papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.
authors: Lukas Aichberger, Adam Golinski, Arno Blaas, Arwen Bradley, Jacob Springer, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Michael Kirchhof, Sinead Williamson
bullets: Hard math problems often have few accepted reasoning traces under independent sampling, limiting post-training data.
DART decomposes rejected traces, ranks uncertain steps, and generates distinct alternatives using reference-answer guidance and meta-thoughts.
On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, it recovers 37% more problems than matched-trace Monte Carlo sampling.
DART has nearly identical cost per recovered problem and 30% lower cost per accepted trace.
Training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on DART-mined traces gives the highest point estimate in five of six MATH-500 and AIME evaluations.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT
authors: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang, Jinze Bai, Bo Wang, Xiang Bai
bullets: Introduces Mixture-of-Loops Attention, which uses keys and values as reusable memory across depths and loops.
MoLT-KV removes same-position cross-loop dependence and supports single-traversal decoding beyond the training loop horizon through loop forcing.
U-MoLT separates memory construction from prediction readout, skipping unnecessary decoder traversals without changing predictions.
Across multiple model scales and settings, U-MoLT improves token efficiency, perplexity, and task accuracy while matching non-looped inference latency in one evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Looped transformer with KV memory reuse directly targets LLM architecture efficiency and inference memory.
papers.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
papers.tldr: MoLT improves the efficiency–expressivity trade-off of looped Transformers by selectively reusing key-value memories across loops, enabling efficient training and decoding without sacrificing quality.

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from.
bullets: Targets self-structuring knowledge bases whose organization controls information retrieval and connections.
Diagnoses answer discrepancies, proposes structural edits, rebuilds the knowledge base, and retains edits that reduce learning loss.
Models candidate-edit loss changes via selection probabilities and evaluates interacting edits jointly.
On document-based experiments, updated cards and graph schemas improved mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions.
Performance on human questions improved for schemas but declined for cards, indicating question-type-specific effects.

papers.title: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering
papers.tldr: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent iteratively edits knowledge-base structures to improve question-answering performance, with gains depending on the question type used for learning.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.
authors: Kumar Shubham, Devendra Vyas, Vidushi Agarwal, Jayin Khanna, Prathosh AP
bullets: Distillation can cause trustworthiness regressions even when downstream capabilities remain intact.
The framework estimates PBRF curvature from a surrogate proxy dataset, avoiding reliance on the original transfer corpus.
An odds-ratio objective incorporates preferred and dispreferred responses while constraining model changes.
It improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors by up to 8% with less than a 1% perplexity increase across distilled models.
The approach applies to both pre-training and post-training models as an alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of post-hoc trustworthiness repair. Left: the shipped student is produced by a distillation process the practitioner does not observe; the distillation corpus Ddistill is unavailable after deployment (dashed), and the student inherits the teacher’s task performance but degraded trustworthiness. Right: our method repairs the shipped student without access to Ddistill, using a generic proxy corpus Dproxy to preserve capability and trustworthiness dataset Dtrust to restore the preferential behaviour, yielding a repaired student that improves trustworthiness at negligible cost to distillation performance.

Table 2: Trustworthiness and capability evaluation before and after repair for pre-training models using FineWeb and OpenWebText (OWT) as proxy datasets. Log-O denotes the log-odds metric and PPL denotes perplexity; lower values are better for both metrics. ∆ denotes the relative change with respect to the distilled model, computed as 100× (Distilled−Method)/|Distilled|. Positive values indicate improvement, while negative values indicate degradation.

Table 1: Trustworthiness and capability evaluation before and after repair for Post training models using S-NI and U-NI based proxy datasets. Log-O denotes the log-odds metric and PPL denotes perplexity; lower values are better for both metrics. ∆ denotes the relative change with respect to the distilled model, computed as 100× (Distilled−Method)/|Distilled|.

papers.selection_reason: Repairing trustworthiness of distilled LLMs, relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models
papers.tldr: A targeted PBRF-based repair method improves trustworthiness in distilled language models without requiring the original distillation data or substantially harming performance.

papers.abstract: LLM routing aims to choose, for each prompt, which model in a portfolio is most likely to answer correctly. This only makes sense when the benchmark contains enough prompt-specific variation for different models to be best on different inputs. On coarse-scored LLM benchmarks, however, many models often tie for the best score, and the single best model may already leave little room for improvement. We therefore propose a routeability-first audit, instantiated as RAP and RouteabilityBench, a runnable claim-verification package. The audit is retrospective: it runs once the benchmark-portfolio score matrix exists and before router comparisons are interpreted as general evidence, rather than certifying a portfolio that has not yet been evaluated. Across four benchmarks and 66 LLMs, generic routing enhancements such as larger embedding sets, dimensionality reduction, selective abstention, clustering, and stronger regressors do not consistently outperform the single best model. The clearest positive evidence is concentrated in portfolio-dependent Omni-MATH settings, while GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval show different ways in which routing can remain hard or predictor-sensitive. Our practical recommendation is that routing gains should be reported together with routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, portfolio construction details, and family-corrected statistical tests.
authors: Yihang Lu, Denica Kjorvezir, Ana Gjorgjevikj, Carola Doerr, Tome Eftimov
bullets: Motivation: coarse-scored benchmarks often produce many tied best models, leaving limited headroom for routing.
Method: retrospectively analyze the benchmark–portfolio score matrix using routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, portfolio details, and family-corrected tests.
Finding: across four benchmarks and 66 LLMs, common routing enhancements do not consistently beat the single best model.
Positive evidence is strongest in portfolio-dependent Omni-MATH settings, while GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval expose different routing difficulties.
Scope: RAP audits already-evaluated benchmark portfolios; it does not certify routeability before portfolio evaluation.

papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures revisit layer parameters across depths. This design increases effective depth without adding parameters. Recent looped MoE studies report substantial gains over the standard MoE at matched budgets (parameters, FLOPs and KV cache). However, the reported gains still confound parameter revisit with other design choices, e.g., network shape and residual scale. We ask, what does parameter revisit itself buy? Using matched non-revisit controls, we find that parameter revisit itself buys almost nothing. We argue that revisit only offers a freedom an MoE already has, i.e., trading experts for depth (more layers, fewer experts each) at fixed parameters. First, at matched budgets, we decompose the state-of-the-art looped recipe, with revisit last. A non-revisit control retains all the gain. Most comes from network shape, and the rest from residual scale. We prove this scale acts as a lower learning rate on revisited layers. This helps under AdamW's uneven layer step sizes, but disappears under Muon, which keeps them nearly equal. Second, beyond matched budgets, we evaluate revisit by adding compute at fixed parameters. One extra visit gains more than doubling the experts. Yet without revisit, a deeper standard MoE at equal parameters and compute obtains 90.2% of that gain under Muon. Overall, gains come from network shape, the optimizer and added compute, which a standard MoE can adopt. Accordingly, we propose LoopTitan-Base as a stronger MoE baseline. Under Muon, it matches the strongest looped recipe without revisit or residual scale. We open-source LoopTitan and release 17 pretrained models (including LoopTitan-Base and the control). Our experiment record is public as GitHub issues, with predictions pre-registered and the full exploration history kept. This is our Phase 1 technical report, laying the foundation for follow-up studies.
authors: Zichen Tian, Yudong Lu, Xuansheng Wu, Na Zou, Xia Hu, Guanchu Wang, Qianru Sun
bullets: Looped MoEs revisit parameters across depth to increase effective depth without increasing parameter count.
Matched non-revisit controls retain nearly all reported gains, implicating network shape and residual scaling rather than revisit itself.
Residual scaling behaves like a lower learning rate on revisited layers under AdamW; this effect largely disappears with Muon.
With extra compute at fixed parameters, revisiting outperforms doubling experts, but deeper standard MoEs recover 90.2% of the gain under Muon.
LoopTitan-Base is proposed as a stronger non-revisit MoE baseline; the authors release 17 pretrained models and public experiment records.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.
bullets: Memory hallucinations stem from conflicts between parametric knowledge and external memory, causing memory-ignoring, misapplication, and version confusion.
TASK stores content in text, uses a knowledge edit as an in-model address, and applies query-dependent steering to control memory use.
On frozen models, it reduced memory-ignoring errors to at most 1.5% across all tested model-dataset cells.
It improved over BM25 RAG by 16.4 percentage points on a 300-memory library, with gains persisting at 3,000 memories, and added 7.5 points on multi-hop accuracy.
The method resolved revised facts without fact IDs and outperformed three context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.

figures.caption: Figure 3: TASK memory overview. (a) Write. A visible observation (s, p, o∗) is compiled into a memory object bound to the model hash, scope and version. The object contains a text record T, an address key km at layer ℓE with a threshold τm calibrated at write time, a closed-form, low-rank and removable patch E keyed on the same address, and steering vectors S = (v+m, v−m) trained on the frozen model; these are kept in a text store, a patch library and a steering bank. (b) Read, against memory-ignoring (Type I) and memory-misapplying (Type II) hallucination. Candidates are retrieved by BM25 or semantic search, and one partial forward pass to layer ℓE computes each candidate’s address response rm. The shared gate gm = ⊮[rm ≥ τm] decides whether the note is shown, whether the patch is loaded as W +BA, and whether v+m or v−m is added at the decision positions of layer ℓS ; multi-hop composition uses v+ only. All hooks and patches are unloaded after generation. (c) Revise, against version confusion (Type III). A new observation is matched to the top-2 active records by BM25, checked with the address and judged by the agent’s own model. On UPDATE the old version’s T, E and S are retired together; on DIFFERENT the existing record stays active. No fact IDs are used.

Figure 1: Memory hallucination: the memory is correct, the answer is not. (a) Text-only memory or RAG puts the retrieved note into the prompt and leaves the rest to the frozen model, where the note in the context conflicts with the stale fact in the weights. On a question about the memory, the weights win and the model answers with the stale fact (Type I, memory-ignoring). On a question about another entity, the note wins and the model assigns the memory to the wrong entity (Type II, memory-misapplying). Across our five models these rates reach 46% and 24%, and Type II reaches 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing. (b) TASK memory goes beyond text-only memory. Each memory object holds Text content, a Knowledge edit ∆Wm whose key ûm serves as the in-model address, and a pair of Activation-Steering vectors (v+, v−) that carry no content. For a query x, the address response rm(x) is compared with the threshold τm. A relevant query shows T, loads E and adds v+, so the model adopts the memory; an unrelated query leaves T and E off and adds v−, so the model keeps its own answer.

Figure 4: TASK reduces both types of use-time memory hallucination on five models and two datasets (test). (a) Type I, memoryignoring: reversion to the stale parametric answer on queries whose stale fact is in the weights. (b) Type II, memory-misapplying: misuse on neighbour questions that the no-memory model answers correctly. This subset is why the values differ from the misuse over all neighbours in Table 3 (e.g. 24.3% vs. 39.2% for Qwen3-8B with T). Bars give values in %. Per-cell bootstrap CIs are in Section A.

Figure 2: Use-time memory hallucinations caused by the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory (test splits, text memory in context, greedy decoding). (a) Type I, memory-ignoring: adoption of the memory’s answer on paraphrased questions. Filled markers: queries on which the no-memory model states the stale fact, i.e. the old fact is in the weights. Hollow markers: all other queries. The gap is in percentage points; ∗ marks a paired world-level bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. (b) Type II, memory-misapplying: on neighbour questions (same relation, different subject) that the no-memory model answers correctly, the rate at which the model instead states the memory’s answer. Without memory this is ≤0.9%. With text memory it rises on every model, and with text memory plus a weight edit (T+E) it rises further on four of the five models. All numbers come from frozen predictions (Section A).

Figure 5: Scaling the library to 3,000 memories (CounterFact test queries; distractors are training-split memories written by the same writer). Dashed: BM25 retrieval; solid: address-verified reading. Colours follow the carriers as in Figures 2 and 4. papers.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
papers.tldr: TASK memory combines text notes, removable knowledge edits, and activation steering to substantially reduce use-time memory hallucinations in LLM agents.

papers.abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.
bullets: Chorus augments transformer inputs and attention with hashed bigram and trigram tables.
On Polish pre-1918 text, similarly performing Chorus models match plain models 1.34× larger at 16M parameters and 1.16–1.20× larger at 107M–349M.
With tables roughly the backbone’s size, each added table parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters.
Separate learning-rate tuning reduces Chorus’s gain at 47M parameters by about one third.
Chorus trains slower than an equally sized plain model, while quiz differences are comparable to variation across random seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the effect of an n-gram module in language models, relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
papers.tldr: Chorus N-gram tables can replace some transformer backbone capacity, but their benefit shrinks in larger models and comes with slower training and narrow experimental scope.

papers.abstract: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.
authors: Jiacheng Zhang, Qixing Zhou, Haiyang Wang, Qipeng Gu, Shuzhe Wu, Feiyang Pan, Lue Fan, Dandan Tu, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses unstable mixed-task learning, inefficient rollout allocation, and continual domain expansion without separate specialists or distillation.
Uses a quota-based asynchronous rollout scheduler to balance gradient contributions and reduce off-policy effects across task domains.
Introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling to prioritize samples by mastery, encouraging frontier exploration while preserving learned capabilities.
Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5-27B improves from 43.6 to 54.2 and then 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier of Qwen3.8-27B.
Outperforms single-task RL while using less compute for policy updates, supporting MixRL as a compute-efficient post-training approach.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS). Frontier, Reinforcement, and History buffers receive fixed sampling quotas for exploring unsolved instances, consolidating emerging capabilities, and replaying instances from earlier stages, respectively.

Figure 3: Overview of Maco-RL. TBS samples instances from each task pool. Rollouts run asynchronously across task types and in parallel with training. A shared rollout buffer collects completed trajectories for joint policy updates on mixed batches.

papers.abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.
authors: Yifei Xu, Li Yu, Zhaoyang Liu, Ce Wang, Sen Huang, Yanyan Shen, Yun Lin, Linpeng Huang, Hong Mei
bullets: Targets the largely manual optimization of memory-system code, prompts, and configurations.
Iteratively evaluates and edits previously tested harnesses, using session-level memory versions and execution traces to localize shared failures.
Promotes structural exploration with candidate gating and lowers evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and memory reuse.
Validated with ReMe on LongMemEval-S and BEAM; after six formal evaluations per benchmark, it found harnesses with better end-task performance and fewer query-time tokens than the original harness.

papers.abstract: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.
bullets: LLM optimizers are unnecessary for core weight-space programming regimes.
FWSP combines probing, localization, stratified operators, blind routing, and paired verification without extra per-token computation.
Protected FisherGate enables a closed-form, reasoning-state-orthogonal readout edit for math-calibrated reasoning models.
On DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, one frozen patch reaches 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 and improves over 512-token budget forcing by 14.6 percentage points with fewer tokens.
Across five modalities and thirteen models, FWSP identifies subspace entanglement and frozen representation span as operator boundaries; localized LoRA can bridge these limits.

papers.abstract: Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4. In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection. On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
authors: Praveen Kumar Bodigutla, Yizhi Zhang, Sai Vivek Kanaparthy, Arup De
bullets: OKF-indexed memory organizes interactions by lineage to retrieve temporally and project-relevant episodes.
Procedure Memory learns reusable hiring decision procedures through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning.
OKF retrieval reaches 0.93–0.95 low-priority preference F1 and uses 69% fewer context tokens than full-history context.
Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39%; on PersonaMem-v2, the combined approach reaches 50.2% accuracy with 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history.
Smaller Jev-class models improve efficiency but more often miss temporally relevant evidence, emphasizing evidence selection.

papers.abstract: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.

papers.abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.
authors: Jon Carmona, Jon Irureta, Jon Imaz, Aizea Lojo, Juan Mart\'inez-Romo, Lourdes Araujo
bullets: Published watermark designs enable two attacks: rewording to erase the signal or learning it to copy the signal onto ungenerated text.
The proposed attacker selects whichever attack is more effective for each known watermark, defeating all compared existing methods.
KeyedLex derives its secret key from the previous sentence’s grammar, which tends to remain stable under rewording.
Its detector does not need to recover the key exactly, improving robustness to attacks.
On both tested models, KeyedLex retains about half its signal versus two thirds lost by the best alternative, with no additional text-quality cost.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes KeyedLex, a sentence-keyed watermarking technique for LLMs that is robust against attacks that reword text or learn the watermark pattern.
papers.title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
papers.tldr: KeyedLex is a sentence-keyed LLM watermark designed to withstand attackers who choose between rewriting text and learning the watermark to forge it.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.
authors: Runguo Li, Dezhen Lu, Zixiang Ni
bullets: Targets recurrent-depth language models where each token repeatedly applies shared layers until convergence.
Uses a learned linear change-of-coordinates warm start fitted in closed form on the frozen model, costing under 5% of one loop.
On Huginn-0125, matches the strongest training-free baseline with 14–19% fewer decoding layers.
Improves batched throughput by 16–18% in two serving engines and adds 10–14% gains alongside self-speculative decoding.
A contraction analysis predicts loop savings and indicates warm starts help most when convergence normally requires more loops.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a warm-start method to reduce decoding loops in recurrent-depth LLMs, directly improving inference efficiency.
papers.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.tldr: FlyingStart accelerates fixed-point decoding by predicting each token’s converged state from the previous token, reducing iteration cost without changing accuracy or stopping criteria.

papers.abstract: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.
authors: Ilkin Masimov, Rufana Baghirli, Muhammad Rashid
bullets: Only 44.7–50.6% of claims flagged by the verifier were confirmed hallucinations by human review.
Correction loops converged in 85.2–95.1% of cases, but introduced 35% of genuine final errors.
Three independent runs improved true-hallucination recall from 35.6–41.2% to 71–80%.
The verifier showed moderate agreement (κ=0.505), while the final genuine-error rate was 1.7%.
The study supports measuring verifier reliability rather than treating verifier output as ground truth.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the effectiveness of verify-and-revise pipelines in mitigating hallucinations for medical question answering, identifying verifier reliability as a critical limiting factor.
papers.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
papers.tldr: In ESC cardiology QA, claim-level verification substantially reduces hallucinations, but verifier errors and correction-induced mistakes remain the main limitation.

papers.abstract: We formalize Agentic Waterfall Feed, a new problem of personalized information discovery in which users actively direct recommendations and the system adapts to evolving needs inferred from both explicit requests and browsing behavior. We address this problem with the Agentic Waterfall framework, whose language-model controller maintains persistent user state and coordinates content retrieval, ranking, and state updates. To evaluate systems on this task, we contribute the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol. The dataset combines real content metadata with simulated interaction histories. The protocol compares systems under shared histories using relevance scores and blind judgments of how well recommendations satisfy current user goals and constraints. Agentic Waterfall remains competitive with strong baselines on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks. On the Agentic Waterfall Dataset, it outperforms the strongest baseline in both evaluations, with relative improvements of up to 16.1%.
authors: Yige Luo, Shining Zhang, Jikun Liu, Hongjiao Qiang, Ran Guan
bullets: Targets personalized discovery where users actively steer recommendations rather than passively receiving feeds.
Uses a language-model controller to coordinate retrieval, ranking, and updates to persistent user state.
Introduces the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol with relevance scores and blind goal-satisfaction judgments.
Remains competitive on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks.
Outperforms the strongest baseline on its dataset by up to 16.1% in the reported evaluations.

papers.title: Agentic Waterfall: An Intent-Driven Information Discovery Framework for Reclaiming User Control in the Attention Economy
papers.tldr: Agentic Waterfall is an intent-driven recommendation framework that uses persistent user state and feedback from requests and browsing to adapt information discovery to evolving goals.

papers.abstract: Even a correct operator reply can be an unreliable training target for a customer-support agent. About a quarter of the factual claims in these replies lacked full support in the agent's knowledge base and tool records. We treat operator replies as claims to verify rather than answers to imitate. Unverified claims guide revisions to the knowledge base and tools. Verified claims serve as coverage targets in a claim-level GRPO reward that scores factual precision against the evidence the agent retrieved for its answer. On an offline benchmark, 8.6% of the GRPO agent's text answers were flagged for hallucinations, compared with 13.6% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. In a randomized A/B test against the existing procedural bot, the deployed system increased the share of conversations closed without a human operator from 63.3% to 80.8%.
authors: Dmitrii Stoianov, Olga Tsymboi, Danil Taranets, Daniil Strizhakov, Ilya Buryak, Almaz Dautov, Dmitry Fatnev, Arthur Babkin, Aleksandr Fida, Daniil Dryabin, Maksim Shilenko, Nikita Surnachev, Anatolii Potapov

papers.selection_reason: Develops a claim-level GRPO reward mechanism for customer support agents to learn from potentially unreliable operator references, improving factual precision and reducing hallucinations.
papers.title: Learning from Unreliable Operator References: Claim-Level Rewards for Customer Support Agents
papers.tldr: A claim-verification and claim-level reward approach improves factuality and autonomous resolution for customer-support agents trained from unreliable operator replies.

papers.abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
authors: Abhinav Sharma, Li Li, Chien Van Nguyen, Sai Karthik Navuluru, Bo Ni, Xiangbo Gao, Xiaolei Huang, Yue Zhao, Nesreen K. Ahmed, Tyler Derr, Yu Wang, Hongjie Chen, Zhengzhong Tu, Thien Huu Nguyen, Ryan A. Rossi, Franck Dernoncourt
bullets: The benchmark contains 23,777 community-verified puzzles spanning riddles, ciphers, logic, wordplay, mathematics, and image-based tasks.
It supports analysis by hints, categories, dates, and a post-training-cutoff contamination check, with released data, scoring, and provenance.
Nine evaluated models were scored using normalized exact match plus an LLM judge validated across model families.
GPT-6.1 achieved 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set, while 17 puzzles stumped every model and failures were strongly correlated.
In a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, removing images reduced the two best models’ scores by 24 and 35 points; an oracle combining all models reached 91%.

papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly learn from their own experience, the tasks they learn from and are evaluated on are almost always in English. We ask whether self-evolution transfers from English to Urdu, and release IRTIQA, a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench, built with a matrix-language code-switching pipeline and human verification. Using IRTIQA, we evaluate three self-evolving frameworks, Tool-R0 (self-play RL), AgentEvolver (experience-guided RL), and Autogenesis (protocol-level evolution), against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability: AgentEvolver lifts AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across all conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%. But it rarely closes the language gap. Evolved systems remain stronger in English, by up to 0.26 DROP F1, the gap is largest on multi-step tasks, and code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation. On a shared Gemma-4 31B backbone, the gap exists before evolution, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English. Language parity must therefore be an explicit design target, as it does not emerge from self-improvement alone.
authors: Abdullah Hashmat, Danish Javed, Usman Naseem, Agha Ali Raza
bullets: IRTIQA benchmarks aligned English, Urdu, and Urdu code-switched versions of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench.
It evaluates Tool-R0, AgentEvolver, and Autogenesis against their unevolved backbones.
Self-evolution improves some capabilities, including AppWorld goal completion and SkillsBench pass rate.
English performance remains stronger—especially on multi-step tasks—and code-switching is a distinct evaluation condition.
RL-based evolution can worsen Urdu reasoning, indicating that language parity must be designed explicitly.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces IRTIQA, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving LLM agents across English, Urdu, and code-switched inputs, highlighting the challenges of language transfer in agent evolution.
papers.title: IRTIQA: Evolving in English, Evaluated in Urdu -- Does Agent Self-Evolution Transfer from English to Urdu and Code-Switched Input?

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers decouple computational depth from parameter count, and prior studies have demonstrated promising performance gains with increased computation. However, systematic design principles for configuring these models under strict iso-parameter and iso-FLOP constraints remain scarce. We contribute to this direction by improving information flow in looped models and systematically studying loop parameter configurations. Specifically, we refine this information flow via gated inner-loop state updates and a cross-stage residual connection. Building on this design, controlled studies identify a configuration combining a single-pass Core depth of 25%-35% of the total unrolled depth with reallocating saved parameters into extra routed experts per layer, improving performance at zero extra compute while preserving compatibility with existing training infrastructure. Evaluated after 1T pre-training tokens, our 69B MLA and 51B KDA Mixture-of-Experts models outperform budget-matched non-recurrent baselines by an average of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points across four benchmarks, respectively. Further reproduction experiments on a common backbone with a 200B-token training budget show that our method achieves lower perplexity than other looped methods. Code for these reproduction experiments is available at https://github.com/lxi01766/Scaling-Looped-MoE-Language-Models-under-Matched-Budgets-Information-Flow-and-Parameter-Allocation.
authors: Shipeng Bai, Jiayu Qin, Hong Liu, Xili Wang, Jianchao Tan, Jiacheng Li, He Zhang, Yifan Lu, Jiaqi Zhang, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses the lack of design principles for looped models under strict iso-parameter and iso-FLOP constraints.
Uses gated inner-loop state updates and cross-stage residual connections to improve information flow.
Finds that a single-pass Core occupying 25–35% of unrolled depth, with saved parameters assigned to more routed experts, is an effective configuration.
After 1T tokens, 69B MLA and 51B KDA MoE models outperform matched non-recurrent baselines by average gains of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points across four benchmarks.
Reproduction experiments with a shared backbone and 200B tokens yield lower perplexity than other looped methods.

papers.abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.
authors: Truong Phan, Ngoc-Quan Pham, Dat Quoc Nguyen
bullets: Addresses reactive defenses that can be overridden or require retraining for new attack styles.
Uses mutual information and embedding variance for query-conditioned reranking, without attack detection or training.
Introduces LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark averaging 4,032 words per context.
Evaluated across short- and long-context QA and agent tool-call injection settings.
Reports the best accuracy–security trade-off among training-free defenses, with robustness to adaptive attacks and low long-context latency.

papers.abstract: Transferring reasoning capabilities from large language models to smaller ones often requires extensive teacher supervision or costly student adaptation. We study projected cross-model Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Vector transfer, a two-stage approach that keeps both models frozen. First, we learn a task-level CoT Vector in the teacher using dataset-provided solution traces and final-answer supervision. We then train a lightweight linear projector to map the fixed vector into a smaller student's residual space. Student-side training uses only final-answer cross-entropy on a small subset of task training examples; it requires neither teacher outputs nor intermediate solution traces. We select the student injection layer and intervention scale on a labeled support set and report results on the disjoint remainder of each evaluation split. On GSM8K and MATH, the projected vector improves base students by 10.37-21.98 accuracy points across the evaluated teacher-student settings. On four code-generation benchmarks, the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student gains 3.23-4.67 pass@1 points, while the base Qwen2.5-7B student gains up to 9.65 points. These results show that a teacher-side reasoning vector can be reused across smaller students with different residual dimensions through projector-only adaptation.
authors: Yulin Qi, Shuo Xu, Shuxia Lin, Qingjian Ni, Xu Yang, Xin Geng

Improves GSM8K and MATH accuracy by 10.37–21.98 points across evaluated settings, and boosts code-generation pass@1 by 3.23–9.65 points.
Evaluated with frozen models; injection layer and intervention scale are selected on a labeled support set.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a lightweight reasoning transfer method using projected Chain-of-Thought vectors, enabling small student models to inherit reasoning capabilities from large teachers without intermediate supervision.
papers.title: Lightweight Reasoning Transfer via Chain-of-Thought Vector Projection
papers.tldr: A frozen teacher’s learned reasoning vector can be projected into smaller frozen students using only limited final-answer supervision, substantially improving reasoning and code-generation performance.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
authors: Alessio Devoto, Avinash Vem, Tara Safavi, Sanjay Kariyappa, Yu-Hsuan Tseng, Paul Furgale, Ricardo Silveira Cabral

Evaluated on document research and machine learning engineering across 8K–512K-token budgets.
Effective API use improves performance at tight budgets: GPT 6.1’s OfficeQA Pro v2 score rose from 21% to 56% at 32K tokens, while Kimi used up to 41% fewer input tokens.
Models vary widely in compaction frequency, aggressiveness, and timing; prompt changes also affect when compaction begins.
KV-cache reuse after context edits reduced prefill compute by up to 15% per request without measurable accuracy changes.

papers.selection_reason: Model-driven context management and KV-cache reuse for efficient inference; relevant to LLM memory, long-context handling, and memory-efficient serving.
papers.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
papers.tldr: Model-driven context management can substantially improve agent accuracy and token efficiency under tight context budgets, especially when inference engines support efficient KV-cache editing.

papers.abstract: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.

Initial classification and extraction evaluations suggest the approach is feasible, but the system is work in progress and does not replace substantive legal assessment.

papers.tldr: LEXI uses large language models to assist M&A legal due diligence from data-room document organization through report preparation while keeping lawyers responsible for legal judgment.

papers.abstract: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.
authors: Dat Tat Mai, Hung Tran Quy, Thai Viet Pham, James Jin Kang
bullets: Reviews 2,289 studies from 2017–September 2026 across 20 methodological families using an inspect-then-allocate framework.
Hard selection dominates token-, query-, and task-level research, while computational overhead is a bottleneck at every layer.
Intra-layer gating emphasizes load balancing but seldom uses uncertainty estimation.
Model cascades and agent workflows use confidence thresholds and budgets, but face miscalibration and cascading errors.
Agentic task delegation is growing fastest, yet routing is least often isolated experimentally and carries the highest methodological-bias risk.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic review of conditional computation, expert gating, model cascades, and agent orchestration; directly relevant to efficient AI and LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Not Every Input Needs Everything: Unifying Expert Gating, Model Cascades, and Agent Orchestration
papers.tldr: This systematic review unifies conditional computation across expert gating, model cascades, and agent orchestration, exposing shared bottlenecks and uneven safeguards across scales.

papers.abstract: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.
authors: Xichong Zhang, Xixuan Hao, Zhichen Liu, Le Zhou, Zeyu Zhang, Boyu Chen, Mingfei Lu, Zehao Lin, Bo Tang, Yonggang Zhang, Linyun Liu, Feiyu Xiong, Jianlin Su, Zhiyu Li
bullets: GDN-2 can fail during long-context training because asymmetric erasure creates non-normal state updates whose directional gains accumulate over time.
The proposed method uses symmetric erasure for non-expansive propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to retain flexible updates.
It preserves chunkwise parallel computation and theoretically limits recurrent-state growth to O(√T).
Experiments with approximately 1.6B-parameter models show stable training and improved long-context retrieval.
Relative to GDN-2, it improves the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in recurrent models and nine-task average accuracy by 0.62 points in hybrid models.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses architectural stability in linear attention mechanisms (Gated DeltaNet-2) for LLMs, proposing symmetric erasure to mitigate recurrent state instability.
papers.title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
papers.tldr: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2 prevents recurrent-state explosions with symmetric erasure and regulated writing, enabling stable long-context training and better retrieval.

papers.abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.
authors: Pusala Pavan Teja, Jayasimha Talur, Saab Mansour, Marcello Federico
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 500 HTN-represented workflows covering sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies.
Simulator fidelity declines sharply as workflow complexity increases, with goal drift causing most failures.
Fidelity varies substantially depending on the assistant’s response style.
ReUST, a reasoning and user-state-tracking prompting strategy, improves goal success by over 12 points for mid-sized and large models.
ReUST also reduces sensitivity to the assistant’s response style.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for LLM user simulators in complex multi-step workflows and proposes ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking) to improve fidelity and goal alignment.
papers.title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows
papers.tldr: ReUST improves the reliability of LLM user simulators in complex, multi-step workflow evaluations by tracking user state and reducing goal drift.

papers.abstract: LLM-based interactive learner simulators are increasingly used in educational applications, including teacher training and tutoring system development. A critical requirement for those simulations is cognitive fidelity: the simulated learner should maintain the assigned knowledge, misconceptions, and reasoning procedures throughout interaction. However, LLMs may express knowledge or problem-solving skills beyond the assigned learner's cognitive status, a phenomenon we refer to as competence leakage. In this exploratory study, we examine 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner simulator transcripts across three learning scenarios and identify over-competence as a prominent direction of cognitive-profile misalignment during interaction. We then investigate the recurrence of previously observed competence leakage cases under four matched-trigger evaluation protocols, ranging from isolated questioning to multi-turn interactions, across five model configurations. Overall, we observe higher violation recurrence under multi-turn protocols than under isolated question answering. More capable models generally show lower recurrence, whereas increased reasoning effort does not consistently improve cognitive fidelity and is even associated with slightly higher recurrence under multi-turn protocols in our matched-model comparison. These findings provide exploratory evidence of competence leakage phenomena in interactive learner simulation and suggest that single-turn question-answering type of evaluations alone may be insufficient, motivating the development of more systematic and reliable multi-turn protocols for evaluating cognitive fidelity in learner simulation.
authors: Zhen Xu, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Jamie N. Mikeska
bullets: Studies 3,339 utterances from 130 transcripts spanning three learning scenarios.
Identifies over-competence as a prominent form of cognitive-profile misalignment.
Tests recurrence of competence leakage using four matched-trigger protocols across five model configurations.
Violations recur more often in multi-turn interactions than in isolated questions.
More capable models generally reduce recurrence, while greater reasoning effort does not consistently improve fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies and analyzes 'competence leakage' in LLM-based learner simulators, providing insights into cognitive fidelity and evaluation protocols for educational AI.
papers.title: Too Smart for Its Own Good? Cognitive Fidelity and Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners
papers.tldr: LLM learner simulators often leak knowledge beyond their assigned cognitive level, especially in multi-turn interactions, making single-turn evaluations insufficient for assessing cognitive fidelity.

papers.abstract: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($\tau = 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.
authors: Shohei Hisada, Keisuke Orimo, Kenji Igarashi, Kota Sato, Masahiro Kazama, Mitsuhisa Ota, Shoko Wakamiya, Eiji Aramaki
bullets: Creates a Japan-localized benchmark of 79 patient consultations and 1,022 rubric criteria.
Uses LLM drafting plus specialist revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review; most criteria were retained with limited rewriting.
Across 18 LLMs, translation-only evaluation maintained coarse rankings but changed verdicts on many modified criteria and produced false penalties under Japan-specific clinical standards.
Finds context awareness and locally appropriate clinical criteria remain key weaknesses, while Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training improve localized performance.
Datasets, revision logs, and evaluation code are publicly available.

papers.selection_reason: Constructs a localized medical evaluation benchmark (JHealthBench-L) for LLMs in Japan, addressing regional clinical context and translation issues in evaluation.
papers.title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan
papers.tldr: JHealthBench-L adapts HealthBench to Japan through multi-stage physician review, revealing that machine translation can preserve overall rankings while misjudging clinically important item-level performance.

papers.abstract: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).
authors: Filippos Ventirozos, Ioanna Nteka, Tania Nandy, Peter A. Appleby, Matthew Shardlow
bullets: Frames feature extraction as contextual named entity recognition conditioned on the exact vehicle’s feature catalogue, with an entity-linking interpretation.
Contains 430 human-gold adverts and 925 LLM-silver adverts.
Uses validation and targeted remedies for malformed outputs, hallucinations, and out-of-catalogue links.
On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM achieves 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% entity-linking performance.
Performance on unseen catalogue features is 54.5% span F1 for the LoRA-tuned LLM versus 49.0% for the encoder.
