papers.selection_reason: Presents an LLM-assisted corpus creation methodology for feature NER, utilizing LoRA for efficient fine-tuning and a robust validation pipeline for LLM-generated data.
papers.title: Auto-Features: An LLM-Assisted Corpus for Contextual Recognition of Standard and Optional Car Features
papers.tldr: Auto-Features introduces a validated human- and LLM-annotated corpus for recognizing catalogue-specific car features in varied advertisement text.

papers.abstract: We introduce Dual Mutual Information Regularization (DuoMI), a method for regulating expert routing across rounds in looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers. When two rounds of computation share an expert pool, their routers may favor different expert subsets, limiting the reuse of individual expert parameters across rounds. Even when aggregate expert usage is identical across rounds, we would still prefer each token to retain some experts while switching to others. DuoMI addresses both aspects of routing: it uses round-level marginal mutual information to limit the dependence of aggregate expert usage on the round, and token-level conditional mutual information to penalize average cross-round routing changes that fall outside a target interval. During training, DuoMI computes differentiable penalties from soft routing distributions over all experts. It adds no model parameters and leaves sparse Top-$k$ routing strategy unchanged at inference. On a looped OLMoE backbone in which paired adjacent layers share experts, DuoMI improves the average score across $15$ downstream tasks from $50.08\%$ to $51.82\%$, a gain of $1.74$ percentage points over the looped baseline.
authors: Xinlai Kang, Zhenhe Wu, Haoyu Wang, Weihua He, Yaping Jin, Jie Hu, Hanting Chen
bullets: Targets inconsistent expert selection across rounds, which can limit parameter reuse.
Combines round-level mutual information regularization for aligned aggregate expert usage with token-level conditional mutual information to control routing changes.
Uses differentiable penalties on soft routing distributions, while adding no parameters or changing sparse Top-k inference.
On a looped OLMoE backbone with shared experts, it raises the average score across 15 downstream tasks from 50.08% to 51.82%.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Cross-round expert selection patterns. Rows denote tokens and columns denote experts; colored cells indicate selected experts. The bar charts show expert selection counts in each round. Both G and D are computed using uniform hard Top-k distributions. (a) The aggregate distributions are identical, and each token retains half of its experts: G = 0, D = 0.5. (b) Each token retains its entire expert set: G = 0, D = 0. (c) Each token selects disjoint expert sets across rounds: G = 0, D = 1. (d) Each token again retains half of its experts, but the rounds favor different expert subsets: G = 0.5, D = 0.5. These patterns illustrate aggregate expert reuse and token-level routing change as distinct statistical dimensions; they do not specify the soft regularization thresholds used in training.

Figure 3. Cross-round routing trajectories for the OLMoE-Loop baseline and DuoMI under its default configuration. From left to right: round-level marginal mutual information G̃, token-level conditional mutual information D̃, and the fraction of Top-8 experts retained for the same token across rounds. Horizontal dashed lines mark the thresholds applied to the soft statistics during training.

Figure 4. Cross-round routing under different constraint thresholds. papers.abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.
authors: Phong Le, Ngoc-Quan Pham, Dat Quoc Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the limited study of diffusion adaptation for efficient hybrid architectures.
Progressively makes LFM2’s causal gated convolution bidirectional to capture local context.
Uses masking warm-up together with joint autoregressive–diffusion training.
In controlled experiments, performs comparably to fine-tuned LFM2.5 AR models.
Provides consistent speedups at 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4× on average and up to 1.79×.

papers.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.
authors: Mingyuan Li, Tong Jia, Haoran Wang, Wenbo Qi, Ziyuan Yang, Bowen Ma, Jie Gui, Baosheng Yu
bullets: Medical LLM agents struggle to select specialized tools because tool outputs are uncertain and distribution-shifted.
EATS stores queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback from prior interactions.
Relevant experiences are retrieved to guide tool selection for new medical queries.
Evaluated on visual question answering and report generation across four public datasets and three multimodal LLMs.
The abstract reports consistent improvements in tool selection and downstream medical reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in chemical knowledge and reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether they can solve problems whose answers must be discovered through experimentation. We investigate this question through Unknown Chemical Identification, where a model must actively design experiments, interpret observations, update hypotheses, and ultimately identify a hidden substance. We introduce ChemDeduce, an interactive evaluation framework for assessing LLMs through simulated experiments. ChemDeduce formulates chemical identification as a sequential decision process and provides a stateful simulated laboratory with explicit instrument and operational constraints, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation of iterative experimental reasoning. We benchmark eight frontier LLMs on 200 chemicals, yielding 1600 model--target pairs and 4800 episodes over three independent repetitions, and evaluate identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality. Despite generating seemingly plausible experimental plans, current models achieve an average identification accuracy ranging from 23.83% to 67.33%, revealing substantial limitations in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement.
authors: Hengyi Cai, Yuqi Tang, Zichang Li, Huajun chen, Qiang Zhang, Keyan Ding
bullets: Frames unknown chemical identification as sequential decision-making under instrument and operational constraints.
Introduces a stateful, reproducible simulated laboratory for evaluating iterative experimental reasoning.
Benchmarks eight frontier LLMs across 200 chemicals, 1,600 model–target pairs, and 4,800 episodes.
Measures identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality.
Observed average identification accuracy ranges from 23.83% to 67.33%, highlighting weaknesses in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and hypothesis refinement.

papers.abstract: Massively multilingual translation models usually have one tag per language and no control over regional varieties, and they cover a region's smaller languages poorly or not at all. We report three fine-tunes of MADLAD-400-3B-MT, each adding target tags with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), back-translation of monolingual text and replay of the base model's own translations: for Spanish as written in Spain, for Latin American Spanish, and one model for three Romance languages of the Iberian Peninsula, Asturian ( ), Aragonese ( ) and Aranese ( ). For the Spanish varieties we annotate the 250.9M documents of MADLAD-400's Spanish split with a domain-supervised Spain vs. Latin America classifier and select variety text with a rule that admitted no Latin American document in a 340-document reference set. The Castilian model chooses Spain's everyday vocabulary in 97% of a targeted test (base model 62%) and vosotros for informal plural address in 70% (10%), while improving chrF++ on human references. A first finding is tag collapse: with a new tag initialised from , the parent tag drifts to the new variety (84-87% identical outputs). In the Iberian model, contrastive pairs and a separate learning rate for the tag embeddings keep each tag in its own language. Trained only on publicly available data, mostly the TAN-IBE Wikipedia corpora, the Iberian model matches or beats the TAN-IBE Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on FLORES+, is 1.9 BLEU behind in Spanish->Aranese, and is second only to SalamandraTA-7B in most directions. The exception, Spanish->Aragonese, reflects a difference of written variety between Aragonese Wikipedia and the FLORES+ reference, not model quality. All three fine-tunes lose 0.6-0.7 chrF++ on average in thirteen other FLORES-200 directions. We release the models, data and variety classifier under open licences

The Castilian model selects Spain-specific vocabulary in 97% of targeted cases and uses “vosotros” in 70%, improving over the base model and improving chrF++ on human references.
The Iberian model matches or surpasses TAN-IBE Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on FLORES+, while trailing by 1.9 BLEU in Spanish→Aranese.
All fine-tunes reduce average chrF++ by 0.6–0.7 on thirteen other FLORES-200 directions; models, data, and classifier are openly released.

papers.abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Yixiao He, Yichen Wu, Ruite Lu, Jiayu Wang, Ying Wei
bullets: Builds a task-relative state space and represents reusable procedures as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies.

Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, it achieves the highest mean performance in four of five settings and uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine.
Partial procedural coverage can hurt performance relative to hidden memory; high coverage helps, while low coverage has little effect.

papers.abstract: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer often-implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. Existing approaches typically adapt individual models or supply external cultural knowledge, while learning norm inference independently of downstream response generation remains underexplored. We introduce NORMCRAFT, a modular framework that decouples norm inference from response generation. Through norm-centric multi-view supervision, we train an LLM as a norm generator to recover shared norms from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios without downstream response labels. The generated norms guide a separate, frozen LLM (the responder). With Qwen3.5-4B as the responder, NORMCRAFT outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics. On SafeWorld, its responses reflect the reference norms more often (Coverage) and more precisely (Faithfulness), exceeding Responder SFT by 18.0 and 14.1 percentage points, respectively. Direct norm evaluation also shows higher norm quality than the base and few-shot generators. The same trained generator improves cultural alignment on SafeWorld across fourteen frozen LLMs spanning five families and 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.
authors: Tangyuan Zhang, Zhuang Li, Fatemeh Shiri, Xiangyu Zhao, Junyu Yan, Xiuzhen Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring culturally appropriate norms without relying on downstream response labels.
Trains a norm generator with multi-view supervision from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios.
Uses generated norms to guide a separate, frozen responder LLM.
With Qwen3.5-4B, outperforms prompting and SFT baselines on four of five downstream metrics, including higher norm coverage and faithfulness on SafeWorld.
The generator transfers across 14 frozen LLMs from five families and 0.8B–27B parameters, with largest gains for smaller models.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.
authors: Yuxuan Sun, Yuanjian Xu, Jianing Hao, Yu Li, Sowmen Das, Zhong Li, Sangwoong Yoon, Miguel R. D. Rodrigues
bullets: Classical forward-KL distillation does not reliably benefit DLMs: more teacher-generated data may not improve perplexity, and it can underperform the original denoising objective.
The framework first uses off-policy distillation on static teacher-generated data to transfer general knowledge.
It then applies on-policy distillation with reverse-process trajectory loss, confidence reweighting, and a trust-region anchor.
On MDLM, the student reaches 24.75 GPT-2 perplexity versus the teacher’s 27.04; on Dream-7B, perplexity improves from 25.23 to 19.83 for a 93M student.
Zero-shot general capability benchmark performance is preserved in the reported Dream-7B distillation setting.

papers.abstract: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained during reinforcement learning (RL). We study how properties of SFT data may affect this retention by constructing Low, Medium, and High SFT datasets with approximately matched token budgets but different tool-call depths. Under the same RL recipe, the three initializations reach similar RL training accuracy yet exhibit markedly different tool-use dynamics: tool initiation increases in Low, declines in Medium, and collapses in High. We observe that these datasets also differ substantially in the amount of reasoning preceding each tool call. In particular, High trajectories contain considerably less pre-call reasoning, motivating the hypothesis that pre-call reasoning may affect how well tool use is calibrated and, consequently, whether the corresponding behaviors are retained during RL. An idealized theoretical analysis provides a selective-retention view of this process: advantages in overall and tool-conditioned accuracy can be preserved under outcome-only optimization, while tool initiation increases only when tool-using trajectories are more successful than the tool-free alternative. Guided by this analysis, we rank the original High trajectories by average pre-call reasoning length and retain the highest-ranked examples while approximately matching cumulative SFT token exposure. This simple filtering strategy improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned final-answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation across multiple benchmarks. These results suggest that pre-call reasoning is a useful dimension of SFT supervision for understanding and improving tool-use retention under downstream RL.
authors: Kaiwen Hu, Hyunin Lee, Joseph Suh, Serina Chang, Shuai Shao, Yong Zhang, Namyong Park, Xiaoqiang Luo, Luke Simon, Somayeh Sojoudi
bullets: Matched-token SFT datasets with different tool-call depths show divergent RL dynamics: tool initiation rises, falls, or collapses depending on the initialization.
High-tool-call trajectories contain substantially less reasoning before tool calls, motivating pre-call reasoning as a calibration and retention factor.
Theory suggests tool initiation grows only when tool-using trajectories outperform the tool-free alternative under outcome-only RL.
Selecting High-dataset examples with the longest average pre-call reasoning improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned success across multiple benchmarks.
The filtering strategy does not consistently increase tool initiation, so its benefit appears focused on retention and answer quality rather than usage frequency.

Figure 4 Tool-use behavior after RL. Together, the two views show that the downstream benefit is better reflected by the effectiveness of retained tool-mediated decisions than by how frequently tools are invoked.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies how SFT pre-call reasoning affects tool-use retention under RL for LLMs, relevant to LLM training and alignment.
papers.title: PRIOR: Pre-Call Reasoning in SFT and Its Influence on Tool-Use Retention under RL
papers.tldr: Pre-call reasoning in SFT is linked to whether tool-use behavior survives RL, and filtering for longer pre-call reasoning improves post-RL performance without reliably increasing tool initiation.

papers.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
bullets: Addresses the linear growth of standard attention’s key-value cache by learning context-dependent memory retention.
Uses a learned scorer to rescore memory chunks as new context arrives, while a standard attention reader accesses retained representations.
Trains retention jointly with reading using either gradual soft-to-hard selection or hard retention from the outset, aided by generated recovery supervision.

Across retrieval, variable tracking, reasoning, and language modeling, SSA substantially outperforms equal-budget bounded attention and can match or exceed attention with roughly four times its readable budget on retrieval tasks.
Its main remaining gap to full attention at small model scale is on RULER; the approach is evaluated across different training and inference context/model scales.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
authors: Tianmai M. Zhang, Hoda Shajari, Amr Hendy, Xiaohu Liu, Piyush Behre, Omar Zia Khan, Ankur Gupta
bullets: Studies how success- and failure-derived procedural memories support continual adaptation across heterogeneous, multi-domain tool-use tasks.
Introduces a retrieval-free workflow with customizable reflection, memory generation from both outcome types, and periodic consolidation under fixed capacity.
Online evaluation finds failure memory broadens coverage, success memory improves execution efficiency, and combining both captures both benefits.
Shows cross-domain memory generalization and continual adaptation over long task streams.
External evaluation on EvoMemBench supports DualPM’s portability as a general long-term procedural memory method.

papers.abstract: Orthogonal finetuning (OFT) adapts a pretrained weight by an orthogonal transform and preserves its singular values and row angles, but existing methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step. We measure how far a transform $A$ is from orthogonal by its orthogonality defect $\|A^\top A-I\|_2$. For OFTv2, which truncates a Cayley-Neumann series, we show that the truncation order does not determine the defect. At its default order, block defects in checkpoints from the reference implementation span five orders of magnitude. We propose Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (RTOFT), which uses the first-order update $W(I+S)$ of a weight $W$ with a skew-symmetric $S$ and restores exact orthogonality by a polar decomposition only when the drift $\|S\|_2$ reaches a tolerance $\tau$. The defect of $I+S$ is exactly $\|S\|_2^2$. Therefore, reading the drift after every update and restoring before the next forward pass guarantees a defect of at most $\tau^2$ in every forward pass, independently of the loss, data, model, and optimizer. A final restoration makes the returned transform exactly orthogonal. On GLUE, RTOFT reduces the training time of block-diagonal, subspace, and butterfly parameterizations from $1.10$-$1.58\times$ to $0.97$-$1.13\times$ that of LoRA, and its block-diagonal version exceeds LoRA by $1.98\pm0.39$ points on the six-task average over five seeds. At $\tau=0.10$, the largest drift read during training stays between $0.10$ and $0.12$ across DeBERTaV3, Qwen, and diffusion models, whereas it ranges from $0.17$ to $1.65$ when restoring once per epoch. In all seven settings of our ablation, the tangent update is worse without restoration than with it, and restoring after every step yields no measurable accuracy gain over restoring at the tolerance and costs $4.5$-$27.5\%$ more per step.
authors: Lanxin Zhao (The University of Sydney), Xiaoyu Li (University of New South Wales), Dai Shi (University of Cambridge), Junbin Gao (The University of Sydney), Andi Han (The University of Sydney)
bullets: Existing OFT methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step, incurring unnecessary overhead and potentially unpredictable defects.
RTOFT applies the first-order update W(I+S), with skew-symmetric S, and uses polar decomposition only when ||S||₂ reaches tolerance τ.
Because the orthogonality defect of I+S is exactly ||S||₂², checking drift before each forward pass guarantees defect ≤ τ²; a final restoration gives an exactly orthogonal result.
On GLUE, RTOFT reduces training time relative to LoRA across several parameterizations and its block-diagonal variant improves the six-task average by 1.98±0.39 points over five seeds.
Restoring only at the tolerance matches per-step restoration accuracy in the reported ablation while costing less; scope includes language and diffusion-model experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Accuracy, training time, general capability, and numbers of restorations of RTOFT. (a) Average score on six GLUE tasks with DeBERTaV3-base against training time relative to LoRA. At the same number of trainable parameters, RTOFT takes 12% less time than OFTv2 and scores 1.09 points higher. (b) One step of RTOFT and one restoration, where Wn is the weight after the n-th restoration. Between two restorations, a forward pass needs one multiplication by the structured matrix S, and the drift ∥S∥2 is read after each update without gradient. Prior methods construct a transform at every step and differentiate through it. papers.selection_reason: Orthogonal fine-tuning with drift-triggered restoration; applicable to LLM and diffusion model adaptation.
papers.title: Amortizing Exact Orthogonality: Drift-Triggered Restoration for Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: RTOFT speeds up orthogonal fine-tuning by restoring exact orthogonality only when drift exceeds a tolerance, while maintaining bounded per-step orthogonality error and competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a severe threat to modern NLP models by embedding hidden triggers that induce malicious behavior at inference time. Recent unlearning methods such as gradient ascent (GA) attempt to remove backdoors by maximizing the loss on poisoned samples; however, these methods can suffer from a critical limitation: they may shift the trigger's influence to other classes rather than eliminating it. In this work, we propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), a framework for mitigating textual backdoor behavior by enforcing prediction and representation invariance to trigger insertion. TICU constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs, then fine-tunes the model so that both inputs produce consistent output distributions and aligned hidden representations. To preserve clean-task performance, TICU also retains the supervised classification loss on clean data and constrains parameter drift from the original model. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings show that TICU improves triggered accuracy and reduces trigger-induced prediction shifts compared with existing baselines, while maintaining competitive label-flipping performance and limiting clean-task degradation.
authors: Santosh Chapagain, Shah Muhammad Hamdi, Soukaina Filali Boubrahimi
bullets: Addresses a limitation of gradient-ascent unlearning, which can shift trigger effects to other classes instead of removing them.
Creates clean/triggered counterfactual pairs and enforces consistency in both predictions and hidden representations.
Retains clean-data classification loss and constrains parameter drift to limit degradation of the original model.
Experiments across datasets, architectures, and attack settings report improved triggered accuracy and reduced trigger-induced shifts versus baselines.
Maintains competitive label-flipping performance while limiting clean-task degradation.

papers.abstract: A common indication that a fine-tuned model has forgotten a deleted record is a membership-inference score near chance (ROC-AUC $\approx 0.5$). This reading is sound only if the comparison population represents how the record should behave after a valid deletion---a counterfactual that is rarely validated. We test this premise in a controlled $2\times2$ study pairing two membership-inference benchmarks, ArxivMIA and BookMIA, with two language models, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B. Exact retraining validates the membership reference: it lies within the prespecified chance band on ArxivMIA but reaches $0.122$ on BookMIA, causing the same metric to reject an empirical deletion reference. A post-hoc BookMIA/Qwen diagnostic replaces benchmark label-0 records with same-pool, never-fine-tuned records and moves the reference from $0.257$ to $0.523$, supporting population mismatch in that cell. Each approximate-unlearning checkpoint is judged jointly on membership removal, deletion-targeted shift beyond non-deletion variation, and utility. On the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama axis, no tested configuration of gradient ascent with retain descent (GA+GD), negative-preference optimization with retain training (NPO-RT), or teacher--student unlearning (SCRUB) passes. A score near chance is not evidence of forgetting until a reference establishes what chance means.
bullets: Exact retraining showed that the expected membership-inference reference can vary across benchmarks and models.
On BookMIA/Qwen, replacing benchmark negatives with never-fine-tuned records shifted the reference from 0.257 to 0.523, indicating population mismatch.
The study evaluates unlearning using membership removal, deletion-specific change beyond natural variation, and utility.
No tested GA+GD, NPO-RT, or SCRUB configuration passed all criteria on the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama setting.
Scope: results cover two benchmarks, two models, and selected approximate-unlearning methods.

papers.abstract: Open-source LLMs that are optimized for reasoning, such as VibeThinker, aim to democratize AI by bringing high-capability models to users with limited resources. They are broadly available but lack regulation and external guardrails; therefore, in order to integrate them safely into human society, it is critical that they perform in a safe manner. There are popular and intuitive arguments for why improved reasoning should improve safety, but recent evidence suggests that, in fact, the opposite may be true. This paper aims to characterize and mitigate this issue. First, it develops a metric for evaluating LLMs optimized for reasoning, and shows that increasing reasoning across multiple model families increases the unsafe rate in all cases. Second, it proposes a method for restoring safety by combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail (ESPG). Compared to alternative methods for safety post-training such as GRPO, ESPG is simple to implement, requires no GPU memory beyond that of inference, and works with remarkably few training samples (e.g.\ 30), yet makes the model significantly safer. The study thus establishes a path towards safe post-training of open-source AI models.
authors: Ehsan Latif, Roberto Dailey, Risto Miikkulainen, Elliot Meyerson
bullets: Introduces a metric for evaluating safety in reasoning-tuned LLMs.
Finds that increasing reasoning raises unsafe rates across multiple model families.
Proposes ESPG, combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail.
ESPG requires inference-level GPU memory and few training samples, while substantially improving safety.
Motivated by the need for safer deployment of broadly accessible, unregulated open-source models.

papers.abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.
authors: Hui Chen, Joshua Elsdon, Can Goksen
bullets: Increasing recurrent depth adds per-token computation while keeping parameters shared.
Deeper passes mostly reweight tokens already favored after the first pass.
Preference write-back trains the shared block from deeper continuations using no reference answers or correctness filtering.
Updated models outperform matched non-recurrent controls across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with reported mean relative gains up to 46.2%.
A one-pass-learned update can improve later passes; the benefit depends on whether input injection is used.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one model that serves many tasks without retraining, but merging many experts this way substantially reduces accuracy. Grouping offers a middle ground: at every layer or weight matrix, the $N$ experts are divided into $K<N$ groups, the experts in a group are merged into one shared module, and a task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Natural choices are to keep the same partners across layers or to group similar experts. Surprisingly, we find that randomly changing partners at every layer outperforms both. We call this Balanced Random Regrouping (BRR): it independently partitions the experts into $K$ equal-sized random groups at each layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix) and merges each group with an existing method. With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 CLIP settings, by 1.0-6.8 points, and BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every setting. A first-order analysis explains this gain. At each layer, merging a task's expert with its partners shifts the task's output features; when the partners are the same at every layer, these shifts tend to point in similar directions and add up, whereas with new partners at every layer they vary independently and add up less on average. A series of experiments supports this analysis, which further guides a grouping search that can outperform BRR.
authors: Kaiyang Li, Shaobo Han, Shihao Ji
bullets: Problem: Merging many fine-tuned experts into one model can substantially reduce accuracy; fixed or similarity-based grouping may limit performance.
Method: Independently partition experts into equal-sized random groups at every layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix), then merge each group with an existing method.
Result: With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform fixed grouping across all 24 CLIP settings by 1.0–6.8 points.
Result: BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every reported setting.
Analysis: Changing partners makes feature shifts vary across layers, reducing their average accumulation; this insight also motivates a search strategy that can outperform BRR.

papers.abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.
authors: Yilin Luo, Jin Hwa Lee, Andrew M. Saxe, Antonio Sclocchi
bullets: The study examines whether fine-tuning removes latent representations or merely suppresses their observable behavior.
Using transformers pretrained on a controlled hierarchical grammar and fine-tuned on restricted rules, it identifies two forgetting timescales.
Generation of excluded rules changes rapidly, with the rate linked to token–latent correlation, while their representations initially remain intact.
Representational forgetting occurs much more slowly as network parameters gradually drift.
Similar dynamics appear in a natural-language setting, suggesting the phenomenon may generalize beyond the controlled model.

papers.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning suppresses previously learned behavior quickly, while the underlying representations persist and are forgotten only through much slower parameter drift.

papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.
bullets: Linear attention treats its recurrent state as an online-learned key-value regression model, making update-pair construction important.
SWGDN replaces short convolutions with content-dependent sliding-window aggregation of queries, keys, and values.
The method produces more similar key-value pairs across consecutive updates, helping the state reinforce learned associations.
It applies to both GDN2 and KDA while preserving their state-update equations and chunkwise parallel algorithms.
Experiments report improvements over the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical question answering, but plausible incorrect answers remain a safety risk in clinical settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground responses in medical literature, while confidence-based adaptive RAG retrieves only when the model appears uncertain. We evaluate this routing strategy on three biomedical QA benchmarks of increasing difficulty and compare models across a broad range of parameter scales. The results reveal a paradox: confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78--0.89) on standard medical exam questions where retrieval adds little value (+2.4\% to -1.4\%), yet becomes \emph{near-random} (AUROC 0.506) on specialist-level questions where retrieval helps most (+11.2\%). Five uncertainty signals---first-token probability, margin, entropy, consistency-based sampling, and verbalized confidence---show the same failure pattern. Five post-hoc calibration correction strategies, including density-ratio reweighting and rank-preserving transformation, do not recover a useful routing signal on hard questions (best AUROC: 0.507). Cross-model comparison shows that larger parameter scale and higher base accuracy do not guarantee reliable confidence-based routing under specialist-domain difficulty shift. These findings challenge the premise of confidence-based adaptive RAG: in high-stakes biomedical settings, defaulting to always-retrieve is safer and more accurate than confidence-based routing when calibration on the target domain is unknown.
authors: Chengying She, Siyu Deng, Haiyan Ge, Lizhuang Liu
bullets: Evaluates confidence-based retrieval routing across three biomedical QA benchmarks with increasing difficulty and models of varied parameter scales.
On standard exam questions, confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78–0.89), but retrieval offers little benefit (+2.4% to −1.4%).
On specialist-level questions, routing becomes near-random (AUROC 0.506) even though retrieval improves performance by 11.2%.
Five uncertainty signals and five post-hoc calibration methods show the same failure pattern; the best corrected AUROC is 0.507.
Larger models and higher base accuracy do not ensure reliable routing under specialist-domain difficulty shifts.

papers.abstract: Transformer architectural modifications frequently measure a statistic on internal representations, observe that it is large, remove it architecturally, and report an improvement. Interpreting that sequence requires evaluating whether the statistic exceeds its noise floor, whether it survives a geometric null, and whether the training gain requires the specific direction removed. We formulate these requirements as three reusable checks and apply them to self-attention removal, which deletes the component of an attention head's output aligned with its own value vector. Across nine multi-head pretrained models (5,408 heads, 124M to 6.9B parameters), an earlier-position causal null accounts for 48% to 63% of the head-value cosine alignment, with no monotone scale trend. Under grouped-query attention, this alignment is specific to each head's own key-value group and reverses across groups (+0.24 to +0.27 within-group, -0.11 to -0.19 across-group). Split-half reliability demonstrates that the per-head intervention effect is resolvable in GPT-2 ($r_Δ= 0.80$) but attenuated in Pythia-160M (0.42) and Pythia-410M (0.53), whereas structural self-cosine reliability is near-perfect in all three ($r_{\text{stat}} > 0.99$); which statistic predicts its own intervention is model-dependent. In a pre-registered 3-arm by 8-seed paired factorial at $4.0 \times 10^8$ tokens per run (399,900,672 tokens), a fixed arbitrary rank-one direction does not differ from baseline (+0.0011 nats, $p = 0.197$), while self-directed removal lowers validation loss (-0.0029 nats, Holm-corrected $p = 0.0023$) and outperforms the fixed arbitrary control directly (-0.0040 nats, $p = 0.0018$). At 50.9M scale the training benefit requires the own-value direction rather than a fixed arbitrary one, but a large cosine alignment alone does not establish redundancy in frozen models.
bullets: An earlier-position causal null explains 48–63% of head–value cosine alignment, with no consistent parameter-scale trend.
Under grouped-query attention, alignment is specific to each head’s own key–value group and reverses across groups.
Structural self-cosine is highly reliable, but intervention-effect reliability and predictive validity vary by model.
In a preregistered factorial experiment, self-directed removal reduced validation loss, while a fixed arbitrary rank-one control did not.
Large cosine alignment alone does not prove redundancy in frozen models.

papers.abstract: Under matched conditions, classifier-head fine-tuning (\textsc{cls}) paradigm consistently outperforms the LLM-as-Judge sequence-to-sequence (\textsc{s2s}) on binary hallucination detection. We trace this gap to the representations induced by the two objectives. Static analysis shows that \textsc{cls} learns a task-specific discriminative direction, pushing hidden states into a clear two-cluster geometry with stronger class separation and linearly decodable label information. By contrast, \textsc{s2s} relies on the pretrained language-modeling head to make decisions. This minimizes the pressure to reorganize representations, leaving the hidden states much closer to the pretrained backbone. Our analysis also reveals that the \textsc{cls} signal saturates before the final layer, after which upper layers form a plateau of statistically interchangeable and largely redundant representations. However, endpoint redundancy alone does not show whether these layers are dispensable during training. Further training-dynamics analysis reveals 1) a lower pretrained substrate, 2) a narrow upper-middle \textbf{InfoWindow} where task information emerges, and 3) a later-synchronizing upper plateau that mirrors this signal. This mechanism motivates us to remove layers above the InfoWindow. Truncating 31\% of the network leaves accuracy unchanged within seed noise on Qwen3-4B and 8B and cuts latency by $1.4\times$. The same depth fraction, fixed before any analysis of the target models, transfers to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, and the layer structure behind it reappears there and on QNLI and SST-2. We hope this helps guide efficient task-specific LLM design.
bullets: Classifier fine-tuning forms clearly separated hidden-state clusters with more linearly decodable labels, while sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning leaves representations closer to the pretrained model.
Task information emerges in a narrow upper-middle-layer InfoWindow, followed by a redundant upper plateau that synchronizes with and mirrors the signal.
Removing layers above the InfoWindow cuts 31% of the network while preserving accuracy within seed variation on Qwen3-4B and 8B.
The same fixed depth fraction transfers to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, with similar layer structure also observed on QNLI and SST-2.
The analysis is based on matched comparisons and training dynamics; the reported efficiency scope covers the evaluated models and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise analysis of fine-tuning objectives for LLM hallucination detection enabling efficient layer truncation.
papers.title: How Fine-Tuning Objectives Shape Layer-Wise Information in LLM Hallucination Detection
papers.tldr: Classifier-head fine-tuning detects hallucinations better than sequence-to-sequence prompting because it creates a localized, discriminative information window that enables substantial upper-layer pruning without accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.
authors: Dawid J. Kopiczko, Tijmen Blankevoort, Yuki M. Asano
bullets: Addresses the challenge of distilling capable closed-model teachers whose chain-of-thought is inaccessible.
Trains students on teacher action trajectories with an empty reasoning block, plus a replay-buffer KL loss to limit policy drift.
Finds cross-format transfer: policies learned without reasoning transfer to inference with reasoning enabled.
Short CoT-proxies improve performance beyond action-only distillation, including gains on AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified.
The approach works with visible outputs and API-provided reasoning summaries from closed teachers.

papers.selection_reason: Distills long-horizon reasoning policies from teacher actions, relevant to LLM reasoning and agent training.
papers.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
papers.tldr: CoT-Proxy distills long-horizon agent behavior from teacher actions—and optionally short reasoning summaries—without requiring hidden chain-of-thought, enabling students to retain their own reasoning style while matching the teacher’s policy.

papers.abstract: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
bullets: The unedited model almost never completes its thinking block within 4,096 tokens and achieves 15.4% on MATH-500.
Fine-tuning only 140–139,750 high-gradient weights on as few as 50 correct training examples raises 4k-token accuracy to 39.0–45.5%.
The gradient concentrates on near-constant channels in the first three layers, behaving like fixed vectors added to the residual stream.
Under the 32k-token evaluation protocol, the reproduced Astra edit reaches 52.1%, while the authors’ edits perform better at budgets up to 16k tokens.
Combining the Astra edit with a half-strength authors’ edit reaches 62.2% at 32k tokens, outperforming Astra alone and using half as many tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates gradient edits to stop reasoning loops in small LLMs, improving performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
papers.tldr: Tiny, gradient-selected edits largely stop Qwen3.5-0.8B’s reasoning loops, and combining them with a frontier-model weight edit substantially improves math performance.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
authors: Yuchao Wu, XingCheng Liang, Xuanze Wang, Yini Huang, Yue Wu
bullets: Addresses retrieval of complementary facts scattered across sessions, including evidence with limited query similarity.

Annotates supported relative-time expressions with calendar interpretations while preserving original wording and temporal granularity.
Achieves the highest reported scores among evaluated methods on LoCoMo (83.08) and LongMemEval (80.20); SAG-Mem-Lite offers lower operational cost with scores of 77.09 and 77.20.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.
authors: Scott Piersall, Yang Gao, Shenyang Liu, Liqiang Wang
bullets: Targets the strong dependence of LLM-generated parallel code on generation guidance.
Combines correctness tests, compiler and static-analysis feedback, runtime data, and load-imbalance profiles into a reward for textual refinement.
Uses external memory to retrieve and accumulate optimization knowledge across runs.
Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, improves runtime, static-analysis quality, and load balance over zero-shot generation and generally over TextGrad.
Ablations and leakage-controlled tests indicate benefits persist with a matched refinement model and transferred knowledge in both skills and memory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: MetaFORGE: An automated meta-learning skill-refinement architecture. MetaFORGE optimizes LLM coding skills through execution-grounded feedback. Generated MPI C code is compiled, statically analyzed, executed, and scored using Eq. (1). Diagnostics and reward trends are converted into a textual gradient for skillprompt rewriting, while iteration artifacts are stored, distilled, indexed, and retrieved as long-term memory, enabling future updates to reuse prior reward-improving strategies.

Figure 8: Held-out cross-task transfer protocol. For each leave-one-task-out fold, METAFORGE is trained sequentially on the two non-held-out tasks across all workload sizes. The resulting transferred skill and cross-task memory are frozen before evaluation. Zero-update transfer isolates knowledge retained in the transferred skill, whereas adaptation transfer evaluates refinement with and without read-only access to the frozen cross-task memory. The held-out task is excluded from all Phase 1 skill updates and memory construction.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.
bullets: Addresses the risk that semantically incorrect LLM-to-FOL translations corrupt downstream reasoning.
Generates candidate readings with tools such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics.
Uses an SMT solver to test logical equivalence between candidate interpretations and the LLM’s formula.
Rejects or optionally repairs unfaithful translations, while abstaining when analysis or checking is inconclusive.
Evaluated on ProofWriter, RuleTaker, PrOntoQA, and the adversarial LongFaithCheck benchmark, achieving near-perfect selective accuracy.

papers.abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.
authors: Shijin Gong, Kai Ye, Victor Chernozhukov, Xinyu Zhang, Chengchun Shi
bullets: GRPO group size is important but is typically chosen by trial and error.
The authors formulate group-size selection as estimating a variance ratio from GRPO’s U-statistic policy gradient.
A pessimistic ratio estimator handles instability when the denominator is small by accounting for estimation uncertainty.
A jackknife-based rule is evaluated on synthetic reasoning tasks plus math and code-generation benchmarks.
The method reduces policy-gradient mean squared error and improves optimization over fixed group sizes with modest extra computation.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low dimensionality of the loss landscape. It relies on a two-point estimate of the gradient that only accesses the function value and not the gradient, bypassing the resource-heavy backpropagation. Recently, it was accidentally discovered that per-sample clipping can improve the performance of the trained model, while running a differentially private version of zeroth-order optimization \cite{zhang2024dpzero} with a very large privacy parameter $\epsilon$ (corresponding to very little privacy). In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and demonstrate that ($i$) the optimal choice of learning rate $\eta$ is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold $c$, satisfying $\eta c =$ constant; ($ii$) clipping drives the zeroth-order optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy; and ($iii$) this phenomenon is only observed with per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization and not other zeroth-order alternatives that also provide robust estimates of the gradient. Further analyses with artificially injected label noise reveals that clipping leads to more robust predictions, which stems from the implicit down weighting of hard-to-fit training examples. Our code is available at https://github.com/SewoongLab/ClipZero
authors: Saket Gollapudi, Elisa Bertino, Sewoong Oh
bullets: The optimal learning rate scales inversely with the clipping threshold, keeping ηc constant.
Clipping leads zeroth-order optimization toward a different solution with higher test accuracy.
The effect is specific to per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization, not other robust zeroth-order gradient estimators.
Under label noise, clipping produces more robust predictions by reducing the influence of difficult training examples.
The study focuses on explaining clipping behavior in zeroth-order fine-tuning of LLMs.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates clipping in zeroth-order optimization for LLM fine-tuning, improving robustness and accuracy.
papers.title: Understanding Clipping In Zeroth-Order Optimization
papers.tldr: Per-sample clipping changes zeroth-order optimization’s solution and can improve test accuracy and robustness by implicitly downweighting hard-to-fit examples.

papers.abstract: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.
authors: Yanlai Yang, Minki Kang, Divyam Madaan, Sung Ju Hwang, Mengye Ren
bullets: Addresses the storage challenge of keeping separate LoRA adapters for many streaming documents.
Finds that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs are more spectrally concentrated and cross-document aligned than directly fine-tuned LoRAs.
Composes intermediate hypernetwork latents, then decodes the merged latent into a LoRA using the frozen generation head.
Evaluated with Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE; latent-space merging consistently improves over weight-space and factor-space methods.
Scope: combines hypernetwork-generated adapters under a fixed output-rank budget.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on external memory to retain and reuse information across interactions. Existing memory systems treat memory as a record of the past and evaluate it by fidelity to the conversation. However, the value of memory lies in whether it improves the agent's response. A memory system decides what to memorize and what to serve before that response exists, and fidelity checks neither decision against it. Faithful memory can therefore fail to improve the response. We instead view memory as a prediction problem and present \textbf{\emph{\leto{}}}, a memory system for LLM agents that focuses on the utility of memory to the future rather than on its fidelity to the past. Because future requests are unknown, \emph{\leto{}} preserves access to conversation details through memory indexing, allowing information to remain available through its sources. When a request arrives, memory replay draws on this index to anticipate and supply the context the agent needs beyond what the request explicitly states. The utility of the served context remains uncertain until the response is generated, motivating a utility loop that uses response outcomes to refine future memory selection. We evaluate our system against six memory systems on five benchmarks across three scenarios. In personalization, it outperforms the strongest compared memory system by 16.3 percentage points in accuracy on PrefEval and by 3.1 points in task completion on PERMA. For long-horizon tasks, it achieves the best overall performance on MemoryArena averaged over five environments with a gain that increases with the chain depth. In long-context understanding, it is on par with retrieval over the raw history while serving fewer context tokens.
bullets: Preserves conversation details through an index instead of permanently compressing or discarding them.
Uses memory replay to anticipate unstated context needs when a request arrives.
Applies a utility loop that learns from response outcomes to improve future memory selection.
Outperforms the strongest compared system in personalization and performs best overall on MemoryArena across five environments.
Matches raw-history retrieval for long-context understanding while serving fewer context tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Utility-centric external memory system for LLM agents, directly relevant to LLM memory.
papers.title: Leto: Utility-Centric Agent Memory
papers.tldr: Leto treats agent memory as a utility-driven prediction problem, selecting context based on its expected impact on future responses rather than fidelity to past conversations.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are built through large-scale pretraining, often followed by post-training, and are then adapted to specific tasks and behaviors. But, does the adaptation add truly new capabilities, or the base model already holds it? We decompose the update induced by different adaptations into a component shared across all inputs and a residual that varies with the input. We find that the shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that learns a constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. We call this the potentiality principle of foundation models: the base model already contains the capacity needed for task-specific expertise. To adapt to a new task, the model just needs to be actualized, i.e., pushed in a certain direction via a constant, input-independent shift. We show the implications of this principle on parameter-efficient adaptation, steering, and convergence across models, and how it explains the neural thickets phenomenon.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Adaptation updates are decomposed into an input-shared component and an input-dependent residual.
A shift adapter using one constant vector per layer reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning for most adaptation gains.
The work proposes the “potentiality principle”: pretraining provides the needed capacity, while adaptation selects or activates it.
The principle has implications for parameter-efficient adaptation, model steering, convergence, and neural thickets.
The abstract does not specify quantitative results or the scope of evaluated models and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Shows constant shift adapters reproduce LoRA/fine-tuning; relevant to foundation-model adaptation and parameter-efficient methods.
papers.title: On Potentiality and Actuality Of Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Foundation models often already contain task-specific capabilities, and adaptation mainly actualizes them through a simple input-independent shift.

papers.abstract: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.
bullets: The study examines why linear attention underperforms softmax attention on associative recall in language modeling.
Synthetic experiments find that recall capacity scales with state size similarly across tested linear-attention architectures.
Even a single sufficiently scaled layer can retrieve thousands of long-distance associations.
In-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting improve recall benchmarks and narrow the gap to softmax attention.
These gains come without architectural or compute-budget changes, but with a slight cost to general language modeling.
