papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokm{\aa}l, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.
authors: Vladislav Mikhailov, Sarfraz Ahmad, Momina Ahsan, Zoia Butenko, Vladimir Dobrovolskii, Preslav Nakov, Erik Velldal, Lilja {\O}vrelid, Ekaterina Artemova

Results across 12 judges show aggregate scores can hide substantial differences by language and evaluation criterion.
Requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences; judges exhibit position, length, and related-model biases.
The benchmark and annotation materials are released under CC BY-NC 4.0 to support more reliable multilingual judge evaluation.

papers.abstract: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.
bullets: Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L underperforms in-context learning for factual question answering.
Adding documents causes substantial interference; errors often retrieve facts from other questions about the same passage.
Layer-wise analysis suggests interference accumulates through depth, with source information present but not reliably resolved by trained readers.
On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and adapter composition approach consolidated text-memory accuracy when episodes remain text, but token savings are modest.
Throughput benefits vary by model and batch size, despite lower analytical compute; the study motivates online-learning approaches for personalized memory.

papers.title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference

papers.abstract: Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support another. We apply the weight-space intervention paradigm of ROME and MEMIT at the granularity of one MLP down-projection column. Our measurement, Empirical Margin Sensitivity (EMS), replaces each coordinate magnitude of a column by its mean while preserving the column's sign pattern and L1 scale, and records the resulting change in the logit margin between the correct option and its hardest-wrong competitor. This isolates the margin's dependence on a column's fine-grained coordinate structure while the column stays in place. We discover high-EMS columns (anchors) on MedQA in ten public checkpoints (four general-purpose bases and six medical post-trained variants) across the Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM families, and measure the same columns on MedMCQA and PubMedQA. Mean-ablating each discovered anchor set lowers MedQA accuracy in all six post-trained models, by 6 to 28 points. In the two pure-SFT checkpoints, crushing anchors raises the PubMedQA margin on correctly answered items (negative EMS), and anchors with this property sit significantly deeper than the same model's other anchors; the four checkpoints trained with RL or mixed recipes show positive PubMedQA EMS and no significant depth shift. The depth association recurs in each of three held-out checkpoints. Because the checkpoints differ in data and pipeline as well as objective, we report these as per-checkpoint observations.
authors: Aniruddh Shreyas, Aarnav Kembhavi, Minal Moharir
bullets: Post-training accuracy alone does not reveal which internal components drive model decisions or transfer across tasks.

EMS intervenes on one MLP down-projection column by replacing coordinate magnitudes with their mean while preserving sign pattern and L1 scale, then measures the change in correct-versus-hardest-wrong logit margin.
Across ten checkpoints, EMS identifies high-sensitivity MedQA columns (“anchors”) in Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM models.
Mean-ablating anchors reduces MedQA accuracy in all six medical post-trained models, by 6–28 percentage points.

PubMedQA effects differ by recipe: pure-SFT models show negative EMS and deeper anchors, whereas RL or mixed-recipe models show positive EMS without a significant depth shift; findings are checkpoint-specific.

papers.abstract: Large language models can have behaviours which only arise in hard-to-anticipate contexts. These hidden behaviours pose a challenge to alignment audits, which seek to uncover problematic model behaviour but are limited by the scenarios the auditor can anticipate. To address this challenge, we explore limited-parameter finetuning (LPF) on examples of a target behaviour. While training 3-25% of LoRA parameters, LPF reveals whether the model has a hidden behaviour, even when standard behavioural evaluations cannot. LPF succeeds on a suite of model organisms with hidden behaviours (8-14B parameters), and also surfaces naturally occurring hidden behaviours in open-weight models (27-35B parameters). LPF can thus distinguish between models which appear behaviourally identical to an auditor, and does not require the context in which the hidden behaviour surfaces. LPF provides a novel affordance that may be useful for auditing frontier AI models. However, we do not evaluate LPF against baselines in a realistic auditing setting, so further work is needed to determine its practicality.
authors: Boyd Kane, Jo J. Jiao, Elizabeth Donoway, Bryce Woodworth, Alex Cloud, Alexander M. Turner
bullets: Addresses alignment audits that are constrained by scenarios auditors can anticipate.
Trains only 3–25% of LoRA parameters on examples of a target behaviour.
Reveals hidden behaviours in model organisms and surfaces naturally occurring behaviours in open-weight models.
Can distinguish models that appear behaviourally identical and does not require the triggering context.
Practicality remains uncertain because it was not evaluated against baselines in a realistic auditing setting.

papers.abstract: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
authors: Da Xiao, Qingye Meng, Shengping Li, Xingyuan Yuan
bullets: Motivation: Standard Transformer circuits have relatively fixed information pathways across heads and layers.
Method: Loom attention interleaves vertical attention over earlier head outputs with horizontal token attention, using normalized, gated linear attention over per-token matrix memories.
Architecture: LoomFormer uses dual residual streams, separating control in vector states from content in matrix states.
Results: Across language modeling and downstream tasks, it matches models trained with over 3× compute and recent residual-stream baselines trained with roughly 1.7–2.8× compute.
Scope: Demonstrated across multiple model sizes and training-token budgets; code is publicly available. ],

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.
authors: Kairong Han, Nuanqiao Shan, Ziyu Zhao, Xinpeng Dong, Zijing Hu, Dian Jin, Leyan Deng, Junjian Ye, Lujia Pan, Fei Wu, Kun Kuang
bullets: Existing reward models rely on outputs or textual trajectories, causing coarse-grained rewards and textual reward aliasing.
The Attention Process Reward Model uses hidden states and attention maps to assess internal reasoning quality.
It is trained with ranking and counterfactual objectives and periodically updated to address distribution shifts.
APRM integrates with representative RL methods and reports an average pass@8 improvement of 2.88%.

papers.abstract: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.
bullets: Paired-seed ablations used the same 3B targets, tokenizer, and training recipe across models ranging from 54M to 759M parameters.
Replacing dense feed-forward blocks with 16 and then 32 routed experts consistently reduced held-out loss in both Greek and English.
Looping a four-layer block recovered roughly 40–44% of the gap between shallow and independently deep models.
Mixer choices such as GQA, GDN, and KDA hybrids changed loss only modestly; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid was the strongest dense variant.
Synthetic mathematics was the hardest Greek component and benefited least from added experts; cached decoding required a fixed-reduction policy and remains qualified.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.
authors: YuanShuo Wang, Jianchao Tan, Lei Gong, Teng Wang, Wenqi Lou, Xuehai Zhou
bullets: Addresses retrieval overhead and the limits of uniform page scoring in sparse attention.
Uses a Lightweight Gate Estimator during prefill to skip low-value regions with under 1% added dense-prefill time.
Extracts compact, calibration-free features for both page- and token-level scoring.
A distance-aware two-level selector ranks near and far pages and candidate tokens under a shared budget.
On Qwen3-8B at 512K context, achieves up to 5.49× operator and 2.97× whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

papers.abstract: An assistant that summarizes old conversations may later need a detail from the original exchange. It can score archived passages against the question, but only passages that fit in the prompt reach the answering model. We tested whether a BM25 filter saves input tokens once that limit is taken into account. We calibrated the filter on passages that individually corrected an answer the model got wrong from the summaries alone. Across 75 LongMemEval questions, filtering changed one prompt and saved 0.096% of input tokens. With and without the filter, the model answered the same questions correctly under a second automated grading. On a random sample, two human graders' settled judgments agreed with the automated grades in 92.9% of definite comparisons (Cohen's kappa = 0.805). Building on earlier work that distinguishes retrieved evidence from delivered evidence, we give an exact test for packers that try whole passages in a fixed order and skip any that do not fit. Run the packer without the filter. The prompt changes exactly when an admitted passage scores below the cutoff. Code and data: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Certfold
authors: John Knight, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
bullets: Across 75 questions, filtering changed only one prompt and saved 0.096% of input tokens.
Answer correctness was unchanged with versus without the filter.
Human and automated grading agreed on 92.9% of definite comparisons, with Cohen’s κ = 0.805.
The paper provides an exact test for fixed-order packers that skip passages exceeding the prompt limit.
The result is scoped to the tested LongMemEval setup and packing strategy.

papers.selection_reason: Examines retrieval and filtering of archived passages for LLM memory and context reduction in long conversations.
papers.title: Why Calibrated BM25 Filtering Barely Reduced Context on LongMemEval
papers.tldr: Calibrated BM25 filtering barely reduced LongMemEval context because prompt-length limits already excluded most irrelevant passages.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.
authors: Junrui Zhang, Zeyu Xu, Runchuan Zhu, Jie Peng, Long Zhang, Zixin Ding, Jiaxin Lin, Kai Wang, Jianmin Ji, Junyuan Hong
bullets: Introduces a benchmark spanning datasets with different reasoning patterns to study when LLMs can engineer effective context.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data, a fundamental capability for LLM-based agents.
papers.title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
papers.tldr: LLM-based context engineering helps inconsistently because its effectiveness depends on how diverse the underlying reasoning failures are and whether the model can extract useful general principles from them.

papers.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical account of Transformer attention by organizing existing probabilistic and information-theoretic results. It identifies the assumptions under which attention computes a posterior mean and the additional conditions required for accurate next-token prediction. Posterior-mean optimality under squared-error loss does not by itself establish predictive sufficiency; even a sufficient representation requires a prediction head that uses its information correctly. An excess-log-loss decomposition makes this distinction precise by separating representation information loss from prediction-head error. The analysis clarifies the conditions required for predictive guarantees. Determining when these conditions hold in trained models, and how architectural or training choices can support them, could guide the development of AI systems that preserve and use predictive information more effectively.
bullets: Organizes probabilistic and information-theoretic results on Transformer attention.
Identifies assumptions under which attention computes a posterior mean.
Shows that posterior-mean optimality under squared-error loss is insufficient for predictive sufficiency.
Uses an excess-log-loss decomposition to separate representation information loss from prediction-head error.
Highlights open questions about whether trained models and design choices satisfy the required conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of Transformer attention and predictive sufficiency; relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Toward a Theoretical Understanding of Transformer Attention: Bayesian Estimation and Predictive Sufficiency
papers.tldr: The paper clarifies when Transformer attention can be viewed as Bayesian estimation and why posterior-mean representations alone do not guarantee accurate next-token prediction.

papers.abstract: Many large language models (LLMs) use chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems, but hide their CoT traces to prevent reasoning capabilities from being distilled. While recent studies have shown that hidden CoTs can be reconstructed, existing methods typically require training a separate attacker for each target LLM. This paper studies model-agnostic CoT reconstruction, aiming to reconstruct hidden CoT traces from arbitrary target LLMs using only input prompts and visible final responses. We propose Final-Output Preference Learning (FOPL), which trains a single reconstruction model that generalizes to unseen LLMs without target-specific adaptation. To achieve this, the reconstruction model must learn which reasoning patterns match a given final response without knowing the target LLM's identity. We address this using preference optimization, training the reconstruction model to prefer native CoTs over synthetic alternatives for the same question and final response. By learning these preferences from LLMs with accessible CoTs, the reconstruction model learns to distinguish reasoning patterns based on visible responses. Experiments show that reconstructed CoTs capture distinct reasoning patterns across LLM families, including a family unseen during training. Moreover, students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Hongli Shen, Shaopeng Fu, Qinbo Zhang, Jian Li, Di Wang
bullets: Addresses model-agnostic reconstruction of hidden reasoning without target-specific attacker training.
Uses preference optimization to favor native CoTs over synthetic alternatives sharing the same prompt and final response.
Learns reasoning-pattern preferences from models with accessible CoTs, without identifying the target LLM.
Reconstructed CoTs capture distinct patterns across LLM families, including one unseen during training.
Students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.
authors: Juntong Shi, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec, Minkai Xu
bullets: RLVR rewards only sampled trajectories, while on-policy distillation provides dense teacher feedback that is not tied to verified outcomes.
VOPD combines both signals in a shared implicit-reward space and projects verifier preferences onto the teacher’s reward direction.
Rao–Blackwellization propagates this verifier-grounded signal across the full vocabulary, including unsampled actions.
The method adaptively extrapolates distillation targets based on teacher–verifier agreement.
Across two teacher–student settings and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD improves final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy baselines.

papers.abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.
authors: Yuxuan Chen, Changwei Lv, Yunfei Li, Zhongjing Du, Kehui Tan, Zijun Liao, Ruochong Zheng, Hao Chen, Can Deng, Zheni Zeng, Chang Liu, Jie Chen
bullets: Addresses the problem of agents storing multimodal records without retaining task-level understanding, causing repeated mistakes.
Uses source-linked multi-view memory for text, images, rendered pages, and cross-record scene images.
Combines source-generated task warm-up, self-training, and task distillation into experiences containing context, conclusions, and supporting links.
Task-aware retrieval supports answering, verification, and evidence-backed long-term reuse.
Outperforms eight baselines across LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2; ablations show benefits from training and memory warm-up.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Motivation and overview of MMMem. Figure 2. MMMem framework. (a) Each memory node holds text, image, page, and generated views of its source records. (b) Tasks generated from the source memory are used to train the reader offline and to warm up the memory. The agent answers with its sources, writes a note, and may generate an image; the resulting experience moves from staged to retained after repeated, source-supported reuse.

(b) A recalled experience links the common and scientific names of a bird in a photo-counting task. (c) The task warm-up example compares answers to a dog-breed question with and without warm-up.

papers.title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation

papers.abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B--14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining \emph{Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs)}, and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.
authors: Sunbowen Li, Dandan Song, Shengkun Ma, Xuanning Cao
bullets: Formalizes how an autoregressive model represents mixtures of latent reasoning modes using prefix-dependent mode posteriors.
In paired breadth-first/depth-first graph-search trajectories, mixed SFT shows no consistent disadvantage versus homogeneous or labeled training under matched token budgets.
Across 0.6B–14B models and data budgets, global mode confusion largely diminishes, shifting the bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions.
Defines Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs) as the small fraction of local errors that determine outcomes; repairing them can rescue failed trajectories when downstream competence is sufficient.
The symbolic graph-search environment is open-sourced; results also extend to natural-language benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Long-lived Web assistants require effective memory and retrieval mechanisms to access information from past user interactions. While these capabilities can be learned through specialized policies, it remains unclear whether specialists trained independently in different environments can be effectively composed without joint optimization. This paper investigates compositional transfer through policy distillation. Memory-writing and sequential retrieval policies are independently distilled from frontier-model action trajectories into 3B models and combined with a fixed answer generator without downstream training. On a LongMemEval-based benchmark, the distilled composition achieves 73.1% accuracy, compared with 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms the evaluated RL-trained compositions on PersonaMem-v2. Component ablations reveal that improvements in individual policies depend on their composition, highlighting the importance of cross-specialist compatibility. Further task-specific adaptation improves accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval through RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 through supervised distillation. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of independent specialist distillation for modular multi-agent systems. Source code and datasets of teacher-generated memory-editing and retrieval trajectories are released to facilitate reproducibility and further research.
authors: Grigorii Davydenko, Artem Sakhno, Igor Pavlov, Julia Belikova, Andrey Savchenko, Maksim Makarenko
bullets: Addresses whether policies trained independently across environments can transfer and work together.
Distills memory-writing and sequential-retrieval policies from frontier-model trajectories into 3B models, then combines them with a fixed answer generator without downstream training.
The composition reaches 73.1% accuracy on LongMemEval versus 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms evaluated RL compositions on PersonaMem-v2.
Ablations show that individual policy gains depend on cross-specialist compatibility.
Task-specific adaptation further raises accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval via RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 via supervised distillation; code and teacher-generated datasets are released.

papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems. However, traditional deep-learning models often rely heavily on high-quality observations. Recent LLM-based approaches incorporate pretrained knowledge to improve forecasting, but they remain sensitive to input perturbations and struggle to preserve long-term patterns. To address this, we propose STMemoLLM, a spatial-temporal memory-augmented LLM for robust traffic forecasting. STMemoLLM introduces memory prototypes to compress inputs into compact summary tokens while extracting reliable dynamics from residual signals, achieving a balance between stability and variability. Specifically, a memory-enhanced tokenizer encodes prototypes and sensor characteristics into attention biases to guide adaptive compression of correlated sensors into semantic summary tokens. A memory-calibrated router further evaluates contextual deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to identify reliable residual signals, which complement the summaries while suppressing noise. Extensive experiments on eight real-world datasets show that STMemoLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments examine point masking, additive Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data, demonstrating strong robustness. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/STMemoLLM-70BF.

A memory-enhanced tokenizer guides compression through prototype- and sensor-informed attention biases.
A memory-calibrated router evaluates deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to suppress noisy residuals.
Experiments across eight real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance and robustness to masking, Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data.

papers.abstract: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.
authors: Sushant Mehta, Logan Ritchie, Edwin Chen
bullets: Evaluates professional-document tasks involving very long sources, visual evidence, and multi-hop reasoning across ten enterprise domains.

On a 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, strict pass rises from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains up to 240K-token inputs while generated tokens remain nearly unchanged.
On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, mean rubric reward increases from 0.571 to 0.746, zero-credit tasks decrease from 54 to 10, and messages per task fall 18%.
Argues that long-context agent evaluation should jointly report accuracy, tokens, and turns, and that document datasets should include both text and image renderings.

papers.abstract: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.
authors: Chen Li, Xiaoling Hu, Chao Chen
bullets: Binary correctness labels miss differences between occasional errors, frequent failures, isolated successes, and consistently correct behavior.
The method combines an individual response’s correctness with query-level empirical success rates from repeated generations.
An independent confidence estimator uses the query and full response, trained with LoRA adapters and a confidence head via mean squared error.
Repeated generations are needed only to construct supervision; inference evaluates each response in a single pass.
The paper proves ordering and mean-preservation properties and derives a selective-risk bound, then evaluates calibration and selective prediction in language and vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=\Omega(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.
authors: Yee Man Choi, Fengchi Wang, Ruiquan Huang
bullets: Studies one-token-context next-token prediction with jointly trained input/output embeddings initialized randomly.
Analyzes untied and tied embeddings using perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on population cross-entropy.
For untied embeddings, dimension scaling as Ω(√V) yields RPG above 7/8 during most late training iterations, with high probability.
For tied embeddings trained on observed states, RPG is 1−O(V/d²), with additional guarantees for unseen states under coverage and embedding-boundedness conditions.
The theory uses a bounded Hessian trace to connect approximate second-order stationary points with high prediction gain; experiments illustrate persistent gain and transfer.

papers.abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).
bullets: Addresses state-tracking weaknesses and per-step latency that limit parallel-trainable recurrent models.
Routes each layer’s transition through a tree using the current token and the lower layer’s state, activating one expert per layer.
Cross-layer routing enables conditional resets while preserving parallel-scan training by avoiding feedback from a layer’s own past.
Active weights fit in a few hundred kilobytes of CPU L2 cache, while the larger expert bank remains in RAM.
It solves all five evaluated state-tracking tasks and reports strong language, genomic, CPU-speed, GPU-throughput, and genomic-classification results.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. As a result, policy optimization can be inefficient, especially when training base models directly from sparse outcome feedback. In this paper, we introduce SAEPO, a Sparse AutoEncoder-guided token-level credit assignment method for outcome-supervised Policy Optimization. Rather than treating correctness only as a rollout-level (sequence-level) signal, SAEPO uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to build token-level semantic representations within reasoning trajectories; it scores each token based on the SAE concepts (e.g., penalizing wrong "final-answer" tokens but rewarding correct "reasoning-process" tokens), learned in an unsupervised manner, to achieve fine-grained credit assignment. SAEPO is a plug-in advantage-shaping module compatible with various policy optimization algorithms. We instantiate SAEPO with both GRPO and GSPO, covering token-ratio and sequence-ratio policy-gradient objectives, and evaluate SAEPO across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks. Empirical results show that SAEPO improves both the math and code benchmark averages over the matched baselines, with gains of up to 6.63% and 5.57%, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, training curves also show faster early accuracy growth. Feature and token-level analyses suggest that the SAE-derived signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens.
authors: Yusong Zhao, Zihao Zhao, Zirui Zhang, Tunyu Zhang, Ziyan Wang, Yi Wang, Chengzhi Mao, Hao Wang
bullets: Targets coarse credit assignment in outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, where verifiers judge only completed responses.
Uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder to represent reasoning trajectories and shape token-level advantages based on semantic concepts.
Can be plugged into multiple policy-optimization methods, demonstrated with GRPO and GSPO.
Evaluated across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks, improving matched-baseline averages by up to 6.63% in math and 5.57% in code.
Analyses indicate the learned signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens; early accuracy growth was faster on Qwen3-1.7B-Base.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of SAEPO. A frozen SAE encodes token hidden states from grouped rollouts into sparse features. For each token, its counts of similar tokens in correct and incorrect rollouts determine its token-level reward, with higher reward assigned when more similar tokens appear in correct rollouts than in incorrect ones. The token-level reward is normalized and added to the outcome advantage, while the verifier reward, policy-ratio construction, clipping rule, and KL regularizer remain unchanged.

Figure 4 SAE features (concepts) associated with the highest and the lowest SAEPO token scores, computed from rollouts on the “Algebra” and “Geometry” subjects in MATH-500. Feature-level rewards are obtained by averaging semantic scores over tokens where each SAE feature is active. Right: Low-reward features mostly capture connectives, copulas, punctuation, stop words, and discourse markers. These results suggest that the SAEPO-derived signal concentrates on semantically meaningful reasoning features.

Figure 1 Comparison of credit assignment mechanisms in outcome-supervised policy optimizations. GRPO assigns the same rollout-level credit to all tokens in a generated reasoning trace, so decisive reasoning steps and incidental tokens receive identical credit. Our SAEPO assigns question-local, token-level semantic credit based on semantic representations from the SAE feature space; therefore it rewards question-relevant reasoning tokens while penalizing uninformative or misleading tokens with more fine-grained credit assignment. Top words of the most related concepts to an example rewarded token “interior” show that our SAEPO can achieve interpretable token-level credit assignment.

Figure 5 Examples of how SAEPO can assign a fine-grained credit signal to each token. Green tokens represent positive credit that rewards the tokens, gray tokens represent near-zero credit, while red tokens represent negative credit that penalizes the tokens. SAEPO tends to reward semantically meaningful tokens like question-relevant tokens in incorrect trajectories and reasoning tokens in correct trajectories, while penalizing uninformative or misleading tokens even when they are in correct trajectories, achieving fine-grained token-level credit assignment over the reasoning trace.

papers.selection_reason: SAE-guided token-level credit assignment improves LLM reasoning policy optimization.
papers.title: SAEPO: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Credit Assignment for Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: SAEPO improves sparse-reward LLM reasoning training by using sparse-autoencoder concepts to assign fine-grained token-level credit instead of relying only on final-answer correctness.

papers.abstract: A transformer language model computes a deep hidden state for every token but uses it only to sample that token. Existing latent-feedback designs, which feed hidden states back across tokens, are mostly built in during pretraining and gain little when added to a pretrained model. We introduce the temporal residual, a second residual stream that every sublayer reads and writes and that is carried from each token to the next. It adds 2,752 parameters to a 4.2B-parameter model and starts exactly at the pretrained network. Retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B tokens of training, it beats a standard model trained on the same data by 7, 13 and 5 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and AMC 2023, writes shorter solutions, and stays ahead at matched training compute. The separate stream matters: prior designs that feed state into the existing stream recover at most 40% of the gain when retrofitted. Validation loss can mislead: the recipe with the lowest loss gains nothing at decoding. Trained with filler tokens in place of reasoning, the model reasons in its hidden state: its GSM8K accuracy with no visible reasoning rises from 21% to 40%, and falls back when the carried state is zeroed.
authors: Ziyang Cai, Xingyu Zhu, Sanjeev Arora
bullets: Addresses the limited effectiveness of adding latent feedback after pretraining.
Adds a separate residual stream that each sublayer reads, writes, and carries across tokens.
Retrofitting Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B training tokens improved AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AMC 2023 performance by 7, 13, and 5 points, respectively, versus a same-data standard model.
The approach supports hidden-state reasoning: GSM8K accuracy without visible reasoning increased from 21% to 40%, but dropped when the carried state was removed.
Separate-stream design and decoding evaluations matter; validation loss alone did not predict gains, and prior retrofits recovered at most 40% of the improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a temporal residual stream carrying latent feedback across tokens in pretrained LLMs, improving reasoning and acting as a lightweight recurrent memory.
papers.title: The Temporal Residual: Fast and Effective Retrofitting of Latent Feedback into Pretrained Language Models
papers.tldr: The temporal residual efficiently retrofits cross-token latent feedback into a pretrained language model, improving reasoning while enabling shorter or hidden reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.
authors: Qiyao Liang, Kajetan Schweighofer, Xin Qiu, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: Both ES and policy gradients estimate the same gradient, but ES explores parameter space while policy gradients explore generated actions.
ES sample cost depends on effective dimension—the number of independent skills—whereas policy-gradient cost depends on effective horizon—the reward-relevant token dependencies.
On a controllable synthetic task, policy gradients win at short horizons; ES wins beyond a skill-dependent crossover horizon.
Across 20 NLP, math, and agentic tasks, policy gradients lead on short horizons and tie on moderate-horizon math tasks; no task reached the predicted ES-favorable regime.
On the much longer-horizon Terminal-Bench, preliminary results show ES without credit assignment outperforming a released policy-gradient checkpoint.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of evolution strategies versus policy gradients for LLM fine-tuning; relevant to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Evolution Strategies (ES) become competitive with policy gradients when tasks have long effective horizons but few independent skills, though most current benchmarks remain too short to show a clear ES advantage.

papers.abstract: Effective long-horizon persuasion in recurring goal-oriented settings requires more than factual memory: it must track how a user's trust, negotiation behavior, and strategic receptiveness evolve across interactions. Existing persuasive dialogue systems are largely single-session, static, and unimodal, while cross-session memory systems, though temporally aware, retain only factual content and overlook persuasion-specific dynamics. We propose MERIT (Memory-augmented Experience-Rationale for Iterative Temporal persuasion), which pairs a graph-based memory of four persuasion-specific memory types with a per-persona experience rationale library that records which strategies succeed for each user and why. Together they enable adaptive persuasion through prompt composition alone, with no parameter updates. To support this setting, we introduce PERSIST (PERSona-driven InSurance Interactions over Time), a dataset of 60 curated personas spanning 10+ years of motor insurance renewal interactions, with probabilistic life events that shift negotiation behavior and receptiveness across sessions, verified through strict human-in-the-loop annotation. MERIT surpasses memory and experience-based baselines on every metric across two policy backbones, reaching persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 (out of 5).
authors: Rohan Kirti, Akash Ghosh, Pratik Amrit, Aryan Vats, Niladri Ghosh, Sriparna Saha
bullets: Targets recurring persuasion settings where trust, negotiation behavior, and receptiveness evolve across sessions.
Uses a graph-based memory with four persuasion-specific memory types plus a per-persona library of successful strategies and rationales.
Introduces PERSIST, a human-verified dataset of 60 personas across 10+ years of motor-insurance renewal interactions and changing life events.
Evaluated with two policy backbones, MERIT outperforms memory and experience-based baselines on every reported metric, achieving persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 out of 5.

papers.abstract: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.
authors: Fu Dai, Haodi Quan, Kamal Taha
bullets: Short-sequence failures are mainly attributed to rotary positional encoding rather than content matching.
Random gaps in position IDs let the indexer and frozen teacher learn long-range positions without processing long sequences.
An 8K-distilled indexer nearly matches 32K- and, on one model, 64K-distilled quality; the reported training-cost reduction is about 6× per token.
3–4-bit key quantization requires no retraining; 4-bit keys change perplexity by at most 0.05 and yield 1.6–2.2× faster scans.
Benefits vary by model and serving setting: position compression can be competitive, and decoding speedups appear mainly for long contexts with multiple streams.

(1) Position-skipped distillation lets the ids of T contiguous tokens jump by a random offset u after a cut point, so every distance up to the range R occurs. (2) The frozen model computes dense attention under the same ids, and each layer’s indexer matches its head-summed attention pt,s with a KL loss; only the indexer receives gradients. (3) Each token keeps one b-bit key, an integer scan scores all keys, and attention reads the k best (orange). Bottom, serving: in every layer H query heads are scored against the b-bit keys by a fused integer scan; beyond R the ids are scaled by ρ = R/L. Blue: our components.

papers.selection_reason: Improves sparse-attention indexer distillation for long-context serving with position-skipped training and quantization, relevant to efficient long-context LLMs.
papers.title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
papers.tldr: Position-skipped distillation trains sparse-attention indexers on short sequences that generalize to long contexts, substantially reducing training cost while preserving quality in several models.

papers.abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
authors: Honghao Feng, Shanhan Qu, Kai Tong, Shuquan Man, Huiping Zhuang
bullets: P-TAP gradually shapes a session’s lightweight adapter with escalating adversarial queries, then uses the accumulated state to answer a final harmful request.
Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, updates increased attack success by 13.00 percentage points with greedy decoding and 22.25 points with best-of-10 sampling.
The attack’s effect largely disappears when adaptation uses unrelated or benign same-topic text instead of adversarial queries.
Incoming-query screening caught every attack stream, whereas a perplexity-based unsafe-adaptation detector missed all successful attacks.

papers.selection_reason: Studies security risks of conversational test-time learning where LLM adapters update during deployment, directly matching test-time adaptation and LLM research.
papers.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Persistent conversational test-time learning can be poisoned through ordinary multi-turn queries, weakening safety alignment and enabling jailbreaks.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.
bullets: The model analyzes its reasoning, weights, and activations in a persistent Python session to design self-edits.
Edits use white-box primitives such as singular directions, activation contrasts, rank-one projections, and tensor computations.
Each candidate is evaluated on a hidden gate set, and only strictly improving edits are merged before the next generation.
On Qwen3.8-27B math problems, five generations improved gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45%.
Held-out performance also improved, indicating that the self-edits generalized beyond the loop’s gate set.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The gradient writes the weights, or the model does. Top: in existing self-improvement the model writes data or chooses hyper-parameters, and SGD computes the weight change. Bottom: in SELFWRITE the model reads its own wrong and right answers, contrasts its activations on them, and writes a program that projects the contrast direction out of one of its layers (code simplified). The rank-one edit is merged only if it improves the model on a hidden gate set, and the edited model Mg+1 writes the next edit. No gradient tool is used and no training step is taken.

papers.abstract: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. All protocols and acceptance criteria are pre-registered; the stack and harness are released.
authors: Fahrell Giovanny, Geby Bayuningtyas, Sahrul Mukharom
bullets: Defines attack layers and proves that each deployment-layer verification tier covers only its own layer; composite vectors can evade per-fragment checks.
Evaluates eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families using a preregistered, released harness.
Pattern-based defenses produced 35–50% benign-session false positives; provenance-gated channel separation achieved zero false positives and zero utility loss.
Instruction overrides without recognizable markers bypassed gates at 47.7–49.5% control-equivalent rates, identifying a model-internal detection boundary.
Storage-layer detection was deterministic across 126/126 cases per model with zero false positives; PoisonedRAG pressure fell from 70% to 0% under the full stack.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (~-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.
authors: Stephen Cheng, Zahra Sodagar, Sandeep Soni, Dinesh Manocha, Sarah Wiegreffe
bullets: Many rollouts repeatedly propose answers despite containing only one unique answer, suggesting potentially unnecessary chain-of-thought backtracking.
A linear direction extracted from verbalized confidence separates high- and low-confidence states and also influences the probability of backtracking.
Steering this direction mid-trace changes response length by roughly −1.3k to +2.5k tokens and answer proposals by −4.18 to +4.75, in both directions.
Applying the direction from generation start shortens traces at comparable accuracy, even without knowing proposal positions.
The findings link internal confidence representations to a model’s tendency to commit or continue reasoning.

papers.selection_reason: Studies internal confidence and backtracking in reasoning LLMs; fits language foundation model reasoning research.
papers.title: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: A latent confidence direction in reasoning models can predict and steer whether they backtrack, substantially changing trace length and proposal count with little accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.
authors: Yoonsung Jung, Sunghun Jung, Louise Nayeong Koh, Yongjun Choi
bullets: Studies length extrapolation in a controlled multi-step state-tracking task.
Atomic operation representations generalize substantially better than multi-token templates.

Scaling the recurrent operator reaches 35.1% exact-match accuracy on 20–40 operations after training on 2–10, while larger fixed-depth Transformers reach 0%.

papers.abstract: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.
authors: Jiayu Huang, Yichao Cai, Xinyu Li, Zhen Zhang, Javen Qinfeng Shi
bullets: Long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making context-aware evidence retrieval difficult.
Studies show memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability; adjacent-turn grouping improves access, while wider windows do not consistently help.
ContextFact links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations across sessions.
At query time, it independently reranks fact and entity views and expands retrieval through entity links.

Using Qwen3.5-27B, it reports 86.49% judge accuracy on LoCoMo and 91.00% on LongMemEval-S while consuming 21% of the evidence tokens used by the strongest baseline; entity readout particularly helps multi-hop questions.
