papers.abstract: Code models are increasingly trained on the full history of software repositories, every version of every file, rather than on a single snapshot. The tools that deduplicate training data were built for snapshots, and what they do to a history has not been measured. We measured it on a pre-registered random sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind the SWE-bench benchmark. A history is mostly repetition: in the vocabulary of text indexing, a pangenome, one text in many near-identical variants. The history of a typical repository holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code, and a mature repository holds 89. The reason is that each edit changes a few lines and leaves the rest of the file in place: nine tokens in ten of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of these copies, since no two versions are identical. Large training pipelines already deduplicate their snapshots by grouping near-identical files and keeping one. Applied across versions, the same step brings the repetition down to about two copies. But two problems remain. The deduplicator keeps one version of each file, and in widely used implementations, including the one we measured, the rule for choosing that version ignores dates, so for half of all files the version kept for training is an old one. Sorting versions newest first before deduplicating fixes the problem at almost no cost. The second problem is benchmark answers. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench test a model on real bug fixes, and a merged fix survives in a median of 18 later versions of the files it changed. Therefore, removing benchmark fixes needs a separate step that checks every version. We turn the measurements into a short set of rules for teams that train on code history, and release the instruments and frozen outputs.
bullets: Repository histories contain roughly 19 copies of current code typically, rising to 89 in mature projects; nine in ten tokens of a changed file already existed before the edit.
Exact-match deduplication removes none of these non-identical historical versions.
Near-duplicate file grouping reduces repetition to about two copies, but version-selection rules may retain old files when dates are ignored.
Sorting versions newest first fixes stale-version selection at minimal cost.
Benchmark fixes can persist through many later versions, requiring a separate all-version scan to remove them from training data.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and optimizes training data curation for code models, addressing data deduplication and history management relevant to LLM pretraining.
papers.title: Git History Is a Pangenome: Repetition in Code Training Corpora and What Deduplication Removes, Keeps and Misses
papers.tldr: Code histories contain massive near-duplicate repetition that snapshot deduplication largely misses, but ordering versions by recency and separately filtering benchmark fixes can reduce leakage and redundancy.

papers.abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.
authors: Tengfei Shao, Asma Rezaei, Ali Reza Kamali
bullets: Treating reports from shared sources as independent can double count evidence; instruction value depends on the receiver’s baseline.
The study constructs an exact reference over binary worlds with 0.65 single-report reliability and four dependence levels, then evaluates raw versus instructed answers on 2,976 worlds.
Agreement with the exact rule and improvement from instruction were distinct: some models already agreed nearly perfectly, while others gained modestly.
The prespecified dependence-level gain contrast was 0.0342 (95% interval 0.0303–0.0382); the grouping endpoint difference was not detected and was bounded within ±0.0031.
The authors recommend estimating paired Brier-score gain on labelled deployment items before adopting the instruction for a given receiver and prompt.

papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average, with no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls isolate the contribution of each stage.
bullets: Targets the unresolved conflicts that arise when LLMs must satisfy competing values.
Decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces.
Uses preference-aware value merging followed by lightweight harmonization with the expert ensemble.
Outperforms strong DPO variants and multi-objective baselines on the average across five preference-alignment benchmarks.
Shows no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls assess each pipeline stage.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.
authors: Xinnan Zhang, Zeyi Liao, Siliang Zeng, Zhongruo Wang, Jiaxiang Li, Xinyan Zhao, Huan Sun, Mingyi Hong
bullets: OPD failures include excessive length, repetition, performance degradation, and spurious agreement with the teacher.
The analysis identifies mismatched states where sampled-token updates fail to correct the teacher–student gap, characterized by the student’s probability mass on the teacher’s top-p tokens.
Gradients from mismatched states can interfere with learning at other tokens, making teacher imitation difficult.
A termination-token mismatch can suppress the student’s existing generation modes and steer sampling toward states where the teacher is unreliable.
The findings support SFT initialization and targeted correction of student–teacher mismatch states.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.
authors: Ruijia Yang, Ruikai Li, Zeyi Wen
bullets: Addresses inefficiency from either serial GPU time-sharing or inflexible whole-GPU partitioning.
Co-resides a persistent rollout engine with a learner on each GPU using CUDA MPS.
Uses host-memory optimizer state and layer-wise weight streaming to fit the learner beside rollouts.
A publication gate and step-time bound control policy staleness and compute sharing.
Across reported platforms and workloads, CTRL delivers 1.11–2.24× the throughput of stronger asynchronous baselines and consistently outperforms time-sharing and measured GPU splits.

papers.abstract: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Shengxiang Xu, Liang Yao, Shuyi Chen, Yishu Wang, Shimin Di, Fan Liu, Bishun Yao, Hanghui Guo, Xinyu Liu, Chengye Liang, Yuyu Luo, Min-Ling Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed toolsets and task-specific experience accumulation in agentic remote sensing systems.
Uses execution feedback to evolve persistent tools and workflow knowledge while keeping the base model parameters fixed.
Acquires specialized tools on demand and distills successful executions into reusable agent skills.
Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench report substantial accuracy gains from the initial system and improvements over existing methods.
Scope: improvements depend on the availability of execution feedback and the harness’s ability to acquire and verify tools and skills.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.
bullets: Targets two failure modes: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep reasoning steps.
Uses auxiliary heads to supervise exact canonical execution states and keep latent trajectories on valid computational manifolds.
Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, RoPE primarily recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%).
Combining RoPE and ORION yields complementary additive gains on joint length-depth extrapolation.
Negative controls show that exact canonical alignment is necessary; hashed state statistics do not constrain depth extrapolation.

figures.caption: Figure 7: The ORION architecture on both domains. An exact simulator emits the canonical state Φ(S) = (µ, ν, ω, T, ans) at every execution step; five read-out heads decode it from one shared latent, and their losses are added to the language-modelling objective. The answer head is one probe among several rather than the privileged output. The identical wiring runs on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT, which is what lets the contrastive term act across domains.

Figure 3: Canonical-state pretraining transfers across domains. Exact match during adaptation to the other domain under an equal 800-step budget, using five seeds. Models are initialized from scratch, from a Transformer pretrained on the source domain, or from an ORION model pretrained on the source domain. The ORION initialization improves target-domain held-out performance over Transformer pretraining by +0.085 ± 0.041 for FOLDING→GRIDSHIFT and +0.035 ± 0.013 for GRIDSHIFT→FOLDING. The improvement is positive in every seed in both directions.

Figure 2: ORION composes with RoPE on depth extrapolation. (a,b) Exact match at execution depths 5–8, after training at depths 1–4, for RoPE alone and ORION + RoPE on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. Bands show ± one standard deviation over three seeds. Printed values give the pairedby-example difference at each depth; stars indicate p < 0.05. Across all held-out depths, ORION + RoPE improves over RoPE by +0.016 on FOLDING (p = 0.036) and +0.024 on GRIDSHIFT (p = 0.002). (c) The corresponding difference across model widths in the five-seed scaling ladder. The gains are +0.000, +0.004, and +0.082 at 3.5M, 11M, and 26M parameters, respectively; the largest model favors the combined condition in all five seeds.

Figure 1: ORION + RoPE keeps computing the canonical state beyond the training depth. Exact accuracy of the canonical-state read-outs by execution depth (seed 0; shaded region: training depths). (a, b) The answer set read directly from the latent at the decision position, without autoregressive decoding, on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. (c) The occupancy map on FOLDING. With absolute positions the read-outs collapse at the first unseen depth (0.04, 0.19, 0.06); with RoPE they remain at 0.63, 0.67 and 0.85 at depth 5 and decay gradually, so the state is still being tracked where it was never supervised.

Figure 4: Canonical supervision confines the latent trajectory. The final-layer hidden state at each executed operation is one point per step, projected on the two leading principal components of the in-distribution states and expressed in units of their spread. Arrows: mean step-to-step displacement of 800 paths through each cell; bold path: mean position from step 1 (square) to step 8. The baseline moves 1.18 spreads per step with no coherent direction; ORION + RoPE moves 0.44 along a coherent field. The effect comes from the supervision, not the positional encoding (0.45 for ORION without RoPE, 1.36 for RoPE alone).

Figure 9: Layer-to-layer linear CKA within each model on FOLDING (seed 0, 384 in-distribution prompts). Both models show the same smooth block structure, with adjacent layers above 0.97 and the embedding layer the most distinct. Canonical supervision does not reorganise the layer hierarchy. Note the colour scale starts at 0.90; on an absolute scale the two panels are nearly identical, which is the point.

Figure 5: An execution trace in the FOLDING domain. Each operation reflects part of the sheet onto the rest and concatenates the stacks, so layer count grows with depth while the footprint shrinks. The canonical state Φ(St) is the stack-valued geometry at each step; the query is a punch through the final stack, scored by exact set match over the original cells it perforates.

Figure 6: An execution trace in the GRIDSHIFT domain. Cyclic row and column shifts permute origin labels over a grid whose extent never changes, so unlike FOLDING the state size is independent of program length. The canonical state is the origin-per-cell permutation and the query asks which positions hold marked origins after execution.

Figure 10: Degradation on FOLDING, from the reduced-budget surface sweep. (a) Exact match against execution depth at the training state sizes; the shaded band is the trained range and the printed values are the endpoints at 2×. The rotary conditions degrade gradually while the two absolute-position conditions fall off a cliff at the first unseen depth. (b) The joint surface for ORION + RoPE over both axes, every cell labelled with exact match; red lines mark the edges of the training region and n/a marks a combination the generator cannot produce. Reading up the left columns shows depth costing accuracy gradually; reading across to the right column shows the size axis costing all of it at once, at every depth. The size axis is not drawn as a separate curve because all four conditions coincide on it (0.195, 0.190, 0.169 and 0.170 at S/Strain = 1.33).

Figure 11: Per-algorithm exact match on the CLRS pilot (single seed). (a) In-distribution (n = 16). (b) The preregistered out-of-distribution endpoint, the mean of the length and structural axes. Only kmp matcher separates the conditions; activity selector and graham scan are at zero for every condition.

FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT models are trained on state size Strain ≤ 6 and execution depth Dtrain ≤ 4; the joint split tests S = 8 at depth 5–8. In-domain, size-only, and depth-only results are averaged over three random seeds and reported as mean ± standard deviation. The joint split uses seed-0 checkpoints and reports the half-width of a 95% bootstrap interval over 1,000 test instances. CLRS is a single-seed pilot over eight algorithms. ↑ indicates higher is better.

Table 3: Ablation against negative controls on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT under joint OOD extrapolation (S = 8, 2×D). Results use seed-0 checkpoints; ± denotes the half-width of a 95% bootstrap interval over 1,000 test instances. The controls retain the auxiliary-head architecture while changing the supervision target.
Table 1: Structural properties and evaluation parameters for the algorithmic reasoning task splits.

Table 11: Hyperparameter settings across model configurations. The scaling ladder of Table 13 varies dmodel ∈ {256, 384, 512} at a reduced step budget with five seeds; all other experiments use the configuration below.

Table 7: Alternative sequence backbones at a matched training budget (6,000 steps, 3 seeds, mean ± s.d.). The recurrent and long-convolution models were run because they carry sequence priors of their own and are therefore confounds for any claim about positional structure. The state-space model does not fit the training distribution in either domain and Hyena fits only FOLDING; RWKV fits both and is the strongest non-rotary backbone on the depth axis (0.099 and 0.175), but none of the three comes near what rotary embeddings reach (0.651 and 0.575).

Table 4: Sensitivity to the availability of canonical supervision on FOLDING using an exploratory seed. The auxiliary loss weight (λ) was fixed at its preregistered value. The experiment varies the fraction of supervised execution steps and the fraction of corrupted labels.

Table 9: Representation geometry of the final layer on FOLDING (seed 0, n = 600 in-distribution prompts). The preregistered hypothesis was that canonical supervision compresses the execution subspace. It does not: the participation ratio, the spectral entropy and the number of dimensions needed for 90–95% of the variance all rise under supervision. The TwoNN estimator is the one measure that moves the other way, so we report the evidence as mixed in direction but uniform in conclusion — no measure supports compression. Layer-wise linear CKA between the supervised and unsupervised models stays high throughout, so the supervised representation is a nearby one rather than a different one.

Table 10: Error taxonomy on FOLDING (seed 0): counts of each failure mode among incorrect predictions. Beyond the training depth the model almost never emits a malformed or reflected answer: the failures are well-formed answer sets that miss cells or are disjoint from the truth, which is the signature of a state that has drifted rather than of a decoder that has broken.

Table 8: Robustness to input corruption on FOLDING (seed 0, in-distribution test set). Token noise replaces a fraction p of program tokens at random. Dropped operation removes one operation from the program and scores against the answer for the shortened program. Canonical supervision leaves both curves essentially unchanged, so the robustness it confers is not visible at the level of the decoded answer.

Table 5: Scaling laws for RoPE versus ORION + RoPE on depth extrapolation in FOLDING. Values are EM percentages, reported as mean ± standard deviation over five seeds. The ladder uses a reduced training budget; therefore, its absolute values are lower than those in Table 2.

The controls lie within the seed spread of the APE baseline and of ORION with APE (0.026 on FOLDING, 0.063 on GRIDSHIFT); the separation in this table is between the rotary column and everything else.

papers.selection_reason: Improves transformer length/depth extrapolation via canonical-state supervision and RoPE, relevant to LLM architecture and long-context research.
papers.title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
papers.tldr: ORION improves Transformers’ systematic generalization by supervising exact canonical execution states, addressing depth-related state drift alongside RoPE’s handling of long-sequence positional corruption.

papers.abstract: Training-free activation guardrails such as kNNGuard score prompts by comparing last-token LLM hidden states (the Layer Ensemble branch, kNNGuard LE) and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Embedding-kNN) against a small reference bank (50 examples per class), combining the two branches into a Fused Ensemble (kNNGuard FE). While effective on short inputs (up to 256 tokens), standard kNNGuard degrades substantially on long inputs (over 1000 tokens): averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it, kNNGuard LE AUROC drops from 0.742 (0.777 and 0.706) to 0.554 (0.587 and 0.521) on Content Harm Moderation (Aegis-2.0), and from 0.994 (0.995 and 0.992) to 0.556 (0.598 and 0.513) on RAG Hallucination Detection (HaluBench). We trace this degradation to three causes: (1) hidden-state drift as sequence length increases, (2) hard 256-token truncation in MiniLM, and (3) signal dilution when a long document is compressed into a single final-token vector. We then evaluate three training-free adaptations: a Length-Routed Dual Bank, a long-context embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and Strided Window Pooling across intermediate token positions. On Content Harm Moderation, dual-bank routing and strided window pooling raise long-context kNNGuard LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 (+0.274 AUROC) and fused kNNGuard FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886 (+0.164 AUROC) with no latency overhead from bank routing. On RAG Hallucination Detection, where the guardrail must verify logical consistency between a generated answer and a retrieved passage, sentence-embedding kNN remains near random chance across all lengths, while length-matched LLM hidden states (kNNGuard LE) recover medium-length detection (AUROC = 0.853) but remain limited on over-1000-token passages (AUROC = 0.607) due to final-token dilution over long contexts.
bullets: Long-context degradation stems from hidden-state drift, MiniLM’s 256-token truncation, and final-token signal dilution.
Length-routed dual banks and strided window pooling improve long-context Content Harm Moderation LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 and fused FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886.
Bank routing adds no latency overhead, while a long-context embedding model is evaluated as another training-free adaptation.
Sentence-embedding kNN stays near random for RAG hallucination detection; length-matched hidden states recover medium-length performance but remain weak beyond 1,000 tokens.
The study evaluates training-free adaptations using small reference banks across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses long-context prompt processing and hidden-state drift in LLM guardrails, fitting long-context model research.
papers.title: Auditing and Adapting kNNGuard for Long-Context Prompts
papers.tldr: kNNGuard degrades sharply on long prompts, but length-aware banks and strided pooling substantially restore harmful-content detection while hallucination detection remains difficult at extreme lengths.

papers.abstract: Language models assign different probabilities to token sequences that decode to the same string. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), a trainer that re-encodes sampled text may train on a different token sequence with the same reward. We ask how far this moves a training update, and whether the movement has a consistent direction. From one checkpoint, we compare updates on the same rollouts, canonical and with selected tokens split into two pieces, against an update on a different batch. On Qwen2.5-0.5B with three-digit addition, splitting about one token in 25 moves the update 0.556 times as far as replacing the batch. The ratio rises with the fraction split in four models and depends on which tokens are split; within a checkpoint, the displacements share a direction across batches. In a tabular model with one table per tokenization and a single sampled string, we prove that whenever two strings below an unsampled prefix differ in probability, only the zero full-gradient step agrees across tokenizations, however it is weighted. In an audit that decodes and re-encodes resampled rollouts, re-encoding touches up to 5.2% of rollouts but at most 0.08% of tokens, far below the split fractions we test. Training on fixed rollouts, the canonical arm finishes ahead in 14 of 18 pre-registered pairs; the interval for the mean accuracy difference includes zero over all pairs and excludes it only under the registered exclusion rule, which favours the canonical arm.
bullets: Re-encoding the same text changes token-level probabilities and therefore the RLVR training update despite leaving rewards unchanged.
On Qwen2.5-0.5B, splitting roughly 1 in 25 tokens moved the update 0.556 as far as using a different batch; the effect increased with split frequency and varied by token.
Update displacements tended to share a direction across batches within a checkpoint.
A tabular analysis proves that, when tokenization-dependent probabilities differ, only a zero full-gradient step is guaranteed to agree across tokenizations.

In an audit, re-encoding affected up to 5.2% of rollouts but no more than 0.08% of tokens; canonical training finished ahead in 14 of 18 pairs, though overall accuracy evidence was inconclusive under the stated analysis.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the impact of lossless re-tokenization on updates in Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
papers.title: How Far Does Lossless Re-tokenization Move an RLVR Update?
papers.tldr: Lossless re-tokenization can substantially alter RLVR updates, with effects that are directionally consistent but usually small in practical re-encoding audits.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.
bullets: Across models, draws, and paraphrases, prediction errors are strongly shared; averaging 20 draws adds no accuracy and can cause overconfidence if treated as independent.
A major error source is describing each feature’s effect in isolation rather than conditional on the other features.
Compared with the best classical prior, LLM centers clearly help on 1 of 4 benchmarks, marginally help on 2, and worsen mean RMSE on 1.
LLM-reported uncertainty is unreliable; estimating prior scale from data reduces the harm of an incorrect center four-fold versus a unit-variance prior.
An external test found mixed outcomes: the center helped on 6 of 18 problems and hurt on 4; evidence-weighted mixtures were safer than a hard trust gate.

papers.selection_reason: Audits the use of LLMs as priors for small-sample Bayesian regression, evaluating their accuracy and uncertainty reliability.
papers.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
papers.tldr: LLM-elicited Bayesian regression priors are highly correlated, often miscalibrated, and provide inconsistent benefits, so data-adaptive safeguards are needed.

papers.abstract: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.
authors: Claudia Carroll, Gabi Kirilloff, Dashiell Leigh
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies in existing benchmarks for direct discourse identification.
Expands evaluation beyond speech-focused discourse forms.
Uses a narrative theory-based framework for classification and evaluation.
Provides 12 text samples with task-relevant metadata.
Covers English-language fictional texts; broader generalization is not established.

papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning distillation requires choosing the language in which teacher reasoning is presented, yet existing recipes often entangle linguistic form with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. We construct content-controlled supervision by rendering the same verified English trajectories into English, translated target-language, and language-mixed shells, and fine-tune two pretrained students in three target languages, evaluating them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. Even with the underlying reasoning content held fixed, we find that shell choice can change downstream accuracy, with effects varying across students, languages, and difficulty levels. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently track these outcomes, and even when our tests find no clear accuracy difference between shells, their output-language behavior can still differ substantially. These results suggest that the supervision shell is a distinct design choice in multilingual reasoning distillation.
authors: Hoejoon Kwon, Jinhee Jang, Byeonggeuk Lim, YoungBin Kim
bullets: Uses identical verified English reasoning trajectories rendered as English, translated, or language-mixed shells.
Evaluates two pretrained students across three target languages and two mathematical-reasoning difficulty levels.
Shell choice changes accuracy, with effects varying by student, language, and difficulty.
Pre-training compatibility does not consistently predict which shell works best.
Even without clear accuracy differences, shells can produce substantially different output-language behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates multilingual reasoning distillation in LLMs, specifically isolating the impact of the 'language shell' on student model performance.

papers.abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
authors: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
bullets: Agent execution histories grow over time, driving shared GPU KV-cache demand and limiting throughput.
Tool-operation provenance identifies earlier outputs and turns superseded by later operations; 64% of final-history tokens are removal candidates.
Contexture separates the complete harness history from the model’s execution context and evicts context based on supersession, cache residency, and GPU pressure.
Across two models, harnesses, and benchmarks, it improves SLO-constrained throughput by 20–73% versus the strongest baseline and reduces GPU energy per session by up to 11%.
Live-agent accuracy improves by 1.4 percentage points on average versus unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points.

papers.selection_reason: A runtime context eviction framework for high-throughput LLM agent serving that uses tool-execution information to manage KV cache and improve memory efficiency.
papers.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
papers.tldr: Contexture improves high-throughput LLM-agent serving by evicting superseded conversation context at runtime while coordinating with shared KV-cache state.

papers.abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
authors: Anika Misra, Chimaobi Okite, Rada Mihalcea
bullets: Existing evaluations may overestimate child-safety alignment by focusing on prompts that name predefined harm categories.

Behavioral and mechanistic analyses suggest lexical and semantic prompt associations partly drive safety reasoning.

papers.abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.
bullets: Studies how unsupported claims evolve as they pass between agents.
Compares homogeneous pipelines using one model with heterogeneous pipelines using different models.
Attaches each claim’s support status, source, evidence, and transmission history; no new evidence is added during transmission.
Evaluates meaning changes, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation.
Tests whether provenance tracking reduces unsupported changes relative to a baseline.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.
authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Ferdinando D'Elia, Greta Tuckute, Evelina Fedorenko, Meenakshi Khosla
bullets: Tests 12 LLMs spanning six model families against randomly rotated representations with identical geometry.
Native axes align more reliably with other models, human language-related brain responses, and interpretable linguistic features.
The findings challenge the assumption that meaning exists only in directions rather than individual coordinates.
Native-coordinate alignment remains below the best achievable level, indicating incomplete canonicality.
A complete theory must explain both shared representation geometry and recurring unit response patterns.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Axis-by-axis alignment under rotation of the coordinates. A. Schematic of the unit matching procedure. Each coordinate axis of an LLM hidden representation X (one axis per unit) generates a response profile across the input stimuli. Each unit of a target representation Y (a unit of another LLM, a voxel in the brain, or an interpretable linguistic feature) is matched to its most correlated axis in X on a training split; the alignment score is the correlation r between matched pairs on held-out stimuli, averaged over target units in Y . B. The stimuli in X are represented as a point cloud in three coordinate frames (with all pairwise distances fully preserved). Left: a random orthogonal rotation (α = 1) moves away from the native axes but keeps the geometry intact. Middle: the native basis (α = 0), where each axis corresponds to one model unit. Right: the optimal rotation Q∗, learned by gradient descent on SO(n) to maximize the pairwise alignment with the target. If the native axes were arbitrary, the matching in A would give identical alignment scores in the left and middle panel; if they were fully canonical, it would give identical scores in the middle and right panels.

Figure 2. Three settings for probing the LLM representation basis. In each setting an LLM’s hidden representation (X) is aligned to a target representation (Y ) via axis-by-axis matching. For each basis of X (native or rotated), we match each target dimension to the single axis of X with which it has the highest absolute correlation on training stimuli and evaluate that match on held-out stimuli. Top: Model-to-model, where Y is the hidden representation of another LLM elicited by the same set of 627 naturalistic sentences (the 384 sentences of Pereira Experiment 2 combined with the 243 sentences of Pereira Experiment 3). Middle: Model-to-brain, where Y is human fMRI responses recorded in the language network while participants read the same 627 sentences across two experiments. Bottom: Model-to-feature, where Y is an interpretable linguistic feature, either a binary well-formedness label from a minimal-pair task (Y ∈ {0, 1}; morphology, syntax, hypernymy) or a multi-dimensional rating vector (Y ∈ Rk; perceptual and affective ratings).

Figure 4. Model-to-feature alignment as a function of rotation. Pairwise alignment of each LLM against five interpretable feature targets that span morphology (Wug), syntax (BLiMP, averaged across 12 sub-tasks) and lexical semantics (hypernymy minimal pairs; perceptual sensorimotor norms; affective valence/arousal/dominance norms). Each curve is the mean over layers; the same decline with α appears in all panels.

Figure 5. Random, native and optimal alignment. From left to right: model-to-model alignment (with Pythia-160M as the reference); model-to-brain alignment (Pereira Experiments 2 and 3); and model-to-feature alignment (grouped by morphology, syntax, and lexical semantics). Each box shows the distribution across models of the alignment under a full random rotation (α = 1, gray), the native basis (α = 0, light blue), and the optimal axis alignment (Q∗, dark blue); thin lines connect the three values of one model. Across all alignment targets, the pattern is random < native ≪ optimal.

Figure 3. Model-to-model and model-to-brain alignment as a function of rotation. A. Pairwise alignment between Pythia-160M and every other model in the set, as a function of the rotation fraction α. The light-blue dashed line is the comparison with an identical model trained with a different seed. B, C. Pairwise alignment of each LLM with human fMRI responses in the language network, separately for Experiment 2 (B) and Experiment 3 (C) of Pereira et al. (2018). Each curve is the mean over layers (and participants); alignment decreases with α in most models and in every panel on average.

Figure 6. Readout sparsity and training dynamics. A. Kurtosis of the ridge readout weights across hidden units in the native basis, for the discrete features (left; Wug, BLiMP and hypernymy labels) and the continuous features (right; perceptual and affective norms). For each model, the line shows the distribution over layers of the native kurtosis (median over tasks); the small dots are the individual layers (darker = deeper; gray if within the null of that layer), and the vertical square is the median over tasks and layers. The gray band is the 95% interval of this median under a full random rotation of the basis (α = 1, 10 rotation samples) using the widest interval across models. B. Basis privilege across training. The difference between native and random alignment across 29 log-spaced Pythia training checkpoints, for five model sizes. The thick line indicates the mean across sizes; the shaded band around it, the SEM across sizes. The basis privilege is positive but small at random initialization and increases with training.
Table 1. The 12 BLiMP sub-tasks used in the model-to-feature alignment analyses, one per broad linguistic-phenomenon class.

For each target and depth (normalized relative to the total number of layers), ∆r is the mean difference between native and random across models at the layer closest to the depth, and n+ the number of models (out of 12) with a positive gap. Asterisks indicate statistical significance (∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the internal representations of LLMs, finding that coordinate axes are partially canonical rather than arbitrary, providing insights into LLM geometry and interpretability.
papers.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
papers.tldr: LLM representation axes are neither arbitrary nor fully standardized: native coordinates show meaningful cross-model, brain, and linguistic alignment, but remain only partially canonical.

papers.abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).
authors: Yang Liu, Shengbo Tong, Xiyuan Chen, Shiwei Hou, Sen Yuan, Hao Wang, Yanfeng Li, Hongwen Li, Yiming Zhu, Zhuolun He, Wenjian Yu
bullets: Addresses poorly documented proprietary APIs, silent failures, and hard-to-maintain hand-crafted scripting knowledge.
Enhances the ZhuLong harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, sandboxed execution, and static checking.
Stores distilled experience in a three-tier memory with ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval.
Achieves 92.4% pass@1 on the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark without self-evolution, outperforming ZhuLong across five LLM backbones.
On an instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution reaches 80.0% pass@1 versus 77.5% for human-crafted experience.

papers.abstract: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with workload configurations and explicitly defined timing targets. It also includes 64 text-generation configurations measured under standardized conditions, each in three separate program launches. We compare three LLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Claude Opus 5.5) with regression baselines and evaluate analytical estimates on a supported forward-pass subset. On 16 held-out generation configurations, the open-weight LLMs underestimate latency by 90-99% on average without examples. Claude's zero-shot mean absolute error is 4.5 times that of a Random Forest fit on 32 configurations. Five labeled examples substantially reduce Claude's generation error, but their benefit varies across timing targets. We will open-source our data and evaluation pipeline upon acceptance.
authors: Ashish Molakalapalli, Kangda Wei, Haonan Duan, Alex Carter, Ruihong Huang
bullets: Targets runtime prediction for shared-GPU scheduling, hardware selection, and compute budgeting.
Provides 801 training records, 1,884 inference records, and 64 standardized text-generation configurations with repeated launches.
Compares three LLMs with regression baselines and analytical estimates on a forward-pass subset.
On 16 held-out generation configurations, open-weight LLMs underestimated latency by 90–99% on average without examples.
Five labeled examples substantially improved Claude’s generation predictions, with benefits varying by timing target.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PreRun, a benchmark for predicting LLM runtime on GPU clusters, directly relevant to LLM behavior and resource estimation.
papers.title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction
papers.tldr: PreRun benchmarks how well LLMs can predict deep-learning training and inference runtimes before execution, finding that zero-shot estimates are often highly inaccurate but improve with labeled examples.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read and rewrite another network's weights without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what it edits. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the few-shot minus zero-shot residual is measured at the final prompt token, the ICL task vector, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and of fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.
bullets: The study examines six tasks, four frontier editors, and three families of weaker language models.
Editors convert few-shot-minus-zero-shot behavior into a task vector and write it into model weights.
The sparsest updates target near-silent MLP units associated with prompt format.
Performance usually matches in-context learning and fine-tuning, including LoRA, while leaving perplexity largely unchanged.
Performance worsens with wording changes; one editor underperforms fine-tuning, and comparable results on unseen items are limited mainly to the strongest editor.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Test accuracy against the number of in-context examples, for the unedited model and the updated models (mean over tasks and completed Qwen2.5-0.5B runs; three draws per k).

papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets
authors: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair
bullets: Targets parameter-efficient continued-fraction channel mixing for language models.
Introduces a non-expanding gated component compatible with MLPs, GLUs, and MoE experts.
Reformulates division using logarithms and exponentials to simplify and stabilize training.
Across GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2, and Llama-MoE variants, performance is similar or better than prior continued-fraction designs with higher throughput.
Eliminates the need for prior incremental-training procedures for stable deeper CoFrGeNets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Above we see our continued fraction inspired architecture that can replace feedforward layers in dense as well as MoE architectures. Our architecture performs a non-expansive gating of the input that then passes through an (ensemble of) continued fraction ladders. The fact that we do not expand the hidden representation and each layer of our ladders requires only a linear number of parameters we obtain significant parameter savings over typical (gated and vanilla) feedforward layers leading to dense models that are ≈ 2 3 the size and MoEs that are ≈ 1 2 the size. In our implementations we create a different class for CoFrGeNet that has the same api as the FFN class, that is, same parameters are passed and the same size output tensor (equal to embedding size) is returned. The depth and width parameters for CoFrGeNet could be additionally passed or just set in the CoFrGeNet class itself. Hence, no changes are made to the residual stream or other aspects of the original architecture. The input x1, ..., xp in the figure is thus simply the output of the attention or SSM layer where the residual stream is added and the representation normalized in the particular block. In other words, nothing else in the model architectures changes and the input and output tensors are both size embedding dimension.

Figure 3: CoFrNet architecture from [14] to simulate FFNs. Two ensembles are used each consisting of specified number of p-variate ladders. Element wise multiplication is done between the representations coming out of the linear layer of each ensemble for higher expressivity.

papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.
authors: Kaustubh Ponkshe, Gyung Hyun Je, Stefan Taga, Colin Raffel, Martin Jaggi
bullets: Motivation: Search is often added only after static-text pretraining, potentially limiting foundational search ability.
Method: Augment ordinary text corpora with web-search queries and responses retrieved from a local index, then train models on the resulting data.
Result: QueryLM models improve knowledge-intensive task performance and follow retrieved evidence more effectively across tested model scales and corpora.
The gains persist after supervised fine-tuning, suggesting the tested post-training methods do not fully recover capabilities learned through search-pretraining.
A 1.4B QueryLM consistently matches or outperforms a FLOP-matched 3.3B conventional baseline on the reported knowledge-intensive tasks.

papers.abstract: We show that reinforcement learning (RL) in reasoning tasks can succeed even when the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is severely corrupted. In a mathematical reasoning dataset (GSM8K), we systematically corrupt training trajectories across 361 configurations by injecting realistic error types, varying error locations, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios up to 100%. While aggregated SFT-only performance steadily deteriorates under corruption (dropping from 43.61% to 13.80%), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training consistently restores model accuracy back to gold-baseline levels (approximately 60%). Crucially, initializing RL with as few as N = 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line "form-only" traces boosts post-RL performance to 69.30%, outperforming standard gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and GRPO without SFT (35.00%). Further, we show that SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r approximately 0), demonstrating a fundamental asymmetry in post-training: SFT primarily establishes structural layout (form), while RL independently discovers functional reasoning (function).
authors: Anika Misra, Shreyas Vinod, Huteng Dai
bullets: Evaluated 361 corruption settings on GSM8K, including errors in locations, trace–answer consistency, and corruption rates up to 100%.
SFT-only accuracy fell from 43.61% to 13.80% as corruption increased.
GRPO generally restored performance to roughly gold-baseline levels (~60%) despite corrupted initialization.
Initializing with just 8 incorrect three-line form-only traces reached 69.30%, versus 60.71% with gold SFT and 35.00% without SFT.
SFT accuracy was nearly uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r≈0), indicating distinct roles for structural form and functional reasoning.

Figure 3: Example of our six corruption types injected into a GSM8K reasoning trace. For each corruption type, we use regex to modify a value and deterministically propagate the error through, resulting in an incorrect final answer.

Figure 5: GRPO displays robustness to corrupted SFT initialization. The absolute accuracy differences between the lowest-performing corrupted configuration and its gold-initialized counterpart are larger in SFTonly (orange) than in SFT+GRPO (purple).
Figure 6: Gold GSM8K SFT + GRPO outperforms the GRPO-only baseline, while minimal form-only initializations achieve the highest overall accuracy.

papers.abstract: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.
authors: Renjia Deng, Yuxi Liu, Yutong He, Xue Wang, Kun Yuan
bullets: Existing gated linear attention uses state-independent gates, which ignore the information currently stored in recurrent memory.
SDG computes element-wise gates from the memory change over each chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary.
The approach preserves parallel within-chunk computation and is implemented with fused kernels for several linear-attention architectures.
Theory connects SDG to improved signal reconstruction and interprets fixed-gate boundary decay as an element-wise ridge proximal step.
Experiments on 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens report improvements across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, and long-context understanding.

papers.abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model, using 146 training runs across 200 unique languages and more than 10,000 evaluations. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
bullets: Compares eight LoRA methods on a frozen base model across 146 training runs, 200 languages, and over 10,000 evaluations.
Shows that reduced-scale searches can find viable configurations but do not reliably predict full-scale rankings.
LoRA consistently improves fit on translation data, with the strongest benefits for low-resource languages.
Reading comprehension degrades consistently after adaptation.
Concludes that LoRA methods are best used as targeted tools for multilingual adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic empirical study of MoE-LoRA methods for multilingual adaptation of LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture and adaptation methods.
papers.title: MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study
papers.tldr: A large empirical study finds that LoRA adapters help multilingual language-model fit—especially for low-resource languages—but consistently hurt reading comprehension and are not reliable general-purpose upgrades.

papers.abstract: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.
bullets: Evaluates whether NLAs can expose latent knowledge, detect misleading hints, and catch silent fabrications.
Extends NLAs to use activation information from multiple layers and positions.
Improves NLA handling of long transcripts and reduces false claims.
Reports improvements on new auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations from prior work.
Finds that auditing performance improves early in training but may decline with extended training.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and improves natural language autoencoders for interpreting LLM activations, contributing to LLM research and interpretability.
papers.title: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
papers.tldr: The paper evaluates natural language autoencoders for auditing LLM activations and introduces extensions that improve their auditing ability while revealing that extended training can degrade some capabilities.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
bullets: Addresses low-diversity reasoning and declining or saturated pass@k performance after SFT and RLVR.
Routes well-solved training problems into an off-mode track for generating distinct solution approaches.
Uses an LLM judge to verify logical validity and strategy distinctness before self-distillation.
On Qwen3.5-2b trained with 1,000 MATH level-5 problems, it raises peak pass@16 by 4.7% and roughly doubles correct embedding cosine distance.
The reported evaluation focuses on a difficult evaluation set and this training configuration.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ROAM-GRPO training pipeline. Well-solved prompts (≥ k of G completions correct) are routed off the GRPO objective onto an off-mode track that self-distills valid, distinct alternative solutions measured by τ, ϕ (abstract functions, instantiated as an LLM judge here in practice).

Figure 4: Method-level diversity at step 7000 using an LLM judge (Claude Opus 5.5). Bottom: fraction of pairs (within the same method bin) judged to be meaningful variants rather than surface level rewrites, among correct completions (c) and all completions (d). Error bars show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over problems, and ∆ shows ROAM − GRPO difference along with the 95% CI. All judged problems require that both arms produce at least one correct completion.

Delayed ROAM also mostly employs the common approach, but also adopts an alternative approach (using the hockey-stick identity) twice (succeeds once, fails once). On one occasion it attempts to solve by recursive summation.

papers.selection_reason: Augments GRPO post-training to enforce reasoning diversity in LLMs, directly relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
papers.tldr: ROAM-GRPO augments GRPO with verified, self-distilled alternative reasoning strategies to reduce policy collapse and improve reasoning diversity.

papers.abstract: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.
bullets: The system extracts each transition from a frozen model and composes updates sequentially with an external integer register.
It targets permutation-tracking tasks that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers are not expected to solve for arbitrary input lengths under the stated complexity conjecture.
A 0.8B model correctly read all events in 299/299 long windows, with a follow-up achieving 472/473; one reported test narrowly missed its 0.99 confidence target.
On room-swap documents, extraction plus the register solved all tested documents for every model, while reasoning alone succeeded less consistently; concurrent extraction also reduced time and cost.
On free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader reached 68.8% accuracy versus 61.0% for a frequency baseline; fixed-format documents were also solved by regex plus execution.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Window accuracy on 𝑆5 streams by length and inference method. Orange: Qwen3.8-27B with reasoning, fraction of windows exact with two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals (100 windows at 2, 4 and 8 events; 50 at 16 and 32; 25 at 64; 8 at 128; 4 at 256). Lengths of 8 and more were added after the first results (shaded). Hollow markers: no visible reasoning. Blue: the frozen 0.8B model with the register, 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events.

Inside the frozen model a selector scores possible transitions from intermediate-layer features aligned to each event boundary, all obtained in one prefill pass.
