papers.selection_reason: Adaptive observation mechanism for post-training self-improvement of LLM capabilities; relevant to language foundation model training and reasoning.
papers.title: Sage-Evolve-Preview:Adaptive Observation for Post-Training Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: Adaptive observation helps post-training self-improvement escape plateaus by refining diagnostic feedback while preserving a fixed anchor objective.

papers.abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.
authors: Alper Kalle, Theo Rudkiewicz, Mohamed-Oumar Ouerfelli, Mohamed Tamaazousti
bullets: Targets post-training low-rank compression that preserves input-output behavior, not just layer weights.
Linearizes the network and uses a Kronecker-factored approximation to reduce compression to a closed-form weighted SVD.
Estimates the otherwise intractable output-side factor unbiasedly with random probes, requiring K backward passes per sequence.
On WikiText-2 calibration, it reports the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity across matched uniform-rank settings and at ratio 0.7 with LEMS allocation.
KL-SVD usually improves calibration perplexity and downstream accuracy but increases cross-corpus perplexity; Complete-SVD improves IFEval accuracy over prior output-aware methods.
papers.selection_reason: Output-aware low-rank SVD compression for LLMs; reduces model memory while preserving logit behavior.
papers.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
papers.tldr: Complete-SVD compresses LLMs by minimizing equal-weighted changes to the model’s output logits, achieving strong perplexity and instruction-following performance in the reported settings.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.
authors: Emre U\u{g}ur, Jiawen Qi, Qinyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the prefill bottleneck of long-context attention, where accurately scoring skippable blocks can be costly.
Uses training-free, content-adaptive delta scoring with fewer anchors in redundant regions and more in heterogeneous ones.
Accelerates scoring through parallel, tile-aligned local scans, then computes selected tiles with the original vectors.
Maintains average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, including RULER up to 128K tokens.
Reports 38% lower scoring-pipeline latency than XAttention at 128K tokens and 3.3× prefill speedup over a FlashAttention-2 PyTorch baseline at 512K tokens on four H100 GPUs.

papers.abstract: When a constraint puzzle has several correct answers, language models tend to give the same one.We study four open-weight models from three families on symbolic puzzles and multi-solution ZebraLogic variants with exactly known solution sets.Repeated samples concentrate on one default solution far beyond uniform sampling, and different models often share it.Yet models usually produce even rarely sampled solutions when added clues uniquely identify them.On held-out symbolic puzzles, we compare visiting entities in name order with visiting those with the fewest initial candidates first. Both searches try values in the stated order. Where their pre-specified predictions differ, the latter matches a larger share of responses in all four models, by 26 to 40 percentage points.Reversing the stated value order or specifying a search order shifts responses towards the solution that the new order favours, on both testbeds. Randomising the presentation or supplying a random search order raises breadth (the effective share of solutions in use) by 26 to 42 percentage points on the symbolic task and 11 to 26 on ZebraLogic. The largest observed validity losses are 3 and 4 percentage points, respectively. Randomised presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in each of the three main models.
bullets: Across four open-weight models, repeated samples overproduce one solution rather than sampling uniformly, often the same solution across models.
Models can usually produce rare solutions when additional clues make them uniquely identifiable.
Searches that select entities with the fewest candidates better predict model responses than name-order searches, by 26–40 percentage points where predictions differ.
Reversing value order or specifying random presentation/search orders shifts responses and broadens solution coverage, with limited validity losses of up to 3–4 percentage points.
Randomized presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in the three main models tested.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of how search order shapes LLM default solutions on constraint puzzles; relevant to LLM reasoning behavior.
papers.title: Many Solutions, One Answer: Search Order Shapes the Default Solutions of Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models’ default answers to multi-solution puzzles are strongly shaped by the order in which search options are presented or explored.

papers.abstract: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.
authors: Yue Che, Jingze Wang, Chen Guoyi, Yujie Wu, Xuming Ran, Mingkun Xu
bullets: Addresses growing storage costs and declining retrieval quality as lifelong edits accumulate.
Retrieves relevant edits in an external semantic space while injecting knowledge into the LLM’s internal representation space.
Uses sparse, storage-efficient updates while leaving base model parameters untouched.
Reduces per-entry storage to about 10.2% of the original and remains resilient through up to 16K edits.
Improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods on a challenging benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BiSpace. Knowledge retrieval is decoupled from injection by constructing edit keys and queries in an external semantic space. Sparse codebook values reduce storage costs and are reconstructed on the fly for updates in the internal representation space.

Figure 3: Overall Performance over 10K sequential edits on ZsRE, WikiBigEdit, and CounterFact using LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. BiSpace maintains consistently higher performance as edits accumulate, with larger advantages on the more challenging WikiBigEdit and CounterFact benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Lifelong model editing with decoupled retrieval and compact memory, relevant to LLM memory and continual updating.
papers.title: Decoupled Knowledge Retrieval and Compact Memory Enable Reliable Lifelong Model Editing
papers.tldr: BiSpace enables scalable lifelong LLM editing by separating edit retrieval from knowledge injection and using compact memory updates.

papers.abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.
authors: Yifan Lu, Gaoyang Guo, Wen Chen, Ziyun Zou, Jian Wu, Han Zhu, Imran Razzak
bullets: Addresses outdated or misapplied preferences caused by storing interaction content without tracking currentness or scope.
Models the user as a latent preference state updated and revealed by every interaction, including the current request.
Stores relevant beliefs with supporting evidence, scope, and status rather than raw history alone.
Uses a trained writer to produce belief records for a frozen agent.
Achieves the best results among evaluated memory systems across two agent families and two benchmarks; request conditioning improves answering, while auxiliary tasks improve tool use.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HabitusMem. The writer takes the retained raw interactions and the current user query as input and infers belief records, each with its evidence, scope, and status. It then projects only the beliefs that bear on the user query to the agent, which answers or acts on the user query. Here, the bland diet and the late-shift hospital address shape the dinner order, whereas the partner-specific vegetarian preference and the one-off oat-milk instruction are kept but not projected. A single writer learns these steps from four tasks: direct writing, state update, request projection, and action projection.

Figure 1: Content-based memory method versus belief memory on a personalized order. The user has repeatedly rejected Penfolds wine and now asks for a bottle of wine without naming a brand. Content-based memory methods pass on fragments such as past purchases and a negative review, and agents using them order the wrong wine or none at all. HabitusMem infers that the user prefers mid-priced layered reds and rejects Penfolds, records the evidence, scope, and status of each belief, and leads the agent to the same order as the ground-truth profile.

papers.selection_reason: Belief-based memory over evolving user preferences for LLM agents, directly relevant to LLM memory and personalization.
papers.title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: HabitusMem represents user memory as revisable, evidence-backed beliefs about evolving preferences, improving personalized LLM agent decisions and tool use.

papers.abstract: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.
bullets: Evaluates an anchor answer against one or two greedy checks from alternate prompts or model families using a pure five-outcome reconciliation function.
Pooling samples from another model family improves semantic-entropy error detection, while same-model temperature checks perform worst.
The three-call contract performs comparably to pooled semantic entropy as a complete pipeline and detects anchor errors better at 3–5 samples.
A strict Agree gate automates 70% of items but still acts on 16% of errors.
The hosted API did not make generation itself reproducible; only the reconciliation decision is replayable from its record.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes auditable cross-prompt and cross-model reconciliation for LLM decisions, relevant to LLM reasoning and reliability.
papers.title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
papers.tldr: A deterministic reconciliation contract makes LLM decisions auditable by acting only when independently generated checks agree with a committed anchor, though it still acts on some errors.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
authors: Filippo Galgani, Ziwei Ji, Omri Homburger, Ganesh Jawahar, Michelle Ramanovich, Ivan Korotkov, Luciano Martins, Utku Evci, Edouard Yvinec, Pooja Consul, Vivek Kumar, Tal Schuster
bullets: Addresses the need for lightweight, accurate draft generation in speculative decoding.
Uses a shared drafting head with target activation injection, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention, and clustered vocabulary projection.
Evaluated with the Gemma 4 family, achieving reported speedups of up to 3.1× on server-side setups and 2.2× on a smartphone GPU.
Introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes that require up to 1.83× fewer target-model forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
Scope: results are reported for Gemma 4 models and the specified hardware environments.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Architecture of the optimized Multi-Token Prediction (G-MTP) module. The input to the drafter is constructed by concatenating the token embedding (𝑒(𝑥)) with the backbone hidden state (ℎ(𝐿)), both of dimension 𝑑target, and reducing to the drafter dimension 𝑑draft. The draft tokens are then propagated through the MTP layers, utilizing cross-attention against the backbone’s frozen KV Cache to bypass prefill computations before recursively triggering the next forward step. For subsequent drafting steps, the drafter’s output state is up-projected (𝑊up), concatenated with the embedding of the sampled draft token, and down-projected (𝑊down) to form the next input (Equation 3).

Figure 2 | The autoregressive G-MTP drafter (blue blocks) is initialized with activations from the main model (gray blocks) and cross-attends to its KV cache. Across successive drafting steps, the positional encoding (𝑝1) remains constant, as the drafter repeatedly queries a static, pre-computed KV snapshot.

Figure 3 | Empirical scaling of theoretical Block Efficiency (BE) and speculative wall-clock throughput across varying lookahead horizons (𝛾). While longer draft sequences monotonically increase token acceptance, throughput degrades for some models (e.g., 26B MoE) as drafting and verification costs exceed generation gains.

Table 4 | Speculative Decoding Domain Adaptation Performance (Gemma 4 E4B). Fine-tuning the model without updating the MTP (row 2) can lead to regression in Block Efficiency (𝛽). Joint finetuning (row 3) matches or exceeds the 𝛽 of the no SFT reference (row 1), and two-stage distillation (row 4) recovers about 96% of it.
Table 2 | Comparison of speedup for three different Gemma 4 31B drafters (2×H100, utilizing FlashAttention 4 kernels, batch size 1) on SPEED-Bench quality dataset.
Table 6 | Batch size scaling performance: Gemma 4 26B MoE (𝛾 = 4, measured on 2×H100)

Table 7 | On-device decoding throughput of Gemma 4 E2B and E4B with LiteRT-LM on the GPU of a Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (𝛾 = 3, greedy decoding, full vocabulary projection). Acceptance rate and throughput values are medians over the 76 prompts; the acceptance rate is the draft acceptance rate reported by the runtime. Speedups are ratios of median throughput with and without G-MTP, over all prompts and per task type.
Table 5 | Throughput across lookahead horizons 𝛾 (Figure 3 extends to 𝛾 = 15).

papers.selection_reason: Optimized multi-token prediction drafting accelerates LLM inference and reduces KV-cache memory overhead.
papers.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
papers.tldr: G-MTP is an optimized multi-token drafter that accelerates speculative LLM decoding across server and mobile hardware while remaining efficient and adaptable under domain shift.

papers.abstract: Organizations monitor their workers' activity for insider threats, in which workers misuse their legitimate access, by copying confidential files before leaving. Detectors score how unusual each day of activity is, flagging the most unusual for an analyst to review. Prominent current approaches use opaque neural networks, so explanations of a flag point to internal features: patterns of neuron activity most active on days of misuse. We audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on CERT's simulated workplace logs. To test an explanation, we see what happens to the detector's score when we remove its features inside the model. We compare this to a control: a change that is as similar as possible to the removal, but without actually removing the features. Because defining "similar" requires choosing a metric, our central contribution is the tipping radius: a first-order prediction of how far that metric must move before the difference between removal and control disappears, a measure of how fragile the result is to that choice. In 33 of 34 runs of seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard choices of metric. Moving that far removes at least 58% of the difference or reverses it, while random moves of the same size leave it largely intact. The result replicates in thirteen of fourteen pre-declared primary runs on openly released models, though on our trained detectors the difference is often too small to measure. We also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is, not what they did, and that the features named depend on whom they are compared against. Audits should therefore fix the control's metric in advance, report its tipping radius, and disclose that comparison.
bullets: The study audits explanations that identify internal neuron features behind anomalous workplace-activity flags.
It introduces the tipping radius, estimating how much a control metric must change before the explanation’s apparent effect disappears.
Across 33 of 34 runs involving seven language models, small metric changes—at most 18% of the distance between two standard metrics—removed or reversed much of the explanation effect.
The findings replicated in 13 of 14 pre-declared runs on open models, while effects were often too small to measure in the authors’ trained detectors.
Flag scores partly reflect worker identity, and identified features vary with the comparison group; audits should predefine and disclose the control metric and tipping radius.

papers.abstract: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps. If changing routing also changes a model's step-level verification judgment, it is tempting to conclude that the judgment follows what routing encodes. We test this inference with RouteVerify, a controlled intervention study that replaces selected internal activations from one solution trace with activations from another, while keeping the evaluated input unchanged. Across nine MoE checkpoints, we compare three intervention interfaces: router logits, MoE outputs, and post-MoE residual states. We vary the layers and token positions at which activations are replaced. We measure changes in a verification margin that quantifies the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. We also evaluate the same input with activations from correct versus erroneous steps to test whether the resulting judgment depends on the source step's correctness. We report four linked results. First, probes on router logits separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88). Second, replacing router logits across all routed layers changes the judgment in all nine checkpoints, and by more than a norm-matched random replacement. Third, this change rarely depends on whether the source step is correct. At one layer, routing from erroneous steps and from correct steps produces indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints. Under all-layer routing, their difference is resolved and positive in only one. Fourth, the same difference is positive for local residual replacements in eight of nine checkpoints, so the measure does detect such dependence where it exists. Correctness is therefore readable from routing, and routing replacements move the judgment, but the movement rarely follows correctness.
authors: Yucheng Du, Ryan A. Rossi, Xiyang Hu
bullets: Across nine MoE checkpoints, router-logit probes distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps in eight models.
Replacing router logits changes verification margins in all nine checkpoints, more than norm-matched random replacements.
The judgment change usually does not depend on whether replacement activations came from correct or erroneous steps.
Local residual interventions reveal correctness dependence in eight of nine checkpoints, showing the measure can detect it when present.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.
authors: Hao Wu, Sipeng Chen, Jingwen Fu, Yuwang Wang
bullets: Diffusion language models can decode multiple tokens in parallel, but quality often drops when denoising steps are reduced.
CaRR is a training-free framework for improving outputs from a fixed editable checkpoint within the existing edit schedule.
Token Commitment Remasking refills selected replacements using updated context, while Submission Commitment Recovery rescues supported candidates that fail output requirements.
Experiments in code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent accuracy gains across four inference budgets, especially under tight budgets.
At one-eighth of the full budget, CaRR raises six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 percentage points, including 11.37 on MBPP and 10.05 on MBPP+.

papers.abstract: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.
bullets: Targets the cost and risk of revising every answer, which can damage already-correct facts.
Routes uncertain answers to an editor that performs bounded exact-text replacements with valid source coordinates and legal edit operations.
On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, it improves over a verified revision chain by 0.82 F1 and 1.24 Judge points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls.
Direct editing improves native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, with gains of 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 F1 points, respectively.
Results support selective editing as an efficient quality–cost tradeoff, but show a completeness gap on an external PerLTQA subset and unresolved source-obligation effects.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

bullets: Addresses the limitation of memories that record what happened but not how experiences shape user behavior.
Maintains an Episodic Graph linking interactions temporally, causally, and semantically, plus an Insight Graph of LLM-extracted behavioral signals.
Retrieves behavioral knowledge directly from insight nodes grounded in supporting events, avoiding repeated episodic traversal.
Projects event-as-edge knowledge into relational embeddings to transfer insights across users and infer missing knowledge for cold-start users.
Reports gains on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, and LongLaMP, including cross-user improvements at 5% graph sparsity.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Zixiong Guo, Shuo Shao, Yu He, Wenli Wang, Meihui Chen, Di Wang, Yuke Hu
bullets: Addresses privacy risks in remote LLM inference, where sensitive user queries are exposed to the service provider.
Hides the real query among dummy queries and randomly shuffles the set before server-side inference.
Uses shared-prefix transformer KV-cache reuse to reduce the efficiency cost of processing augmented queries.
Evaluated on classification, generation, and QIA, EIA, and GPT-based privacy attacks.
Reports strong inference-time privacy, near-plaintext utility, and improved inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.
bullets: Prediction accuracy may not reflect the cost of decisions made from LLM outputs.
DFRL uses negative downstream decision regret as the reinforcement-learning reward and does not require convex or differentiable optimization problems.
Heuristic warm-starting and reward correction reduce the need for expensive exact reward evaluations.

Experiments on synthetic problems, knapsack, and H&M inventory planning show improvements over prediction-loss baselines; the best inventory configuration reduces regret by 31.4% versus SFT and 12.4% versus the strongest conventional forecasting baseline.
The method is evaluated within the reported synthetic, knapsack, and inventory-planning settings; broader generalization is not established by the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1 DFRL pipeline with RLOO as an example. (1) Context. The input x provides task-relevant information, including text and structured data. (2) Predict parameters. The LLM independently samples K parameter predictions ĉ1, . . . , ĉK ∼ πθ(· | x). (3) Solve downstream optimization problems. Each prediction ĉk is passed to the optimizer, which returns a decision w⋆(ĉk) that is optimal under the predicted parameters. (4) Evaluate regret. Each decision is evaluated under the observed parameters c and compared with the optimal decision under c, yielding reward rk = −ℓ(ĉk, c). (5) Update the LLM policy. RLOO subtracts the average reward of the other K − 1 predictions from rk to obtain advantage Ak. These advantages weight the policy gradients used to update θ, without differentiating through the downstream optimizer. The hindsight cost F (w⋆(c), c) is shared across predictions and cancels from the advantages, so solving under c is unnecessary for the RLOO update.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DriftGuard-7F0B.
authors: Licheng Pan, Yuzhou Chen, Zhixuan Chu, Yichen Sun, Han Zheng, Zhiyu Wang, Hao Wang, Yan Wang, Bingyu Zhu, Haiwen Hong, Longtao Huang, Kui Ren
bullets: Persistent agent memory can drift and redirect tool use or task outcomes when memories are misleading or adversarial.
Content signals such as perplexity and retrieval relevance do not reliably identify causally influential memories.
Offline, paired counterfactual replays compare original and single-memory-neutralized trajectories to build component-wise memory drift scores.
An online risk model estimates these scores from pre-action information and flags memories using their maximum component risk.
Experiments show accurate identification of drift-inducing memories and efficient online defense, without serving-time counterfactual rollouts.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

Covers nine RAG development tasks with no starter code or prescribed strategies and a six-hour, single-GPU budget.
Evaluates nine agent configurations, including both final system effectiveness and development trajectories.
GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest reported average score of 56.1, compared with 44.4 for the composite Human-SOTA baseline.
Starting from human-designed systems on seven tasks, the same agent improves scores by 16.6 points on average.

papers.abstract: A prompt for in-context learning (ICL) can describe a task in addition to, or instead of, demonstrating it through examples. Yet how task descriptions work remains poorly understood theoretically. Through the Bayesian view of ICL, we model descriptions as informative priors characterized by their specificity and reliability. We adapt the effective sample size (ESS) from Bayesian statistics, quantifying a description's predictive value as an equivalent number of demonstrations. For in-context linear regression, we show that a reliable description's ESS grows with its specificity and with the task's dimension. A description that may be irrelevant, however, gains little from its specificity unless demonstrations are given. In practice, do in-context learners use descriptions as a Bayes-optimal predictor would? Our experiments show that meta-trained Transformers come close to the Bayes-optimal ESS when tested on their training distribution. Pretrained language models, however, make too little use of highly specific descriptions when answering without reasoning; most of them closely match the Bayes-optimal predictor only when reasoning is enabled. These results extend the Bayesian analysis of ICL from demonstrations to descriptions.
authors: Bruce Nguyen, Bei Jiang, Linglong Kong
bullets: Models descriptions as informative Bayesian priors and measure their predictive value using effective sample size (ESS), interpreted as an equivalent number of demonstrations.
For in-context linear regression, reliable descriptions become more valuable with greater specificity and higher task dimension.
Potentially irrelevant descriptions benefit little from added specificity unless demonstrations provide supporting context.
Meta-trained Transformers nearly achieve Bayes-optimal ESS on their training distribution, while pretrained language models often underuse highly specific descriptions without reasoning.
The analysis extends Bayesian theory of in-context learning from example demonstrations to task descriptions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes in-context learning and task descriptions in LLMs through a Bayesian effective sample size framework.
papers.title: Is a Description Worth a Thousand Demonstrations? Specificity and Reliability of Task Descriptions in In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Task descriptions can substitute for demonstrations in in-context learning, but their value depends on specificity, reliability, and whether the model reasons over them.

papers.abstract: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.
bullets: Defines composability through an interference functional combining cross-task curvature overlap with signed task-vector alignment.
In the quadratic setting, the functional exactly equals merged-model excess loss and uses angles measured in the curvature metric rather than Euclidean space.
A curvature-guided regularizer bounds displacement in the base curvature metric during non-convex training and yields an inverse penalty relationship for the curvature component of interference.
The regularizer does not similarly reduce the first-order term caused by solutions being nonstationary for the task loss.
Experiments confirm the predicted budget and ceiling; the functional tracks merging degradation, but is no more rank-correlated than Euclidean displacement in a transformer study.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents rely on stored records to recover a person's state as facts change. Reliable answers depend on how facts are recorded, retrieved, and presented to the reader. We treat a long-form persona dossier as a memory representation of a known latent state, an invariant identity plus a timeline of facts, routines, and decision rules tied to life phases. We present ChronoDossier, a benchmark of 311 synthetic dossiers of 1k-10k words written by seven generators from dated timelines. Intrinsic metrics evaluate the records against their intended states; extrinsic metrics test recovery by five readers on a seeded 32-persona GPT-5.1 panel balanced across lengths (520 rated turns per condition). The linked states, records, evidence packets, and answers support tests of construction and evidence delivery. In a contextual-stress control, tag-scoped writer inputs remove detected out-of-scope anchor copying. Frozen questions authored on staged dossiers transfer less reliably to one-pass dossiers of the same states. In matched evidence controls, whole sections repair 29 of 32 GPT-5.1 and 25 of 30 Sonnet 4.6 failures labeled as packaging, compared with 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. Attribution uses separate key-based and key-free support measures, with model disagreements retained. Length remains confounded with persona and question composition; the observed between-bucket widening depends on excerpt construction. The benchmark supports offline evaluation against known facts. Memory acquisition from interaction and validation against real users remain outside its scope.
bullets: Models personas as an invariant identity plus time-linked facts, routines, and decision rules across life phases.
Introduces 311 synthetic, 1k–10k-word dossiers from dated timelines, evaluated with intrinsic state-matching and extrinsic reader-recovery metrics.
Matched evidence experiments found whole-section packaging repaired many packaging failures, but rarely corrected answer-formation failures.
Frozen questions transferred less reliably from staged dossiers to one-pass dossiers representing the same states.
Length effects are confounded by persona, question composition, and excerpt construction; interaction-based memory acquisition and real-user validation are out of scope.

papers.abstract: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.
authors: Bochen Han, Anshu Xiong, Mingyang Ma
bullets: The study analyzes a four-stage workflow for incorporating argumentation frameworks into LLM decision-making.
It evaluates design choices for debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification.
Qnt-Arg groups debate arguments by original speakers and combines estimated argument strengths with answer priors using gradual semantics.
Qlt-Arg ranks conflicting evidence by credibility and uses grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for LLM inference.
Qnt-Arg outperforms matched argumentation-augmented methods in debate, while Qlt-Arg improves fact verification over baselines.

papers.abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.
bullets: Pointwise rewards that map correct answers to confidence 1 and incorrect answers to 0 lose useful distinctions between answer confidences.
CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation) rewards confidence rankings across question sets using thresholds induced at different risk tolerances.
This enables models to abstain or defer on lower-confidence questions while maximizing coverage under a target error rate.
On math benchmarks, CARE raises 5% risk coverage from 0.8% to 42.4%; on out-of-distribution QA, it raises coverage from 12.3% to 23.6%.
The approach is evaluated for selective prediction and confidence estimation, with reported gains across several in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of continual-learning-style memory systems that retain information indefinitely.
Uses a fixed-capacity LoRA substrate with k-hot rank combinations to reduce interference and independently control temporal decay.
Trains a lightweight controller to decide what to store, how deeply, and for how long based on incoming user events.
Evaluates long-horizon user trajectories with queries testing recall while facts are valid and abstention after expiration.
Achieves 86% of oracle performance, balancing recall and abstention better than continual-learning and RAG baselines.

papers.abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.
authors: Mark Lovett, Denis Lim, Soroush Vosoughi
bullets: Experts choose positions in a fixed prompt-trait space to maximize their expected share of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses.
A kernel-based stability criterion guides when co-located experts separate and specialize.
On seven safety-related benchmarks, the highest-share expert had the lowest held-out NLL for about 90% of prompts, versus about 15% with permuted allocations.
The fixed router performs comparably to published learned gates and enables tracing harmful behavior to one expert for targeted retraining.
Specialization can be controlled through the kernel, trait-space geometry, and number of experts; the framework is intended to generalize across encoders and data distributions.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.
authors: Ziyan Yang, Taiwei Shi, Jieyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses context-window limits and the information loss caused by summarization, masking, and structured memory.
Uses only an append-only text log plus on-demand grep-style regex search—no embeddings, indexes, memory extraction, or extra models.
Trains Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning across five context-management strategies and evaluates multiple long-context memory tasks.
Achieves 95–97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and beats SUPO summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi.
Remains effective as input streams grow and stays on the accuracy–token-cost Pareto frontier across the evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: GREPMEM Overview. (a) The basic agent loop generates responses and tool calls from its active context, while GREPMEM additionally appends these interactions and tool results to a persistent history log. (b) Context compaction generates a summary when the working context reaches the compaction limit, allowing the agent to resume execution with a compacted context. GREPMEM builds on SUPO’s summarization loop. Extending this framework, GREPMEM enables (c) on-demand retrieval through grep_history and (d) a lossless, append-only full history log containing user messages, tool calls, tool results, summaries, and agent responses. By combining context summarization with a log preserving every message and tool output verbatim, GREPMEM enables grep_history to retrieve matching log lines after the first compaction without embeddings, a retrieval index, or an additional model.

Our method, GREPMEM, combines summarization with a lossless, searchable history log, enabling on-demand retrieval through grep without a retrieval index. papers.abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.
bullets: Constructs matched string-replacement tasks with certified minimum solution lengths of one versus two rules.
Uses complete one-rule enumeration and executable two-rule witnesses to verify task requirements before inference.
Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, certified separation tasks reduced displayed-task completion by 23.53–45.83 percentage points.
Performance on wholly unshown witness pairs increased by 8.40–13.45 points, alongside lower agreement on sampled inputs.
Recertification shows that even one unchanged example can eliminate a shortcut and determine whether two rules are necessary.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a certificate-grounded calibration method for program induction benchmarks to verify task difficulty, providing a rigorous testbed for evaluating LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
papers.tldr: Certificate-grounded calibration verifies whether examples truly require one or two rules, revealing how task evidence changes models’ inferred programs and generalization.

papers.abstract: Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run. In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens. Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale. These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.
bullets: The study analyzes 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3–8B parameters using 1–2T tokens.
Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers; at 8B, they achieve the same MMLU accuracy with about 30% fewer pretraining tokens.
New GLA5 and GDN2 variants improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet; with Canon, simple gated linear attention matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2.
Despite strong standard benchmark scores, linear models fail to reliably retrieve information from 500-token contexts, and no tested model reliably solves a simple two-hop question.
The results suggest incorporating in-context reasoning examples early in pretraining rather than relying mainly on later mid-training or post-training.

papers.selection_reason: Studies LLM architecture differences (Canon layers, linear models) at scale, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality
papers.tldr: At billion-parameter scale, long pretraining reveals architectural differences that standard benchmarks often hide, while synthetic tasks better expose models’ weak in-context reasoning.

papers.abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.
authors: Yu-Hung Wu, Shao-Xiang Yuan, Chan-Hung Yu, Zih-Ching Chen, Kuan-Hao Huang, Shao-Hua Sun
bullets: Generated-token count is an observable proxy for inference compute, but it does not monotonically align with classical computational complexity.
LLM Complexity is defined by the area bounded above by the accuracy–token curve.
Different LLMs produce highly consistent task-difficulty rankings under this metric.
An easy-to-hard curriculum based on LLM Complexity improves accuracy while reducing token consumption.
The metric extends to real-world tasks and yields more stable cross-model correlations than human difficulty labels.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Time complexity does not align with LLMs’ inference-time token usage. We conduct experiments on NEMOTRON-253B and report the relationship between the token budget and accuracy. (a) For problem size 80, sorting (O(n log n)) requires more tokens to reach 50% accuracy than some tasks with higher theoretical complexity. (b) For four sum closest, accuracy at a 10K-token budget does not decrease monotonically with problem size. Together, these results highlight a mismatch between algorithmic complexity and LLM inference behavior.

Figure 4: SFT learns and curriculum improves generalization. Accuracy on seen (training-split) vs. unseen (held-out) instances for each algorithm. Bars compare random-order SFT and curriculum SFT (complexity-based weighted sampling) evaluated on both splits. The dashed line separates algorithms included in SFT training (seen algorithms) from algorithms excluded from training (unseen algorithms). SFT yields higher accuracy on seen instances than unseen instances for seen algorithms, confirming effective adaptation, while curriculum SFT improves held-out performance and transfers better to unseen algorithms.
Figure 2: Illustration of inference utility. We plot accuracy as a function of token budget. The shaded area under the curve represents aggregate accuracy across the budget.

Table 2: Cross-model correlation of task-level complexity rankings. We report Spearman’s ρ / Kendall’s τb between the per-task complexity ranks induced by Model A and Model B (higher is better) on 12 algorithmic problems. Length: The number of tokens in the model’s first phase CoT trace. Budget: the token budget required to reach 90% of the model’s peak accuracy, normalized by the peak accuracy. Peak: the model’s peak accuracy. The results show that LLM Complexity yields the best cross-model correlation among all the other heuristic complexity definitions.

Table 9: Annotated time and auxiliary-space complexity for the 12 algorithmic tasks. Time bounds follow the tightest widely accepted worst-case complexity under the standard computation model. Space reports worst-case auxiliary memory, excluding input/output storage. Here n is input list length; for Longest Common Subsequence, n,m are the two sequence lengths; for Coin Change, A is the target amount and k is the number of coin types; for Knapsack, W is capacity; for Subset Sum, T is the target sum. †Assuming in-place sorting; recursion stack is O(logn) if applicable. ‡Subset Sum is NP-complete in n; we annotate the exponential worst-case in n while noting its pseudo-polynomial DP dependence on T .

Table 7: Cross-model consistency of task-level complexity rankings on RuleArena. We report Spearman’s ρ / Kendall’s τb between the rankings of the nine RuleArena tasks induced by Model A and Model B (higher is better). LLM Complexity achieves the strongest cross-model agreement.

Table 4: Accuracy usage under different curricula. We fine-tune QWEN3-1.7B with teachergenerated supervision from NEMOTRON-253B using 3 different seeds. All curriculum variants use the same sampling form P ∝ exp(−C/τ) with an annealed temperature to induce an easy-to-hard schedule, differing only in the choice of complexity score C: Time (wall-clock execution time), Length, Budget (defined in Table 2), and LLM Complexity; Random uses uniform sampling, and Pre-trained denotes the base model without SFT. LLM Complexity achieves the highest average accuracy and lowest average token usage, supporting its effectiveness for curriculum design.

Table 6: Task-level complexity correlation on DeepMath. We report cross-model correlation (averaged per model over pairwise comparisons) and correlation with DeepMath difficulty annotations using Spearman’s ρ and Kendall’s τb. LLM Complexity shows substantial cross-model consistency but near-zero correlation with humanannotated difficulty, suggesting that it captures a complementary dimension of LLM-specific problem complexity. Full pairwise correlations are provided in Section C.3.

Table 1: Weak alignment between worstcase algorithmic time complexity and LLM token usage. We conduct the experiment with 12 algorithmic problems, each evaluated across 10 problem sizes. For each model, we compute the correlation between the average output length and a task-level time-complexity ranking derived from tight, widely accepted worst-case bounds (e.g., sorting with O(n log n)). Across all five models, both Spearman’s ρ and Kendall’s τb remain small, indicating weak alignment between inference-time token usage and worst-case algorithmic time complexity.

papers.abstract: Developing effective forecasting models for diverse time-series domains requires substantial expert knowledge, evidence from scientific literature on the web, and iterative experimentation. However, translating this knowledge and research experience into model designs requires preserving source context and testing applicability under task-specific assumptions. In this paper, we propose NeoResearch, a literature- and experience-guided autonomous research framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) as researchers to discover lightweight, domain-specific forecasting models. Specifically, NeoResearch establishes an expert-inspired dual-loop research workflow, coupling hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization through experimental feedback. To enable knowledge-grounded discovery, the agent autonomously mines scientific literature from the Web, extracting modeling mechanisms, empirical evidence, and applicability conditions to formulate task-grounded, testable architecture hypotheses. Furthermore, a hierarchical experience memory links literature findings to experimental outcomes and consolidates conditional lessons, guiding architecture discovery and training optimization while supporting reuse across forecasting tasks. Experiments on ten datasets show competitive performance and support dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse. Our code is available.
bullets: Targets the expert knowledge and iterative experimentation typically required for forecasting model design.
Uses a dual-loop workflow combining hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with training and hyperparameter optimization.
Mines scientific literature for mechanisms, evidence, and applicability conditions to create testable architecture hypotheses.
Maintains hierarchical experience memory linking literature insights with experimental outcomes for reuse across tasks.
Experiments on ten datasets show competitive performance and support the framework’s dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse.
