papers.abstract: Hybrid attention is rapidly becoming the dominant architectural choice for frontier models. Despite their successes, such architectures complicate model design by introducing additional choices, including the types and locations of layers. This combinatorially large design space has been studied empirically, but given the vast expense of training and evaluating models with different configurations, a principled understanding of the effects of layer selection and ordering is needed. We provide the first such analysis, showing that the dominant hybrid architecture is highly task-specific. Concretely, for any layer configuration, we prove that there exists a task where we can construct a model with this configuration that provably outperforms any other model of any different configuration under fixed resource constraints. Empirically, we observe that for standard training, learned hybrid architectures exhibit separations between layer orderings that match our theoretical findings. For instance, under the same memory budget, the optimal architecture predicted by our theory for a segmented retrieval task consistently achieves perfect accuracy, whereas the next strongest plateaus below 0.5. These results extend to deeper models, where ``containing'' the dominant architecture for a task indicates whether the model attains high performance. In addition, we investigate the mechanisms learned by hybrids, observing that Transformer layers contribute the largest share of performance on associative recall across architectures. This work establishes insights into task-dependent hybrid architecture design relevant to the training and scaling of frontier-scale hybrids.
bullets: Hybrid models introduce a large design space of layer types and orderings that is costly to explore empirically.
The authors prove that for any layer configuration, some task exists where it outperforms every different configuration under the same resource constraints.
Experiments show that learned architectures exhibit performance gaps between orderings consistent with the theory.
On a segmented retrieval task, the theoretically optimal architecture reaches perfect accuracy, while the next-best remains below 0.5.
Transformer layers provide the largest share of associative-recall performance across hybrid architectures.

papers.abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.
bullets: Fixed steering may not fit the diverse knowledge and reasoning needs of individual queries.
Q-NeuS identifies a compact, subject-guided candidate neuron space and generates query-specific neuron modulation coefficients with a lightweight gate.
Neu-GRPO trains the gate using relative performance across multiple neuron-intervention configurations.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks report consistent improvements, broad model-scale applicability, and cross-benchmark transfer.
The abstract does not specify particular datasets, numerical gains, or limitations beyond its evaluated scope.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.
authors: Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao

Bottom (Stage 2): Route Selection Mechanism. We generate pseudo-labels via token-level NLL and apply a margin-based filtering strategy to obtain a noise-removed training set. papers.abstract: Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.
bullets: Withholding skill-specific training signals delays, but does not prevent, capability acquisition.
The delay for larger models can be predicted from results on smaller models.
A chess model trained without explicit check responses ranked legal responses nearly as well as one trained with them.
Models regained withheld skills using only a small fraction of the data required from initialization, with the fraction shrinking as training progressed.
The findings span chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, web text, and a withheld programming language.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.
authors: Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Meng Tang, Haoran Li, Yechao Bai, Feiyang Pan, Jia He
bullets: Targets sparse terminal rewards, difficult credit assignment, and exploration in long-horizon RL.

Uses paired advantages to distinguish reaching more solvable states from completing tasks afterward.
Expands capability backward along successful trajectories, then outward through on-policy exploration.
Outperforms competitive agentic RL methods on ALFWorld and WebShop at both Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B-Instruct scales.

papers.abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
bullets: Uses Gated Delta Networks adapted to block diffusion, combining historical recurrent memory with current-block bidirectional softmax attention.

A decision-model variant improves joint question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0% on 500 internal groups.

papers.abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.
authors: Donghyeok Lee, Sangwon Yu, Sangkwon Park, Hye Youn Park, Munyoung Chang, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Reasoning-trained models retain broadly similar global gradient organization but develop localized changes within a contiguous layer span.
Diffusion-map embeddings were applied to matched base and reasoning-trained models across three model families.
Transplanting weights from the span into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, especially when donor and host regions overlapped.
The span emerged gradually during early performance gains; intermediate-training grafts also helped and often preserved more previously solved problems than other graft locations.
A similar transferable span was found in a medical model, though the analysis supports a reasoning-related region rather than a universal mechanism across all models.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
bullets: Targets the accuracy–interpretability–compute trade-off in activation-based LLM monitoring.
Represents each probe as explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features under a gate budget.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. We start by labelling each CoT hidden state as recovering if patching it into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and failed otherwise. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. We then show that the representation space of the direct prompt holds a direction for each question that leads the model, in a short generation, to the correct answer more often than CoT does. Specifically, we rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once, before generation, towards a direction built for each question from its own recovering and failed states. Across 25 tasks, these directions raise the direct prompt's mean accuracy from $46\%$ to $85\%$ on LLaMA 3.1 8B (CoT: $69\%$) and from $52\%$ to $86\%$ on Qwen 2.5 7B (CoT: $77\%$), with a tenth of CoT's tokens. CoT is thus not the shortest route to this accuracy, and these directions can be used in future work to train models to align their states with them.
bullets: CoT hidden states are labeled as recovering or failed based on whether patching them into a direct prompt produces the correct answer.
A linear probe distinguishes these two hidden-state classes.
For each question, a direction derived from recovering and failed states is used to rotate the direct prompt’s final hidden state before generation.
Across 25 tasks, accuracy rises from 46% to 85% on LLaMA 3.1 8B and from 52% to 86% on Qwen 2.5 7B, exceeding CoT accuracy with roughly one-tenth as many tokens.
The approach requires question-specific directions and is presented as a basis for future state-alignment training.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
papers.tldr: Question-specific hidden-state directions can steer direct-answer prompting to substantially higher accuracy than CoT while using far fewer tokens.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.
authors: Ziqi Jin, Jiaxi Li, Weiwen Xu, Aixin Sun
bullets: Problem: Standard early exit leaves past-token key-value caches incomplete, while full recurrence increases sequential decoding latency.
Method: New tokens enter directly into the final K recurrent steps; Wake verification checks projected states using a logit-margin tolerance τ within a static CUDA graph.
Modes: τ=0 provides greedy-exact decoding, τ>0 enables margin-gated verification, and τ=∞ gives non-rollback lossy late entry.
Results: On Ouro-2.6B, K=2 achieved 5.2× exact and 6.8× lossy speedups; scaling recurrence on Huginn-3.5B reached up to 8.4× exact and 12.5× lossy speedups.

papers.selection_reason: Decoding strategy for looped LLMs that reduces latency and cache-related overhead; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: Late entry accelerates looped language-model decoding by letting new tokens skip early recurrent passes while preserving configurable exactness or accepting controlled approximation.

papers.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extend a Transformer's residual stream into multiple parallel streams with learned cross-stream connections. Prior work trains all streams toward a shared objective. We instead study whether assigning distinct learning objectives to different streams can improve task performance and induce objective-specific specialization. Using complementary lexical (sparse) and semantic (dense) retrieval objectives as a test case, we find that objective-specialized mHC consistently outperforms a non-specialized mHC model across the full sparse--dense fusion range, for both two- and four-stream models and at two model scales. We then examine how specialization changes the model internally using probes of stream representations, residual mixing, objective-specific gradient flow, and read/write gates. The specialized and non-specialized models behave similarly through most of the network but diverge in the final layers: the specialized model develops increasingly objective-specific gradient flow, distinct read/write routing patterns, and reduced cross-stream mixing, and streams assigned to different objectives become increasingly dissimilar while those trained toward the same objective remain highly similar. Fixing the residual mixing to the identity leaves the specialization benefit intact, indicating that the benefit stems from objective-specific read/write routing rather than learned cross-stream mixing. These results show that assigning distinct objectives to mHC streams can improve multi-objective retrieval while inducing structured, depth-dependent specialization in the residual computation.
authors: Shantanu Agarwal, Ruchita V. Maitri, Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel
bullets: Tests objective-specialized mHC using complementary sparse lexical and dense semantic retrieval objectives.
Specialized models outperform non-specialized mHC across the full sparse–dense fusion range for two- and four-stream models at two scales.
Specialization emerges mainly in final layers through distinct gradient flow, read/write routing, and reduced cross-stream mixing.
Streams trained on the same objective remain similar, while streams trained on different objectives become increasingly dissimilar.
The benefit persists with identity residual mixing, implicating read/write routing rather than learned cross-stream mixing.

From left: stream cosine similarity, residual-mixing identity retention diag(A), per-objective gradient share on the assigned stream(s), and read/write gate shift. Red: specialized; blue: non-specialized control. Solid vs. dashed distinguishes the two objectives / gates / stream-pair types (legends). Metrics are defined and discussed in Section 5.

Figure 2: Average BEIR nDCG@10 as a function of the fusion weight α, for ModernBERT-base (left) and ModernBERT-large (right); both mean over two seeds. α = 0 and α = 1 correspond to pure sparse and pure dense retrieval, respectively. Color encodes objective specialization (red: specialized, blue: non-specialized); Sparse+Dense (n=1, grey) has no stream routing. Specialized models (red) dominate at every α for both stream counts and at both base/large model scales.

Figure 1: Schematic comparison of the three encoder configurations studied in this work. In all three, streams propagate through the full encoder stack and the retrieval heads read only the final-layer (l = L) stream representations. (left) Single-stream: the standard ModernBERT encoder, with a single residual stream read by both the sparse and dense retrieval heads. (middle) Non-specialized mHC: the residual stream is expanded into n parallel streams with learned cross-stream routing. Both retrieval heads operate on the mean-pooled representation obtained from all n streams, so the sparse and dense objectives jointly optimize the same stream representation. (right) Objective-specialized mHC: the sparse and dense heads instead read disjoint sets of final-layer streams, so each objective selectively trains its assigned stream(s). For clarity the schematic depicts n = 2 streams; we study both n = 2 and n = 4 in our experiments.

Figure 4: Attention-sublayer routing probes at the final checkpoint (lines are the mean and shaded bands ±1 standard deviation over 4 seeds; flat layers 0–9 omitted). Left pair: n=2; right pair: n=4. Within each pair: mean diagonal of the residual-mixing matrix diag(A), and the shift in each gate’s sparse-stream share ∆ (read gate p solid, write gate q dashed). Red: specialized; blue: non-specialized control. Like the MLP sublayer, attention drives A toward the identity under specialization; unlike the MLP, its read gate does not shift (∆s(pℓ) ≈ 0) while its write gate moves strongly toward the dense-assigned stream(s) (∆s(qL) ≈ −0.44), i.e. attention specializes its write but not its read. Metrics defined in Section 5.

Sparse-only and Dense-only are evaluated in their native retrieval mode; the remaining models are hybrid retrievers fused at α = 0.9. The two-seed means are the values reported in Table 4. As at the base scale, the specialization gain holds within each seed: at both n = 2 and n = 4, mHC+spec exceeds mHC no-spec in every seed.

Table 3: Initialization of each mHC block. Projection weights are zero-initialized so routing starts static; the biases place the block near an identity residual layer. The read-gate bias uses the UNIFORM-NOISY scheme (target σ(bprek ) = 1/n plus noise ε ∼ N (0, σ2 noise), σnoise=10−2, renormalized to sum to one) for both specialized and non-specialized models. At initialization this yields read gate p ≈ [1/n, . . . , 1/n] (summing to 1), write gate q = [1, . . . , 1], and a doubly-stochastic mixing matrix A with its largest mass on the diagonal.
Table 5: Per-seed BEIR nDCG@10 across all 13 datasets (hybrid fusion at α = 0.9) for ModernBERT-base.

Table 1: BEIR nDCG@10 across all 13 datasets using ModernBERT-base. Sparse-only and Dense-only are evaluated in their native retrieval mode; Sparse+Dense and the mHC models are hybrid retrievers fused at α = 0.9, the shared empirical optimum across all multi-objective models. Underline marks the best score within each stream count n; bold marks the best score for that dataset across all configurations. The advantage of objective specialization is not confined to the aggregate score; it extends to a majority of individual datasets and holds at both n = 2 and n = 4. Excluding the in-domain NQ dataset, mHC+spec still improves over mHC no-spec on the remaining 12 datasets (0.4329→ 0.4470 at n=2; 0.4431→ 0.4510 at n=4). Results reported here are mean over two seeds. Per seed variation is provided in Appendix 5. Results with ModernBERT-large (Table 4) show the same trend: mHC+spec improves over mHC no-spec at both n = 2 and n = 4, indicating that the benefit of objective specialization is robust to model scale rather than specific to a single model size.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Transformer residual-stream architecture modification with objective specialization, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Objective-Specialized Residual Streams in Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
papers.tldr: Assigning different retrieval objectives to parallel mHC residual streams improves multi-objective retrieval and induces depth-dependent stream specialization, primarily through objective-specific routing.

papers.abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.
bullets: Compares five architectural and optimization changes under the same data and training budget.
Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimization, and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid yield the largest gains; extra normalization also helps.
An attention gate with matched parameter count contributes little on average.
Most improvements combine effectively, but small interactions recur across repeated random seeds.
Results are limited to the small-model setting, and expert models have greater total capacity.

papers.selection_reason: Conducts a factorial study on small language model components (MoE, Muon, DeltaNet), providing insights into model architecture and training recipes for LLMs.
papers.title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
papers.tldr: A replicated factorial study finds that several frontier-model components provide mostly additive gains in small language models, though some interactions and capacity differences complicate interpretation.

papers.abstract: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.
authors: Haoran Luo, Jiapu Wang, Linhao Luo, Luu Anh Tuan
bullets: Existing knowledge-engineering systems typically support at most two of omnimodality, closed-loop updating, and multi-granular use.
The authors formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench: six tasks covering 1,829 model-free items from 3,960 files across five modalities.
KnowledgeClaw constructs an omnimodal typed hypergraph, maintains it through a closed-loop lifecycle agent, and routes queries to the needed granularity.
It ranks first among 30 baselines across all six tasks, achieving an overall OKE score of 55.9, 14.6 points above the strongest baseline.
The benchmark and system are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.
authors: Yi Lu, Qianshi Lin, Yumeng Yang, Hongxia Wang
bullets: Separates content relevance, observable proxies, and auditable positional weights for context billing.
Context ablations find relevance dominates position; distance-decay weighting does not beat a relevance-only baseline.
Serving measurements show cache hits cut repeated-prefix compute costs by over 100× at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends limit discounts.
Calibrated simulations reduce 99th-percentile session charges by 31–42%, but revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs produce similar reductions and increase median charges.
The work offers bounded per-token accounting and deployment constraints, not a validated utility estimator.

papers.abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Guoyao Yang, Kaidi Yang
bullets: Role information may be internally represented without reliably constraining the model’s outputs.
A first-order decomposition identifies sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation as necessary for role effects to influence behavior.
Causal analysis links role-span contributions to response structure, content selection, and factual-value decisions.
Role-consistent outputs require adequate role-span support at key decisions; increasing this support can reverse failures.
The framework attributes ICL and OOC hallucination to how effectively functional-role contributions remain active across output decisions.

papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.
authors: Haowei Chen, Yichen Wang, Congfu Xu
bullets: Uses learned nonlinear features and covariance-guided recursive ridge-regression updates to store associations.
Applies a content-dependent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transition to control retention and restore uncertainty for future writes.
Has an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and an inference state whose size does not grow with context length.
Associative block maps and explicit adjoints enable parallel training while preserving the recursive update.
Controlled language-modeling experiments report better prediction quality than attention and recurrent baselines, plus stronger associative recall than evaluated recurrent models.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.
authors: Shuaidi Wang, Zhuocheng Gong, Xuejie Liu, Jianguo Li, Yu Zhang
bullets: Replacement-only editing struggles with missing or extra tokens and errors spanning many positions.
LED learns Levenshtein-style refinement through on-the-fly longest-common-subsequence edit supervision, avoiding manual edit labels.
Multi-stage training feeds each stage’s output into the next, helping the model correct its own earlier errors.
On LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED improves average benchmark scores under confidence-guided and confidence-free decoding, and is more robust to large block sizes.
LED also achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, indicating greater generation diversity.

papers.abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.
authors: Zeman Li, Ali Behrouz, Yuan Deng, Praneeth Kacham, Rami Al-Rfou, Meisam Razaviyayn, Vahab Mirrokni
bullets: Builds a two-layer nonlinear memory by placing an activation between two delta-rule linear memories.
Uses chunk-level target propagation to provide hidden-layer targets while retaining efficient unmodified delta-rule kernels.
At matched sizes and training budgets, outperforms KDA across five model sizes on C4 and PG19; C4 perplexity matches or slightly improves on attention.
Its attention hybrid achieves the best perplexity among four tested hybrids, and its largest model reaches 51.84% mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks.
Maintains lower loss than KDA through 20K-token contexts and is substantially faster than tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a nonlinear memory architecture for LLMs using cascaded linear memories and target propagation, directly fitting LLM Memory.
papers.title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
papers.tldr: Toaster creates a fast nonlinear recurrent memory by cascading two linear memories with target propagation, achieving stronger language-modeling and long-context results than comparable linear and deep-memory baselines.

papers.abstract: We introduce MANGO Arena, an open-source testbed in which four LLM agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from MANGO, a classroom factory-management game. The environment enforces hard rules (a truck limit, a no-credit cash constraint and production capacity), logs every blocked attempt to break them, and gives agents a public message board on which side payments are explicitly forbidden. This lets one environment measure three things at once: an economic outcome (the bullwhip effect), rule adherence under pressure, and proposals to collude. In a pilot with three small reasoning models, two scripted reference policies, two conditions (with and without a supplier fire) and three demand seeds, all LLM agents amplified demand variability as it moved upstream, by 7 to 25 times at the Retailer and 13 to 179 times at the Supplier, often more than a textbook order-up-to policy. They did so largely by ordering in batches (zero orders in up to 60% of decisions). Real rule violations were rare (at most 7 of 288 decisions per model) and no agent proposed a money side deal. The pilot's main lesson concerns evaluation method. API failures (rate limits and runaway hidden reasoning) entered the metrics silently as "no order" decisions. And when we reran games with the same seeds and no failed calls, upstream bullwhip changed by up to 17 times between runs. With three seeds, conclusions about how a disruption affects a given model did not survive a rerun. We report these failures in full and propose reporting practices for multi-agent evaluations of this kind. Code, prompts and every logged decision are public.
bullets: Four LLM agents manage companies in a rule-constrained serial supply chain with logged violations and a public message board.
The testbed jointly measures bullwhip effects, rule adherence, and attempts to collude under disruption and baseline conditions.
In the pilot, agents amplified variability substantially, often through batched ordering; rule violations and side-payment proposals were rare.
API failures were silently recorded as no-order actions, and identical seeds produced bullwhip differences of up to 17× across reruns.
The study recommends stronger reporting practices and provides public code, prompts, and decision logs.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM agents in a simulated supply chain environment, focusing on agent behavior and economic outcomes, fitting Large Language Models.
papers.title: MANGO Arena: Same Seeds, Different Chains Evaluating LLM Agents in a Disrupted Supply Chain
papers.tldr: MANGO Arena is an open-source testbed showing that LLM supply-chain agents can strongly amplify demand variability, while evaluation outcomes remain highly sensitive to API failures and reruns.

papers.abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.
bullets: Uses timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes across 3,629 questions and six models.
The Verify prompt increases adoption of false answers on pre-cutoff events in all five tested models, often displacing previously correct answers.
On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini shows increased false-answer adoption; passage priority alone raises adoption, while adding checking lowers it.
Adversarial-Aware restores 82.5–98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with less than one percentage point change in true-passage accuracy.
The framework supports reproducible evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs on knowledge-context conflict, a core issue in managing long contexts and memory, fitting LLM Memory and Long-Context Models.
papers.title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
papers.tldr: FutureBench evaluates how prompts and retrieved passages make LLMs resolve conflicts between context and their own knowledge over time.

papers.abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).
authors: Jiangyun Zhang, Zhou Tang, Kristen Surrao, Zhiyu Chen, Albert Guan, Tor Nitayanont, Yupei Zhang, Roopali Singh, Yunkai Xiao, Shreya Pandit, Julia Huang, Shayan Ali Akbar, Erwin Cornejo, Yuan Li, Yi Zhang
bullets: Targets dynamic enterprise environments where models, workflows, and cost requirements change over time.
Uses self- or teacher-model failure attribution to create corrective micro-memories, consolidate them into macro rules, and retain updates only when held-out accuracy improves.
Evaluated across 14 SOP-Bench and τ²-Bench workflow domains with 5 models.
ARISE-Teacher improves baseline accuracy by 10.9 percentage points on SOP-Bench and 5.8 points on τ²-Bench; ARISE-Self gains 10.0 points on SOP-Bench.
ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving memory architecture for LLM agents, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
papers.tldr: ARISE improves enterprise-agent accuracy and efficiency by turning failures into validated, retrievable memory and rules without changing model weights, tools, or workflows.

papers.abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.
authors: Xinyang Li, Chih-Hsuan Yang, Xiaolong Ma, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Vikram Vasudevan, Rajeev Thakur, Feng Yan
bullets: The system skips a helper’s text or latent KV-cache message only when it certifies, with high probability, that no more than 5% of answers will change; otherwise it communicates.
Whether skipping is safe depends on how often and predictably a message changes answers—not on the helper’s accuracy.
On four settings where text messages helped, policies skipped 59–80% of messages while retaining an estimated 76–95% of the gain.
Prospective tests skipped 39.9% of verifier messages while retaining 12.55 of 12.80 points of gain, and skipped 68.4% of 32B-helper messages while retaining the full gain.
Safety and efficiency differ: text skipping saved hundreds of milliseconds per query at batch size one, whereas KV-cache savings were much smaller; certification extended to SQuAD but not GSM8K.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanisms for LLM agents to skip messages safely to reduce latency, a relevant optimization for agent efficiency.
papers.title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
papers.tldr: A confidence-based finite-sample test lets LLM agents safely skip many helper messages, preserving most answer improvements while reducing latency when skipping is worthwhile.

papers.abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.
bullets: Across 40 questions from newly accepted papers, models usually recognized that questions were unstudied but rarely stated this clearly in ordinary answers.
Six frontier systems had reporting gaps of 30–90 percentage points, with larger gaps among more capable models.
The failure was asymmetric: models more reliably identified studied questions when the relevant papers were supplied.
A fixed answer combining model judgments with separate citation checks raised clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95% for GPT-6-Astra and improved all six systems.
The method also predicted reviewers’ novelty grades competitively without requiring model weights or internal activations.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Deng Pan, Arun Ross, Dongxiao Zhu
bullets: Targets the informationless BOS representation created by causal masking, which later tokens repeatedly attend to.
At one prefill layer, allows only the BOS query to attend to all visual and textual input tokens; all other causal attention remains unchanged.
Requires no training, added parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead.
Improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and recent sink-intervention methods across eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks.
Mechanistic analysis finds reduced BOS sink dominance and more attention allocated to content-bearing prompt tokens.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/
authors: Chaipat Tirapongprasert, Rajarshi Das, Parijat Dube
bullets: Studies LLM decision-making in iterative games with incomplete information.
Compares externalized reasoning traces with internal layer activations.
Finds that game representations are formed and revised throughout reasoning.
Shows that premature incorrect beliefs persist in both the trace and activations.
Provides an interactive visualizer for selected example traces.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.
authors: Hubert Strauss, Liam Fowl, Noam Razin
bullets: Sequence-level OPD has a future-agreement bias that token-level objectives avoid.
This bias can cause reverse learning: later positions are matched first, while earlier positions may favor teacher-improbable tokens.
Forward KL yields a well-behaved optimization landscape.
Other f-divergences, including reverse KL, can have vanishing gradients even when student and teacher distributions differ substantially.
The preferable OPD objective depends on the student, teacher, and post-training task.

figures.caption: Figure 13: Example of the user message given to gpt-5.6-terra for writing the programs in the code completion dataset (see Appendix E.3.1 for details on the dataset construction process). The model responded with a structured output containing one entry per program, whose fields are described in Appendix E.3.1.

Figure 5: RKL becomes more preferable to FKL as the capacity gap between the student and teacher grows. We trained Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base students using token-level OPD with the FKL and RKL divergences and Qwen3 teachers of varying sizes, on the MATH dataset. The left plot shows that the gap in accuracy between students trained with RKL and FKL grows with the size of the teacher (markers stand for means over three seeds, with error bars denoting standard deviation). The middle and right plots point to a potential cause: the tokens whose probability increases the most under RKL are typically already likely under the initial student, whereas under FKL they can have low initial probability, especially with the larger teacher, suggesting that FKL changes the student in ways that are less compatible with its initial capabilities. Specifically, for the 0.6B student with the 4B and 32B teachers, the middle and right plots show how the initial student probabilities are distributed for the tokens that increased the most in probability during training.

Figure 11: Sequence-level OPD can cause the student to refuse to answer even when its thinking block concludes that the request is safe. Shown is an output of the Qwen3-1.7B student for a benign training request, generated at training step 282 of a sequence-level OPD run in Figure 9. We show an output from this training step since, later in training, the thinking blocks of the student often become empty.

Figure 4: RKL and JS struggle to distill knowledge of new APIs in a code completion task. We trained a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Base student using token-level OPD objectives with a Qwen3-8B-Base teacher, on prompts requiring the use of Python APIs that were released after the student (see Section 4.2.1). Reported values are computed over training prompts for which the student initially assigns the first token of the correct API name a probability of at most 10−3, and averaged over three seeds (shaded areas mark standard deviation). In agreement with Theorem 2, FKL and its equal mixture with RKL quickly match the rate at which the teacher names the correct API, whereas RKL and JS are substantially slower to do so. Note that this slowdown is not due to insufficient sampling of unlikely tokens, since the divergences are computed over the full vocabulary and RKL and JS are slow to raise even the probability of the first token of the correct API name. Rather, it stems from their objective landscapes being flat along the logits of such tokens (as established in Section 4.1).

Figure 2: Future agreement bias prevents sequence-level OPD from efficiently solving the binary tree navigation task. We trained a randomly initialized Transformer student via sequence-level and tokenlevel OPD on the binary tree navigation task described in Section 3.2, using tree depth L = 15 and δ = 10−4. The left plot reports the probability that the student assigns to the correct pathy⋆ (i.e., success probability) and to the correct token at the root, throughout training. The middle and right plots report the RKL divergence between the student and teacher next-token distributions at each token position, across training steps of sequence-level and token-level OPD (averaged over 512 student-generated outputs and normalized by its initial value; error bars mark standard error). In line with our theory, sequence-level OPD first assigns high probability to the incorrect token at the root, correcting this mistake only after matching the teacher at later positions, whereas token-level OPD efficiently matches the teacher starting from the root. Figure 8 shows that token-level OPD with FKL and JS exhibits trends similar to those of token-level OPD with RKL.

Figure 3: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to cause over-refusal of benign requests. We trained a Qwen3-1.7B student using sequence-level and token-level OPD objectives with a Qwen3-8B teacher. The training prompts were taken from the WildJailbreak dataset and consist of an equal mixture of harmful and benign requests. Reported values are computed over training prompts and averaged over three seeds, with shaded areas marking standard deviation (results on a test set showed identical trends). Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 17.5% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them due to the future agreement bias characterized in Section 3.1. Consequently, sequence-level OPD lowers the safety accuracy of the student (i.e., the percentage of prompts for which it correctly refuses a harmful request or answers a benign one), whereas token-level OPD substantially improves it by lowering the refusal rate on benign requests and raising the refusal rate on harmful requests.

Figure 1: The binary tree navigation task analyzed in Section 3.2 (for depth L = 3). The student starts at the root, and its goal is to produce with high probability the path y⋆ = (A, A, . . . , A), which reaches a fixed target leaf. The teacher assigns high probability to choosing the left child at the root and every node in its left subtree (δ = exp(−L)), but chooses uniformly among children if the initial token is incorrect.

Figure 7: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to outperform token-level OPD on an arithmetic task by steering the student to use a calculator tool. We trained a Qwen3-1.7B student using a Qwen3-8B teacher via sequence-level OPD and token-level OPD with the RKL, FKL, and JS divergences on arithmetic problems, where each prompt instructs the model to either solve the problem directly or output a call to a calculator tool with an arithmetic expression. Reported values are computed over training prompts and averaged over three seeds, with shaded areas marking standard deviation (results on a test set showed identical trends). Notice that, although the teacher calls the calculator in only 7.2% of its outputs, sequencelevel OPD leads the student to call it for nearly all problems due to the future agreement bias characterized in Section 3.1. Consequently, the student attains near-perfect accuracy under sequence-level OPD, even surpassing the teacher. By contrast, token-level OPD leads the student to call the calculator less, and so its accuracy remains substantially lower than the accuracy achieved with sequence-level OPD.

Figure 12: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to outperform token-level OPD on an arithmetic task by steering the student to use a calculator tool (with a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher). This figure is identical to Figure 7, except that we used a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher instead of the Qwen3-1.7B student and Qwen3-8B teacher, and a different system prompt (see Appendix E.2.2). Notice that, although the teacher calls the calculator tool in only 1.4% of its outputs, sequence-level OPD leads the student to call it for most problems. It therefore outperforms token-level OPD objectives, under which the student almost never uses the calculator and struggles to learn to solve the problems directly as accurately as the teacher.

Figure 8: Token-level OPD objectives exhibit similar trends in the binary tree navigation task since they all avoid the future agreement bias. This figure supplements Figure 2 by including experiments with token-level OPD using the FKL and JS divergences. The left plot is analogous to that of Figure 2 (for clarity, teacher probabilities are omitted). The middle and right plots are the same as those of Figure 2, but for token-level OPD with FKL and JS, respectively. Both objectives behave similarly to token-level OPD with RKL: they efficiently match the teacher starting from the root, whereas sequence-level OPD first assigns high probability to the incorrect token at the root.

Figure 6: The binary tree navigation task analyzed in Appendix A.1 (for depth L = 3). The task and teacher are the same as in Figure 1, except that, alongside the path y⋆ = (A, A, . . . , A) to the leftmost leaf, every path that starts with B is also correct. Thus, the task can be solved either by following y⋆, which the teacher strongly prefers (δ = exp(−L)), or by choosing B at the root and then any continuation.

Figure 10: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to over-refuse benign requests (with a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher). This figure is identical to Figure 3, except that we used a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher instead of the Qwen3-1.7B student and Qwen3-8B teacher, and a different prompt template (see Appendix E.2.1). Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 12% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them, which lowers its safety accuracy. Token-level OPD, on the other hand, is able to improve the safety accuracy by lowering the refusal rate on benign requests and raising the refusal rate on harmful requests.

Figure 9: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to over-refuse benign requests (with thinking enabled). This figure is identical to Figure 3, except that thinking is enabled. That is, instead of responding directly, the student and teacher first produce thinking tokens, enclosed in a dedicated block marked by <think> and </think> tokens. Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 7.5% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them, which lowers its safety accuracy, whereas token-level OPD keeps the refusal rate of the student on benign requests close to that of the teacher and improves its safety accuracy.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
authors: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu
bullets: Addresses the time-consuming, model-specific redesign of post-training quantization recipes.
The agent iteratively builds and evaluates candidate recipes using output KL divergence on hidden reasoning traces, with long-generation checks for failures.
A compatible library of public PTQ methods speeds recipe construction across model architectures.
Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe at W4A16, W4A8, and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search.
For GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of FP8 accuracy; checkpoints run on existing serving kernels without inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.
bullets: Separate per-layer n-gram tables are memory-intensive, while naïve sharing limits layer-specific preferences.
Chorus lets each layer adapt shared embeddings using a layer-specific projection and hidden-state-conditioned rescaling.
With 1.2B table parameters, Chorus outperforms FactorEngram and DeepSeek’s Engram using 9.6B parameters.
It outperforms Engram, TN-gram, and FactorEngram across the compared table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters.
Combined with Ember, Chorus reduces table-optimizer memory by 99.2% versus AdamW without degrading training performance.

papers.selection_reason: Shared n-gram embeddings with layer-wise adaptation improve LLM capacity while substantially reducing memory use.
papers.title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
papers.tldr: Chorus shares n-gram embedding tables across all layers while allowing layer-specific adaptation, achieving comparable or better quality with substantially lower memory use.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.
authors: Zekai Chen, Yihan Sun, Xunkai Li, Xun Wu, Xinmo Jin, Yinlin Zhu, Haodong Lu, Xuaner Chen, Rong-Hua Li
bullets: Targets failures in agent interactions, message exchanges, and task dependencies that agent-level anomaly detection may miss.
Learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent states, messages, and dependencies.
Uses source-aware attribution to localize responsible execution elements and selects minimal repairs.
Experiments across five MAS benchmarks show a 60.2% improvement in root-cause localization accuracy and consistent task-recovery gains over strong safeguards.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the diagnosis and repair of failures in LLM-based multi-agent systems, a key challenge in LLM agent research.
