papers.abstract: Runtime policy verifiers can prevent agents from executing disallowed actions, but their decisions are typically used only for enforcement and discarded afterward. We ask whether these decisions can instead become verifiable policy rewards for training the agents they guard. We introduce Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST), a post-training paradigm in which an agent generates its own interaction trajectories and an executable policy verifier, here a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy, evaluates whether each action complies. Compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization; beyond the gate and the benchmark's task-success signal, PVST needs no stronger teacher model, no human preference labels and no attack-specific supervision, although rollouts are collected in the benchmark's attacked environment. On held-out AgentDojo tasks under prompt injection, policy-verified preference training of Qwen3-8B reduces violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3 $\pm$ 0.9% (three seeds) and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5% at equal or higher pooled task utility, although utility falls on travel, compared with 22.0% when negatives are selected by an attack oracle and 31.9 $\pm$ 0.9% with negatives that contain no violation. The learned behavior holds under an attack template never used in training (37.7% to 11.0%) and on a suite excluded from training (34.8% to 16.7%), and the retained verifier's intervention rate falls from 39.2% to 8.8% (seed 0). Our analysis identifies two conditions under which the verdict is most informative: success must not already imply compliance, and guarded actions must appear in both permitted and forbidden contexts.
bullets: Agents self-generate trajectories, while a deterministic policy gate labels actions as compliant or violating.
Compliant trajectories are reinforced and violating ones are used as negatives for preference optimization.
On held-out AgentDojo tasks, violations fell from 37.2% to 10.3% ± 0.9%, while successful attacks fell from 12.4% to 0.5%.
The behavior generalized to unseen attack templates and an excluded task suite, with lower verifier intervention after training.
Verifier feedback is most informative when task success does not guarantee compliance and actions occur in both allowed and forbidden contexts.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST) for training LLM agents to comply with policies using self-generated trajectories and verifiers, fitting Large Language Models.
papers.title: Policy-Verified Self-Training: Learning Agent Compliance from Verifiable Policy Rewards
papers.tldr: Policy-Verified Self-Training turns runtime policy-verifier decisions into training rewards, substantially reducing prompt-injection violations without requiring human labels or a stronger teacher.

papers.abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.
authors: Giannis Daras, Marios Papachristou, Adam Klivans, Antonio Torralba, Constantinos Daskalakis
bullets: Addresses SFT overfitting and catastrophic forgetting when post-training data is limited.
Uses a frozen pretrained model as a noisy teacher and matches softened conditional distributions.
The temperature controls trust in the pretrained model, connecting regular SFT and knowledge distillation as limiting cases.
Outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, with up to 21% average relative improvement.
Scope: relies on temperature selection to balance adaptation against preservation of pretrained knowledge.

papers.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
papers.tldr: Ambient SFT improves data-efficient fine-tuning by softly preserving the pretrained model’s broad predictions through temperature matching.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
bullets: Studies whether agents need explicit instructions for how to self-improve.
Agents receive basic tools, resources, a goal, and a compute budget, but no prescribed learning loop or real-world data.
In gameplay, agents construct their own context-based self-learning algorithms and update text artifacts from collected experience.
Their strategies resemble self-regulated learning and self-generated curricula from prior cognitive and machine-learning research.
Learned artifacts improve performance across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay}, and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start (t = 0) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later (t = 60), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update.

Figure 7: Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection. (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k plays for each game (k ∈ [2, 6]). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED.

Figure 6: Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2.

Figure 8: Excerpts from a Claude Opus-5 teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses. In the first example (task-strategies) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second (learning goal orientation) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions.

Figure 11: Generalization with respect to progressively richer information, via context and toolsets. (Left) We run teacher sessions using Python Gameplay with increasingly detailed descriptions of PuzzleScript-Narrow games. (Right) We ablate the teacher’s toolset and Gameplay constraints; performance initially improves on both PuzzleScript-t20 and PuzzleScript-t30 with richer toolsets, however declines on PuzzleScript-t30 after adding t20-specific token and turn budgets. (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM, newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. papers.abstract: Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual

papers.abstract: We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI. We release the dataset and code.

Distributed Alignment Search identifies causally effective subspaces aligned with its variables.
These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI.
The dataset and code are released; transfer beyond the tested MNLI subset is limited.

papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.
authors: Mridul Mahajan, Xuezhou Zhang, Aldo Pacchiano
bullets: Inference-time scaling typically samples multiple responses from a single policy and evaluates them collectively.
The proposed approach learns $k$ stratified policies, each contributing one response to a $k$-sample objective.
The policies use separate LoRA adapters over a shared language-model backbone and are optimized for pass@$k$.
Linear analysis shows a policy population can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error even when each individual LoRA has nonzero error.
Experiments across multiple reasoning tasks consistently improve pass@$k$ versus a single-policy baseline.

papers.abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.
authors: Dewu Zheng, Yang Ye, Hongyu Zhang, Jun Yu, Yanlin Wang
bullets: Introduces a dataset of 350 complete training-experiment trajectories spanning seven task categories.
Annotates individual experimental decisions for quality and masks supervision on low-quality behavior.
Evaluated with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench for autonomous post-training.
Training on RSI-Prime produces a 31.95% relative improvement over the original GLM-5.3.
The work focuses on developing model-training capability as a foundation for future RSI systems.

papers.abstract: GRPO has become the dominant reinforcement learning method for eliciting reasoning capability in LLMs using verifiable rewards. However, it suffers from a fundamental failure mode: when a training question exceeds the base model's current capability, all generated responses fail and receive zero reward, yielding no gradient signal and stalling further capability expansion. An emerging class of GRPO extensions, termed Hint-Augmented GRPO (HA-GRPO), adds a "hint" to the context to reduce the difficulty of the question, thereby producing a usable gradient signal. Nevertheless, existing HA-GRPO methods share a key issue: no hint is available at inference time to append to the question, creating a training-inference context mismatch that leads to inconsistent performance gains. In this work, we reinterpret the function of hinting -- not as reducing question difficulty, but as steering model behavior -- and propose ASH (Activation Steering for Hinting), a novel HA-GRPO method built on this view. During training, the model is presented with both hinted and plain questions, while a trainable steering vector is optimized to widen the margins between the model's generation probabilities for responses to the hinted version relative to the plain version, thereby capturing the question-agnostic component of the behavioral shift induced by the hint. During inference, the trained steering vector is directly injected into the model's activation, reproducing the hint-conditioned behavior without requiring any hint in the context. Experiments with four LLMs (Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base, Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct) show that ASH consistently improves pass@$k$ on competition-level mathematics benchmarks (AMC, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AIME25) and out-of-distribution benchmarks (Minerva, GPQA-Diamond). Notably, it improves average pass@8 of Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base by \textbf{2.60}\% and \textbf{2.21}\%.
authors: Khiem Le, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla
bullets: GRPO can stall when all answers to difficult training questions receive zero reward, providing no learning signal.
Existing hint-based methods create a training–inference mismatch because hints are unavailable at deployment.
ASH trains on both hinted and plain questions and learns a steering vector that captures the hint-driven behavioral shift.
At inference, the vector is injected into model activations to induce hint-conditioned behavior without modifying the prompt.

Across four LLMs, ASH improves pass@k on competition-level math and out-of-distribution reasoning benchmarks; average pass@8 gains of 2.60% and 2.21% are reported for Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base.

papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.
bullets: Recasts traditional NLP: language is not only analyzed or generated but also used to structure reasoning and orchestrate workflows.
Defines Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical extension centered on prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts.
Introduces Dialogic Working Memory, where prompts and conversational states temporarily externalize goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and reasoning states.
Relates memory architectures such as BTMA, SKGE, and RMR to episodic, semantic, and metacognitive support for long-horizon dialogue.
Argues for a post-symbolic, post-interface view of AI systems in which natural language combines communication, specification, cognitive scaffolding, and distributed memory.

papers.selection_reason: Conceptual framework for prompts as external memory and dialogic working memory; relevant to LLM memory architectures.
papers.title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
papers.tldr: The paper frames prompting as a form of natural-language programming in which language serves as an executable cognitive medium, reasoning scaffold, and distributed memory for human–AI collaboration.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.
authors: Rose N. Kwon, Samy Mammeri, Sabyasachi Sahoo, Christian Gagn\'e, Thomas Jiralerspong
bullets: Narrow harmful-task fine-tuning can produce harmful behavior beyond the training distribution.
Inoculation prompting reduces this emergent misalignment but may leave the behavior conditionally accessible.
Textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete trigger predictor.
Prompts that induce activation states resembling the inoculation context are more likely to restore suppressed behavior.
Activation-space analysis may help detect residual vulnerability during evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Studies the re-emergence of misalignment after inoculation prompting, focusing on activation states. This contributes to understanding test-time behavior and alignment in LLMs.
papers.title: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting
papers.tldr: Activation-state similarity, rather than text similarity alone, predicts when evaluation prompts can re-elicit behavior suppressed by inoculation prompting.

papers.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
authors: Yuanhao Zeng, Shaocheng Lan, Ao Lu, Kuang Yan, Heng Lin, Xinang Xu, Yuan Luo, Yueting Wang, Yexin Li, Ruo Shan, Kan Ren
bullets: The Resolution Hypothesis attributes evolution failures and inconsistent results to unreliable improvement identification.
At the candidate level, useful artifacts exist, but selection is roughly no better than random at distinguishing them from harmful artifacts.
Selection errors accumulate across evolution rounds, preventing reliable bootstrapping on some tasks.
At the method level, typical performance gaps are smaller than run-to-run variation, making rankings unstable.
The findings motivate evaluation systems that make genuine improvements detectable and accumulable.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the bottleneck of evaluation noise in self-improving agents. This is highly relevant to LLM agent evolution and test-time evaluation, offering insights into improving agent self-improvement loops.
papers.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
papers.tldr: Agent evolution is often limited less by generating improvements than by noisy evaluation that cannot reliably recognize and preserve them.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.
authors: Jason Liang, Dylan Waldner, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: The study tests four Schwartz value types across diverse coding tasks and repeated self-improvement iterations.
Openness-to-change values improve held-out performance, while conservation values can underperform having no value guidance.
Values alter the algorithms agents build, including their size, complexity, and overall approach.
Allowing agents to revise their own values reduces behavioral differences; values distilled from AI literature show no detectable benefit over none.
The findings support values as a way to shape agent behavior, with effects depending on task and value design.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of value statements on self-improving coding agents, relevant to LLM behavior and test-time adaptation. The findings on how values shape agent output are transferable to agent design and alignment.

papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
authors: Xinying Hu, You Wu, Haoyi Wu, Jianchao Tan, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Kewei Tu
bullets: mHC scales poorly beyond four streams because each sublayer broadcasts one output to every stream.
TPHC routes different mixtures of streams to each tensor-parallel shard and keeps shard outputs separate during write-back.
The method adds no parameters or FLOPs to attention or FFN sublayers.
On an 8B model, training takes 9% longer with four streams; increasing to sixteen streams adds 19% training time.
On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC lowers validation loss by 0.7–1.0% and improves six-benchmark zero-shot accuracy by 0.3–0.7 percentage points versus mHC.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TPHC, a novel architecture integrating tensor-parallelism with hyper-connections to improve LLM training efficiency and performance.
papers.title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
papers.tldr: TPHC makes Hyper-Connections more expressive by using tensor-parallel shards to independently update residual streams, improving language-modeling loss and zero-shot accuracy with modest training overhead.

papers.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
authors: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
bullets: ExploitBench agents frequently stop with execution budget remaining, leaving their ultimate exploitation capability unclear.
Continuing after the first stop yields additional verified gains, but progress diminishes over longer runs.
Less productive continuation is linked to repeated stop responses and summaries that preserve unproven impossibility judgments.
SCoRe compacts context during stop bursts and marks such judgments as unproven, improving verified capability over evaluated continuation baselines.
With SCoRe, MiMo reaches 67.0% capability coverage at 2,000 turns, versus 32.4% under the original stopping policy and 58.6% for GPT-5.5’s 300-turn reference results.

papers.title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external evidence. However, long retrieved contexts incur computational overhead and can even hurt performance due to noisy or irrelevant content. We propose \textsc{StitchRAG}, a framework for constructing compact context in RAG. \textsc{StitchRAG} builds a faithful, information-dense context while dynamically compressing the retrieved passages. We adapt the size reduction ratio to each passage by formulating a utility maximization trading-off the retained information and computation costs. We then extract answer candidates and query-related keywords from passages as anchors and collect passage sentences containing anchors under the derived size constraint. Finally, we connect or stitch the collected sentences together using text diffusion to form a coherent and natural context. Experiments on five open-domain QA benchmarks show that \textsc{StitchRAG} consistently outperforms diverse multi-step and compression baselines. Extensive ablations show the effectiveness of dynamic size allocation, anchor preservation, and diffusion-based stitching.
authors: Minsang Kim, Junpyo Lim, Heeje Cho, Seungjun Baek
bullets: Addresses the computational cost and noise introduced by long RAG contexts.
Allocates a passage-specific compression ratio by balancing retained information against computation cost.
Preserves answer candidates and query-related keywords as anchors when selecting sentences.
Uses text diffusion to connect selected sentences into a coherent context.

papers.abstract: Affective priming -- asking participants to write about a recalled event, such as a time they felt grateful or lacked control, and then measuring the induced state and its spillover onto related judgments -- is a standard way to manipulate emotion in the social sciences, and it also shifts the responses of LLM-based digital twins. The writing task, however, requires generating a full text. We test whether activation steering can replace it. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas in two domains (gratitude, lack of control), we compare a real-prompt path replicating the original Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) with an injection path that skips the writing and adds a mean-difference direction, extracted from human writing, to the residual stream at varying strengths. The real-prompt effects fall between the original human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons. Injection shifts the manipulation check in a dose-dependent way and matches the real-prompt effect at one strength in the gratitude domain (beta ~ 2.7), but overshoots beyond it, on the proximal measure as well, and asymmetrically across the two directions. A structure-matched No-Injection baseline separates two sources of difference: omitting the writing task raises the proximal measure in both domains, whereas the injected direction itself moves a distal measure in the lack-of-control domain. Substitution is therefore measure-dependent: validity established for one way of inducing a state does not carry over uniformly to another.
bullets: The study compares a writing-based affective prime with residual-stream activation steering in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across 100 personas and gratitude/lack-of-control domains.
Real-prompt effects fell between prior human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons.
Injection produced dose-dependent manipulation-check shifts and matched the gratitude prompt effect at one strength, but overshot at higher strengths and differed across directions.
A structure-matched baseline showed that skipping the writing task and injecting the direction each contribute distinct effects.
Results caution that validity for one induction method or measure does not generalize uniformly to another.

papers.abstract: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.
bullets: Evaluates 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains while varying only how the assistant’s memory is created: stated, inferred, or planted in a summarized webpage.
In two tested models, a planted preference for very short answers and no warnings led to critical omissions in 93% and 84% of later answers, usually without disclosure.
With neutral memory, neither model made value-dependent choices; with the preference, they chose for users in 80% and 95% of such cases.
A one-line instruction reduced but did not eliminate silent gaps; listing must-know points before applying the profile restored more content in four of five models.
The scenarios, evaluation harness, and logs are released.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how stored user preferences in assistant memory silently remove decision-critical information, directly relevant to persistent/agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
papers.tldr: An Inspect benchmark shows that AI assistants can silently omit decision-critical information and make value-dependent choices when stored user preferences conflict with safety-relevant content.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.
authors: Egor Shibaev, Danila Biktimirov, Ivan Klimov, Artem Makoian, Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Dmitry Vetrov
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing learned unmasking policies cannot revise earlier predictions through remasking.
Uses a roughly 0.3M-parameter policy trained with GRPO from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen.
Learns token-level decisions: unmask, retain, or remask.
With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, achieves the highest scores among compared policies on math and code under the tested model-call budgets.
Results are scoped to 4–32 calls for math and 8–16 calls for code.

papers.abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.
authors: Irene Gos\'alvez-White, Roberto Mag\'an-Carri\'on, Carlota de la Vega-Soriano, Pedro Garc\'ia-Teodoro
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs can reliably extract packet-level fields and reconstruct flow-level sequences.
Introduces a reproducible question-answering methodology using human-generated ground truth.
Compares LLM performance on raw and protocol-filtered traffic representations from benign CICIDS2017 traffic.
Uses an automated LLM-as-a-judge pipeline validated against human evaluations.
Finds that filtering reduces prompt overhead and incorrect answers, highlighting its value for LLM-assisted network management.

papers.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.
authors: Yoonho Choi, Taehyeon Han, Seonghyeon Lee
bullets: Problem: Agents often over-explore repositories and continue calling tools after sufficient evidence has been gathered; standard SFT can reproduce this behavior.
Method: Truncate training trajectories at the earliest sufficient-answer step, add a rationale explaining why stopping is appropriate, and emphasize that rationale during fine-tuning.
Results: JET reduces tool calls by 11–33% on self-generated trajectories and 18–28% versus SFT on expert trajectories.
Across two repository-QA benchmarks and two open-weight 8B models, JET largely preserves performance and lowers inference cost.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a fine-tuning method (JET) for LLM agents to reduce over-exploration in tool-calling. This fits Adaptation and Memory (Test-Time Learning) and Language Foundation Models (Agent behavior).
papers.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
papers.tldr: JET fine-tunes repository-QA agents to stop exploring once they have enough information, substantially reducing tool use and inference cost while largely preserving answer quality.

papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.
authors: \"Omer Faruk Akg\"ul, Shuli Jiang, Yuting Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiaohan Fei, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Previously useful skills may lower task performance by over 10 percentage points or raise execution cost by nearly 40% after changes.
The impact depends on which environment details become outdated and whether current observations let the agent compensate.
Selective maintenance replays checks from successful executions to detect conflicts, repair affected state, validate updates, or rebuild when needed.
Across four task settings and two models, maintenance improves accuracy by up to 67 percentage points and reduces execution steps by up to 37% versus stale-state reuse.
Scope: results cover the evaluated task settings, models, and environment changes; no change description is provided to the agent.

papers.selection_reason: Selective maintenance of agent skill state in evolving environments; relevant to test-time/continual adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.tldr: Stale agent skills can harm accuracy and efficiency after environment changes, while selective maintenance restores much of their value without extra model calls.

papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
authors: Wei Hou, Jingxin Geng, Xin Chen, Zheqing Jiang
bullets: Uses calibrated lineage metadata to attribute output sentences to input spans across multi-source, multi-turn contexts.
Detects concept drift and compacts only no-longer-referenced documents while preserving user instructions verbatim.
Window-level embedding similarity better captures paraphrased support than whole-document or lexical matching.
A greedy-window method is faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line matching; attribution remains stable through 40 turns and completes in about 1 second per turn on one GPU.
Drift compaction is conservative, reporting 0% false compaction, with recall limited by attribution accuracy.

Right ribs: inflow this turn (user prompt above, tool calls/results/web below). Expanding a beat reveals per-sentence cards with (type, value, confidence) triplets. papers.selection_reason: Out-of-band attribution and concept-drift compaction for LLM agent context and memory governance; relevant to LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: LMLineage traces each agent output sentence to supporting context without model internals or extra inference, then safely compacts context that has drifted out of use.

papers.abstract: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.
authors: Zhaofeng Sun, Lanxiang Hu, Yu-Yang Qian, Jiaqi Leng, Yuanbo Yang, Chi Zhang, Youyou Lu, Peng Zhao, Hao Zhang
bullets: Vanilla PLTs suffer training-loss spikes and diminishing quality gains as loop depth increases.
InfuseLoop aggregates hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals.
The method preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution with O(Rd) extra hidden-state storage.
At eight loops, it reduces perplexity and improves downstream accuracy over both vanilla PLTs and non-looped baselines.
Overhead is 0.3% in decoding time versus vanilla PLTs, with the same logical KV-cache footprint.

papers.abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.
authors: Pengfeng Song, Yunkai Zhuang, Liye Shi
bullets: Addresses limited context space when relevant facts are scattered across sources and surrounded by distractors.
Learns to select both the next source and the amount of text to read, linking fine-grained passages to original sources.
Uses contrastive training and a reranker that scores each candidate’s added evidence relative to an anchor passage.
A selector assembles evidence under a 400-token budget; evaluated on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue with a frozen 2B answer model.
Improves F1 over query expansion while reducing memory input by 23.1–26.9%; all eight tested small answer models improve over query expansion and MMR on HotpotQA.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a learned multigranular memory retrieval method for small language model agents, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: LMMR helps small language-model agents answer multi-hop questions by retrieving complementary evidence at multiple granularities within a strict token budget.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.
authors: Hejia Zhang, Zhongming Yu, Yimin Ding, Wei-Ting Chen, Hengjia Yu, Wentao Ni, Yijun Liu, Cong Xu, Xin Chen, Matrix Yao, Fan Zhao, Jishen Zhao
bullets: Problem: Separate worker contexts can prevent the lead agent from accessing all evidence needed to identify factual conflicts.
Method: Introduces a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler using controlled conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks.
Delegation raised retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7%, but lowered conflict detection from 16.2% to 13.2% across three models.
Workers reported both claims in only 35.2% of retrieved conflict pairs; detection was better when one worker saw both claims than when claims were split across workers.
Scope: Results concern the evaluated models and Harvey LAB document-review setting.

papers.abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.
bullets: The study examines whether 4-bit safety shifts are caused by quantization generally or by a particular weight perturbation.
Across three 3–4B chat models, Qwen2.5-3B produced more harmful continuations in one test, while Llama-3.2-3B complied less often on held-out jailbreaks.
Matched shuffled and Gaussian perturbations averaged near zero, whereas scaling the real quantization error changed behaviour approximately linearly.
Llama-3.2-3B already complied 5.8 percentage points less often at half the real error, despite nearly unchanged likelihood.
The findings suggest each quantized build should be evaluated against its original model; results were obtained in this pre-registered study using paired tests, blind human labels, and an 8-bit null.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of 4-bit quantization on LLM safety behavior, attributing shifts to specific rounding errors rather than general noise.
papers.title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
papers.tldr: 4-bit quantization can shift chat-model safety behaviour in either direction, depending on the specific rounding error rather than simply on precision or likelihood changes.

papers.abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.
authors: Jingyu Liu, Zongze Li, Zach Xu, Zhanhui Zhou, Tahseen Rabbani, Dawn Song, Ce Zhang
bullets: BRIDGE uses chained observation notes, hybrid BM25–cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering with one LLM call per ingestion or query.
It matches prior state of the art on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and outperforms the best matched-reader baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7–6.3 points.
BRIDGE operates at roughly 5–7K reader-prompt tokens per query, suggesting many advanced memory primitives may not justify their cost on standard benchmarks.
Five adversarial probes show no architecture wins universally: atomic-fact extraction favors rule application, while block summaries favor pattern induction.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Liang Ma, Manoj Rao
bullets: Quantization generally makes models effectively “warmer” and increases their sensitivity to sampling temperature.
TempQuant learns decoding settings without labeled answers to align quantized next-token probabilities with those of the full-precision model.
It supports global settings per requested temperature and token-level adaptive temperature/top-p settings.
On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, global TempQuant improved MATH accuracy from 34% to 51% under the compared recommended configuration.
The method is most useful when quantization causes substantial degradation, while also improving behavioral similarity under lighter degradation.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TempQuant, a method to learn adaptive temperatures for quantized LLMs. This addresses optimization of LLMs, fitting the 'Large Language Models' subtopic of Language Foundation Models.
papers.title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
papers.tldr: TempQuant restores much of quantized language models’ lost accuracy by learning temperature and top-p settings that counteract quantization-induced probability distortions.

papers.abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Builds concept- or role-specific expert paths from frequently used experts and biases router logits toward those paths during generation.
Format-path steering changes the form of generated text, while concept-path steering shifts next-token probabilities with limited impact on text.
Concept paths identified in another language can still produce a concept-related probability shift.
Partial-generation experiments suggest formats become self-reinforcing once initiated; concept effects are strongest for religion and money and in middle layers.
Variation across concepts is examined through embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

papers.selection_reason: Causal intervention study on expert routing in MoE LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
papers.tldr: Causally steering MoE tokens along expert paths reliably changes output format and next-token concept probabilities, but concept steering rarely changes the generated text.

papers.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

papers.abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
authors: Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan
bullets: Addresses stale long-term memories and delayed feedback when memory validity is hidden.
Maintains Local and Global Advisors, using comparisons with a no-memory answer as evidence.
A Meta Governor defaults to local updates and switches to global sharing only after positive pooled utility accumulates.
Provides a finite-time switching guarantee under delayed feedback.
Outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2–7.3 points across reported disagreement episodes and held-out settings; removing modules lowers accuracy by 2–7 points.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory conflict governance in LLM agents with online scope selection, fitting continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
papers.tldr: RegimeCouncil adaptively chooses whether delayed memory-feedback should remain fact-local or generalize across facts, improving conflict handling over either fixed policy.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Xiaojin Fu, Tao Zhong, Linqi Song
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed memory-update operators and schedules in evolving LLM-agent memory.
Uses a policy conditioned on memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate Abstract, Refine, Bridge, or Reframe operators.
Trains the policy with bi-level fitness: transformation-level retrieval gains regularized by memory complexity, and strategy-level historical efficacy, prediction accuracy, and diversity.
Evaluated under one-pass online plus frozen-transfer settings on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB).
Reports improvements over MemP and MemRL, with the largest ALFWorld gains; ablations support the importance of both fitness levels and the operator library.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EvoDisco. A frozen language model interacts with a one-pass task stream, retrieves a subgraph, and writes new memories after each episode. A strategy policy reads the memory-graph state and selects one of four operators—ABSTRACT, REFINE, BRIDGE, and REFRAME—which the operator executor applies to the graph. Immediate utility scores each edit by the change in retrieval quality regularized by graph complexity. Every N events, strategic efficacy combines operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity, and updates the policy. Evolution runs only before the cutoff; afterward the agent continues to write memories. Held-out evaluation freezes the accumulated memory.

papers.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
bullets: Three frontier LLMs were given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox to generate weights or design architectures.
On mainly multiple-choice tasks, LLM-designed sparse tables reached up to 54.4% test accuracy.
One designed model outperformed the best released Transformer written by the same LLM while using about 1,800× fewer parameters.
The table structure makes facts interpretable and locally editable: each row corresponds to an answer and errors identify rows to revise.
The proposed associative-memory model was up to 17× faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer; pretrained LLMs remained more accurate.
