papers.abstract: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.
bullets: Evaluates stale retrieval on 892 real-world updating facts with source-derived validity labels.
Shows retrieval rankings can look identical even when reader accuracy differs by up to 65.6 points without dates.
Introduces Contamination@5, which identifies stale-memory failures that current@1/current@5 miss.
Finds removing lexical anchors severely harms freshness, while entity resolution on writing and querying recovers most of the loss.
Compares supersession handling in Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem, and ERASE, and releases data, evaluation tools, and baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The keying ladder as the lexical anchor is withdrawn. The inventory-based keying rungs are indistinguishable at a=0, and at a=1 the gazetteer falls 65.8 points below the oracle; the entity linker (handed the alias inventory) tracks the oracle, while the two mechanisms deployed memory systems use do not. The oracle keys perfectly but still retrieves by similarity, so the two rungs that resolve the query as well are not bounded by it — and the upper one, which resolves symmetrically with a complete alias table, is close to flat across the whole axis (0.994 to 0.912). Withdrawing the anchor costs almost nothing to a system that resolves entities on both paths.

Figure 1: StaleBench in one picture. (a) Real updating facts become a chronological stream with one value-agnostic query per fact and a source-defined current label; two knobs set how hard same-fact detection is. (b) A policy is store-all retrieval, optionally time-aware, or retention = a keyer (is this a fact already stored?) × a mechanism (overwrite, or invalidate and keep), run on the write path, the read path, or both. (c) Each top-k is scored by retrieval metrics, by what its text says, and by what a reader answers.

Figure 3: Left: retrieval current@1 against reader accuracy for the primary reader; the dashed line is what a retrieval metric would predict. The arrow is the controlled pair — two keyers that return the same statement at rank 1 on every query of this configuration, so they share an x exactly and the vertical distance is what contamination of ranks 2–5 costs. Right: constructed contexts, where contamination is manipulated rather than observed.

Table 5: Three deployed systems and ERASE, reimplemented, under the rungs’ harness, streams and encoder (test subsample, n=150 facts, p=0.5). cur@1 attributes the top memory to its source statement, by text scores what it says, cont.@5 is contamination@5 by text, and reader is qwen2.5:14b answering from the system’s own top-5. The Mem0 and Graphiti rows have qwen2.5:14b in the loop. The lower block is the ladder on the same streams. Per-system tables, gates and the second adjudicator are in Appendix K.
Table 6: Positioning: what each line of work measures, and what it cannot see.

Table 3: current@1 as the lexical anchor is withdrawn (a = alias_p: the probability a non-introducing statement uses a short form). Test split, p=0.5, every policy re-tuned on val at every level. The last column is the keying deficit at a=1: points of current@1 below the true-key oracle, which isolates the same-fact decision from the retrieval difficulty that aliasing also creates (and which the oracle pays too). The oracle is a write-path oracle — perfect same-fact detection, ordinary similarity retrieval — so it is an upper bound only within that family, and the rungs that also resolve the query post a negative deficit against it (§5.2).

Table 19: Each policy’s own top-5 handed to qwen2.5:14b (anchored, n=150; rows carry the harness’s policy ids — reconsolidation is the threshold keyer, lexical-key the gazetteer, fuzzy-key the fuzzy linker, fuzzy-rw-key symmetric keying; the system’s row is its own rewritten memories in its own words, from the 0.1.118 run — 2.0.11 is in the text). as retrieved is what a deployment gets; the next two pairs apply this paper’s read-path fix post hoc to those same contexts, resolving the query through the keyer of §5.2 and then keeping one memory per resolved entity, at no ingestion and no model call. The two middle cur@1 columns are identical wherever the readers beside them differ by up to 1.000 against 0.293: the retrieval metric cannot see the difference the reader is made of. The last column keeps the oldest memory per entity instead of the freshest. Because facts arrive as they become true, freshest-is-current is free here (150/150 facts); withdrawing it leaves only what each write path had already removed, so the column reads near zero for anything that stores every version and near one for anything that merges on write. It is a write-path purity measure that uses no identifiers and no timestamps in its favour, and it is where the deployed system is priced.

Table 7: Where each policy’s errors go in the anchor-free regime (a=1, test, p=0.5). contamination@5 is shown with current@5 because it is not monotone (§3): the entity linker’s near-zero contamination is partly the absence of any version of the fact, not only the absence of conflict.

Table 17: Mem0 scored under the same harness as the idealized rungs, on the same streams, with the same encoder (test subsample, n=150 facts, p=0.5; anchored unless the column says otherwise; contamination@5 by id). The rightmost column is the system’s own decision histogram over its 329 ingestion calls. The library version is part of the result, not provenance: see the text.

Table 18: Every (release, vector store) pair we probed, and whether its numbers are usable. writes: the system can record its own ADD/UPDATE decisions. retrieval: a hand-scored query returns the right fact first from what the store holds. Two pairs fail, in opposite halves, and both produce plausible-looking metrics that measure the backend rather than the system — which is why the selection of runs quoted in this section is made by this table and not by which result file was written last.

Table 16: A language model as the same-fact keyer, against the mechanical rungs (test, p=0.5). For each arriving statement the model is shown the top-4 stored candidates by cosine and asked which, if any, describes the same fact; it sees statement text only — never an id, a key, or a timestamp. % split is the retrieval-independent share of facts scattered over more than one slot (§G).

Table 20: The second deployed system. Graphiti (graphiti-core 0.29.2, FalkorDB, qwen2.5:14b adjudicator, MiniLM encoder) on the identical 150-fact streams, scored by id, by text and at the reader (qwen2.5:14b, own top-5), by three read paths over the same stored graph: the library’s default search (as returned), the same hits with non-invalidated edges ranked first (the temporal-KG rung’s read path), and invalidated edges dropped. Ladder rows are the same stream; contamination@5 is by id here and by text in Table 5. An empty reader cell means that arm was not run.

Table 10: The two temporal signals, corrupted separately and together (test, p=0.5; current@1, mean over 3 permutation seeds; hyperparameters are the val-tuned values of the clean regime, since a deployment cannot retune for a corruption it does not know it has). clock permuted: timestamps permuted across statements, arrival order intact — unreliable logging, imports, clock skew. arrival permuted: arrival order permuted, each statement keeping its own timestamp — delayed or out-of-order ingestion. Every time-aware or retention policy reads one signal and is blind to the other; with both corrupted nothing recovers. The per-seed spread is at most 5.8 points in any cell.
Table 8: current@1 by per-fact version count (test, p=0.5). The cheap fix collapses on the facts that changed most — exactly the motivating population.

Table 9: A late stale report: for a fraction q of the 468 test facts the final version arrives before its predecessor, timestamps intact (p=0.5; current@1, mean of 3 draws). Overwrite loses its margin in proportion to q with contamination@5 fixed at 0.000: one confidently stale memory, not a contradiction.

Table 21: A second adjudicator model. Mem0 0.1.118 (chroma) under its stock, user-centric extraction prompt and under a prompt that admits facts about any named entity, each driven by qwen2.5:14b and by glm-4.6; Graphiti with both models, as returned and with valid edges first. Same 150-fact streams as Table 17; contamination@5 by id. slots for Graphiti is active/total edges; the last column counts UPDATE+DELETE decisions (Mem0) or invalidations (Graphiti).

Readers are qwen2.5:14b, glm-4.6; the last two columns repeat both readers with the stored year surfaced in the context. Retrieval hyperparameters are inherited from the val tuning of §5.1 and are never tuned against reader accuracy. The two read-path rows are the controlled pair: identical retrieval columns except contamination@5, because they return the same statement at rank 1 for all 468 queries of this configuration.
Table 1: Terms used throughout.

Table 2: TempLAMA test split (468 facts), paraphrase p=0.5. Mean over queries; brackets = bootstrap 95% CIs; tuned hyperparameters from val (k=2 for time-rerank, τ=0.60 for the threshold keyer). Reconsolidation (τ ) is the threshold keyer and Lexical key the gazetteer keyer, both with overwrite. All four pre-specified paired comparisons (sign-flip permutation, Holm-corrected; the family is hard-coded before test evaluation and its store-all comparator is selected on val) are significant at p < 10−3. Two go against our own policies: time-rerank > cosine, and the best store-all fix > the threshold keyer on current@1; two go with them: the threshold keyer < the best store-all fix on contamination@5, and oracle > threshold keyer.

Table 12: Same-fact decisions scored directly as a clustering of statements against the true fact partition, independent of any retriever. Merge err. counts slots holding statements about more than one fact; % split is the fraction of facts scattered across several slots.

Table 14: current@1 on the 7,078-statement corpus (6,083 distractor statements from fact keys that are never queried). Keyers hold either an open-world inventory (the 468 queried subjects) or a closed-world one (all 2,995 subjects in the stream). Store-all policies use no inventory, so their columns coincide.
Table 13: Retention mechanism at fixed keyer (p=0.5): invalidation matches overwrite’s accuracy and contamination while keeping every superseded statement recoverable.

Table 15: The anchor-free ladder at a=1 with short forms drawn from Wikidata aliases and English Wikipedia redirects instead of generated mechanically (test, p=0.5; current@1, and the keying deficit in points against the write-path oracle of the same configuration; every tunable re-tuned on val, whose own inventory covers 288 of its subjects). natural: a subject with no real short form stays anchored (270 of the 467 distinct subjects behind the 468 test facts have one; 59.6% of alias-eligible statements are aliased). natural+fallback: such a subject takes the mechanical forms instead (95.1%), the like-for-like comparison with Table 3.

Table 22: The third deployed system. LangMem 0.0.30 (LangChain’s long-term memory: one structured-output call per statement returns the memories to insert or patch; inserts and updates on, deletes off, as installed) on the identical 150-fact streams with the benchmark’s MiniLM encoder as its store index, scored by id, by text and at the reader (qwen2.5:14b, own top-5). Ladder rows are the same stream. contamination@5 is by text, since the library rewrites what it stores and adds memories no statement wrote.

Table 23: The fourth mechanism: ERASE, rewrite-on-arrival (Li et al., 2025), reimplemented from the paper because no release pins it. When a statement arrives, the 5 stored facts nearest to it are retrieved and one model call decides, for each, KEEP, REWRITE or DELETE; the statement is then inserted. Same 150-fact streams, MiniLM encoder, reader (qwen2.5:14b, own top-5). contamination@5 is by text, since a rewrite can keep the superseded value’s string in a past-tense clause.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.
authors: Qi Chen, Zifeng Cheng, Zhiwei Jiang, Qing Gu
bullets: Addresses pseudo-autoregressive behavior and function-word-first bias in diffusion language models.
Uses token-level gradients to identify semantic tokens and prioritizes preserving them during progressive masking.
Reweights semantic-token losses to reinforce their early prediction.
Matches strong autoregressive baselines in text writing and code generation while improving semantic coherence.
Achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.
bullets: Across three instruction-tuned model families, the best probing direction was not the best steering direction for truthfulness or sentiment.
This separation held in 59 of 60 layer–model–concept combinations and also under rotation-based steering.
An intermediate direction sometimes outperformed the mean difference for sentiment steering, but the gain was unstable and depended on text matching, layer, and operator.
Probe directions transferred across models more reliably than steering directions.
Steering toward “unknown” increased abstention mainly on uncertain errors, with little correction of otherwise answerable errors.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates probing versus steering directions in LLM hidden states, relevant to understanding and controlling large language models.
papers.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
papers.tldr: Probing and steering generally favor different hidden-state directions: probes favor covariance-adjusted directions, while steering favors directions closer to the mean difference.

papers.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.
authors: Lucia Licakova, Niklas Schmidinger, Lukas Hauzenberger, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Depth recurrence increases effective depth but normally grows autoregressive KV memory with each iteration.
The authors evaluate looped Transformer hybrids using recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks plus periodic attention anchors.
A Parcae-style recurrent workspace and stabilising adapter are tested to constrain recurrence and improve stability.
Recurrent KV replay trains later iterations to reuse KV states written by selected earlier iterations.
Hybrid quality depends on sufficiently frequent attention anchors and the choice of recurrent mixer; KV replay retains near-baseline performance while reducing cache sharing overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Depth-recurrent language model architectures with KV replay reduce memory, relevant to LLM architecture and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
papers.tldr: The study reduces depth-recurrent language-model decoding memory by sharing key-value (KV) caches across recurrence iterations, with recurrent KV replay preserving performance close to separate-cache baselines.

papers.abstract: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.
bullets: Compares AdamW, diagonal AdaGrad, two Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon under a common forward-KL objective and fixed budget.
Evaluates four dense Qwen student–teacher pairs across scales.
AdamW generally achieves the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale.
SOAP often matches AdamW’s KL but has substantial trainer-time overhead; Shampoo variants vary by model pair.
Optimizer conclusions depend on the distillation objective and feasible systems recipe.

papers.title: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
papers.tldr: Pretraining optimizer improvements do not automatically transfer to short-horizon KL distillation, where AdamW remains the strongest overall quality–time baseline.

papers.abstract: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.
authors: Ruihong Zeng, Puning Yang, Jinghui Zhang, Shen Gao, Xiangliang Zhang, Preslav Nakov, Xiuying Chen
bullets: Introduces Role-playing Unlearning: removing target-role style and knowledge, not just factual information.
Maps roles to more independent Mixture-of-Experts subspaces for finer control and interpretability.
Uses specialization and disentanglement losses to separate role-specific expert distributions and capabilities.
RoleBench-Unlearn evaluates the task across multiple backbone LLMs.
Experiments report precise target-role forgetting with better preservation of non-target roles’ language quality, knowledge, and persona consistency.

papers.selection_reason: MoE-based role unlearning for LLMs; relevant to LLM architecture and controllable generation.
papers.title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
papers.tldr: RoleMoE enables interpretable, selective unlearning of target personas in LLMs while preserving the capabilities and behaviors of other roles.

papers.abstract: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it. We fixed the rules in advance and ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without this reminder, using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness. The reminder made no measurable difference: across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with it and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% interval [-8.3, +6.3], exact McNemar p=1.0). The primary outcome (a documented deviation from our preregistration), the first 48 pairs, was 29/48 with memory against 25/48 without (+8.3 points, [-2.1, +18.3], p=0.22); the extension of 50 tasks, decided after that result, pointed the other way (18/50 against 23/50, -10.0 points, p=0.125), so the sign did not replicate. With 19% of tasks flipping between two identical no-memory runs, the combined interval excludes harms larger than about 8 points and gains larger than about 6, and the design had 80% power only for effects of about +-12 points or more. The model almost never wrote notes (2 of 16 and 4 of 32 runs), and memory cost context: the first request is larger and something was injected at only 47% to 65% of compactions. The registered secondary, repeated actions per compaction, was also null. Two directional hypotheses found on Modal did not replicate on Kaggle. We also report an A/A calibration and a validity funnel (129 tasks, 105 valid). Together these results show that single-run memory claims on task sets of this size sit inside run-to-run noise. The treatment is a harness mechanism and does not test agent-written memory.
bullets: The study tested a fixed reminder mechanism that reinserts the agent’s last finding after context loss.
Across 98 tasks, 47 were solved with reminders versus 48 without; the estimated effect was compatible with ordinary run-to-run noise.
An initial 48-task result favored reminders, but a later 50-task extension reversed direction and did not replicate the finding.
The agent rarely wrote notes, and reminder injection occurred in only 47%–65% of compactions; repeated actions per compaction were also null.
The results do not evaluate agent-written memory and suggest that task sets of this size cannot reliably support single-run memory claims.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD
authors: Zhi Xu, Yinqi Wu, Feng Zhang, Xiaotong Zhang, Hong Yu, Han Liu
bullets: Addresses training settings where ground-truth solutions are unavailable.
Generates briefs from questions alone, covering relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls without giving a final solution.
A frozen teacher uses each brief to guide the student’s on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching.
Evaluated on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 across three Qwen3 model sizes.
Both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD in these evaluations.

The initial model generates static briefs, while a saved student checkpoint generates refreshed briefs. The current student generates its solution trajectory from the question alone. The frozen teacher receives the question and brief, evaluates the same student prefixes, and provides token-level feedback.

papers.abstract: LoCoMo is a widely reported benchmark for long-term conversational memory, but published scores mix memory quality with choices of answer prompt, judge and baseline layout that are rarely reported together. We measure how much these choices move a score, and evaluate Becos, a team memory system for coding agents, as a black box under all of them: ten conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts and three LLM judges, against a whole-conversation baseline rerun under identical conditions. Changing only the judge moves a score by up to 7.2 points and changing only the answer prompt by up to 9.3. A blind human check of 150 answers finds the judges reliable when they agree, and the primary judge's errors on disputed answers working against Becos rather than for it. Becos answers from a context with 90% fewer characters than the whole conversation. Its configuration was developed on LoCoMo itself, so there is no held-out set. With gpt-4o-mini answers it scores clearly higher than the whole conversation (79.7 vs 73.0 with the short prompt, paired 95% interval for the difference +3.8 to +9.5; 88.8 vs 77.5 with a step-by-step prompt). With gpt-4.1-mini answers the two score about the same (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1). We release every answer and verdict and the scoring script.
bullets: Judge choice changes scores by up to 7.2 points, and answer-prompt choice by up to 9.3 points.
The study evaluates Becos across 10 conversations, 1,540 questions, two answer models, two prompts, and three LLM judges.
Becos outperforms the whole-conversation baseline with gpt-4o-mini, but performs about the same with gpt-4.1-mini.
A blind human check suggests judges are reliable when they agree; disputed- answer errors by the primary judge favored the baseline over Becos.
Becos was configured using LoCoMo itself, so the evaluation has no held-out set; answers, verdicts, and scoring code are released.

papers.abstract: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.
authors: Jianhao Huang, Allan Zhang, Ali Payani, Baharan Mirzasoleiman
bullets: Reasoning traces expose multi-step structure but may omit facts available through atomic supervision.
The study measures generalization to transitions seen atomically but absent from training traces.
Analysis shows the optimal weight on atomic signals grows with reasoning-chain length and falls as reasoning-trace coverage increases.
These patterns persist in a full transformer layer and are validated in controlled multi-hop and mathematical pretraining settings.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.
authors: Joshua Ryo Cheng, Thomas L. Griffiths, Jake C. Snell
bullets: Targets social biases such as name–nationality, occupation–gender, and racial stereotypes.
Uses prompt–response observations from bias benchmarks to infer a low-dimensional latent distribution.
Develops a mathematical formulation and practical reconstruction algorithm for this Bayesian inverse problem.
Demonstrates the approach on the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) in ambiguous social contexts.

papers.abstract: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.
bullets: Full attention recalls well but has quadratic training/prefill cost and a linearly growing inference cache.
The method complements the existing recent-context hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence start, enabling finer access to both early and recent tokens while remaining causal.
Recurrent and chunkwise-parallel formulations retain log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage.
Mean associative-recall accuracy improves from 76.37% to 96.12%; selected RULER retrieval scores improve from 26.97% to 50.03% at 6,144-token context.
It outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.
authors: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh, Tyler Romero, Yashas Samaga, Jacob Morrison, Iz Beltagy, Taira Anderson, Noah A. Smith, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
bullets: MoE training costs can grow with total stored parameters because of memory, communication, and kernel-launch overhead, even when active compute remains similar.
The stack replaces FSDP with DDP and adds expert, pipeline, and optimizer parallelism plus activation recomputation.
NVSHMEM-based rowwise expert parallelism and GPU-managed routing avoid dispatch/combine permutations and synchronization overhead.
Integrated MXFP8 reduces compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, while topology-agnostic checkpoints allow parallel layouts to change between runs.
On NVL8 B300 nodes, it scales from 12.9B to 1.2T parameters across up to 512 GPUs; the authors also report Token Gerrymandering and cases where communication overlap hurts kernel speed.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Throughput as total expert parameter size grows at nearly fixed active FLOPs. These preliminary measurements use an eight-layer bfloat16 (BF16) model on one 8×B300 node without pipeline parallelism (PP; Section 6); MoE uses top-4 routing, and the new MoE path uses EP8. The old, dense-oriented FSDP path loses throughput as total expert parameter size grows, whereas the new DDP+EP path keeps MoE throughput within a modest margin of its dense baseline. This is a composed-system result, not an isolated FSDP-versus-DDP or EP ablation.

Figure 5 Subsystems of the Olmo-core DDP training stack. Colors mark the layers: configuration (green) and train-module orchestration (purple) sit above the MoE model (yellow), the parallel runtimes (blue), and supporting systems (orange). Low-level libraries, kernels, communication systems, and hardware interconnects (gray) form the substrate below. The layout groups system responsibilities rather than prescribing an execution order.

Figure 59 Kernel-time breakdown, throughput, and memory across the four MXFP8 modes. The combined recipe reduces the rank-0 kernel-duration sum by a quarter. Panels (a,b) use profiled kernel durations to identify changed work; panel (c) uses unprofiled runs for throughput because tracing perturbs the launch-heavy combined path. (a) Kernel-duration sums per captured train batch on rank 0 by kernel family, means of three captured batches per mode. Teal families are the ones MXFP8 targets, gray families are not targeted, and pink is the added quantization, scale-swizzle, and dequantization work (75.5, 203.1, and 262.1 ms per batch; 3.0%, 8.0%, and 10.3% of the BF16 sum). Family sums overlap across streams and are not an additive wall-time model; the triangle marks the union of kernelbusy intervals, which shrinks by 1.3%, 16.3%, and 20.2%. (b) Change of the three targeted families relative to BF16; the bars in each row are, top to bottom, dense GEMM, grouped GEMM, and EP transport, in the colors of (a). The EP-transport family includes barrier kernels; the payload-moving kernels alone fall by 41% in both the MLP+EP and combined modes, so part of the combined −50% is reduced waiting. (c) Throughput change over three fresh distributed jobs per mode; bars are means of the three ten-step windows and dots are the repetitions. The BF16 reference is 54.74K tokens/s/GPU and the largest sample standard deviation is 0.14K, smaller than the dot markers. (d) Peak active memory change in the same runs from the 103.40 GiB BF16 reference. Four B300 GPUs, EP = 4, uniform routing, and identical initialized weights, inputs, and routing in every mode (Table 26); these are systems measurements at one operating point, not training-quality evidence (Section 11.3.5).

Figure 2 Equal FLOPs do not imply equal HBM traffic. The forward fused up/gate and down GEMMs of a dense FFN with intermediate width Kh are compared with N experts of intermediate width h, selecting K per token. Here N = 64, K = 4, and the model width and expert intermediate width are d = h = 4096. (a) GEMM-side HBM byte categories, each normalized separately to dense. These ratios are not additive: each category contributes according to its absolute byte volume, not equally. The intermediate row counts up/gate output writes and down input reads, excluding the pointwise activation’s own accesses. (b) Analytical ceilings in bfloat16 (BF16), normalized to peak FLOPs, with balanced routes and one HBM read/write per operand/result. Each curve adds the two GEMM times; pointwise activation, packing, combine, network, and backward costs are excluded. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities; assumptions are detailed in Appendix A.8.

Figure 3 A FLOP advantage can shrink or survive in wall time. This illustrative, simplified comparison uses two power-law-shaped loss traces that run for 10,000 equal-token steps and end at the same loss. Panel (a) assigns the 3.5B-active/13B-total MoE a normalized useful-FLOP cost of 1 per step, versus 2 for the 7B dense model. Panel (b) maps the same MoE loss samples onto two hypothetical runtimes: normalized wall-time costs of 1.85 for inefficient infrastructure and 1.2 for optimized infrastructure, versus 2 for dense. The corresponding time-to-target advantages are only 2/1.85 ≈ 1.08× and 2/1.2 ≈ 1.67×. All costs and loss curves are illustrative assumptions, not measurements or predictions for an Olmo run.

Figure 1 MoE and Dense Transformer blocks. Both blocks retain attention and residual connections. The dense block (right) applies the same feed-forward network to every token. The MoE block (left) illustrates one token routed to K = 2 of N = 4 routed experts—experts 0 and 2 in this example—and combines their outputs with an optional always-active shared expert before the residual addition. Here, K = 2 is a per-token choice. Other tokens can select different experts, so a training batch can collectively use all N experts.

Figure 74 Captured timelines show the two submission regimes. Both Nsight Systems profiles run the same eight-layer development model (128 routed experts, top-8, one shared expert, EP8, BF16, two sequences per rank microbatch) on eight B300 GPUs; only the expert-parallel path differs. This capture predates and differs from the reduced profiling workload of Table 46. In the synchronized trace (a), the per-block host wait appears as cudaEventSynchronize in the CUDA API lane, the CPU and GPU ranges of each forward block stay in lock step, and the GPU kernel rows show recurring gaps. In the rowwise trace (b), no host wait interrupts submission: the CPU finishes submitting the microbatch while the GPU is still executing earlier work, and the GPU-side forward blocks run back to back. Each panel is one captured instance of one rank; the two traces are separate runs, so this figure illustrates the submission mechanism rather than a controlled throughput comparison.

Figure 6 A four-GPU DDP example with no model-parallel sharding. With DP = 4, every GPU holds a static replica of the same attention layers and complete routed-expert pool, experts 0–15, while processing different input data. DDP synchronizes the gradients of these replicated weights; it does not itself shard the model shown here.

Figure 36 A host loop executes exact-size expert GEMMs. It avoids padded arithmetic, but GPU-produced row counts must become host-visible before the runtime can submit the per-expert operations. The separate streams in this conceptual drawing are not required by the method; the legacy Olmo fallback submits its GEMMs on the current stream.

Figure 65 Under a pipeline schedule, static per-layer replay needs one saved-context slot per in-flight microbatch. (a) Without a pipeline the backward of each microbatch consumes the layer’s saved context before the next forward overwrites it, so one graph per layer serves every microbatch. (b) With three microbatches in flight, a shared slot is overwritten by F1 and F2 before B0 reads it; three slots, each with its own graph and static buffers, are recycled as each microbatch’s backward for the layer completes. Conceptual illustration after the design described for Megatron-Core (Yan et al., 2026); no measured quantities.

Figure 56 Round-ceiling MXFP8 follows the BF16 training trajectory. The top plot reports cross-entropy loss; the bottom reports total gradient norm. The model has 8.36B active and 166.72B total parameters across 31 layers, with top-4 routing over 128 routed experts and one shared expert. The common step-6000 checkpoint was trained from scratch with MXFP8 OCP-floor scaling on approximately 56B tokens. Step 7179 corresponds to approximately 67B tokens, so the plotted continuation spans approximately 11B tokens. The main panels use a 21-step centered moving average, while the final-50-step panels use a lighter 7-step centered moving average; faint lines show the raw measurements. Over the final 50 steps, rceil differs from BF16 by +0.00048 mean loss and −1.9% mean gradient norm, whereas floor differs by +0.02200 mean loss and +51.1% mean gradient norm.

Figure 38 Grouped GEMM and capacity-padded BMM across routed-row counts. Grouped GEMM is faster throughout the shaded mid-to-large-model range. The experiment isolates one BF16 square expert projection on one B300 with Nlocal = 16 and d = h = 4096. The horizontal axis is total routed rows across the 16 local experts; routed rows count expert rows, not unique input tokens, since each token contributes one row to each of its top-K experts, and balanced routing gives M/16 valid rows per expert. The green band marks the representative 16K–96K rank-local operating range. Its endpoints summarize variation in microbatch and routing choices rather than one fixed microbatch size, sequence length, top-K, or local-expert count; Appendix Table 42 gives concrete configurations. BMM reserves exactly 1.25× capacity per expert, while grouped GEMM executes only valid rows. Left: useful throughput counts only valid-row FLOPs. Right: values above one indicate that grouped GEMM is faster. Each point is the mean of 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups; all timed operations are submitted behind one device-side gate and released only after the host has queued the complete batch, so small shapes are not dominated by Python launch gaps.

Figure 8 Global-batch and model-size sweeps expose different limits. Preliminary single-node measurements use eight B300 GPUs, an eight-layer BF16 MoE model, top-4 random routing, no PP, and approximately 3.2B active parameters. Left: with EP disabled and 48 routed experts (19B total parameters), DDP useful-model FLOPs utilization (MFU) rises from 25.2% to 41.4% between 128-Ki and 4-Mi-token global batches (1 Ki = 210 and 1 Mi = 220 tokens), while FSDP rises from 26.4% to 29.8%. Right: total parameters grow from 4.6B to 47B; no-EP DDP runs out of memory at 64 and 128 experts, no-EP FSDP continues to fit but loses useful-model MFU, and DDP+EP8 remains nearly flat. Each point is one run, so the curves show preliminary scaling behavior rather than run-to-run variance. They do not decompose peak memory or attribute the trend to a specific communication phase.

Figure 71 Grouped GEMM also wins across the small-model training range. This one-B300 experiment fixes 16 local experts and a square BF16 projection with d = h = 2048. The green band marks the 96K–192K routed-row range represented by the small configurations in Table 42; their exact widths and local expert counts vary, so the band is an operating-range guide rather than an exact reconstruction of every model. BMM reserves 1.25× capacity per expert, while grouped GEMM executes only valid rows. Each point averages 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups.

Figure 54 Conversion and layout costs in MXFP8 execution. MXFP8 is faster only when its GEMM savings exceed these costs. This is a schematic cost model, not measured timing. The displayed O(MK + KN) conversion term assumes both operands are quantized on the critical path. In Olmo training, the K × N weight conversion is normally paid during cache refresh and reused across microbatches, leaving activation conversion as the principal per-invocation cost. For small GEMMs, that remaining overhead can still turn the expected speedup into a slowdown.

Figure 9 The distributed optimizer and EP reduce different parts of DDP’s persistent parameter-sized training state. Under the illustrated BF16-execution, FP32-gradient, and two-moment FP32 optimizer policy, naive DDP uses 18 bytes per parameter. Sharding the FP32 main weights and optimizer states evenly over D replica ranks reduces this to 6+12/D bytes while compute weights and gradient buffers remain replicated. Sharding routed-expert compute weights and gradients over the expert-parallel model-sharding degree ME (EP-MP; defined in Section 5) further reduces their per-rank memory contribution to 6/ME + 12/D bytes when D = MEDE . Dense and shared parameters follow their separate replica groups. This accounting excludes execution working memory, including activations, routing and communication buffers, kernel workspaces, execution caches, and allocator fragmentation, as well as uneven shards and small auxiliary tensors that are not sharded.

Figure 62 Block recompute removes nearly two thirds of activation memory at a one-fifth throughput cost in this matched configuration. Bars show the arithmetic mean of three fresh-process repetitions; dots show the individual ten-step windows, and the sample standard deviations are smaller than the dot markers. Normal training in this campaign sustains 54.68K tokens/s/GPU at 103.03 GiB peak active memory; recomputing every transformer block sustains 43.22K tokens/s/GPU at 76.90 GiB, 20.95% lower throughput for 26.13 GiB (25.36%) less peak memory. Figure 30 Submission headroom is the queued, not-yet-executed device work. Both curves are computed exactly from the drawn boxes: headroom jumps up by a kernel’s device duration when the CPU completes that kernel’s submission and drains at unit rate while the GPU executes, so the GPU is idle exactly where the curve sits at zero. (a) Cheap submissions of large kernels (k1–k3) build the lead; a host-heavy stretch of small kernels (k4–k7) spends it faster than it is replaced, and after the lead reaches zero the GPU waits for k7’s submission. (b) Within one microbatch, each Python-driven forward submission costs the CPU more time than its kernel costs the GPU, so the lead carried in from the previous backward drains layer by layer and grazes zero just as the last forward submission arrives. The autograd-driven backward inverts the imbalance, and while the GPU executes it, the CPU is already submitting the next microbatch’s forward: the rebuilt surplus is the lead that forward will spend. Each CPU box’s width is the full host cost of its submission, including Python and dispatcher time. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities.

Figure 31 A per-block synchronization point stops the CPU from running ahead. papers.selection_reason: Efficient and scalable MoE training stack for large language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture/training and AI efficiency.
papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.tldr: A redesigned Olmo-core stack makes large-scale MoE training more efficient and scalable by combining specialized parallelism, communication-free routing, MXFP8, and flexible checkpointing.

papers.abstract: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.
authors: Yupei Wang, Neil Mallinar, Mikhail Belkin, Alex Warstadt
bullets: Introduces Concept Energy, measuring alignment between a concept’s representation subspace and directions emphasized by the loss’s average gradient outer product.
Analyzes 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and Pythia-1B.
The first Concept Energy peak generally occurs at or before the steepest rise in probe decodability.
Concept Energy may show sustained or repeated peaks, suggesting continual reinforcement or multi-stage concept learning.
Shows that probe performance alone can miss important variation in how the loss supports concept acquisition.

papers.abstract: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.

Achieves the highest average accuracy across five math benchmarks for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode.

papers.abstract: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller's value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.
bullets: Addresses reserve pricing for highly differentiated products whose demand information is embedded in unstructured listing text.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.
authors: Lei Zhou, Youwen zhu, Rongke Liu
bullets: Output-level verifiers may infer unlearning from provider-controlled predictions without confirming removal of training-data influence.

Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV) compares intermediate representations between original and unlearned models.
RUV analyzes activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support, using retained controls and joint permutation calibration.
Across tested settings, ODR deception was highly effective, while RUV achieved high verification accuracy and rejected most deceptive submissions.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.

papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

papers.abstract: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.
authors: Maikel Yelandi Leyva-Vazquez, Alexis Matheu Perez, Florentin Smarandache
bullets: Projects intermediate-layer readouts onto support, refutation, and hedging lexicons to estimate truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) profiles.
Initial signatures—refutation under conflict, indeterminacy under false belief, and verdict collapse—largely disappear under matched prompt controls.
The balance B = log10(F) − log10(T) remains sensitive to evidence polarity across tested layers and also distinguishes false from true first-person beliefs.
The two-battery design shows why template controls are essential and provides a reusable protocol for auditing lens-based measurements of model internals.

papers.tldr: A template-controlled Jacobian-lens analysis finds that neutrosophic internal verdict balance tracks evidence polarity in Qwen3.5-4B, while many apparent truth, indeterminacy, and falsity signatures are prompt-grammar artifacts.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can improve long- horizon interactive decision-making through test-time evolu- tion, yet existing methods face three information bottlenecks: memory retrieval overemphasizes textual similarity, candi- date harnesses are often behaviorally redundant, and whole- harness rewriting may overwrite useful evidence or introduce cross-component inconsistency. We introduce Trident, which improves experience utilization, behavioral exploration, and harness evolution through boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion- based updating, respectively. We evaluate Trident on five benchmarks spanning text games, web interaction, and cod- ing tasks. Across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt- oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and consistently outperforms non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and automated prompt optimization base- lines. Compared with the strongest baseline, APEX, Trident yields relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3% on the three backbones, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity stud- ies further show that the three designs provide complementary gains and remain robust to parameter variations.
authors: Kaijie Chen, Liang Yan, Yilan Wei, Jiachen Luo, Zhihao Dou, Jiashu Qu, Haoran Liu, Junli Wang
bullets: Addresses three bottlenecks: similarity-biased memory retrieval, redundant candidate harnesses, and risky whole-harness rewriting.
Uses boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion-based updates.
Evaluated across five text-game, web-interaction, and coding benchmarks with three LLM backbones.
Achieves the best average performance and outperforms several non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and prompt-optimization baselines.
Ablations show the components provide complementary gains and are robust to parameter variations.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time evolution of LLM agents with memory reading and inference-time updating; fits test-time learning and agent memory.
papers.title: Read, Route, Patch: Robust Test-Time Evolution for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Trident robustly improves LLM agents’ test-time evolution by better retrieving experiences, routing diverse candidates, and incrementally updating harnesses.

papers.abstract: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.
authors: Fei Ding, Yongkang Zhang, Yuhao Liao, Zijian Zeng, Huiming Yang
bullets: LLM reasoning errors can propagate because existing verification typically occurs only after generation finishes.
A vocabulary marker triggers analysis, error localization, truncation, and rewriting at any point in the reasoning stream.
The token carries no reasoning content and introduces approximately 13% overhead, analogous to ECC parity bits.
Speculative forking reduces false-positive latency, while segmented rewards make trigger timing learnable end to end.
On HMMT25 with Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-Next, it improves performance by 10.8 percentage points at 1.13× overhead and is reported as 88× more token-efficient than Best-of-8.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. Stage 1: Vocabulary extension adds check token c; SFT finetunes on constructed data (auxiliary trigger loss guarantees pmin > 0), providing the model with triggering and localization capability. Stage 2: RLOO with segmented reward finetunes trigger precision; the optimal threshold q∗ has a closed-form solution. Inference: upon outputting c, speculative forking creates a main branch (speculative continuation) and a check branch (correction analysis); true positives trigger truncation-rewriting, false positives directly use the main branch (zero latency).

Figure 3: Check token workflow (true-positive path). After the error segment s4–s6 (orange), outputting c (red) triggers self-checking. After precise localization, s1–s3 (green) are retained, and truncation-rewriting (blue) proceeds. On false positives, the check branch is discarded, and the main branch’s speculative continuation directly becomes the final sequence (zero latency cost).

Table 1: Functional comparison with existing methods. “Precise Loc.”: text-level localization finer than reasoning-step granularity; “Learned”: trigger mechanism learned through endto-end training; “General Reas.”: systematically evaluated on multi-step reasoning tasks. Detailed analysis of each method is in Appendix C.

Table 3: Main results (Qwen3-32B, Acc avg@32 %, mean ± 95% bootstrap CI over 5 random seeds). †PRM uses base model weights (Appendix J). All three predictions are validated: (H1) HMMT25 +10.8 > AIME25 +9.2 > LiveCodeBench +7.2 pp; (H2) token efficiency 10.8/0.13 ≈ 83 pp/×, Best-of-8 efficiency 6.6/7.0 ≈ 0.94 pp/×, ratio ≈ 88×; (H3) precise truncation advantage: HMMT25 +7.0 > AIME25 +5.7 > LiveCodeBench +4.0 pp, monotonically increasing.

Table 4: Ablation study (Qwen3-32B, AIME25 Acc avg@32). Key findings: (1) optimal r− = −0.2 matches closed-form prediction; (2) Ca=100 is saturated; (3) precise truncation yields +2.8 pp over step-level truncation; (4) auxiliary trigger loss contributes +1.7 pp and reduces FP rate by 5.5 pp; (5) RL contributes an additional +5.0 pp on top of auxiliary loss. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a check-token mechanism for built-in self-verification and truncation in LLM reasoning chains, a novel architectural/methodological advance for LLMs.
papers.title: Check Token: Real-Time Self-Verification and Precise Truncation in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Check Token adds an ECC-like trigger to LLM reasoning that enables real-time self-verification and precise error truncation with low overhead.

papers.abstract: Parallel mechanisms pose distinctive challenges to large language models (LLMs), as valid reasoning depends jointly on mechanism topology, loop closure, geometry, joint types, and modeling assumptions. Yet existing LLM benchmarks provide little systematic coverage of such domain-specific knowledge, constraint-sensitive analysis, and constructive design. To fill this gap, we introduce MECHBENCH, a 2,541-question benchmark for evaluating LLMs in parallel mechanisms across professional knowledge, mechanism analysis, and design. MECHBENCH contains standard and challenge tiers spanning six capability categories and nine executable analysis and design tasks. It is constructed through MECHFORGE, a domain-grounded framework that combines expert-organized knowledge, LLM-assisted question generation, programmatic instance generation, two-stage expert review, and task-aware scoring with exact matching, rubric-based evaluation, and program verification. We further develop MECHGPT as a diagnostic domain-adapted model. Experiments show that strong knowledge performance does not directly translate into executable mechanism reasoning: leading closed-service models achieve over 95 on the standard tier but only 47-60 on the challenge tier, while domain adaptation substantially improves MechGPT over its Qwen3-8B baselines but leaves a large gap in constrained analysis and design. These results establish MECHBENCH as a systematic testbed for measuring domain-specific LLM capabilities in mechanism science.
bullets: Introduces a 2,541-question benchmark covering professional knowledge, mechanism analysis, and design.
Includes standard and challenge tiers, six capability categories, and nine executable analysis/design tasks.
Built with MECHFORGE: expert knowledge organization, LLM-assisted generation, programmatic instances, expert review, and task-aware scoring.
Strong models exceed 95 on the standard tier but score only 47–60 on the challenge tier, indicating difficulty with constrained reasoning.
Domain adaptation improves MechGPT over Qwen3-8B baselines, but substantial gaps remain in analysis and design.
