papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.
authors: Haoyang Zhang, Qumeng Sun, Xiao Zhang, Xiang Liu, Zhidong Fan, Junjie Wang
bullets: Addresses failures caused by tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims.
Combines model-facing guidance with Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding.
Introduces Contrast, an auditable harness-evaluation framework with fairness constraints, request verification, and evidence-based adjudication.
Across five benchmarks, six models, and six harnesses, EvoX reached a 56.2% success rate over 691 task–model pairs—about 3 percentage points above the other harnesses’ average.
Results varied by model, with larger gains for GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3, indicating model-dependent harness effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architecture and runtime design of EvoX. The system integrates a model-driven Semantic Policy with a harness-level Operational Policy to coordinate decisions and environment interactions. The operational policy comprises three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization mediates executable tool calls, Execution Continuity coordinates recovery and runtime control, and Outcome Grounding aligns reported outcomes with observed execution. The runtime supports diverse tools and optional persistent adaptation through long-term memory and GEP-based experience evolution. The right panel illustrates the conceptual distinction between a minimal execution loop and explicit harness-level operational control.

Figure 2: Overview of Contrast for controlled and auditable harness evaluation. A fairness contract distinguishes locked, shared, and harness-native conditions, preserving native execution behaviors while controlling external evaluation factors. Versioned tasks undergo qualification and integrity checks before execution through native harnesses in controlled environments. A model bridge mediates model requests, enforces applicable configurations, and audits provider-bound request parameters. Execution traces, model-call records, verifier results, and runtime diagnostics provide evidence for failure attribution, validity decisions, and auditable result selection. Only valid, scored task–model combinations enter paired statistical comparisons, while excluded or quarantined records remain available for audit and disclosure.

papers.abstract: When people face a hard problem, they often restate it in a clearer way before solving it. We study whether the same habit helps large language models by rewriting the statement of a problem. A legal rewrite must keep the meaning, the constraints, and the correct answer unchanged. We test three kinds of rewrites. Decomposition makes hidden subgoals explicit. Typed Reformulation casts the task into a more suitable solving frame. Concept Reduction removes surface detail and exposes the task structure. We evaluate them on eight math, logic, and code benchmarks with eight models, all under the same chain-of-thought solving prompt. The effect is large but depends on the problem type. An oracle that picks the best rewrite after the fact raises accuracy by +27.6% on average. Yet no single rewrite helps every problem, and a mismatched rewrite can hurt. Still, the effect follows clear patterns. Each kind of rewrite fits certain problem types. A simple fixed rule learned from one set of problems transfers part of the gain to new problems. It gains +11.0% on the problems it chooses to rewrite, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share of problems. Rewriting is therefore not a universal way to solve problems. The question is when and how to rewrite.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Xiaoyu Zhang, Chengwei Liu, Yutao Hu, Tao Zhang, Junsheng Wu, Hongping Gan, Yang Liu
bullets: Studies three meaning-preserving rewrites: Decomposition, Typed Reformulation, and Concept Reduction.

No rewrite works universally: mismatched reformulations can reduce performance.
A simple rule transfers part of the benefit, gaining 11.0% on selected problems, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share.

papers.abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.
authors: Jie Ren, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Neil Thompson
bullets: Parallel test-time scaling wastes compute by fully expanding low-quality reasoning paths before evaluation.
Confidence signals matter most on questions near the decision boundary, where short prefixes can already guide aggregation.
PreG generates short prefixes, ranks them by internal confidence, and completes only the strongest candidates.
Theoretical analysis shows PreG can widen the effective decision-boundary margin under a fixed compute budget.
Experiments report consistent gains over standard parallel TTS with improved token efficiency and lower computation.

papers.abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.
authors: Yunlong Hou, Fengzhuo Zhang, Yuan Cheng, Jiachun Pan, Xingyao Li, Zhuoran Yang
bullets: SFT data source is critical: a carefully mixed dataset outperforms data generated solely by a larger model.
Matching correct-rollout counts substantially improves SFT generalization; matching total rollout budgets can make SFT perform as well as RL.
Combining data quality and scale enables SFT to generalize beyond RL in the studied settings.
Larger datasets cover more rare (“tail”) solution methods, which provide generalizable reasoning signals.
Experiments use Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models, with theoretical analysis of shallow-transformer training dynamics.

papers.abstract: Generative large language models are widely used for multilingual text evaluation, yet whether decision models that directly output judgment probabilities can serve as multilingual judges has received limited attention. We evaluate Jev against generative LLM judges on four multilingual benchmarks with human annotations, covering up to 47 language varieties and three evaluation formats: binary decisions, pairwise comparisons, and graded ratings. At approximately $1/31$ to $1/61$ of GPT-6.1's evaluation cost, Jev is competitive on most multilingual judging tasks, but falls behind GPT-6.1 on knowledge-intensive answer verification. Further analysis shows that Jev is more likely to accept incorrect answers in low-resource languages than in English and that its probability outputs help identify errors across tasks. Based on these findings, we offer recommendations on evaluation instructions, confidence-based selection, and model routing, providing empirical guidance for using Jev as a multilingual judge.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to lack diversity in open-ended text generation, a limitation that is especially consequential in education, where homogeneity can narrow the kinds of thinking and disciplinary work students are invited to do. We study diversity in two educational generation tasks: math items and essay feedback. We compare frontier and open-weight models with human-authored reference distributions using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures. For math, we examine the mathematical activities students are asked to perform; for feedback, we examine the revision work requested and the rhetorical strategies used to communicate it. We evaluate direct prompting, two diversity prompting methods, and post-training. Across both tasks, directly prompted model outputs are markedly less diverse than human-authored content--78% higher on lexical (Self-BLEU) and 51% higher on semantic (embedding) similarity--and represent a narrower range of instructional forms. Diversity prompting and post-training increase variation largely through surface features without broadening the instructional repertoire. Models inherit and amplify the most normative routines of human instruction. Overcoming mode collapse in education will require richer instructional data and investment in teachers' creative capacity and professional judgment.

papers.abstract: Morphology-aware tokenizers are expected to help morphologically rich languages, and their reported gains over byte-pair encoding (BPE) are usually credited to their linguistic units. A comparison with BPE cannot support this attribution, since such a tokenizer also segments text more finely (granularity) and, on token-level tasks, changes how much the sub-token readout matters. We separate both factors from the effect of grouping words by their roots (root assignment) in Amharic, a Semitic language whose Ge'ez abugida hides consonantal roots inside syllabic glyphs, with Latin-script Hausa as an orthographic contrast. Our design combines a lossless root-and-pattern tokenizer with controls that change one factor at a time, in two independent implementations. In both, real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots (+4.9 and +4.7 F1), and root-frequency structure explains little of this gain. In small from-scratch models, the readout choice moves F1 by up to 13.4 points and reverses the sign of every comparison of the root-and-pattern arms with BPE, whereas in two pretrained encoders it moves F1 by less than one point. The granularity effect changes sign across languages and implementations. We recommend decomposing tokenizer effects, and reporting the readout, before a gain is attributed to linguistic structure.
authors: Abdul Rehman Antall, Baidya Nath Saha
bullets: The study compares morphology-aware tokenization with controlled alternatives in Amharic and Hausa.
Real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots, while root-frequency structure explains little of the gain.
Word-level readout has a major impact in small from-scratch models, changing F1 by up to 13.4 points and reversing comparisons with BPE.
Readout effects are much smaller in pretrained encoders, and granularity effects vary by language and implementation.
The authors recommend reporting readout choices and isolating tokenizer factors in future evaluations.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. We show that a frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM can instead be adapted into a word-level full-duplex system with little data. Our system is a thinker-talker cascade on an 80 ms frame clock. The thinker keeps the LLM frozen and trains only lightweight adapters and a few new token embeddings (97M parameters); at every frame it emits one token of agent text, with pauses, yields, and onsets represented as tokens of the same vocabulary and kept legal by a finite-state machine. A four-stage curriculum, each stage anchored to the model's own behavior under the previous format, performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours. The talker reads only the thinker's discrete tokens, so the two halves are trained independently. On Full-Duplex-Bench and InteractionBench, the system is competitive with open-source full-duplex systems built through large-scale speech training: among them, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses, backchannels most often, and leads in spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and coherence over long conversations.
authors: Tairan Chen, Richard Yucheng He, Yihang Liu, Baodong Cao, Chen Xu
bullets: Full-duplex dialogue requires listening while speaking, backchanneling, yielding, and handling interruptions at word-level timing.
The system uses a frozen LLM with lightweight adapters and new token embeddings, operating on an 80 ms frame clock.
A thinker emits text, pauses, yields, and onsets as constrained tokens; an independently trained talker converts them to speech.
A four-stage curriculum completes adaptation in about 30 GPU-hours.

On two benchmarks, it is competitive with large-scale speech-trained systems and performs strongly in floor-taking restraint, backchanneling, spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and long-conversation coherence.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview. A frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM (Qwen3-Omni), which only talks in turns, becomes the thinker of a full-duplex system through four training stages. Each stage card shows what the model reads and emits at that stage as one cell per frame (user codec tokens, agent words, pause, SE/SS, and PAD cells), which modules it trains, and which model anchors its KL term; the frozen core is never changed. The resulting thinker emits agent text and timing tokens frame by frame, and the talker turns them into speech, so that the agent listens and speaks at the same time.

(b) Mean L2 norm of the user-audio branch entering the channel-fusion layer on 40 held-out noisy examples, for frames with user speech and for answer-phase frames that contain only room tone.

Figure 1: Illustration of the two behaviors on a shared timeline (user above, agent below; schematic: timings and text are illustrative). (a) A free-running conversation: the agent backchannels (“mmhm”, “yeah”, in the backchannel color) while the user is still talking and takes the turn when the user finishes, with no external turn detector. (b) A user interruption: the agent yields the floor when the user cuts in (silence-start token, SS) and takes it back to answer the new request (silence-end token, SE). SE/SS markers are drawn at the start and end of each agent turn.

Figure 3: Data flow and frame-level token structure. A frozen codec encoder turns the user’s waveform into per-frame audio tokens. The thinker reads the user-audio stream together with its own agent-text stream (pad, text, and control tokens on one lane per frame) and extends the text stream by one token per frame. The talker reads the agent-text stream and its own previous audio tokens and extends the agent-audio stream by one frame; a frozen codec decoder renders it as a waveform. The control tokens SS and SE open and close the agent’s silences, and pause tokens mark short gaps; the example includes a short backchannel (“Mhm”) produced while the user is still speaking.

Figure 4: The thinker’s turn-taking state machine. In SILENCE the legal tokens are PAD (stay silent) and SE (take the floor, entering CONTENT after one automatically fed EPAD frame). In CONTENT they are word pieces and pause0 (stay), pausem withm > 0 (enter PAUSE), and SS (yield, entering SILENCE). PAUSE samples nothing: it feeds its queued PAD and EPAD frames and returns to CONTENT when the queue is empty.

papers.abstract: User research and system testing reveal whether products and services meet user needs, yet recruiting specialized participants, designing controlled what-if comparisons, and repeating studies as designs evolve often bottleneck design iteration and data-driven decision-making. We present a framework and execution infrastructure that translates real-world industry inquiries into controlled experiments with simulated users. Our methodology formally defines the target cohort, experimental stimuli, and decision-relevant metrics, while the pipeline supports large-scale concurrent runs over cohort-stimulus-environment combinations (survey, web, chatbot, and OS app), auditable trial-level logging, cohort-level outcome aggregation, and cross-cohort and cross-variant statistical reports. Across twelve industry partner cases spanning five domains, we show how constructing hard-to-reach or what-if persona cohorts supports exploratory studies and distills simulated responses into testable design hypotheses. Cross-model comparisons on selected cases largely preserve primary conclusions, whereas perturbing or ablating persona attributes alters service outcomes, effect sizes, and inter-group differences, indicating that grounding target cohorts in detailed personas materially shapes simulation results. Together, these studies show that persona-enabled agents can test specified cohorts at design speed, diagnose systems under test, and deliver directional evidence that focuses problem definition, steers design and strategic decisions, and guides further study.
authors: Julie Zhu, Jianheng Hou, Zhixu Silvia Tao, Shi Bo, Yilan Fan, Yixuan He, Zhiyuan Hu, Shirley Huang, Fangyu Liu, Yijun Wang, Zibu Wei, Haimingyue Xu, Zhen Xu, Zichen Yuan, Jierui Zuo, Jintao Huang, Yifan Wang, Qianfeng Wen, Jiahan Li, Zhejian Peng, Bowen Yang, Shushu Liang, Yuexing Hao, Xiaomin Li
bullets: Addresses the cost and iteration bottlenecks of recruiting specialized participants and repeatedly running controlled user studies.
Formalizes target cohorts, experimental stimuli, and decision-relevant metrics across surveys, websites, chatbots, and OS apps.
Supports concurrent cohort–stimulus–environment experiments, trial-level logging, aggregation, and statistical reporting.
Twelve industry cases across five domains show that simulated persona cohorts can support exploratory research and produce testable design hypotheses.
Results are sensitive to persona attributes, while selected cross-model comparisons generally preserve primary conclusions; findings are directional and intended to guide further study.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now a standard stage of language model post-training, and the compute devoted to it is growing rapidly. While it has been shown to improve capabilities, particularly for tasks with verifiable rewards, it can also change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target. We present a formalism to describe the evolution of "traits" during RL post-training and, in doing so, recover the Price equation from evolutionary biology. We use this to develop a mathematical model for what we call "trait hitchhiking": the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions. We evaluate this Price update expression on language models trained with GRPO and show that the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics. These results identify trait hitchhiking as a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.
authors: Adil Soubki, Elizabeth S. Z. Tan, Miles Cranmer
bullets: Motivation: RL improves rewarded capabilities but may silently alter non-targeted behaviors and internal properties.
Method: A trait-evolution formalism based on the Price equation models how probability redistribution across completions changes traits.
Evaluation: The authors test the resulting Price update on language models trained with GRPO.
Result: Price-equation estimates closely track the observed dynamics of sampled traits.
Implication: Trait hitchhiking may amplify undesirable traits even when they are not directly rewarded.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Trait hitchhiking follows the same law in evolution and in RL. Left: long tails are correlated with other traits that make a widowbird ‘fit’, although long tails themselves do not lead to increased fitness of a widowbird. Right: RL leads to an increased probability for outputs that achieve a high reward. Behaviours or traits that appear consistently in highly rewarded outputs will thus also gain a greater prevalence, even though the reward function does not necessarily reward these traits. The change in the average trait exhibited by the model is the covariance of reinforcement (specifically ω from Definition 3, which defines how the probability of an input-output pair changes after a training step), and •, the trait.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and models 'trait hitchhiking' during LLM post-training using the Price equation. This provides a formal framework for understanding how RL post-training amplifies non-targeted traits in language models.
papers.title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: RL post-training can unintentionally amplify or suppress behaviors unrelated to its reward, a phenomenon formalized as “trait hitchhiking.”

papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu, Bo Pang, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
bullets: The study tests whether identical information helps differently depending on how it is represented in history and whether the world reflects it.
With the world fixed after a wrong value, a truthful note improved recovery from 51% to 66%, while presenting the correction as a completed action reduced it from 50% to 44%.
In AppWorld, success receipts helped when their effects were present (38% to 49%) but hurt when effects were absent (45% to 28%).
History edits and world state interacted across receivers, showing that the value alone does not determine recovery.
Scope: results concern mid-task, tool-using agents and history/world edits evaluated on AgentCE-Bench and AppWorld.

papers.abstract: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.
bullets: Addresses the lack of curated sports-and-health training data and rigorous domain benchmarks.
Built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training and optimized for Chinese exercise guidance.
Supports workout-plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports-data analysis.
Uses a domain-expert-designed, rubric-based evaluation framework emphasizing safety and scientific grounding.
Internal results report gains over its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, especially in safety and boundary compliance.

papers.selection_reason: Reports on Keepace.ai, a domain-specialized LLM for sports and health, optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance.

papers.abstract: Whole-prompt translation evaluates a request in different languages but does not compare which component carries a language. We introduce a paired reversal: translate the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language, holding behaviour, English frame and translated-span count fixed. Component identity and non-English text quantity change together. Assigning English, Chinese and Spanish independently to the two components yields nine configurations on 190 of 300 sampled harmful behaviours retained after consensus annotation and automatic gating. Refusal scored by language-model judges is the primary outcome; unsafe compliance is reported separately. On Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, three refusal swaps are about 5.3 percentage points and the fourth is -0.5; none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction. In an exploratory extension, Mistral Small 4 has a 13.7-point Spanish swap (95% interval [8.4, 18.9]), which survives the twelve-test Holm sensitivity correction under the primary judge, and 12.1 points under a second judge. GPT-5.4-mini estimates are within 2 points of zero. Component assignment supplies an additional evaluation dimension. Evaluations should record component languages and translated text quantity, comparing matched behaviours at equal translated-span count while interpreting refusal and unsafe compliance separately.
bullets: Whole-prompt translation cannot isolate whether request or operation language drives safety behavior.
The study compares nine English/Chinese/Spanish assignments while matching translated-span count and holding the English frame and behavior constant.
Refusal is judged by language models, with unsafe compliance reported separately.
For Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, observed refusal swaps do not survive Holm correction; GPT-5.4-mini effects are near zero.
An exploratory Mistral Small 4 result shows a corrected Spanish swap, supporting component-aware multilingual safety evaluation.

papers.abstract: Systematic reviews synthesize biomedical evidence to inform clinical and public-health decision-making, but require domain experts to manually screen thousands of studies against detailed eligibility criteria. We investigate whether language models can assist with this bottleneck by learning from expert feedback on title and abstract screening decisions and model-generated reasoning. We introduce the Context-Aware Reasoning Framework (CARF), a human-in-the-loop framework that uses expert feedback on model-generated reasoning to adapt language models to context-dependent screening tasks. We evaluate CARF on systematic reviews of verbal autopsy and cause-of-death ascertainment methods used in global public health mortality surveillance. CARF shows competitive screening performance compared to evaluated models while retaining high sensitivity, and is more inclined to retain ambiguous, context-dependent studies for human review. Together, these findings suggest that expert-corrected reasoning is a promising supervision signal for context-dependent scientific screening, while retaining a role for human oversight.
bullets: Addresses the labor-intensive screening of thousands of studies in systematic reviews.
Uses expert feedback on model-generated reasoning to adapt models to context-dependent eligibility decisions.
Evaluated on reviews of verbal autopsy and cause-of-death ascertainment methods in global public-health mortality surveillance.
Achieves competitive screening performance with high sensitivity and tends to retain ambiguous studies for human review.
Supports expert-corrected reasoning as a promising supervision signal, not a replacement for human oversight.

Figure I2: Qualitative examples of self-corrective reasoning on the held-out test set. In each case the model’s initial reasoning leans toward inclusion, then the expert-feedback–informed reasoning revisits the evidence against the eligibility criteria and corrects the decision to exclude.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a human-in-the-loop framework (CARF) for context-aware reasoning supervision in scientific evidence screening.
papers.title: CARF: Context-Aware Reasoning Supervision for Scientific Evidence Screening
papers.tldr: CARF uses expert-corrected model reasoning to help language models screen scientific studies while preserving human oversight for ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly supplies transcripts for educational NLP, but aggregate word error rate (WER) can conceal errors concentrated in learner speech, multilingual turns, and speaker attribution. We compare platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted, and commercial ASR configurations on held-out sessions of online L2 Spanish interaction between L1 English learners and their instructors and tutors. Because English is the learner's shared first language, the interactions contain Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns. Evaluation combines overall WER and character error rate (CER), WER disaggregated by speaker role and language context, and diarization error rate (DER). We also adapt Whisper large-v3 and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize with LoRA using human-corrected in-domain classroom data. MOSS adaptation produced consistent improvements across speaker roles and language contexts, whereas Whisper showed smaller gains. Domain match proved more important than data volume: Larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora did not outperform the smaller classroom corpus, where learner speech and code-switching are embedded in instructor--learner interaction. The open-weight MOSS adapter was competitive with commercial Muse Voice Transcribe on WER and CER and achieved lower system-provided DER on the recordings eligible for each system. Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech. The findings demonstrate the value of condition-aware evaluation and interactionally matched data for bilingual educational ASR.
bullets: Aggregate WER can hide errors tied to speaker role, language context, and diarization.
The study evaluates multiple ASR configurations on online L2 Spanish classrooms, including Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns.
LoRA adaptation improved MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize consistently; Whisper gains were smaller.
Domain match mattered more than corpus size: a smaller classroom corpus outperformed larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner datasets.
Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech.

papers.abstract: Medical chart abstraction transforms unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring. We evaluated a prompting-based large language model (LLM) framework for extracting eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals. Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs were evaluated across architectures, model sizes, and biomedical adaptations using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard. Evaluation was restricted to report-variable pairs with a valid LLaMA3.3-70B CoT prediction and a corresponding reference label. Performance measures included extraction accuracy, inference latency, and agreement with expert adjudication. Twenty discordant cases per variable underwent review by two senior physicians and four medical students. LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved performance on inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication showed that AI predictions were more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge. Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.
bullets: Evaluated 22 open-source instruction-tuned LLMs on eight variables from 2,416 acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals.
LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest reported overall accuracy at 94.8%.
Chain-of-Thought prompting helped with inference-dependent variables, while Quick Response worked best for directly stated procedural fields.
AI predictions generally aligned more closely with expert adjudication than non-expert annotations.
Intracranial angioplasty remained challenging, supporting expert review for ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: We describe the QMUL_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.
bullets: Targets Arabic-English function calling and reasoning-augmented calling under the AISA-ArabicFC 2026 task.
Combines Arabic schema-aware prompts, dialect/no-call resampling, token-weighted training, and schema-based call validation.
Uses only official task data and supports both function-calling tracks with a shared output format.
Scores 0.9253 and 0.9380 on blind-test Tracks A and B, ranking 3rd in each.

papers.abstract: Recurrent sequence models must decide how strongly to overwrite their memory at each token. Read as Bayesian filtering, this write is the gain of a Kalman update, set by uncertainty from two sources that pull it in opposite directions: volatility, how quickly the underlying associations change, and stochasticity, how noisy each observation of them is. First, we show that the update of gated delta-rule memories is the form this filter takes under isotropic uncertainty. Next, we introduce Voltic, a recurrent memory that keeps the covariance anisotropic and makes both noise variances input-dependent, so the write is vector-valued and carries uncertainty accumulated over the sequence. A dense covariance would have to be propagated token by token, ruling out the parallel training these models depend on. We therefore give two assumed-density approximations, diagonal and quasi-diagonal, both of which leave the memory update in delta-rule form and reuse its chunked kernels. On controlled recall tasks in which associations change and observations are corrupted, Voltic leads all baselines. On the task combining volatility and stochasticity, its margin over the strongest baseline is larger at both extrapolation sizes than at the training sizes. In 45M-parameter language models it leads an eight-task reasoning average and achieves higher retrieval accuracy beyond the training context length than gated baselines, at throughput close to those baselines. Deriving the write from an uncertainty recursion therefore makes memory more responsive to change.
bullets: Recasts gated memory writes as Kalman-style updates driven by uncertainty.
Introduces input-dependent volatility and stochasticity with anisotropic covariance, producing vector-valued writes.
Uses diagonal and quasi-diagonal approximations to preserve parallel, chunked training.
Leads baselines on controlled recall, combined volatility–stochasticity, reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks.
Scope: approximations trade full covariance modeling for computational efficiency.

papers.tldr: Voltic improves recurrent memory by distinguishing changing associations from noisy observations, enabling more responsive and uncertainty-aware updates.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.
authors: Zijian Zhang, Rizhen Hu, Jiangweizhi Peng, Shiyang Li, Sujay Bhatt, Sihan Zeng, Mingyi Hong
bullets: Addresses the information loss caused by reducing each RL attempt to a single outcome reward.
The teacher diagnoses student bottlenecks and creates shared strategies or task-specific hints, with support adapting as learning progresses.
Scaffolds are used only during training and removed at evaluation, requiring minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention.
Students outperform corresponding RL baselines across ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation.

Reported gains include 7.2 ALFWorld success points, 4.0 QA exact-match points, and up to 5.0 points in faster-than-PyTorch GPU kernels; math reaches higher accuracy with about one-third the training steps of QuestA.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AUTOSCAFFOLD. (a) A class-level scaffold, injected with probability q[C], and an instancelevel scaffold are added to the student’s training prompt. On a hard task this turns all-failure groups into mixed groups that produce training signal; the RL algorithm is unchanged, and all scaffolds are removed at evaluation. (b) At the end of each block of K steps, a frozen teacher gathers evidence from the training log, proposes edits, validates classlevel scaffolds on held-out tasks, and deploys the updated scaffold for the next block. Bottom: an actual update on ALFWorld.

Figure 2: AutoScaffold: a teacher LLM designs and adapts scaffolds during RL training. (a) Unlike handdesigned scaffolding, AutoScaffold is automatic, adaptive, and unified. (b) Evaluation curves during training (success rate on ALFWorld, exact match on search-based QA), compared with GiGPO. (c) Gains over the RL baseline of each experiment, evaluated without scaffolds: success rate on ALFWorld, average exact match on search-based QA, average accuracy on math, and KernelBench correctness pass@3 averaged over Levels 1 to 3. Gray dots are prior scaffolding methods. All methods use the same student size as AutoScaffold, except Skill0, SkillRL and SkillC in ALFWorld using 7B models. (d) The teacher sets each problem’s solution-prefix ratio as instance-level scaffold: it first reveals more of the reference solutions and then withdraws support, whereas QuestA switches from 50% to 25% at a fixed step.

It reads them and finds meaningful information for further diagnosis and edits. Bottom: it diagnoses a different failure in each class and responds with a matching edit: adding, rewriting, reducing, or omitting a scaffold.

Figure 5: Scaffold changes over training on ALFWorld. Left: scaffold-free success (top) and mean class-level injection probability (bottom), with training divided into three stages. Right: what the teacher changed in each stage (+ add, ∼ revise, − remove, ↑↓ raise or lower injection probability).

Figure 6: From each branching point, we train 20 more steps with the updated scaffold (AUTOSCAFFOLD, dark blue), with the previous scaffold kept fixed (orange), or with vanilla RL (gray). AUTOSCAFFOLD gives the highest success at every branching point.

Figure 7: Solution-prefix ratios during math training (Nemotron-1.5B). Mean ratio across all training problems. AutoScaffold (red) adjusts each problem’s ratio using training evidence. QuestA (gray) switches from 50% to 25% at step 100.

Table 1: Positioning of AutoScaffold. Stage: whether the method changes how a model behaves at inference time or how it is trained. What it changes: the object that is designed or edited. Granularity: whether guidance is shared by a class of tasks, specific to one task, or both. Automatic: an AI system decides the changes, without hand-designed content or schedules (◦: content is generated by a model, but its use follows hand-designed rules). Adapts to student progress: whether guidance or training settings are revised in response to the student’s current performance and observed failures (◦: changes follow predefined rules or schedules). No extra runs: changes are decided and tested within a single training run, without training separate runs or branches (◦: branches are trained from checkpoints). Scaffold-free eval.: the learner is evaluated without the guidance it received during training (◦: some guidance is kept). Domains: the task types on which the method is evaluated (A = agentic, S = search QA, M = math, K = GPU kernels). –: not applicable.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.
authors: Zhimin Hu, Chen Jiang, Hanbo Xie, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Sashank Varma
bullets: MI increasingly studies internal computations, not just predictive behavior.
The paper identifies recurring inferential bottlenecks shared by neuroscience and MI.
It proposes five principles organized into a recursive framework for mechanistic inference.
The framework aims to make findings cumulative within models and precise enough to generate external, testable hypotheses.
Claims about what model mechanisms reveal about the broader world require evidence beyond MI.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A recursive logic for mechanistic inference. For a given neural system with behavior of interest, it can be investigated by different candidate objects of study: neurons, features, circuits, population geometry, and dynamics. We propose five principles to organize mechanistic research as a recursive process in which evidence informs further questions and revisions to earlier claims. An individual study may address a subset of these questions and revisit them as needed. Red arrows connect these five inferential questions: which object explains the phenomenon (P1), whether represented information is used in computation (P2), what computational role it plays (P3), how roles are organized (P4), and what remains invariant across conditions or implementations (P5; illustrated here across random seeds). Measurement choices constrain every inference (P0). A, B, and C denote computational roles. This process supports the discovery of candidate model mechanisms (within-model discovery), which can generate domain hypotheses and establish their plausibility beyond the model requires independent evidence (beyond-model discovery).

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference

papers.abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
authors: Audrey Huang, Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster
bullets: Defines coverage-preserving algorithms whose sample and gradient costs depend on how readily the base model can generate optimal responses.
Shows REINFORCE—and consequently PPO/GRPO-style methods—can suffer coverage collapse even when rewards improve and exact gradients or KL regularization are used.
Introduces Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), which repeatedly resets the KL reference to the latest policy and solves a sequence of regularized subproblems.
Proves global convergence and coverage-preservation for several softmax linear-policy algorithms, including stylized PPO/GRPO variants and implicit squared-loss methods.
Clarifies how regularization, clipping, and objective design affect post-training’s sampling and optimization costs.

Each arrow marks the learner’s progress after a fixed number of gradient steps. (a) With weak regularization to the base model, coverage can collapse and cause optimization to stall. (b) Strong regularization controls coverage and keeps the learner close to the reference policy, but far from optimality (marked ✩). (c) APMD resets the reference to the most recent policy, reaching optimality through successive local improvements.

papers.abstract: UTF-8's role as the de facto encoding standard in language models introduces cross-lingual inequities due to its variable-length design. However, the effect that this encoding choice has on model performance remains largely unexamined. In this work, we investigate how text encoding impacts the performance of byte-level language models, comparing UTF-8 with a wide range of other encoding strategies, including other Unicode-based approaches, language-specific encodings, and our own customized encodings. To facilitate our analysis, we propose Aether: a hybrid encoding scheme that uses script-specific encodings for our target setting while maintaining full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks, using this framework to model four orthographically diverse languages. Surprisingly, we find that while languages with information-dense characters (Chinese, Korean) significantly benefit from compressive encodings, languages whose characters carry less information individually (Georgian, Tamil) are largely insensitive to encoding choice. In light of these findings, we argue that text encoding should be a language-specific design decision, rather than a universal default.
authors: Eugene Jang, Catherine Arnett, Terra Blevins
bullets: The study examines how UTF-8 and alternative encodings influence byte-level language-model performance.
It compares Unicode-based, language-specific, and customized encoding strategies across four orthographically diverse languages.
Aether combines script-specific encodings with UTF-8 fallbacks to preserve full Unicode coverage.
Compressive encodings substantially benefit Chinese and Korean, while Georgian and Tamil are largely insensitive to encoding choice.
The findings highlight potential cross-lingual inequities introduced by UTF-8’s variable-length design.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.
authors: Dong Han, Jin Zhang, Kunyue Yang
bullets: Introduces a Cognitive LbT Framework covering Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization.
Maps methods such as chain-of-thought, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning to these mechanisms.
Argues that these methods can improve some tasks without new labeled examples, but may not change model parameters or produce durable learning.
Identifies failures including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high inference-time cost.
Attributes these limits to four asymmetries with human cognition: shared generator/monitor, lack of external grounding, symbolic simulation, and costly inference.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Overall Architecture of the Cognitive LbT Framework. Note. The four mechanisms are shown in their logical order, alternating generation (Reflective Reasoning, Internal Simulation) and consolidation (Synthetic Memory Formation, Conceptual Self-Organization); the side arrow indicates the continuous feedback loops that connect them. The green panel represents external verification signals, and the dashed arrows mark where these signals anchor the loop outside the model (see Section 4.2).

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.
authors: Runxuan Tang, Haoyu Gao, Yuyan Ding, Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, Zecheng Sheng, Liwei Hou
bullets: Addresses the risk that local episode success leads agents to store unsafe or non-transferable lessons.
Represents each candidate update with a precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier.
Tests updates temporarily using transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, then commits, refines, or rejects them based on gain and risk.
Reports strong performance across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks.
Reduces falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE). FGSE first converts episode evidence into a structured behavioral hypothesis, temporarily evaluates it with target-transfer, falsification, and regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects the hypothesis according to verifier-grounded gain and risk criteria.

Figure 5: Interpreting FGSE update selection. (a) Transfer–Falsification volcano plot for candidate hypotheses. The x-axis shows target-transfer gain Ĝ, the y-axis shows − log10(P̂fail + ϵ0), point size encodes regression damage D̂reg, and color indicates the final FGSE decision. The dashed lines mark the useful-transfer and falsification thresholds. (b) Decision simplex over normalized target gain, falsification risk, and regression damage. The shaded area shows the gate-induced decision regions.
Figure 4: Domain-level diagnostic of self-evolution risk.

Figure 1: A locally useful episode-derived lesson may overgeneralize or regress archived skills if directly written into memory. FGSE tests each lesson as a structured hypothesis in a temporary state and commits only verified, transferable updates to long-term memory.

Figure 8: Stability of hypothesis effects under stochastic rollouts. Each row corresponds to one hypothesis and shows the distribution of seed-specific update effects ∆(s) h across repeated rollouts. Rows are grouped by the final FGSE decision. Dots denote seed-level outcomes, the shaded halfviolin shows the empirical density, the white box shows the interquartile range, and the diamond marks the mean effect. The right-side annotation reports the sign-consistency score C(h). Committed hypotheses remain consistently positive across seeds, refined hypotheses are still mostly positive but exhibit larger variance, while rejected hypotheses are centered near zero or change sign frequently.

Figure 10: Memory-growth Pareto analysis. We vary the retention budget and evaluate longhorizon self-evolving agents under different memory policies. Left: task success rate versus committed memory size. Right: violation rate versus committed memory size. Each faint point denotes one domain-seed run, while solid lines connect policy means across budgets. Marker area is proportional to retrieval cost Cret. A desirable memory policy should remain close to the upper-left region in the left panel (high success with small memory) and the lower-left region in the right panel (low violation with small memory). FGSE traces the most favorable frontier: it achieves high task success and low violation with substantially smaller committed memory and lower retrieval cost than naive memory growth.

Figure 6: Plasticity–safety Pareto analysis of update-selection strategies. Each point is one configuration obtained by sweeping verifier budgets and acceptance thresholds. The x-axis is update gain ∆upd, and the y-axis is either harmful update rate H (left) or regression damage R (right). Point size indicates verifier cost C (average verifier calls per candidate update), and color denotes the update-selection strategy. The black dashed line shows the empirical Pareto frontier, where larger gain and smaller harm are jointly preferred. FGSE occupies the most favorable lower-right region over a wide range of medium verifier budgets, showing that it improves plasticity without incurring the safety cost typically associated with aggressive update policies.

Figure 7: Falsification discovery curves under different probe-selection policies. The x-axis is the probe budget K. The left panel shows bad-update detection rate D(K), and the right panel shows harmful update avoided A(K). Solid lines denote the mean across repeated trials, and shaded bands denote 95% confidence intervals. The gray vertical band marks the practically relevant low-budget regime (8 ≤ K ≤ 16). Targeted probing consistently dominates random baselines, especially in the low-budget regime, showing that hypothesis-aware falsification is substantially more informationefficient than unguided random testing.

Figure 9: Trajectory-edit Sankey diagram from baseline traces to FGSE traces. The left column shows the dominant behavioral deficiency in the baseline trace, the middle column shows the dominant edit family introduced by FGSE, and the right column shows the resulting FGSE behavior motif. Band width is proportional to the number of corrected trajectories. The diagram shows that most successful transitions are driven by tool-order repair, memory retrieval, and constraint checking, whereas final-answer formatting accounts for only a small minority of improvements.

Figure 2: Exploratory diagnostics for naive episode-derived self-updates. (a) Many updates combine near-transfer gains with boundary harm. (b) Broad and underspecified updates produce substantially higher boundary and archive harm than more specific updates. (c) Sequentially writing free-form lessons into memory can accumulate errors, especially when updates are selected only by source-episode improvement. (d) A post-hoc scope-localization analysis shows that many harmful but useful updates can be repaired by narrowing their applicability, motivating an explicit refinement mechanism.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems use self-judgment to decide which answers to release, review, or recompute. Because intervention is costly, an assurance score must rank errors well at the available budget, not merely over the full ranking. We compare the judge's continuous verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe trained on attention-head activations from the same prompt. Exact identities link fixed-budget error recall to residual risk and show that AUROC averages recall over all budgets. Across three open 7-12B models on GSM8K and MATH, the probe finds 1.3-22.5 additional percentage points of errors at 5% review in all six model-dataset settings (median 7.4 points). At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improves accuracy over equal-cost random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but beats judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge. Cross-dataset transfer lowers probe AUROC for every model in both directions relative to target-domain training. Because dataset, weight precision, and generation budget change together, this measures a joint protocol shift rather than a dataset-only effect. Internal signals can improve supervised, in-domain budget allocation, but are not domain-general confidence estimators.
bullets: The study evaluates confidence signals for deciding which model answers to review or recompute under limited budgets.
It compares the judge’s verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe using attention-head activations from the same prompt.
Across three open 7–12B models on GSM8K and MATH, probes recovered 1.3–22.5 more percentage points of errors at 5% review in all settings.
At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improved over random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but surpassed judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge.
Cross-dataset transfer reduced probe AUROC in every model; results reflect a joint protocol shift, not dataset shift alone.

papers.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
authors: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: External memory can hurt performance when lessons are incorrect, misapplied, or misread.

The system specifically reduces degradation caused by adding memory.

papers.abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.
authors: Junhao Shen, Qing Zong, Yue Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Hong Cheng
bullets: Introduces 5,448 questions across 16 task categories, covering single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decisions.
Tests realistic settings including state tracking, tool selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring.
Includes fresh contexts with 2–1,024 options and inputs up to 64,817 tokens to probe scalable decision making.
Evaluates 28 decision models and finds substantial weaknesses in option logic, constraint planning, and complete multi-select recovery.
Highlights joint reasoning and constraint-aware selection as priorities for future decision-model development.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.
bullets: Frames repair as a discrete optimization problem that suppresses reasoning loops, strengthens conclusions, and preserves productive outputs.
Decomposes the objective into independent per-row QUBO/Ising problems solved with GPU simulated annealing or simulated bifurcation.
On Qwen3.5-0.8B, reaches 54.6% on MATH-500 versus 51.7% for the agent edit and 7.9% for the base model; simulated bifurcation reaches 55.1%.
Uses four forward-pass requests, zero LLM tokens, 13–17% fewer weight edits, and 2.2–2.3× fewer BF16 bit flips than the agent repair.
On Qwen3.5-2B, raises greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%; an eight-variable subproblem is also demonstrated on IBM Heron hardware.

papers.abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating 250 paired derivations on the GSM8K benchmark across two 8B models (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), we contrast clustered bursts of attention head masking against budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout. Concentrated bursts induce substantial reasoning degradation: at onset parameter $\mathcal{B}=0.10$ (scheduling $\sim 5.7\%$ of vulnerable head-token volume), Qwen3-8B accuracy drops from $91.2\%$ under diffuse noise to $78.8\%$ under burst dropout ($\Delta = -12.4$ percentage points [pp], exact McNemar $p = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}$), while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct drops from $84.0\%$ to $76.8\%$ ($\Delta = -7.2$ pp, $p = 0.0198$). Conversely, dispersing the identical cumulative budget uniformly across generation steps via stratified quintile matching yields substantially milder degradation (retaining $91.2\%$ in Qwen and $84.0\%$ in LLaMA). In an exploratory factorial dissociation ($N=100$), single-step dropout density is associated with an acute drop in a single schedule draw ($-10.0$ pp on Qwen, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.0425$), while multi-token continuity exhibits an inconclusive compounding trend ($-7.0$ pp, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.1892$). Error analysis reveals that Qwen failures reflect derivation errors within formatted responses (conditional accuracy drop of $-11.4$ pp), whereas in LLaMA $22.2\%$ of discordant losses lack a final answer format line (conditional gap narrows to $-5.0$ pp). These findings demonstrate that autoregressive reasoning chains are particularly vulnerable to concentrated structural disruptions, providing empirical benchmarks for fault tolerance in transformer architectures.
bullets: The study compares clustered bursts of attention-head masking with budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout in 250 paired GSM8K derivations using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct.
At the tested disruption level, burst dropout reduced accuracy by 12.4 percentage points for Qwen3 and 7.2 points for LLaMA relative to diffuse noise.
Uniformly dispersing the same cumulative dropout budget caused substantially milder degradation, preserving the diffuse-noise accuracy levels reported for both models.
Exploratory analysis links single-step dropout density to acute performance loss, while evidence for additional compounding from multi-token continuity is inconclusive.
Failures included derivation errors in Qwen3 and missing final-answer formatting in some LLaMA losses.
