papers.tldr: Concentrated attention-head dropout disrupts autoregressive multi-step reasoning far more than the same dropout budget spread diffusely across generation steps.

papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.
authors: Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces fundamental representational units (FRUs) as basic units of neural representations.
Defines fidelity and stability as criteria for evaluating FRUs.
Proves that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions.
Finds that more stable FRUs are more monosemantic and can be composed across layers to recover human-like semantic organization.
Supports the framework with large-scale experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of the framework for defining, evaluating and identifying representational atoms. a, Representational atoms are defined as fundamental representational units (FRUs) that faithfully reconstruct model representations while remaining distinguishable. This definition is characterized by three properties: representability, sparsity and separability under the atomic inner product (AIP). b, Candidate FRUs are evaluated along two quantitative dimensions. Fidelity, quantified by the coefficient of determination R2, measures the reconstruction of the original representations, whereas stability, quantified by q∗, measures the extent to which atoms remain distinguishable under the condition µq < 1/(2Kq − 1). Higher values indicate better performance for both metrics, with R2 ∈ (−∞, 1] and q∗ ∈ [0, 1]. Stability captures the distinguishability of atoms and their compositions and constitutes a prerequisite for monosemanticity. c, Representational atoms are identified using threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs). The encoder acts as a detector that activates atoms when its response exceeds the positive or negative threshold, while the corresponding decoder vectors constitute the atom set and reconstruct the original representations.

Fig. 3 Monosemanticity is positively correlated with stability across datasets and models. a, Overall relationship between stability and monosemanticity across all datasets, models and SAE architectures. Each point denotes one dataset-model-SAE combination (N = 40). For language models, stability and monosemanticity are averaged across the six evaluated layers; for Stable Diffusion v1.5, across three diffusion timesteps; and for FLUX.2-klein-9B, across six layer-step combinations. The positive correlation indicates a consistent association between stability and monosemanticity across heterogeneous representation settings. b-d, Relationships within Wikipedia (b; N = 15), Wikidata (c; N = 15) and LAION-COCO (d; N = 10), using the same model-SAE-level averages as in a. Positive correlations within all three datasets show that the overall association is preserved within individual datasets and modalities. e-l, Relationships within individual models: Gemma2-2B (e), Gemma2-9B (f) and Qwen3.5-9B (g) on Wikipedia; Gemma2-2B (h), Gemma2-9B (i) and Olmo-Hybrid-7B (j) on Wikidata; and Stable Diffusion v1.5 (k) and FLUX.2-klein-9B (l) on LAION-COCO. For language models, each point denotes one SAE architecture at one layer; for Stable Diffusion v1.5, one SAE architecture at one diffusion timestep; and for FLUX.2-klein-9B, one SAE architecture at one layer-step combination. Monosemanticity is averaged across the manually evaluated features at each corresponding layer, timestep or layer-step combination. These model-level results show that the positive correlation persists at finer representational granularity, although its strength varies across models. Colors denote SAE architectures (BiJumpReLU, JumpReLU, ReLU, TopK with K = 50, and AbsTopK with K = 50), and marker shapes denote datasets. Black lines show linear regression fits with 95% confidence bands. Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients (ρ) and two-sided P values are shown in each panel.

Fig. 2 Existing representational units exhibit distinct limitations in fidelity and stability. a–c, Fidelity (R2, top) and stability (q∗, bottom) of neurons and learned features across layers of Gemma2-2B (a), Gemma2-9B (b) and Llama3.1-8B (c). Angular coordinates denote layer indices, and radial coordinates denote the corresponding metric values. The dashed red circle marks the ideal-atom reference, for which both fidelity and stability attain their maximum value of 1. Neurons consistently exhibit high fidelity but substantially lower stability, whereas learned features from Gemma Scope and Llama Scope show improved stability to varying degrees but generally sacrifice fidelity, with neither class simultaneously approaching the ideal reference on both criteria. Across model scales and feature widths, these results reveal a systematic gap between existing candidate FRUs and the criteria for ideal representational atoms.

Fig. 4 Human sememes are compositionally represented by multiple representational atoms. a, Sememe– atom structural map for Gemma2-2B. Large light-blue circles denote human sememes and smaller blue circles denote representational atoms selected for their compositional recovery. Solid orange circles indicate the best single atoms that are retained in the final composition, whereas dashed orange circles indicate the best single atoms that are not selected. Circle sizes reflect the sizes of the corresponding semantic sets, and the geometric overlap between an atom and its sememe reflects their single-atom precision. Representative examples show that near one-to-one sememe–atom correspondence is rare, whereas compositional recovery by multiple atoms is common. More complete sememe–atom structural maps for Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B, and Llama3.1-8B are shown in Extended Data Figs. 3–5, respectively. b, Distribution of the number of atoms selected for each sememe across Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B and Llama3.1-8B, grouped into 1, 2–3, 4–6 and > 6 atoms. Most sememes are recovered using more than six atoms. c, Semantic recovery of the best single atom and the corresponding atom combination across the three models. Each point denotes an individual sememe, and F1 measures the agreement between the recovered representational set and the corresponding HowNet sememe set. Atom combinations consistently achieve substantially higher semantic alignment than the best single atoms. d, Relationship between sememe complexity and the number of atoms selected for its compositional recovery across the three models. Sememe complexity is measured by the number of entities associated with each HowNet sememe. Each point denotes an individual sememe with merged F1 ≥ 0.5, and dashed lines show model-specific linear regression fits in log–log space. More complex sememes tend to require more atoms for recovery.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon personalized agents maintain an evolving memory by continuously deciding what to add, modify, or discard. However, learning an optimal update policy remains challenging. Conventional training relies solely on terminal question-answering accuracy, yielding a coarse feedback signal that treats all intermediate updates identically. Furthermore, update utility is inherently user-specific, as identical memory actions may yield opposite effects across different user personas. Existing methods fail to address this heterogeneity, relying on globally shared evaluation standards with at most a single scalar intermediate reward. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{Personalized Memory Rubrics} (\textbf{PMR}), a framework that translates terminal feedback into fine-grained, per-step, and per-user credit assignment. PMR decomposes evaluation into a universal layer capturing cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user adaptive layer modeling individual traits as a specialized delta over the universal baseline. Through \textbf{Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment}, PMR redistributes credit at the token level, selectively amplifying validated decisions on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones to avoid unreliable attribution. The rubric and memory policy \textbf{co-evolve} in a closed loop with anti-circularity guarantees. Crucially, PMR incurs zero inference overhead, operating without any rubric or external judge during deployment. Extensive experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines.
authors: Yupeng Han, Kai Zhang, Shuochen Liu, Ze Liu, Xianquan Wang, Zhihong Pan, Xiangyu Zhao, Qi Liu, Enhong Chen
bullets: Addresses coarse terminal-only feedback and the fact that memory actions can help one user but harm another.
Uses a universal rubric for cross-user failure patterns plus an adaptive per-user layer capturing individual traits.
Redistributes credit at the token level, reinforcing validated decisions on successful trajectories and using standard policy optimization on failed ones.
Co-evolves the rubric and memory policy with anti-circularity safeguards.
Shows consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines across four benchmarks, with zero inference overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PMR. PMR first induces a personalized rubric 𝑅𝑢 from shared cross-user patterns and residual per-user failures, and then uses it to shape direction-safe, per-step credit while preserving the trajectory-level update direction. A co-evolution loop iteratively updates the student, rubric, and credit assignment, with standard GRPO used as a fallback for failures. At inference, only the student model is required.

Figure 1: Long-horizon memory learning involves multiple updates but only a terminal QA reward, making fine-grained credit assignment difficult. Hand-crafted methods use fixed, non-personalized rules, while RL-based methods rely on sparse scalar feedback with ambiguous step/token attribution. PMR decouples direction from magnitude: the QA advantage determines the learning direction, while personalized rubric evidence modulates credit magnitude through direction-safe gating.

Figure 4: Case study of learned personalized rubrics. PMR selectively adapts rubric dimensions to user behavior: Malia emphasizes timeliness and conciseness, Maria largely retains universal criteria, and Alex strengthens completeness and conciseness. Consistency remains universal across all three personas.

Figure 3: Co-evolution dynamics across 8 rounds on PersonaMem 32K. Left axis: accuracy; PMR (full, rising) and w/o co-evolution (frozen rubric, plateauing). Right axis: |Runi | (growing) and active Rspec (decreasing as student learns).
Figure 5: Per-user gains from Rspec across four persona groups defined by median splits of volatility and interaction frequency. Δ = Acc(PMR) − Acc(PMR-Global), with larger gains for stable users.

Figure 6: Sensitivity to credit modulation strength 𝜆 and coevolution rounds. (a) Held-out accuracy across the 𝜆× rounds grid. (b) Accuracy versus 𝜆 at rounds 4 and 8, with shading indicating the robust plateau (𝜆 ∈ [0.25, 1.0]).

Table 2: Overall comparison across twelve evaluation settings. PersonaMem (32K/128K) is in-domain; PrefEval (Explicit/Implicit), PersonaBench (4 noise levels), and PERMA (C-S/C-M/N-S/N-M denote Clean/Noise × Single/Multi-Domain) are out-of-domain. Higher is better. Best results are in bold.
Table 4: Ablation on rubric structure components. Cell color indicates drop from Full ( <3 to ≥15 pp).
Table 3: Ablation on credit assignment components. Cell color indicates drop from Full ( <3 to ≥15pp). Rows ordered by average drop.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.
authors: Lirui Luo, Kelong Mao, Xinwei Yang, Rongqing Li, Luyu Chen, Kieran Wong, Yudong Guo, Xinrui Wang, Jiayin Zhu, Gu Simiu, Sulong Xu, Cong Fang
bullets: Long-horizon agents need to decide what information to save, retrieve, and when, as histories exceed active context.
CAMG-II evaluates memory behavior across Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual environments using Bash and persistent workspaces.
CAMP-II jointly trains one policy across all five environments with a frozen teacher that already understands file operations.
The learned file-based memory behavior transfers to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2 with improved success rates.

figures.caption: Figure 2 CAMP-II distils file-based memory across five environments. Top: the student acts in the environment and writes and revises memory files. At each context boundary it compresses its state into the continuation file, which a later read restores. Bottom: completed episodes enter the queue, a frozen teacher scores the tokens the student actually sampled, and the OPD learner updates the student weights from the teacher–student log-probability gap, closing the loop back to the rollout.

Figure 1 File-operation priors improve supervision formemory distillation. A frozen teacher scores studentgenerated memory responses that retain (Keep) or omit (Omit) the same Download requirement. Compared with dedicated memory tools and context-compaction protocols, ordinary Bash/file operations draw on the teacher’s existing prior, yielding a clearer preference for retaining task-critical information and thus more effective supervision. The student’s general notes and bounded continuation file persist across context replacements, so it can recover the saved Download requirement through Bash.

Figure 4 A Visual episode continues from its own saved file. We follow one episode from a late training update on the fitness-product showcase task. papers.abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the nature of expert specialization remains controversial. Reports of domain-associated expert preferences contrast with analyses attributing routing primarily to token identity or syntactic patterns. To clarify these differing accounts, we look beyond expert-level routing to investigate the neuron-level organization of domain-specialized computation using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a measure developed for this analysis. Using mixed-domain calibration data, we identify domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across multi-source samples of the same domain, compared with 15-24% across domains. To understand how this organization evolves during training, we trace neuron importance throughout pre-training and post-training across three fully open MoE families. Neuron importance continues to reorganize between pre-training checkpoints despite comparatively stable expert-level importance rankings, while post-training largely preserves neuron rankings. Building on these neuron-level perspectives, we further introduce RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr) to select neurons across experts for balanced multi-domain capability preservation. At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves average 91-98% of original full performance across six models. At 50% retention, our pruning method can reduce resident GPU memory by 36-43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17-39% effectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/Neuron-Level-Specialization-in-MoE
authors: Zhenhong Zhou, Mao Zheng, Mingyang Song, Qiankun Li, Kun Wang, Junfeng Fang
bullets: Finds domain-specialized neuron sets with 58–74% overlap within domains versus 15–24% across domains.

At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves 91–98% of original performance across six models.
At 50% retention, RAMPr reduces resident GPU memory by 36–43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17–39%.

papers.selection_reason: Neuron-level pruning in MoE LLMs for memory and throughput efficiency, plus MoE architecture analysis.
papers.title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries
papers.tldr: Neuron-level analysis reveals domain-specialized organization within MoE experts and enables pruning that preserves most performance while reducing memory and improving throughput.

papers.abstract: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. However, they typically divide inputs into flat token segments without preserving structure or hierarchy, causing three limitations for structured data such as API responses or HTML documents. First, fixed-length segmentation can split fields of the same record, breaking their relationships. Second, segments lack hierarchical information, obscuring their structural context and positions. Third, successive memory updates may discard details of earlier sibling records needed for reasoning on later segments. To address these limitations, we propose TreeAgent, a structure-aware agent that uses the input hierarchy to guide both segment-wise context processing and access to past information. Specifically, TreeAgent constructs segments from complete subtrees and groups of adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structural relationships. We provide theoretical guarantees on segment counts to guide token budget selection toward matching the segment count of fixed-length segmentation. We further attach structural paths to the segments for the agent to identify their ancestors and hierarchical positions. We also introduce residual memory links from the segments of low-level children to the segments of high-level parents, enabling direct information flows beyond successive memory updates. We evaluate TreeAgent with four representative memory agents on eight retrieval and aggregation tasks. The inputs are derived from real-world application data in JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript and range from 8K to 1M tokens. TreeAgent improves the average score across the four datasets for all four agents, with 3.61% performance gain on average.
authors: Wei Gu, Weiwei Qi, Jiajun Tang, Tianhang Zheng, Bo Chen, Zhibo Zhang, Jinfei Liu, Kui Ren
bullets: Targets flat, fixed-length segmentation that breaks relationships, loses hierarchy, and forgets earlier sibling details.
Builds segments from complete subtrees or adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structure.
Attaches structural paths to expose each segment’s ancestors and position.
Adds residual links from low-level child segments to high-level parent segments for direct information flow.
Evaluated on retrieval and aggregation tasks over JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript inputs spanning 8K–1M tokens; improved all four tested memory agents on average.

The memory-agent block represents the agent’s original workflow, including its internal actions and stopping behavior. After processing each section, TreeAgent saves the updated memory. Parent–child relations determine which saved states are linked and accessed by later updates.

papers.title: TreeAgent: Structure-Aware Memory Agent for Processing Long Hierarchical Data
papers.tldr: TreeAgent improves long hierarchical-data processing by preserving structure during segmentation and memory access, yielding an average 3.61% gain across evaluated memory agents.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.
authors: Lorenzo Cirillo, Irene Amerini, Andrea Cavallaro
bullets: Deep neural networks are difficult to interpret because their layered activations encode complex, interdependent relationships.
Individual neurons may represent multiple concepts, complicating direct interpretation.
Mechanistic interpretability analyzes components whose activations are causally responsible for model behaviors.
The article reviews advances, methods, and frameworks for causal analysis across image, audio, and language-processing systems.

papers.tldr: This article surveys mechanistic interpretability methods for uncovering how internal neural-network components causally produce specific behaviors.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.
authors: Ruize Zheng, Xuyang Liu, Siyu Ren, Xiaobing Tu, Yinggui Wang, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Standard next-token prediction has model-dependent effects: it helps Llama-3.2-3B but degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base on the same mathematical corpus.
OPMD replaces passive imitation with active, query-driven knowledge acquisition from states visited by the student.
At selected anchor positions, it samples student-policy trajectories and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher.
On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves Qwen over its base model and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline.
The method adds no inference-time overhead and is designed to integrate with continual pre-training pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the OPMD compared with standard NTP, along with training dynamics. (a) Standard NTP: Rigid token-by-token imitation on specialized domain corpora leads to severe policy collapse. (b) OPMD Pipeline: (1) Anchor Token Identification (ATI) & Alignment: A proxy model identifies informative trigger tokens via predictive entropy, followed by context deduplication and strict budget alignment. (2) On-Policy Rollout & Distillation: The student generates continuations from prefix prompts and receives dense teacher guidance through a student-weighted Top-16 log-ratio reward at each rollout step. (c) Performance Dynamics: OPMD completely eliminates NTP policy collapse and achieves substantial, stable reasoning gains across benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces on-policy distillation for continual pre-training of LLMs, directly relevant to LLM training and domain adaptation.
papers.title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
papers.tldr: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD) makes continual pre-training model-aware by distilling a frozen teacher on trajectories sampled from the evolving student, improving mathematical adaptation where standard next-token training can hurt.

papers.abstract: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Sarun Kumar K S
bullets: Covers 322 native-language messages in 12 languages and 9 scripts, plus 156 code-mixed or romanised messages and 967 optional training examples.
Provides a fixed routing protocol, baselines, a 13-system leaderboard, and evaluations on four withheld languages.
The shipped multilingual model scores 77.3% overall, the best fine-tune 96.6%, and TF-IDF with logistic regression 91.9%.
On withheld languages, multilingual systems score 77%, 90%, and 93%; code-mixed results show no statistically clear advantage for the multilingual checkpoint.
Labels were generated by LLMs and independently agreed upon for 97.2% of test items; the benchmark resolves differences only above roughly 4 points.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.
authors: Dara Varam, Taraneh Aminosharieh Najafi, David Atienza
bullets: Applies weight-space programming to biosignal models trained on EEG and ECG data.
Language models can identify and fix planted faults without being told what they are, and generate all network weights from architecture, task, and minimal training data.
In one experiment, a language model matched standard training using 6× fewer training subjects without gradient descent.
Claude Opus 5.5-built networks outperformed handcrafted EEG baselines when trained from the same 5 subjects.
Models could not reliably improve already well-trained classifiers or infer the task from weights alone; practical use remains premature.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed. In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).
bullets: Focuses on attacks that manipulate agents’ semantic memory and alter their behavior.
Uses signed knowledge-base entries to prevent unauthorized or malicious knowledge manipulation.
Combines a local Prolog-like Horn-clause inference system with private access to an external knowledge base.
Describes Python implementations offering privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy via IT-PIR.
Scope is semantic memory; episodic and short-term memory attacks are not addressed.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language models by distilling teacher predictions on student-generated trajectories, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for an external teacher by using a reference-conditioned copy of the model as the teacher. Despite its great early improvements, we find that OPSD does not remain consistently effective under continued training and can eventually suffer substantial performance degradation. We study this training behavior and link the degradation to a growing mismatch between the evolving reference-free student and the frozen privileged teacher. In the early stage of OPSD, the privileged teacher remains closely aligned with the student and provides useful guidance for improving the student's generation trajectories. However, as training progresses, the growing distributional mismatch between the privileged teacher and reference-free student can cause the teacher to provide misleading supervision, ultimately degrading student performance. This phenomenon motivates us to first leverage privileged reference supervision to acquire useful knowledge and then transfer it to a fresh student. We introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Distillation (BOPD), a two-stage framework that first uses OPSD to internalize task-relevant information from reference-conditioned supervision into an intermediate model, and then distills this reference-free intermediate model into a fresh copy of the initial model. Experiments across models show that BOPD improves mathematical reasoning and code generation beyond both the initial models and the constructed OPSD teachers. These results suggest that privileged reference supervision can be more effectively exploited by first transferring its task-relevant signal into a task-adapted model and then distilling from that model without reference conditioning.
authors: Yue Wu, Xueyu Zhou, Yangrong Hu, Jian Huang
bullets: On-policy self-distillation can initially help but eventually degrades as the student diverges from its frozen, reference-conditioned teacher.
The proposed BOPD framework uses two stages: OPSD first adapts an intermediate model, then its reference-free behavior is distilled into a fresh copy of the initial model.
Across models, BOPD improves mathematical reasoning and code generation over both the initial models and the corresponding OPSD teachers.
The approach is motivated by reducing misleading supervision caused by distributional mismatch during continued OPSD training.

papers.abstract: Transformer feed-forward blocks combine several design choices: squared activations, gating, and tied versus untied parameter sharing, whose separate contributions to expressivity remain poorly understood. We introduce CP-MLPs, a tensor framework in which each multiplicative unit contributes a rank-1 interaction with three roles: detecting an input feature, reading a value, and writing to the output. Tied gated blocks such as ReLU$^2$ force the detector and value roles to share the same direction; untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU let them differ. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at https://github.com/rarefin/CP-MLPs.
authors: Md Rifat Arefin, Farzaneh Heidari, Irina Rish, Guillaume Rabusseau
bullets: Models each multiplicative unit as a rank-1 interaction that detects input features, reads values, and writes outputs.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.
authors: Zhiyuan Huang, Shengan Zheng, Chenghu Yang, Song Zhang, Lingyun Li, Chen Yu, Weiquan Huang, Linpeng Huang

In AppWorld and WebShop, it achieved 270 successes—29.8% more than Base—and replaced 4,987 diagnosis calls.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Synapse-Control, an agent runtime that manages memory and advice selection, relevant to LLM memory mechanisms and test-time adaptation for agents.
papers.title: Synapse-Control: Making Agent Experience Actionable with Lightweight Runtime Control

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, yet the mechanisms by which they acquire reasoning capabilities and the efficiency of their reasoning remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the path-finding problem over directed graphs, a symbolic abstraction of multi-step reasoning. We first characterize the architectural requirements for this task, proving that one-layer transformers require $\Omega(N^2)$ size on dense graphs to implement the key DFS child-selection primitive. While a two-layer transformer implements full DFS with $O(N\log(N))$ size. Thus, a second layer is necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning. We then extend this expressivity analysis to deeper models: for every $k\geq3$, a $k$-layer transformer implements a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon $1+2^{k-3}$, establishing an exponential increase in reachability horizon with depth. Finally, going beyond expressivity, given appropriately curated training data, we show that two-layer transformers can provably learn to execute DFS via gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs. Together, our results provide a mechanistic account of how transformers implement graph search, how depth expands bounded look-ahead, and how such reasoning algorithms can emerge through training.
bullets: One-layer transformers need Ω(N²) size on dense graphs for the key DFS child-selection operation.
Two-layer transformers implement full DFS with O(N log N) size, making a second layer necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning.
A k-layer transformer achieves a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon 1 + 2^(k−3) for k ≥ 3.
Under appropriately curated training data, two-layer transformers can learn DFS through gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs.
The analysis is theoretical and focuses on directed-graph path finding as a symbolic model of multi-step reasoning.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization, defined as the ability to train on some combinations of modules (e.g., functions such as sort, filter) and then generalize to unseen combinations. Despite substantial empirical work evaluating compositional generalization in transformers, findings have been inconsistent because evaluations were often conducted on a limited set of train-test splits, defined in an ad hoc manner. Through a systematic evaluation, we identify two key aspects of the train-test distribution that strongly affect performance: composition equivalence and module coverage. We show that the apparent performance of direct models (trained only on final outputs) results primarily from exploiting composition equivalences, meaning different sequences of modules that reduce to identical end-to-end functions. When benchmarks eliminate these equivalences, performance drops significantly, showing their inability to generalize to compositions of known modules that produce novel end-to-end functions. We further demonstrate that performance degrades monotonically as module coverage shifts increase (when modules appear in different contexts between train and test), affecting both direct and step-by-step models (trained on intermediate and final outputs). These findings have concrete implications for benchmark design: benchmarks that include compositional equivalences can lead to significant overestimation of the generalization abilities of direct models, and benchmarks that include both module coverage violations and compositional equivalences can exacerbate shortcut learning. As a case study, we demonstrate the role of compositional equivalence on the generalization performance of the pre-trained model Llama3-8B on the code-output prediction task in the coding benchmark LiveCodeBench.
authors: Purva Pruthi, Andrew Yuan, Alexander D'Amour, David Jensen
bullets: Systematically evaluates how train–test distribution design affects compositional generalization.
Finds direct models often appear strong by exploiting different module sequences with identical end-to-end functions.
Removing composition equivalences causes substantial performance drops on novel functions built from known modules.
Performance declines monotonically as module contexts shift between training and testing, for both direct and step-by-step models.
Shows benchmark design can overestimate generalization and encourage shortcut learning, including in a Llama3-8B LiveCodeBench case study.

Figure 1: (a) A sequential composition task combines “atomic” functions (e.g., sort, mode, filter). Task-based compositional generalization is the ability to generalize to unseen sequences after training on a subset. (b) Composition equivalence: Different sequences are composition equivalent if they reduce to the same end-to-end function. For example, one equivalence class consisting of the first four sequences reduces to returning the most frequently occurring vowel in a set of strings; direct models succeed on the test sequence (mode ◦ filter ◦ sort) from this class but fail on the remaining two test sequences from a different composition equivalence class. (c) Module coverage: Examples of coverage failures include position-wise (e.g., function 2 never appearing in the first position, shown with dashed lines) and pair-wise (e.g., missing pair (2,1) in the training set, shown with solid lines).

Figure 3: Cross-k evaluation: For the diverse benchmark (a–b), direct models perform well near training k as equivalences persist across nearby k values. Direct models fail on the uniform benchmark (c–d) regardless of identity tokens, since identity-based equivalences in the uniform benchmark are k-specific. Step-by-step models are more robust but still exhibit significant variability.

Figure 2: Within-k evaluation: Direct models fail completely (0% accuracy) on uniform bijections without identity tokens (Figure (d)), while step-by-step models maintain near-perfect performance across all conditions. We observe that including identity tokens or diverse function types seems crucial for the generalization performance of direct models.

Figure 7: Uniform benchmark (without identity), N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3, Direct (Relative): We observe that the models learn to predict the outputs of training compositions for both K=2 and for K=6, while the test accuracy on unseen compositions remains 0% throughout. We report two metrics: (1) sharp accuracy, where a prediction scores 1.0 only if the entire output sequence is correct and 0.0 otherwise; and (2) mean token accuracy, average accuracy of predictions in the output sequence, with both metrics averaged across compositions from each split. For reference, 100 epochs correspond to roughly 20k iterations (batch size 512, 100k training samples, 195 iterations per epoch).

Figure 8: Diverse benchmark, N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3, Direct (Relative): We observe non-trivial compositional generalization, as the models perform well on training and validation compositions, the test performance also increases. We observe better generalization for K = 6 than for K = 2 due to more training diversity and shared equivalences.
Figure 5: Effect of position-wise distribution shift: As the position-wise KL divergence increases, the compositional generalization performance of both direct and step-by-step models decreases.

Figure 10: Equivalence class necessity and training requirements: (a) Generalization performance to unseen sequences is strongly correlated with the degree of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) Models need to see at least 4–5 composition equivalences (per class) in training to generalize to the corresponding test equivalences.

Figure 14: Composition equivalence encourages shortcuts in step-by-step models: We observe that composition equivalences in the diverse benchmark cause discrepancies between final output accuracy and full output (intermediate and final output) accuracy for both within-k evaluation and cross-k evaluation. Final accuracy > full accuracy implies the model is learning shortcuts to reach the final answer. If we eliminate composition equivalences, the performance difference is zero between full and final outputs (see Figures 15(a), 15(b))

Figure 15: Eliminating composition equivalences removes shortcut learning in step-by-step models : We observe that the lack of compositional equivalence in the uniform benchmark removes shortcut-learning behavior in step-by-step models. This is shown by the exact same step-by-step accuracy, and the final accuracy is the same for both within-k evaluation (k = 6) and cross-k evaluation (train-k = 6).

Figure 19: Effect of pairwise-wise distribution shift: (a) As the pairwise-wise KL divergence increases, the compositional generalization performance of both direct and step-by-step models decreases in the diverse benchmark. (b) For the uniform benchmark, the effect of divergence is primarily observed at the extreme right end for support violations.

Figure 25: Effect of number of samples per composition (diverse benchmark, direct model): For the diverse benchmark, direct models are less sample efficient than the uniform benchmark to generalize on the validation set, especially for K= 2. We observe significant compositional generalization behavior, as seen in Figure 2(b) for large samples, especially for K=6.

Figure 24: Effect of number of samples per composition (uniform benchmark, step-by-step model): We observe that step-by-step models are more sample efficient than direct models due to access to intermediate outputs providing extra information.

Figure 23: Effect of number of samples per composition (uniform benchmark, direct model):. Number of training compositions N = 24 for K = 2, and N = 576 for K = 6. We vary the number of input-output samples per training composition in this experiment. We observe that with a small number of training samples, the train/val gap is large, and the model struggles to generalize to training compositions with novel inputs. The train-val gap reduces as the number of samples increases. Test accuracies remain 0%, as expected.

Figure 26: Effect of number of samples per composition (diverse benchmark, step-by-step model): Step-by-step models are more sample efficient than direct models, and a similar difference between uniform and diverse benchmarks for K=2 is observed as for direct models.

Figure 22: Effect of number of unique training sequential compositions (randomly sampled, K=6):: We observe that (a) step-by-step models with relative global embedding need fewer training compositions to generalize faster than absolute embedding models, and (b) For the diverse benchmark, as compared to direct models, step-by-step models need fewer unique training compositions due to extra information available using intermediate outputs.

Figure 16: Gemma-1B visualization of per-class distribution for 100% sharing: We observe that most of the equivalence classes are shared and the model has overall high accuracy over test sequences in the shared equivalence classes.

Figure 17: Gemma-1B visualization of test accuracy for the split with no shared equivalences: We observe that none of the equivalence classes are shared, and the model has poor accuracy over test sequences in those classes.

Figure 13: Leaking test equivalence classes without swapping (K = 6): (a) Generalization performance to unseen sequences is strongly correlated with the number of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) The mean accuracy of shared equivalence classes is significantly higher than that of non-shared equivalence classes.

Figure 20: Combined effect of position-wise shift and reduced diversity: Shows (1-accuracyKL) to demonstrate accuracy degradation as in Figure 5, revealing combined effects of coverage shift and reduced compositional diversity due to biased sampling. Here, accuracyKL is the performance with biased sampling.

Figure 21: Isolating position-wise shift by controlling diversity: Shows accuracyzero_shift − accuracyKL, where accuracyzero_shift and accuracyKL are accuracies under random and biased sampling with n unique compositions at each Dpos, respectively. For the diverse benchmark, positionwise shift alone has a reduced but still significant effect compared to Figure 20, indicating that both coverage shift and reduced diversity contribute to degradation. For the uniform benchmark, the negligible difference confirms that degradation is driven primarily by coverage shift alone.

Figure 11: Visualization of learned equivalence classes for the diverse benchmark (K=6): We show two equivalence classes (out of a total of 14 classes). papers.abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. (ii) An eight-test black-box sovereignty audit that a buyer can run without access to weights. (iii) A regime argument: under energy and liability constraints, accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk should replace raw accuracy as design objectives, with metrics that abstention cannot inflate. We close with preliminary internal measurements from a proprietary architecture built around these objectives, reported with their limitations. Data and measurement code are included.

A Portuguese-derived vocabulary reduces premiums for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages, including about 24% for Guarani and Quechua.
Introduces an eight-test black-box sovereignty audit requiring no model-weight access.
Argues for optimizing accuracy per joule, calibration, and selective risk rather than raw accuracy; proprietary preliminary measurements are reported with limitations.

papers.title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South
papers.tldr: Fine-tuned language models inherit tokenization and sovereignty costs from their base models, often disadvantaging Global South languages and motivating buyer-accessible audits and efficiency-aware objectives.

papers.abstract: How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds. The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.
bullets: Studies rotation-invariant kernel machines on an ICL linear-regression task using a kernel-eigenbasis decomposition.
As sample size grows, models learn increasingly higher-degree components tied to higher-order statistics of the training tasks.
Generalization appears first, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds.
The results suggest feature learning is not essential for ICL in this setting.
Empirically trained transformers show the predicted memorization through higher-order task statistics.

Figure 4: Task diversity trades pretraining-task accuracy for novel-task accuracy. Following Raventós et al. (2023), we sweep the number of training tasks T and report test MSE on the pretraining tasks Dtr (left) and on novel tasks Dnovel (right). Our data is drawn with d = 8, L = 15, ϵ2 = 0.25. In blue, we show a fit random features network trained with SGD (see Section B for random feature network details), with the memorizing (dMMSE) and generalizing (ridge) oracles shown. As T grows, the training task distribution’s cumulants approach that of the prior’s (Gaussian) and all three curves converge. Evaluated on novel tasks, the random features model initially tracks the memorizing solution up to a task diversity T of 4, continuing to approach the generalizing solution until T ≈ 26 = 64 tasks. All models are trained with enough samples such that they can fully realize the optimal degree-3 term, indicated by the green background. We note two exceptions: a blue background for one training task is used to signify that the model uses the mean task alone, and the seafoam background for two tasks signifies the mean task still being heavily utilized. The trained models do not exactly reach the generalizing solution, in part due to the finite context length L we use for training (see Section 7). Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 7: One-dimensional ICL data breaks Gaussian universality. We compare the eigenframework’s predicted test MSE (line) against kernel regression trained on true ICL contexts (circles) and on a Gaussian surrogate with matched moments (diamonds), for T = 4, d = 1, L = 8. We use a Gaussian kernel with kernel width σker = √ 3 and in-context data with covariance Σx ∼ Id/(dL). The left panel is ridgeless (δ = 0) and the right uses a small ridge (δ = 5× 10−3). The Gaussian surrogate tracks the theory at every n. The true contexts agree away from the interpolation peak but exceed the prediction near it, most visibly at small ridge. Both datasets share the same theoretical curve, so the mismatch comes from the non-Gaussianity of one-dimensional ICL data rather than from the predicted eigenstructure. We observe no such failure for d > 1.

Figure 3: Random feature models can perform ICL even with only T = d+ 1 tasks. We train a random feature network using SGD with exactly T = 4 = d+ 1 tasks (d = 3), with context length L = 96. We manually construct a training task pool such that Σ̂ = Id and µ̂ = 0. As is predicted in Section 7, this training task distribution allows the model to near-perfectly generalize once the optimal degree-3 term ∑ i yix ⊤ i xL+1 is learned. We evaluate the random features model’s test error on novel tasks β⋆ ∼ Dnovel, normalized by E[y2]. When the model has not seen many samples in phase one, the model uses the average training task, which we manually set to 0. At approximately 106 samples, the model enters phase two and begins fitting the generalizing degree-3 term. Even though there are only 4 training tasks, the model does not memorize the tasks with up to 109 samples! Given infinite training samples, the model will eventually memorize. Further details in Section B.

Figure 5: Transformers memorize through non-Gaussian statistics of their training tasks. We train 12-layer GPT-2-style transformers with Adam on T = 256 training tasks (d = 8, L = 16, ϵ2 = 0.25) and evaluate the test MSE on (a) fresh tasks and (b) the training tasks. All pools are centered and whitened (see Section 7.2 for a discussion of the implications) and differ principally in their fourth cumulant. Whiten consists of i.i.d. Gaussian draws, partial kurtosis is made of a symmetric pool whose κ̂4 is rescaled to 0.3× that of its initial Gaussian pool, no kurtosis uses a symmetric pool with κ̂4 = 0. Dashed and dotted lines mark the generalizing (ridge) and memorizing (dMMSE). In (a), each pool’s dMMSE is shown to highlight that the slight difference in oracle does not explain the onset of task memorization. All models first approach the generalizing solution, with the scale of the kurtosis setting when memorization begins. Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 1: As sample size grows, kernels learn successively higher-degree target function components in in-context linear regression. They first learn the mean training task (phase 1), then approximate the degree-three generalizing solution (phase 2), and finally memorize the training tasks (phase 3). (Left) A visualization of a kernel machine’s inferred task in task space B = Rd decomposed into vector components learned in each phase (arrows). Grey dots indicate training tasks Btr = {β(t)} and a grey star indicates an unseen task β∗ /∈ Btr. In phase 1, the kernel learns the mean training task µ̂β := Eβ∼Btr [β]. In phase 2, the kernel learns approximately β∗− µ̂β , nearly recovering the true task β∗. In phase 3, learned higher-degree terms pull the prediction towards the nearest task in Btr. (Right) We plot learning curves for KR on the in-context linear regression problem with d = 5, L = 7, T = 16. (Top) Evaluated on the training tasks, the error falls monotonically, eventually reaching that of the memorizing solution (Equation (3)). We show both theoretical predictions (lines) and experimental values (dots) in the experimentally-accessible region n ∈ [1, 5 × 104]. (Middle) Evaluated on novel tasks (β ∼ N (0, Id)), error is minimized at the end of phase 2, approaching that of the generalizing solution (Equation (4)), before rising to that of the memorizing solution in phase 3. Background shading indicates the three phases of learning. (Bottom) We also plot the predicted overlap between the function f̂ker learned by KR and various polynomial functions gi. The functions gi correspond to the vector components in the cartoon on the left, and are given explicitly in Section B. The function gi is determined by the i-th order statistics of Btr. The component g1 is responsible for generalization and is learned in phase 2. We show theoretical predictions (lines) for the kernel’s error out to 1012 samples, finding excellent agreement between theory and experiment in the experimentally accessible region.

Figure 2: Transience is explained by learning higher order task statistics. We train lazy random features networks (RFNs) (see Section B.2 for a description of RFNs) with online SGD on ICL linear regression data. Using RFNs, we empirically find that the error on novel tasks rises when the higher degree terms are learned, as was theoretically predicted in Figure 1. We observe the same three phases of predicting from the mean task alone, then generalizing to any task, followed by memorizing using higher-degree terms. (Top) Test MSE on novel tasks β ∼ Dnovel, with the memorizing (dMMSE) and generalizing (ridge) oracles for reference. Unlike the kernels trained in Figure 1, the random feature networks train with enough samples to empirically probe phase 3. (Bottom) Overlap of the learned predictor with the leading terms of the memorizing solution, E[f̂gi]/E[g2i ]. Similar to Figure 1, the functions gi are determined by the i-th order statistics of Btr, and are explicitly given in Section B. Novel-task error drops below the memorizing oracle as ϕ3 is learned (n ≈ 105–106) and is lowest once ϕ3 (g1) saturates. The error then rises back toward the memorizing oracle as the network learns higher order statistics through g2 (n ≳ 107). Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 6: Analytically solved random feature models outperform the memorizing oracle on novel tasks. We show test MSE on novel tasks (Dnovel) and on the training tasks β ∈ Dtr of a random feature model whose readout layer weight has been analytically solved, as a function of the number of training samples n. The limiting kernel function is the ICL kernel of Equation (11), set with kernel width σ = 3. We use T = 8, L = 4, d = 4, ϵ2 = 0.05, and tasks drawn from an isotropic prior. Shading shows the standard deviation over 5 trials. Past n ≈ 4× 103, the model’s error drops below that of the memorizing oracle (dMMSE). It remains well above the generalizing oracle (ridge) throughout.

Figure 9: Gaussian kernel learning curves on ICL Regression data. For four different settings (colors) of the task diversity T , we compute the expected test MSE as a function of the number of training samples n, and compare it to empirical errors obtained across 20 trials. Theoretical learning curve equations are provided in Section D, with validation of the eigensystem the equations are built off of provided in Sections E and F. Our data uses a Gaussian kernel with kernel width σker = √ 3, d = 5, L = 7, ϵ2 = 0.1 where our data is drawn x ∼ N (0, Id/(dL)). Additionally, as T → ∞, we find that the errors on the pretraining distribution match those of the true distribution, as expected. Further experimental details are in Section B.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.
authors: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li, Rui Zhang, Hong Yu
bullets: Evaluates five memory approaches across four LLMs in biomedical reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversation settings.

HMRU improves results by an average of 8.6%, reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9%, and closes 48.0% of the gap to full-context inference.
The study highlights persistent challenges in retrieving relevant information, preserving fidelity, and using memory effectively for biomedical reasoning.

papers.abstract: Quantifying uncertainty over an entire LLM completion is critical for selective prediction and adaptive compute. Zero-cost signals such as mean token entropy and log-probability are local to tokens or to one completion, and self-consistency needs many extra completions. We show that Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which gives the sequence-level R'enyi entropy (SRE) of the model's completion distribution at zero marginal cost, with a guarantee at every particle budget. A R'enyi chain rule extends this readout to a family of stepwise entropies of any order. We prove that orders above one are tied to the most likely token of each step, which explains why they track log-probability, while the order-1/2 member accumulates the log of per-step search effort. This member is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 its AUROC is 0.022 to 0.044 above log-probability with all four models and within length quartiles, and the same order is selected when each setting is held out. An 8-particle probe identifies the problems that benefit from more particles, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy on MATH500 with 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.
authors: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Milad Heidari Sorkhehdizaj, Shahab Rahimirad, Aliasghar Pourghani, Seyedarmin Azizi, Souvik Kundu, Abolfazl Hashemi, Joseph Campbell, Vijay Gupta
bullets: Sequence-level uncertainty is needed for selective prediction, but token-level scores and self-consistency have limitations.
Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) power sampling estimates the completion distribution’s normalizing constant, yielding sequence-level Rényi entropy at every particle budget.
A Rényi chain rule provides stepwise entropy signals; order 1/2 captures cumulative per-step search effort and outperforms log-probability in 10 of 13 settings.
On MATH500, order 1/2 improves AUROC over log-probability by 0.022–0.044 across four models and length quartiles.
An 8-particle probe enables adaptive compute: a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy while using 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.

papers.title: Free Lunch Uncertainty: Sequence-Level R\'enyi Entropy from Particle Decoding for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Particle decoding provides sequence-level Rényi entropy at no extra decoding cost, enabling stronger uncertainty estimates and adaptive allocation of LLM reasoning compute.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen computation without adding parameters, yet caching full-context key-value (KV) states across layers and rounds severely bounds serving batch size. We design a looped causal encoder-decoder (CED) that achieves recurrent depth with zero round-wise KV growth, addressing where and how to loop an asymmetric stack in which only sparse encoder layers generate global KV. We find that recurrence must be placed in the encoder to iteratively refine global KV representations rather than re-reading static decoder projections, which both drives language-modeling gains and preserves long-context scaling. Furthermore, training the encoder loop under stochastic recurrence depth induces a fixed-point equilibrium where every round losslessly shares the last round's KV cache. Compounding cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing, the resulting Looped CED matches an unlooped CED's minimal memory footprint and recovers 86-93% of a looped Transformer's gain with 1/6 of its global KV. To test serving at production scale, we loop the 552B-parameter DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for 8 rounds on one 4xGB200 node: with per-layer and per-round KV the loop cannot fit a single 128K-token request, whereas Looped CED holds 36.8x less KV per token, fits 38 such requests (as many as the unlooped model), and serves 3.6x higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.
authors: Jiaqi Leng, Minshen Zhang, Zhaofeng Sun, Yu-Yang Qian, Peng Zhao, Hao Zhang
bullets: Problem: Standard looped Transformers grow KV caches across layers and rounds, limiting batch size and long-context serving.
Method: Place recurrence in sparse encoder layers to iteratively refine global KV representations, and train with stochastic recurrence depth to encourage KV sharing across rounds.
Contribution: Cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing yields recurrent computation without round-wise KV growth.
Results: Looped CED recovers 86–93% of a looped Transformer’s gain using one-sixth the global KV, while matching an unlooped CED’s memory footprint.
At production scale, it uses 36.8× less KV per token, fits 38 128K-token requests on one node, and delivers 3.6× higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.

papers.selection_reason: Looped causal encoder-decoder with recurrent depth and zero round-wise KV growth; directly targets KV-cache and memory-efficient LLM serving.
papers.title: Looping Deeper Without Growing the KV Cache: Recurrent Depth for Causal Encoder-Decoders
papers.tldr: Looped CED adds recurrent depth while keeping KV-cache memory effectively unchanged, enabling long-context serving at substantially higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
authors: Saber Malekmohammadi, Kevin Kuo, Virginia Smith, Golnoosh Farnadi
bullets: Shows that frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ LoRA with Gaussian initialization approximates full fine-tuning through rank-dependent stochastic gradient perturbations.
Freezes and periodically resamples client-side $\mathbf{A}$ matrices to decouple adaptation gradients and ease low-rank constraints.
Finds that gradient signal-to-noise ratio increases linearly with adaptation rank, motivating rank-aware client learning rates.
Proves convergence under heterogeneous client resources.
Experiments on benchmark datasets report consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art baselines with half the client overhead.
