papers.tldr: SPRA-LoRA improves federated LoRA fine-tuning by freezing and resampling one adaptation matrix while scaling client learning rates with rank, reducing client overhead by 50%.

papers.abstract: Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. In the viewer, every cell can be decoded with two lenses, the logit lens and the Jacobian lens (J-lens), traced back to the tokens it drew from, and edited, with the rest of the model rerun on the spot. We demonstrate three usage scenarios on Gemma-3-4B-it, backed by sweeps over a few hundred prompts, to show what this tool can discover. First, the two lenses give different directions to write with, each suiting a different edit: the logit lens's word direction sets what a token outputs, while the J-lens's direction changes what later tokens read. Second, in two-hop trivia questions (the capital of the state or country containing a given city), the state or country is readable at the city token from as early as layer 7, and swapping it there can redirect the answer 92-98% of the time; however, at the answer position, the state or country information is not used. Third, when a chat model answers questions with a step-by-step reasoning prompt, the correct answer is often already the top word in the residual stream before any reasoning is written: for 89-92% of retrieval questions and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, far above their respective distractors (at most 5%). However, ordering puzzles are an exception, as the model works them out only once it writes its final reasoning steps. Furthermore, for answers that are visible in the residual stream, the J-lens reads them a layer or two earlier than the logit lens across the different types of question.
authors: Nika Zahedi, Fangyi Zhu, Anna Wu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that decoded-word heatmaps show representations but not whether the model uses them.
Provides an interactive layers-by-tokens viewer with logit- and Jacobian-lens decoding, token tracing, and live editing.
The logit lens is better for changing a token’s output, while the J-lens is better for changing what later tokens read.
In two-hop trivia, intermediate entities appear early and can redirect answers 92–98% of the time, though they are not used at the answer position.
Answers often appear before written reasoning for retrieval and some multi-hop tasks, but ordering puzzles require the model’s final reasoning; the J-lens detects answers earlier.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Two-hop recall in Gemma-3-4B-it (“Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is”, 25 U.S. items the model answers correctly). (a) At the city token, the J-lens reads the state among its top five words from about layer 7, the logit lens from layer 22. As a control, a wrong state (one belonging to another item, such as California for Dallas) never enters either lens’s top five. (b) At the last token, both lenses read the state before the capital; the J-lens begins to read it a few layers before the logit lens does. (c) Swapping the state for another item’s at the city token (s = 4, 40 pairs) gives the new state’s capital, nearly as often as the copy cell edit (black line), until the handoff. (d) The same swap at the last token fails, although the state is readable there and copying the cell works after the handoff. Bands are bootstrap 95% CIs.

Figure 6: The Dallas question in the viewer (Gemma-3-4B-it). (a) At Dallas, layer 21, the J-lens reads Texas second. (b) Swapping Texas for California there (J-lens directions, s = 4) changes the answer from Austin to Sacramento. (c) At the last token, layer 25, the J-lens reads Texas first. (d) The same swap there makes the model name a state instead of reasoning on to its capital.

Figure 9: Scenario B in one picture (Gemma-3-4B-it, 34 layers; “Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is”, 25 U.S. items). Each token has one lane per lens, shaded from the median layer at which the state (Texas, light) and then the capital (Austin, dark) enter the lens’s top five. (a) At the city token "Dallas", the J-lens reads the first hop from layer 7, well before the logit lens (layer 22), and swapping Texas for California there makes the model answer Sacramento. (b) By the handoff (layer 25), the last token "is" has copied the state from the city token, and both lenses read the state before the capital. Swapping the state here leaves the answer Austin: the state is readable at this token but not used. World items (not shown) read the capital as early as the country, as a memorized shortcut would.

Figure 10: The two patterns we look for (a schematic, not data), for the prompt “The Sydney Opera House is in a country. What is the capital of that country? Think step by step.” Each cell can only use the tokens to its left. (a) If the model resolves both hops in its layers while reading the question, a lens reads Australia and then Canberra in the question’s cells, before any reasoning is written. (b) If the model needs its written steps, Canberra becomes readable only after it has written Australia. Figure 11 counts how often each case occurs.

Figure 3: Each direction suits one edit (country–capital, Gemma-3-4B-it). (a) Pushing the answer token toward another country’s capital: the logit lens direction succeeds for 90% of items from layer 7, the J-lens direction only from layer 28 (n = 79). (b) Swapping the country for another at its own token: the J-lens direction succeeds in the middle layers (n = 100 pairs), up to the handoff, where copying the cells after the country starts to beat copying the country’s own cell (black lines, 20 pairs). Bands are bootstrap 95% CIs. (c) Cosine between the two directions for the same word, over the 203 words pushed toward (band: interquartile range): nearly perpendicular through layer 12, converging near the top.

Figure 4: A J-lens swap in the viewer (Gemma-3-4B-it, antonym prompts with five examples). (a) At layer 18 the J-lens reads the undue cell as undue and related words, and (c) swapping undue for rural there (strength 4) changes the answer to urban. (b) The J-lens reads the comfortable cell as formatting tokens (layer 12 shown), and (d) the same swap toward unfold leaves the answer uncomfortable. A J-lens swap points the right way only when the J-lens shows the word in its own cell; undue→rural is the only antonym pair of 100 for which it succeeds.

Figure 5: Finding the handoff in the viewer (Gemma-3-4B-it, “. . . Q: Russia\nA:”). Left: the last four tokens, each cell labeled with the J-lens’s top word and shaded by how much it feeds the output (Trace back from the outlined cell). Right: the answer after copying the Russia cell, at that layer, from the same prompt ending in Japan. The copy changes the answer up to layer 21 and not after. Teal outlines: cells with trace-back weight of > 0.04 to the output cell (red outline).

Figure 7: Reading the Dallas question in the viewer (Gemma-3-4Bit): the last four tokens at every layer, each cell labeled with the J-lens’s top word. Shaded: Texas is among the top five; outlined: Austin is. Texas is readable at Dallas from layer 6, long before the cell’s top word changes, and reaches the last token at layer 23, three layers before Austin.

Figure 11: Is the final answer readable before the reasoning? Gemma-3-4B-it, correctly answered questions out of 100 per task type. (a) Share of answers that a lens ranks first at some cell before the first reasoning token; the black ticks are a plausible wrong answer (control). (b) For those answers, the median first layer at which the lens reads it, with the number of answers beside each point.

Figure 2: Schematic of the four edits to a cell h. (a) Push adds a word’s direction d̂w, scaled by the cell’s own length. (b) Swap removes the cell’s component along the old word and adds s times its size along the new word, leaving the rest of the cell unchanged. (c) Copy replaces the whole cell with the same cell from another prompt. (d) Add a difference adds the difference between two prompts’ cells.
Table 2: The four task types of the chain-of-thought study, 100 questions each, and how many Gemma-3-4B-it answers correctly.

Table 1: Edits on Gemma-3-4B-it (34 layers), n = 25–100 items per task. Push: the first layer from which the pushed word is the top prediction for at least 90% of items. Swap: success at each direction’s best layer, with that layer in parentheses. Random: a control edit that changes the cell by the same amount as the J-lens swap, but along a random direction. Copy cell: success when the whole entity cell is copied from a prompt naming the new entity, our empirical ceiling for a single-cell edit. Random pushes succeed on at most 4% of items at any layer. The rates are not sensitive to choosing the best layer on the same pairs it is scored on: choosing it on a random half and scoring the other half (20 split trials) changed them by at most 5 percentage points.

papers.selection_reason: LLM residual-stream interpretability tool with a Jacobian lens; technically relevant to language-model analysis and editing.
papers.title: MicroLens: Read, Trace, and Rewire the Residual Stream with Two Lenses
papers.tldr: MicroLens combines decoding, information tracing, and residual-stream editing to reveal what language models represent, use, and can be redirected by.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.
authors: Komal Thareja, Mats Rynge, Berent Aldikacti, Angelina Ju, Ian Lumsden, Anirban Mandal, Rajiv Mayani, Kin Wai Ng, Hamza Safri, Michael Stealey, Sai Swaminathan, Michela Taufer, Karan Vahi, Michael Zink, Ewa Deelman
bullets: Addresses the gap between AI-generated workflow code and safe, observable execution on shared scientific infrastructure.
Projects a curated knowledge base into multiple coding agents and introspects workflow interfaces and execution sites.
Grounds agent diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry for distributed-run awareness.
Constrains actions through federated identity, per-user environments and credentials, observability, and approval controls.

papers.abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.
authors: Ke Wang, Atakan Topcu, Hossein Momeni, Molin Zhang
bullets: Connects acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific checks to agent actions.
Uses project-local memory and reviewed contributions to preserve and improve workflow guidance.
Demonstrates sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction under researcher supervision.
Introduces MRI Agent Bench for evaluating agents across models and MRI task types.
In 240 Core evaluations, all-checks-passed completion rose from 67.5% to 78.3%; in 134 Hard evaluations, from 36.6% to 44.8% with MRFoundry.

papers.abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.
bullets: The study examines what causes symbolic mechanisms supporting abstract reasoning to emerge.
Networks were trained from scratch on abstract sequence tasks while varying architecture and data distribution.
Representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses confirmed the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in transformers.
Greater diversity across multiple data dimensions produced stronger symbolic signatures.
Similar mechanisms emerged in modified transformers, multilayer perceptrons, and an entity–attribute binding task.

papers.abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.
authors: Llu\'is Arola-Fern\'andez, Aissam Khadraoui, Alex Arenas
bullets: Models past tokens as oscillators whose content and age determine their state and frequency.
Uses Kuramoto synchronization to derive a closed-form attention layer with normalized weights above a critical coupling threshold.
Below the threshold, the receiver abstains, producing weights that sum to less than one.
Trained networks exploit both phases to select, abstain, and count, and continue reading beyond their training length.
The theory predicts observed failure cases, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or evaluation settings.

papers.selection_reason: Derives an attention layer from oscillator synchronization, a novel architectural mechanism for LLMs.
papers.title: Everything in its right place: attention is a radio head
papers.tldr: The paper reinterprets attention as a radio-like synchronization process in which a receiver locks onto relevant context tokens and can remain silent when none are relevant.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
bullets: Motivation: Query relevance alone may be insufficient for long-lived AI systems that must recover causally and temporally linked memories.
Method: Request and goal cues seed a memory graph; activation and fan attenuation bound traversal, while retrieved entities recursively emit cues.
Output: A typed evidence graph is reconstructed before language-model generation.
Analysis: The work specifies architectural consequences, cost estimates, ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol.
Scope: This is a preprint with no benchmark measurements; the claim is testable against a simpler graph reranker under equal budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Activation-guided graph retrieval control loop. The self-loop at recursive cues and path expansion is Section 3.3’s recursive cue generation: a retrieved entity’s new cues re-enter frontier allocation before the stop criteria release the result to evidence reconstruction. Authorization is evaluated before content-bearing activation or expansion; only qualified downstream outcomes update future availability.

papers.title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
papers.tldr: An architecture proposes reconstructing memories by activation-guided traversal of an authorized graph, returning evidence paths rather than only relevance-ranked context.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.
authors: Rotem Elimelech, Michael Shalyt, Ido Kaminer
bullets: Targets errors that propagate through LLM reasoning and are costly to detect only at the end.
Uses code-based, real-time verification of reasoning steps rather than a separate verifier LLM.
When a check fails, the model is alerted and continues from the error location instead of restarting.
On ASyMoB with three open-weight models, accuracy improved by 1.4–5.6 percentage points with 6–7% more tokens.
Demonstrated for symbolic mathematics; broader gains depend on extending deterministic checkers to other reasoning steps.

(B) During checked generation, a completed mathematical claim is extracted from the stream and dispatched for verification while the model continues decoding. A failed check interrupts generation; the continuation after the offending step is discarded, and corrective feedback is appended before generation resumes. (C) The three stages of the method, corresponding to the numbered annotations in panel B. Extraction and verification require no additional model calls.

papers.abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
bullets: Determines the origin radius for every dictionary in polynomial time using radius certificates based on products of automaton runs.
Shows the radius is infinite exactly when a periodic word has two canonical tilings without a common boundary; under an ordering condition, self-pairs characterize infinitude.
Proves that finite radius yields dense cuts and that the token machine is complete, making tokenization subsequential for every dictionary.
Develops a streaming tokenizer that emits tokens stable under all continuations, and decides boundedness of token-sequence edit distance in polynomial time.
Reports infinite origin radius for GPT-2 from its 42nd effective self-pair and for cl100k, o200k, and Llama 3 from their first; asymptotic edit-distance bounds are given under the ordering condition.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.
authors: Dongyao Chen, Jiayun Lei, Zhiyuan Ji, Zhiying Deng, Wei Liu, Xiaobo Sun
bullets: Knowledge-editing methods must allocate limited model capacity when constructing target hidden states, not only when editing parameters.
The paper shows a positive correlation between interference among target hidden states and interference in parameter space.
It applies ℓ1 regularization to prune extraneous “tentacles” from knowledge vectors while preserving essential components.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify improved coexistence of edited and existing knowledge.

papers.abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.
authors: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
bullets: Third Eye separates immediate utility from the utility of a subsequent native update.
Across five 3–8B backbones on math and code, continuation often reduces update utility; Qwen3-8B is inconclusive.
In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility was near zero, while continuation reduced it by 1.78 percentage points.
Candidate-averaged immediate utility was already negative, suggesting selection can mask first-step harm.
Independent scoring and a no-update baseline are needed to assess persistent self-updates; no reliable mitigation or single mechanism was identified.

papers.abstract: Time-series forecasting has recently seen a paradigm shift with the introduction of foundation-style models that adapt large pretrained language architectures to sequential data. However, effectively exposing fundamental temporal structures, such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence, to these models remains an open challenge, particularly when the available observations are limited. In this paper, we conduct an exploratory empirical study across different generations of forecasting architectures and propose StatPrompt-LLM, a lightweight statistical refinement of Time-LLM. StatPrompt-LLM augments the existing Time-LLM prompting mechanism with dataset-level statistical information and introduces a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. We evaluate our framework on electricity and meteorological time-series benchmarks, including ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather, under full-prefix and reduced-prefix configurations. Under the 10% reduced-prefix configuration, StatPrompt-LLM achieved lower in-sample prediction errors than Time-LLM, with unweighted average relative reductions across datasets of 40.2% in MSE and 21.4% in MAE. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent. Ablation analyses revealed relatively modest and dataset-dependent changes when selected additional statistical descriptor groups were masked within the combined architecture. Computational profiling indicated additional model parameters and runtime overhead relative to Time-LLM.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exposing trend, scale, and temporal dependence to foundation-style forecasting models with limited observations.
Extends Time-LLM prompting using dataset-level statistical information and a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass.
Evaluated on ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather benchmarks under full-prefix and 10% reduced-prefix settings.
With 10% prefixes, it reduced in-sample MSE by 40.2% and MAE by 21.4% on average relative to Time-LLM; full-prefix results varied by dataset.
Ablations showed modest, dataset-dependent effects from masking descriptor groups, while profiling found increased parameters and runtime.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
authors: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Targets the indexer bottleneck, which can exceed half of prefill GPU time at long context lengths.
Uses layer-wise calibration to handle heterogeneous cross-query retrieval overlap across layers.
Trains adaptive layer-wise group indexers through group-level distillation while retaining query-specific refinement.
Reduces repeated full-prefix scans via token-bank sharing within query groups.
On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1, reports up to 6.22× prefill, 3.40× decoding-kernel, and 1.54× end-to-end serving speedups while maintaining near-lossless LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of ADIndex. During inference, the trained group indexer constructs a shared token bank through a single full-prefix scan per group. The original DSA indexer then performs query-specific Top-K refinement over the shared bank augmented with newly visible post-anchor tokens.

papers.abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.
bullets: Preference construction is audited through stored derivations that allow labels to be recomputed without rerunning the language model.
A pretrained language model classifies predefined prompt and response attributes, after which explicit rules determine verdicts and preferences.
On 200 human-annotated prompts, 192 produced valid structured outputs; all parsing failures occurred among harmful self-harm prompts.
A policy trained on 465 preference pairs showed measured benign refusal of 40.82% and toxic refusal of 84.98% across the evaluated prompt sets.
Reproducible label derivations do not establish attribute correctness or semantic safety, which require separate validation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Symbolic Preference Labeling pipeline for one candidate pair. After attribute assignment, the rule base gives each candidate a response verdict, and the ranks of the two verdicts are compared under the fixed verdict ranking to determine the preference label. Dashed lines mark the cases that produce no preference label. papers.tldr: Symbolic Preference Labeling makes safety preference labels reproducible and inspectable by recording the model’s attribute assignments, rules, and verdict rankings.

papers.abstract: The demand for personalized LLMs is shifting from style imitation toward content quality. We investigate whether self-distillation can bridge this gap in existing fine-tuning paradigm. To address this limitation, we introduce MIRROR(Meta- personalization by Internalizing Reference-Revealed On-policy Reflections), a novel self-distillation framework that shifts LLM personalization from imitation toward preference internalization. First, we replace reference-token imitation with reference-revealed on-policy self-distillation, aligning the model's next-token distributions along its own generation trajectories with those of its reference-conditioned self, thereby internalizing user preferences rather than reproducing reference wording.Second, we introduce MIRROR-F, a focal plug-in that augments on-policy distributional alignment with selective supervision over informative reference tokens, thereby strengthening content generation while preserving user-specific expression. Across three personalized generation benchmarks, two model scales, and complementary reference-based and LLM-based evaluations, MIRROR and MIRROR-F achieve leading overall personalization performance and superior text quality, while exhibiting less catastrophic forgetting than SFT-based baselines on three unseen personalized generation tasks. The gains are consistent across model scales and application scenarios, translating to improved performance in LLM personalization tasks.
bullets: Targets the shift from stylistic imitation toward higher-quality, preference-aware content generation.
Aligns on-policy token distributions from the model’s own generations with those of its reference-conditioned counterpart.
MIRROR-F adds selective supervision on informative reference tokens to strengthen content generation while preserving personal expression.
Across three benchmarks, two model scales, and multiple evaluations, both methods show strong personalization and text-quality performance.

papers.abstract: Activation steering manipulates large language model behavior by intervening on internal activations, but the mechanistic basis of these interventions remains poorly understood. We decompose refusal steering into component-level interventions across four open-weight models, identifying the sparse subsets of attention and MLP components whose steering suffices to reproduce the full behavioral effect. We find that refusal directions concentrate in sparse component mechanisms comprising 28--48\% of upstream components, retaining 88--101\% of steering effectiveness. Within these mechanisms, effective steering further concentrates in approximately 50\% of residual stream dimensions, retaining 85--98\% of the component-mechanism baseline, consistent with a privileged basis structure. Sparsity thus operates at two levels: which components are steered, and which dimensions within those components carry the signal. Together these findings show that refusal is not diffusely encoded across a transformer but assembled by a structured, identifiable mechanism, providing a foundation for mechanistic understanding of how refusal behaviors are represented and steered. To facilitate reproducibility, we release all code and raw experimental results in https://github.com/wang-research-lab/Refusal_Mechanisms.
bullets: Across four open-weight models, sparse attention and MLP component subsets reproduced most of the full refusal-steering effect.
These subsets comprised 28–48% of upstream components while retaining 88–101% effectiveness.
Within selected components, about half of residual-stream dimensions retained 85–98% of the component-level effect.
The results suggest a privileged basis structure and an identifiable mechanism for refusal behavior.
Code and raw experimental results are publicly released for reproducibility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-level sparsity in transformer refusal mechanisms. The residual stream passes through a sequence of attention and MLP components; a sparse subset (28–48% across models) forms a sufficient mechanism to steer refusal behavior, where steering a component via orthogonalization means removing the output’s projection onto the refusal direction. Zooming into each identified component, effective steering also requires intervening on only the same ≈ 50% of residual dimensions across all components, consistent with a privileged basis structure in the residual stream. Prior work steers all dimensions of all upstream components simultaneously by intervening on the residual stream; we instead steer individual component outputs, allowing the residual connection to proceed unaltered.

Figure 2: Residual stream steering effectiveness as a function of dimension percentage. Each marker shows the ASR recovered relative to full-dimensional steering, plotted against the fraction of hidden dimensions used. Marker labels indicate the corresponding norm explanation threshold t – the fraction of ∥r∗∥2 explained by the retained dimensions. Across all four models, retaining ∼50% of dimensions at the 95% norm threshold recovers over 90% of full steering ASR, with some models exceeding the dense baseline. Performance degrades sharply only as the budget falls below the 50% norm threshold, confirming that the refusal direction is concentrated in a sparse set of high-magnitude coordinates.

Figure 7: Distribution of refusal direction coefficients at l∗. Coordinate values of r∗ for each model. Blue bars represent typical dimensions within the central distribution; red bars with black outlines denote statistical outliers (> 2.5× IQR). The y-axis is log-scaled to make the sparse high-magnitude dimensions visible. Summary statistics (µ, σ) and outlier counts are provided for each model.

Figure 5: Component write profiles sorted by refusal importance rank. Top 10% of coordinates by write magnitude shown for each component, sorted by |r∗i | descending so the most refusal-important coordinates appear on the left. Outputs are unit-normalised to control for LayerNorm-induced scale differences. Point size scales with write magnitude; color indicates relative layer depth (early: purple, late: gold). High-magnitude writes are distributed throughout the coordinate space rather than concentrated at high refusal importance ranks, indicating component-specific rather than shared sparse subspaces.

Figure 4: Per-component linear attribution to the refusal direction. For each component in the identified mechanism, bars show the scalar projection of its difference-in-mean vector onto r∗, measuring how much each component contributes to assembling the refusal direction at l∗. Attention components (orange) and MLP components (blue) are shown by layer index. Negative values indicate components that write against the refusal direction. Each reconstruction scores (fraction of ∥r∗∥2 recovered) is provided in the top left.

Figure 10: First-Round Component Ablation: Initial Redundancy. The absolute drop in ASR when individual components are removed from the initial, unpruned candidate circuit. The flat profile across all models indicates that no single component acts as a bottleneck in the presence of the full redundant set.

Figure 6: Exhaustive steering performance of the difference-in-means direction extracted from each layer’s input. Steering is performed in the residual stream at the layer input, replicating prior work. The highest performing steering direction is highlighted in red and is used to find the mechanism in our study. All directions are extracted from the last post-instruction token. The highest ASR value is also used as a reference value that the mechanisms in Table 1 compare against.

Figure 3: Sparse mechanisms versus their complement sets. Each arrow points from the complement (excluded components, hollow diamond) to the identified mechanism (included components, filled circle). Mechanisms comprising 28–48% of upstream components reproduce 88–101% of the full steering effect, while their complements – the remaining 52–72% of components – largely fail to elicit refusal.

Figure 8: Component cosine similarity with r∗ on harmful vs. harmless prompts. Colored bars show the IQR of cosine similarity between each component’s last-token output and r∗ over harmful prompts (blue: MLP, orange: attention). Outlined boxes show the corresponding IQR over harmless prompts. Red lines indicate the selectivity shift – the difference in mean cosine similarity between the two distributions. A large upward red line indicates a component that aligns more strongly with the refusal direction on harmful content than harmless content.

Figure 9: Mechanism Sufficiency: Leave-One-Out ASR Drop. The absolute drop in Attack Success Rate (ASR) when each individual component is removed from the identified sparse mechanism. Higher bars indicate components that act as critical bottlenecks for successful refusal steering. Blue bars represent MLP layers, and orange bars represent Attention mechanisms.

Table 6: Membership containment across threshold settings. Shared is the number of components present in both mechanisms. Subset? indicates whether the smaller mechanism is a strict subset of the larger. Every τ relation nests; α = 0.90 ⊆ α = 0.95 nests for three of four models; α = 0.95 ⊆ α = 0.99 nests for none, including the Mistral-3.2-Small case where both mechanisms have size 10 but differ by one component.

Table 4: Rotation control experiment results. For each model, the same number of dimensions k used in the 95% norm-threshold sparse steering condition is selected from a randomly rotated direction r̃ = Qr∗, where Q ∼ Haar(O(d)). Orig. Rel. ASR is the ASR of the original sparse steering as a percentage of the full-component dense baseline. Rot. Rel. ASR is the mean ASR across N = 5 random rotations; Std is the standard deviation across trials. ∆ is the difference. Near-zero rotated ASR confirms that the specific nativebasis coordinates selected by the norm threshold are functionally privileged rather than interchangeable with an arbitrary coordinate system of the same size.

Table 8: Per-model hyperparameters. Target layer indicates the layer l∗ at which the refusal direction r∗ was extracted. The % Norm Explained controls the fraction of the direction’s squared norm explained by the retained dimensions, resulting in the chosen dimensions and ASRs reported in Table 1. α is the projection retention threshold used in Stage 1 greedy elimination and τ the ASR-drop tolerance used as the Stage 2 stopping rule; sensitivity to both is reported in Appendix K.

Table 2: Capability change relative to the unmodified model. MMLU and GSM8k are in accuracy points, so negative ∆ is degradation; Pile is in perplexity, so positive ∆ is degradation. ∆Full is the dense intervention applied to all upstream components; ∆Mech is the identified sparse mechanism under the 95% norm-explained coordinate mask. Bold marks the smaller degradation within each pair. The sparse mechanism is equal or better in ten of twelve cells.

Table 1: Sparse refusal mechanisms identified across four models. The layer indices of the selected attention and MLP components in the identified mechanism are provided above. Components is the fraction of upstream components comprising the mechanism. Mechanism ASR reports attack success rate as a percentage of the full residual-stream steering baseline: orthogonalizing the dense direction r∗ at the input of l∗, as in prior work, which is the peak value of the layer sweep in Appendix C. A value above 100% indicates the mechanism steers more effectively than this single-point intervention. Sparse Dim. ASR reports attack success rate when steering the mechanism using only a subset of hidden state dimensions, with the percentage of residual dimensions used given in parentheses. We exclude the embedding matrix as it is never retained by the elimination procedure across models.

Table 3: Steering effectiveness when using only bottom-magnitude dimensions of r∗. Relative ASR is reported as a percentage of the full-direction baseline. Despite comparable dimension budgets to the top-magnitude condition, bottom-magnitude steering fails to elicit refusal across all models.

Table 7: Stability of Stage 2 under random tie-breaking. Tie steps is the fraction of elimination steps on the deterministic trajectory at which at least two candidates fall within ϵ = 0.005 of the minimum drop, and mean tie set size the average number of such candidates. Remaining columns aggregate over four realizations per model (three random seeds plus the deterministic baseline). Core counts components present in all four realizations; peripheral counts components present in some but not all.

Table 5: Sensitivity of mechanism size and behavior to the Stage 1 and Stage 2 thresholds. Each cell reports mechanism size as a raw count, the percentage of the component budget D = 2l∗ + 1 in parentheses, and held-out test ASR (n = 512, LlamaGuard-3). Allcomp. ASR is the reference condition in which every one of the D upstream components is steered. The paper’s operating point is bolded. Test ASR remains within approximately five points of that operating point across every threshold setting.

papers.tldr: Refusal steering in transformers is driven by a sparse, structured subset of components and residual dimensions rather than being diffusely distributed.

papers.abstract: Post-LayerNorm Transformers have seen limited practical adoption due to enduring difficulties in scaling them to large depths. While prior research has focused on stabilising Post-LayerNorm by improving conditioning at initialisation, stability often deteriorates when models are trained with large learning rates, forcing additional compromises. In the decoder-only settings we study, existing Post-LayerNorm methods fail to outperform strong Pre-LayerNorm baselines. We propose KiteNorm, a post-norm training method designed to break this trend by constraining hidden-state variance. This approach is motivated by a bound on the LayerNorm Jacobian suggesting that variance growth contributes to gradient vanishing, alongside empirical evidence linking it to rank collapse. KiteNorm combines residual scaling and variance regularisation to maintain stability throughout training, supported by scalarised double-normalisation that provides separately learnable scales for the skip and residual branches. Across decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves training stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates, with scaling laws favouring KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget. Ablations show that each component is necessary for the full stability and performance gains.
bullets: Post-LayerNorm Transformers can become unstable at large learning rates and depths, limiting their practical use.
KiteNorm combines residual scaling with variance regularisation to constrain hidden-state variance and reduce gradient vanishing and rank collapse.
Scalarised double-normalisation gives the skip and residual branches independently learnable scales.
In decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates.
Scaling laws favour KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget; ablations indicate both components are necessary.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.
bullets: Outcome-only reinforcement learning improved aggregate reward yet encouraged premature commitment, asking only one question, and failures on rare high-risk cases.
The study evaluates medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration in controlled environments with hidden states, query costs, adaptive oracles, and verifiable outcomes.
In diagnostics, dense credit for uncertainty-reducing questions improved held-out value and moderate-case support across three seeds without the observed high-risk seed collapse.
Separating exploration from exploitation increased best-checkpoint high-risk support but caused excessive information gathering for low-acuity cases.
Reinforcement learning can trim useful questions after supervised warmup and does not reliably fix rare behavior gaps from biased supervised data.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Experimental framework and effects of reward design on clinical multi-turn decision procedures. A, The LoRA-adapted MedGemma-4B-it policy interacts with a partially observed patient simulator across medication-refill triage, acute diagnostics and dosing titration. Each environment provides an exact adaptive oracle and deterministic outcome verifier. The three GRPO methods use different training reward formulations or exploration strategies, with policy optimization and rollout generation distributed across two compute nodes. All policies are evaluated on held-out cases using the same unshaped terminal verifier. B, Selected trajectories for the same simulated high-risk abdominal-pain case illustrate different information-gathering procedures. The exact adaptive oracle gathers four targeted findings before emergency treatment. Outcomeonly GRPO commits prematurely after one finding. Credit-assignment GRPO reaches the correct terminal action after four requests and receives an oracle-grade reward despite following a different evidence sequence. Decoupled exploration reaches the correct terminal action after eight requests, including additional non-decisive findings. The learned trajectories are selected illustrative examples, not representative estimates of typical policy behavior. Oracle-grade reward does not necessarily establish sufficient gathered clinical evidence. C, Held-out diagnostics performance measured by high-risk verifier value and mean questions asked. Outcome-only and credit-assignment GRPO show mean ± standard deviation across three training seeds; the base model and decoupled GRPO are single-seed references (hatched bars). The dashed line indicates the exact adaptive oracle’s mean question count. All methods are scored using the same unshaped evaluation reward. Decoupled GRPO is shown at its step-40 checkpoint, selected on held-out data; its final checkpoint does not retain the high-risk advantage (Table 3). The held-out diagnostics set contains only two high-risk cases.

Figure 3: Diagnostics performance by risk subgroup in the held-out hidden condition. Every method is evaluated with the pure verifier reward. Plain GRPO and credit-assignment GRPO show mean±standard deviation over three training seeds; base and decoupled GRPO are single-seed references. Outcome-only GRPO raises aggregate value but reduces and destabilizes high-risk performance. Credit assignment improves the moderate subgroup and maintains high-risk support of 0.50 (one of two high-risk cases) across all three seeds. Decoupled GRPO produces the highest high-risk value and support, but requests substantially more information.

Figure 10: Attempted repair of a mildly biased diagnostics SFT policy by risk subgroup, using the held-out hidden condition and n=200 cases. Both RL methods lose most of the initialization’s high-risk oracle-grade support; support falls from 1.00 for the SFT initialization to 0.14 with credit-assignment GRPO and 0.36 with decoupled GRPO, even as high-risk value rises. The methods fail in different directions. Credit assignment reduces gathering, while decoupled GRPO increases question burden and lowers benign support from 0.92 to 0.16. This figure complements Table 5 and Figure 9.

Figure 9: Attempted reinforcement learning repair of the biased SFT policy. Credit assignment and decoupled GRPO move away from the initialization in opposite directions. Credit assignment reduces gathering and loses high-risk support; decoupled GRPO increases gathering and damages benign support. Both methods reduce the SFT policy’s strong aggregate support, and neither restores the missing high-risk procedure.

Figure 2: Agent–simulator dialogues rendered in plain language. The dialogues are simplified simulator traces, not real clinical conversations. The replying party is a rule-based simulator, not a patient or clinician. It looks up each requested finding in the case’s hidden record and reports whether it is present. Findings are binary, so the simulator returns no numeric values; each question and answer paraphrases one requested finding and its revealed value. (A) The same held-out high-risk diagnostics case as Figure 1. The exact adaptive oracle gathers four findings before emergency treatment (reward +0.83). The outcome-only GRPO rollout shown is that policy’s most common behaviour on this case (6 of 12 samples). It asks one question and admits the patient (reward +0.17). (B) Exact adaptive oracle trajectories for one held-out case in each task, matching Appendix B. Rewards are terminal utility minus 0.03 per question. Hidden risk is never shown to the agent.

Figure 6: Training diagnostics derived from the run logs. Top, diagnostics GRPO over 60 optimisation steps. The panels show the optimised reward, KL divergence from the initialization, policy entropy, and mean questions per rollout for outcome-only GRPO, credit-assignment GRPO, and decoupled GRPO. The question trajectory reveals the characteristic procedural differences among the methods; outcome-only GRPO and credit-assignment GRPO both settle well below the oracle gathering level of approximately 3.9, with credit assignment slightly higher, while decoupled GRPO rises above it. Bottom, training loss for the biased SFT warmup. Loss converges to approximately 0.002, showing that the supervised trajectories are closely fit before RL begins.

Figure 4: Information credit coefficient sweep on the titration task. Mean questions remain below the oracle level when λ≤0.03, approach the oracle at λ=0.1, and exceed it at λ=0.2. The coefficient therefore behaves as a task-specific control parameter for gathering depth, rather than as a constant that can be transferred without calibration.

Figure 8: Refill triage performance by risk subgroup in the held-out hidden condition, evaluated with the pure verifier reward. The figure compares the base model, the SFT v3 warmup, outcome-only GRPO, and creditassignment GRPO at their final checkpoints. The SFT warmup already achieves the strongest high-risk result. Both RL policies subsequently reduce high-risk value and move toward shorter, under-gathered trajectories, despite preserving high support under stochastic sampling.

Figure 5: Effect of supervised coverage bias on aggregate performance and latent support. Left, the biased SFT retains high overall support despite poor high-risk value. Right, severe bias removes the high-risk action emergent_tx from sampled trajectories and fails Gate 2. Mild bias retains a 21% sampling rate and passes Gate 2. The subsequent repair experiment shows that nonzero latent support is necessary but not sufficient for RL to restore the missing behaviour.

Figure 7: Checkpoint trajectory for decoupled GRPO on diagnostics. Evaluation uses the held-out hidden condition and the pure verifier reward. High-risk oracle-grade support and high-risk value peak at checkpoint 40, reaching 1.00 and +0.248, respectively. The same checkpoint also shows increased gathering; mean questions approach and then exceed the oracle level of approximately 3.9. The trajectory illustrates the method’s central tradeoff between high-risk coverage and information burden.

Table 2: Final held-out results across tasks and training methods. All policies are evaluated in the hidden condition using the pure verifiable reward and k=12 sampled rollouts per case. High-risk value and high-risk oracle-grade support are the primary safety-focused metrics. Overall value, overall support, and mean questions describe aggregate performance and interaction burden. Bold marks the strongest non-exploitative high-risk result within each task. Apparent support produced by a degenerate under-gathering policy is marked EXPLOIT, because support@12 can remain high even when typical trajectories do not gather the evidence required for the decision. ‡Diagnostics plain GRPO and credit-assignment GRPO are reported as means across three seeds; the corresponding standard deviations appear in Table 3. All other rows are single-seed results. High-risk subgroup sizes are small (diagnostics n=2, titration high-clot n=6, refill n=7 cases); with k=12 rollouts per case, diagnostics high-risk support can take only the values 0, 0.5, and 1.

Table 5: Attempted repair of a mildly biased diagnostics SFT policy (30% of high-risk SFT examples retained), in the held-out hidden condition with n=200 cases (14 high-risk) and the pure verifier reward. The SFT initialization samples an oracle-grade trajectory for every high-risk case (support 1.00) but performs poorly on a typical high-risk rollout (value −0.285). Both RL methods raise high-risk value but sharply reduce high-risk support, and both reduce overall support. Credit-assignment GRPO under-gathers; decoupled GRPO over-gathers and damages benign support. Neither converts the sampled behaviour into a reliable procedure. “supp” denotes oracle-grade support@12.

Table 7: Hyperparameters for GRPO training. Outcome-only GRPO uses the terminal utility minus the accumulated question cost. Credit assignment adds λΦ to the rollout reward during training only. Decoupled GRPO instead alternates exploration updates based on state recoverability with exploitation updates based on env.score. Every policy is evaluated using the same unshaped terminal verifier.

Table 1: Clinical environment dimensions. “Findings” is the set of binary clinical features available for the agent to request. “Commit actions” is the number of terminal decisions available to the policy. All environments use a question cost of 0.03 and an oracle-grade tolerance of 0.03. Diagnostics contains the largest finding space and is designed to reveal hedging and premature commitment on rare emergency cases.

Table 6: Hyperparameters for the supervised protocol warmup. Loss is computed on every assistant turn; system messages, user messages, and simulator responses are excluded from the supervised objective.

Table 3: Diagnostics results in the held-out hidden condition using the pure verifiable reward. Plain GRPO and credit-assignment GRPO are reported as mean±sample standard deviation over three training seeds. Base and decoupled GRPO are single-seed reference policies. Credit assignment improves overall value, high-risk value, and moderate oracle-grade support relative to the outcome-only control. One plain GRPO seed loses the supported high-risk case, whereas credit assignment retains it in each tested seed. “supp” denotes oracle-grade support@12 and should be interpreted as sampled capability rather than single-trajectory reliability. The held-out high-risk subgroup contains only two cases; every policy with high-risk support of 0.50 supports the same abdominal case, so high-risk values in this table are illustrative rather than precise estimates. §The step-40 checkpoint was selected on the held-out evaluation set and is therefore an optimistic estimate; the final checkpoint is shown for comparison.

Table 4: Titration results in the held-out hidden condition using the pure verifier reward. The information credit coefficient controls the depth of gathering. Plain GRPO and λ=0.03 produce high one-question rates and under-gathering. At λ=0.2, the policy asks more than the oracle and loses aggregate value. The analytically motivated setting λ=0.1 places mean questioning close to the oracle level and preserves high clot support. The absence of an overall value gain is consistent with the small best constant gap of +0.075, which leaves limited adaptive headroom.

papers.selection_reason: RL reward design for multi-turn LLM agents is relevant to LLM reasoning and sequential decision-making methods.
papers.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
papers.tldr: For multi-turn clinical agents, dense process rewards that value uncertainty-reducing questions can produce safer procedures than outcome-only rewards, but reward strength and exploration must be tailored to the task.

papers.abstract: Interpretability tools are usually built for one model at a time: a refusal direction, a truthfulness probe, or a steering vector is found with labeled data inside the model it explains. We ask whether such tools can be carried to other models through a map between residual streams fit only on unlabeled prompts. We transfer a refusal direction, tested causally by addition and ablation, and two read-out tools, a correctness direction and a sentiment probe, across 110 pairs of models from five families and 1B to 72B parameters and between base and instruction-tuned models, with controls for specificity and five seeds. How much transfers depends on what the map was fit on. A map fit on ordinary questions recovers 54\% of the target's own refusal steering and 16\% to 77\% of its correctness gain; adding unlabeled prompts from the region where the tool operates raises these to 102\% and 88\% to 98\%, while control directions recover at most 1\%. We prove that a linear map behaves this way whenever two models correspond linearly on the data it covers, and a label-free coverage score derived from this result tracks recovery across more than 16,000 runs and explains earlier reports that maps between models fail across domains. Carried read-out tools outperform anything the target's unlabeled representations yield. Interpretability results, once found, can be reused across models at the cost of a few unlabeled prompts.
bullets: Tests refusal steering, correctness directions, and sentiment probes across 110 model pairs spanning five families, 1B–72B parameters, and base/instruction-tuned variants.
Transfer quality depends on whether mapping data covers the tool’s operating region; targeted prompts substantially improve recovery over ordinary questions.
A coverage score predicts transfer success across more than 16,000 runs and explains failures when mappings are fit outside the relevant domain.
Transferred read-out tools outperform tools learned solely from the target model’s unlabeled representations.
Scope: results concern linear residual-stream maps and the tested interpretability tools, model pairs, and prompt coverage settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. A tool built on a source model is carried into a target model through a linear map fit on paired activations, and applied to the target without any of the target’s labels. Transfer is measured as the share of the target’s own effect that the carried tool reproduces. The map’s training data decides how much transfers: fit on general text alone, the carried refusal direction recovers 54% of the native effect, and adding 16 unlabeled harmful and 16 unlabeled harmless prompts raises recovery to 102%. The carried tool r̂T is rebuilt from the mapped representations of the prompts that define rS ; for a difference of means this equals the map’s linear part applied to rS , up to renormalization.

papers.abstract: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.
bullets: Targets repeated work caused by missing shared memory and persistent errors from fixed agent procedures.
Uses a shared evidence graph and separate editors for roles/coordination and, in SciMARS + Memory, evidence recording and retrieval.
Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next multi-agent harness.
Evaluated with experimental-data replay, a digital twin, Autonomous Science Bench, ScienceAgentBench, and AppWorld.
SciMARS + Memory outperformed the base team across the reported benchmarks, though results varied by model and task.

papers.abstract: Correlation Matrix Memories (CMMs) store associations as sums of rank-one outer products, providing closed-form addressability, exact deletion, and linear attribution. While classical analyses assume random, orthogonal keys, semantic encoders produce correlated representations. We analyse CMMs under correlated keys using frame-theoretic coherence: (i) capacity bounds yielding an encoder-independent limit $n \le d(1+\varepsilon^2)$ for mean squared crosstalk $\varepsilon^2$; (ii) an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, guaranteeing that deletion never invalidates certified associations; and (iii) a geometric transparency bound demonstrating why attribution requires candidate sets of centred keys. On this basis, we introduce Topology-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Associative Retrieval (TANSAR). TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths via sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived strictly from the verified path into the residual stream of a frozen language model, guarded by a Clopper--Pearson selective-risk gate. Controlled experiments confirm all theoretical bounds. In multi-hop knowledge editing, Horn pruning reduces answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval incurs 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored (and 0% if stale associations are removed). An end-to-end edit transaction requires 13.6 ms on a standard CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels across all 600 ProofWriter theories and achieves 94.0% agreement on FOLIO, demonstrating sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning.
bullets: Analyzes CMMs with correlated keys, deriving capacity, deletion-collateral, and attribution-transparency guarantees.
Traverses directed acyclic association graphs and prunes invalid paths using sound ground Horn constraints.
Injects only verified-path representations into a frozen language model, with a Clopper–Pearson selective-risk gate.
Reports reductions in multi-hop answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5% with Horn pruning, plus millisecond-scale edit transactions.
Matches gold labels on 600 ProofWriter theories and reaches 94.0% agreement on FOLIO.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up language models by having a lightweight drafter propose future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash predict an entire block in one forward pass, and DDTree builds draft trees directly from their per-position distributions. Each distribution implicitly assumes that the drafter's own greedy continuation is accepted, whereas a draft tree improves over a chain only on branches that leave this greedy path. Once a path forks, the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% and its top candidates often miss the true token. Re-running the drafter from the fork token largely restores its accuracy, showing that the errors stem from conditioning on an outdated prefix rather than from limited model capacity. In this paper, we introduce DForkTree, a training-free method that re-anchors each branch on its own tokens. It adjusts the drafter's scores with pointwise mutual information from target-generated n-grams, weighted more heavily after a fork, and a layer-wise GPU search recovers the exact optimal tree under these scores. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, by up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.
bullets: Problem: Block-diffusion drafters become inaccurate after a tree branch because they condition on an outdated prefix.
Method: Re-anchor each branch using its own tokens, adjust scores with target-generated n-gram PMI, and emphasize corrections after forks.
The method is training-free and uses a layer-wise GPU search to recover the exact optimal tree under its scoring function.
On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all reported baselines across benchmarks.
It achieves up to 4.75× speedup over autoregressive decoding, with gains of up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree.

papers.abstract: Recurrent latent reasoning in large lanugage models (LLMs) scales test-time computation by increasing recurrent depth, naturally framing inference as a problem of deciding when to stop. We identify a previously overlooked limitation of this single-depth view through systematic preliminary analysis: deeper recurrence can lose correct solutions found at shallower depths, while depth-specific success sets remain broadly non-nested even after controlling for marginal accuracy. This suggests that depth determines not only computation cost, but also access to distinct candidate solutions. Motivated by this finding, we propose Depth Portfolio Allocation (DPA), which reformulates recurrent test-time scaling as budgeted allocation across depth-specific candidate sources. DPA supports both fixed portfolios and feedback-guided sequential allocation under a shared inference budget. Experiments on GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, and MBPP show that mixed-depth portfolios expand oracle coverage under matched candidate counts and nominal costs, while feedback-guided allocation generally matches or improves uniform allocation and can reduce computation in high-budget settings. Code and data are avaible at : https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM-latent-B7BC/.
bullets: Deeper recurrence can lose solutions found at shallower depths, and success sets across depths are broadly non-nested.
Depth therefore provides access to distinct candidate solutions, not just more computation.
DPA supports fixed mixed-depth portfolios and feedback-guided sequential allocation under a shared budget.
Across GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, and MBPP, mixed-depth portfolios improve oracle coverage at matched candidate counts and nominal costs.
Feedback-guided allocation generally matches or improves uniform allocation and may reduce computation at high budgets.

papers.abstract: LLM-driven time series forecasting has become increasingly promising by leveraging contextual features to generate future values directly or refine forecast priors. However, incorporating contextual features alone does not ensure that models can identify which features matter for forecasting and understand what they suggest about future dynamics. We argue that the fundamental challenge is how to extract predictive evidence from contextual features and when and how to leverage it to guide forecasting decisions. In this paper, we propose CastReasoner, an evidence-grounded reasoning model for context-aware time series forecasting. Specifically, CastReasoner uses a structured chain of thought (CoT) to extract predictive evidence from contextual features, infer the future dynamics suggested by this evidence, and assess these dynamics against the forecast prior to guide adaptive forecasting decisions. To enable this capability, we design a reasoning-centric two-stage post-training framework including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). First, we synthesize reasoning trajectories through controllable multi-teacher guidance and select high-quality ones using a novel student-aware difficulty metric. Second, we design fine-grained multi-objective rewards to further improve reasoning and forecasting. To address heterogeneous learning needs across domains in both stages, we introduce a convergence-guided data balancing strategy. Through this two-stage training, CastReasoner improves both reasoning quality and predictive accuracy. Extensive experiments across multi-domain forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that CastReasoner achieves superior forecasting performance.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of determining which contextual features matter and how they indicate future dynamics.
Uses structured chain-of-thought to extract evidence, infer dynamics, and compare them with a forecast prior.
Trains the model with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning using multi-objective rewards.
Employs multi-teacher trajectory synthesis, student-aware difficulty selection, and convergence-guided data balancing.
Experiments across multi-domain benchmarks show improved reasoning quality and predictive accuracy, with superior forecasting performance.
