papers.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.
bullets: Targets non-stationary crypto markets, opaque decisions, and fixed signal-aggregation rules.
Coordinates agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading across prices, indicators, news, and charts.
Uses Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative trader agents whose influence is learned by a PPO-based gating policy.
Combines post-trade reflection via a Financial ReasoningBank with counterfactual trader-contribution estimates to adapt across market regimes.
Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP report higher total return and Sharpe ratio than traditional, ML, RL, and existing LLM-based baselines.

The Market Execution and Feedback Alignment stage executes at the current Open and sends next-Open portfolio outcomes, trader-level counterfactual feedback, and distilled experience lessons back to the gating policy and memory.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
bullets: The study compares REAP expert pruning with REAM expert merging across five web-hosting production tasks and two 30B-parameter MoE models.
At 25% expert removal, REAP preserves 93.6% of Qwen3-30B’s generative quality, versus 62.5% for REAM.
Across 20 matched comparisons, REAP performs significantly better in 16, while REAM does so in 2.
Most quality loss in email generation comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts, and runaway generation—not loss of content.
Cross-perplexity, logit divergence, and repetition-loop rates track production quality; n-gram diversity does not.

papers.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates. We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher's current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same protocol by 11.0 and 7.6 percentage points, respectively. In an ablation study, supervising only executable commands rather than the Actor's full response raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.
bullets: Self-written skills can propagate errors when guidance is weighted by token-likelihood shifts instead of behavioral improvement.
ECOS estimates command-level advantages by comparing commands taken in similar observations.
These advantages weight Teacher preferences and reinforce skills that favor higher-advantage commands.
Without inference-time skills, ECOS achieves strong performance on seen ALFWorld and WebShop tasks and outperforms GRPO on unseen ALFWorld tasks.
An ablation shows that supervising only executable commands substantially improves 3B WebShop success over supervising the full response.

papers.abstract: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.
bullets: The study compares rule-sheet-only targets with targets generated using rule sheets plus program-written worked solutions.
With six training passes, sheet-only targets improve composition accuracy by 24.3 percentage points in a prospective test.
On unseen arguments, forward accuracy is identical at 87.5%, while composition accuracy is 58.3% for sheet-only versus 23.6% with worked solutions.
More passes with shorter worked-solution targets narrow the gap, but do not consistently eliminate it across target-bank pairs.
Worked solutions reduce capture tokens and update time, yet require 2.1–2.6× more generated tokens per successful composition.

papers.title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
papers.tldr: Worked solutions make self-generated training targets cheaper but can substantially impair a model’s ability to compose newly learned rules, despite equal forward accuracy.

papers.abstract: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.
bullets: Orchestrates 15 specialized LLM agents through persisted, validated artifacts and deterministic Python utilities.
Includes three human checkpoints for study inclusion, corpus adequacy, and synthesis-outline approval.
Introduces QualityScore, a 0–100 index combining network, bibliometric, semantic, and process measures.
Two case studies demonstrate end-to-end feasibility and show that corpus improvements can raise the quality score and increase coverage of older studies.
Audits found incomplete retrieval, inconsistent counts, undocumented checkpoint decisions, and sensitivity to citation-data handling; independent human validation remains pending.

papers.title: PARIS: A multi-agent LLM framework for end-to-end, PRISMA-guided systematic literature reviews with pre-synthesis corpus quality assessment

papers.abstract: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $ρ$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that $ρ$ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between $-0.55$ and $-0.74$ across four bias-free RoPE models spanning $135$M to $7$B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use $ρ$ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/rho-invariant.
bullets: ρ measures each attention head’s capacity to couple with rotary positional encodings.
Across four bias-free RoPE models (135M–7B parameters), ρ predicts induction heads with Spearman correlations from −0.55 to −0.74.
Applying YaRN only to the top 50% of positional heads causes less perplexity degradation than applying it uniformly.
The study focuses on bias-free RoPE models and presents targeted YaRN application as a preliminary proof of concept.

papers.abstract: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.
bullets: Addresses the challenge that skills can become redundant or harmful as the model changes during reinforcement learning.
Uses on-policy skills to guide parameter updates through OPD, while a response-based Strength score ranks candidate skills.
Periodically consolidates high-impact skills into a persistent Global skill set that guides future interactions and updates.
With Qwen3-4B, reports 98.57% success on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, outperforming the matched SEED-API baseline.
Ablations indicate that response-based selection and Global consolidation improve performance; retained-skill benefits depend on content and model compatibility.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.
bullets: Addresses memory loss, unbounded storage, and inefficient retrieval in long-running LLM agents.
Uses six typed memory agents, a provenance hypergraph with n-ary frames, explicit retrieval budgets, and optional AutoDream consolidation and skill distillation.
Leads compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks, including 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S.
Achieves the highest mean success among compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop, and 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench.
Runs with closed or open models, requires no fine-tuning, and is faster than HyperMem across five timed benchmarks when AutoDream is disabled.

papers.abstract: Large language models offer a promising technique for translating natural-language optimization problems into solver code, but their reliability remains constrained by the quality of template retrieval. While recent structured methods improve over flat prompting through hierarchical taxonomy search, their traversal rules remain fixed or LLM-driven at inference time, leaving retrieval unable to improve from past successes and failures. This motivates treating template retrieval as a policy that can be learned from modeling experience, rather than as a static inference-time rule. We propose COMPASS, a policy-amortized framework for retrieving optimization templates in LLM-based solver modeling, which represents the template library as a directed acyclic graph and formulates retrieval as a sequential decision process over template nodes. A deep Q-network learns a reusable traversal policy from template-level judgments and execution feedback, reducing reliance on fixed heuristic traversal through feedback-driven graph navigation. To support extensible retrieval, COMPASS embeds problem descriptions and template nodes in a shared semantic space, allowing newly inserted templates to be scored from their text descriptions without redefining the action space. Experiments across multiple LLM backbones and optimization-modeling benchmarks demonstrate that COMPASS consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval, with the largest gains on complex and mixed-category problems.
bullets: Targets unreliable template retrieval in LLM-based optimization modeling.
Models templates as a directed acyclic graph and retrieval as sequential graph navigation.
Trains a deep Q-network using template judgments and execution feedback.
Uses shared semantic embeddings to score newly added templates without changing the action space.
Improves over heuristic structured retrieval across LLM backbones and benchmarks, especially on complex and mixed-category problems.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable natural-language skills, yet growing skill collections remain accumulations of isolated text artifacts that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose. We argue that the reusable content of a skill lies not in its surface wording but in its procedural transitions: which operation to execute under a given state and which observable outcome to produce. Based on this observation, we propose State-Move-Outcome (SMO), a compilation-like framework that decomposes raw skills into reusable procedural bricks and organizes admitted bricks as an externalized symbolic structure. When compiling a skill, SMO first retrieves and composes existing bricks, dynamically connects them through Outcome-to-State conditions, and creates a candidate brick only for an uncovered procedure; the candidate becomes reusable only after validation and admission. Experiments on SkillsBench v1.1 demonstrate that SMO represents 232 rawSkills from 87 underlying tasks with 95 shared bricks, reducing the corresponding skill representations from 366,472 to 149,154 tokens--a $\mathbf{59.3}\times$ reduction and $\mathbf{2.46}\times$ compression. Across 232 skill-conditioned evaluation instances, SMO raises the average task score from $\mathbf{0.6379}$ to $\mathbf{0.7478}$ and increases 5/5 Pass instances from $\mathbf{138}$ to $\mathbf{164}$, while matching or outperforming rawSkill on $\mathbf{208}$ of $\mathbf{232}$ instances. It also reduces average runtime token consumption by $\mathbf{38.38\%}$. These results show that compiling natural-language skills into shared procedural units can jointly improve skill reuse, representation efficiency, and downstream execution.
bullets: Addresses skill collections that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose because they remain isolated text artifacts.
Decomposes skills into procedural bricks linked by Outcome-to-State conditions, reusing validated bricks and creating new ones only for uncovered procedures.
On SkillsBench v1.1, represents 232 skills from 87 tasks with 95 shared bricks and reduces representation tokens by 59.3%.
Improves average task score from 0.6379 to 0.7478, raises 5/5 Pass instances from 138 to 164, and matches or beats raw skills on 208/232 instances.
Reduces average runtime token consumption by 38.38%, though the abstract does not specify broader limitations or scope beyond the reported benchmark.

papers.abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering diverse, multi-level, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks.
Evaluates six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours.

Agents discovered solutions surpassing human-designed baselines; Claude Opus 5.5 improved mean KV-cache compression from 6.82× to 19.86× on one task.
Trajectory analysis highlights task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained optimization.

papers.abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.
bullets: Addresses emotion errors when verbal, vocal, and visual cues conflict.

Across 5,507 MME-Emotion items, Recognition improves by 7.6–13.4 points over video-only calls for four students and two Builders.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a deployed language model on one task after another can change behaviour that should stay fixed, such as earlier skills, general chat or refusals. Today, such forgetting is found only after training, on the benchmarks someone chose to run. This work bounds, before training, how often its outputs change on chosen prompt distributions. FireGate places each task's update, such as a new LoRA, behind a gate, which is a classifier on the model's frozen lower layers that decides for each prompt whether the update is used. Where no gate fires, the model computes exactly what the old one computes. As a result, on any prompt distribution, every bounded behaviour score changes by at most the gates' firing rate there over a whole task stream. Calibrating each gate on unlabeled prompts of what must not change fixes that rate before training, with a PAC guarantee, whatever weights training produces. Forgetting is thus bounded by the gate's false-alarm rate, and its price is the gate's power: no update, gated or not, that changes as few protected outputs can change new-task outputs more often than the best test of that level tells new-task prompts from protected ones. On reinforcement-learning streams of up to five tasks, gated training keeps the earlier tasks and changes 3.3% of held-out chat responses, whereas ungated training changes 91.8%. Across seven models, the gain kept behind the gate follows its firing rate on new-task prompts, measured before training. The certificate covers the gated model as deployed, on the prompt distributions sampled for calibration, not against an adversary who searches for prompts that fire the gate.
bullets: Addresses forgetting of earlier skills, general chat, and refusals that is typically detected only after training.
Places each task update behind a classifier over frozen lower-layer features; when it does not fire, the original model is unchanged.
PAC calibration on unlabeled protected prompts bounds any protected-behaviour score change by the gate’s firing rate over a task stream.
On streams of up to five RL tasks, gated training changed 3.3% of held-out chat responses versus 91.8% for ungated training.
The guarantee applies to calibrated prompt distributions, not adversarially selected prompts; new-task gains depend on gate firing there.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual learning and forgetting in LLMs using a gating mechanism to bound behavior change, directly relevant to Adaptation and Memory and Language Foundation Models.
papers.title: FireGate: Bounding Behaviour Change Before Training in Continual RL Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: FireGate uses pre-training prompt gates to certify and limit behavioural changes during continual RL fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.
bullets: Scores candidate witnesses between item pairs at zero temperature, retaining the best score and tie count rather than dispersed soft weights.
Rebuilds pair states from the input and comparison bits at each loop, avoiding unresolved score gaps and drifting soft states.
Achieves at least 99.95% accuracy on maximum retrieval sets 1,000× larger than training; a soft-count variant drops to 42% at 4,096 items.
On CLRS-30, the generalized layer beats the best published hinted model; the full cold layer is exact on 9 of 12 comparison-based tasks.
Supports exact 2-SAT, two-colouring, family chaining, and CLUTRR reasoning, while improving frozen language-model performance on text-based relational tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 4 | One block, run K times, and the four kinds of block we train. Cobalt: the yes-or-no tests, exact counts and verdict bits (cold); rose: real numbers, which a block carries from loop to loop. a, The network keeps one vector of 128 numbers for every ordered pair of items, its pair state. In the general setting the input’s items, facts and numbers enter it once, through a learned embedding. One block then reads the state and writes back to it, with the same weights in every loop. It reads through two learned tests per channel, A(i, k) and B(k, j). Half of its 128 channels count, for every pair, the middle items k that pass both tests (the witnesses) and hand on only two verdict bits per pair of channels: is one count larger, and are the two equal? The other half keep the strongest witness and hand on its strength, a number between 0 and 1. A gated mix of the bits and strengths is added to each cell, then the output of a small network applied to each pair. After the last loop a read-out takes the answer from the pair state: here, for shortest routes, each node points to the one before it. The block has 146,552 parameters, shared by every loop, and one loop costs n3 per channel. b, The four kinds of block in one grammar: the pair state (small square; rose tints, real numbers; cobalt cells, bits), the block (box, naming the channels it holds: count, the count-and-compare channels of a; best, the best-witness channels; or the general and the cold half), what one loop hands to the next (the arrow back; rose, a carried real state; cobalt, bits from which the state is rebuilt), and where numbers enter (into the state through an embedding, rose; into the block as comparisons only, cobalt; from a frozen language model, grey box). General: the general block of a, 97.04% on CLRS-30 with one block per task and 97.20% with one block for all thirty tasks. Cold: the cold block, into which numbers enter only as comparisons made inside the layer, its state rebuilt from bits every loop (kept bits, which only turn on, or free bits; with kept bits it rebuilds twice, and its comparison channels read a state without the bits their learned tests made); right on every test input, on every seed, on 9 of the 12 tasks whose answer depends on the numbers only through comparisons. General and cold halves: the general-and-cold block, one block for all thirty tasks, 96.55% at its registered read (weight-averaged parameters, K(n) loops) and 96.40% read like the general block (final parameters, eight loops), a loss of 0.46 points against our first general block for all thirty read the same way. Beside a language model: three kept bits per pair of mentions, monotone tests, tied legs and a read-out that can only say yes, reading relations from a frozen model; exact to 1,000 statements. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a higher-order attention layer with zero-temperature reading for exact reasoning, relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Attention at Absolute Zero
papers.tldr: A zero-temperature, count-aware higher-order attention layer enables exact or highly scalable discrete reasoning from answers alone, outperforming soft-attention variants and strong baselines across retrieval, algorithmic, logical, and relational tasks.

papers.abstract: In most LLM agents, weights are fixed after deployment, so new information must be retained in external memory. Existing approaches often rely on predefined records and fixed organizational rules, which cannot readily accommodate evolving tasks and interactions. This raises the question: can LLM agents organize their own memory using ordinary documents? We introduce self-organized memory (SoMem), a framework that stores memory in linked documents. The agent decides what to summarize, how to group related information, and when to revise existing topics, and every summary it produces stays linked to the original interactions as evidence. The runtime validates updates and automatically derives temporal, relational, and recent-memory views from the organized content. At query time, the agent chooses what to search and read, following document links and inspecting original evidence as needed. On LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. The constructed memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can further improve answer quality. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of agents organizing and using their own persistent memory through ordinary documents. Code is available at: https://github.com/Qi202/SoMem.
bullets: Fixed model weights require agents to store new information in external memory, but predefined records and rules struggle with evolving tasks.
The agent decides what to summarize, how to group information, and when to revise topics, while linking summaries to original interactions as evidence.
Runtime validation and automatically derived temporal, relational, and recent-memory views support flexible retrieval and inspection.
SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points on LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, respectively.
Organized memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can improve answer quality.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.
bullets: Late reasoning answers can be valuable when they differ from a safe fallback, while on-time answers may add little value if they match it.
In a replay of 1,200 decisions, missed-deadline thinking answers were worth about five times as much as on-time ones.
Estimating value as on-time rate × mean answer value overstated thinking’s advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision; a 300-decision repeat showed a 0.0191 overestimate.
Under burst load on a single-GPU Qwen3-8B setup, meeting a 45-second deadline fell from 79.2% at 8 requests to 1.4% at 56, despite tripled output.
Laboratory-agent evaluations should score the action actually executed, jointly accounting for answer quality and arrival time.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.
bullets: Addresses the overlooked matrix structure of transformer weights in existing unlearning methods.
Combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured, spectral optimization.
Derives the spectral update as the steepest-descent direction for transformers with linear layers and normalized inputs/outputs.
Evaluates memorization, privacy, and utility using their harmonic mean.
Outperforms a broad range of baselines and approaches a retain-trained reference across these measures.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce explicit chains of thought to improve transparency, but they frequently overthink, generating long yet inefficient reasoning chains that inflate computational costs and risk introducing errors. While numerous reinforcement learning methods struggle to penalize verbosity to achieve conciseness, they typically apply the penalty uniformly across lengthy sequences, which leads to credit confounding, that is, the failure to distinguish essential reasoning steps from superfluous ones. In this paper, we study a measurable proxy for this confounding: high-entropy tokens that often coincide with surface transition points where reasoning re-enters verification. Based on this insight, we propose Adaptive Entropy-Sparing (AES), which selectively spares high-entropy tokens that occur before an efficient in-group reference, while penalizing overlength high-entropy suffix tokens associated with superfluous branching. Our AES thereby navigates the suppression-exploration trade-off, reducing overthinking while preserving average reasoning accuracy. We also present an entropy-length model that motivates why local uncertainty can serve as a proxy for future reasoning cost. Across eight reasoning benchmarks, AES reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% while increasing mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over the base models, consistently outperforming existing efficiency-oriented methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/MobiusDai/AES.
bullets: Addresses overthinking in large reasoning models, where uniformly penalizing long outputs can suppress essential reasoning steps.
Uses high-entropy tokens as a proxy for reasoning transitions and future computational cost.
Spares high-entropy tokens before efficient in-group references, while penalizing high-entropy suffixes linked to unnecessary branching.
Across eight reasoning benchmarks, reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% and increases mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over base models.
Scope: targets verbosity and efficiency in explicit reasoning chains; the abstract does not specify broader generalization beyond the evaluated benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces overthinking in large reasoning models by selectively penalizing high-entropy tokens, improving reasoning efficiency.

papers.abstract: Answer probes applied to chain-of-thought hidden states are often read as evidence that a language model has already decided its final response. This reading overlooks a competing signal, the candidate the model is about to mention. We introduce emission-controlled dual-target probing (ECDP), which fits the same low-rank reader family separately to the imminent mention and to the final answer at identical positions, with target-specific nulls and thresholds fixed before any fit. On correct DecisionDepth (DD) rollouts in which a distractor is mentioned before the final answer, Qwen3.5-4B decodes the next mention at .966 (null .234) but the final answer only at .221 (null .186), an emission gap of .696 [.648, .744]; Llama-3.1-8B gives .575 [.514, .632]. This pattern is not universal. In a pre-specified evaluation of Qwen3-8B with thinking enabled on held-out MMLU questions, using a full-prefix attention reader over every thinking position, both targets are decodable and the final answer is read far more strongly (mention-minus-answer lift -.398 [-.459, -.336] at layer 22 over 467 questions). Model, task, positions, and reader change together between these settings, and an attempted matched comparison on DD produced no valid statistics because the imminent-mention probe did not train reliably, so we do not identify what reverses the order. On DD, planted-signal controls show that the reader recovers an injected final-answer signal at one tenth of full dose. Answer-candidate decodability is therefore target-relative and protocol-dependent: a strong answer readout does not by itself establish when a model commits, and a probe that fails to train is not evidence that the information is absent. ECDP is a practical control for distinguishing imminent text emission from evidence of a settled decision.
bullets: ECDP fits separate low-rank probes for the imminent mention and final answer at identical chain-of-thought positions, with pre-fixed target-specific nulls and thresholds.
On correct DD rollouts with an earlier distractor, Qwen3.5-4B strongly decoded the next mention (.966) but weakly decoded the final answer (.221); Llama-3.1-8B showed the same direction.
The pattern is protocol-dependent: on held-out MMLU with Qwen3-8B, both targets were decodable and the final answer was more strongly read at one layer.
Because model, task, positions, and reader changed across settings—and a matched DD comparison failed to train—the study does not explain why the ordering reverses.
Planted-signal controls show the reader can recover an injected final-answer signal at one-tenth of full strength.

papers.abstract: An answer can match the reference for a complete agent history even when the reader's visible history does not determine it. We study this distinction using executable device logs. Our protocol separates reference agreement, certified evidence sufficiency, and context-appropriate behavior. Insufficiency requires two legal histories yielding byte-identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology and query cutoffs certify sufficient prefixes. On 80 confirmation histories, Qwen3-32B matches 87 hidden references among 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, with only seven appropriate abstentions. A fixed-input DeepSeek-V4-Flash replication matches 85 and abstains on 21 of the same 203 instances. Each reader makes 1,600 requests. Compact CSV's estimated appropriateness effects remain inconclusive: +3.16 percentage points, clustered 95% interval [0.00,6.57], for Qwen and +2.46, [-1.84,6.94], for DeepSeek. A separate held-out judge study achieves 99.38% correctness but retains support errors and truncations; a deterministic baseline solves all constructed cases. These results support an evaluation diagnosis across two hosted reader configurations, not gains for a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.
bullets: Using executable device logs, the protocol tests whether visible histories uniquely determine the reference answer.
Insufficiency is certified by finding two legal histories with identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology certifies sufficient prefixes.
On 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, Qwen3-32B matched 87 hidden references and abstained appropriately only seven times; DeepSeek-V4-Flash matched 85 and abstained 21 times.
Compact CSV’s estimated appropriateness effects were inconclusive for both readers, and a separate judge study still showed support errors and truncations.
The findings diagnose evaluation issues across two hosted configurations, not improvements to a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.
bullets: Decomposes noise robustness into knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning.
Uses an adaptive task scheduler to tailor the training curriculum to the generator’s learning progress.
Applies inter-group advantage estimation to reduce mode collapse under limited output spaces.
Evaluated on 2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA, with reported improvements in noise robustness and output quality over baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall framework of ARMOR. (Left) The Adaptive Task Scheduler functions as a Teacher, dynamically prioritizing one of the three robustness sub-tasks (Knowledge Boundary Perception, Retrieval Verification, and Robust Reasoning) for each training batch based on the Absolute Learning Progress (ALP). (Right) The RAG Generator (Student) generates multiple rollouts to learn the selected task. (Bottom Right) Inter-Group Advantage Estimation computes reward advantages across the global batch scope rather than within groups, effectively mitigating mode collapse and stabilizing the decoupled training process.

papers.abstract: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving simulation models request arrivals, queues, and cache transfer. For Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B, it predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy use than using the larger model for both prefill and decode phases.
bullets: Targets the compute-heavy prefill phase and memory-bandwidth-limited decoding phase with different model sizes.
Uses a lightweight KV-stitching module with local layer mixing and separate nonlinear key/value mappings to reconcile cache differences.
Trains the translation module with both models frozen; optional low-rank adapters support further task adaptation.
Across six model pairs and five datasets, it outperformed matched-budget fine-tuned small-model baselines in all 30 settings and closed up to 80% of the quality gap to the large model.
Reported serving gains include 3.0× faster requests for an 8B-to-1B pair and simulated gains up to 33.86× faster with 27.5% lower energy for a 70B-to-1B pair.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache translation for heterogeneous prefill/decode; directly targets memory efficiency in LLM inference.
papers.title: BridgeKV: Large-Model Prefill and Small-Model Decoding for LLM Inference via KV Cache Translation
papers.tldr: BridgeKV accelerates LLM serving by using a large model for prompt prefill and a small same-family model for decoding, translating the large model’s KV cache between them.

papers.abstract: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. We show these observations are compatible and characterize update directions during training. For singular values following $σ_i \propto i^{-α}$ with $0 < α\leq 1/2$, we prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension increases. Full singular value decompositions of selected OLMo-2-7B updates confirm this separation: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy. We next compute consecutive checkpoint-displacement cosines from full-model inner products. Across nine publicly released reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stages, all 131 adjacent pairs have negative cosines on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning comparisons across four model families show configuration-dependent alignment, including negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama. Finally, a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds and a 2,048-token response cap compares group-relative advantages against a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.
bullets: Stable rank and fixed-energy rank measure different properties; power-law spectra can make stable rank small even when many singular components capture most energy.
Full SVDs of selected OLMo-2-7B PPO attention updates found stable ranks of 9.6–18.3, while 532–1,222 components were needed for 80% energy.
All 131 adjacent checkpoint pairs across nine RLVR stages had negative displacement cosines on their native grids, including PPO and GRPO.
SFT direction alignment was configuration-dependent, with negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama.
In a controlled OLMo-2-1B comparison, critic-based GAE produced less aligned late-training directions than group-relative advantages, with a paired cosine difference of -0.247.

papers.title: Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training
papers.tldr: Language-model post-training can produce updates that are nearly full-rank yet energy-concentrated, while successive update directions often reverse—an effect influenced by the advantage-estimation system.

papers.abstract: Compression can preserve a language model's average accuracy while selectively degrading individual capabilities. Whether these losses follow method-specific patterns or a transferable order is unclear. We applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned models, scoring 16 tasks in four answer formats against preregistered predictions. Short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order under four random perturbations with different mechanisms (median correlation 0.90) and, within each model, under pruning and quantization (0.875). Intact answer margin, answer frequency and answer format predicted this order. Fragility profiles measured under random perturbation predicted which tasks and facts compression removes first and, after four-task calibration, held-out task accuracy (median absolute error 0.11-0.12, against 0.20-0.21 for uniform decline); profiles borrowed from other model families did almost as well. The order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or hold for long-form tasks. Within short answers, what compression removes is predictable before deployment.
bullets: Across four random perturbations, short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order (median correlation 0.90).
Within individual models, pruning and quantization produced similarly ordered failures (correlation 0.875).
Answer margin, answer frequency, and answer format predicted which capabilities degraded first.
Random-perturbation fragility profiles predicted compression-related task loss and held-out accuracy after four-task calibration.
The ordering did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization and did not apply to long-form tasks.

Top, the answer of Qwen2.5-7B to one item as the noise dose rises. b, Every damage removes the same capabilities first, each at its own dose. c, Three separable axes: how securely the task is held, how familiar the answer is and how much of it must be produced. Because the effects add, the failure front is a plane, and more damage moves it towards the robust corner; the fact axis was measured within recall tasks only. d, Measured once under random damage, in the model itself or in other models, the profile predicts what compression removes first and how much accuracy it leaves. papers.selection_reason: Analysis of LLM capability ordering under compression.
papers.title: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
papers.tldr: Language-model capabilities tend to fail in a predictable, shared order under many perturbations and compression methods, but this predictability is limited across model families and long-form tasks.

papers.abstract: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.
bullets: Targets the access problem in continual instruction tuning: selecting the correct task module from a prompt alone.
Uses a frozen LLM with task-isolated latent memories and adapter banks; memories gather causal-prefix information and inject task-conditioned context.
The memories’ persistent states serve as routing prototypes for a shared prompt-only router.
On an 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, it reports 65.19 acquisition, 63.98 final macro score, and 1.38 average forgetting; results are similar under reversed task order.
Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9%, while oracle routing adds 1.21 final macro points, highlighting routing as a remaining limitation.

papers.abstract: A deployed language model does not merely answer questions. It spends computation, consumes time, consults evidence, exposes memory, invites or avoids human review, and sometimes makes mistakes whose consequences are radically unequal. Yet LLM systems are still commonly compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the relevant outcome were a single benchmark score. This paper argues that the unit of analysis should instead be the deployment policy: the mechanism that decides when to retrieve, when to remember, when to call a larger model, when to verify, and when not to answer at all. We introduce risk-adjusted deployment efficiency (RADE), a system-level objective that scores the utility a deployment delivers net of inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected failure cost, while treating harms that cannot be priced as hard budgets alongside constraints on latency, privacy, and resources. The framework brings selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and human escalation into a common account. We then examine five deployment regimes in which the same nominal LLM capability leads to different rational architectures, and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load. The central claim is modest but consequential: frontier capability should be treated as a resource to allocate, not a default state to maintain. A safe and sustainable system is not the one that always uses the strongest model; it is the one that spends capability where the reduction in risk or increase in utility justifies the cost.
bullets: Argues that deployment policy—not a standalone model or benchmark score—is the proper unit of analysis.
Defines risk-adjusted deployment efficiency as utility minus inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected-failure costs.
Treats unpriced harms, latency, privacy, and resource use as constraints or hard budgets.
Unifies routing, retrieval, governed memory, specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and escalation.
Proposes reporting risk-coverage, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load across five deployment regimes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A deployment-first control architecture. A low-cost gate estimates complexity and consequence; retrieval and governed memory provide context; heterogeneous execution paths produce candidate outputs; and verification determines whether a verified answer is released or the case is withheld and escalated. The figure is architectural rather than an empirical benchmark result.
Table 2: A minimum reporting set for risk-adjusted evaluation of deployed LLM systems.
Table 1: Five representative deployment regimes. The relevant "failure budget" concerns the tolerated probability and severity of consequential failure, not ordinary benchmark error.

papers.selection_reason: Framework for LLM deployment policies involving governed memory and routing aligns with LLM memory.
papers.title: RADE: Risk-Adjusted Deployment Efficiency, A Framework for Routing, Memory, and Escalation in Safe LLM Systems
papers.tldr: RADE evaluates LLM deployments as risk-aware policies that allocate computation, memory, retrieval, verification, and human review rather than always using the strongest model.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation trains a student language model to match a teacher's predictions on the training text. We ask whether learning the teacher's behavior beyond the training text can further improve the student. We investigate this using three input perturbations: additive token noise, blending two documents, and blending neighboring tokens. Specifically, for an early part of pretraining we perturb the inputs and train the student to match the teacher on them, and we spend the rest of the same token budget on ordinary distillation. When pretraining from scratch, the best method improves on standard distillation at both scales we tried, by 0.025 nats at 135M parameters and by 0.020 nats at 0.5B (mean of three seeds). At 135M this is 1.45 times the gain that distillation itself provides over next-token training. We also observe promising downstream transfer: at 0.5B, the best variant improves average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks. It also retains its validation-loss advantage after low-bit weight quantization. We also test a data-limited setting in which training data must be reused, and find that the gains persist. Finally, ablations suggest that, for additive noise, perturbing the teacher's inputs contributes most of the gain, while perturbing only the student's inputs yields much less.
bullets: Studies additive token noise, document blending, and neighboring-token blending during an early distillation phase.
The best perturbation method improves validation loss at both tested scales: 135M and 0.5B parameters.
At 0.5B, it increases average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks.
Benefits persist when training data is reused and after low-bit weight quantization.
Ablations indicate that perturbing the teacher’s inputs is more beneficial than perturbing only the student’s inputs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (a) In standard distillation, teacher and student read the same clean text and the student is trained to match the teacher’s prediction on it. In the early stage of our method, both read a perturbed version of the text, and the student matches the teacher’s prediction on that perturbed input: the inputs on which the teacher supervises the student change, not only the student’s input. The bars under each token sketch its input vector over a toy vocabulary, one-hot for clean text and spread over several vocabulary items when perturbed (Fig. 2). The rest of training is standard distillation on clean text. (b) Clean validation loss of two 0.5B students trained from the same initialization on the same data order, one with standard distillation and one with adjacent blending (λ=0.5) for the first 30% of training, and their difference (symmetric log scale). While its inputs are perturbed, the blended student lags by about one nat. After the switch it recovers quickly, overtakes the baseline at about 47% of training and finishes 0.020 nats below it.

Figure 3: Change in final validation loss against standard distillation (below zero is better). (a–c) 135M student with the SmolLM2-1.7B teacher, 4.2B tokens. The dashed line is next-token prediction without a teacher. (a) Noise size, with a 50% perturbed stage. The open markers in (a) are Gaussian noise added to each model’s input embedding; their σ is relative to the embedding’s rootmean-square value, so it is not in the same units as token noise. (b) Blend weight for both blends, with a 30% perturbed stage. (c) Length of the perturbed stage at each family’s best size. (d–f) 0.5B student with the Qwen2.5-1.5B teacher, 10B tokens, scored on the full validation split. Error bars are ±2 paired standard errors. (d) Noise size and (e) blend weight, with the same perturbed-stage lengths as in (a, b). (f) Length of the perturbed stage at each family’s best size.

Bars show the mean over initialization seeds and dots the individual seeds, each compared with standard distillation from the same seed. (a) Each family at its best setting, with and without the teacher, each compared with its own unperturbed baseline (standard distillation or next-token prediction). (b) Token noise given to both models, to the teacher only, or to the student only. The grey bar is the sum of the two one-sided gains. (c) Clean inputs, with the teacher’s target softened instead, either by a temperature τ (τ=1.15 matches the entropy of the teacher’s prediction on σ=0.4 inputs) or by label smoothing to the same entropy. (d) Clean inputs for the first half of training, distilled from a weaker model (an early checkpoint of the teacher, or a smaller model) instead of the teacher. (e) Adjacent blending at λ=0.8, as in the main runs and on the same raw tokens as the baseline, and the overlapping variant described in the text (one seed).

(a) Final validation loss of standard distillation with and without noise (token noise σ=0.4 for the first 50% of training) as a function of AdamW weight decay. papers.selection_reason: Improves pretraining distillation for language models via input perturbations; fits LLM training and foundation models.
papers.title: Perturbing Inputs Improves Pretraining Distillation
papers.tldr: Perturbing pretraining inputs during knowledge distillation improves student language models over standard distillation, including in transfer and quantized settings.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. In practice, users may identify problems in the current outcome without specifying the desired result, so learning user intentions requires interpreting each correction against the agent's preceding and revised outcomes. These expectations are often connected to a particular context, making it hard to know when they apply and how to ensure the agent later acts as the user expects. To this end, we propose LiveAsset, an intent harness that learns reusable intent assets from corrective interactions and uses them for runtime control of agent execution. LiveAsset jointly interprets each correction with the agent's original and revised results to infer user intent, incrementally updating the assets while preserving earlier requirements that remain applicable. The learned requirements guide agent execution from task entry and provide criteria for runtime verification, which uses the explanations to assess applicability before each reply is delivered and directs the agent to revise the result to address unmet requirements while preserving those already satisfied. Following a learning phase in which simulated users progressively reveal requirements through multi-turn corrections, we evaluate LiveAsset using same-task replay of the original requests on π-Bench, PERMA, and Vita and cross-task transfer on PAST-Bench and SkillEvolBench. Experiments show that LiveAsset better fulfills requirements learned from corrective interactions and improves performance on these benchmarks compared with memory, skill, and rule-based harness baselines. Code is available at github.com/landian60/LiveAsset.
bullets: Addresses underspecified goals where users correct outcomes without explicitly stating the desired result.
Interprets each correction alongside the agent’s original and revised outputs to infer and incrementally update intent assets.
Guides execution from task entry and verifies each response, prompting revisions while preserving already satisfied requirements.
Evaluated through same-task replay and cross-task transfer across five benchmarks after simulated multi-turn requirement learning.
Outperforms memory-, skill-, and rule-based harness baselines in fulfilling requirements learned from corrections.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces 'LiveAsset,' a mechanism for LLM agents to learn and store user intent (intent assets) from corrective interactions during runtime. This directly addresses the LLM Memory subtopic by providing a persistent memory mechanism for user preferences, and the Test-Time Learning subtopic by updating the agent's state based on deployment-time interactions.
papers.title: LiveAsset: Learning Intent Assets from Corrective Interactions for Agent Runtime Control
papers.tldr: LiveAsset learns reusable user-intent requirements from corrective interactions and uses them to control and verify LLM agent behavior at runtime.

papers.abstract: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.
bullets: The paper compares gates driven by the current input, recurrent state, or both in diagonal state-space models.
State gating strictly increases expressivity: scalar models solve induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary sizes and sequence lengths.
Under standard stability assumptions, input gating fails on a finite induction-head instance.
Experiments confirm state-gating advantages on induction tasks and input-gating advantages on selective copying.
The two gating mechanisms provide complementary capabilities when combined.

papers.selection_reason: Expressivity analysis of input vs. state gating in diagonal state-space sequence models relevant to LLM architectures.
papers.title: Where Should a Gate Look? Input vs. State Gating in Diagonal State Space Models
papers.tldr: State-based memory-update gates make diagonal state-space models more expressive on induction tasks, while input-based gates excel at selective copying; combining both is strongest overall.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. We trace this degradation to three coupled mechanisms: (1) tool-token imbalance produces negative overall tool credit when incorrect trajectories contain more tool tokens per turn than correct ones; (2) aggregation amplification can further strengthen this negative signal as token-mean aggregation gives longer incorrect trajectories greater weight in policy updates; and (3) failure-driven retries prolong trajectories as models tend to call tools again after execution errors, extending potential negative credit to recovery attempts. To counter this suppression, we propose Transition-Aware Credit Assignment (TACA), which targets the transition from reasoning to tool use through supervision of both call initiation and generation. Specifically, TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens within each prompt group through a minimal uniform shift. Additionally, TACA guides tool-use decisions with Decision Contrast, comparing rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers to the same prompt. Through Supervised Replay, it reinforces tool-call generation using calls from previously sampled correct trajectories. Across models and tasks, TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training, raising mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TACA.
bullets: Identifies three causes of tool-use degradation: tool-token imbalance, length-amplified credit aggregation, and failure-driven retries.
Uses Advantage Projection to ensure tool-call tokens receive nonnegative mean advantage within each prompt group.
Applies Decision Contrast to compare tool-assisted and direct answers, plus Supervised Replay from correct trajectories.
Improves mean accuracy over MT-GRPO by 4.61 points on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 points on Qwen2.5-3B across six reasoning benchmarks.
Scope: targets multi-turn tool interactions trained with verifiable rewards.

papers.selection_reason: Credit assignment method for improving LLM reasoning and tool-calling in agentic reinforcement learning.
papers.title: When Credit Turns Against Tools: Transition-Aware Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: TACA prevents tool-use suppression in agentic RL by correcting negative credit around reasoning-to-tool transitions, improving reasoning accuracy and tool reliability.

papers.abstract: Random perturbations around a shared checkpoint can produce experts for distinct tasks, but shared origin does not ensure that their gains survive composition. We formulate expert-pair selection for joint base-relative retention, measured by strict joint success and worst-task gain with unconditional abstention accounting. An exact finite-difference decomposition and an arbitrarily small orthogonal counterexample show why proximity and orthogonality alone are insufficient. We instantiate this formulation with quality-constrained spectral selection, a fixed-budget framework combining cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, and Base fallback. Across six checkpoints, 21 task pairs, and five independent perturbation pools, the procedure improves strict joint success over Top-1 averaging throughout and leads the four-method model-scale comparison on four of six checkpoints. For the five models with at least 1.5B parameters, matched quality-only, global-cosine, and spectral ranking attain 49.1%, 50.5%, and 53.1% joint success. Under this matched protocol, the spectral selector also yields the highest worst-task gain and Weak Pareto rate and the lowest regression rate. Mean worst-task gain reaches +0.61 percentage points, while 17.1% regression and 13.0% abstention show that composability remains conditional. Project page: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Thickets-Merge/.
bullets: The work selects expert pairs by joint base-relative retention, strict joint success, and worst-task gain, with abstention counted explicitly.
An exact finite-difference decomposition and an orthogonal counterexample show that proximity and orthogonality alone do not guarantee successful composition.
The proposed fixed-budget method combines cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, spectral ranking, and Base fallback.
Across six checkpoints and 21 task pairs, spectral selection consistently improves strict joint success over Top-1 averaging and leads model-scale comparisons on four checkpoints.
For models with at least 1.5B parameters, spectral ranking achieves 53.1% joint success versus 49.1% for quality-only and 50.5% for global-cosine ranking; regression and abstention remain nontrivial.
