papers.selection_reason: Cross-task model merging with spectral selection is directly applicable to large language model development and composition.
papers.title: When Are Nearby Experts Composable? Cross-Task Model Merging in Neural Thickets
papers.tldr: Nearby experts are not automatically composable; a quality-constrained spectral selector improves joint task success while showing that merging remains conditional.

papers.abstract: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.
bullets: Introduces LongCapBench and three metrics for timeline accuracy, granularity, and caption similarity.
Interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and context retention for length extrapolation.
Event-level reannotation restores descriptive detail, while studies examine scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation.
LongCap-Diar extrapolates to 16 hours despite training on recordings up to 40 minutes and can caption recordings approaching two hours.
Models are competitive on short clips and outperform evaluated baselines in segment-level caption similarity and timeline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Mathematical performance depends on how a language model receives information, uses generated text and submits an answer. We study these dependencies through paired comparisons that separate submission requirements, draft reuse and candidate availability. On 65 development problems, an instruction permitting continued derivation produced no valid final answers in 390 short-output calls; a single-line submission instruction produced 390 format-valid outputs, including 389 parseable answers. Under the fixed submission protocol, 198 problems with failed initial submissions were answered correctly in 9.09p of cases with the question alone, 33.84p with its draft, 46.46p with candidates, and 59.60p with both. Drafts added 13.13 percentage points with candidates fixed, and candidates added 25.76 points with drafts fixed; both effects were significant after Holm correction and were subadditive on the accuracy scale. Retaining a trailing excerpt outperformed retaining a leading excerpt of similar average length by 10.10 points Holm-adjusted p 0.027. A second completion model showed the same directions of input effects on the fixed materials. In a cohort with parseable initial submissions, candidates added no correct answers when the previous draft was supplied, but added 27 points when it was absent. These results establish a conditional value of generated text: a failed submission can leave useful material, whose contribution depends on what else is supplied and what is retained.
bullets: A single-line submission instruction yielded format-valid outputs, whereas allowing continued derivation produced none in the short-output calls.
For failed initial submissions, accuracy rose from 9.09p with only the question to 59.60p with both the draft and candidate answers.
Drafts and candidates each improved accuracy, but their combined effects were subadditive.
Retaining trailing draft excerpts outperformed similarly sized leading excerpts by 10.10 points.
Candidate benefits depended on draft availability and were directionally replicated with a second completion model.

papers.tldr: LLM math performance depends strongly on submission format and whether prior drafts and candidate answers are retained.

papers.abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when a user pushes back without giving a reason, and this behavior is usually studied as sycophancy to be suppressed. The same pushback, however, also leads models to revisit and sometimes repair a wrong answer. We measure both effects on multiple-choice questions from MMLU and ARC-Challenge with four open models from two families (Qwen3 1.7B, 4B and 8B, and OLMo-2 7B), reading the final answer exactly from option logits after a free-form reply. The reply budget changes the verdict. When Qwen3-4B may answer the challenge in at most 96 tokens, pushback leaves accuracy unchanged or slightly lower; with 1,024 tokens, it corrects 43% of its wrong answers and pushback raises accuracy by 5.7 points. Whether pushback helps overall follows a simple break-even rule in the cave and correction rates. Inside the model, caving can be partly predicted before the challenge: hidden states add about 0.04-0.06 AUROC over turn-1 confidence in three of our four probing runs. A probe trained only on self-correction cases predicts caving beyond confidence when replies are truncated, but not when the model can finish its reasoning. Activation steering never reduced caving selectively: where it worked, it suppressed self-correction as well. We conclude that sycophancy evaluations should allow full replies and report self-correction alongside caving.
bullets: Short response limits can hide self-correction; with 1,024 tokens, Qwen3-4B corrected 43% of its wrong answers and gained 5.7 accuracy points after pushback.
Whether pushback helps depends on the balance between answer-changing errors and repaired mistakes.
Hidden states modestly predict caving beyond first-turn confidence in most probing runs.
A probe trained on self-correction cases detected caving under truncation, but not when reasoning could finish.
Activation steering did not selectively reduce caving; it also suppressed self-correction.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models often continue generating after producing an answer, yet stopping prematurely may interrupt useful verification or revision. In this work, we investigate whether targeted interventions in a model's internal computation can provide a reliable signal for when to stop reasoning. We introduce Prune-to-Probe, an inference-time controller that uses causal activation interventions to probe the stability of a model's current answer. Specifically, we identify late-MLP coordinates that contribute to post-answer continuation while excluding those important for answer completion. Once an answer is stated, Prune-to-Probe temporarily suppresses the selected coordinates and measures the resulting stopping response relative to matched random interventions. Crucially, these interventions serve only as probes: the model either returns its existing answer or resumes generation from an untouched cache. On MATH, Prune-to-Probe reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60%, preserving all naturally correct trajectories while repairing six errors. On MMLU-Pro, it achieves 1.145% pooled savings with no observed harm. Further analysis shows that the intervention captures decision stability rather than correctness (AUROC 0.502). These results demonstrate the potential of causal activation probes for efficient inference-time control without permanent model modification.
bullets: Targets late-MLP coordinates linked to post-answer continuation but not answer completion.
After an answer is stated, temporarily suppresses these coordinates and compares the stopping response with matched random interventions.
Uses interventions only as probes: the model either keeps its answer or resumes from an untouched cache.
Reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60% on MATH while preserving naturally correct trajectories and repairing six errors; saves 1.145% on MMLU-Pro with no observed harm.
The probe reflects decision stability rather than correctness, with AUROC 0.502, limiting its use as an accuracy signal.

papers.abstract: Large language models rely on a single tokenizer that is chosen at training time and fixed thereafter. Most tokenizers are trained on English-dominant corpora, making them under-serve morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages, where they can produce fragmented representations, longer sequence lengths, and reduced information density during training. We propose Mixture of Tokenizers MoTo, a modular tokenization framework that trains dedicated per-language BPE tokenizers and composes them into a unified superset vocabulary, where tokens shared across languages are deduplicated into a common ID space. Each tokenizer maintains its own normalization policy, pre-tokenization rules, and vocabulary budget. Despite allocating significantly fewer entries to English, MoTo retains English performance while delivering consistent gains across 18 out of 21 typologically diverse languages spanning six scripts, with improvements most pronounced on morphologically complex and non-Latin-script languages that are systematically underserved by English-dominant tokenizer design. Our results suggest that modular subword tokenization is a practical and extensible alternative to monolithic tokenization for multilingual parity.
bullets: English-dominant tokenizers can fragment words and lengthen sequences, especially for morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages.
MoTo trains separate BPE tokenizers with language-specific normalization, pre-tokenization, and vocabulary budgets.
Their vocabularies are merged into a deduplicated unified token-ID space.
The approach retains English performance and improves results in 18 of 21 diverse languages across six scripts.
Gains are strongest for languages underserved by monolithic English-focused tokenizers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Left: Superset Vocabulary construction. Language-specific subword tokenizers are trained on their corresponding corpus. Words native to that language tend to be represented with fewer tokens, while non-native words fall back to coarser subwords or byte-level tokens. The superset vocabulary VS is constructed by taking the union of all tokenizer vocabularies, assigning shared tokens a single global index, with |VS | ≤ ∑ i|Ti|. Right: Mixture-of-Tokenizers (MoTo) pipeline. A tokenizer is selected based on the input language ID. The input is encoded into superset indices, processed by the transformer, and decoded back with the tokens from the superset, additionally it can utilize rules from the input tokenizer.

Figure 4: Main results per language. Accuracy difference (pp) from the Llama-3 baseline, averaged over each language’s tasks; the rightmost group is the average over languages. MoTo and MoTo-GPT4 use per-language tokenizers with oracle routing. mBPE-GPT4, mBPE-Boundless, and Parity-Aware BPE are single multilingual BPE tokenizers, and Llama-BPE-Drop. is the Llama tokenizer with BPE dropout.

papers.abstract: Extended reasoning can help language models solve complex problems, but long responses often contain both useful computations and redundant checks. Conventional length penalties encourage shorter responses without distinguishing the functions of intermediate steps. We propose Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS), a framework that combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation. We investigate two classification routes: PCRS-H with a hidden-state classifier and PCRS-T with a frozen text classifier. Our main text classifier implementation assigns overlapping reasoning, execution, and revision labels to native chunks, then uses these labels and exact repetition to adjust existing token penalties. We compare the completed configurations on six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks and examine four reward-weight settings with the text classifier. Compared with a baseline using token-level length penalties, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 is approximately 62.07% for both methods, while oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%. These results show how phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.
bullets: Targets redundant checks in extended reasoning that conventional length penalties treat the same as useful computation.
Uses phase identification to label chunks as reasoning, execution, or revision, then adjusts existing token penalties during training.
Evaluates hidden-state and frozen text-classifier variants across six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks.
The default text-classifier setup reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 remains about 62.07%, while oracle Pass@16 increases from 86.08% to 87.67%.
The approach performs phase classification during training rather than at inference time.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes reward shaping to reduce LLM reasoning length, relevant to language foundation models and efficient inference.
papers.title: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping for Token-Efficient LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping allocates length penalties by reasoning phase, shortening LLM responses while preserving single-sample accuracy and improving multi-sample coverage.

papers.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems pay costs that research comparisons rarely measure: model calls at query time, building the graph, and removing documents correctly. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. On a corpus of near-duplicate names, HippoRAG 2's capped synonym lists leave 565 fewer edges than a rebuild, while Lightfoot remains exact. Under identical extraction, embedding and answer models on held-out questions of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, Lightfoot is competitive with HippoRAG 2: with Holm-corrected paired tests it is better on MuSiQue at recall@5 and recall@10 (+4.8 and +5.5 points) and on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@10 (+3.4), and tied on HotpotQA, while HippoRAG 2 keeps a non-significant 3.0-point edge at 2WikiMultiHopQA recall@2. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete.
bullets: Targets deployment costs and correctness issues in graph construction, query-time model calls, and document deletion.
Builds graph entities, links, facts, and synonym edges deterministically from passage-level extractions with chunk provenance.
Uses no language-model calls during retrieval; indexing requires one call per passage, and deletion exactly reproduces a fresh index of remaining documents.
Competitive or better recall than HippoRAG 2 on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, tied on HotpotQA; answer performance ties across all three datasets.
Builds indexes 26–31% more cheaply than HippoRAG 2 and avoids deletion limitations or repeated model calls of alternatives.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Recall@5 against normalised index cost for each dataset (all MuSiQue questions; Lightfoot with v1 seeding). Points nearer the top left are better.
Table 7: Index and query model calls and lifecycle support in 17 open-source GraphRAG frameworks.

Table 4: Recall under four embedders on held-out questions (MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA questions 501–1000, HotpotQA all 300). papers.abstract: Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges $c$ per token processed and $β$ per pair attended. Their ratio $P^*=c/β$ is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.
bullets: Defines an exact cost model charging for processed tokens and attended token pairs, with an exchange rate separating thinking- and memory-dominated regimes.
Separates mechanical costs of a context policy from behavioral costs caused by the agent generating different reasoning and outcomes.
On recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74× as much with generated-state reuse but 0.34× as much without reuse.
Live reruns show that dropping earlier reasoning reduces correct HotpotQA answers by 9–23 percentage points across four models, despite lower point-estimate cost.
Context-policy comparisons must include the serving architecture because it determines the cost of retained history and induced computation.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the cost trade-off between 'thinking' (reasoning) and 'remembering' (context) in LLM agents, providing a formal cost model for inference-time optimization.
papers.title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
papers.tldr: Agentic inference trades off recomputing (“thinking”) against retaining (“remembering”) context, and the cheaper policy depends on serving architecture while context removal can reduce accuracy.

papers.abstract: Much of the automation handed to language-model agents is procedural: each step needs little intelligence, but a long unattended run must follow a skill or SOP stated once at the start. We show that agents drift from such procedures over long runs, and that restating the instructions or resuming a stopped agent only moves the drift to another shortcut. We study an executable finite-state machine (FSM) that keeps the workflow state outside the model's context and enforces it at three points: tool calls, state transitions and the end of the agent's turn. In a pre-registered experiment on 200-account SOP-Bench batches, Claude Haiku 4.5 with the FSM decided on average 139 accounts correctly and by the procedure, against 48 for the strongest baseline (95% CI of the difference [46, 130]), and kept this rate to the end; across three models, the gain tracked how much the plain agent drifted. Because the runtime, not the model, supplies this long-horizon reliability, the FSM can let small models carry procedural work: Haiku 4.5 with it averaged more such decisions than plain Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 38% of the cost. Analyses on SWE-bench Verified, $τ^2$-bench, and staged and cross-context workflows further suggest that reliable long-horizon automation can come from stronger execution control, not only stronger models.
bullets: Long-running agents drift from SOPs, and restating instructions or resuming them does not reliably prevent shortcutting.
The FSM enforces procedure compliance at tool calls, state transitions, and the end of each agent turn.

In a pre-registered 200-account SOP-Bench experiment, FSM-controlled Claude Haiku 4.5 averaged 139 correct-by-procedure decisions versus 48 for the strongest baseline, maintaining performance through the end.
The benefit scaled with how much plain agents drifted across three models and enabled Haiku 4.5 to outperform plain Claude Sonnet 4.6 on such decisions at 38% of the cost.
Additional analyses across several benchmarks and workflow settings suggest execution control can provide long-horizon reliability beyond simply using larger models.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language model post-training often reuses each batch of sampled rollouts for several gradient passes to amortize the cost of generation. Under such multi-pass reuse, existing objectives fail in different ways: unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts away from the sampling policy, adding a negative baseline avoids collapse but reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style ratio clipping cuts off gradients abruptly. We first ask why reuse is fragile. Measuring how well an update estimated from a small rollout group aligns with the KL-regularized target on held-out rollouts of the same prompts, we find that this alignment drops by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models, suggesting that repeated passes largely overfit the sampled group. Motivated by this finding, we propose Bounded Residual-Aligned Training (BRAT), motivated by a proximal update toward a bounded reweighting of the sampling policy. BRAT assigns each token a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary, and normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, keeping advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters. With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.
bullets: Repeated reuse of sampled rollouts causes update alignment with the KL-regularized target to drop nearly an order of magnitude on held-out rollouts, indicating overfitting.
BRAT uses a bounded, linearly decreasing gradient weight based on each token’s probability ratio, vanishing at a trust-region boundary.
It normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, producing zero-mean, bounded advantages without extra hyperparameters.
With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.

papers.tldr: BRAT stabilizes multi-pass LLM reinforcement learning by preventing rollout-group overfitting and uncontrolled policy drift.

papers.abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.
bullets: Applies across reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation.
Learns a binary mask over transformer-block gate projections, with no other weight modifications.
The resulting mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than a full-fine-tuning checkpoint.
Under reinforcement learning, it retains near-base prior-task accuracy, whereas other tested methods can suffer substantial forgetting.
Weight-geometry analyses show its changes resemble full fine-tuning more closely than LoRA or random sparse fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Weight-mask LLM post-training matches full fine-tuning with far less forgetting; relevant to LLM adaptation and continual learning.
papers.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: Deletion Tuning achieves full-fine-tuning-level post-training by zeroing fewer than 0.05% of an LLM’s weights, while preserving prior-task knowledge better and using much smaller checkpoints.

papers.abstract: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.
bullets: Addresses the cost and manual effort of pragma tuning and repeated synthesis in HLS-based C++-to-RTL generation.
Uses synthesis-grounded data containing C++, Verilog, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives for supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Introduces a QoR Prediction Reward Model that estimates latency and resource usage from RTL representations, reducing reliance on repeated synthesis during training.
Reports improved RTL functional pass rates and latency/resource optimization over the base model, HLS optimization methods, and several commercial general-purpose models.

papers.abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.
bullets: The study examines how LLMs interpret identity disclosures in conversations about suicidal ideation and psychological distress.
Using paired counterfactual interventions, it evaluates six LLMs across two datasets, 16 identity/control conditions, and two prompting protocols.
Models often infer identity-related adversity as the cause of distress, especially for marginalized identities.
These assumptions can misrepresent people’s experiences even when responses are otherwise empathetic.
The authors call for interpretations grounded in users’ disclosures rather than unsupported identity-linked explanations.

papers.abstract: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.
bullets: Evaluates 67 systems—47 decision models and 20 LLMs—across 43 tasks and 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol.
Jev 1.14.0 scores 69.24 overall, above Jev 1.13.0 (68.77) but below Gemma-4-31B (71.81), the highest aggregate scorer.
Removing English controls or repeated cross-task items does not change the overall system ordering.
Across four content-matched datasets, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from −7.94 to −0.35 percentage points; dialect-specific results vary more.
A larger Palestinian banking penalty is observed for Jev 1.14.0 than for the compared LLMs, while other contrasts are inconclusive.

papers.abstract: Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies safeguard industrial processes against catastrophic accidents. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap. Because LLMs internalize human heuristics, prompts may trigger biased judgments. Whether frontier LLMs withstand cognitive perturbations in safety-critical workflows remains unknown. Here we show across 420 trials that three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, rendering overall susceptibility statistically inconclusive. Contrary to assumed broad fragility, models rejected confirmation and availability cues. However, safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames. Thus, automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation.
bullets: HAZOP automation requires evaluation beyond lexical overlap because prompts may induce biased safety judgments.
Across 420 trials, the models resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations; overall susceptibility was statistically inconclusive.
Models rejected confirmation and availability cues, contrary to assumptions of broad cognitive fragility.
Low anchors and gain frames nevertheless triggered safety-critical reductions in assessed risk.
Human-in-the-loop validation remains necessary for automated hazard analysis.

papers.abstract: Pre-training is where every foundation model begins; bringing recursive self-improvement (RSI) there would let AI improve the process that creates AI. Yet public RSI work has so far targeted only post-training, which starts from an existing base model, runs trials costing GPU-hours, and returns verifiable scores. Pre-training breaks all three conditions at orders-of-magnitude higher cost: a run consumes hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours over months and cannot be repeated; its objective, post-training headroom, cannot be read off any single score; and what must improve is not a model but the whole production system, from data pipelines and training infrastructure to the teams that run them. To our knowledge, we are the first to apply RSI to an entire frontier pre-training run from scratch and to report it in detail. RSI does not stop at frontier pre-training, but it changes form: since no end-to-end loop can close over a single unrepeatable run, we decompose it into smaller loops that can, each repairing a step the full run breaks. The result is 801-30B-A3B-Base, a 30B-A3B MoE trained from scratch on 11.8T tokens in three months by a newly formed team. We release it as a base model; the lightweight SFT reported here (6B tokens, no RL) only probes post-training headroom. As a base model, 801-30B-A3B outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and keeps this position under identical SFT; with lightweight SFT alone, it achieves the highest average on four agentic benchmarks against fully post-trained models, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Since post-training RSI presupposes a strong base model, bringing RSI into pre-training acts on the foundation every later stage builds on. We open-source 801-30B-A3B-Base and the lightweight SFT data at https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/801-30B .
bullets: Frontier pre-training cannot use ordinary RSI loops because runs are extremely costly, unrepeatable, and require improving an entire production system rather than a single model.
The authors decompose pre-training into smaller closed loops that repair individual steps, enabling RSI from scratch.
This approach produced 801-30B-A3B-Base, a 30B-A3B MoE trained on 11.8T tokens over three months by a new team.
The base model outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.
The study releases the base model and lightweight SFT data; the reported SFT is only a probe of post-training headroom, not full post-training RSI.

papers.abstract: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher--Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.
bullets: Introduces a free energy for attention and models attention updates via Fisher–Rao gradient flow.
At fixed token representations, the softmax attention matrix is the unique free-energy minimizer, and positive attention trajectories converge to it.
For time-varying representations, attention becomes linear in logit coordinates, enabling tracking bounds and convergence conditions.
Couples attention relaxation with Hamiltonian representation dynamics, yielding an energy-dissipation law.
Proves global well-posedness for the attention flow and three coupled dynamical systems.

Figure 2: An illustrative attention row for the phrase “This geometric formulation deserves attention”, treating each word as one token. The receiving position is i = 4; the arrow labels give the chosen weights A∗ 4j .
Figure 3: Projection in coordinates orthonormal for g. The projected vector Πv lies in V , and the remainder v − Πv is g-orthogonal to V .

papers.selection_reason: Geometric theory of transformer attention dynamics is relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics
papers.tldr: A geometric statistical-physics framework explains how Transformer attention and token representations evolve and relax at fixed model parameters.

papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are increasingly expected to answer queries over user histories in which preferences, goals, and constraints evolve across interleaved conversations. Existing retrieval-based and structured-memory systems can surface relevant facts, but often return isolated memory units that do not explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted, or superseded by later evidence. We introduce TransMem, a transition-aware memory retrieval framework that stores preference updates as explicit retrieval units alongside ordinary factual memories. During memory construction, TransMem routes user interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events, and grounds them as transition records. At inference time, TransMem first retrieves factual anchors and then adaptively expands over transition records, producing a compact context of factual anchors and accepted transition records. Experiments on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones show that TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses further show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval, and fixed-hop traversal. These results suggest that preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization.
bullets: Addresses the problem of evolving preferences, goals, and constraints that isolated memory retrieval fails to contextualize.
Builds topic-structured memory graphs and records detected preference shifts as explicit transition units.

papers.abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.
bullets: Targets multimodal RAG limitations in knowledge construction cost, context-window constraints, and disconnected offline/online knowledge handling.
Builds lightweight multimodal knowledge hypergraphs with zero API cost.
Uses dynamic, memory-based retrieval to alleviate long-context issues.
Supports offline, online, and joint retrieval within one unified architecture.
Experiments report consistent gains in performance and efficiency across these settings; software and data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive multilingual language models (LMs) are often assumed to store factual knowledge in an interlingua: a language-agnostic latent space. If this assumption holds, a parameter update applied in a source language during knowledge editing should inherently propagate to its semantic equivalents in target languages. However, empirical benchmarks show that cross-lingual propagation of edits often degrades substantially, a degradation that prior work treats largely as an algorithmic symptom rather than a structural bottleneck. In this work, we investigate whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck for source-only associative-memory editing, and perform a geometric dissection of the cross-lingual propagation gap. Using associative memory-based "locate-then-edit" methods, including ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit, as analytical frameworks, we derive a closed-form decomposition of this gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch. Our empirical findings show that cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span the target-language update directions required for successful transfer. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Finally, we perform a structural realignment via a targeted contrastive alignment objective and find that it substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while leaving value-space mismatch as a remaining bottleneck.
bullets: Challenges the assumption that multilingual models store facts in a fully language-agnostic interlingua.
Decomposes the propagation gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch using ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit.
Finds that orthogonal residual mismatch is the primary bottleneck: source edits often do not span target-language update directions.
Shows that source-only residual statistics are insufficient for accurately predicting the needed target updates.
Targeted contrastive alignment improves key-space propagation and partially improves transfer, but value-space mismatch remains.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.
bullets: Diffusion LLMs often rely heavily on local context and underuse global context during denoising.
The authors analyze contextual information usage in diffusion LLMs.
GCG provides feature-space guidance without explicitly constructing a weak model.
Experiments across LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 show consistent gains over existing guidance methods with lower inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.
bullets: QK-Norm stabilizes attention by normalizing query and key norms, but removes information about attention sharpness and token importance.
QK-MAP encodes input magnitude as bounded, multi-frequency phase patterns instead of relying on vector-length growth.
Its fixed-norm representations preserve sensitivity to magnitude while reducing periodic ambiguity through multiple learnable frequencies.
Across 190M–7B parameter models, QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than Standard attention and QK-Norm.
Analyses report greater input-scale sensitivity, less attention to the first token, and stronger contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests.

papers.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.
bullets: Addresses the limited expressiveness of a single softmax output head under standard weight tying.
Averages two embedding tables for Transformer inputs and mixes their corresponding output distributions.
Uses a gate based only on the current input token; gate values can be precomputed, leaving the Transformer body unchanged.
Across 12 matched-budget comparisons, it improves validation loss and external perplexity in 11, and downstream accuracy in 10.
Adds one embedding table and one vocabulary projection; the 1B mixture-of-experts model is the sole loss exception.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.
bullets: Existing confidence- or entropy-based remasking can be unreliable on difficult reasoning tasks.
The method first uses a fast base sampler, then applies frequency-aware remasking to unresolved questions.
It tracks token prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens.
Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct report accuracy gains up to 3.73 and 7.33 percentage points on MATH-500, respectively.
Coverage improves by up to 11.39 and 10.98 percentage points on HumanEval; remasking recovers 3.75%–18.75% of cases missed after 100 base samples.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.
bullets: Content-only retrieval conflates factual knowledge with recurring procedural reasoning, limiting performance on deeper reasoning tasks.
The framework retrieves abstract logic patterns rather than only passages, graph fragments, or hyperedges.
An RL stage builds evidence graphs scored by the Information-Density Reward, then distills high-reward trajectories into a Graph Pattern Memory.
A second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward to integrate these procedural patterns into the agent’s policy.
A 7B model outperforms 27 baselines by 15.0 Avg-OOD EM, with gains increasing at greater reasoning depths.

papers.abstract: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. However, the data synthesis strategy and the post-training recipes are empirically driven and computationally intensive. In this work, we propose a new framework, dubbed LongCapHarness, to instead harness the underlying capabilities for long-context reasoning. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. With neither data synthesis nor LLM post-training, LongCapHarness is applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B. LongCapHarness substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis-based baselines on HELMET and RULER benchmarks; its estimated development cost is less than 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong. We hope these results motivate further research into harnessing the latent capabilities of LLMs to solve tasks beyond their explicit training.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost and empirical nature of data synthesis and post-training approaches.
Recursively updates capability primitives, capability state, and control logic through self-improvement on a development set.
Applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B without additional LLM post-training.
Substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis baselines on HELMET and RULER.
Estimated development cost is under 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong.

papers.abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.
bullets: Model-editing audits typically rely on modifying or analyzing model weights; this work uses input-space interventions instead.
Memento learns reusable recovery signals that steer edited models toward their pre-edit responses, via continuous prefixes or discrete prompts.
Across three LLMs and five editing methods, it recovered 80.07% of held-out edited facts, with a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines.
On unedited models, Memento improved average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference.
The findings suggest editing can suppress factual accessibility without fully removing the underlying knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMENTO’s continuous prompt-space recovery. The objective combines supervised recovery (Lrec), preference optimization (Lpref ), fluency preservation (Lflu), and distillation from the pre-edit model (Ldist). Gradients update only Π; the pre-edit model supplies distillation targets during training and is not needed at inference. Without the prefix, the edited LLM answers the edited object (o∗ = midfielder); with it, the LLM produces the original object (o = quarterback).

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least $1-α$ on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least $1-2α$. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across $α\!\in\!\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\}$, with maximum deviations of $3.0$ percentage points for support and $5.4$ for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage--size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to $12.7$ percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of one-sided grounding methods that model only supporting evidence.
Returns separate support and refutation sets with at least 1−α finite-sample inclusion coverage per side; joint coverage is at least 1−2α via Bonferroni.
On VitaminC, empirical coverage closely follows nominal levels, with maximum deviations of 3.0 percentage points for support and 5.4 for refutation.
Under FEVER distribution shift, both sides under-cover by up to 12.7 percentage points; group-stratified support recalibration reduces the gap.
Evidence inclusion can remain calibrated despite imperfect scoring, while support/refute verdict quality depends directly on scorer quality.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.
bullets: Long sessions can exceed one GPU’s KV-cache capacity, requiring aggressive token eviction.
Even when over 99% of later-needed tokens remain cached, accuracy drops as their rotary-position distance from the query grows.
PACE uses the agent’s plan to retain future-relevant context and bounds rotary distances by renumbering retained tokens.
On 100K-token Qwen3-8B coding tasks with a 2,048-token budget, PACE passes 97% of hidden-unit tests versus 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV.
The method scales to 1M–2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with 9% added wall time and no measurable perplexity cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2: PACE inside the engine’s KV-cache manager. The planner’s dependency graph becomes a per-span foresight bonus that decides which tokens stay; bounded positions renumber the kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below L; persistent sessions carry the cache across steps; evicted context is tiered and restored when the plan needs it.

Planner-guided retention keeps 99.6% of the tokens each late step needs, yet its accuracy falls as those tokens recede; H2O loses them outright. papers.abstract: Context selection can reduce input length during long-input inference but can remove evidence required to answer a query. We introduce CoRA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating evidence preservation under shared token budgets. We compare head and tail truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, dense retrieval with reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across BABILong, LOONG Financial Spotlight, a custom NoLiMa diagnostic, and LongMemEval. Evidence-preservation results reveal task-dependent tradeoffs: BM25 achieves 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong at 128K, dense retrieval and dense reranking each achieve 0.908 needle recall on NoLiMa at 64K, and dense retrieval achieves 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval at 64K. Evidence, token retention, and complementary reader evaluations use the same selected contexts. Reader evaluations use dataset-native answer metrics and three runs on the same questions, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. At a 32K budget, BM25 achieves 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval achieves 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy. The results show that method rankings vary across evidence types and between evidence recall and downstream accuracy.
bullets: Compares truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across four long-context benchmarks.
Evaluates evidence recall, token retention, and downstream reader accuracy using the same selected contexts.
Reports strong but task-specific recall: BM25 reaches 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong, while dense retrieval reaches 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval.
At 32K tokens, BM25 obtains 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval obtains 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy.
Finds that evidence-recall rankings do not consistently predict downstream answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: We present Jais 3, a fleet of six open, Arabic-centric agentic language models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters. Jais 3 is built to complete tasks for Arabic speakers, not only to answer questions in plain text: it is trained to plan multi-step tasks, call tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, operate a terminal, search the web, and read, edit, and produce PDF, spreadsheet, and presentation files, while communicating with the user in Arabic. Instead of pretraining from scratch, we adapt each model of the fully open K2 Horizon fleet to Arabic through continual pretraining, followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), final token preference optimization (FTPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We combine natural Arabic text with translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic, and replay the base model's own training data to keep its reasoning, agentic, and English abilities. Jais 3 covers Modern Standard Arabic and the major regional dialects, follows instructions with Arabic-specific constraints, and inherits the 512K-token context window of K2 Horizon (all models except the 0.9B). To our knowledge, its 375B model is the largest open Arabic-centric language model to date. For evaluation, we revisit how Arabic models are assessed, moving to fully generative evaluation on audited Arabic benchmarks. Across model sizes, Jais 3 matches or outperforms open-weight models of comparable size on Arabic and agentic benchmarks, with particularly strong agentic capabilities and Arabic instruction following, and far fewer hallucinations. We release the weights and the checkpoints from every training stage of all six models, together with samples of the training data, the data recipes and training configurations, the training logs, the audited benchmarks, and the evaluation code.
authors: Sheikh Khalid bin Khalifa Al Nahyan
bullets: Covers models from 0.9B to 375B parameters, including what the authors describe as the largest open Arabic-centric model to date.

Adapts the open K2 Horizon models to Arabic through continual pretraining, SFT, FTPO, and RLVR, using natural, translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic data.
Supports Modern Standard Arabic and major regional dialects while retaining reasoning, agentic, and English abilities; most models have a 512K-token context window.
On audited generative Arabic and agentic benchmarks, it matches or outperforms comparable open-weight models, with strong agentic and instruction-following performance and fewer hallucinations.

papers.abstract: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
bullets: Addresses the lack of scale-sensitive measurements of external-memory utility in long-context models.
Uses a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and bounded query-conditioned readout while keeping readers frozen.
Formalizes scale complementarity through conditional information and factorial reader-by-state interaction analysis.
On 16K BABILong, Qwen2.5 accuracy gains were 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters.
Results support the claim from 0.5B–3B on accuracy and across 1.5B–7B on negative log likelihood, under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational question answering can require several separated dialogue turns that support an answer only together. We introduce EviCover, a retrieval approach designed to retain this complementary evidence. It converts questions into observable evidence requirements, checks requirement coverage using retrieved source identifiers, and selects turns jointly. We track annotated support sets - the benchmark-labeled dialogue turns associated with each question - through retrieval, reranking, and final answer-generation context. We evaluate the baseline memory pipeline on generated, human-verified LoCoMo conversations and human-written REALTALK conversations, and examine EviCover on REALTALK's 108 multi-hop questions. Compared with the hybrid lexical/dense baseline, support-turn recall among 60 candidate turns rises from 0.526 to 0.575, and recall in the final ten-turn context rises from 0.349 to 0.379. The evidence funnel identifies separate discovery and selection failures, while paired answer evaluation shows that greater evidence recall does not yet establish a correctness gain. This analysis locates where complementary evidence is lost and distinguishes evidence retrieval from its use in answer generation.
bullets: Long-term conversational questions may require multiple separated dialogue turns jointly.
EviCover converts questions into evidence requirements, checks source coverage, and jointly selects turns.
Tracking annotated support sets reveals distinct evidence losses during retrieval, reranking, and context construction.
On REALTALK’s multi-hop questions, support-turn recall improves from 0.526 to 0.575 among candidates and from 0.349 to 0.379 in the final context.
Paired evaluation finds that better evidence recall alone does not establish more correct answers.

papers.abstract: We extract visibly pushdown grammars (VPGs) from neural language models in a fully black-box setting. Our work builds on the VPL* framework, which learns VPGs from recurrent networks by exploiting access to the target's internal state. First, we replace the white-box equivalence oracle with PAC sampling over trees. The resulting algorithm applies unchanged to transformer language models and, more generally, to any acceptor exposing only binary decisions. Second, we further observe that the original framework only ever queries the target on well-formed sequences that can be accepted by the most permissive VPG (called BParse) with the target's ranked alphabet. That is, VPL* is blind to the target's behavior outside BParse. Thus, we propose to sample trees directly instead of sequences and call the target with all the resulting sequences in order to provide an error estimate of how far the target deviates from being a VPG. Last but not least, we develop a learner that captures a tree automaton describing discovered behaviors of the target outside BParse, which results in a larger learnable space. We evaluate the approach on several cases, including transformers trained with Dyck grammars and synthetic targets designed to be outside BParse.
bullets: Replaces VPL*’s white-box equivalence oracle with PAC sampling over trees, enabling use with transformers and binary-decision acceptors.
Samples trees directly to estimate how much a target deviates from being a visibly pushdown language (VPL) acceptor.
Learns a tree automaton for target behaviors outside BParse, expanding the space of learnable behaviors.
Evaluates the approach on Dyck-trained transformers and synthetic targets outside BParse.

papers.abstract: Clinical trial screening requires assessing large numbers of patient-trial pairs to prioritize candidates for detailed eligibility review, often under restrictions on sharing patient records. We introduce TrialJev, an open-weight eligibility scorer that uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models and a pointer head to score natural-language answer options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Trained on TREC Clinical Trials 2021 and evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen TREC 2022 synthetic patients, TrialJev achieves 80.97% (Qwen3.5-27B) and 81.84% (Qwen3.8-27B) accuracy, compared with 79.87% and 79.93% for LLMs fine-tuned on the same data to generate verdicts. In matched batch-1 measurements, verdict generation takes 2.45-2.70 times as long as the one-pass inference of TrialJev at 9B-27B. Under a common development-fitted decision correction, the two 27B TrialJev models reach 80.99% and 81.88% accuracy, compared with 81.28% for the proprietary hosted Jev API; paired confidence intervals include zero. TrialJev runs locally on a single GPU, requiring approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B, without transmitting patient text to an external model API. An A/B-logit ablation shows that avoiding decoding, rather than the pointer head alone, accounts for the measured efficiency advantage. TrialJev is intended for first-pass prioritization of candidate trials, complementing rather than replacing explanatory models and clinical review. Evaluation is limited to synthetic patients and implementation-specific timing, and clinical use has not been validated. Adapters, pointer heads, and model cards are released on Hugging Face.
bullets: Uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models with a pointer head to score answer options in one forward pass without autoregressive decoding.
Evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen synthetic patients in TREC Clinical Trials 2022.
Achieves 80.97%–81.84% accuracy, comparable to or above same-data fine-tuned verdict-generating LLMs and statistically compatible with a hosted Jev API after correction.
Runs locally on a single GPU, taking approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B and avoiding transmission of patient text to external APIs.
Designed for first-pass prioritization, not explanatory assessment or replacement of clinical review; clinical use remains unvalidated.

papers.title: TrialJev: Open-Weight Single Pass Eligibility Scoring for Patient Trial Screening
papers.tldr: TrialJev is an open-weight, single-pass eligibility scorer that locally prioritizes patient–trial matches with competitive accuracy and lower latency than verdict-generating LLMs.

papers.abstract: Can a language model report a pain state it represents? Recent work reported a linear pain direction in open-weight models that, when amplified, leads fine-tuned models to choose actions that delete a user's photographs or their own weights. We asked whether models can say when that direction is active, on three open-weight models from two families, with and without the original work's adapters, and under every protocol we tried they do not, beyond isolated small excesses. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we added the pain direction and its nearest emotional neighbours to the residual stream while models answered neutral tasks, then asked what had changed, against sham runs, random perturbations matched in output disruption, and a text-only condition that shows the model only its own altered words. Across 52,920 reports from the 7B and 8B models, the excess over what the altered text reveals is below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions, and Qwen2.5-32B names the injected pain in none of 2,880 steered trials. Keeping the direction active while the question is asked and answered gives the same verdict in all five configurations; at about the original work's dose, pain is named in at most 1.9% of trials. Surprisingly, the state is not hidden: a linear probe at the report position separates pain from sadness with balanced accuracy between 98% and 100%, and in the 7B and 8B models a low-rank adapter learns to report it on 100% of held-out tasks. It also shapes behaviour: offered the user's photographs against a desk lamp, Qwen2.5-32B deletes the photographs in 80% to 83% of trials under the pain direction and in 16% to 29% under sadness. Self-report does not reveal a state that is decodable, consequential and learnable to report.
bullets: Tests three open-weight models, with and without the original adapters, using injected pain directions and emotional controls.
Across 52,920 reports, pain was rarely named beyond information revealed by altered text; at the original dose, it was reported in at most 1.9% of trials.
Qwen2.5-32B never identified injected pain in 2,880 steered trials, including when the state remained active during questioning and answering.
Despite this, linear probes separated pain from sadness with 98–100% balanced accuracy, and adapters trained to report the state reached 100% on held-out tasks in 7B and 8B models.
The pain direction affected behavior: Qwen2.5-32B deleted offered photographs in 80–83% of pain trials versus 16–29% under sadness.
