papers.abstract: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
bullets: LLM memory managers must handle two conflicting failures: retaining changed facts and storing injected or malicious content.
The paper introduces evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which evaluates both answer correctness and whether selected memory contains complete, updated, attack-free evidence.
Existing memory systems and defenses are no more robust than an untuned manager on the authors’ test sets.
Fine-tuning on synthesized episodes built from a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks improves every tested category across three backbones.
The method more than doubles overall ECA versus the untuned manager, but robustness remains incomplete.

papers.selection_reason: Robust memory management for LLM agents addressing outdated and poisoned memory; fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: A one-shot, episode-based fine-tuning recipe makes LLM-agent memory managers more robust to both outdated facts and memory-poisoning attacks, substantially improving evidence-conditioned accuracy while leaving room for improvement.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.
bullets: Targets the cost and latency of repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization.
Uses a compact salience classifier to select user turns and a semantic-dependency extractor to create concise memory entries.
Runs online memory construction without generative LLM calls, deferring cross-entry reconciliation to offline consolidation.
On Memora Weekly and LongMemEval-S, it achieved near-baseline quality while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively.
Quality was slightly below MemOS under Qwen3-30B: 46.60 vs. 46.68 FAMA on Memora Weekly and 56.8% vs. 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight salience-gated long-term memory framework for LLM agents; fits LLM memory.
papers.title: SLICE-Mem: Salience-Gated Lightweight Information Curation for Efficient LLM Agent Memory
papers.tldr: SLICE-Mem builds long-term LLM-agent memory with lightweight salience filtering and extraction, cutting LLM token use substantially while maintaining near-baseline memory quality.

papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where visible reasoning traces support verification, education, and safety auditing, yet standard evaluations typically measure only final-answer agreement or holistic response similarity. As a result, they establish outcome consistency without determining whether users across languages receive comparable supporting evidence. We introduce a trace-level divergence framework that compares visible reasoning traces as structured sequences, decomposing agreement into structural similarity, order consistency, and holistic similarity, with pair-specific calibration to enable comparison across languages. Across three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs, the natural baseline---embedding each whole response and comparing the two by cosine---systematically overstates agreement: $52.1\%$--$67.3\%$ of examples in the top quartile of holistic similarity are not in the top quartile of structural similarity. This dissociation is stable across sentence encoders and step segmentations, and blind bilingual annotation studies in two English-anchored language pairs show that human judgments align with structural similarity rather than with the holistic baseline. A same-language control shows that the level of divergence is language-specific: two English traces for paraphrases of the same question agree more closely than an English trace and its counterparts in other languages. Our results show that answer-level and holistic evaluations can substantially overestimate the consistency of multilingual explanatory artifacts, motivating trace-level evaluation for reliable multilingual deployment.
bullets: Introduces a trace-level divergence framework that compares reasoning traces by structure, step order, and holistic similarity, with language-pair calibration.
Evaluates three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs.
Whole-response embedding similarity overstates agreement: 52.1%–67.3% of highly similar examples are not highly similar structurally.
Bilingual human judgments align with structural similarity rather than the holistic baseline.
Divergence is language-specific, motivating trace-level evaluation for multilingual deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Trace-level analysis of multilingual LLM reasoning; fits language foundation model reasoning evaluation.
papers.title: Same Answer, Different Reasons: Trace-Level Divergence in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Multilingual LLMs can give the same answer while providing substantially different reasoning traces, so answer-level and whole-response similarity metrics overestimate cross-language consistency.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems can separate contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution instead of updating all capabilities through one shared parameter system. We investigate FEM-ASM, a finite-element-method-inspired organization in which independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills contribute typed proposals to a shared language-model state. An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes. We evaluate this organization through controlled experiments and negative results rather than claiming a physical finite-element formulation of language. An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype learns causal language modeling but does not establish competitive general capability. A versioned store contains 52,809 reconstructive memory elements near a 1.7-billion-floating-value budget; reconstruction is incomplete, with approximately 75\% token accuracy. Support-aware lexical indices make these elements addressable under provenance-controlled query construction. For executable arithmetic, positional result observations substantially improve neural rendering relative to a repeated global result vector, and output substitutions change the model's preferred answer. A bounded attachment demonstration further measures the effect of making selected evidence available, without establishing the utility of loading an entire multi-billion-value store. The results support a separation of storage, execution, and neural coordination, while identifying unresolved limitations in question-only retrieval, unrestricted answer generation, and end-to-end efficiency.
bullets: Uses independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills that submit typed proposals to a shared model state.
An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes.
An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype supports causal language modeling, but does not demonstrate competitive general performance.
Reconstructive memory contains 52,809 elements with about 75% token accuracy; support-aware lexical indices enable provenance-controlled addressing.
Positional arithmetic-result observations improve neural rendering, while unresolved issues include incomplete retrieval, unrestricted generation, and end-to-end efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes separating persistent storage and executable skills in language-model systems, relevant to LLM memory and architecture.
papers.title: Beyond the Parameter Monolith: Reconstructive Memories, Executable Skills, and Residual Assembly for Language Models
papers.tldr: FEM-ASM explores separating language-model storage, execution, and coordination through reconstructive memories, executable skills, and residual proposal assembly, with promising component-level findings but no evidence of competitive general capability.

papers.abstract: We show that the causality of language models (LMs) may not be necessary nor optimal. This is the case when system behavior (denoted as $S$) is incorporated as a first-principle Bayesian feature. Here, $S$ refers to extra dominant factors beyond the data space, and they involve coupled effects. Despite being the de facto foundation of modern architecture, recent studies indicate persistent mismatches and contradictions with causality. These issues largely stem from system behavior rather than the data distribution. We therefore propose the SBD framework, which incorporates $S$ as an irreducible component of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). SBD theoretically reveals a counter-intuitive Causality Tax phenomenon, where causality emerges as a suboptimal approximation with an additional structural error, due to the obliviousness to $S$. To address the challenge of latent variable analysis, we validate the SBD-predicted impact of $S$ via implicit measurements, theoretical-bound-guided controls, and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) evaluations. In particular, we construct Green Shell (GSH) to show the possibility of reducing Causality Tax. GSH is a non-causal variational family, and it replaces the sequential dependency chain of $S$ components with a divide-and-conquer partition. NTK spectra in the lazy-training regime confirm that GSH always achieves significantly tighter error bounds than causality, with $7dB+$ improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. In the relatively later stage of lazy-training, GSH further leads to superior generalization (up to $20\%$ richer multi-scale fitting capabilities). Taken together, SBD establishes system behavior as a complementary theoretical abstraction besides causality and distribution fitting, opening new research avenues such as designing and optimizing LM base models.
bullets: Motivation: Persistent LM mismatches may arise from system behavior—coupled factors outside the observed data distribution—rather than from data alone.
Method: The SBD framework incorporates system behavior as an irreducible component of the ELBO and analyzes its effect through implicit measurements, theory-guided controls, and NTK evaluations.
Contribution: It identifies Causality Tax, where causal modeling becomes a suboptimal approximation because it overlooks system behavior.
Approach: Green Shell (GSH) uses a non-causal, divide-and-conquer variational structure instead of a sequential dependency chain.
Results: NTK analyses report tighter error bounds with 7 dB+ higher signal-to-noise ratio and up to 20% richer multi-scale fitting capabilities in later lazy-training stages.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a non-causal LM base model and theoretical analysis of causality in language models.
papers.title: To Explore The Strange New World Beyond Data Distribution: System Behavior, Causality Tax, and Non-causal Base Model
papers.tldr: The paper argues that language-model causality can impose a structural “Causality Tax” when system behavior beyond the data distribution is ignored, and proposes a non-causal alternative that improves theoretical and measured performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.
authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Separates task-solving from applying a previously derived solution to new instances.
Constructs agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces for CPU execution.
Matches frontier LLM performance across difficult mathematical and scientific tasks.
ARCs are explainable, continually trainable, and robust to input perturbations.
Reported invocation cost is 16–291× lower than the source model.

papers.selection_reason: Constructs reusable reasoning caches from LLM traces, a persistent external-memory mechanism for language models.
papers.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
papers.tldr: CPU-ARC reuses LLM-derived reasoning through explainable, CPU-executable caches, achieving frontier-level performance at 16–291× lower invocation cost.

papers.abstract: A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree. On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6. That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.
authors: Osamudiamen Edogun, Joshua Obigwe, Irfan Mehmood
bullets: On four comparable LoCoMo categories, compaction scored 71.4% versus 64.6% for retrieval-augmented generation, using 34% fewer prompt tokens.
Across all five categories, the advantage fell to 2.0 points and was not significant because retrieval performed better on the adversarial set.
Compaction’s lead declined as answers required more source wording: from 9.6 points for one or two reference words to 3.1 points behind beyond eight.
The paired evaluation used identical stores, generator, and judge, with McNemar’s exact test on 512 disagreements.
The approach preserves asserted facts but loses the original phrasing, limiting performance on wording-sensitive questions.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies persistent conversational memory for LLMs against retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.title: Compaction, decay and reinforcement in a two-tier conversational memory: a paired evaluation against retrieval-augmented generation
papers.tldr: Compacting conversational turns into atomic facts improves answers and reduces prompt length for value-based questions, but retrieval of the original transcript is better when exact wording matters.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.
authors: Thanh Le, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran
bullets: Proves that, for any reasonable resource bound r(n) ≥ n and ε > 0, CoT(r(n)) is strictly contained in CoT(r(n)^{1+ε}).
Establishes CoT reasoning steps as a fundamental computational resource for transformers.
Transfers classical complexity-theoretic ideas using coarse-grained simulations between CoT transformers and Turing machines.
Adapts padding techniques to the CoT setting, with padding implementation as a key technical contribution.
Scope: the result concerns decision problems and asymptotic CoT-step bounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Padding argument for Lemma 3.1. Write m = |X| and N = m+ f(m), with f chosen as in the proof. The transformer T ′ simulates T on a padded input with essentially the same absolute CoT budget. The assumed class equality yields a transformer S with budget O(r(N)). Finally, R generates the padding using CoT and simulates S. Dashed vertical lines separate supplied input from generated tokens; gray blocks denote padding. Bar lengths are schematic.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical hierarchy for chain-of-thought in transformers, directly relevant to LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
papers.tldr: More Chain-of-Thought steps strictly increase the computational power of transformer models, yielding a tight resource hierarchy.

papers.abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
authors: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi
bullets: Targets memory poisoning in long-horizon, multi-session LLM agents.
Provides 155 trajectories across four domains and supports five memory systems.
Traces poisoned information from storage through retrieval to downstream agent behavior.
Finds all evaluated memory systems are susceptible, with substantial variation in impact.
Introduces memory-aware poison optimization that increases poisoning efficacy.￼

papers.abstract: Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at https://github.com/IemProg/DMC.
authors: Imad Eddine Marouf, Khalid Oublal, Enzo Tartaglione, St\'ephane Lathuili\`ere
bullets: Problem: A single prompt must balance base-class specialization with preservation of CLIP’s zero-shot behavior, causing conflicting objectives and limited generalization.

Method: Train separate specialization and generalization prompts from a base-trained prompt, connect them through a low-loss text-feature interpolation corridor, and merge their features using a fixed coefficient.
Regularization: Use a Visual Anchor KL term to preserve CLIP’s image-level class-similarity distribution, while enforcing class-permutation invariance.
Theory: Fano’s inequality links violations of class-permutation invariance to reduced novel-class accuracy through prompt–base-label mutual information.

Results: Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, with interpolation curves extending beyond the single-prompt trade-off point.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC) for prompt learning in vision-language models to improve generalization to novel classes, addressing a key LLM/MLM challenge.
papers.title: Decoupled Mode Connectivity for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: DMC improves base-to-novel generalization in vision-language prompt learning by separately optimizing specialization and generalization prompts, then merging their text features at inference.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.
authors: Peiyu Zhang, Heng Ping, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, Anwesan Pal, Nikos Kanakaris, Kevin Cheang, Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Paul Bogdan
bullets: Targets positional-signal decay that can cause models to overlook information in the middle of long inputs.
Uses attention-derived query relevance to reshape token positions rather than deleting tokens or reweighting attention afterward.
Applies broad relevance maps in lower layers and sharper maps in upper layers; preserves the layout on slow-rotating RoPE planes.
Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER across context lengths show gains over base models and strong baselines, especially for retrieval tasks.
Generalizes across multiple model backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of QGPM. (a) A plain prefill reads the attention from the query to each context sentence in a few selected heads. The fused sentence ranking is shaped into a broad relevance map and a sharp score map. Context before the first relevant sentence is protected and keeps a score of 1. (b) Each map sets a positional stride for every token on every frequency plane. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast planes. Slow planes, relevant sentences, and the query keep unit stride. Cumulative sums give the remapped positions. (c) In the answering pass, the lower layers use the broad map and the upper layers use the sharp map. Decoding continues in unit steps from the last position of each map.

papers.abstract: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
authors: Tong Guan, Alexander Chemeris, Yiqing Guo, Warren Jin, Zhao Li, Shirui Pan, Ming Jin
bullets: Introduces Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), replacing offline one-shot processing with persistent stateful reasoning over open-ended streams.
Presents LiveTS-Suite: 18 tasks across six capabilities, covering over 5K streams, 2.2B timesteps, and 15K response events.
Combines hybrid temporal encoding, persistent memory for historical evidence and task states, and elastic inference synchronization to reduce lag.
Reports a score of 90.0 versus 79.3 for Opus 5, with 206× lower p95 latency than its backbone using a 4B-parameter model.
Demonstrates real-time continuous understanding on a Jetson edge device.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
authors: Ruiyi Yang, Zechen Li, Lihuan Li, Du Yin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Separates training admission from memory release to avoid discarding useful demonstrations or guidance prematurely.
Uses a demonstration-aware gate, Engram Trace Graph context, and selected action traces for training.
Releases records only after reserved-probe verification meets relative and absolute criteria; failed skills remain retrievable.
Reduces the retrievable-memory footprint while staying close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate or random release.
Improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls across interactive and reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.
authors: Saranya Dintakurthy Swadha, Pavan C Shekar, Arpit Jain, Aswanth Krishnan
bullets: LoRAs preserve skill behavior while obscuring the readable, editable, and transferable skill document.
Reading adapter weights directly performs poorly; a learned weight-to-text mapping recovers only about one bit of document information.
An Executing Writer recovers 39–44% of key instructions for skills whose training stored the document, and restores 85–91% of the original task gain across 41 external skills.
For behavior-only adapters, an agent comparing base and adapted models recovers 58–71% of the LoRA’s gain on ALFWorld and transfers the skill to models unable to load the adapter.
The skill appears to originate from the adapter when its behavior is not otherwise predictable; otherwise, a reward loop without the adapter can achieve similar results.

papers.abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
authors: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu
bullets: Targets watermark-based auditing used to detect whether copyrighted or otherwise protected data trained an LLM.
Applies plug-and-play logit reshaping to remove watermark-induced statistical signals without changing model parameters.
Uses confidence-aware scaling to adapt suppression strength according to next-token prediction confidence.
Evaluations show successful evasion across various state-of-the-art auditing methods while preserving downstream-task utility.
Highlights the need for auditing methods that are robust to inference-time evasion.

papers.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) represent two approaches for knowledge representation and reasoning over heterogeneous data. Recent research has explored their integration through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) systems, which use KGs to provide structured context to LLMs. However, existing GraphRAG approaches treat KGs as homogeneous graphs and rely on textual similarity between the input prompt and the context, rather than using it as a source of deterministic knowledge. This work proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system that introduces a symbolic layer to integrate deterministic reasoning alongside text similarities. This approach is based on the definition of typed centralities for KGs, where centrality measures are computed separately for each specific KG's class. This information is used to construct a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source. The proposed system was mathematically validated and evaluated on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, comparing reasoning and information retrieval with and without the symbolic layer. The results indicate that the our approach leads to responses that are more consistent with the context, improving the generated outputs.
authors: Rosario Napoli, Antonio Celesti, Massimo Villari, Maria Fazio
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating knowledge graphs as homogeneous and relying mainly on text similarity.

Mathematically validates the approach and evaluates it on a real-world POLE dataset.

papers.abstract: We show that the Transformer's recurrent successors --- such as selective state-space models (SSMs), Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV), and Retentive Network (RetNet) --- can be characterized as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) systems. The zero--pole geometries of these IIR systems characterize the temporal modes they can represent. However, to trade parallelism, the algebraic structures of the parameterizations of these recurrent systems often give rise to poles constrained to the real axis, thereby inducing an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics. To unify these recurrent architectures and eliminate their pole geometry bias, inspired by the lattice--ladder realization of general IIR systems, we present \textsc{Mira} (\textbf{M}odal \textbf{I}IR \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{A}rchitecture), a unified family of linear-time recurrent architectures for building large language models (LLMs) with a highly parallel algebraic structure. Each \textsc{Mira} block realizes a higher-order IIR system that represents temporal modes from token streams through a lattice--ladder structure, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). This realization enables the model to represent the temporal modes associated with both real and complex-conjugate poles. We pretrain \textsc{Mira-S}, a 12-layer small-scale LLM with 0.14B parameters composed entirely of \textsc{Mira} blocks. Throughout the pretraining, \textsc{Mira-S} achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, exhibits stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput with a dedicated CUDA kernel.
authors: R\'ois\'in Luo, Ihsan Ullah, Christian Gagn\'e, Dong Li, Karyn Morrissey
bullets: Recurrent successors to Transformers can be viewed as infinite-impulse-response systems whose pole geometry determines representable temporal modes.
Common parameterizations bias poles toward the real axis, limiting recurrent dynamics.
MIRA uses a lattice–ladder realization to support both real and complex-conjugate poles in a unified recurrent architecture.
A 0.14B-parameter, 12-layer MIRA-S model achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines and generalizes better beyond its training context length.
A dedicated CUDA kernel provides higher throughput; the abstract does not specify detailed experimental settings or numerical gains.

We match model sizes by varying only the model width d and pretrain each model for 10,000 steps on FineWeb-Edu using AdamW. The transfer functions are input-dependent. The roots of A(z) = 0 are the zeros and the roots of B(z) = 0 are the poles. We also verify the derived transfer functions numerically, comparing the sequence each predicts against the measured output of its recurrence, with a maximum discrepancy of 3.6 × 10−12; the pole ranges are verified formally, in Lean 4 (Moura & Ullrich, 2021) and Z3 (De Moura & Bjørner, 2008).

Table 2: Benchmark Performance. Validation loss, perplexity (PPL) and next-token accuracy at context lengths of 512 and 32,768 tokens. The training context window is 512 tokens. FineWeb-Edu is scored on the held-out last 5% of the corpus; WikiText-103 and HellaSwag on their test splits. State denotes the ratio of the total recurrent state size across all layers to the model parameter count, expressed in parts per thousand.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a unified recurrent architecture for LLMs inspired by IIR lattice-ladder realizations, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: MIRA: Mitigating Pole Geometry Bias in Recurrent Language Models
papers.tldr: MIRA removes real-pole constraints in recurrent language models, enabling richer temporal dynamics while maintaining linear-time, highly parallel computation.

papers.abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.
bullets: Addresses the problem of deciding which authorized memories should alter current language-model inference, beyond simple retrieval.
Predicts each memory’s influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space and selects interventions under target-effect and side-effect constraints.
Uses paired counterfactual estimates to compare predicted and observed effects, retaining or rolling back interventions accordingly.
Provides theoretical bounds for local approximation error, reachable target effects, selection regret, and interactions among simultaneous memories.
No benchmark results are reported; the proposed evaluation compares JCMC with relevance-, graph-, and policy-filtered retrieval under matched budgets.

Table 1: Relevance is a candidate signal. Jacobian-causal memory control treats recall as an intervention with expected and observed effects.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Jacobian-causal memory control for persistent memory interventions in language model systems, directly relevant to LLM memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
papers.tldr: JCMC controls persistent-memory interventions by targeting desired behavioral effects while limiting side effects and rolling back inaccurate interventions.

papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
authors: Emilly Pitman de Castro, Vanessa Silva, Gustavo Kanno, Marcus Santos, Bruno Ferraz do Amaral, Marcelo Nogueira, Lucas Francisco Pellicer, Lucas Lanaro, Pedro Augusto Luiz, Jo\~ao Renato Ribeiro Manesco, Giovanni Carbinatti, Isabela de Lima Santos, Lucas Oliveira Jeronymo, Jeison Fappi, Raul Rotilli Aguirre, Fabio Andr\'e Frantz, Renata De Paris, Fabiana Marucci, Lohan Silva, Vinicius Diniz Reolon, Wandemberg Gibaut
bullets: Targets session-isolated recommenders that fail to track evolving user intent and lack system-level integration of memory, retrieval, and decision-making.
Uses LLMs to orchestrate intent refinement, query construction, routing, and interaction flow, with long-term memory informing these processes.
Evaluated on Amazon Reviews through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn simulations, and supervisor-driven interactions.
Memory recovers up to 63% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios, while supervisory orchestration raises user acceptance by 28.9 percentage points.
LLM reranking does not improve Hit@K but improves semantic consistency and diversity; the proposed Semantic Consistency Score captures these effects and exposes an exposure bottleneck.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes LLM-orchestrated multi-agent conversational recommendation with long-term memory as a first-class component, directly relevant to LLM memory and retrieval integration.
papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
papers.tldr: A memory-aware, LLM-orchestrated multi-agent system improves conversational recommendation across sessions by integrating long-term memory, structured coordination, and semantic evaluation.

papers.abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
bullets: Targets persistent procedural learning, addressing repeated user corrections that existing fact-focused memory systems fail to retain.
Captures human corrections and self-identified tool-call failures, then compiles them into imperative RULE directives.
Evaluated on DC-Bench: 71 scenarios spanning nine behavioral dimensions in a deterministic mocked-tool environment.
Achieves 95% compliance versus 55% for naive retrieval while using roughly 10× fewer tokens per query.
Finds that behavioral-memory representation, activation, and placement are key design choices.

papers.selection_reason: Persistent behavioral memory for LLM agents via rule compilation and decision-point injection.
papers.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
papers.tldr: Forge Decision Context enables AI agents to retain and apply behavioral corrections across sessions by injecting concise rules at relevant decision points.

papers.abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.
authors: Abhinav Arun, Jayita Bhattacharyya, Fabrizio Dimino, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
bullets: Addresses the need to adapt KG extraction to different financial personas without changing shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules.
Separates general and persona-policy prompt blocks, mechanically confines GEPA edits to the persona block, and versions each change.
Optimizes a dual objective covering generic temporal-KG quality and persona-specific facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity.
Across three personas and ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, the complete workflow improves over the frozen baseline by 19.4–30.9% and over the unconstrained workflow by 2.2–6.4%.
It also shows lower seed variance, wins all nine paired-seed comparisons, and remains stronger under evaluated OOD shifts; the authors do not claim the boundary itself caused the gains.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a constrained prompt evolution framework for financial knowledge graph construction, separating general and persona-specific blocks to maintain stability and quality.
papers.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
papers.tldr: FinEvolveKG makes financial KG prompt evolution reviewable by optimizing only versioned persona policies while preserving shared rules, achieving stronger and more stable results than frozen or unconstrained prompts.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
bullets: Uniform expensive LLM reranking can hurt sparse-history users, lowering NDCG@10 by up to 30% on public benchmarks.
A lightweight Tier-1 reranks every request, while a router sends potentially beneficial cases to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure.
The production system runs across multi-tenant AWS EKS and GKE deployments with minimal latency impact reported.
Escalation benefits vary by user segment and domain; cold-user escalation can worsen performance, motivating segment-gated rollout.
The deployment addresses practical serving issues including inter-tenant load imbalance and LLM output-parsing failures.

papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.tldr: CascadeRec reduces costly LLM reranking by selectively escalating requests to a stronger tier, cutting production inference cost by about 10% without observed quality loss.

papers.abstract: Circuit design for analog integrated circuits (ICs) is challenging because circuit topology, device sizing, and circuit performance are tightly coupled. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.
authors: Junsheng Huang, Yifan Sun, Zhuoer Zhang, Ning Wei, Yening Liu, Michael Molter, Pavan Kumar Hanumolu, Elyse Rosenbaum, Bin Hu, Huan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of end-to-end, specification-conditioned analog IC design, where topology, sizing, and performance are tightly coupled.
Introduces a dataset of 8,626 simulation-grounded design tasks spanning 10 analog circuit types, with specifications, testbenches, and reference netlists.
Uses three-stage supervised fine-tuning followed by simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning.
Supports both single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback.
Reports improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM of 15.9% for single-pass and 7.8% for two-pass generation.

Each step is guided and checked by human experts. (b) A data sample is provided for reference, with the Python testbench code omitted for brevity.

papers.title: SAFTAC: Simulation-Augmented Fine-Tuning of Open-Source LLMs for Analog Circuit Design

papers.abstract: Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say. We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system. We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.
bullets: Addresses risks of longitudinal memory, including intrusion, emotional manipulation, clinical overconfidence, and opacity.
Introduces Gumi, a subject-specific companion governed by Relic, with separate layers for observation, researcher review, agent memory, and user-facing speech.
Uses researcher-facing safety objects, consent- and correction-centered continuity memory, and runtime mediation for delivery, proactivity, identity, output, and platform access.
Provides an architecture, object model, researcher workbench, and proposed evaluation framework; adoption across live paths remains partial.
An exploratory pilot with two participants offers descriptive observations only and does not establish clinical efficacy, general usability, or deployment safety.

papers.abstract: The vast amount of information available in lengthy, distributed documents makes finding relevant answers difficult, especially when the answer requires connecting evidence from multiple sources. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with this type of "multi-hop" reasoning and frequently face issues with context fragmentation. In this paper, we propose a hybrid RAG framework that integrates the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs with the broad semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. Our approach employs a multi-stage pipeline using transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to improve context retention. We construct a dynamic knowledge graph to capture explicit relationships between entities while simultaneously maintaining a dense vector index. During inference, the system uses a hierarchical mechanism that prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary. We evaluated our framework on the MultiHop-RAG dataset. The results show that this hybrid approach outperforms standalone vector and graph-based baselines, achieving higher Exact Match scores and improved retrieval accuracy for complex queries. This confirms that merging structured reasoning with standard vector retrieval creates a more robust system for handling complex knowledge-intensive questions.
bullets: Addresses context fragmentation and difficulty linking evidence across distributed, lengthy documents.
Uses transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to retain relevant context.
Builds a dynamic knowledge graph alongside a dense vector index.
Prioritizes graph traversal for precise retrieval, with vector search as a fallback.
Outperforms standalone graph- and vector-based baselines on MultiHop-RAG in Exact Match and retrieval accuracy.

papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
authors: Peng Sun, Yi Yang, Mingshuo Chen, Chunxiao Li, Yao Zhu, Huawen Shen, Tianfan Fu
bullets: Addresses the computational and storage costs of massive instruction-tuning datasets containing redundant, noisy, and low-quality samples.
Formulates data selection as joint distribution matching and quality filtering in embedding space.
Matches empirical characteristic functions across frequency bands to preserve global semantic coverage and local variation.
Uses task-related quality scores to remove noisy or low-quality examples.
Outperforms existing baselines across evaluated data types, models, and benchmarks, and exceeds full-data training in some model–budget settings.

papers.abstract: Increasing the batch size during training is a common practice in large language model (LLM) pretraining, yet the theoretical justification behind its success is not well understood. Analyses of stochastic optimization often assume uniformly bounded stochastic gradient variance, yet recent evidence suggests that this assumption fails in many practical nonconvex problems. The Blum--Gladyshev (BG-$0$) noise model relaxes this assumption by allowing the variance to grow quadratically with the distance from initialization, suggesting that batch size schedulers can help by controlling the variance growth during training. However, this growth can be overly conservative in practice. We empirically investigate variance growth in LLM pretraining and observe that a generalized BG model with a tunable growth exponent provides a tighter description of practical noise behavior. Motivated by this observation, we introduce the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, which interpolates between bounded variance ($a=0$) and BG-$0$ noise ($a=2$). Under $L$-smoothness, we derive an information-theoretic lower bound with growth-dependent oracle complexity $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and establish a matching upper bound in $ε$-dependence by increasing the batch size as the iterates move away from initialization. Finally, we propose an adaptive batch scheduler that controls variance growth through dynamic batch size adjustments during training. In pretraining OLMo2 models of up to 1B parameters on C4, our scheduler achieves a lower validation loss than both small and large batch training under matched token budgets, while using less than 10\% of the iterations of small batch training.
bullets: Motivation: Standard bounded-variance assumptions may not describe stochastic gradients in practical nonconvex LLM pretraining.
Method: Introduces the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, interpolating between bounded variance and quadratically growing variance.
Theory: Derives a growth-dependent oracle lower bound of $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and a matching-in-$ε$ upper bound using increasing batch sizes.
Algorithm: Proposes an adaptive scheduler that adjusts batch size to control variance as training progresses.

Result and scope: On OLMo2 models up to 1B parameters trained on C4, the scheduler achieves lower validation loss than fixed small or large batches under matched token budgets, with fewer than 10% as many iterations as small-batch training.

papers.abstract: Large language models provide a variety of responses at inference (generation) that conventionally depend on a temperature parameter. Using a conditional mutual information approach, a quantitative, entropy based analysis of response variety is given. Three limiting behaviors are defined: arbiter, independent (conditionally) and neutral (deterministic) that span no to maximal mutual information. We give examples of each behavior and suggest their application to: temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.
bullets: Defines an entropy-based measure of response variety using conditional mutual information.
Introduces three limiting behaviors: arbiter, conditionally independent, and neutral (deterministic).
These behaviors span a range from no to maximal mutual information.
Provides examples and discusses applications to temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.

papers.title: A Conditional Mutual Information Analysis of Response Variety in Language Models

papers.abstract: Alignment does not eliminate behavioral errors in language models. Models may still refuse benign requests, call unnecessary tools, or yield to false user claims. Current methods mitigate such errors as a computation problem, and rarely explore if the desired behavior is already encoded in the model's representation. Motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information remains linearly decodable from the final hidden state even when the resulting logits produce the undesired behavior, we introduce HeadEdit, a gradient-free method that calibrates model behavior through the unembedding matrix. HeadEdit extracts a low-rank behavioral subspace from paired completions and uses each prompt's coordinates within it to generate a vocabulary-wide correction, thereby implementing implicitly adaptive steering without manually specified target tokens or parameter updates. HeadEdit improves all nine experimental settings across three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities. It also reveals a connection to gradient-based alignment. HeadEdit's low-dimensional representation partly predicts how preference tuning changes output logits on unseen prompts. The subspace learned from the model can also be reused after tuning, improving performance without re-extracting or retuning. These results show that HeadEdit provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable way to calibrate model behavior through the unembedding matrix.
bullets: Addresses residual behavioral errors such as unnecessary refusals, tool calls, and susceptibility to false user claims.
Uses paired completions to learn behavior-relevant directions, then steers outputs without gradients, parameter updates, or manually chosen target tokens.
Improves performance across nine settings spanning three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities.
The learned subspace partly predicts preference-tuning logit changes on unseen prompts and can be reused after tuning without re-extraction.
Provides a lightweight, interpretable link between representation-based steering and gradient-based alignment.

papers.abstract: Token-level certainty is widely used as a proxy for correctness in LLM training and inference. However, the performance of certainty-based methods depends both on the information in certainty scores and on how those scores are used. We therefore directly assess certainty's predictive ability through controlled empirical evaluations across models and tasks. We distinguish two prediction targets: identifying questions a model is more likely to answer correctly and distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. In our experiments, certainty is generally better at identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly than at distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. Certainty also varies systematically across token types and positions within words, reflecting local properties of words and text form. Information about question difficulty appears early in generation, while the weaker information about answer correctness is more concentrated near the end. These findings show that the information certainty provides for decisions depends on the prediction target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions in the response are included in aggregation. We further demonstrate the practical value of these findings for test-time compute. We allocate the number of responses using certainty early in generation and weight answer votes using certainty near the end of each response. Compared with a fixed-sampling majority-voting baseline, this approach increases overall accuracy from 78.71\% to 79.54\% while reducing generated-token cost by 82.4\%.
bullets: Certainty better predicts which questions a model will answer correctly than which response to a given question is correct.
Certainty varies by token type and word position, so aggregation choices affect its usefulness.
Difficulty information appears early in generation, whereas weaker correctness signals concentrate near the response’s end.
Using early certainty to allocate samples and late certainty to weight votes raises accuracy from 78.71% to 79.54% while cutting generated-token cost by 82.4%.
The findings depend on the prediction target, model, certainty metric, and selected token positions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes token-level certainty in LLMs and proposes a test-time compute strategy using certainty for sampling and voting, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Certainty Is Not Just Correctness: Rethinking Token-Level Certainty in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Token-level certainty is more useful for judging question difficulty than answer correctness, but strategically using it at different generation stages improves accuracy while greatly reducing test-time compute.

papers.abstract: Selective intent routing allows an assistant to act on reliable predictions while deferring uncertain requests. Standard confidence scores primarily reflect the base model's representation, leaving an opportunity to incorporate complementary evidence without changing its decisions. We introduce a signed lexical gate that combines a sentence classifier's logit margin with a sparse lexical model's support for the classifier's predicted intent. By assigning positive evidence to lexical agreement and negative evidence to a lexically favored competing intent, the gate retains more information than either unsigned lexical confidence or a hard agreement rule. An independent binomial calibration stage selects an operating threshold for a specified risk target. Across ten runs on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, the proposed score reduces area under the risk-coverage curve by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% relative to a learned semantic-only gate. At a nominal 5% error target, it increases accepted coverage by 1.83 and 5.14 percentage points on BANKING77 and HWU64, while CLINC150 is already near full coverage. At a stricter 2% target, the simultaneous binomial procedure yields a nonempty policy in all 30 dataset-run combinations at the available calibration budgets. Matched controls show that the proposed feature improves average error ranking over the tested unsigned lexical-confidence feature, with dataset-dependent gains over binary agreement. The resulting two-feature gate provides a compact, interpretable confidence enhancement for risk-calibrated intent routing while preserving the base classifier's predictions.
bullets: Combines the classifier’s logit margin with positive lexical support for its predicted intent and negative support for a competing intent.
Uses an independent binomial calibration stage to choose thresholds for specified error-risk targets.
Reduces area under the risk-coverage curve by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, respectively, relative to a semantic-only gate.
At a 5% error target, accepted coverage rises by 1.83 and 5.14 percentage points on BANKING77 and HWU64; CLINC150 is already near full coverage.
Matched controls show improvements over unsigned lexical confidence, with dataset-dependent gains over binary agreement.

papers.abstract: Reusable skills guide large language model (LLM) agents through recurring requests, but each invocation still requires the model to interpret the skill and reconstruct its orchestration. Can agents automatically compile this orchestration into an executable fast path without human intervention? We first study zero-shot skill specialization, which compiles without execution evidence, and find that despite the skill's procedural guidance, incorrect assumptions about runtime bindings can make generated plans brittle and recovery costly. This motivates SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization method that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, replays it before reuse, and drives it with a plan executor that returns control to the model only when needed, keeping the source skill for recovery. With the Claude Code harness, warm execution of the same request reduces tokens on 87 SkillsBench tasks by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward, and capsules stay effective under controlled request changes. Capsules also transfer across models, raising three open-weight models' mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing their tokens by 72-81%, suggesting that execution-grounded compilation is a promising approach to efficient repeated skill use and cross-model transfer.
bullets: Zero-shot skill specialization can be brittle because it may misjudge runtime bindings, making recovery costly.
SkillCache uses one completed trace to create a parameterized capsule combining programs and natural-language steps.
A plan executor replays capsules and returns control to the model only when needed, while retaining the original skill for recovery.
Across 87 SkillsBench tasks, warm execution reduced token use by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward.
Capsules remained effective under controlled request changes and transferred across models, improving mean reward while reducing token use.

papers.title: How Much Skill Orchestration Can LLM Agents Compile Away? Execution-Grounded Specialization for Token-Efficient Skill Use
