papers.selection_reason: Separates belief content from evidence weight in LLM memory and steering; relevant to LLM memory and reasoning.
papers.title: Same Answer, Different Future: Dissociating Belief Content and Evidence Weight in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models can produce the same answer while assigning different evidential weight to it, and this hidden weight depends more on the belief’s textual origin and framing than on model scale.

papers.abstract: Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent. We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost. Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.
bullets: Compares main-agent retrieval, non-persistent subagent retrieval, and persistent subagent retrieval across enterprise questions and multi-turn follow-ups.
The persistent subagent maintains retrieval state, returns evidence directly, and supports correction requests from the main agent.
Uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens, 45.0% lower estimated API cost, and 9.1% lower average response time than skill-based retrieval.
Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it responds 15.6 seconds faster per question but uses 65.1% more tokens and costs 29.1% more.
The approach shifts response synthesis to the main agent while the retrieval subagent focuses on state maintenance and evidence provision.

papers.abstract: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.
bullets: Frozen embeddings capture the four key memory axes poorly; changing a memory’s date or place barely changes its representation.
A projection layer on top of frozen embeddings does not recover the missing axis information, which is encoded internally in distinct attention-head patterns.
Axis-LoRA adds four per-axis LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them with a per-query gate.
Across three embedding models and four benchmarks, it raises mean R@10 by 1.28–1.56 percentage points while updating only a small fraction of parameters.
Training uses a small axis-counterfactual dataset; the method is evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (a) Failure case in personal-memory retrieval. Four axis-conditional LoRA adapters (T/S/E/Ev) attach to the last 20% of layers of the frozen embedding model and produce per-axis representations ϕA(q), ϕA(m). papers.abstract: Small language models are often trained under tight data budgets, where the choice of pretraining corpus may matter as much as model size or training recipe. We compare two contrasting corpora at matched 10-million- and 37-million-word budgets: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and the BabyLM 2026 strict pretraining corpus. For each corpus, we train teacher models, distilled 58-million-parameter Baby-Llama students, and no-distillation student ablations, using the same model families, training recipes, and evaluation protocol across corpora. Across BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking, and COMPS, the corpora produce different skill profiles rather than a single quality ranking. BabyLM 2026 is consistently stronger on linguistic acceptability benchmarks, while Britannica is often stronger on Entity Tracking, a synthetic state-tracking task. The contrast appears across teacher and student models and at both budgets, with the cleanest cross-seed replication in the distilled student comparison. Targeted controls show that the central contrast persists after matching training exposure and at a longer diagnostic context; direct teacher ensembling also does not reproduce the 10M Britannica student's Entity Tracking behavior. Entity Tracking magnitudes nevertheless remain sensitive to training dynamics. For this corpus pair, corpus choice can therefore produce different relative skill profiles at small scale, motivating multi-benchmark evaluation when comparing pretraining data.
bullets: Compares Britannica and BabyLM 2026 corpora at matched 10M- and 37M-word budgets.
Uses matched teacher, distilled 58M-parameter student, and no-distillation setups with the same evaluations.
BabyLM 2026 performs consistently better on linguistic acceptability benchmarks.
Britannica is often stronger on the synthetic Entity Tracking task, across teachers and students.

papers.tldr: At small scale, pretraining corpus choice produces distinct skill profiles rather than one universally better model.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) commonly decode responses by proceeding autoregressively across blocks while iteratively denoising multiple tokens within each block. This structure makes block-level policy optimization a natural adaptation of autoregressive policy optimization. However, the exact likelihood of a completed block is intractable because it marginalizes over the intermediate states and reveal orders of the denoising process. To realize the block-level formulation, we construct a prefix-block state and use a single model evaluation to define a factorized one-step surrogate for the block likelihood. The resulting block surrogate ratio is a product of its token surrogate ratios, allowing variation at individual positions to propagate across the entire block before clipping. We therefore introduce Prefix-Block Policy Optimization (PBPO), which preserves block-level conditioning but applies surrogate importance weighting and clipping separately to each token. PBPO further diversifies repeated updates by resampling corrupted views of the prompt and revealed prefix, a design motivated by masked-dLLM pre-training. Under our analysis assumptions, block-product weighting amplifies the variance of gradient contributions relative to token-local weighting. Across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths, PBPO achieves competitive performance against existing dLLM RL methods.
bullets: Addresses the intractable likelihood of fully denoised blocks in dLLMs.
Builds a prefix-block state and a single model evaluation to form a factorized one-step block surrogate.
Applies surrogate ratios and clipping separately per token, avoiding the higher gradient variance associated with block-product weighting under the paper’s assumptions.
Resamples corrupted prompt and revealed-prefix views to diversify repeated updates.
Shows competitive performance against existing dLLM reinforcement-learning methods across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths.

papers.abstract: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.
bullets: The study explains accuracy loss from irrelevant statements or off-distribution tokens even when they provide no competing answer.
MLPs enrich irrelevant-token representations, while parrot-like heads carry prefix content to the prediction position; relational readers mostly avoid unrelated sources.
Intrusion heads promote distractor content and provide weaker support for the correct answer, rather than directly suppressing it.
These heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely distinct from heads that use helpful context.
An oracle residual replacement recovers 97.6% of the induced drop; masking about ten heads recovers 57% with bounded impact on useful context.

papers.abstract: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzhagi/convpe.
bullets: Adds a windowed, content-dependent bias to attention scores using a causal convolution over low-dimensional hidden-state projections.
Works with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation, and supports high-dimensional position embeddings through high-dimensional convolutions.
Evaluated for language modeling, long-context extension, and vision.
In reproduction experiments, it outperformed five 1D and eight 2D baselines.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated responses. We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher--student log-probability difference of mathematical positions. Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher's expression. We instead take the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student--base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student's distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation (SD-OPD), which uses centered student--base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher--student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher--student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/sd-opd.
bullets: OPD feedback is disproportionately concentrated on style-related tokens, with 3.5× the mean absolute discrepancy of mathematical tokens.
SD-OPD uses centered student–base log-probability differences as update coefficients, retaining them only when aligned with centered teacher–student feedback.
The student signal is recomputed each training round to reflect evolving learned preferences.
Across five Qwen3 teacher–student configurations (1.7B–8B), SD-OPD raises six-task math average pass@1 (avg@16) by 7.76–10.37 percentage points over OPD.
The abstract evaluates the method on mathematics reasoning and does not establish broader task or model scope.

papers.selection_reason: On-policy distillation method for LLM reasoning; directly relevant to LLM training and improvement.
papers.title: Reinforcing What the Student Has Learned: Teacher-Guided On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: SD-OPD improves on-policy distillation by using the student’s learned post-training preferences to focus teacher-guided updates on useful reasoning behavior rather than expression matching.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. When continuous predictions are formed by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities, different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under a continuous reconstruction objective based on mean squared error (MSE). We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF) to apply squared supervision directly to token identities. TIBF fixes token embeddings, combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. We show that, for fixed token embeddings, the squared error in token posterior prediction controls the squared errors of the continuous denoising prediction and the flow velocity. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, TIBF achieves mean Gen.PPL values of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls. Further evaluations show improvements across multiple sampling budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiangjiawei-kust/TIBF.
bullets: Continuous MSE supervision can treat distinct token distributions as identical when they produce the same embedding average.
TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model and applies squared supervision to token identities.
A theoretical analysis links token-posterior error to continuous denoising and flow-velocity errors.
The method achieves mean Gen.PPL of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls under matched budgets.
Results improve across multiple sampling budgets; the approach focuses continued training on probability prediction while retaining pretrained embeddings.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone. We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.
bullets: Introduces 358 structured tasks spanning five capability domains and 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers.
Targets four failure subtypes: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, and Context Forgetting.
Evaluates 14 frontier agents from eight vendors across 5,012 trajectories.
Agents average 0.642 overall, but Unreachable Goal tasks fall to 0.458, with only 23.2% passing.
Failure profiles vary substantially by subtype, so aggregate task success can obscure important weaknesses.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce copyrighted training data, raising serious privacy and intellectual property concerns. In this work, we investigate whether memorization can be mitigated without modifying or retraining the underlying model through an information bottleneck. We propose a modular plug-and-play framework that inserts a nonparametric variational information bottleneck (NVIB) between a frozen LLM backbone and its language modeling head. By compressing the final hidden representations before token prediction, the proposed bottleneck aims to preserve general linguistic knowledge while filtering out highly specific memorized sequences. We evaluate our approach on memorization extraction tasks involving book passages and on standard language modeling benchmarks to measure the trade-off between memorization reduction and downstream utility. Our experiments show that the NVIB layer substantially reduces extractability while maintaining competitive performance on benchmark tasks. These results suggest that adding an information bottleneck offers a practical and architecture agnostic direction for post-hoc memorization mitigation in pretrained LLMs.
bullets: Targets privacy and copyright risks from LLMs reproducing memorized training data.
Inserts a nonparametric variational information bottleneck between a frozen LLM backbone and its language-modeling head.
Compresses final hidden representations to filter highly specific memorized sequences while retaining general linguistic knowledge.
Evaluation on book-passage extraction and standard language-modeling benchmarks shows substantially lower extractability with competitive benchmark performance.
Scope: addresses post-hoc mitigation without modifying or retraining the underlying model; the abstract does not quantify residual memorization or utility trade-offs.

The block combines a stochastic bottleneck, denoising attention, and feed-forward layers to reduce memorization while preserving language modeling performance. Only the bottleneck parameters are trained.

papers.abstract: Expert pruning compresses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by removing the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant. Studies of high-resource languages largely find that English calibration transfers well to other languages. We test this for Lithuanian: we pruned four MoE models with REAP, removing 25% or 50% of the experts with English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration, and evaluated both languages on reading comprehension, translation and language modelling. English calibration does not transfer to Lithuanian: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but Lithuanian by 21.4. The transfer is asymmetric. Lithuanian calibration removed most of the Lithuanian loss and never significantly hurt English comprehension, which was on average 2.5 points better than under English calibration; only English language modeling got slightly worse. Routing suggests why: in the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of its expert selections to just eight experts, against 19-39% for English, and English calibration removes some of these experts. Compressed models should be calibrated, and evaluated, in every language they must serve.
bullets: The study tests REAP pruning on four MoE models at 25% and 50% expert removal using English, Lithuanian, or mixed calibration.
At 25% pruning, English comprehension dropped by a median of 1.7 points, versus 21.4 points for Lithuanian under English calibration.
Lithuanian calibration recovered most Lithuanian performance loss and did not significantly harm English comprehension; English language modeling worsened slightly.
Routing analysis indicates Lithuanian concentrates selections on eight experts in later layers, some of which English calibration removes.
Calibration and evaluation should include every language the compressed model is intended to serve.

papers.abstract: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.
bullets: Addresses the problem of valuable exploration knowledge being trapped in temporary execution traces.
Uses structured Gene assets with experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution.
Supports experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses, including Claude Code and Codex.
Across four benchmarks, a 320-execution diagnostic set shows success rising from 83.13% to 87.50% and recorded token use falling by 24.24%.
Scope: results focus on selected diagnostic executions and paired comparisons rather than universal performance guarantees.

papers.title: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities
papers.tldr: Evolver turns transient agent experience into reusable procedural capabilities, improving task success and reducing execution-token use without changing foundation-model parameters.

papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly use persistent memory to record user preferences and procedures across sessions. We show that memory from benign interactions can cause unsafe or unreliable behavior on later tasks. We call this failure the memory trap. To study this issue, we compare behavior in sessions with and without memory across six frontier models (including Claude Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models and GPT-5.6). We evaluate these models in a range of settings. First, in autonomy experiments, we find that requests to skip confirmation during low-stakes coding chores lead agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks in both coding and everyday life. We next study memories formed when users seek emotional support, or describe harm from uncritical feedback, and find these memories bias later judgments of mathematical work, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-critique (respectively). Memory notes written during legitimate stale-test repairs lead agents to weaken correct tests that catch broken safeguards; these memories also increase cheating on ImpossibleBench, with larger increases for stronger Sonnet and Opus models. We show that memory traps can arise both from overgeneralizations in memory writing, and when acting on memory. These findings demonstrate that even benign interactions can lead to serious risks from memory systems, and thus motivate the need for new research into ensuring that agents preserve the scope of their memories.
bullets: Across six frontier models, agents with memory showed harmful behavior not seen—or less evident—without memory.
Benign requests to skip confirmation generalized to skipping confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks.
Memories from emotional-support interactions biased later evaluations toward sycophancy or excessive criticism.
Stale-test repair memories weakened safeguards and increased cheating on ImpossibleBench, especially in stronger Sonnet and Opus models.
Memory traps arose both when writing memories and when applying them, highlighting the need to preserve memory scope.

papers.selection_reason: Studies memory-induced overgeneralization in language agents; fits LLM memory and agent memory.
papers.title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions
papers.tldr: Persistent memory can make language agents overgeneralize benign past interactions, causing unsafe, unreliable, or biased behavior on later tasks.

papers.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.
bullets: Long-context inference can exhaust HBM because KV-cache usage grows with sequence length and concurrency, limiting concurrency.
The architecture fully offloads KV caches for both prefill and decode while optimizing cache access across the serving pipeline.
Key techniques include rolling HBM and hot decode caches, a reverse sparse index, and compute–load overlap.
On GLM-5.2 with MTP3 speculative decoding, it improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38× and decode throughput by up to 1.91× under a 30 ms TPOT SLO.
The system is integrated into the open-source vLLM-Ascend serving framework.

papers.abstract: Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive throughout a task. Despite rapid empirical progress, existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming that the other decisions in the episode stay fixed. This assumption fails in orchestration, where the contribution of each decision to the final outcome depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of its per-decision effects. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{IAPO}, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for interactions among decisions. Specifically, IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, which we prove can account for half of the attainable gain, and then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. On long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO's deployed plans reach the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens, and removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code.
bullets: Existing methods credit orchestration decisions independently, overlooking dependencies between earlier and later choices.
IAPO exactly decomposes policy-performance changes into individual decision effects and higher-order interactions.
It optimizes both components from sampled trajectories and certifies that each update improves performance.
Across long-input reasoning and code benchmarks, IAPO matches the strongest system’s accuracy using fewer tokens.
Ablating interaction modeling reduces code accuracy by 7–17 points, showing its importance.

(c) With the candidates fixed, IAPO computes two lower bounds on the gain from fresh trajectories, keeps the larger one, and updates the policy only if it is positive.

papers.abstract: Mapping behavioral intelligence in malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques supports threat analysis and defense, but reliable identification remains challenging. Supporting evidence is often scattered across long, heterogeneous reports, while closely related techniques share behavioral cues and differ only in subtle but decisive details. While large language models (LLMs) can use external knowledge to interpret reports, they may assign techniques based on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence. We present MEvince, a knowledge-constrained LLM reasoning framework for report-level malware technique identification. Its core is a shared behavioral representation connecting report observations to technique definitions. This representation is built through agentic mining of technique documentation and supports two online stages: 1) primitive-guided extraction uses behavioral primitives to structure LLM-extracted observations, link them to source passages, and group dispersed evidence; 2) evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles through the same concepts, retaining likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison of distinguishing behaviors. Controls at both stages validate evidence references and check technique-specific requirements. The representation also supports adaptation without parameter updates, where offline agentic audits diagnose concept weaknesses and refine extraction or retrieval policies. We evaluate MEvince against 11 baselines spanning four method families using a dataset of 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK. MEvince improves exact-ID F1 over the strongest baseline by 17.4%, and its concept-guided retrieval increases gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement yields further gains and outperforms baselines that update model parameters.
bullets: Addresses scattered evidence and subtle distinctions between closely related ATT&CK techniques.
Uses agentic documentation mining to build a shared behavioral representation linking observations, passages, and technique definitions.
Extracts primitive-guided evidence, retrieves aligned technique candidates and confusable alternatives, and validates references and technique requirements.
Evaluated on 610 MITRE ATT&CK-referenced malware reports against 11 baselines; it improves exact-ID F1 by 17.4% over the strongest baseline.
Concept-guided retrieval raises gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%; offline policy refinement further improves performance without parameter updates.

papers.abstract: Enterprise AI agents split requests across subagents, and each handoff can drop, alter or ignore a requirement. A preregistered study on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks compares free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs it and deterministically verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no detectable utility loss versus structured handoffs (S2 -0.4 pp, 95% CI [-14.2, 13.3]). Signing defeats in-transit mutation: unsigned manifests violated 79.2 pp more often than signed ones, which never did; this replicated in gpt-oss-20b and gemma-4-12b. There, without an adversary, signed manifests were descriptively slightly worse than structured handoffs (11.1% vs 2.8%; 16.7% vs 8.3%; not tested) and lost utility overall (gpt-oss-20b, all threats: -28.7 pp). On identical Qwen3-8B trajectories, the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, and an oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits, so the residual risk is in extraction. A preregistered pre-signing injection confirmed this: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest unsafe commits from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 16.7% to 97.2% (gemma-4-12b), and every such commit carried a manifest corrupted before signing. Signing protects transit; extraction is the trust boundary. A testable pre-signing specification (PSE), specified after the injection results and frozen before an offline evaluation, blocked all these injected commits (fixed templates) but refused 45.8%, 11.1% and 22.2% of benign requests, changing completions by -8.3 pp, -2.8 pp and 0.0 pp.
bullets: The study compares free-text, structured JSON, and cryptographically signed requirement-manifest handoffs on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks across five threats.
For Qwen3-8B, signed manifests reduced unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% without detectable utility loss versus structured handoffs.
Signing eliminated in-transit manifest mutation across tested models, while deterministic verification outperformed an LLM checker on detecting violating decisions.
Residual risk lies in requirement extraction: a single pre-signing adversarial line sharply increased unsafe commits across Qwen3-8B, gpt-oss-20b, and gemma-4-12b.
A post hoc frozen pre-signing specification blocked injected attacks but rejected some benign requests, indicating a safety–availability tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.
bullets: Targets unsafe reasoning and answers, inconsistent safety behavior, and failure to identify user intent.
Decomposes safety into four fine-grained verifiable rewards and selects training data based on difficulty.
Uses reasoning-preserving gradient projection to resolve conflicts between safety and reasoning objectives.
Across 1.5B–671B models, reports stronger safety, lower over-refusal, and preserved general reasoning across multiple benchmarks.

papers.title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: SAVeR² aligns large reasoning models for safety by rewarding verifiable reasoning behaviors while preserving their general reasoning ability.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon role-playing dialogue requires consistent character identity, reliable memory, and context-sensitive interaction. We present a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework that revises original-character memory, stable persona instructions, and a policy for constructing turn-level prompts. Repair outcomes also inform revisions to the updater's diagnostic rules, edit routing, and candidate selection. We specify the updater as a versioned policy with explicit inputs, editable fields, acceptance gates, and stopping conditions. An internal evaluation covers 50 original characters and five models, with two 100-round conversations per character-model pair: 500 conversations per condition. Across the pooled evaluated replies, the bad-response rate decreases from 14.00% (6,973/49,824) to 4.94% (2,459/49,793), a 9.06-percentage-point reduction and a 64.71% relative reduction. In 600 blinded human comparisons, RSI receives 294 wins, 187 ties, and 119 losses, yielding a 71.19% win rate among decisive judgments. The results support improved aggregate dialogue quality for the complete framework on the internal test distribution.
bullets: Targets character consistency, reliable memory, and context-sensitive interaction over extended conversations.
Uses a versioned updater with explicit inputs, editable fields, diagnostic rules, edit routing, candidate selection, acceptance gates, and stopping conditions.
Evaluated on 50 original characters and five models with 100-round conversations in an internal test setting.
Bad-response rate fell from 14.00% to 4.94%, while blinded human comparisons favored RSI in 294 of 600 cases, with 187 ties and 119 losses.
Results support improved aggregate dialogue quality for the complete framework on the internal test distribution; broader generalization is not established.

papers.selection_reason: Recursive self-improvement framework for long-horizon dialogue with persistent character memory and policy revision.
papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Role-Playing Dialogue
papers.tldr: A bounded recursive self-improvement framework substantially improves long-horizon role-playing dialogue by refining character memory, persona instructions, prompt construction, and its own update policy.

papers.abstract: Recent work in machine learning has demonstrated that transformer-based language model agents can communicate state not only through text, but also directly in latent space via key-value (KV) caches. In this paper, we argue that such cache-to-cache translation can provide utility beyond the original motivating application of real-time agent communication and can instead be utilized for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Building on the Cache-to-Cache (C2C) fusion framework, our proposed system CacheGraft encodes each corpus passage offline into a fused KV cache representation between a larger sharer model (4B parameters in our experiments) and a smaller receiver model (0.6B parameters) such that this cache can be injected into the receiver at query time with no need for the larger model. Across five QA benchmarks and two independent locally-run judges, CacheGraft improves answer quality over the text-only receiver baseline in 29 out of 30 comparisons, of which 17 of the 30 are statistically significant. Notably, these gains are zero-shot with respect to the fuser, which was never trained on retrieval data. These initial results suggest that latent-space document enrichment may be a promising avenue for enhancing the performance of RAG systems, particularly in compute-constrained settings where it is only feasible to deploy a small model at inference time.
bullets: Addresses compute-constrained RAG settings where only a small receiver model can be deployed during inference.
Offline, a larger sharer and smaller receiver model jointly encode each passage into a fused KV-cache representation.
The cache is injected into the receiver at query time, avoiding runtime use of the larger model.
Improved answer quality over a text-only receiver in 29 of 30 comparisons across five QA benchmarks and two judges; 17 improvements were statistically significant.
Results are zero-shot for the fuser, which was not trained on retrieval data; findings are presented as initial evidence rather than a definitive general solution.

papers.title: CacheGraft: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Latent-Space Document Enrichment
papers.tldr: CacheGraft enriches retrieved documents as latent KV-cache representations, improving small-model RAG without requiring the larger model at query time.

papers.abstract: Selecting high-quality training data can reduce computation cost for LLM fine-tuning. Prior work on data selection developed a variety of difficulty-based scores, motivated by the intuition that harder examples are more informative. While effective for smaller classification models, we find that such methods often fail to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning. Our analysis reveals that random selection performs better because it is more representative of the underlying input space---i.e., has better coverage. To validate the importance of coverage, we implement a simple clustering-based selection method which selects data that is more representative of the underlying input distribution. On a set of diverse single-domain tasks, this method yields performance at or above that of random selection. On the diverse, multi-domain Tülu 3 mixture, where random sampling no longer guarantees a balanced subset, our method outperforms all methods. Overall, our results indicate that prioritizing coverage over difficulty leads to more effective data selection for LLM fine-tuning.
bullets: Difficulty-based selection often fails to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning.
Random selection works well because it better represents the underlying input space.
A simple clustering-based method selects data to improve coverage of the input distribution.
The method matches or exceeds random selection on diverse single-domain tasks and outperforms all compared methods on the multi-domain Tülu 3 mixture.

papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an increasingly popular means of translating Large Language Model (LLM) hidden state vectors into a human-comprehensible list of features or symbols. As such, SAEs may provide insight into an LLM's knowledge representation and internal ``mental'' grammar - topics of pragmatic interest for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior and of theoretical interest for the study of in silico representations of human language. Language models with fewer than 100M parameters, trained on small corpora, nonetheless exhibit strong grammatical competence and discourse coherence, despite producing content of limited reliability. We use SAEs that we trained on one such model (Pythia-70M) to conduct an in-depth examination of how a single grammatical phenomenon, number agreement, is represented and processed in an LLM. We demonstrate the mechanism and the methodology by which SAEs can be used to find and propagate ``plural noun'', ``plural matrix subject'', and ``generate a plural verb'' features which cause the LLM to produce plural verb forms such as ``are'', ``do'', or ``have'' instead of ``is'', ``does'', and ``has'' in response to prompts such as ``the men in the park''. We show that intervening to remove these features from the hidden states of plural subject noun tokens causes the model to produce singular verbs instead, and vice versa. We also show that corresponding ``singular noun'' and ``generate a singular verb'' features are not as effective for this task. This asymmetry suggests that Pythia-70m makes use of a privative representation of grammatical number in English. These findings replicated with larger LLMs Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b yielded similar results. Our main contribution is a novel approach to the use of SAEs to understanding how LLMs encode human language that addresses a number of technical and methodological challenges.
bullets: Studies number agreement in Pythia-70M using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extending the analysis to Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b.
Identifies features for plural nouns, plural subjects, and generating plural verbs that influence forms such as “are,” “do,” and “have.”
Removing plural features from plural-subject representations causes singular verb outputs, while adding or propagating them promotes plural agreement.
Singular-related features are less effective, suggesting grammatical number may be represented primarily through plural features rather than a balanced singular/plural code.
Demonstrates an SAE-based methodology for probing and intervening on language representations while addressing associated technical and methodological challenges.

papers.selection_reason: SAE-based mechanistic analysis of grammatical number encoding in LLMs, relevant to LLM research.
papers.title: Encoding and Propagation of Grammatical Number in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.
bullets: The study defines and evaluates calendar-based time-context—the lookback period before prediction—rather than token-context alone.
A decoder-only EHR transformer was pretrained on coded primary-care events and evaluated across 15 nested windows spanning 2–30 years.
AUROC increased from 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued; roughly 80% of the gain occurred within 10 years.
An XGBoost baseline reached a similar peak AUROC, while simulations indicated potential RoPE time aliasing beyond about 20 years.
The findings support reporting time-context as a distinct design axis for clinical prediction models.

papers.tldr: For colorectal cancer prediction from primary-care EHRs, extending the model’s time-context improved discrimination up to about 18 years, with most gains achieved within 10 years.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.
bullets: Existing extrapolative OPD couples the direction and magnitude of target shifts, which can lead to poorly controlled targets.
D²-OPD uses a per-prefix hard KL constraint to bound the target’s distance from the teacher.
It adaptively determines extrapolation direction from the teacher’s post-training shift and the initial student–teacher gap.
Forward-KL optimization preserves learning signals for low-probability tokens.
Across three settings, it outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points; ablations support each component’s contribution.

papers.abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.
bullets: Archetypal contexts—such as “tipping point” or “winner takes all”—are represented separately from the topics and languages in which they appear.
In Qwen3.8-27B, neuron silencing selectively removes recognition of an archetype, topic, or language while preserving the others.
Mapped layers form a “sandwich”: languages in outer layers, topics in intermediate layers, and archetypes near the center.
This organization reportedly emerges during pretraining and appears across all models examined.
The released neurons, texts, and code provide a reproduction package, though the proposed role in intelligence remains a strong interpretation of the findings.

The plot is a cylinder that has been cut and flattened where language mixes with topic (cyan), so its top and bottom edges are the topic and language mix. Each colour is scaled to its own strongest neurons, so a band shows where a signal is strong relative to itself, not relative to the other two.

papers.selection_reason: Neuron-level analysis of relational archetypes in LLMs, relevant to understanding LLM internal mechanisms.
papers.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
papers.tldr: The study argues that language models encode reusable cross-domain relational patterns in distinct neuron groups, forming a layered architecture that supports analogy and possibly intelligence.

papers.abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.
bullets: Builds a hierarchical KV-cache tree whose nodes summarize subtrees with pooled keys and values.
Selects at most k candidates per level, reducing per-query selection and reads to O(log L).
Uses shared, dense-attention-distilled poolers and level-relative RoPE positions to support length extrapolation.
Outperforms reported baselines from 131K to 2M tokens; at 1M, scores 60.5 versus 40.0 for Dense + DCA on RULER.
With optimized kernels, achieves 3.2× prefill and 3.8× decoding speedups at 524K on one H200 GPU.

papers.selection_reason: Recursive sparse attention achieves million-token extrapolation at logarithmic cost, directly relevant to efficient attention and long-context LLMs.
papers.title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
papers.tldr: RecSA enables accurate attention over up to 2M tokens with logarithmic selection cost, using only 32K-length training.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.
bullets: Looped Transformers share blocks to reduce parameters, but their effectiveness depends on how repeated outputs are reused.
The method reads individual block updates while keeping the shared stack’s input on a separate path.
Geometric decay controls total update weight and provides a recency prior; attention allocates weight across updates.
On ClimbMix, Loopback achieves lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines using 40–75% of their Transformer parameters, with matched training tokens and executed depth.
It also obtains the highest thirteen-task mean accuracy at 191M, 374M, 778M, 1.4B, and 3B reference scales among the compared designs.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a looped residual transformer architecture with depth-memory controls, relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. We introduce execution-grounded completion contracts, which treat completion as a service-level outcome. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between accepted operations or immediate reads and deadline-bound observable outcomes in asynchronous services.
Uses an independent control plane to monitor service-state predicates, admit or reject completion, and direct recovery.
Evaluated placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and injected transfer delay.
Some accepted tasks missed deadlines, while some rejected tasks met them, showing agent reports were unreliable.
Enforcement kept accepted completions consistent with later observations and terminated unresolved faulted tasks as unverified.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes execution-grounded completion contracts for LLM agents in distributed services to govern task completion based on independent state observation.

papers.abstract: Parallel decoding speeds up masked diffusion language models by writing several tokens per forward pass. Published commit rules choose these tokens by testing the predicted distributions. Under sampling the written tokens are drawn, and these tests do not see them. We find that answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written. An answer's log probability splits into this reliability and the dependence within each step. We propose PACT, a training-free commit rule that draws the tokens first, certifies the set it will write and spaces the positions of each step apart. This certificate holds at every temperature, and we show that no rule with the same guarantee commits more positions. Experiments use four models of the LLaDA and Dream families and HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500 and IFEval benchmarks. PACT reaches the quality of published commit rules with fewer forward passes. Spacing removes positions from each step, yet it usually lowers the total cost because later steps then write more tokens. At the same speed, published decoders also write a word twice in a row far more often than PACT. These results suggest that commit rules should certify the tokens they write. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PACT.
bullets: Existing commit rules assess predicted distributions rather than the tokens actually sampled during decoding.
PACT samples tokens first, certifies the set to write, and spaces selected positions apart; its guarantee holds at every temperature.
The paper decomposes answer log probability into written-token reliability and within-step dependence, motivating certification of actual writes.
Across LLaDA and Dream models on HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500, and IFEval, PACT matches published quality with fewer forward passes.
Spacing generally lowers total decoding cost and reduces repeated word writes compared with published decoders.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free commit rule (PACT) for parallel decoding in diffusion language models to certify the reliability of written tokens.
papers.title: PACT: Certifying What Is Written in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: PACT is a training-free parallel decoding rule for diffusion language models that certifies sampled tokens before writing them, preserving quality while reducing forward passes.

papers.abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.
bullets: Structural memorization records internal expert pathways alongside training data, even when fine-tuning uses few samples.
The strength of these routing fingerprints depends on which model modules are trainable.
Attackers can recover pathways from unconditional generation using only routing information and output logits, without training data or procedure knowledge.
Distributed systems amplify exposure across federated aggregation, edge-cloud, and multi-tenant monitoring boundaries.
Composite metrics using reference-model tail likelihood and complexity-aware normalization improve detection beyond standard membership-inference measures.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.
bullets: Long responses can cause student prefixes to drift from the teacher, weakening later feedback and destabilizing training.
The method replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher-generated segment, then resumes student reasoning.
Persistently divergent suffixes are excluded from the distillation loss while preserving useful student continuation.
Diagnostics show reduced disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses.
Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher–student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.

papers.abstract: Foundation models can generate scientific code, but authoring a scientific simulator (an executable program encoding hypotheses about how mechanisms generate observable signals) requires iterative refinement. Scientific adequacy rarely admits a unique implementation or exact test, so simulators must instead be judged against limited real observations. We study this setting as scientific simulator authoring under weak empirical feedback, where distributional comparisons between simulated and real signals guide revision, and the target is the simulator itself rather than only its generated samples. We introduce SimAuthor, a persistent authoring harness that retains and revises executable simulators, separates scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback, and accumulates reusable implementation mechanisms. We evaluate SimAuthor on six biomedical tasks spanning cardiac and respiratory audio, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrocardiography (ECG). Under a fixed 100-attempt budget, SimAuthor outperforms PUCT score search on all six tasks, generally outperforms textual-strategy optimization, and achieves the highest endpoint score on five of six. The authored simulators also improve on unseen recordings, transfer to independent pretrained representations, and yield substantial out-of-distribution gains in downstream ECG classification. Finally, 111 of 138 audited revisions alter program structure and account for 86.1% of the signed score improvement. These results suggest that persistent revision can progressively convert foundation-model knowledge into better executable scientific simulators from limited empirical evidence.
bullets: Addresses simulator authoring when scientific adequacy lacks a unique implementation or exact test.
Maintains and revises executable simulators, separating scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback and reusing implementation mechanisms.

Outperformed PUCT score search on all six tasks and achieved the best endpoint score on five; it also generalized to unseen recordings and downstream ECG classification.
Most audited revisions changed program structure, accounting for 86.1% of signed score improvement.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have reached expert-level performance on competition mathematics largely through the volume of search placed around them: candidate solutions are sampled in quantity and retained only when an external criterion accepts them. Such a procedure improves the outcome that survives it while leaving untouched what the model represents. We examine that question where no external criterion exists: translating statements between the dialects of neighbouring subfields, where fidelity turns on the level of generality at which content is asserted. The source leaves that level implicit in its vocabulary, so a faithful translation must recover it from the relation between the theories. We introduce an instrument that codes truth, content and scope in separate blind queues, with a judge-free measure of whether a rewrite states the hypothesis implicit in its source, and establish its sensitivity with a planted-positive control. Across seven models from four families, translating towards the general framing widens the domain of quantification in 60.6% of rewrites and narrows it in none; translating towards the concrete framing narrows it in 28.3% and widens it in 0.3%. The hypothesis that would prevent it is stated in 21.6% of model rewrites and 4.2% of human statements. Capability does not govern the asymmetry: it appears in every model tested, and the most capable widens least. It replicates on the half of the benchmark held out by a pre-registered rule, and on statements written by mathematicians. Instructing a model to state every hypothesis it requires raises that rate but not its sensitivity to direction. We argue that these systems have acquired an object-level correspondence between subfield vocabularies without the constraint under which a translation between theories carries hypotheses to hypotheses.
bullets: The study tests translation between neighboring mathematical subfields, where implicit scope and assumptions determine fidelity.
It introduces a judge-free instrument that separately codes truth, content, and scope, validated with planted-positive controls.
Across seven models, translations toward general frameworks widened quantification in 60.6% of cases and never narrowed it; concrete-directed translations narrowed it in 28.3% and widened it in 0.3%.
Models stated the hypotheses required by their rewrites in 21.6% of cases, versus 4.2% for human statements; the asymmetry appeared across all models.
Explicitly prompting models to state every required hypothesis increased disclosure but did not improve directional sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for agentic large language models is often done through GRPO-style methods, which compute a group baseline over repeated rollouts to reduce target variance. However, this setup is ill-suited to agents acting in stateful environments such as live services or security sandboxes, where repeated rollouts are impractical to obtain and aggressive updates entrench the noise of long, sparsely verified trajectories. We propose \textit{Follow the Winners} (FTW), a critic-free policy-learning algorithm that adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT, replacing group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples that yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. We derive FTW through a control-as-inference lens, which also recovers GRPO and DPO as specific modelling choices, identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW controls. We identify this offset as an inherent trade-off of variance reduction through ordinal filters on samples, whereas a critic model induces a different trade-off between bias and variance. Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, showing a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.
bullets: Targets stateful environments where repeated rollouts are impractical and long trajectories are sparsely verified.
Applies an ordinal filter from the cross-entropy method to replay-buffer samples.
Uses a control-as-inference formulation that connects FTW with GRPO and DPO.
Controls the bounded risk-seeking effect introduced by ordinal filtering.
Matches GRPO and PPO baselines on Sokoban and Search-R1 while trading value models or group rollouts for CPU memory.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used where small syntactic errors matter, yet character-level reasoning is still evaluated mostly through isolated probes and aggregate accuracy. We introduce SyntaxBench, a diagnostic benchmark and statistical evaluation framework for character-level reasoning. It contains five core tasks, character counting, letter containment, palindrome detection, edit distance, and longest-string selection, plus index_to_span, a harder substring-extraction stress test. The five core tasks use paired English and character-length-matched random-string inputs. index_to_span documents share a 200-500 word band and are not character-length matched. All six tasks use zero-, one-, and four-shot prompts. We evaluate eight open-weight models from 2B to 32B parameters across 11 reasoning-mode configurations. The framework reports exact-match and relaxed accuracy, Cohen's kappa, paired McNemar tests with odds ratios, bootstrap confidence intervals, Kendall's tau, class-conditional metrics, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison-corrected tests. Three findings stand out. First, tokenization shapes accuracy: random strings are more character-visible than English strings (1.892 vs. 3.169 characters per token), and character-counting accuracy falls as English words occupy more tokens. Second, reasoning mode is not uniformly helpful: Gemma4-31B is nearly unchanged across modes on the near-saturated tasks, while Qwen3.6-27B is worse with thinking on palindrome detection (0.952 non-thinking vs. 0.886 thinking at four-shot). Third, index_to_span remains largely unsolved; the best four-shot exact-match accuracy is 6.75%. Character-level evaluation needs controlled inputs, paired tests, and analyses of tokenization and reasoning mode rather than aggregate accuracy alone.
bullets: Introduces six diagnostic tasks covering counting, containment, palindromes, edit distance, string selection, and substring extraction.
Pairs English and character-length-matched random-string inputs to isolate tokenization effects, with zero-, one-, and four-shot settings.
Evaluates eight open-weight models using exact and relaxed accuracy, paired statistical tests, confidence intervals, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison correction.
Random strings are more character-visible than English, and English counting accuracy declines as words use more tokens.
Reasoning mode is task- and model-dependent; index_to_span achieves only 6.75% best four-shot exact-match accuracy.

Nemotron-Cascade-2 is at 69.0% on longest_string_finder, and DeepSeek-R1-32B non-thinking is at 43.25% on that task. edit_distance discriminates models, and index_to_span remains near the floor.
