papers.abstract: Recurrent memory requires learning useful updates, but attention added to assist learning can also compromise length generalization. We study bounded delta attention: causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update. Its implementation in TraceRelay combines additive phase recurrence with attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5, trained at lengths 1--40, three findings characterize its behavior at length 80. First, upper delta attention attains $70.81\pm8.26$% accuracy across seven seeds, versus $69.21\pm22.42$% for the local-attention recurrent baseline (mean $\pm$ sample SD): a 63.2% reduction in SD with a similar mean. Upper state attention also reduces variation, reaching $74.75\pm6.24$%, so this benefit is not unique to update-level attention. Disabling the upper delta correction retains $70.62\pm8.60$%. Second, blocking gradients at the delta-attention inputs changes accuracy to $65.25\pm12.40$% in the matched seven-seed comparison, increasing SD by 50.2%. It also delays a 99% validation threshold on average among the same six seeds that reach it; the 95% threshold is reached earlier on average with input-gradient blocking across all seven seeds. Third, lower delta attention exhibits substantially less extrapolation degradation than lower state attention: 62.60% versus 19.40%, against a 71.06% baseline. Removing its correction reduces accuracy to 22.56%; its advantage over lower state attention also persists under input-gradient blocking. These observations motivate bounded update-level attention as a recurrent learning scaffold, combining reduced seed variation with less severe degradation in a placement where state attention fails.
authors: Sungwoo Goo, Hwi-yeol Yun, Sangkeun Jung
bullets: On modulo-5 extrapolation from lengths 1–40 to 80, upper delta attention achieved 70.81% accuracy with substantially lower seed variation than the local-attention baseline.
Upper state attention also reduced variation, indicating the stability benefit is not unique to update-level attention; removing upper delta correction had little effect in this setting.
Blocking gradients into delta-attention inputs increased variability and altered validation-threshold timing, suggesting these gradients support stable learning.
Lower delta attention degraded less under extrapolation than lower state attention, whose performance fell sharply; removing the lower correction largely eliminated the benefit.
Findings are based on seven seeds and a specific prefix-supervised modulo-5 task, so broader generalization remains unestablished.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates memory mechanisms in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to improve length generalization and reduce seed variability, relevant to the architecture and memory of LLMs.
papers.title: Attending to Memory Writes Reduces Seed Variability in Recurrent Length Generalization
papers.tldr: Bounded delta attention can make recurrent length extrapolation more seed-stable, especially when attention is applied to update proposals rather than recurrent states.

papers.abstract: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. Across evaluations of frontier models with full context, retrieval methods, and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, especially for distributed and conflicting memories. Together, two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints bring consistent gains, showing that group memory systems must improve use, not recall alone.
authors: Zhanghao Hu, Linhai Zhang, Qian Zhao, Qi Zhu, Yuan Hua, Di Liang, Jiasheng Si, Xin Zhao, Yulan He, Zhumin Chen, Lin Gui
bullets: Introduces a real-world benchmark built from 80,299 messages across 50 groups using a deployed group assistant.
Evaluates both recall against reference answers and open-ended assistance requests without fixed answers.
Covers single, distributed, and conflicting memories, reflecting revisions and disagreements in group conversations.
Memory systems can approach full-context performance on recall but lag substantially on memory use.
Relating retrieved memories and enforcing remembered facts as response constraints consistently improve assistance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.
authors: Liyan Tan, Yequan Zhao, Ziyue Liu, Yupeng Su, Ruijie Zhang, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited device memory, lack of labeled data, and the cost of backpropagation for on-device specialization.

Reported phone-use success rates increase from 6–23% to 89–100%; FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies and stronger than LoRA- or quantized-ES baselines on INT4 RLVR benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.
authors: Yao Cui, Zhen Yang, Yuandong Wang, Yangfu Zhu, Tianyu Wo, Zhenzhou Shao
bullets: Direct decoding failures may reflect policy limitations rather than missing reasoning capability.
A recoverable capability frontier identifies failures that can be elicited through trajectory-level search.
Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search generates and verifies candidate solutions, then selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR.

Three one-shot RLVR stages improved the reported MATH500 and WE-MATH average from 78.71 to 80.16; frontier-guided selection also outperformed random selection in the matched setting.

papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.
authors: Rounak Sen, Divya Kumari, Deeksha Varshney
bullets: BLEURT-based labeling treats similarity as a proxy for factuality, despite limitations including English-centric supervision and unbounded scores.
Experiments compare 15 automatic judges, seven detection baselines, two generators, two QA datasets, and five languages.
Detector results vary substantially depending on the supervision judge used to create labels.
Human validation finds QGen-9B most reliable among tested judges, while BLEURT-based methods show much higher misclassification rates.
The study motivates judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers extend inference-time computation through repeated latent-state updates, but final-depth training does not directly encourage useful intermediate alternatives. We introduce Best-of-Depth (BoD), which trains a recurrent trajectory as a candidate set by minimizing prediction loss across depths. Different valid targets can be matched at different depths without architectural changes or depth-specific labels. An exact-match analysis connects this objective to solution coverage. On N-Queens completion and graph coloring, BoD improves coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives. N-Queens coverage reaches 91.03%, versus 45.75% for final-depth training. Further experiments show discovery beyond the training depth and recovery of solutions withheld from teacher pools on familiar inputs. Fine-tuning a pretrained looped language model with BoD yields higher pooled code-generation success than final-depth training when programs are generated separately at evaluated fixed depths. These results support training recurrent computation for solution discovery along its trajectory.
authors: Shota Takashiro, Takeshi Kojima, Masanori Koyama, Kohei Hayashi, Yusuke Iwasawa
bullets: Addresses the limitation that final-depth training neglects useful intermediate alternatives in recurrent inference.

Shows discovery beyond training depth, recovery of withheld solutions, and higher pooled code-generation success at fixed evaluation depths.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.
authors: Yangrong Hu, Xueyu Zhou, Yue Wu, Jian Huang
bullets: Token-level weighting changes the target distribution learned during SFT.
Dynamic weighting can overly sharpen the target, while static weighting depends strongly on the prior model’s quality.
SPFT uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information as a prior for token weighting.
A Bayesian decomposition shows that SPFT gives higher weights to tokens informative for predicting the ground-truth outcome.
Experiments in mathematical reasoning and code generation show improvements over standard SFT and other baselines.],

papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supports Web information seeking and fact verification by recovering complementary evidence across related pages within a limited retrieval budget. Scoring evidence independently against the original question can miss supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts. Iterative retrieval incorporates these facts into subsequent queries, while graph retrieval explicitly models relations among evidence units. Yet fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query condition to accumulated relational context. We view multi-hop evidence recovery as the coupled evolution of evidence representations and query conditions, with accumulated context informing both what the retriever represents and how it searches for complementary evidence. QueryFlow realizes this perspective by recurrently integrating query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation. Across four representative multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets, QueryFlow achieves macro Recall@10 (R@10), Full Recall@10 (FR@10), and LLM-Acc gains of 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines, respectively.
authors: Manzong Huang, Chenyang Bu, Yi He, Jiapu Wang, Xindong Wu
bullets: Addresses missed evidence whose relevance emerges only through intermediate facts.
Recurrently summarizes query-conditioned graph context into a shared evolving query state.
Uses the updated query to control boundary inputs and relation features during later graph propagation.
Evaluated on four multi-hop QA datasets, improving macro R@10, FR@10, and LLM-Acc by 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines.

papers.abstract: Compiling a natural-language agent skill into model parameters removes the skill text from the prompt and leaves behind a small artifact that can be distributed and reused. Existing methods differ in where they inject the compiled quantity, and all of them assume that the artifact carries the content of the skill. We test that assumption. Through three controls on a retrieval agent, we find that a compiled skill shift carries a domain-general behavioural prior, not the content of the skill. A wrong skill document performs on par with the correct one, a single averaged bundle matches per-skill routing under a two-sided equivalence test, and a same-norm random direction collapses to the no-injection baseline, which shows that the trained direction stays load-bearing. We then introduce SKILL2STEER, a one-pass hypernetwork that reads a skill document once and maps it to low-rank activation shifts added at the output of every decoder block. Each skill compiles to 2.36M parameters, 9.25 times fewer than a weight-space adapter, while the base weights stay frozen and the generator runs only at compile time. The shift can be scheduled across retrieval steps and deployed as one routing-free bundle. On SearchQA, a seven-dataset benchmark, SKILL2STEER reaches 37.9 exact match, 9.8 points above the frozen model and 2.3 points above a weight-space method that ships 9.25 times more parameters per skill.
bullets: Compiled skill shifts encode a domain-general behavioral prior rather than the specific skill document’s content.
Controls show wrong-skill inputs perform similarly to correct ones, an averaged bundle matches per-skill routing, and random same-norm directions provide no benefit.
A one-pass hypernetwork maps each skill document to low-rank shifts applied after every decoder block; the generator runs only during compilation.
Each compiled skill uses 2.36M parameters—9.25× fewer than the compared weight-space adapter—and can be deployed as one routing-free bundle.
On SearchQA, SKILL2STEER achieves 37.9 exact match, improving over the frozen model and the larger weight-space method.

papers.abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.

papers.abstract: Muon has recently shown strong empirical performance in training Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), yet its optimization dynamics remain poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we analyze the training dynamics of Muon for next-token prediction (NTP) in Transformers. The training procedure consists of two phases: the preprocessing phase learns the output-value component, while the main phase learns the key-query component. For the preprocessing phase, we characterize the optimization trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update. For the main phase, we establish nonasymptotic convergence rates for the training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention. These results suggest that Muon's update rule can help models efficiently learn which tokens matter for prediction, offering a possible explanation for its strong performance in large language model training. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical insights with experiments on next-token prediction tasks.
authors: Shengwei Wu, Yixuan Yang, Gao Huang, Song Li
bullets: Analyzes Muon training through preprocessing and main phases: learning output values first, then key-query structure.
Exactly characterizes the preprocessing trajectory and shows optimal normalized spectral margin after every update.
Derives nonasymptotic convergence rates for training loss and normalized margin gap under softmax attention.
Argues that Muon efficiently learns which tokens matter for prediction and provides a generalization guarantee to unseen contexts.
Validates the theoretical findings on next-token prediction tasks, without reporting specific quantitative results in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.
bullets: Addresses LoRA’s flat optimization directions and linear effective-rank scaling.
Relaxes the shared-block constraint in perfect-shuffle factorization to span low- through full-rank adaptations.
Its effective rank can scale quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full rank.
Collapses the invariance manifold to a diagonal group, potentially easing optimization.
Consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks with greater parameter efficiency.

papers.abstract: Agile Earth observation satellites must coordinate imaging tasks within limited observation windows, while accounting for attitude maneuvering and onboard energy constraints. Competition among observation opportunities makes scheduling performance sensitive to the heuristic rules used for task selection. This letter proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted adaptive heuristic search method for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling. The LLM generates an initial heuristic rule according to the characteristics of the scheduling instance. During the subsequent ant colony search, search performance and scheduling information are fed back to the LLM to refine the heuristic rule. The proposed modifications are evaluated through paired solution constructions before being incorporated into the search process. A unified scheduling procedure determines task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing under the operational constraints. Experiments on six scheduling scenarios involving 50--200 imaging tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 4.3\%--9.6\% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline.
authors: He Wang, Yeye Liu, Ruijie Li, Xuemei Jiang, Junyu Wu, Lining Liu Zhuoqi Man, Tao Li, Yanjie Song

papers.abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + \delta$, $\delta \in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.
authors: Xin Liu, Boyuan Sun, Yuxin Wang, Haoran Song, Mingjian Zhao, Mengyu Liu
bullets: Among surveyed repositories, 52.6% of untied gated or hybrid checkpoints had reachable embeddings with norms below 10⁻⁶, versus 0% for weight-tied models.
At zero input, gated architectures suppress historical-state readout and can amplify embedding gradients by over 30 orders of magnitude.
Pre-RMSNorm can further amplify gradients, causing FP32 global-norm clipping to overflow and discard entire batches; one continual-pretraining run lost updates on about 20% of steps.
GroupClip separates embedding clipping using higher-precision or rescaled norms, eliminating update loss and healing affected rows in one step.
GateFloor adds a small positive offset to SiLU gates, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude with comparable perplexity in experiments up to 370M parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses training stability of gated sequence models (Mamba, etc.), a type of LLM architecture.
papers.title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Near-zero untied token embeddings can silently stall gated-model training by causing gradient explosions, norm-clipping overflow, and repeated zeroed updates, while GroupClip and GateFloor largely prevent the failure.

papers.abstract: Automated research pipelines pair an LLM proposer with a verifier on an implicit bet: discovery quality rises with verification strength. Under a pre-registered protocol we test this bet in two real-data domains -- job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading on Beijing T-Drive trajectories -- across 100 matched LLM/random pairs per domain and three verifier tiers. The manipulation binds -- a 429-case mutation battery shows scores rising across tiers -- yet the paired LLM-over-random advantage does not scale with it (A, one-sided p=0.1115; D, p=0.9994), and in D shrinks under the strict tier (margin contrast -0.040, p=0.0013). The two lower gates promote identical candidates in 100/100 and 99/100 pairs, so the strict order is untestable when they coincide. Constructively, LLM proposals carry a real paired advantage over random controls, but a post-hoc union-pool analysis shows the fastest path to better discovery is widening the pool, not tightening the gate: mixing the two pools adds +1.52 holdout-value units in domain A (one-sided Wilcoxon, n=100, p=0.0002) -- evidence that pool composition, not verification strength, is the lever. Criteria, ledgers and scripts are archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23308866).
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Siyuan Zhang
bullets: A pre-registered test evaluated LLM proposers with three verifier strengths in job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading.
Verifier tiers were behaviorally distinct, but stronger verification did not increase the LLM-over-random discovery advantage.
In one domain, the advantage decreased under the strictest verifier.
A post-hoc union-pool analysis found that mixing proposer pools improved holdout value, supporting pool composition as the key lever.
The study’s criteria, ledgers, and scripts are publicly archived on Zenodo.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM-based automated research pipelines, testing the interaction between proposers and verifiers in a scientific discovery context.
papers.title: Verifier strength does not buy discovery quality: a pre-registered two-domain test of LLM-based automated research, with post-hoc evidence pointing to proposer-pool composition
papers.tldr: Across two domains, stronger verification did not improve LLM-driven discovery; expanding and diversifying the proposer pool appeared more effective.

papers.abstract: On a public agent leaderboard, a general-purpose agent trails a scaffold built for an airline customer-service benchmark by 13 points on the tasks that touch its database, and a reader could conclude that generality costs accuracy. The gap comes from the grader. The general agent often ends its conversations in a way that never triggers grading, so only about half of its episodes were scored and the rest were stored as failures. Grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the pooled gap, without rerunning any agent. We audit two carefully maintained public leaderboards, HAL and tau2-bench, from their published artifacts alone and find three more instrument errors. A cost column counts nested model calls twice, unevenly across rows. Archived trajectories record grader-written actions as agent actions. Re-grading saved trajectories under a newer evaluator is itself a new measurement: a correct and announced fix reorders a leaderboard, and a mode check that misreads four files collapses their scores by 59 to 82 points while printing no error. Each produced a plausible number, and the HAL maintainers confirmed their three within five weeks. Together the cases show that the infrastructure of agent evaluation, meaning the code that grades, logs, replays and versions an evaluation, is part of the measurement and fails silently, so scores and orderings can move with no visible sign. These failure modes follow from how agent evaluation pipelines are built, and those pipelines change as fast as the agents they measure, so we expect more of them elsewhere. We propose cheap checks that expose the instrument: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of every recorded action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.
bullets: Auditing HAL and tau2-bench found four errors in grading, cost accounting, trajectory logging, and evaluator/version handling.
A general agent’s apparent 13-point deficit disappeared when episodes that had not triggered grading were scored under the benchmark’s own rule.
Double-counted nested model calls, mislabeled grader actions, and a faulty mode check each produced plausible but incorrect measurements.
Regrading archived trajectories under a newer evaluator changed leaderboard rankings, showing that evaluator updates are new measurements.
Recommended safeguards include reporting graded fractions, aggregating cost from root spans, tagging action provenance, and publishing evaluator-version re-grade diffs.

papers.selection_reason: Audits the infrastructure of agent evaluation, highlighting how logging and replay mechanisms (memory) can silently affect leaderboard scores.
papers.title: Silent Instrument Errors Reorder Agent Leaderboards
papers.tldr: Silent errors in agent-evaluation infrastructure can substantially distort scores and reorder public leaderboards without producing obvious failures.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning data can include metadata that predicts the correct answer, such as a reward-model score or a quality label. We ask whether a model learns to rely on this metadata even when every training label is correct. We fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions in which (Reward: 5) always marks the correct option; when this annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models select that option on 97-100% of CommonsenseQA items. Removing it leaves most answers correct, so evaluation without it misses the dependence. Cue-following rises sharply with training-time reliability and develops even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, although test-time wording affects its strength. A Qwen3 experiment also finds cue dependence in option-letter scores after direct preference optimization. Audits can test for this dependence by moving or removing visible annotations while holding the task and correct answer fixed.
bullets: Fine-tuning 7–9B open-weight models with a reward or quality annotation marking the correct option induces strong metadata dependence.
When the annotation is moved to a wrong option, models follow it on 97–100% of CommonsenseQA items.
Removing the annotation often preserves accuracy, so standard evaluation can miss this hidden reliance.
Cue-following increases with training-time reliability and can emerge from neutral or nonsense annotation words; test wording changes its strength.
A Qwen3 direct-preference-optimization experiment shows similar dependence in option-letter scores.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the unintended behavior of LLMs when fine-tuned on metadata, a relevant finding for understanding and controlling LLM behavior.
papers.title: Correct Labels Are Not Enough: Reliable Metadata Can Silently Control Model Behavior
papers.tldr: Models can silently learn to trust reliable metadata over the actual task, even when all training labels are correct.

papers.abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoeResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoeResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.
authors: Hei Yi Mak, Hoang Le, Mehran Taghian Jazi, Yunke Peng, Huan Lin, Zhengzhi Tang, Zhexu Liu, Yao Wang, Yaoyuan Wang, Anandharaju Durai Raju, Tanzila Rahman
bullets: Dense-model FP4 recovery methods provide no improvement over naive FP4 baselines for MoE models.
Discrete expert routing makes MoE training–inference policy alignment highly sensitive to asymmetric recovery.
Asymmetric corrections sharply reduce probability correlation and router-selection matching between training and inference.
MoeResQ applies symmetric corrections on both sides, restoring alignment and substantially narrowing the accuracy gap to full precision.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Visualization of the alignment between training and inference probabilities for BF16, HiF4, RC Inference, RC Training, and RC Both.

Table 2: Training-inference alignment base on three metrics: the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) between training and inference probabilities, the fraction of tokens whose top-k expert set matches exactly (top_k_match_frac), and the mean pairwise overlap of the top-k sets (topk_overlap_mean). For top_k_match_frac, we measured the values for layer 0, 12, 23, 35, and 47. RC denotes applying RC when quantizing both attention linear projections and expert linear projections, and RC (Experts only) denotes applying RC when quantizing expert linear projection only.

papers.selection_reason: Studies FP4 RL post-training for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs, directly relevant to LLM training and architecture.
papers.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: MoeResQ shows that symmetric training–inference quantization recovery is essential for effective end-to-end FP4 RL on MoE language models.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
authors: Vimal William, Yuanzhe Li, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang
bullets: Long-context retrieval is concentrated in a small number of layers, while other recurrent states encode similar information via layer-specific transformations.
Anchor places recurrent TTT memory only at these anchor layers and uses a cross-layer state read by many layers.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, it achieves 2.3–3.1× higher recall and 6.7–8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs.
It uses a 10× smaller recurrent state, retains 91–95% of teacher MMLU accuracy, and reduces latency by up to 4.3× versus softmax attention.
The approach also generalizes to other hybrid-attention designs.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Anchor architecture and recurrent-state coverage. Left: Anchor-F maintains a private recurrent state in every layer, while Anchor keeps one shared state per anchor group and removes the interior states entirely, reducing recurrent state by 16× (201.0 → 12.6MB at 32k context). Each reader accesses the shared state through its own learned read map χ(·). Right: coverage over query (rows) and key (columns) positions. Green marks the local sliding window, red the span served by the recurrent state. Anchor-F requires one such state per layer; Anchor serves layers l1, . . . , L from a single shared state.

Figure 9. Cross-layer similarity generalizes across linearization methods. Debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity for every pair of layers, on the recurrent-state readouts of our TTT hybrid (Anchor-F), LoLCATs, and Liger on Mistral-7B over identical PG-19 and WikiText inputs. In all three models, layers share information while their cosine similarity remains small, indicating that this information is encoded in different bases.

Figure 7. Hybrid architecture of ANCHOR and full self-attention. ANCHOR and full self-attention layers are interleaved at a 3:1 ratio, so that softmax attention accounts for 25% of all layers. Within each group, the three ANCHOR layers retain their own sliding-window attention for local context but share a single recurrent state for long-range context: the leading layer writes the state, and each layer reads it through its own learned read map χℓ(·). The subsequent full self-attention layer attends over the entire sequence, providing exact retrieval at regular depth intervals, while the recurrent state per group remains constant in sequence length.

Figure 2. Layer-wise contribution of each branch to long-context retrieval. ∆CE (nats) on AR-32k when the TTT (top) or SWA (bottom) branch is removed at a single layer, broken down by the distance between a query and its target. Warm cells indicate degradation, that is, a larger increase in loss when the branch is removed. The TTT branch contributes almost nothing across the interior layers (ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) but dominates at the boundary layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}), whereas SWA contributes broadly at every depth. The color scale is symmetric-log with a linear region below 0.01, and both panels share one scale.

Figure 3. Improved Attention Transfer in Stage-1 Linearization. Held-out attention-transfer loss LMSE (left) and perplexity (right) during Stage 1. (a) Training on LMSE alone matches the teacher’s attention outputs closely, reducing the loss by over 25×, yet perplexity rises from 5.3K to 236K: the student reproduces each layer’s output while losing the ability to model language. (b) Adding next-token supervision LCE resolves this, lowering both losses together and reaching a perplexity of 34, which provides a stable initialization for the TTT parameters.

Figure 10. Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. Accuracy across context lengths (1K–8K) and needle depths for Llama-3.1-8B, a LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention), and the ANCHOR 3:1 hybrid. ANCHOR reaches a mean accuracy of 0.95 (baseline 1.00), whereas the LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention) (0.33) retrieves reliably only at 1K or when the needle lies near the end of the context.

Figure 6. Study on Performance–efficiency trade-off. ANCHOR evaluated on reasoning (MMLU) and recall (SWDE, FDA, SQuAD) benchmarks, together with end-to-end throughput and recurrent state size. (a) Reasoning accuracy of the ANCHOR series against LoLCATs; targeted placement of the cross-layer recurrent state improves reasoning. (b) Throughput (tokens/s) against reasoning accuracy; ANCHOR attains 4.3× higher throughput than the baseline at comparable accuracy. (c) Recall accuracy against recurrent state size; ANCHOR improves recall over LoLCATs by 2.3–3.1× while using a 10.2× smaller state.

Figure 4. Representational similarity of TTT states on (a) PG-19 and (b) WikiText. Each point is one layer pair, plotted as debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity on cross-window targets, that is, those whose source lies beyond the local window. Interior pairs ( , ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) are drawn separately from anchor pairs (▲, ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}). Anchor pairs are more strongly aligned than interior pairs on both corpora (0.97 versus 0.82 on PG-19, 0.92 versus 0.49 on WikiText). High CKA with near-zero cosine indicates closely related information encoded in different bases.

Figure 1. Recurrent states across layers are redundant, so one shared state suffices. Left: Debiased CKA between the TTT states of every pair of layers in Llama-3.1-8B, measured on WikiText for targets beyond the local window. The anchor layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}, dashed boxes) are strongly aligned with one another (mean CKA 0.92), whereas the interior layers are not (0.49). Right: Number of recurrent states per block as the ratio of hybrid to softmax-attention layers grows. A per-layer design keeps one state per hybrid layer; ANCHOR keeps a single shared state, reducing the count by 3–6×.

papers.selection_reason: Uses test-time training with recurrent memory for efficient long-context retrieval, fitting TTT, memory efficiency, and long-context models.
papers.title: Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Anchor improves long-context retrieval and efficiency by storing TTT memory only in a few anchor layers and sharing it across layers through learned read transformations.

papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
authors: Sosuke Kobayashi, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Builds a prompt-specific index by clustering noncontiguous keys into large semantic blocks.
Each query scores block centroids, then attends to the original keys and values within selected blocks.
Groups queries selecting the same blocks to keep prefill efficient despite query-specific routing.
On one H200, whole-model speedups reach 2.3–2.4× for 512K prefill, 1.7–2.0× for 512K decoding, and 2.9–3.0× for 1M prefill.
The 35B-A3B model remains close to dense attention on several long-context evaluations; the 4B model mainly degrades on multi-key retrieval.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.
authors: Qinghua Mao, Xi Lin, Yuxin Qi, Zihao Xu, Jinze Gu, Yuliang Chen
bullets: Standard debate may override evidence-grounded safety boundaries through conformity pressure, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry.
SafeConflict-Bias evaluates these effects with invariant queries and retrieved evidence across six Web risk categories.
Across tested backbones, unsafe adoption under standard debate ranged from 0.0% to 100.0%, despite isolated models rejecting the guidance.
RiskTrace-Debias combines evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration.
The framework limited worst-case unsafe adoption to ≤2.0% without reported over-refusal and produced provenance traces for auditing manipulation.

papers.abstract: LLM-powered semantic queries increasingly combine relational processing with multiple LLM-based operators over unstructured data. Efficiently serving such queries is challenging due to runtime dynamism at two coupled levels. Across queries, dynamic arrivals and heterogeneous resource demands continuously change scheduling priorities. Within a query, heterogeneous characteristics across fine-grained input batches cause operator costs and selectivities to vary throughout execution, making a statically optimized plan unreliable. These two forms of dynamism create a circular dependency: inter-query scheduling requires estimates of remaining LLM work, while the remaining work depends on runtime plan choices whose costs become observable only during execution. We present SeqoFlow, a runtime framework that jointly adapts query plans and schedules concurrent semantic queries. SeqoFlow enumerates equivalence-preserving plan alternatives under operator dependencies and decomposes queries into fine-grained units, enabling safe plan adaptation and query preemption at batch boundaries. To support both decisions without exhaustively profiling candidate plans on the target LLM, SeqoFlow uses lightweight speculative estimation to capture runtime costs. These estimates jointly guide plan adaptation and inter-query scheduling, closing the loop between query optimization and LLM inference. Experiments across diverse query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show that SeqoFlow substantially reduces end-to-end latency compared to existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.
bullets: Semantic queries face dynamism across queries—changing arrivals and resource demands—and within queries, where batch-level costs and selectivities vary.
These dynamics are coupled: scheduling needs remaining-work estimates, while remaining work depends on runtime plan choices.
SeqoFlow enumerates dependency-preserving plan alternatives and decomposes queries into fine-grained units for safe adaptation and batch-boundary preemption.
Lightweight speculative estimates guide both plan selection and inter-query scheduling without exhaustively profiling every candidate plan.
Experiments across varied query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show substantially lower end-to-end latency than several existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large pretrained models. However, standard LoRA typically assigns a fixed rank profile despite layer- and stage-dependent adaptation needs, while recent adaptive-rank variants often rely on heuristic or first-order signals that provide only an indirect link between rank reallocation and local loss behavior. This leaves the rationale behind each rank reallocation insufficiently interpretable. Motivated by this gap, we propose LIRA (Loss-Informed Rank Allocation), a dynamic-rank LoRA method designed to make online rank reallocation more interpretable. LIRA scores each layer by the estimated magnitude of the local loss perturbation associated with its recent LoRA-factor movements under a second-order approximation, making the basis for each rank change interpretable term by term. By periodically applying DELTA (Displacement-Evaluated Loss-Trajectory Allocation), a displacement-based algorithm for LoRA rank reallocation, LIRA produces discrete effective ranks under matched budgets while remaining compatible with standard (A,B) adapters. On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, LIRA outperforms the uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines reported under this protocol; Trajectory EMA attains performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.
authors: Sihao Wang, Bozheng Li, Xuemiao Xu, Haoxin Yang, Yujie Xu, Jie Tang
bullets: Addresses fixed rank profiles and opaque heuristic signals in adaptive-rank LoRA.
Scores layers using a second-order estimate of local loss perturbation caused by recent LoRA-factor movements.
Uses DELTA to periodically reallocate discrete effective ranks under matched parameter budgets while retaining standard (A,B) adapters.
On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, it outperforms the reported uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines.
Trajectory EMA achieves performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.

papers.abstract: Self-attention has become the standard for modern sequence modeling, enabling Transformers to model long-range dependencies across a wide range of modalities. Despite these advances, its quadratic cost with respect to sequence length remains a significant computational bottleneck. Recent work addresses this limitation by introducing linear variants of self-attention, namely with kernel approximations of the softmax operator. However, their first-order aggregation restricts expressivity and struggles to capture higher-order structure. We propose Linear Stochastic Attention (LiSA), a linear attention plug-in module that enables higher-order token interactions via a stochastic diffusion process based on truncated random walks. LiSA incorporates adaptive locality, favoring semantically similar neighbors to preserve fine-grained structures, while maintaining stable and efficient training. We conduct extensive experiments on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks and show improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Sahar Dastani, Fereshteh Shakeri, Samuel Barbeau, Kunal Mahatha, Ismail Ben Ayed, Herve Lombaert, Christian Desrosiers
bullets: Addresses the quadratic sequence-length cost of standard self-attention and the limited expressivity of first-order linear attention.
Uses truncated random walks to enable higher-order token interactions within a linear-attention framework.
Employs adaptive locality to emphasize semantically similar neighbors and preserve fine-grained visual structure.
Evaluated on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, with improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
The abstract does not specify numerical gains or experimental datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LiSA. We patchify the input image into tokens and treat them as nodes in a graph G = (V,E), where edge weights define a row-stochastic transition matrix S. Aggregating the truncated terms on S yields a global attention map that captures transitive (higher-order) dependencies. In parallel, we compute content-based similarity within each token’s local neighborhood to form a local attention map. The layer output is a convex combination of the two, blending sharp local context with long-range structure.

papers.abstract: Tokenization is a fundamental component of modern language models: before a model sees data, its tokenizer has already determined how the data appears. We identify and challenge three myths in the tokenization research literature. Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is agnostic to the tokenizer and/or the vocabulary size: BPB is tokens per byte times bits per token, and the two factors do not cancel; using untrained models, we show that BPB prefers some tokenizers over others: the model has learned nothing, but the tokenizer--model pair has. Myth #2: lower BPB means a better model: On untrained models, BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes, even though accuracy remains at chance, and on real models trained on the same data, BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance. Myth #3: different "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics yield consistent results: The "unigram-normalized loss" is not tokenizer-agnostic; its reported correlation of 0.989 with BPB comes from a confounder and falls to 0.057 once fixed; from the same data the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size. We present a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can score only the true distribution best, give the same predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric is choosing a research question. We conclude with a caution for reading the tokenization literature and a conjecture for future work.
bullets: Challenges three myths about Bits-Per-Byte (BPB), including that it is tokenizer-independent and that lower BPB implies a better model.
Using untrained models, shows BPB can prefer tokenizer–model pairs and vocabulary sizes despite chance-level accuracy.
Finds BPB correlates only weakly with downstream performance in models trained on the same data.
Shows unigram-normalized loss is confounded: its apparent 0.989 correlation with BPB falls to 0.057 after correction, and the metrics select different vocabularies.
Proposes a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can simultaneously assess only the true distribution, score identical predictions equally, and tie all untrained models.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Myth #2: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Option-Letter Scoring). Untrained models that output uniform distributions. Top: BPB of the correct label drops one step at each merge that shortens a label (inset), then rises with log V . Bottom: accuracy is constant, at the fraction of items whose correct answer is listed first. Red band, for reference: central 95% of a uniform random guesser; black dashed: always choosing the first option. BPB strongly prefers a vocabulary of a few hundred tokens, whereas accuracy finds all models to be equally useless.

Figure 4: Myth #2: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Answer-Text Scoring). Untrained models that output uniform distributions, scored on answer text (WinoGrande: on a shared continuation). Top: BPB of the correct answers has an interior minimum on every benchmark (star), between 8K and 39K. Bottom: accuracy on the same strings moves by at most a few points and has no common preferred vocabulary size. Red band, for reference: central 95% of a uniform random guesser; dashed: always choosing the first option. BPB concludes that vocabulary sizes between 8K and 39K are strongly preferable, whereas accuracy finds all models to be equally useless.

Figure 6: Myth #2, Continued: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Where the Differences Lie). Each marker is the least-squares slope of the decision term on BPB across the tokenizers of one set, with its 95% bootstrap interval; the format term’s slope is one minus it. Most of the difference lies in the format term, which accuracy ignores, not in the decision term, which it reads.

Figure 8: Myth #3: Different “Tokenizer-Agnostic” Metrics Yield Consistent Results (Minima). Left and center: the 56 digitized runs of Figure 11 of Tao et al. (2024) against vocabulary size; stars mark each model size’s minimum, and hollow diamonds show candidate vocabularies for five runs whose match is ambiguous. Right: the vocabulary at each minimum. BPC is always lowest at the largest vocabulary trained, and its optimum may lie beyond it (arrows); Lu is lowest inside the grid. Unigram-normalized loss and BPC pick different vocabularies from the same data.

Figure 5: Myth #2: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Trained Models). Each point is one model-tokenizer pair from Meister (2026): every model has the same layers and saw the same documents in the same order; the tokenizer varies. The horizontal axis is BPB on the benchmark’s own text; for BLiMP, the grammatical sentence of each pair, scored alone. Each panel gives the Pearson (r) and Spearman (ρ) correlations between BPB and downstream performance. Dashed line and band: least-squares line with a 95% bootstrap band. On trained models, the correlation is relatively weak, with or without the outlier tokenizer (red cross, Appendix F).

papers.abstract: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.
authors: Roberto Dailey, Kajetan Schweighofer, Jamieson Warner, Conor F. Hayes, Elliot Meyerson, Babak Hodjat, Risto Miikkulainen, Xin Qiu
bullets: The paper characterizes this counterintuitive behavior across models, tasks, and modalities.
In high-dimensional spaces, perturbations often reduce performance but reveal informative directional signals.
Aggregating these signals enables local parent-model improvements despite uniformly worse sampled offspring.
The phenomenon arises from the interaction between reward-landscape curvature and the ES estimator’s noise.
The findings offer guidance for using perturbation-based optimization in LLM fine-tuning and other high-dimensional problems.

The paradox occurs when the magnitude is at a distance where all perturbations have a reward worse than the current model, but they still differentiate the good directions from the bad. (b) A demonstration of the tradeoff in perturbation size empirically, with performance of Qwen 2.5 7B on the Sudoku task after 300 ES iterations varying σ, holding all else constant. Thus, the same good directions can be identified at various perturbation magnitudes, even at which all the perturbations are worse than the parent.

papers.abstract: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execution. The AlgoPilot framework contains three components: 1) a SteerLM, trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), that adaptively selects the solving strategy (paradigm and modes) based on input problems, 2) the corresponding expert GuideLM, trained via SFT, that generates structured formulation guidance tailored to the selected strategy, and 3) an ExecutionLM that generates solutions conditioned on both the selected strategy and its formulation. Unlike prompting-based methods that rely on fixed reasoning templates, our approach learns to adaptively choose and structure problem-solving strategies based on the input. We build AlgoPilot on Qwen3-8B and evaluate across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, comparing against both the latest similarly scaled small models and large LLMs. AlgoPilot significantly improves average accuracy for the same model from 38.4% to 72.9%, outperforming the best large LLM prompting baseline GLM-5 by 11.7%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. Notably, we show that the learned steering and formulation modules can transfer across execution models, suggesting their potential to improve other LLMs. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/algopilot.
authors: Yilun Hao, Ruixiao Yang, Hudson Hilal, Yongchao Chen, Kaizhi Qian, Yada Zhu, Yang Zhang, Chuchu Fan

Ablations support the value of each component, while steering and formulation modules transfer across execution models.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already handle well while underexploring harder ones that require departing from those representations. Through our controlled experiments and large-scale analysis, we show that RLVR training on mixed data tends to further sharpen performance on easier problems while yielding only marginal gains on harder ones. We find that although hard problems lead to modest gains overall, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model's reasoning capabilities and pushing the representations. However, prolonged training on these hard problems may also hurt and lead to forgetting on easy problems. These findings help to better understand some of the prior conflicting observations about RLVR, specifically, why on (OOD) domains where the base model performs poorly, improvements on hard problems can expand reasoning; while on well-trained domains, forgetting can reduce performance and mask genuine gains obtained from hard problems.
authors: Phuc Minh Nguyen, Ngoc-Hieu Nguyen, Parshin Shojaee, Chinh Duc La, Duy Minh Ho Nguyen, Rui Zhang, Khoa D. Doan, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawl
bullets: Mixed-data RLVR disproportionately improves problems the base model already solves well, with limited gains on harder problems.
Hard problems produce modest overall improvements but contribute most to pushing beyond existing representations.
Prolonged training on hard problems can degrade performance on easy problems through forgetting.
The findings reconcile conflicting RLVR results across in-distribution and out-of-distribution domains.

papers.abstract: Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However, new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data or reliable supervisory signals for further training. We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store what it learns: domain-specific skills and instructions on when to apply them, along with memories of past task experiences and reflections on what to improve. Recursa bootstraps the repository from domain materials and then refines it through recursive self-improvement. It uses parallel learners to execute tasks and synthesize local improvements, then validates and merges the improvements into the knowledge repository. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.

Improves held-out all-pass rates on Harvey LAB’s Firm Knowledge benchmark for both evaluated models.
Scope: evaluated on a single benchmark and two model settings described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
authors: Peizhi Niu, Ge Shi, Vaibhav Gorde, Sarthak Ghosh, Christos Faloutsos, Min Cheng, Kevin Chen

Controlled studies find that human-defined schemas and explicit deduplication can hurt performance, whereas human diagnosis substantially improves failed-trace learning.
One round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0–10.9%, suggesting agents should organize memory while humans diagnose failures.

papers.abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) transforms a natural language problem description into a collection of candidate probabilistic programs and performs inference within each model, combining their predictions using Bayesian model averaging. While this provides a flexible framework for probabilistic inference without manual model specification, the resulting candidate model set is often misspecified in practice, and likelihood-based aggregation can concentrate on a single model, under-representing uncertainty across the sampled models. We propose a stacking-based aggregation method for LLB that selects model weights by optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood, while preserving the original language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline. Because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable in latent-variable models, we derive a variational lower bound that yields a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective. Across real-world probabilistic inference tasks, our method achieves comparable predictive performance to Bayesian model averaging while yielding more dispersed model weights, reducing concentration on a single candidate model under misspecification.
authors: Anant Bhide, Akarsh Gupta, Edmond Cunningham, Justin Domke
bullets: Addresses candidate-model misspecification and overly concentrated Bayesian model averaging in LLB.
Preserves LLB’s language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline.
Optimizes model weights for predictive performance using a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective.
Uses a variational lower bound because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable for latent-variable models.
On real-world probabilistic inference tasks, matches Bayesian model averaging’s predictive performance while producing more dispersed weights.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.
authors: Sinuo Wang, Jiacheng Lu, Zeyu Zhang, Maojia Song, Rui Sun, Beidi Luan, Yutong Xie, Jing Li, Daxin Jiang, Qi Wu, Zuo Bai
bullets: Addresses the slow or imbalanced recovery of expert capabilities during multi-teacher on-policy distillation.
Treats the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a differentiable model optimized with the distillation objective.
Uses expert parameters as priors while keeping the student trainable, avoiding confinement to the experts’ parameter span.
Evaluated across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales; it surpasses MOPD’s final average recovery in half the training steps.
At 1.7B, it reaches 94.7% average recovery versus 80.9% for MOPD at the end of training.

papers.abstract: Small language models (<=9B parameters) can support local medical question answering (QA) while reducing privacy and latency concerns, but effective fine-tuning remains challenging. This paper compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervised fine-tuning methods: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS), which applies equal loss weighting to the full CoT-and-answer sequence, and Segment-weighted (SwS), which separately weights CoT and answer losses. We evaluate six general- and medical-domain models on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA) and free-text QA (Med-O1). Results show that neither method is universally best: on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA), SwS generally performs better, with general-purpose models benefiting most; notably, Qwen3.5-4B improves by up to 44.8% over its zero-shot baseline on MedQA. In contrast, medical-domain models show smaller or even negative gains on MCQs. On free-text QA (Med-O1), UaS performs best for nearly all models and provides consistent improvements across both model types, with the 3B Llama-3.2 model approaching the performance of much larger 7B medical-domain models. We also find that excessively long CoT generation is associated with lower performance in some models on either multiple-choice or free-text QA tasks, suggesting that limiting the CoT length during training may benefit selected models. Overall, the results show that CoT loss weighting should be matched to the task format and the knowledge already encoded in the base model, rather than using a single fine-tuning strategy for all clinical QA tasks.
authors: Le Zhou, Xiao Luo, Chinmay Chandra, Zhan Zhang
bullets: SwS, which weights reasoning and answer losses separately, generally works better for multiple-choice QA, especially with general-purpose models.
UaS, which weights the full sequence uniformly, performs best for nearly all models on free-text QA and improves both general- and medical-domain models.
Qwen3.5-4B gains up to 44.8% over its zero-shot MedQA baseline, while medical-domain models show smaller or negative MCQ gains.
A 3B Llama-3.2 model approaches much larger 7B medical models on free-text QA when fine-tuned with UaS.
Excessively long chain-of-thought outputs can correlate with lower performance, suggesting that limiting reasoning length may help selected models.
