papers.abstract: A stored experience may answer one future question and offer little help with another. We measure this task-conditioned utility rather than assigning each memory a single importance score. A task-blind writer stores a memory without seeing the later task; a frozen reader then answers that task with and without the memory, using identical filler. A cost ledger records the resources used to form, store and expose the memory. On single-call factual-recall tasks built from LongMemEval-V2 web-agent memories, the same memory helps more when it contains information needed for the answer. Its mean paired reward gain on these answer-bearing task pairs exceeds that on matched-control pairs by $+0.33$ (95% interval $+0.21$ to $+0.46$). The tested task-blind summaries and structured records yield smaller gains than Raw, including at fixed total context; a budget sweep is consistent with retention of answer-bearing content contributing to the difference. The bearing--control contrast remains positive in a new session with randomized memory position and under a second reader, although individual memory--task labels change. Generic retrieval performs above chance but misses most screen-defined answer-bearing memories. The factual-recall gains do not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where even raw memories have no measurable effect. We provide a public, versioned Conditional Memory Utility Dataset of paired measurements and costs. The practical takeaway is to evaluate memory compression by the task utility it preserves alongside its costs. Task-conditioned measurements make this comparison possible; their stability must also be checked.
authors: Chih-Hsuan Yang, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Feng Yan, Rajeev Thakur
bullets: Measures how much a memory changes a frozen reader’s answer to a task, using identical filler with and without the memory.
On factual-recall tasks, answer-bearing memories produced a larger mean paired reward gain than matched controls: +0.33, with a 95% interval of +0.21 to +0.46.
Tested task-blind summaries and structured records yielded smaller gains than raw memories, including at fixed total context; budget results suggest retaining answer-bearing content matters.
The effect persisted with randomized memory position and a second reader, but generic retrieval missed most screen-defined answer-bearing memories.
The effect did not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where raw memories had no measurable impact.

papers.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
bullets: Long reasoning traces improve problem-solving but can be expensive due to repetition and low-value text.
The study compacts earlier reasoning before pending tool results are revealed, then compares generation from original versus rewritten histories without retraining.
Across tested models, accepted compact histories generally shortened subsequent reasoning; a coding case showed less repeated verification.
Software-agent deployments achieved lower total spending, but task quality and rewrite-inclusive time varied by target and compressor.
The results motivate model-specific compaction policies that balance efficiency with retained capability.

papers.abstract: Long-to-Short (L2S) model merging seeks to combine the strong reasoning capability of long chain-of-thought models with the concise style of base models, but existing methods that rely on linear interpolation and first-order activation statistics fail to capture how the loss landscape responds to parameter displacement, leading to degraded accuracy on hard tasks. We propose Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM), a training-free framework that replaces heuristic statistics with lightweight second-order curvature information. LHM consists of three components: (1) a low-rank Hessian approximation that efficiently estimates per-layer Hessian traces via Hutchinson's estimator on random inputs, eliminating the need for task-specific data; (2) a Layer Second-Order Sensitivity (LSOS) index that combines Hessian trace with task-vector norm to quantify per-layer fusion difficulty; and (3) a Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM) that converts LSOS scores into layer-adaptive merge coefficients while jointly satisfying a fusion-error bound and a global length-reduction target. Experiments across six mathematical benchmarks on 1.5B and 7B models show that LHM outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as ACM-TIES and ORCA, achieving over 4\% accuracy gain and up to 93.1\% reduction in output length relative to the long-CoT model.
authors: Zeqiu Yu, Xuesheng Zhang, Wenxiao Zhao, Shixiao Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of linear interpolation and first-order statistics in merging long-chain-of-thought and concise models.
Uses low-rank Hutchinson-based Hessian estimates, an LSOS layer-sensitivity score, and DCCM layer-adaptive coefficients.
Requires no task-specific data and jointly enforces a fusion-error bound and target length reduction.
Across six mathematical benchmarks and 1.5B/7B models, it reports over 4% higher accuracy and up to 93.1% shorter outputs than the long-CoT model.
The abstract evaluates mathematical reasoning; broader task or domain scope is unspecified.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall framework of Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM). The framework then comprises three modules: (1) Low-Rank Hessian Approximation, which estimates loss-landscape curvature using Rademacher random vectors to compute per-layer Hessian traces; (2) LSOS Index, which combines these traces with the ℓ2 norms of the task vector via element-wise multiplication to evaluate layer importance; and (3) Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM), which applies min–max normalization and dual orthogonal constraints (balancing accuracy preservation and length reduction) to generate layer-wise merge coefficients λi. The merged model θmerged preserves strong reasoning accuracy while producing substantially shorter outputs.

papers.tldr: LHM is a training-free, curvature-aware model-merging method that improves long-to-short reasoning while substantially reducing output length.

papers.abstract: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts the diagnoses documented at a patient's next encounter, turning retrospective electronic health records into prospective clinical prediction. However, conventional aggregate evaluation obscures its multifaceted nature: distributionally, models must handle variable-size diagnosis sets and long-tailed labels; temporally, they must distinguish persistent, newly recorded, and recurrent diagnoses; and both vary with observed history depth. We introduce an evaluation framework along these dimensions and apply it to rule-based heuristics, LLM-based prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent approaches. This reveals that repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses, and that retrieval and memory exhibit distinct profiles whose relative strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones. Motivated by this, we propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework combining evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory. Using cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, it preserves shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive with them on aggregate metrics.
bullets: Aggregate metrics can hide differences in predicting persistent, new, and recurrent diagnoses, especially across varying history depths.
The proposed evaluation framework compares heuristics, prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent methods along distributional and temporal dimensions.
Repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM approaches overall but cannot predict new or recurrent diagnoses.
LONGINUS uses retrieved patient-record evidence, trajectory memory, and cross-view agreement to preserve or adjudicate predictions.
Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, it achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive on aggregate metrics.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.
authors: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble, Daniel M. Bikel
bullets: DSA’s full-cache indexer scan dominates decode time at long contexts, while adjacent layers choose nearly identical tokens.
MLI lets each layer attend to the preceding layer’s selection, allowing indexer computation to overlap with attention.
It requires no retraining or new weights; the default implementation runs in SGLang without kernel changes, with an optional fused kernel.
Combined with IndexCache, MLI improves decoding speed by up to 14.5% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at equal retention.
Long-context accuracy on LongBench, RULER, and LongBench v2 remains within a few percentage points of IndexCache.

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes sparse attention and long-context LLM decode, directly fitting efficient attention and long-context model developments.
papers.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) hides DeepSeek Sparse Attention’s expensive indexer scans by reusing the previous layer’s token selection, delivering faster long-context decoding without retraining.

papers.abstract: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.
authors: Damien Teney, Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Hemanth Saratchandran, Simon Lucey
bullets: The study tests small language models trained from scratch on web text, code, and mathematics.
It replaces standard transformer activations with learned splines tuned to specific datasets.
Cross-domain evaluations show that architectures tuned for natural language transfer better within language domains, while math-tuned variants perform poorly on natural language.
Improvements appear across all seven tested datasets, with mechanisms linked to wider loss basins and more abundant lottery tickets.
The findings suggest domain-specific learning strategies could improve data efficiency while supporting general-purpose models.

This likely requires different inductive biases than standard subword tokenization because of longerrange interactions, different typical entropy in the predictions, etc. As a result, the architectures optimized for this dataset (SHAKESPEARE-CHAR, vertical axis) work badly on others (FINEWEB, ENWIK8) and vice versa.

We specialize a transformer variant for a source domain D1 (left) by replacing nonlinearities with parameterized splines, pre-trained in a warm-up phase. We then reuse these frozen components to train a model on a target dataset D2 (right). Only very few parameters are transferred.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that domain-specific inductive biases (e.g., learned splines) improve LLM training efficiency and generalization, relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
papers.tldr: Domain-specific transformer inductive biases can improve language-model training efficiency or generalization, but their benefits often do not transfer across domains.

papers.abstract: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.
bullets: Models answer typed finance questions with probabilities in one forward pass across 0.8B–32B parameters and multiple model families.
Narrow fine-tuning reduces general decision competence by 9–45 percentage points, with the effect weakening as models scale.
On realized-return questions, models show no detectable conditional edge and instead produce flat, well-calibrated probabilities that follow horizon-specific base rates.
Calibration is strongest at mid-scale, while larger models degrade under prior drift.
A mixed-corpus adapter preserves policy performance and near-specialist outcome calibration, supporting domain-specific temperature regimes and escalation by confidence bands.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates small LLMs for finance, focusing on calibration, honesty, and specialization collapse, relevant to efficient and robust LLM deployment.
papers.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
papers.tldr: Small finance decision models can be fast and calibrated, but narrow specialization erodes general reasoning; mixing policy and real-outcome data restores broad competence while preserving honest uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) estimates learners' evolving knowledge states from interaction histories to support adaptive learning. Retrieval-augmented KT improves these estimates using cross-learner behavioral evidence, but existing approaches typically separate evidence retrieval from downstream prediction. This creates a retrieval-inference alignment gap because evidence relevance varies with the learner's evolving state and prediction context. We propose CaRe-KT, a query-adaptive framework that maintains relevance continuity between evidence acquisition and inference without equating retrieval relevance with predictive utility. CaRe-KT introduces an Evidence-Graph Cache (EGC) that combines persistent question-level relational compatibility with interaction-level temporal validity to construct query-specific evidence subgraphs. Historical learning trajectories retrieved through these subgraphs are encoded alongside the target learner's history in a shared representation space using outcome-supervised contrastive learning. An attention mechanism combines acquisition relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility, allowing relevance to inform, rather than determine, each trajectory's predictive influence. Experiments across five benchmarks show that CaRe-KT outperforms strong KT baselines and remains robust under sparse-history and cold-start conditions. These findings support relevance continuity as a design principle for retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing.
authors: Mehrnoush Mohammadi, Kamal Berahmand, Mohammad Morsali, Shazia Sadiq, Wojtek Tomaszewski, Hassan Khosravi
bullets: Addresses the retrieval-inference alignment gap in retrieval-augmented KT, where relevant evidence may not be predictively useful.
Uses an Evidence-Graph Cache to build query-specific evidence subgraphs from persistent question relations and temporally valid interactions.
Encodes retrieved learning trajectories with the target learner’s history using outcome-supervised contrastive learning.
An attention mechanism combines retrieval relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility to determine predictive influence.
Outperforms strong KT baselines across five benchmarks and remains robust with sparse histories and cold-start learners.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.

papers.abstract: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.
authors: Ankitkumar Patel, Jigarkumar Patel, Amit Kumar, Supreetha Sreeram, Venkatesh Kulkarni
bullets: Evaluates LLM causal discovery across model scale, graph complexity, prompting, metadata quality, data quality, and uncertainty.

Shows that conventional metrics can overstate performance when uncertainty is ignored; uncertainty-aware evaluation lowers scores.
Larger models perform better, but their gains degrade sharply with lower-quality metadata.
Provides practical guidance on when LLMs may support causal discovery and when they risk misleading researchers.

papers.abstract: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.
authors: Tavish Mankash, Vardhaman Kalloli, Keshava Prasad, Deepan Muthirayan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of interpreting concepts distributed across many model dimensions.
Routes inputs to selected experts that read the full representation but write to disjoint, fixed coordinates.
On a controlled task, MoWE outperforms dense models in predictive performance and improves coordinate specificity over dense and standard MoE models, though standard MoE has lower cross-entropy.
Native MoWE coordinates approach the readability of sparse-autoencoder features and can reveal causal paths and steer predictions.
Demonstrations include detecting hazardous requests, inducing refusals, and changing an angle-related prediction from “sides” to “degrees.”

papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.
bullets: The study extends steering vectors from inference-time behavior control to parameter updates during SFT, distillation, and RL with verifiable rewards.
It tests hidden-state injection for supervised training and correctness-contrast advantage repair on wrong GRPO rollouts.
Supervised steering improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains increasing with the off-policy gap and reaching up to 12% when distilling from thinking-mode teachers.
In RL, advantage repair restores learning signals for otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups and transfers to held-out math benchmarks.
Effectiveness has boundaries: directions may fail for code generation, layer placement may not transfer across model families, and inference-time steering may fail on SV-trained checkpoints.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation can transfer reasoning from stronger teachers to frozen students through reusable prompts, but avoiding weight updates does not eliminate supervision. Without ground-truth answers, teacher solutions are unverified, and agreement with the teacher can reward shared mistakes. We introduce Knowledge-to-Prompt (K2P) for label-free knowledge distillation to prompts. K2P synthesizes reusable instructions from teacher solutions, refines them using paired teacher and student responses, and guides search and selection with answer agreement. It retains candidates that adaptive search may undervalue and selects on reserved questions. Deployment uses only the frozen student and selected prompt. Our theory separates generation and selection gaps and gives conditions under which agreement-guided construction yields accuracy guarantees despite imperfect teacher references. Across reasoning tasks and students, K2P outperforms label-free alternatives overall and remains competitive with supervised prompt optimization. Ablations and archive diagnostics assess the contributions of teacher solutions and refinement, while revealing the limits of agreement-guided selection.
bullets: Addresses unverified teacher solutions and shared-error risks in label-free distillation.
Synthesizes instructions from teacher solutions and refines them with paired teacher and student responses.
Uses adaptive search, agreement-guided selection, and reserved questions to retain and evaluate prompt candidates.
Provides theory separating generation and selection gaps, with conditions for accuracy guarantees under imperfect references.
Outperforms label-free alternatives overall and remains competitive with supervised prompt optimization, while exposing limits of agreement-based selection.

papers.abstract: We introduce Type-6 logic, a variant of dynamic epistemic logic augmented with two operators (uncertainty and recurrence), designed to model the inferential dynamics of contemporary large language model (LLM) chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Type-6 accounts for common LLM reasoning pathologies such as unlicensed revision, enthymemes, loopbacks, and unverifiable/incorrect claims. We propose a verifier based on Type-6 logic that builds a graph out the trace, and checks it against Type-6's axioms and inference rules. We evaluate our framework on LLM-generated CoTs four splits spanning formal and informal reasoning. Our verifier detects structurally unsound reasoning steps that surface-level heuristics miss, and allows for easy visualisation of the model's reasoning process. In our corpus, our verifier shows that derived contradiction is the most common hard-fail category in CoT, and that only about 3\% of the propositions of a trace have impact on the final derivation. Ablation studies show that other verification methods (LLMs-as-judges, other neurosymbolic approaches, etc.) cannot be considered interchangeable: for example, agreement between LLMs-as-judges and LINC is $κ\approx 0.034$, and this persists within a method across underlying models. Type-6, however, is the most agreed-with method amongst the ones we tested. We prove our verifier runs on average-case linear time; and release our logic specification and artefacts.
bullets: Models CoT as dynamic epistemic processes with uncertainty and recurrence operators.
Builds a graph from each reasoning trace and checks it against Type-6 axioms and inference rules.
Evaluated on four formal and informal reasoning splits; derived contradictions were the most common hard-fail category.
Finds that only about 3% of trace propositions affect the final derivation.
Runs in average-case linear time and supports visualisation; the authors release the logic specification and artefacts.

papers.abstract: Linear activation steering is a powerful approach for controlling and specializing large language models by adding linear representations of concepts to their activations at inference. While effective, existing methods often steer with a fixed strength, independent of how much steering any given input requires. In this work, we introduce Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), which decomposes activation steering into a fixed steering direction and a context-dependent steering coefficient. This decomposition preserves the interpretability of the steering direction while enabling the steering strength to vary with context. It also enables CLAS to perform selective steering: steering multiple behaviors across different portions of a single generation, which cannot be achieved using a fixed steering strength. In addition, across a wide range of steering benchmarks and language models, CLAS consistently outperforms standard linear activation steering and matches or exceeds ReFT and LoRA in settings with limited labeled data. Notably, CLAS achieves this using directions that also serve as reliable concept monitors, a property that directions learned via fine-tuning lack. We therefore propose CLAS as an interpretable and accurate method for controlling and specializing large language models.
authors: Brandon Hsu, Daniel Beaglehole, Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan, Mikhail Belkin
bullets: Fixed-strength steering applies the same intensity regardless of the input’s needs.
CLAS separates a fixed, interpretable steering direction from a context-dependent steering coefficient.
This supports selective steering of multiple behaviors within different parts of one generation.
Across diverse benchmarks and language models, CLAS outperforms standard linear steering and matches or exceeds ReFT and LoRA with limited labeled data.
Its steering directions also function as reliable concept monitors, unlike directions learned through fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.
authors: Dengzhe Hou, Lingyu Jiang, Deng Li, Zirui Li, Fangzhou Lin, Kazunori D Yamada
bullets: Introduces a working-memory-inspired probe with program-computed answers, 3–100 updates, and final-, intermediate-, or multi-target queries.
Across 18 LLMs, accuracy drops from 84.9% on single-step arithmetic to 31.7% on core tasks with 3–7 updates; beyond 50 updates, no model exceeds 10%.
Accuracy reaches 88.0% when models are instructed to write steps and put the answer on the last line, driven mainly by the protocol change rather than a larger budget.
Core accuracy positively correlates with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores.
The released generator, items, scoring code, and responses support reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.

papers.title: WMIP: A Working-Memory-Inspired Programmable Probe of Cumulative State Tracking in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.
bullets: Studies how training epochs and ensemble size jointly affect generalization in the data-limited regime.
FineWeb experiments show logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration and delays optimal stopping.
Ensembles can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a shared training horizon.
Develops a dynamical mean-field theory for multi-epoch SGD that tracks cross-epoch and cross-model error correlations.
Derives compute-allocation laws: ensemble size should grow at least as quickly as each member’s training time, with excess loss decreasing as a power of compute.

papers.abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.
bullets: Addresses GPU memory growth caused by retaining gradients for all MoE experts until the optimizer step.
Updates batched expert tensors in backward, limiting retained expert gradients to one layer at a time.
Reduces peak memory by 19–22% and step time by 17–23% in the reported bf16 fine-tuning experiments.
Preserves bitwise-identical updates without expert gradient clipping, while held-out loss remains within 0.003 of baselines.
Whole-batched-tensor updates avoid the slowdown associated with updating experts individually; dense parameters can still use gradient clipping.

papers.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.
bullets: Addresses the fixed layer ordering used by standard language models.
Uses a global library of transformer blocks whose runtime routing determines layer order.
A single library-size hyperparameter spans parameter reuse and sparsity, unifying efficiency tradeoffs across dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture-of-experts models.
Matches the performance of these baselines on text pretraining and exhibits distinct routing patterns for sudoku, mazes, languages, and scripts.
Routing can be intervened on to force solution strategies, while router probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC.

figures.caption: Figure 1: We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), a novel architecture where the next executed transformer layer is chosen at runtime. Figure 2: Library of Layers uses strided window attention and a top-1 router to allow for efficient training. LoL is made up of a prelude, a routed core, and a coda. The layers in the prelude and coda can attend over the whole sequence. In the core, the sequence is split into windows of W tokens, and at every routed depth a router selects one layer from the shared library per window (topleft). Attention is restricted to each window, but the window boundaries shift by S tokens between successive routed depths, allowing information to flow across windows (Strided Window Attention, top-right). Window 0 has no history, so its router uses the first token and a learned vector e(ℓ) for routed depth ℓ (bottom-left). For window i > 0, the router averages the mean hidden states of earlier windows 0, . . . , i − 1 and selects one layer (bottom-right). With W = 4 and S = 2, Layers 1 and 3 share the same boundaries while Layer 2 is offset, so information can pass between neighboring windows. Token 5 is highlighted in red to show this: in Layer 1 it is the first token in a new window, while in Layer 2 its window includes tokens 3 and 4.

papers.abstract: A memory-augmented agent must decide which memories to keep, merge and retrieve, and its only evidence of their value is its retrieval log: the memories it retrieved in each episode and whether it succeeded. Existing methods assign every memory a value from this log, even when the log cannot separate one memory's contribution from another's. We treat the log as an experiment that nobody designed and ask which memory values it determines. Two counts answer this before any outcome is observed: how often each memory was retrieved, and how often each pair was retrieved together. From these counts, we prove that top-$k$ retrieval leaves every memory value undetermined, however many episodes are logged, and that a question with its own memories, asked once, determines at most one of their values. On fourteen standard memory benchmarks, no memory value is determined in any of 55 configurations. Both causes are choices about retrieval. We introduce LEDGER, which estimates each determined Shapley value in closed form with a confidence interval and reports every other value as undetermined. It merges memories with identical histories without losing a determined value, and it retrieves so that the next log determines more. On pooled HotpotQA, LEDGER raises the fraction of memories determined from 0.001 to 0.797, at a cost of 2.6 accuracy points on HotpotQA and with a gain of 2.7 on LoCoMo.
bullets: Memory value is identifiable only when retrieval histories distinguish a memory’s contribution from others.
Two retrieval statistics—individual counts and pairwise co-retrieval counts—determine identifiability before observing outcomes.
The authors prove that standard top-$k$ retrieval leaves every memory value undetermined, regardless of log length; single-use question memories determine at most one value.
Across 55 configurations on 14 benchmarks, no memory value was determined.

LEDGER estimates determined Shapley values with confidence intervals, merges memories with identical histories, and improves the determined-memory fraction from 0.001 to 0.797 on pooled HotpotQA, with a 2.6-point HotpotQA accuracy cost and a 2.7-point LoCoMo gain.

papers.abstract: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.
bullets: Uses two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, DPO, or on-policy distillation.
Builds self-contained reasoning through model-aware synthesis and adversarial problem strengthening.
Extends reasoning to tool use via diverse, automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data and deterministic computation.
Reinforcement learning improves long-horizon reasoning and interaction with tools and environments.
Reports strong results across agentic benchmarks, including competitiveness with leading commercial models on several tasks; releases the full development recipe and code.

papers.abstract: LLM agents compact long histories to fit their context windows, but the compacted context must still carry the operating rules that govern later actions. Prior work shows that violations rise after compaction, but measures compliance outside a complete agent harness and does not identify where each violation comes from. We introduce ARCBench(Agent Rule Compliance Benchmark), a configurable benchmark built on the open-source pi agent harness. Its tool-calling agent loop lets us measure rule compliance from actions taken during execution, bringing the evaluation closer to deployed agent workflows. Using ARCBench, we examine where violations after compaction come from, and how different compaction configurations and adversarial settings change their sources. We find that compaction rarely deletes the rule: most violations after compaction occur while the rule is still in the compacted history, with the agent treating a later request as permission, ignoring the rule, and proceeding anyway. Where violations come from depends on the configuration: how the rule is delivered decides whether the agent would break it even without compaction, while the compaction strategy and budget decide whether the rule survives. The strongest compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting the rule in the summary and changing how the agents behave, whereas the strongest defense restores the rule in most summary but still violates. Finally, retaining a rule does not guarantee compliance: compacted runs that retain the rule violate more than twice as often as runs with the full history.
bullets: Introduces ARCBench, a configurable benchmark that measures rule compliance through tool-calling actions in an open-source agent harness.
Most post-compaction violations occur even when the rule remains in the compacted history: agents treat later requests as permission or ignore the rule.
Violation sources depend on configuration: rule delivery affects baseline willingness to break rules, while compaction strategy and budget affect rule preservation.
A compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting summarized rules; the strongest defense restores rules in most summaries but does not eliminate violations.
Retaining a rule is insufficient: compacted runs with retained rules violate more than twice as often as full-history runs.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how context compaction affects LLM agent rule compliance, relevant to long-context processing and context management.
papers.title: Do Agents Still Follow the Rules? Benchmarking Rule Compliance under Agent Context Compaction
papers.tldr: ARCBench shows that context compaction usually preserves rules but can still sharply reduce agent compliance, especially when summaries corrupt rules or alter behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. It uses one indexing query per KV group and shares selected chunks across queries in that group. During prefill, QShare reuses selections across adjacent queries to reduce indexing cost and improve KV reuse and GPU utilization. We evaluate CISA on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano and Ultra, and Inkling-Small. In one-layer BF16 benchmarks at batch size 32 using Ultra's per-device attention dimensions, core attention is 11.7x faster for prefill queries near the end of a 1M-token prompt and 13.0x faster during decode. Including chunk scoring, selection, and all other measured GPU work, speedups are 8.6x and 3.0x. On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly reading growing KV histories during long-context inference.
Indexes fixed-size KV chunks using compact key summaries, with one query per KV group and shared selections across group queries.
QShare reuses chunk selections across adjacent prefill queries to reduce indexing overhead and improve KV reuse.
Reports up to 8–16× fewer KV reads, 2.29× end-to-end throughput, and quality within roughly 1.5–2.05 percentage points of dense attention in evaluated settings.
Using fewer chunks raises throughput to 2.61× but widens the GraphWalks quality gap to 3.59 percentage points.

papers.title: CISA: Retrofitting Dense Attention Models with Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: CISA retrofits pretrained dense-attention LLMs with chunk-level sparse attention, achieving substantially faster million-token inference while keeping quality close to dense attention without retraining.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining high-quality work on complex productivity tasks with sustained monitoring and decision-making.
Separates task strategy from execution management: models choose actions, delegation, and acceptance while the runtime maintains state and feedback.
Supports direct or delegated execution, synchronous or asynchronous subagents, and shared editing of documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes.
Uses hierarchical workspaces, persistent semantic memory, and job logs to make work resumable across agents and sessions.
Across 12 benchmarks and six application categories, it was highly competitive with Codex and DeepSeek Harness; a five-round post-training case study improved average scores from 33.19 to 42.95.

papers.abstract: Knowledge is how understanding accumulates across people and generations: durable records that outlive their producers and that others can check, combine, teach, and correct. AI agents are now built and run by many independent users and organizations, and each agent is upgraded, replaced, or retired within months. Yet what an agent learns stays trapped in model parameters, a transient context window, or a system-specific memory store that is appended to and retrieved from rather than processed. We argue that the next generation of AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent. In this loop, agents discover knowledge from their environments and trajectories; the layer internalizes it by turning fragmented, heterogeneous records and experience into composable, revisable understanding; and agents across systems and generations use the result and return new outcomes for revision. While discovery and use have advanced rapidly with large language model agents, internalization remains the bottleneck. We argue that internalization should become a persistent object of training and maintenance-centered on condition-preserving conceptualization of events and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning across noisy, heterogeneous representations (text, tables, graphs, rules, and programs). To power this layer, we call for knowledge foundation models that provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation, and outline a research agenda showing how an explicit knowledge layer delivers reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.
bullets: Current agents keep learning trapped in parameters, context windows, or system-specific memories, limiting reuse and continuity.
The proposed loop separates knowledge discovery, internalization, and use, with internalization identified as the main bottleneck.
Internalization requires condition-preserving conceptualization and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning over heterogeneous, noisy representations.
The paper calls for knowledge foundation models to provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation.
An explicit knowledge layer could improve reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The knowledge-centric loop across agents and generations. Independent agent systems, built on different models and run by different organizations, discover knowledge and contribute it to an explicit knowledge layer. The layer is internalized by transformations and reasoning, and the results are used by other systems and by later generations, which inherit, revalidate, and revise them.

Figure 2: A knowledge foundation model inside the knowledge layer. It combines explicit knowledge, supporting observations and experience, and the implicit capacities of existing models, organizes shared computation across transformation and reasoning layers while delegating exact computation to symbolic components, and produces deductive, inductive, and abductive results whose status is recorded before they are written back. Implicit priors inform inference but do not become knowledge without evidence.

papers.tldr: The paper argues that future AI should use a shared, explicit knowledge layer that agents continuously discover, internalize, revise, and reuse across systems and generations.

papers.abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.
bullets: Sharpening improves accuracy but reduces behavioral coverage, hindering difficult-task progress.
Closed-form analyses of KL-regularized pass@k and max@k explain their prompt-difficulty-adaptive learning pressure.
The same optimal policies can be achieved with standard @1 objectives using adaptive regularization or reward transformation.
KAPPO applies this adaptation to existing policy optimizers after a one-time reference calibration.
Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show single-completion KAPPO can match multi-completion @k optimization at lower cost.

figures.caption: Figure 3: MATH Level 5 validation performance of the starting checkpoints, @k-A⋆PO checkpoints, and PKPO checkpoints. @k-A⋆PO matches the performance of PKPO at a fraction of the on-policy training rollouts, requiring only a single-time reference calibration at ≤ 5% training time overhead.

Figure 2: pass@keval on AIME 2026 as the sampling budget at test time (keval) increases. Setting k > 1 during training consistently reduces sharpening. In Figure (a), we plot standard GRPO and @k-A⋆PO trained with k ∈ {1, 2, 4}. In Figure (b), we plot @k-DPO trained with k ∈ {1, 2}.

Figure 1: Adaptive pressure induced by @k objectives. (a) For binary rewards, increasing k strengthens regularization on easy tasks while retaining greater optimization pressure on difficult tasks. papers.selection_reason: Provides closed-form analysis and a general framework for pass@k objectives in LLM post-training, a meaningful contribution to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: KAPPO adapts standard single-completion RL objectives to control LLM sharpening, emphasizing harder prompts while reducing unnecessary pressure on easy ones.

papers.abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.
bullets: Addresses information dilution in deep Pre-LN language models without adding substantial cross-layer computation or memory access.
Uses stride-aligned shallow–middle source pairs to reconstruct deep-layer keys and values.
KV-sharing edges provide non-local gradient paths that sharpen key retrieval directions and enrich value representations.
Evaluated on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters under GQA and MLA, with consistent downstream gains.
On a 16B MoE model, reports improvements of 7.0% on MMLU-Pro, 6.6% on CMMLU, and 6.4% on C3.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hierarchical KV-sharing LLM architecture that reduces KV cache by a third while improving downstream performance, fitting both efficiency and LLM architecture interests.
papers.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DepthGraft hierarchically reuses KV projections across layers to regularize deep representations, reduce KV-cache memory by roughly one third, and improve language-model performance.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates the student's exposure bias by optimizing on student-generated trajectories. However, student-generated prefixes may contain reasoning errors or follow patterns unfamiliar to the teacher, undermining the reliability of its token-level supervision. This degradation becomes more pronounced as prefixes grow longer. To address this teacher-side distribution mismatch, we propose Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA), which adapts the teacher to the states on which it is queried during distillation. Specifically, before OPD starts, we collect student rollout prefixes with random lengths and continually train the teacher to continue from the prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). By treating each prefix as context and rewarding correct final answers, the teacher learns to recover from student-induced states rather than imitate the student's reasoning. Then, the adapted teacher is used for standard OPD, with no changes to the distillation objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our SPTA improves average student performance over standard OPD and OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. These results highlight the importance of adapting teachers not only to solve problems independently, but also to provide reliable guidance on the states their students actually visit.
bullets: Problem: Longer or erroneous student prefixes create a teacher–student distribution mismatch that weakens token-level supervision.
Method: Train the teacher on randomly sized student rollout prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards before standard OPD.
The teacher learns to recover from student-induced states and produce correct continuations rather than imitate student reasoning.
SPTA leaves the standard OPD objective unchanged.
Experiments show higher average student performance than standard OPD and OPD using task-level RLVR-adapted teachers.

papers.title: Meet Students Where They Are: Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation for On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: SPTA adapts the teacher to student-generated reasoning states before on-policy distillation, improving guidance and average student performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class's state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks. Mamba 3's multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1's per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3's complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases. On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations. In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.
bullets: Characterizes diagonal equivalence via commuting, jointly diagonalizable transition families, while distinguishing it from input-output equivalence and tracking conditioning under coordinate changes.
Shows that time-shared token-local matrix maps yield state-mediated kernels equivalent to unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks.
Introduces SSD-MIMO and HybridMamba to support retrieval rank above one and combine real decays, complex rotations, multiple heads, and two-endpoint writes.
Fused kernels improve training time over matched Mamba 1/3 SISO recoveries; Mamba 2 is near parity at SSM-core scope, with memory effects depending on the measurement.
Higher routing ranks improve small-model multi-token recall, but routing gains do not translate to lower language-model loss; the best models remain behind Mamba 3 variants.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical study of state space model architectures for language modeling.
papers.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes diagonally equivalent SSMs, connects them to scalar-mode linear attention, and proposes higher-rank retrieval extensions that improve recall but do not consistently improve language-model loss.

papers.abstract: Theoretical limitations of transformers on state tracking---the ability to track information about entities or variables over long contexts---have motivated new recurrent language modeling (LM) architectures such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN). These architectures have, in particular, been benchmarked against the $S_5$ word problem, a theoretically hard state-tracking task that captures abilities such as code evaluation under arbitrary variable assignment. It, however, remains open whether other, simpler forms of state tracking might both be more relevant in practice and already explain observed differences between these architectures. We propose evaluating state tracking using a hierarchy of word problems with four increasing levels of difficulty: r-trivial, corresponding to immutable assignment to variables in programming; aperiodic, where assignments are mutable; soluble, where assignments are self-referential; and general finite state tracking. Theoretically, we show that the class of problems transformers are thought to length-generalize on does not even contain all aperiodic state tracking. On the other hand, we prove that GDN with positive eigenvalues expresses all aperiodic problems, and the regular languages recognized by certain transformers are precisely all soluble ones, thus providing a fine-grained picture of state tracking capabilities of various architectures. Taking these ideas to practice, we construct StateBench, a 4-tier long-horizon state-tracking benchmark. Our systematic direct training experiments across architectures largely align with theoretical expectation, albeit with interesting observations at very large scale length-generalization. Additionally, we also evaluate pretrained models---both open hybrid and closed frontier ones---on StateBench, finding that none of them robustly solves even soluble state tracking, suggesting a direction for future improvement.
bullets: State tracking is organized into r-trivial, aperiodic, soluble, and general finite-state problems of increasing difficulty.
Theoretical results show transformers may fail on some aperiodic tracking, while Gated DeltaNet can express all aperiodic problems; certain transformers correspond precisely to soluble problems.
StateBench provides a four-tier, long-horizon benchmark for systematic evaluation across architectures.
Direct training results broadly match theory, but pretrained open and closed models do not robustly solve even soluble state-tracking tasks.
Very large context lengths reveal additional, notable deviations from expected length-generalization behavior.

papers.selection_reason: State tracking hierarchy and benchmark for language model architectures.
papers.title: A Fine-Grained Hierarchy and Benchmark for State Tracking in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a four-level hierarchy and StateBench to analyze and evaluate how language models track state over long contexts.

papers.abstract: Long-lived agents rely on persistent memory of users, tasks and decisions, and this memory must stay consistent with a world that keeps changing. When an upstream fact changes, however, memory systems can revise the contradicted memory itself while the beliefs, plans and actions derived from it remain accepted, even though they have lost their support. We therefore formulate dependency-aware state revision, which asks not only what changed but also which dependent states should no longer be trusted. To address it, StateGraph maintains an evolving state dependency graph whose edges are recovered from interaction histories. Its core design is counterfactual verification: each candidate edge is tested by asking whether the dependent state would survive the loss of its premise, which separates support dependence from semantic relatedness, and revision then invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path survives. To test this design, we introduce StateChangeBench, a controlled benchmark of 50 author-constructed cases annotated with cascade depth, hard negatives and action consequences. On it, StateGraph's Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 percentage points at depth 1 and 26.0 at depth 3+. On public long-term memory benchmarks, its point estimates are comparable to or higher than those of the evaluated baselines on most datasets. These results provide initial evidence that explicit dependency tracking can improve selective memory revision under changing conditions.
bullets: Targets a key consistency problem: revising an upstream fact can leave its dependent memories incorrectly accepted.
Builds an evolving dependency graph from interaction histories.
Uses counterfactual verification to distinguish true support dependence from mere semantic relatedness.
Invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path remains.

On StateChangeBench, its Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 points at depth 1 and 26.0 points at depth 3+; results on public benchmarks are comparable to or higher than evaluated baselines on most datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The StateGraph pipeline. (A) Direct revision settles what the observation itself contradicts, yielding the seed set It. (B) Dependency reasoning—this paper’s contribution—proposes candidates from six bounded sources, then verifies each counterfactually, so the verified graph is a subgraph of the candidate graph. (C) Conservative revision maps each verified edge to a status instead of invalidating everything reachable. (D) Premise and action gating turns status into behavior. Panels correspond to §4.1–§4.5.

Figure 1: A state change is local, but its consequences are not. The new observation contradicts only s1. Left: a system that revises only the contradicted memory marks s1 stale but retains s2, permitting the pending action a1 to confirm an infeasible meeting.
