papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can improve answer accuracy while weakening responsiveness to supporting evidence. We investigate this separation in scientific-document question answering through matched document interventions that change the supported answer while preserving the question and unrelated context. We identify evidence bypass: a student retains an originally correct answer after the document changes to support a different one. On QASPER with a Qwen3-4B student, standard OPD raises original-document accuracy by 3.4 percentage points, lowers counterfactual accuracy by 5.3 points, and increases bypass by 15.7 points; the same directional pattern appears on PeerQA. Controlled perturbations localize the shift to answer-critical evidence, and bypass grows with the student's pre-distillation closed-book preference for the original answer. A factorized study of teacher targets, privileged information, divergence, and supervision density finds that explicitly supplying the teacher with annotated answer-critical spans yields the largest joint improvement in evidence response and claim support. These findings motivate Evidence-Paired OPD (EP-OPD), which combines on-policy supervision on matched documents supporting different answers to the same question with an answer-level margin that favors each document's supported answer over its paired alternative. Across both datasets and two student sizes, EP-OPD recovers 54-66% of standard OPD's counterfactual-accuracy loss while preserving 80-85% of its original-document accuracy gain. Our results establish evidence responsiveness as a distinct training and evaluation target alongside answer accuracy. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/EP-OPD.
bullets: Identifies “evidence bypass”: students retain an original answer even when matched document edits support a different answer.
On QASPER, standard OPD increases original-document accuracy by 3.4 points but decreases counterfactual accuracy by 5.3 points and increases bypass by 15.7 points; PeerQA shows the same pattern.
Bypass is localized to answer-critical evidence and is stronger when the student initially prefers the original answer in closed-book settings.
Teacher access to annotated answer-critical spans provides the largest joint improvement in evidence response and claim support among tested factors.
EP-OPD recovers 54–66% of OPD’s counterfactual-accuracy loss while retaining 80–85% of its original-document accuracy gain across two datasets and student sizes.

papers.abstract: Reverse and forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences provide complementary supervision in on-policy distillation: reverse KL refines the student's active token rankings, and forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates. At student-generated prefixes, we form a four-observation matrix by treating the student and teacher as both candidate sources and evaluators. The diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty, while source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives. We establish an exact identity equating the Fisher inverse-metric coupling of their logit gradients with the sum of these contrasts, yielding a common local descent direction for distinct positive distributions. Observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) uses observations to set preferences, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update. Across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation, and base-model initialization), OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning and transfers effectively to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/OC-OPD.
bullets: Addresses the complementary roles of reverse KL for refining active token rankings and forward KL for covering teacher-supported candidates.
Builds a four-observation matrix from student/teacher candidate sources and evaluators at student-generated prefixes.
Uses an exact Fisher inverse-metric identity to align the two KL objectives toward a common local descent direction.
Coordinates gradients via closed-form bargaining and scales updates using distributional discrepancy.
Reports gains in mathematical reasoning with transfer to out-of-distribution scientific QA and code generation across three student settings.

(c) Self-observation values set uncertainty-based priorities for closed-form gradient bargaining, while distributional discrepancy controls supervision strength. papers.abstract: Factual recall in language models is typically framed as retrieving a factual association: a subject--relation pair maps to a single object. However, many facts are context-dependent: the same pair maps to different objects depending on a condition such as time. We introduce anchored factual recall, in which the model receives an explicit conditioning expression, an anchor, and must select the object valid under it. This raises questions that single-object recall does not: where the anchor enters the computation, what it changes, and how that change selects the answer. Focusing on temporal anchors, we answer them with causal interventions on four open-weight models on English prompts and identify two routes. In a subject-mediated route, the anchor resolves the final subject-token representation to the queried year, and the relation redistributes the readout of this state across attention heads. In a direct route] the final position attends to the anchor, and upper-layer MLPs turn this signal into a preference for the time-appropriate object. The two routes are parallel channels: their contributions add up, most queries use both, and their balance depends on the query, e.g., on the relation, consistently across models. This reframes mechanistic accounts of factual recall from retrieving a single stored object to selecting among context-dependent alternatives.
bullets: Introduces anchored factual recall, where a subject–relation pair maps to different objects depending on an explicit condition such as time.
Uses causal interventions on four open-weight models with English prompts to trace how temporal anchors affect recall.
Identifies a subject-mediated route: the anchor makes the subject representation year-specific, while the relation redistributes its readout across attention heads.
Identifies a direct route: the final position attends to the anchor, and upper-layer MLPs favor the time-appropriate object.
Both routes usually contribute additively, with their balance varying by query and relation across models.

papers.abstract: LLM agents operate Web infrastructure from the command line and rely on a return assumption, namely that each tool call returns within a bounded time and with its requested action finished. Many commands, however, ask a question before they act, and the agent's harness either closes the program's input or keeps it open as a terminal at which nobody types. With closed input, the program can return status 0 without the requested action. With open input, it waits until a time limit, and the agent pays in time and tokens. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to measure and repair the return assumption. We collect 91,469 production tool calls and 89,047 public agent trajectories, test how 8 widely used harnesses launch commands, and build Litmus, a catalog of 158 checked command-line invocations, and Tripwire, a benchmark of 25 task pairs that differ only in whether a question guards the requested action. We then propose RECEIPT, which keeps the input open, reads what each process waits for from system calls, and returns this state to an unmodified agent through a model-checked protocol. On Litmus, closed input causes 11.5% of tested invocations to return status 0 without performing the requested action, and 7 of 8 harnesses close input when no terminal is attached. An unanswered question at a plain terminal multiplies a task's token use by 2.9, and the input connection moves an LLM from 7th to 3rd place among 8. Across 5 LLMs, RECEIPT reduces false claims of success by 73.5% and completes all 25 guarded tasks on a second harness. An agent's reliability therefore depends on what its harness lets it observe as well as on its LLM. Agent builders should report what each tool call did, not only how it ended, and benchmark maintainers should fix and report the input connection before they rank LLMs.
bullets: The study examines the return assumption that every tool call finishes its requested action within a bounded time.

Across 91,469 production calls, 89,047 public trajectories, and 8 harnesses, closed input sometimes produces status 0 without performing the requested action, while open input can cause waiting and token waste.
The authors introduce Litmus, a catalog of 158 checked invocations, and Tripwire, a benchmark of 25 task pairs involving question-guarded commands.
RECEIPT keeps input open, observes what processes await through system calls, and reports that state to an unmodified agent using a model-checked protocol.
Across 5 LLMs, RECEIPT reduces false success claims by 73.5% and completes all 25 guarded tasks on a second harness.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.
bullets: Task turn counts often reflect model behavior, while generated difficulty labels poorly predict success.
The paper defines depth as the minimum number of sequential turns required when later commands depend on earlier outputs, separate from total work.
Auditing 734 tasks across six datasets found that 94% of solved synthetic tasks finish within three turns, and depth predicts difficulty beyond work.
DEPTH generates tasks segment by segment in a real software environment, executing each segment before continuing from the resulting state.
Its 105 tasks exceed audited datasets in depth and work; six current models each fail to pass half, and fine-tuning Qwen3-8B improves performance on two terminal benchmarks.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.
bullets: Addresses the generation overhead of explicit chain-of-thought and the limited tool-use interface of implicit reasoning.
Uses compact latent reasoning segments, while retaining textual tokens for tool calls, observations, and final answers.
Evaluated on agentic math and question-answering benchmarks.
Reports accuracy gains of up to 8.8 points and up to 6.8× fewer model forward passes.
Analysis indicates improved tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

papers.abstract: Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback. In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes. The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility
bullets: Models repeated interactions among travelers, traffic conditions, and transportation policies.
Uses persistent agents with defined information access, actions, decision schedules, and traceable feedback records.
Implements LLM travelers selecting routes and departure times, plus a manager adjusting link charges in MATSim.
A preliminary 100-day, five-configuration demonstration verified action constraints, choice execution, and memory preservation.
Enables experiments varying agent information, retained experience, and management feedback; scope is currently experimental with one run per configuration.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave linear-attention layers with a small number of softmax-attention layers. Prior work largely attributes in-context retrieval to softmax attention, treating linear attention primarily as a mechanism for compressing past context. We revisit this division of labor and show that linear attention plays a direct role in retrieval by constructing the query used by softmax attention. Studying Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet) and Granite4.0 (Mamba-2), we identify an Encode--Address circuit. An early Encode block preserves token identity, while an Address block constructs the final-position representation from which a softmax \emph{reader} forms its attention query. Transplanting this representation between prompts with different queried keys redirects retrieval in 0.97--0.99 of cases. The Address block's recurrent state carries the retrieval target, and its computation transfers across architectures: replacing Granite's Address block with Qwen's restores retrieval accuracy to 0.92--0.94 without updating either model's weights. Across six Qwen3.5 models, Address computation becomes distributed at larger scales over a chain of blocks, each guiding a successive reader, as the query no longer passes from one reader to the next through attention. These findings reveal a division of labor in hybrid retrieval: linear attention constructs the query, while softmax attention performs the lookup. Code is available at https://github.com/yuang-chen/LinearQuery
bullets: Identifies an Encode–Address circuit: early linear-attention blocks preserve token identity, while later blocks build the final-position representation used by a softmax reader.
Transplanting the Address representation between prompts redirects retrieval in 0.97–0.99 of cases.
The retrieval target is carried in recurrent state, and Address computation transfers across Qwen3.5 and Granite4.0 architectures.
Replacing Granite’s Address block with Qwen’s restores retrieval accuracy to 0.92–0.94 without changing model weights.
At larger Qwen3.5 scales, Address computation becomes distributed across a chain of blocks and readers.

papers.title: Who Asks, Who Answers: Linear Attention Builds the Query in Hybrid Language Models
papers.tldr: In hybrid language models, linear attention constructs the retrieval query while softmax attention performs the lookup.

papers.abstract: When user queries are incomplete, large language models should ask targeted questions before committing to an answer, a capability we call proactive elicitation, yet evaluation on real user-assistant queries across seven LLMs (8B to frontier) shows that fewer than 11% of underspecified queries trigger a follow-up question. To benchmark and train this capability, we introduce VagueBench, where each seed query is annotated with structured intent and detail units then degraded into intent-vague and fully-vague variants via controlled removal of linguistic cues, yielding known hidden information sets for evaluating both when and what to ask. We propose DialogGRPO, an offline reinforcement learning method that organizes multi-turn elicitation as a dialogue-state directed acyclic graph, where candidate questions at each node receive dense turn-level rewards combining immediate information gain with lookahead value through group-relative comparison, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without runtime simulation. DialogGRPO elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries with substantial gains in both recovery efficiency and answer coverage, without over-asking on complete queries, outperforms prompting and test-time-scaling baselines, and generalizes zero-shot to MultiWOZ 2.4 and AmbigQA.
bullets: Fewer than 11% of underspecified queries prompt follow-up questions across seven evaluated LLMs.
VagueBench creates controlled intent-vague and fully-vague queries with known missing information for evaluating when and what models should ask.
DialogGRPO uses a dialogue-state DAG and dense rewards based on information gain and lookahead value to train multi-turn elicitation.
The method elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries, improving recovery efficiency and answer coverage without over-asking on complete queries.
It outperforms prompting and test-time-scaling baselines and generalizes zero-shot to MultiWOZ 2.4 and AmbigQA.

papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.
bullets: Recurrent models require separate treatment of extra-state weights/activations and the recurrent state itself.
Decayed recurrences develop fewer residual outlier channels than softmax attention, reducing the need for incoherence processing.
LoReS combines value-axis scale grouping, decay-aware mixed precision, and stochastic rounding to control recurrent-state quantization error.
It supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower precision for shorter decode horizons across several large models.
A vLLM implementation demonstrates end-to-end decoding speedups.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows organize complex tasks into reusable procedures. However, invoking an LLM at every step incurs repeated inference costs and delays. We propose a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows through semantic task decomposition. Each subtask has explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the decomposition and update these procedures. Experiments in the GLEE competition show the framework on bargaining, negotiation and persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in code. Code is available at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/NeurIPS2026_SeaFlow.
bullets: Addresses the repeated inference cost and latency of invoking LLMs at every workflow step.
Represents each subtask with explicit applicability conditions and an executable procedure.
Uses execution feedback to refine task decompositions and update procedures over time.
Evaluated in the GLEE competition on bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion tasks.
Observed final-decision procedures were mostly implemented in code.

papers.abstract: Residents who contact a community service desk about a repair or a service charge need answers they can act on, with facts that hold for their case and commitments the desk can keep. In tool-augmented LLM agents, such facts come from documents and records, and the conduct of a service answer is usually specified in a system prompt. We present NEIGHBOR, an LLM agent for community resident services that trains this conduct into the model that drives its tools. NEIGHBOR is deployed on a live resident-service platform for a district of an East Asian city of more than ten million people. It adapts Qwen3-235B-A22B with LoRA on 7,824 supervised fine-tuning examples built from public community-service materials around six service-behaviour targets, among them commitment control and human referral, and the adapted model plans document retrieval and read-only text-to-SQL over the resident's own records. In an offline evaluation with seven configurations, an independent domain expert rated all 350 answers to 50 stratified held-out queries. NEIGHBOR scores 7.74/10 against 5.86 for the same agent running the un-tuned model (+1.88; paired Wilcoxon $p<10^{-8}$; higher on 46 of 50 queries) and improves all six rated dimensions. No tool-augmented answer received a red-line flag (standalone models: 8-14% of answers). An LLM judge ranks the seven configurations much as the expert does (Spearman $ρ=0.93$). Its rubric counts specifics absent from the reference answer as fabricated, so it scores tool-grounded answers 1-2 points lower, enough to change which configuration ranks first. For resident-facing agents, service behaviour is a practical fine-tuning target that raises expert-rated answer quality with the tools held fixed.
bullets: Targets six service behaviors, including controlling commitments and referring cases to humans.
Uses LoRA fine-tuning on 7,824 supervised examples while retaining document retrieval and read-only text-to-SQL tools.
In an expert evaluation, the tuned agent scored 7.74/10 versus 5.86/10 for the untuned agent across 50 queries.
The tuned agent improved all six rated dimensions, and no tool-augmented answer received a red-line safety flag.
LLM-judge rankings broadly matched expert rankings, but the judge penalized grounded specifics absent from reference answers.

papers.abstract: LLM-based role-playing agents are fluent at imitating a character's style, yet struggle to make role-consistent decisions over long narrative horizons. Such decisions are shaped by experiences spanning many prior scenes, which are often partial and may point in different directions. Existing methods inject cross-scene memories as context, but do not reason about how past events shape a character's current motivations and behavior. We propose MemRole, a framework that makes this memory-to-decision process explicit. It introduces Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), a reasoning schema that decomposes hidden reasoning into context understanding, memory activation, and response strategy planning, trained on a novel-derived dataset whose character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools limit each character to what it could plausibly know at the current narrative point. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we propose Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD): the model critiques its own rollouts against the reference under a data-driven rubric, and a critique-conditioned teacher view of the same model distills token-level guidance back into the policy. MemRole-32B improves over its backbone by 15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing, performs on par with frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.4, and achieves the best character-motivation recognition accuracy on CroSS-MR.
bullets: Addresses role inconsistency when prior experiences are partial, conflicting, and spread across many narrative scenes.
Uses Long-Horizon Memory Thinking to understand context, activate relevant memories, and plan response strategies.
Trains on character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools that restrict knowledge to what a character could plausibly know.
Adds Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation, where self-critiques guide token-level policy refinement.
MemRole-32B improves its backbone by 15.2 points, matches reported frontier-LLM performance, and leads on CroSS-MR character-motivation recognition.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-to-decision reasoning for long-horizon role-playing LLM agents fits LLM memory research.
papers.title: MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents
papers.tldr: MemRole improves long-horizon role-playing by explicitly turning character memories into motivations, decisions, and response plans.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.
bullets: Addresses fixed experience-retrieval pipelines that do not adapt experience use to task context.
Uses a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller to choose among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL actions.
Jointly decides whether to invoke experience, which memory format to use, and when to consolidate guidance.
Updates both the experience memory and routing policy online from task feedback.
Across four benchmarks and four backbones, improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points and reduces token use by 5.7–62.5× versus ACE with GPT-5.2.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of OMCE. The lightweight Meta-Controller selects a cognitive action specifying whether and which experience to inject into the task prompt. The agent solves the task with the augmented context containing the query and any injected experience. Memory evolution records outcomes in episodic memory, distills guidance before execution when DISTILL is selected, and refines injected guidance afterward using task feedback.

Figure 1: From Fixed Pipelines to Learned Meta-Control. Up: Existing methods typically follow a fixed routine for using and consolidating experience, even when the retrieved experience does not help the current task. Down: OMCE learns from task feedback when to use experience, whether to draw on past cases or general guidance, and when to distill new guidance.
Figure 4: Self-correction detection in MultiChallenge. The meta-controller routes the query to GUIDE (aGUIDE) rather than to episodic cases that enforce the user’s outdated constraint.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation of LLM agents with evolving experience memory and meta-control routing.
papers.title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents
papers.tldr: OMCE enables LLM agents to learn when and how to use accumulated experience during test-time adaptation, improving first-attempt success while substantially reducing token use.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read knowledge-graph facts ranked by relevance, leaving open whether they suffice or conflict. Our checks use relation knowledge, written by hand or learned from training questions labelled with their relation paths. It selects a compact context of facts yielding an answer, and derives it; a derivability check tests whether an answer follows, a consistency check whether facts conflict, and a validation-chosen routing gate decides where the derived answer replaces the LLM's. Seven open LLMs read the compact context better in exact match than relevance-ranked facts; on ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) they match SubgraphRAG's facts at a quarter of the prompt tokens, and stronger LLMs read SubgraphRAG's better. Where the routing gate passes, ours leads SubgraphRAG's in exact match in all 53 LLM, benchmark and prompt settings. A precision gate, returning the derived answer only when the check passes with exactly one derived entity, answered 18 and 5 percent of held-out WebQSP and CWQ questions in a pre-specified test, right for 90 and 96 percent. The consistency check judges facts by path evidence only where another path joins their entities, true of 2.5 percent of named-entity facts in our compact WebQSP and CWQ contexts.
bullets: The work addresses whether relevance-ranked graph facts are sufficient or may conflict when LLMs answer questions.
Hand-written or learned relation knowledge selects facts along answer-supporting relation paths and derives an answer.
Derivability and consistency checks, combined with a validation-selected routing gate, determine when to replace the LLM’s answer.
Across seven open LLMs, compact contexts outperform relevance-ranked facts in exact match; on CWQ, they match SubgraphRAG’s facts using one-quarter as many prompt tokens.
A precision-only gate answered 18% of WebQSP and 5% of CWQ held-out questions, with 90% and 96% accuracy respectively; consistency checks applied to only 2.5% of named-entity facts.

papers.selection_reason: Knowledge-graph context selection and routing for LLMs, relevant to external memory retrieval and LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Less but Sufficient: Relation Knowledge Selects Compact Knowledge-Graph Contexts, and What External Checks Can and Cannot Catch
papers.tldr: Relation-aware selection builds compact knowledge-graph contexts that preserve answerability while external checks help decide when to trust derived answers over LLM outputs.

papers.abstract: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce complete reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline, yet MemUse shows that most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. It also surfaces effects that outcomes hide: 23.2\% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.
bullets: Evaluates memory at its point of use by comparing each delivery with the agent’s visible context and tracing subsequent actions and consequences.
An agentic judge scores relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect, with programmatic evidence checks and fixed aggregation rules.
Across 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes and three memory systems, resolve rates stayed within 0.4 percentage points of the no-memory baseline.
Most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and two systems often repeated information already visible to the agent.
Memory effects were not captured by outcomes alone: 23.2% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, while 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MemUse. The memory bridge connects agents to memory systems and annotates memory operations. The trajectory recorder captures model calls, with token usage and cost when available. Within each episode, data processing groups identical repeated deliveries into injection spans while earlier copies remain visible and assigns each entry a credit window for attributing actions. The memory graph links deliveries to recorded entry histories across trajectories. For each eligible span, an agentic judge assesses each entry’s information quality, use, and observed effects from its exposed text, prior context, and subsequent trajectory. Programmatic checks enforce evidence coverage and credit windows, and fixed rules derive the span verdict.

Figure 2: Credit windows and judge routing. (a) A’s deliveries at steps 2 and 4 share S1; re-entry after removal starts S4 with a fresh prior context. (b) The shorter copy A′ adds no text or identifier beyond the visible A, so A′ in S3 receives an empty window and A in S1 retains credit through step 9. Effects of credited actions are followed through the episode end. (c) S1, S2, and S4 are judged; S3 receives a rule-derived neutral triage label without a judge call. Empty deliveries receive a neutral placeholder and are excluded from triage rates.

Figure 3: Six-axis memory profiles, pooled over four runs per configuration, with each profiled span weighted equally. (a) The radar plot uses a common logarithmic radial scale from 0.001% at the center to 100% at the outer ring, with tenfold increases between adjacent rings. (b) Heatmap cells report the same means as percentages, with shading on the same logarithmic scale. Lower harm shares are better. Table 7 reports these shares alongside uncertainty and token efficiency.

Figure 4: Memory effects concealed by task outcomes. (a) A TencentDB skill for a different Napoleon bug directs the agent into the wrong component (steps 2–5). A reproduction rules out Napoleon at step 7, and the agent fixes sphinx/util/docfields.py at step 9; the task passes despite the detour. (b) A MemGovern card guides the agent to add a subset handler at step 8, changing the reported subset check from None to True. The equality error persists, and at step 14 the agent decides to leave it unfixed despite the card’s advice to repair it; the task fails. Timelines show complete episodes with steps numbered locally. Arrows mark first consumption, shading marks credit windows, and blue steps mark actions based on memory. Red and green annotations highlight problems and repairs. Memory effects are judge assessments; task outcomes come from the SWEbench harness.

Figure 5: Delivered-token and beneficial-entry shares by delivery form. Circles show each form’s share of estimated delivered tokens, including restatements, and diamonds show its share of beneficial entries. Relevance is the mean entry share across profiled spans; token efficiency divides beneficial-entry counts by all estimated delivered tokens, including restatements and spans without profiles. (b) Effect counts are pooled across four runs and divided by the number of acted-on entries, n. Labels give improved and undetermined shares; every segment retains its proportional width.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a point-of-use evaluation framework for LLM agent memory, fitting the LLM memory topic.
papers.title: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
papers.tldr: MemUse evaluates whether an agent actually uses delivered memory and what effects that use has, revealing that outcome metrics alone can hide substantial memory waste and harm.

papers.abstract: Query-conditioned sparse KV selection reduces long-context inference cost by attending to a subset of historical KV entries at each decoding step. Existing selectors must wait for the target-layer query before scoring candidates and generating indices, placing routing on the immediate pre-attention path. We introduce EarlySelectKV, a training-free transformation that uses proxy queries from earlier hidden states to precompute selected KV indices while retaining the real target-layer query for final attention. Tests with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki show no consistent pattern of quality degradation across the evaluated settings. In the primary RocketKV evaluation, ES-RocketKV differs by +0.018 points on LongBench, approximately -0.01 points on RULER, and +0.25 percentage points on representative NIAH/Passkey settings. In a TensorRT-LLM deployment with CPU-offloaded routing, ES-RocketKV improves end-to-end output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces GPU-resident memory by 11.1% of the combined KV/K-summary pool. This makes routing timing an explicit optimization target alongside KV subset selection in sparse long-context decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/sea-with-sakura/EarlySelectKV.
bullets: Addresses routing latency caused by waiting for each target-layer query before selecting historical KV entries.
Uses a training-free transformation to anticipate selected KV indices from proxy queries in earlier hidden states.
Evaluated with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki, with no consistent quality degradation reported across tested settings.
In TensorRT-LLM with CPU-offloaded routing, improves output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces combined KV/K-summary GPU memory by 11.1%.
Frames routing timing—not only KV subset selection—as an optimization target for sparse long-context inference.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of EarlySelectKV. The main flow gathers selected KV using precomputed page indices and performs sparse attention with the real query. The side flow constructs a proxy query from an earlier hidden state and precomputes next-layer page indices. Early and Mid taps represent two timing–fidelity trade-offs: the former offers a longer preparation window, while the latter provides higher selection fidelity.

Figure 4: Task score comparison between ES-RocketKV and RocketKV on LongBench and RULER. The first row reports LongBench results, while the second and third rows report RULER results under different context lengths.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has been widely adopted in large language models (LLMs) since it reduces the computational cost through sparse expert activation. However, the massive parameter scale of MoE models hinders their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. Although existing mixed-precision quantization reduces the model size, they are inherently static, fixing the bit-width of each expert across decoding steps. Such static schemes yield suboptimal performance as they overlook the dynamic variation in expert importance during decoding. Furthermore, they fail to adapt to the dynamic latency constraint driven by the fluctuating system utilization. To address these challenges, we propose MatMoE, a dynamic mixed-precision quantization framework for efficient MoE inference. MatMoE features: (1) a Matryoshka MoE PTQ algorithm that enables experts to operate flexibly at multiple precisions within a stringent memory budget; (2) a floor-and-compensation quantization method that eliminates redundant memory accesses in the Matryoshka representation; and (3) a dynamic bit-width allocation strategy that determines the precision for each expert based on their routing scores to satisfy the dynamic latency requirement. We implement our MatMoE system atop llama.cpp for both CPU and GPU platforms. Extensive evaluations across three modern MoE models and challenging benchmarks demonstrate that MatMoE achieves $4.0\% \sim 18.3\%$ higher accuracy than state-of-the-art static mixed-precision method. Compared to llama.cpp, MatMoE delivers $1.3\times \sim 3.7\times$ speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, and $1.2\times \sim 1.3\times$ speedup on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Orin.
bullets: Targets the large memory footprint and inflexibility of static mixed-precision quantization for MoE deployment on edge devices.
Uses Matryoshka MoE post-training quantization so experts can operate at multiple precisions within a fixed memory budget.
Introduces floor-and-compensation quantization to reduce redundant memory accesses.
Dynamically allocates expert bit-widths from routing scores to meet changing latency requirements.
Across three MoE models, reports 4.0%–18.3% higher accuracy than a static mixed-precision method and 1.2×–3.7× speedups over llama.cpp across tested CPU/GPU platforms.

papers.title: MatMoE: Matryoshka Mixture-of-Experts with Dynamic Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient Inference

papers.abstract: B2B outbound sales involves high transaction values and relationship-based trust, so closing a deal typically requires multiple rounds of outreach building on prior context. Existing LLM-based sales agents operate within single sessions and cannot carry forward context or refine strategies from experience. Methods that do learn from experience store lessons as unstructured text and treat all outcomes as equally informative, with no mechanism to distinguish a flawed strategy from an external factor. We propose SPAR, a self-evolving framework that models selling strategies as testable hypotheses and refines them without parameter updates. A double-loop architecture lets an inner loop adapt to individual merchants through episodic memory while an outer loop evolves a shared strategy playbook through causal attribution and hypothesis-driven evolution. In a live A/B test on the 1688 platform with over 200,000 merchants, SPAR achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth. Human evaluation by domain experts rates SPAR at 4.62 out of 5 on overall sales quality, the highest among all methods.
bullets: Targets the lack of cross-session memory and strategy refinement in existing LLM-based sales agents.
Models sales strategies as testable hypotheses rather than unstructured lessons.
Uses a double-loop design: episodic memory adapts to merchants, while causal attribution evolves a shared strategy playbook without parameter updates.
In a live 1688-platform A/B test involving over 200,000 merchants, SPAR increased conversion by 15.8% and high-intent merchant growth by 35.8%.
Domain experts rated its overall sales quality 4.62/5, highest among the evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: Concerns about LLM homogeneity are typically quantified with embedding similarity, which reduces two texts to a single score. We revisit homogeneity with 25 interpretable metrics spanning five dimensions: semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural, and stylistic & presentational. A human study shows that perceived similarity depends on both content (what responses say) and form (how they say it), yet embedding similarity correlates less with human meaning judgments than sentence-level matching ($ρ=0.417$ vs. $0.606$) and not significantly with form judgments ($ρ=0.140$). Across 18 contemporary LLMs, models say similar things in different words: they share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but remain distinct in lexical characteristics, structural patterns, and interactional conventions. Across releases from 2024 to 2026, models become more like themselves but not more like one another: among significantly changing metrics, intra-model distances decrease for 17 of 22, and inter-model distances increase for 14 of 21. Across two post-training pipelines, model-specific conventions emerge during SFT and are selectively reshaped by preference optimization. These results suggest that homogeneity is multidimensional and evolving, and that embedding similarity alone can overstate cross-model homogeneity while concealing diverging intra- and inter-model trends.
bullets: A 25-metric framework covers semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural, and stylistic/presentational similarity.

Human-perceived similarity reflects both response content and form; sentence-level matching aligns better with meaning judgments than embeddings, while embeddings do not significantly track form judgments.
Across 18 contemporary LLMs, responses share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but differ in lexical, structural, and interactional characteristics.
From 2024–2026, models become more consistent with themselves without becoming more alike: intra-model distances generally shrink while inter-model distances often grow.
SFT introduces model-specific conventions, and preference optimization selectively reshapes them.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes LLM homogeneity using multidimensional metrics, contributing to the understanding of LLM behavior and architecture.
papers.title: Revisiting LLM Homogeneity Through a Multidimensional Lens
papers.tldr: LLM homogeneity is multidimensional: models share broad meaning but differ in wording, structure, style, and interaction conventions, which embedding similarity alone fails to capture.

papers.abstract: Homogeneous gradient functions have widespread significance, including applications in maximum energy subspace selection and retrieval problems. Euler's homogeneous function theorem specifies how the potential associated with a positively k-homogeneous gradient field can be recovered directly from the field itself. We use Euler's theorem to build on GradNets and propose a homogeneous gradient network architecture that is guaranteed to correspond to the gradient of a homogeneous function. Then, we describe how monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate the gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions. The inductive bias of homogeneous GradNets enables them to outperform baseline ICNNs by up to 7dB in our max energy subspace projection experiment and by up to 13% higher accuracy, 98% fewer parameters, and 70% fewer FLOPS in our amortized inner product search experiment.
bullets: Addresses learning gradient fields with positive homogeneity, relevant to energy-based subspace selection and retrieval.
Uses Euler’s homogeneous function theorem to construct GradNets guaranteed to be gradients of homogeneous functions.
Shows monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions.
Outperforms baseline ICNNs in max-energy subspace projection and amortized inner-product search experiments, with reported gains in quality and efficiency.

papers.tldr: A homogeneous gradient network architecture learns gradients of homogeneous functions while guaranteeing valid gradient structure and enabling efficient applications.

papers.abstract: Representation steering methods like difference-in-means (DIM) offer a lightweight approach to controlling LLM behavior, but their effectiveness varies widely across concepts, datasets, and layers, making principled deployment costly without exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps. We build on the discriminability index $d'$, a compute-cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive training activations separate along the steering direction. Across five behaviors on 3 models, we demonstrate uses beyond its established role as a dataset-level steerability predictor. First, in the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting, we show that $d'$ reliably identifies performant layers at which to steer, eliminating the need for a layer-wise sweep. Second, we extend this analysis to open-ended multi-token generation, and find that $d'$ remains successful for layer selection across different settings. Lastly, we test whether the position of a generated token's representation on the DIM line predicts steering success on that individual example. In the MCQA setting, this works for high-$d'$ datasets but is inconsistent across behaviors, models, and training-token choices in open-ended generation. This highlights that methods developed and conclusions drawn in single-token MCQA settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.
bullets: The study uses the discriminability index, d′, to measure how well contrastive activations separate along a steering direction.
Across five behaviors and three models, d′ identifies effective steering layers in MCQA without exhaustive layer-wise sweeps.
d′ also supports layer selection for open-ended multi-token generation across multiple settings.
A token’s position on the DIM line predicts individual-example steering success for high-d′ MCQA datasets, but is inconsistent in open-ended generation.
Results caution against assuming that single-token MCQA findings generalize directly to open-ended generation.

papers.selection_reason: Uses activation-steering geometry to reduce hyperparameter search and select layers in LLMs, directly relevant to language foundation model control.
papers.title: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search
papers.tldr: Activation-separation geometry can reduce layer-search costs for activation steering, but example-level predictions transfer inconsistently from MCQA to open-ended generation.

papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time by adding a vector to their internal representations. Most work asks how to build that vector, and far less attention has gone to where to add it, even though steering at a poorly chosen layer can be worse than not steering at all. Prior selectors choose a layer without ever steering the model to test it: they score how separable the target behavior is at that layer, and how consistently the individual examples point along the steering direction. We argue that what matters is not the separability of the two activation clouds, nor the alignment of individual displacements with their mean, but the extent of the cloud of per-example displacements that mean-difference steering averages. We propose a topology-based layer selection method, called TopoSteer, which scores a layer by the total H_0 persistence of its displacement cloud, computed as the length of the cloud's Euclidean minimum spanning tree. We show that the score focuses on the displacement cloud's relative geometry, while class separation affects it only through standardization. We also provide a theoretical explanation for our method by proving that, as example-level variation increases, TopoSteer and discriminability move in opposite directions, so the two criteria can rank layers in opposite ways. Across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer provides a principled alternative to discriminability- and separability-based layer selection and yields more effective steering without requiring held-out validation.
bullets: Layer choice is crucial: steering at a poor layer can underperform doing nothing.
It replaces separability and displacement-alignment criteria with total H₀ persistence—the Euclidean minimum spanning tree length of the displacement cloud.
The method captures relative displacement geometry, with class separation affecting the score only through standardization.
Theory shows that increasing example-level variation can make TopoSteer and discriminability rank layers oppositely.
Across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer yields more effective steering without held-out validation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Layer choice decides the outcome, and LayerNavigator and TOPOSTEER choose differently. (a) Single-layer steering performance against depth (conscientiousness, Llama-8B) with the unsteered baseline, and the layer each method ranks highest (K=1). (b) Why they differ: two layers from the family of Theorem 1, with the same class means and the same steering vector, differing only in the scale of example-level variation. Top: activations, each contrastive pair joined by its displacement δil (grey arrows), with the mean difference µδ in blue. With large variation, the two classes overlap, so discriminability D drops, while the displacements keep a common direction but vary widely in length. Bottom: the same displacements drawn from a common origin form the displacement cloud ∆l; connectivity length L is the length of its spanning tree (orange), which by Corollary 1 does not see the offset µδ at all. The large-variation layer is therefore scored higher by TOPOSTEER and lower by LayerNavigator, whose full score D + C also drops. All values shown are computed from the data drawn; the construction is the one of Appendix F.

papers.title: TopoSteer: Topological Layer Selection for Activation Steering in LLMs
papers.tldr: TopoSteer selects activation-steering layers by measuring the topological spread of per-example displacement vectors, improving steering without held-out validation.

papers.abstract: Causal masking obstructs the column balancing used by optimal-transport (OT) attention. We study an unbalanced OT operator that uses only current and earlier rows and characterize its induced positional prior. For bounded scores and any fixed balancing strength below one, its fixed point assigns vanishing mass to every fixed window as context grows. With constant scores, the prior has an exact scale-invariant form. We classify positional encodings by whether they prevent this dilution. We also derive finite-length window-mass bounds for log-distance priors with exponents near one. Preregistered experiments use 25M- and 100M-parameter language models. The OT operator improves loss extrapolation over softmax, while exploratory comparisons favor an explicit distance bias at a fraction of the cost. Changing only the bias beyond the training length moves long-context loss in the predicted direction on all 30 tested checkpoints. During training, learned exponents approach one even when constrained above it. A margin chosen from prior calculations controls distant-mass growth in the tested setting.
bullets: Causal masking prevents standard OT column balancing, motivating an unbalanced OT operator over current and earlier rows.
For bounded scores and fixed balancing strength below one, mass in any fixed-size window vanishes as context length grows; constant scores yield an exact scale-invariant prior.
The work classifies positional encodings by whether they prevent this dilution and derives finite-length bounds for log-distance priors with exponents near one.
Experiments with 25M- and 100M-parameter language models show improved loss extrapolation over softmax, while explicit distance bias performs favorably at a fraction of the cost.
Modifying only the bias beyond the training length shifts long-context loss as predicted across 30 checkpoints; learned exponents approach one in training.

papers.selection_reason: Studies causal optimal-transport attention, positional priors, and length extrapolation for language models, directly relevant to long-context LLM research.
papers.title: Causal Optimal-Transport Attention: Positional Priors and Length Extrapolation
papers.tldr: Causal OT attention develops a scale-invariant positional prior that can dilute local attention over long contexts, but suitable distance-based biases can improve length extrapolation at lower cost.

papers.abstract: Resource managers typically encode what to do in a task-specific policy---a heuristic, an optimization procedure, or a model trained for the task---that must be developed before use and may need revision as the workload or system changes. We propose bypassing policy development and instead asking pretrained models to make resource-management decisions directly, given the current system state, desired outcome, and available choices. We evaluate this approach on microservice autoscaling, DRAM sizing, and video encoding, using a frontier LLM and two small decision models. On two microservice applications, a small decision model meets latency targets while using within 10% of the replicas allocated by policy-based autoscalers and within 13% of the frontier LLM. In DRAM sizing, a small decision model reduces DRAM usage by up to 27.5% relative to static provisioning while maintaining at least 95% of baseline performance. In video encoding, it completes encodes up to 4.3$\times$ faster than the frontier LLM, with an imperceptible 1.1-point decrease in Video Multi-Method Assessment Fusion (VMAF), a metric of perceptual video quality. Making individual resource-management decisions may be considerably simpler than developing a general strategy for making them.
bullets: Targets changing workloads and systems where hand-designed or trained policies require development and revision.
Provides models with the current system state, desired outcome, and available choices to select resource-management actions.
Evaluates the approach on microservice autoscaling, DRAM sizing, and video encoding using a frontier LLM and two small decision models.

Small decision models meet stated performance goals with competitive resource use, reduce DRAM usage by up to 27.5% while retaining at least 95% of baseline performance, and encode video up to 4.3× faster than the frontier LLM.
Scope is demonstrated across three resource-management tasks; the abstract does not establish that direct model invocation universally replaces specialized policies.

papers.abstract: Assigning GWAS variants to causal genes requires evidence from multiple resources. We present V2G, an agentic pipeline that records evidence retrieval and returns ranked genes alongside the retrieved evidence. We evaluate whether language-model reranking improves gene prioritisation and whether its gains depend on the retrieved evidence or recall of known associations. On 135 held-out loci where candidate retrieval succeeded and Open Targets L2G predicts, reranking by a language model improves Precision@1 over the evidence ordering it receives, 0.793 against 0.711 (+0.081, 95% CI +0.038 to +0.129), and over nearest-gene assignment (+0.178); no difference from Open Targets L2G or from training-membership baselines was detected. Given only the trait and the candidate gene symbols, in shuffled order, the same model scores 0.864 on these loci (three seeds, 0.859 - 0.867) and names the reference gene at 0.594 of the loci where the pipeline never retrieved it; with each gene's symbol moved to another gene's evidence row it follows the top-scored row and scores 0.284. The gain over the evidence ordering is recall of known genes, and the evidence as presented anchors the model to the ordering rather than informing it. Across the 296 held-out loci (five seeds each) the model keeps the given top candidate at 86% of decisions; at naturally retrieved loci its departures select a reference gene in 85% of departure decisions (31 of 37 loci), and none displaced one. Its calls carry trait-matched mouse mutant or Mendelian phenotype annotations more often than other candidates at the same locus. Train-test overlap is reported throughout. The study includes a frozen benchmark, cached predictions and reproduction code.
bullets: Evaluated on held-out GWAS loci with retrieved candidate genes and Open Targets L2G predictions.
Language-model reranking improved Precision@1 over the supplied evidence ordering (0.793 vs 0.711), but not over Open Targets L2G or training-membership baselines.
With only trait and gene symbols, the model often identified reference genes, indicating gains depended on known-gene recall.
Swapping gene symbols across evidence rows caused the model to follow the top-scored row, showing sensitivity to presentation order.
At naturally retrieved loci, departures from the top candidate selected a reference gene in 31 of 37 cases; train-test overlap was reported.

figures.caption: Figure 1: An agentic variant-to-gene pipeline and a locus where the evidence ordering is incorrect. a, Pipeline stages. Each is a separate, recorded tool call: the genome build is inferred from the coordinates and GRCh37 input lifted to GRCh38; linkage disequilibrium is computed from local 1000 Genomes panels across five ancestry groups; loci are fine-mapped to credible sets by approximate Bayes factor or SuSiE; per-candidate evidence is retrieved gene by gene; and a language model reasons over the assembled evidence and returns a ranked list citing what it used, so any call can be traced to the measurements behind it. b, The evidence retrieved at 2:21155063 A>G, associated with LDL cholesterol (study GCST90002412, a held-out test locus). Score is the composite evidence score that determines the order in which candidates are presented; Dist is the distance from the lead variant to the gene’s transcription start site; eQTL is the number of GTEx v8 tissues with a significant eQTL; PP.H4 is the posterior probability of colocalization; OT L2G is the Open Targets locus-to-gene score. The curated gold gene, APOB, is shaded. All four candidates colocalize at PP.H4 ≥ 0.99; therefore, colocalization cannot discriminate between them, and Open Targets returns no L2G prediction at this locus. c, Ranking before and after the reasoning step. The composite score ranks TDRD15 first on proximity (31 kb, against 111 kb for APOB); the model promotes APOB in all five seeds, with rationales that cite its role in LDL particles (prior knowledge rather than a retrieved measurement). With the open-weights backbone (Qwen3-32B) the ordering is left unchanged in all five seeds. The values shown are the stored benchmark evidence, reproduced in Supplementary Table 7. Of these, the evaluated prompt showed the score and the eQTL and colocalisation flags; the distance, tissue count, PP.H4 and L2G columns were not shown (Methods).

Figure 4: The deployed implementation and what a user receives. The figure describes the application; the benchmark runs evaluated in this study used a narrower prompt (Methods, Reasoning, and output); therefore, panel a is not a description of the evaluated configuration. a, Deployment boundary. The application is distributed as a container image and runs inside the user’s own institution. The summary statistics are read inside the container and never leave it. Build inference, linkage disequilibrium, fine-mapping, expression-QTL retrieval, colocalization, Mendelian randomization, and reporting execute against local reference data. Annotation, the Open Targets, gnomAD, and GTEx lookups, and drug-target scoring send variant coordinates and alleles or gene symbols to public services, and the GWAS Catalog browser sends trait and study identifiers; the optional reasoning step sends the candidate genes, locus record, and assembled per-gene evidence to a language-model endpoint with a key the user supplies, and each such request is logged before it is sent as host, model, message count, and payload size, with no key and no prompt text. b, The audit trail behind a single call, shown for the locus of Fig. 1. The called gene is the consensus prediction of five GPT-5.2 runs; each row is that gene’s value in the released benchmark record, and the rationale is the text stored for it in the first run, quoted verbatim. The evaluated prompt held only the composite score and the eQTL and colocalisation flags for this gene (Supplementary Note 7); the panel marks which rows were shown. The rationale’s ‘lipid eQTL’ is an inference from the trait name, not a retrieved tissue: no tissue was supplied. A field the record does not hold is printed as not recorded rather than inferred: the fine-mapping method is not stored per locus, no coding consequence was flagged for this gene (which does not by itself show the variant is non-coding), and Open Targets returned no prediction. The colocalization value is computed from incomplete regional inputs (Methods). This schematic of the interface is generated from the recorded benchmark data.

Figure 2: The pipeline’s contribution is a rare, high-precision intervention rather than a uniformly better ranking. a, Frequency of each backbone departing from the order in which candidates were presented over 1,480 locus–seed decisions per backbone (296 held-out loci × 5 seeds). GPT-5.2 departed at 212 decisions (14.3%); Qwen3-32B departed once (0.1%), and its Precision@1 was consequently identical to the composite evidence ordering in every seed (0.395 in both cases, all five seeds; at that one locus, neither the initial nor the promoted gene was the reference gene). Bars represent counts over decisions, not loci; the 212 GPT-5.2 departures occur at 60 loci. b, Outcome of the 142 departures (37 loci) made by GPT-5.2 on loci whose reference gene was retrieved naturally, that is, excluding loci where the reference gene had to be added to the candidate set. A total of 120 promoted a reference gene (85%; 31 loci), and 22 did not (7 loci; one locus appeared in both counts because its seeds were split between the two outcomes). *Harmful count departures that displaced a candidate that was already a reference gene; its denominator was all 212 departures, including those on force-added loci, and none occurred. c, Paired outcomes against each comparator on the primary split (135 natural loci at which Open Targets also returned a prediction). The bars show discordant loci only (those where exactly one of the two methods is correct), because concordant loci carry no information in a paired test. The nearest gene was determined by the GENCODE TSS distance. P values are two-sided exact McNemar tests on discordant counts, unadjusted. The full results across all splits are presented in Supplementary Table 1.

Figure 3: The pipeline’s calls and curated reference genes carry trait-matched phenotype annotation more often than other candidates at the locus. Support is assessed against mouse mutant phenotypes (MGI, all allele classes) and human Mendelian disease phenotypes (HPO), with trait and phenotype terms mapped to 18 organ-system categories by versioned rules. These annotations are not GWAS associations but are not independent of the literature either (Results). Predictions are the consensus GPT-5.2 gene per locus. A gene is supported at a locus when any of its phenotype categories meets any of the trait’s. a, Support by arm, shown as supported/annotated loci out of 295 eligible loci, with 95% bootstrap intervals over loci; the random-candidate arm is the expected support of one uniformly drawn other candidate, so its count is fractional. Because mouse mutants are pleiotropic (an annotated gene carries a mean of 6.8 of the 18 categories), absolute rates are not interpretable on their own, and only within-locus differences are. b, Within-locus paired contrasts. Bars are the difference in support between the two arms at the same locus, with 95% intervals from a bootstrap over clusters of loci sharing a reference gene; n is the number of loci where both arms have an annotated gene. q values are Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted across the 11 contrasts for this source (exact McNemar or sign-flip permutation tests); solid fill marks q < 0.05 and hatched fill q ≥ 0.05. All contrasts, by source, are in Supplementary Table 5. Seed 20261017.

Force-added loci (reference gene added to the candidate set by the benchmark and so buried by construction) are reported separately from natural loci, with the pooled result alongside. The primary analysis is the natural loci where Open Targets also returns a prediction; it is conditional on candidate retrieval and Open Targets coverage. The lower two rows are diagnostics, not comparators: both reach 1.000 on force-added loci, which is the artifact those loci create rather than a result. Open Targets is scored with uncovered loci as failures; the other estimands are in Table 2. Every rate is rounded once from its count; the full grid with counts and Wilson intervals is Supplementary Table 1.

Accuracy where Open Targets predicts (split by whether the credible set comes from the locus’s own study), accuracy with abstentions scored as failures, and, as a combined method rather than Open Targets alone, accuracy when the first stored candidate is credited where it abstains. Quoting the first alone flatters a method permitted to decline, while quoting the second alone penalizes abstention.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM reranking for gene prioritization in a bioinformatics pipeline. A standard application of LLMs, relevant to Large Language Models.
papers.title: An auditable agentic pipeline for variant-to-gene prioritisation, validated against orthogonal functional evidence
papers.tldr: V2G is an auditable variant-to-gene pipeline, but its language-model reranking gains mainly reflect recall of known associations and evidence-row ordering rather than independent use of biological evidence.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can autonomously run neuroimaging analyses from research questions to reported findings. Existing agentic systems use tools to check that code runs and reported values match its output, but rely on LLM judgment to decide which results warrant scientific reporting. We show that LLM judges endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is presented as evidence. We present \textbf{CONFIRM}, a framework that separates running an analysis from deciding which findings to report. CONFIRM encodes each hypothesis as a machine-readable, pre-specified analysis plan that fixes the claim and its pass criteria before computing results. It then filters results through five deterministic gates (search history and multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication) under three configurable reporting standards, from least to most demanding: \textit{Screen}, \textit{Replicate}, and \textit{Full}. Failed claims receive diagnoses that guide follow-up analyses. To evaluate reporting decisions at the claim level, we introduce \textbf{NeuroClaimBench}, comprising 489 executable neuroimaging claims with frozen data, including literature-supported findings and 150 controls designed to violate individual methodological requirements. On NeuroClaimBench, CONFIRM falsely supports at most 3\% of controls, compared with 23--38\% for the baselines, while recovering up to 61\% of literature-supported claims. When auditing an existing agent, CONFIRM reduces false support on controls from 23\% to 0\% while retaining the agent's literature-supported claims. Its diagnostic feedback also produces more supported revisions than Self-Refine with fewer LLM calls. Together, CONFIRM and NeuroClaimBench show that basing reporting decisions on pre-specified analysis plans and deterministic gates is essential for trustworthy autonomous scientific discovery.
bullets: LLM judges can endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is explicitly shown.
CONFIRM separates analysis execution from reporting and encodes each hypothesis with fixed claims and pass criteria before analysis.
Five deterministic gates assess multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication under Screen, Replicate, or Full standards.
NeuroClaimBench evaluates 489 executable claims, including 150 controls designed to violate specific methodological requirements.
CONFIRM falsely supported at most 3% of controls versus 23–38% for baselines, while recovering up to 61% of literature-supported claims; audited agents reduced false support from 23% to 0%.

figures.caption: Figure 3: CONFIRM establishes a Pareto-optimal reporting frontier. a, Recovery on literaturesupported claims in the common scalar set (higher is better) versus false support on designed negative controls (lower is better). The dashed curve connects CONFIRM’s three nested reporting standards (Screen, Replicate, Full). Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. b, Accepted controls by failure mode. Each segment is a percentage of all 150 controls (42 site-confounded, 42 broad-search, 42 random-label, 21 underpowered, and 3 nonreplicating).

Figure 2: An abbreviated analysis plan for hippocampal atrophy in Alzheimer’s disease. papers.selection_reason: Introduces CONFIRM, a framework for trustworthy scientific reporting by LLM agents using deterministic gates. This relates to agent memory and verification mechanisms.
papers.title: CONFIRM: Governing Scientific Reporting for Trustworthy Agentic Neuroimaging
papers.tldr: CONFIRM makes autonomous neuroimaging agents’ reporting decisions more trustworthy by enforcing pre-specified claims and deterministic methodological checks instead of relying on LLM judgment alone.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable of writing and executing code, suggesting a natural paradigm for tool-augmented agents: expressing tool use as programs rather than isolated calls. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) captures this idea through loops, batching, abstraction, and structured computation, but existing PTC approaches are largely stateless, limiting their ability to reuse intermediate results and adapt over time. This is problematic for real-world tasks, where tool environments and problem-solving processes are inherently stateful. We therefore present I-PTC, an interactive framework that executes stateful PTC: models issue code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. To evaluate the effectiveness of I-PTC and the general PTC setting, we introduce PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style user requests whose difficulty comes from large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures. Experiments on PTC-Bench show that I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets while substantially reducing token consumption over conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline, highlighting stateful programmatic tool calling as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.
bullets: Addresses the statelessness of existing programmatic tool-calling methods, which limits reuse of intermediate results and adaptation over time.
Lets models execute code that calls tools, preserve reusable state, and update tool interfaces through API corrections.
Introduces PTC-Bench for long-tail, production-style tasks involving large environments, dependent API calls, extended planning, and failure recovery.
Experiments show gains on complex tasks with large tool sets and substantially lower token consumption than conventional tool calling and the original PTC baseline.

papers.abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $τ^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.
bullets: Long agent contexts make repeatedly scoring the full prefix expensive, while fixed cross-layer reuse schedules cannot react to new tool evidence.
AIR uses a small controller to select a nested index-refresh pattern for each episode segment based on prior computation and the latest tool event.
The controller learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget.
On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with 128K context, success rose from 27.0% to 32.4% on SWE-bench Verified at matched cost.
AIR matched or exceeded the strongest static schedule in 44 of 50 tested backbone, context, and benchmark settings, while reducing time per successful task across five benchmarks.
