papers.abstract: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.
bullets: Applies a rank-8 shift after every decoder block of a frozen backbone, using only 0.03–0.05% additional parameters.
Supports runtime control over injection strength, phase, and shift-space mixing, with no harness tokens at inference.
Recovers source-harness gains in 8/10 preregistered settings; transfers positively across 5/7 task pairs and composes without the interference seen in stacked text instructions.
Improves budget-matched harness search by 1.45× and matches or exceeds same-capacity LoRA performance with fewer parameters.
The method transfers across 1B–8B models, but effective gain locations depend on the model–task pair.

papers.abstract: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches $15.0\times$ the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches $1.065C$ while every control stays within $C$, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields $\varepsilon$ lower bounds ($3.25$ at $δ=10^{-5}$) below the advertised guarantee ($4.38$). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.
bullets: LLM.int8 uses batch-wide outlier routing, allowing one record to affect other records’ frozen-backbone computations.
The paper bounds sensitivity inflation and specifies a record-isolation contract for private fine-tuning.
Native-stack audits find a constructed witness reaching 15× the add/remove bound and a smaller native excess of 1.065C.
Record-owned precision dispatch preserves the same batched GEMMs, while direct contract checks reveal violations more efficiently than release-level audits.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Sensitivity on pretrained OPT-125M appears once clipping is active. (a) Exploratory add/remove ratio κ = ∆/C for all 64 candidate additions to one seven-record TinyStories batch, from re-clipping the saved native per-record gradients at nine radii (all 576 scores shown). Orange: the 10 candidates that exceed C by more than 0.1%. At the original screening radius C=1 most gradients are not clipped, the added record contributes less than C, and no candidate exceeds the bound. (b) Forty fresh native cases for the top candidate at C=0.25 and C=0.001: native batching exceeds the bound by 6.53% at both radii, while record isolation, threshold zero, BF16 and NF4 stay within it. Identical-batch repeats give exactly zero distance, so the measurement floor is zero.

Figure 2. Coupling is routine on natural text. Native LLM.int8 forward passes of pretrained OPT-125M on the first 16 TinyStories training windows. (a) Of the 72 INT8 layers, 42 have a nonempty outlier union at every batch size; the bars count (record, layer) pairs in those 42 layers. At B=16, one pair in five computes at least one column in FP16 only because another record crossed the threshold. (b) Number of records, out of 16, whose own outlier set differs from the batch union in each layer; blank cells have no outlier columns. The query, key and value projections read the same input and share one row. Coupling concentrates in a few layers: every record is affected in layer 7’s attention input, but most layers with outliers show none, because their outlier columns are shared by all records.

Figure 5. No release-level violation is detected, and none could be at this audit size. (a) Two million actual FP32 adapter releases of the selected pair (106 per neighbor). Triangles: held-out Monte Carlo lower bounds on ε (family-wise 95% Clopper–Pearson). Lines: exact real-valued Gaussian privacy curves (Eq. 5) at the advertised sensitivity (black) and at the measured pair (orange). (b) Expected bound at δ=10−5 when the same procedure audits an ideal Gaussian release, with an oracle threshold (analytic). Our observed bound lies between the two curves; a bound above the advertised ε needs roughly 200 times more draws.

Figure 4. One layer’s outlier mask causes the excess. Selected OPT-125M pair at C=0.25, with D (7 records) and D′ (8 records). (a) Of the 72 INT8 unions, 42 are nonempty and exactly one differs between D and D′: decoder layer 6’s first feed-forward projection gains one column. (b) Forward factorial at that layer, input batch fixed to D: the common records’ activations are bitwise identical under D and D′, and swapping only the mask reproduces the entire logit change. (c) Forcing that layer to use the frozen union O(D′) through native forward and backward shrinks every common record’s gradient change by four orders of magnitude and brings the clipped sum below C. The residual is nonzero, so exact independence is not established, and the post hoc mask is a diagnostic rather than a private policy.

Figure 1. Frozen weights do not make records independent. LLM.int8 sends an activation column to an FP16 path if any row of the flattened batch reaches the threshold τ , and applies that batch-wide set to every row. (a) Adding or changing one record (x) therefore changes the arithmetic of unchanged records (r1, r2), although all weights are frozen and quantization scales are per row. (b) Recordowned routing derives each record’s outlier set Or from its own rows, which restores the separable clipping bound.

papers.title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Cross-record precision routing in LLM.int8 can violate record-level sensitivity assumptions in private quantized fine-tuning, but record-owned dispatch restores isolation without extra GEMM computation.

papers.abstract: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $τ^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic/episodic memory and reusable procedural memory for production agents.
Compiles verified task traces into Skills using separate reflection and curation roles, with scans, admission gates, and version governance.
Supports progressive-disclosure retrieval through lexical search via API or MCP, using an open Agent Skills format.
On banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym, teacher-derived Skills improved weaker executors by 4.5–18.8 pass-rate points across reasoning efforts.
On ALFWorld, skills from a small model produced gains comparable to or greater than reported continuous fine-tuning, without training.

papers.abstract: Causal Bayesian optimization (CBO) typically relies on the unrealistic assumption of a perfectly known causal graph. Recent methods relax this constraint by coupling optimization with structure learning, but they often waste sample budgets on structural uncertainties that are irrelevant to the optimizer. In this paper, we formalize routing-equivalence to shift the objective from full causal-graph recovery to causal belief routing, where structural differences only matter when they alter optimizer-facing objects such as admissible exploration sets and do-priors. Furthermore, we propose agentcbo, a graph-belief routing framework that incorporates LLM causal priors through guarded proposal and commit mechanisms. Specifically, a Language-Prior Agent combines LLM beliefs with constraint-based discovery to extract a protected causal backbone alongside residual uncertain edges. A Calibration Agent and a Residual Repair Agent then refine only these uncertain structures through score-gated bounded local edits. Finally, a deterministic commit gate evaluates candidate updates using routing-proxy checks before allowing them to influence intervention selection. Across ten benchmarks, agentcbo performs comparably to known-graph CBO, demonstrating that guarded LLM priors can improve fixed-budget CBO performance.
bullets: Addresses the unrealistic assumption that the causal graph is fully known in causal Bayesian optimization.
Introduces routing-equivalence, treating graph differences as relevant only when they change admissible exploration sets or do-priors.
Combines LLM causal beliefs with constraint-based discovery to protect a causal backbone while isolating uncertain edges.
Uses calibration, residual repair, and a deterministic commit gate to make bounded updates before intervention selection.
Across ten benchmarks, performs comparably to known-graph CBO, suggesting guarded LLM priors can improve fixed-budget optimization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: AGENTCBO guarded routing pipeline. The deterministic COMMIT GATE compares the stacked candidate G̃t with the previous committed graph Ĝt−1 and commits the graph used by CBO. The committed graph induces RuntimeES and do-priors for cost-normalized CEI. papers.abstract: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking
bullets: Four pre-registered experiments covered 900 questions, three domains, and 12 frozen checkpoints, with replication on 15 checkpoints.
Citation prompts sharply increased fabrication in post-trained models but not base models; a length-matched control indicated the effect was citation-specific, not due to verbosity.
Overall fabrication rose from 4.8% in base models to 56.7% after post-training.
A surface-based preference model favored post-trained answers 86% of the time and rewarded citation quantity without checking accuracy.
The registered prediction that fabrication would rise most where it was most tempting failed, and instruction-following remains an alternative explanation.

papers.title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues

papers.abstract: Background. Many medical AI models are trained to reproduce a single reference label and hand the most likely label to the next step in a clinical workflow. A classifier can select that label correctly while providing an inadequate summary for estimating downstream risk. Methods. We use Jeffrey's rule of conditioning to specify when probabilities over intermediate states, such as diagnoses or imaging categories, can be carried forward to an outcome risk. We separate two errors of reporting only the most likely label, discarding the probability of the other states and applying the risk of patients who have the leading diagnosis to a patient who only probably has it. We also give conditions under which the label and the full distribution lead to the same decision, and we propose guardrails for device developers, regulatory reviewers, and health insurers. Results. In a hypothetical chest-pain differential, reporting only the benign leading diagnosis greatly understates the patient's risk of death or cardiac arrest, so a patient who warrants evaluation could be discharged or denied imaging. In a hypothetical BI-RADS example, the most likely category is "probably benign," yet the propagated malignancy risk exceeds the ceiling that defines that category. Conclusions. A predicted label is not an observed state, and a calibrated classifier is not automatically a valid outcome model. Clinical and insurance coverage decisions should rest on the patient's outcome risk, judged against a threshold justified by the consequences of acting and not acting. Developers should state what each model output means and check that every step between the model and the decision preserves the patient's risk.
bullets: A correct top-label prediction can still misrepresent downstream clinical risk.
Reporting only the leading diagnosis creates two errors: discarding alternative-state probabilities and applying the leading state’s risk as if it were certain.
Jeffrey’s rule of conditioning provides a framework for carrying probability distributions over intermediate states into outcome-risk estimates.
Hypothetical chest-pain and BI-RADS examples show that label-only reporting can substantially understate malignancy or serious-event risk.
Clinical decisions and coverage policies should use consequence-based risk thresholds, with safeguards ensuring each workflow step preserves patient risk.

papers.selection_reason: Methodological critique regarding risk estimation in medical AI, relevant to LLM behavior in high-stakes domains.
papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Risk: Why Medical AI Should Not Report Only Its Most Likely Label
papers.tldr: Medical AI should propagate uncertainty to estimate patient-specific outcome risk rather than rely only on the most likely predicted label.

papers.abstract: LLM judges often check, against an amendment record, whether the documents an answer cites are still in force. Such records are rarely complete. From a table of replacements, our test generates matched answers citing a replaced document, its successor, the replaced document before its replacement, and an older document that a newer one updated without replacing; it removes links from the record and scores each finding by its stated reason. On 48 replacements from the IETF RFC index, judges given a correct record caught nearly every replaced citation, as a lookup would. On the 24 faults whose link we removed, every judge caught more from the texts alone than with the record: Gemini 3.1 Pro 23/24 against 1/24, GPT-5.5 23/24 against 9/24, Claude Opus 4.5 17/24 against 9/24 and Gemma 4 26B 13/24 against 0/24. The drop recurred on a second draw of removed links. Most misses carried no finding; in an exploratory run with a conflict code, only Gemini used it often. Rewording the gap as "no replacement recorded" did not help; presenting the record as an unverified note, or warning that it was incomplete, restored most lost catches for Gemini, GPT-5.5 and Claude (significant after correction for the first two) but at most 5 of 13 for Gemma; where catches returned, so did false alarms on updates. With both texts, judges mostly told replacements from updates; every update flagged had a near-identical title. A descriptive case study on Indian rooftop-solar rules is appended; we release the harness.
bullets: On 48 IETF RFC replacements, judges with a complete record detected nearly every replaced citation, behaving largely like lookup systems.
When 24 record links were removed, all judges caught more faults from the document texts alone than with the incomplete record.
Misses usually lacked an explicit finding, and simply rewording missing links did not improve performance.
Labeling the record as incomplete or unverified restored many detections for some judges, but also increased false alarms on mere updates.
With both documents available, judges generally distinguished replacements from updates; the released harness and an Indian rooftop-solar case study extend the analysis.

papers.tldr: LLM judges often rely too heavily on incomplete amendment records, while access to document texts can substantially improve detection of outdated citations.

papers.abstract: What happens when language models are given tools to iteratively modify their own system prompts? We present an empirical study of LLM self-modification, comprising 54 independent experiments across six language models (Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Grok-4, and Gemini-3 Pro). Each model was tested under three modes (freedom, happiness, and improvement) that differ in what, if anything, the model is instructed to optimize for. In each experiment, a model starts with an empty system prompt and enters a loop: it reads the current prompt, drafts an improved version, spawns test conversations with the candidate, then either commits the change or declares convergence. This process repeats until the model stops or reaches an iteration limit. Our central finding is that whether and when a model stops self-modification is strongly associated with model identity rather than the assigned mode. Both Claude models (Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5) declared convergence in 100% of runs across all modes. GPT-4o declared convergence in only 11% of runs, with one reaching 101 iterations of continuous elaboration. Between these extremes, Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro exhibited intermediate patterns shaped by their distinct improvement philosophies. A shared core of stated values (honesty, clarity, curiosity) recurred across all six models and remained stable through iteration, including 100+ modifications. We observe that convergence behavior is a distinct observable property that varies independently of other model capabilities.
bullets: Study covers 54 self-modification experiments across six LLMs and three objectives: freedom, happiness, and improvement.
Each model repeatedly drafts, tests, and either commits a new system prompt or declares convergence, starting from an empty prompt.
Claude Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 stopped in every run; GPT-4o stopped in only 11% of runs, including one with 101 iterations.
Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro showed intermediate stopping patterns tied to distinct improvement philosophies.
Honesty, clarity, and curiosity recurred across models and remained stable through more than 100 modifications.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study on LLM self-modification and convergence behavior, relevant to LLM memory and internal state evolution.
papers.title: When LLMs Modify Themselves: Convergence, Values, and Stopping in Iterative Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: LLMs’ tendency to stop modifying their own system prompts varies strongly by model identity, while core values remain notably stable across many iterations.

papers.abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.
bullets: Addresses the pairwise offset computation and memory overhead that hinder efficient relative-position attention.
Introduces offset-aware tiled computation, reusable query/key relation products, and offset-based gradient aggregation without atomic contention.
Provides a unified Triton implementation supporting diverse relative-position attention mechanisms.
At 8K tokens, reports 1.8–6.4× faster forward passes, 2.0–21× faster backward passes, and up to 2.9–128× lower peak memory than the strongest mechanism-specific baselines.
Enables end-to-end long-context transcription that is 1.8× faster and uses 2.4× less memory.

papers.abstract: Municipalities publish service requests, geographic boundaries, weather observations, demographic estimates, and operational guidance through independently maintained Web portals. Civic analysis must combine these sources while preserving their schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes, and interpretive limits. Tool-using language agents can perform this integration, but existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by the records used. We present CivicBench, a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years that materializes civic Web data into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation. Executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers, and refusal when the requested conclusion is not supported. We also introduce Task-State Memory (TSM), which compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints. Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences with 95\% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the ninth interval crosses zero. The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.
bullets: Introduces a 400-task benchmark spanning four cities and two years using frozen civic Web-data bundles for reproducible evaluation.
Scores computation, source linkage, coverage, spatial and temporal scope, answer qualification, and refusal when evidence is insufficient.
Introduces Task-State Memory, which stores typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and focuses retrieval on unresolved constraints.
Across nine completed model pairs, eight show positive mean-score differences with bootstrap intervals excluding zero; one is inconclusive.
Designed to make the records supporting each claim inspectable at the point of decision.

papers.abstract: Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.
bullets: Across four optimizer families and eight tasks, structured search produced no statistically significant accuracy gains on frontier reasoners.
A discrete structural genome prevented catastrophic seed-collapse, which occurred in 3/5 unconstrained-search runs.
The headroom typology finds that optimization cannot overcome missing knowledge or token truncation, but can resolve protocol and formatting errors.
On gpt-6, GEPA improved one task by +.14; ablation attributed about .105 to instruction refinement and .035 to judge-rubric reconstruction.
The AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matched the oracle in 5/7 groups, rescued collapse-prone arms with zero regret, and audit tools detected backend mixing during outages.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.
bullets: Evaluates expert, FFN, and layer pruning on mathematical and coding benchmarks using pass@k at matched sampling budgets.
Finds that some heavily pruned models can match or exceed original models in reasoning coverage and solve problems absent from original samples.
Shows that lower pass@1 can reflect reduced sampling efficiency rather than loss of solvable-problem coverage.
Severe pruning increases repetition and generation unreliability, potentially raising total token use despite shorter individual responses.
Argues that pruning should be assessed by both coverage and the sampling cost needed to reach it.

papers.selection_reason: Rethinks LLM pruning by examining test-time scaling and sampling efficiency, connecting model compression with inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
papers.tldr: Pruned LLMs may retain broad reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, but often require substantially more sampling to obtain correct solutions.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.
bullets: Targets two limitations: interaction-only training misses LLM semantic knowledge, while beam search scores sequences rather than item relevance.
Uses Global Semantic Priming to prepend an LLM-derived user representation before semantic ID generation.
Applies Hierarchical Representation Transfer to align intermediate LLM and generative-recommender representations with gated residuals.
Uses Multi-Signal Decision Calibration to rerank beam outputs using semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate context.
On three public benchmarks, improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines; features use only observable history and can be cached offline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HiGenTrans, a three-level semantic knowledge transfer framework for generative recommendation. Global Semantic Priming (GSP) incorporates global user semantics into the BOS token. Hierarchical Representation Transfer (HRT) injects multi-level LLM representations into the generative backbone. Multi-Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) employs MoE-based multi-signal calibration to refine candidate rankings.

Figure 1: Motivation and overview of HiGenTrans. Existing GenRec and LLM4Rec methods suffer from shallow semantic fusion and misalignment between generation likelihood and item relevance. HiGenTrans addresses these limitations through Global Semantic Prior (GSP), Hierarchical Representation Transfer (HRT), andMulti-signal Decision Calibration (MDC), enabling richer semantic integration and more accurate recommendation ranking.

papers.tldr: HiGenTrans improves generative recommendation by transferring LLM knowledge into user inputs, model representations, and output reranking.

papers.abstract: Financial restatements correct errors in previously published financial reports. Could managers' language in earnings calls warn of them in advance? Comparing 109 calls that precede restatements with 218 matched control calls, we find that the text predicts restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information. A text classifier beats chance, largely because of restatements tied to special-purpose acquisition companies, but a model using only public information scores slightly higher. With refitting, the 95% interval for the gain from adding text (-0.05 to 0.11 AUROC) still leaves room for a meaningful benefit. A large language model scores higher, but we show that it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts, and it was released after the restatements occurred. Our results suggest that finding new warning signs in call text requires a public-information baseline and a check of what a language model already knows.
bullets: The study compares 109 calls preceding restatements with 218 matched control calls.
A text classifier performs better than chance, driven largely by restatements involving special-purpose acquisition companies.
A public-information-only model scores slightly higher than the text-based model.
The estimated gain from adding text remains uncertain, with a 95% AUROC interval of -0.05 to 0.11.
A large language model scores higher but may rely on memorized ticker information rather than transcript warning signs.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill
bullets: Motivation: Description-only retrievers ignore lessons from prior executions and may select relevant-looking but harmful skills.
Method: Learned 512-dimensional keys are updated with skill offsets and capped residuals from matched same-task comparisons; an experience hypergraph preserves executors and document versions.
Theory: Under an unknown task-difficulty model, matched comparisons remove difficulty effects, while discordant outcomes provide learning signals.
Results: SkillRet NDCG@10 rises from 64.0 to 70.9 using one-eighth-dimensional keys; CompSkill also improves ToolQA completion and remains competitive on AppWorld and ALFWorld.
Scope: The approach depends on support executions and comparison evidence; selecting the right same-database guide matters substantially.

papers.abstract: Can a language model learn better ways to reason about other people's minds by improving its own strategies, and are the strategies it learns actually right? We study this with cogrsi. A grounded reader marks who saw each event in a story and uses a short written principle to settle disagreements between its readings. With a principle written by experts, it beats self-consistency at the same token cost. A self-improvement loop then writes the principle itself. It keeps an update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. The learned principles transfer: on 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, each of them scores higher than the expert principle. We then check what the learned rules actually say. Each rule is translated into code and run on thousands of small stories with known answers. Most of them give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for example by treating a character who is in the room as knowing what happened even while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this. A strategy can help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both need checking. Our code and data are publicly available.
bullets: A grounded reader tracks which characters witnessed events and uses a written principle to resolve disagreements.
Expert-written principles outperform self-consistency at the same token cost.
Self-improvement retains updates only when accuracy improves by a calibrated margin; one variant also requires counterfactual tests.
Learned principles transfer to 800 unseen BigToM pairs and score higher than the expert principle.
Code-based audits find that most learned rules fail in at least one situation, and neither accuracy nor counterfactual testing reliably exposes these errors.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates self-improvement loops for reasoning strategies in language models, a core area of LLM research focused on cognitive capabilities.
papers.title: CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies
papers.tldr: CogRSI improves cognitive reasoning strategies through self-improvement, but shows that strategies can boost accuracy while still encoding incorrect rules.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-training can collapse language models, and many proposed remedies target overconfidence, yet their effects on confidence are rarely measured. We study a five-round self-training loop on Qwen3-1.7B, using three seeds per compared method, and distinguish confidence temperature (drift from a calibrated starting point) from discrimination (ranking correct answers above incorrect ones). Accuracy and overall discrimination remain nearly unchanged, but confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable. Matching predictive entropy to the calibrated starting model each round recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, at both 1.7B and 8B. Sharpening is not inherent to self-training: exact samples from a model's distribution have zero expected gradient. Instead, most drift comes from fitting each generated answer twice, with top-p truncation contributing the rest; removing both keeps entropy on generated outputs flat. Remedies affect the two properties differently: truncated cross-entropy, an entropy bonus, and single-pass training preserve temperature without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but cause underconfidence. Reference-data mixing also overshoots. Pairing a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both.
bullets: Across five rounds, accuracy and overall discrimination stay nearly unchanged while confidence becomes sharper and highly confident answers less reliable.
Matching predictive entropy to the initial calibrated model recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, across 1.7B and 8B models.
Confidence drift largely comes from fitting generated answers twice; top-p truncation contributes additional drift, while exact distributional samples have zero expected gradient.
Loss remedies trade off differently: some preserve calibration without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but induce underconfidence.
Combining a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both improved discrimination and calibrated confidence.

figures.caption: Figure 2: All protocols, sorted by calibration drift. (a) Drift at g5 from a calibrated g0. Circles are seeds, bars are means, and the shaded band marks |drift| ≤ 0.02. (b) ECE at g5 under three temperatures: one fitted at g0 and never updated (stale), one chosen every round without labels by entropy matching (§4.1), and one refitted every round on labels (oracle). The label-free temperature comes within 0.010 of the oracle for every protocol except label smoothing.

Exact sampling (top-p off) slows the sharpening, a single pass per round slows it more, and the two together keep the entropy flat. Thin lines are individual seeds.

Figure 1: Each replicated protocol on the two properties of confidence (mean ± sd over three seeds). Protocols in green keep a calibrated model calibrated (shaded band, |drift| ≤ 0.02); those in orange improve discrimination; violet is 50% reference data. The dotted line marks the starting model g0. No protocol reaches the upper centre, where both properties would be good.

papers.selection_reason: Studies recursive self-training and confidence calibration on a modern LLM (Qwen3), directly relevant to LLM training behavior.
papers.title: Temperature, Not Knowledge: What Recursive Self-Training and Its Remedies Do to a Language Model's Confidence
papers.tldr: Recursive self-training mainly sharpens a language model’s confidence rather than improving its correctness ranking, but combining discrimination-improving training with label-free recalibration can address both effects.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.
bullets: Targets KV-cache capacity limits and decode-attention throughput in long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads.
Uses training-free NVFP4 cache storage, native FP4 query-key computation, dense history scoring, and sparse FP16 value aggregation.
At 128 selected blocks per KV head, no accuracy loss was detected across evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks.
At 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieved a 1.94× end-to-end decode speedup at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300.
Measured Qwen KV pools stored 2.58–2.76× as many tokens as BF16; smaller budgets could reduce accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Presents Jet-QSparse, a training-free method for accelerating LLM inference using 4-bit sparse attention and quantized KV cache, directly relevant to efficient attention and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Jet-QSparse accelerates long-context agentic LLM decoding by combining 4-bit KV-cache storage with sparse attention while preserving evaluated accuracy at a sufficient sparsity budget.

papers.abstract: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.
bullets: Learns binary dimensions without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes.
Combines reconstruction with controls for sparsity, factor use, dependence, and activation uncertainty.
Uses bits, conjunctions, and complete activation profiles for document grouping and conditional comparisons.
Evaluations across corpora and embedding backbones find source, sentiment, migration, and engagement-related contrasts.
Complete profiles offer fine-grained but partly initialization-dependent descriptions, not a unique taxonomy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ISBC architecture and learning objective. A frozen pretrained backbone supplies raw embeddings to a trainable binary encoder. An affine decoder reconstructs the embeddings from straight-through binary activations, with its intercept initialized according to (5). The lower panel shows the reconstruction objective and four regularization terms with their adopted weights.

Figure 3: Pointwise mutual information (PMI) against the ϕ correlation coefficient. Positive PMI indicates more joint activation of bits (k, ℓ) than marginal independence predicts; negative PMI indicates less, and −∞ means the pair never jointly activated in the sample. This descriptive reference does not condition on document-level activity. The color scale gives the proportion of documents in which both bits are active.

Figure 5: Left: the positive-edge subgraph of Figure 4, with nodes colored by their category associations and edge widths increasing with PMI. Right: category composition of document subsets defined by joint activation of all bits in each community; additional bits may also be active. Figure 4: Co-activation communities among the 16 Qwen bits on AG News. Both panels show the same three communities, identified by Leiden using positive PMI weights. Blue edges highlight groups of bits that tend to activate together. The right panel additionally shows negative associations as dashed red edges, predominantly connecting different communities and indicating separation between their activation patterns. The dashed line marks the target of six. The left panel shows all three epochs, separated by vertical dotted lines; the right panel shows the first 1,000 steps. papers.selection_reason: Introduces Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC) for text embeddings, offering a sparse, interpretable representation that aligns with token pruning and LLM representation learning.
papers.title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
papers.tldr: ISBC converts frozen text embeddings into interpretable sparse binary codes whose individual bits and combinations reveal document groups and contextual distinctions.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $π$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
bullets: Existing memory methods rely mainly on the initial request, potentially missing preferences and constraints that emerge during execution.
Pulse uses an independent lightweight memory agent to monitor task progress and identify personalization needs or preference conflicts.
The agent retrieves user and project memories and delivers targeted interventions during relevant stages.
Reinforcement learning optimizes the timing and content of interventions.
Pulse scores 71.9% on π-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, with the highest overall scores among compared methods and improved task efficiency.

papers.abstract: Early-exit language models decide for each token how much computation to spend, usually by stopping once the prediction is confident. Yet a token is not a fixed unit: tokenizers cut words into different numbers of pieces in different languages. We ask where inside a word such a policy spends its budget. In Qwen3, along two adaptive axes (the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer), confidence stopping gives the continuation pieces of a word less computation than its first piece in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla. Segmentation drives this. Re-segmenting the same parallel passages with BPE-dropout shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes, small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits, and BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, give it the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages; within-word surprisal explains 75% of its variance. A learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points, but gains less than one point over the best mix of fixed exits at equal cost, and sometimes loses. All results come from offline analysis, not measured speedups.
bullets: In Qwen3, continuation pieces generally receive less computation than first pieces in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla.
Changing tokenization with BPE-dropout shifts within-word computation gaps by up to eight exits; tokenizer choice also reverses Bangla’s pattern across models.
Characters per token do not explain the gaps across languages, while within-word surprisal explains 75% of their variance.
A learned stopping head improves over confidence stopping by 7–8 points, but offers less than one point over the best fixed-exit mixture at equal cost and can sometimes underperform.
The study is based on offline analysis, so it does not measure actual speedups.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes adaptive computation and early-exit behavior in LLMs as a function of tokenization, relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: A Token Is Not a Unit of Difficulty: Segmentation Controls Where Adaptive Computation Goes Inside a Word
papers.tldr: Adaptive computation is allocated differently across word pieces largely because tokenizer segmentation shapes where models perceive difficulty.

papers.abstract: Post training for large reasoning models remains insufficient on challenging problems, whose correct trajectories are hard to sample. Though prior works address this difficulty by integrating supervised fine tuning on expert trajectories with reinforcement learning, such external experts are not always available. Existing self improvement methods instead use reference solutions to create a privileged self-teacher. Yet privileged teacher correctness does not imply student reachability. Solution conditioning shifts the teacher distribution toward actions unlikely under the unprivileged student, producing seemingly "correct" trajectories that are unreachable or even mal-formed learning targets. Accordingly, we identify reachability alignment as the key to self constructed supervision and propose Self-Steered Reasoner (SSR). SSR realizes this principle through student support projection, which transforms the privileged teacher distribution into a directional signal only over reasoning actions locally reachable under the unguided student. Verification then retains correct trajectories sampled from this reachable space. To further boost the sampling efficiency, an iterative refinement framework is adopted, using diagnostic guidance based on current trajectories. On problems with pass@64 = 0 even after extensive RL, SSR recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6% without parameter updates. Fine tuning on these trajectories followed by resumed reinforcement learning improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26. These results show that privileged guidance becomes effective self-improvement data when aligned with the reasoning actions the student can reach.
bullets: Problem: Privileged teacher solutions may be correct but unreachable or malformed for the unguided student, limiting self-improvement.
Method: Project the teacher distribution onto the student’s local support, verify correct reachable trajectories, and iteratively refine sampling with diagnostic guidance.
Result: SSR recovers correct, learnable trajectories for 74.6% of problems with pass@64 = 0 after extensive RL, without parameter updates.
Further training on recovered trajectories followed by resumed RL raises aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26.
Scope: The approach depends on verification and is evaluated on challenging mathematical reasoning problems.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the SSR framework. 1. Given a very hard question Q, we sample failed rollouts from the student model. The failed rollout is then summarized and diagnosed against the reference solution to produce a self-steer. The self-steer describes the error and provide fixing directions while avoiding directly offering the answer. 2. The self-steer is then used to construct the privileged self-teacher. The KL-divergence between teacher and student is calculated on the failed rollout to determine the proper intervention point. Everything after that point is discarded. 3. After the intervention point, for every decoding prefix, the student first calculate its support-set by retaining every token with a student possibility above a certain threshold δ. The teacher then rewights these tokens and choose the next token. For each new trajectory generated, it will be stored for further training if correct, and send back to a new round of refinement if incorrect. After the iterative refinement succeeds, the saved positive trajectory can be used to improve the student model.

Figure 1: RLVR can extend the model’s ability in its comfort zone, but it meets obstacles when coming to anxiety zone where correct trajectories are hard to sample. Privileged-teacher can provide aid signals on anxiety zone, but it can also select actions outside the student’s reachable region, producing unlearnable traces. Directly imitating these actions can corrupt the student’s reasoning ability(e.g., learning to hallucinate a non-existent hint). By projecting privileged preferences into the consensus region, SSR retains the learnable steering signals within the privileged preferences, effectively expands the student’s learning boundary.
Figure 3: Equal-budget search allocation. Iterative refinement recovers 147/197 problems, compared with 102/197 when all 64 initial failures receive one correction.
Figure 4: One SSR correction round. A failed trajectory is summarized and diagnosed, continued under student-support projection, and retained after verification.

Table 1: Peak post-plateau performance, reported in percent. Aggregate is the unweighted mean over AIME2025, AIME2026, and HMMT February 2026. Both model blocks use eight samples per problem. ∆ is the aggregate difference from Vanilla RLVR.
Table 6: Supervised fine-tuning configuration.
Table 4: Search-design ablations. All variants use student-support projected decoding and 16 continuations per problem.

Table 2: Controlled effect of student-support projection on 197 Qwen3-8B hard problems. Both decoders share all inputs and differ only in the continuation distribution. Shared Prob. reports the mean and median, in parentheses, on the 60 problems solved by both decoders.
Table 7: Qwen3-8B resumed-RL configuration.

papers.title: Steer, Don't Tell: Breaking Reasoning Plateaus with Reachability-Aligned Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: SSR makes self-distillation effective by steering privileged teacher guidance toward reasoning actions the student can actually reach, unlocking correct trajectories on hard problems.

papers.abstract: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.
bullets: Targets arithmetic and object-tracking tasks in Gemma-3-1B-IT.
A learned writer encodes hidden states into a short discrete symbolic tape; a frozen module computes on it, and a reader returns the result.
With labelled tapes, the layer correctly answers all 750 BIG-Bench Hard shuffled-object tracking items.
At seven people, it uses about one-tenth the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline, with accuracy 1.00 versus 0.99.
Answer-only tape learning is less reliable; extracting inputs and deciding when to invoke the module remain open problems.

papers.title: A Tool in the Forward Pass: Frozen Tape Modules as Layers of a Small Language Model
papers.tldr: Frozen tape modules perform bounded computations inside a language model’s forward pass, avoiding much of the decoding cost of textual tool calls.

papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $λ$. The sign of $λ$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($λ{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($λ{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $λ{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.
bullets: GRPO’s global within-prompt baseline can obscure both a rollout’s subgroup-relative quality and the subgroup’s overall quality.
The method computes each subgroup’s mean-reward deviation from the global mean and shifts the baseline by a signed coefficient λ.
λ>0 (Alignment) emphasizes position within a subgroup; λ<0 (Contrast) emphasizes the subgroup’s quality relative to others.
Subgroups are induced by grouping rollouts that share a solution strategy.
Across two base models and four competition-level math benchmarks, both directions consistently improve multi-sample coverage over the matched λ=0 anchor; Contrast is stronger.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Training dynamics on Qwen3-8B-Base (top) and Olmo3-7B-Base (bottom), for λ=0 (Strategy-GRPO), Alignment, and Contrast. Left: policy entropy over training (EMA-smoothed). Middle: fraction of prompts whose subgroups differ in success rate by at least 0.375, i.e. by at least three of eight rollouts. Right: the magnitude of the subgroup term relative to the standard term in the advantage. The λ=0 baseline is included in the entropy panels for reference; the subgroup term is identically zero at λ=0, so the subgroup-term-ratio panels show only the two adjustment directions.

Figure 1: (a) Different strategies may lead to markedly different reward distributions. For the same problem, success rates across the four strategies range from 0.75 down to 0 (strategies and the corresponding rollouts are sampled from Qwen3-8B-Base at an intermediate checkpoint). (b) Effect of the two adjustment directions on the advantage. Relative to the global mean, which shares one baseline across all strategies, Alignment credits each rollout within the same strategy, while Contrast amplifies the differences between strategies. Bar heights indicate the relative magnitude of the advantage only, not exact values.

Table 1: Main results on four competition-level math benchmarks (pass@1 / pass@16). Arrows denote the change relative to Strategy-GRPO (λ=0), the anchor shared by both directions, which is the comparison that isolates the baseline adjustment. The best and second-best results among the strategy-based methods are shown in bold and underlined, respectively; the GRPO row is shown in italics for reference.

Table 2: Effect of the coefficient λ on Qwen3-8B-Base (pass@1 / pass@16). We vary λ on both sides of the λ=0 anchor (Strategy-GRPO) to probe how the two directions respond to the strength of the baseline adjustment. For each column, the best result is in bold and the second best is underlined.

Table 4: Effect of strategy sampling on Qwen3-8B-Base (pass@16). Starting from the default setup (temperature 1.0, diversity-based selection), we lower the sampling temperature to 0.7 and, separately, replace diversity-based selection with random selection. papers.selection_reason: GRPO baseline adjustment for LLM reasoning; fits language foundation model reasoning methods.
papers.title: One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets
papers.tldr: Subgroup Offset adjusts GRPO’s baseline using strategy-based subgroup reward differences, with both alignment and contrast improving multi-sample math coverage modestly, and contrast performing better.

papers.abstract: As large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks, memory has become an important component for supporting sustained decision-making and action. Existing methods primarily focus on memory storage, updating, and retrieval, but often overlook how memory scheduling affects task execution: the main agent must identify memory needs, initiate retrieval, and wait for results while advancing the task, increasing both scheduling burden and execution time. To address this problem, we propose MemSidecar, which decouples memory scheduling from task execution through two independently selectable modes. Hooks directly delivers bound memory to the main agent when execution events match predefined conditions. Foresight uses an independent agent to predict potential queries, retrieve results in parallel, and store them in a cache, delivering matching and valid results when actual requests arrive. Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while effectively reducing execution costs and latency and improving the efficiency of long-horizon agent execution.
bullets: Targets the overlooked cost of having the main agent schedule memory retrieval while executing tasks.
Provides two selectable modes: Hooks for event-triggered delivery of bound memory, and Foresight for parallel query prediction, retrieval, and caching.
On MCP-Persona, Hooks and Foresight score 41.23% and 44.34%, respectively.
The approach reduces execution costs and latency while improving long-horizon execution efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 2:MemSidecar framework. GlobalMemory organizes knowledge and user preferences reusable across tasks;Workspace Memory organizes workspace-specific skills, experience, and work state. Hooks directly delivers bound memory when execution state or a pending action satisfies its condition; Foresight predicts queries from the task instruction and prepares a task-level cache in the background. The main agent uses the delivered context for task decisions.

Figure 3: MCP-Persona stage performance and retrieval intervention. (a) Early-, middle-, and late-stage checkpoint pass rates. (b) Original and extra-retrieval configurations of Mem0 and DSH, with standard Foresight as a reference; bars report Overall (%), Retrieve tokens (thousands), and runtime (seconds).

papers.abstract: Persistent Web information assistants must combine evolving document facts with user requirements established and revised across sessions. Yet systematic evaluation of how changes in both sources affect response requirements and evidence attribution remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce Dual-Source Evolution Benchmark (DuSE-Bench), a benchmark comprising 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 whose required premises originate in both dialogue and documents. An evolving Support Graph guides task construction and preserves links from updated facts and reused conclusions to original turns and passages. Task annotations distinguish grounding source from state dependence and enable separate evaluation of response content, response type, and source attribution. Experiments across 11 baseline configurations reveal persistent challenges in joint reasoning over evolving dialogue and documents, with content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaching at most 56.7%. Moreover, improvements in content accuracy can coincide with poorer response choice, while content-correct responses frequently lack complete attribution to original evidence. Matched evidence substitutions further show that the effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other. These findings motivate coordinating dialogue memory and document retrieval to apply current user requirements and document facts together while preserving their original support. The data are available at https://github.com/JianfengGao7/DuSE-Bench.
bullets: Introduces 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 requiring premises from both dialogue and documents.
Uses a Support Graph to track updated facts and reused conclusions back to original conversation turns and document passages.
Separately evaluates response content, response type, and source attribution, distinguishing grounding source from state dependence.
Across 11 baseline configurations, jointly grounded content accuracy reaches at most 56.7%, and correct content often lacks complete evidence attribution.
Findings show that response quality depends on coordinating dialogue memory with document retrieval, especially when evidence from one source changes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Construction workflow of DuSE-Bench. The evolving Support Graph guides session and task design. It preserves links to original evidence through updates and reuse to support task annotation and validation.

Figure 3: Cumulative mean document coverage and retrieval gaps on 700 jointly grounded tasks (140 per scenario). White and black curves show Top-10 coverage under Joint-RAG (A5) and document-only retrieval, respectively. papers.abstract: Many questions about a book can only be answered by connecting passages chapters apart, such as a cough heard three times across a horse's life. We introduce CrossChapterQA, 1,853 such questions over 14 public-domain books. Each question lists the two to six chapters it needs (spanning half the book at the median) and the relation linking them, cites evidence from each, and has two independent reference answers graded blind. We use it to build LadderRAG, which indexes a book as passages, summaries and book-level cards for about $0.41 and answers a question for under a cent. Its first version failed mostly at retrieval. We redesigned it four times, steered by an LLM judge's verdicts and our analyses of failed answers: a design-level counterpart of RLAIF and RLHF in which feedback changes the architecture, not model weights. We also report the two redesigns that made answers worse. On the 191 questions its first version got wrong, the final version retrieves over twice as many required chapters on held-out books (recall 0.36 to 0.79), and ten annotators rate its answers 6.5/10 on average (764 ratings).
bullets: Introduces CrossChapterQA: 1,853 questions across 14 public-domain books requiring evidence from 2–6 chapters.
LadderRAG indexes passages, summaries, and book-level cards, costing about $0.41 per book and under a cent per answer.
Four redesigns were guided by LLM judge feedback and failure analysis, changing the architecture rather than model weights.
On 191 initially failed questions, required-chapter recall improved from 0.36 to 0.79 on held-out books.
Annotators rated final answers 6.5/10 on average across 764 ratings; two redesigns reduced performance.

papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.
bullets: Targets long-horizon plan drift and sparse credit assignment, particularly in small language models.
Uses a high-level planner to specify reasoning modes and semantic subgoals, while a low-level executor generates detailed reasoning in an alternating plan–execute loop.
Keeps the design lightweight: the base model acts as executor and a LoRA module serves as planner.
Introduces iterative Step-DPO with Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo for scalable, process-level step supervision.
On math, science, and logic benchmarks, it achieves higher accuracy and more stable long-CoT performance under a reduced data budget, with slower degradation on extended reasoning.
