papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs for molecular property prediction and uncertainty estimation, demonstrating in-context learning capabilities.
papers.title: Do LLMs Know When They Are Wrong About Molecules? In-Context Property Prediction with Self-Reported Uncertainty
papers.tldr: LLMs can predict molecular properties effectively from in-context examples, but their self-reported uncertainty only weakly indicates when they are wrong.

papers.abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.
authors: Yukiya Horiba, Hakaze Cho, Takahiro Yakoh
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding of task vectors as seemingly atomized steering directions.
Uses candidate-label unembeddings to formulate a TR/TL/residual decomposition and Bayesian optimization of component coefficients.
Evaluates the approach across multiple model families, classification tasks, and instruction- or demonstration-based task vectors.
The optimized TR/TL interventions outperform original task vectors, with especially reliable gains for instruction-based vectors.
Component-specific interventions produce distinct logit effects consistent with their intended functional roles.

papers.selection_reason: Decomposes task vectors into interpretable components for LLM steering, offering a method for controllable intervention.
papers.title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components
papers.tldr: Task vectors can be decomposed into task-recognition, task-learning, and residual components that enable more interpretable and effective model steering.

papers.abstract: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.
authors: Burak Bakkar, Hana Moalla, Mohamed Salem Jedidi, Haifa Ben Messaoud, Nicolas Lopez Carranza
bullets: Clinical-trial failure motivates better phase-level outcome prediction using information in registration text.
BioBERT and BioMistral represented trials as text from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields and were evaluated with fine-tuning or frozen-embedding probing.
All four variants exceeded published HINT results in ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, with reported relative PR-AUC gains of 10–20%.
Fine-tuning was strongest in Phases I–II, while frozen BioMistral embeddings performed best in Phase III; most variant differences were small and untested for significance.
F1 gains were limited: no approach clearly surpassed the trivial always-success classifier on F1.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates domain-specific LLMs (BioBERT, BioMistral) for clinical trial outcome prediction, comparing fine-tuning and probing strategies.
papers.title: Advancing Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Domain-Specific Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Domain-specific language models improve clinical-trial outcome ranking over HINT, while computationally cheaper probing performs similarly to fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.
bullets: The study addresses the tension between correlated model errors (monoculture) and conflicting decisions among similarly accurate models (multiplicity).
It separates reasoning as a controlled intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior.
Across nine models, two developers, and three classification tasks, increased reasoning effort raises agreement on the same individuals.
Individuals producing longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models.
Both effects remain after accounting for model accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates reasoning behavior in LLMs, a core aspect of modern LLM research and architecture.
papers.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
papers.tldr: Reasoning has opposite effects on language-model agreement depending on how it is studied: prompting more reasoning increases agreement, while longer observed reasoning traces signal less consistent predictions.

papers.abstract: Sparse tuning is widely used to adapt large language models due to its parameter efficiency. However, its effectiveness depends not only on the number of trainable parameters, but also on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's structural support. Limited or uneven connectivity in this support may isolate subsets of feature dimensions, forming information islands that restrict direct task-specific interactions through the trainable update. To address this issue, we propose Small-World Induced Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a sparse tuning framework inspired by small-world connectivity. SWIFT combines block-diagonal sparse updates for local feature mixing with a fixed deterministic scattering permutation that routes the mixed outputs across feature groups without additional trainable parameters. We further show theoretically that certain random sparse-update models and block-diagonal updates can exhibit information islands, whereas a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees positive block-level expansion when the trainable block-diagonal factor consists of equal-sized, structurally dense square blocks. Extensive experiments on commonsense reasoning, natural language generation, and image classification demonstrate that SWIFT outperforms the evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning. Implementation is available at https://github.com/xianchaoguan/SWIFT
authors: Xianchao Guan, Zijun Xiong, Yifeng Wang, Yubo Cui, Yaowei Wang, Guo-Sen Xie, Xin Li, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Sparse tuning can suffer from limited feature connectivity, creating information islands in the update structure.
SWIFT uses block-diagonal updates for local feature mixing and a fixed scattering permutation to route information across feature groups without extra trainable parameters.
Theoretical analysis shows block-diagonal and some random sparse updates can form islands, while sufficient scattering provides positive block-level expansion under stated conditions.
Experiments across commonsense reasoning, text generation, and image classification show SWIFT outperforms evaluated PEFT baselines on average and can match or exceed full fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SWIFT, a sparse tuning framework that improves feature interaction topology in LLMs by introducing small-world connectivity to prevent information islands.
papers.title: Breaking Information Islands in Sparse Tuning via Small-World Connectivity
papers.tldr: SWIFT improves sparse fine-tuning by adding deterministic small-world-style routing that connects otherwise isolated feature groups.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. However, existing approaches typically optimize entire responses without explicitly identifying the knowledge to be forgotten, resulting in coarse and uncontrolled forgetting. To address this, we revisit the forgetting target of LLM unlearning and introduce Knowledge Association (KA), which characterizes the association between a query context and its target knowledge and is instantiated by the corresponding conditional predictive distribution, as the fundamental target of forgetting. Based on KA, we propose Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a unified reinforcement learning framework that suppresses forgotten knowledge associations while preserving retained ones. Specifically, KARU derives complementary mechanisms from the KA-based formulation: token-level reward construction for finer-grained forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularization for precise knowledge suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to mitigate collateral degradation. Experiments across diverse LLMs on representative benchmarks demonstrate that KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.
authors: Wutong Xu, Yun Qu, Haiyan Feng, Qi Wang, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Existing unlearning methods can forget coarsely because they optimize complete responses without isolating the knowledge to remove.
The paper defines Knowledge Association (KA) as the conditional predictive distribution linking a query context to target knowledge.
KARU uses reinforcement learning with token-level rewards, distribution-level suppression, and proximity-aware sampling of retained knowledge.
Experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks show improved forgetting effectiveness with comparable retention and general utility.
The method targets selective knowledge removal, with scope determined by the identified knowledge associations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a framework for selectively removing specific knowledge associations from LLMs while preserving general capabilities.
papers.title: What Should LLMs Forget: Reinforcement Unlearning of Knowledge Associations
papers.tldr: KARU treats context–knowledge associations—not whole responses—as the target of LLM unlearning, enabling more precise forgetting while preserving retained knowledge and general utility.

papers.abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Ying Xu, Siyuan Zhang
bullets: Audits 25 claimed cognitive-architecture mechanisms using static code tracing, falsifiable predictions, interventions, replication, and repair controls.
In 18 of 25 modules, computed values never reached production outputs; three previously undescribed idle-wiring patterns were identified.
Across 12 interventions and 61 frozen criteria, 53 were confirmed, five falsified, two partially adjudicated, and one remained ambiguous.
Repair experiments improved planner task success and reduced state-controller error, showing that implementation defects can materially affect behavior.
Findings are case-level across two systems; the authors argue module names and actual computations must be evaluated independently.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a transferable verification protocol to audit whether LLM-based agents actually implement claimed cognitive mechanisms (e.g., Theory of Mind), addressing the claim-implementation gap.
papers.title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
papers.tldr: A pre-registered audit finds that many named cognitive modules in LLM agents do not perform meaningful computation, and offers a reusable method for verifying implementation claims.

papers.abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Nekruz Maxudov, Bedil Karimov, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
bullets: The model is adapted from LFM2.5-2.6B-Base for Tajik tool calling on modest hardware.
LoRA continued pretraining uses 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents, followed by SFT on translated Tajik tool calls, English replay data, and Tajik instructions.
Strict Tajik full-call accuracy increases from 20.69 to 64.14, while English performance remains essentially unchanged.
All continued-pretraining checkpoints score zero on tool calling, indicating loss of the native format and some underlying skill—not just formatting mismatch.

papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.
authors: Ruurd J. A. Kuiper, Robert A. Bagheri
bullets: Addresses the high pretraining and full-fine-tuning costs of building diffusion language models.

Converted models support fully masked generation, bidirectional context, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge.

papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan, Xin Li, Linqi Song
bullets: Targets failed prerequisites and flawed decompositions, rather than relying on another plausible action.
Extends ReAct with a bounded goal stack and dual-horizon checks for goal relevance and current feasibility.
Uses typed failure attribution to trigger Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo-parent operations.
Improves over ReAct and reflection-based control across all tested backbone–benchmark pairs; AppWorld gains reach up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct.
Ablations show verification and diagnosis are complementary, with removing either sometimes reducing performance below ReAct.

The executor receives the root task text together with the active goal—here g2—not the full stack.

papers.abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.
authors: Mahmoud S. Mayaleh, Fetia Bannour, Nour-El-Houda Yellas
bullets: Multi-domain slice placement jointly decides function hosting, inter-domain routing, and admission under an NP-hard online setting.
Fixed planning strategies do not generalize across topology regimes, and many rejected requests may have feasible but undiscovered placements.
ORION combines LLM-based intent and plan generation with multi-agent RL for cross-domain selection and per-domain function placement.
Its outcome-driven episodic memory stores network conditions, plans, and verified success or failure outcomes to guide future planning.
On held-out topology families, memory improves admission by 4.6–11.5 percentage points; importance-based retention outperforms FIFO storage.

papers.abstract: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses class imbalance and ambiguous boundaries between adjacent CEFR levels.
Combines focal loss to emphasize difficult or underrepresented examples with supervised contrastive learning for more discriminative representations.
Evaluates sentence- and document-level assessment in monolingual and multilingual settings.
Consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple CEFR benchmarks.

papers.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.
bullets: Compares closed-source LLM prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, SLM–LLM enhancement, and newly proposed hybrid strategies.
Introduces two manually annotated NLP datasets covering academic abstracts and full-text articles.
LoRA-adapted T5 achieves macro F1 scores of 0.7408 on abstracts and 0.7013 on full text.

Combining strategies with complementary error patterns further improves KERE performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.
authors: Alessandro Previti, Konstantinos Vandikas, Mario Alviano, Mats Carlsson, Albin Larsson Forsberg, Alexandros Nikou, Athanasios Karapantelakis, Aneta Vulgarakis
bullets: Refines the decoding grammar at each step by removing values that cannot lead to a specification-satisfying output.

A backtracking variant revises earlier choices when later constraints leave only values the LLM considers unsuitable.
Model-agnostic and compatible with existing grammar-constrained decoding, with modest symbolic-reasoning overhead.
Evaluated on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks, improving specification adherence and alignment with the model’s prompt interpretation.

papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
authors: Alexandros Christoforos, Chadbourne Davis, Paul Raj
bullets: Models long-context diffusion costs using two budgets: attention-graph edges and activated feed-forward experts.
Unifies local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming sparsity preserves document-level information.
Defines normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
Evaluates the DualBudget configuration on scientific summarization, multi-hop QA, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction.
Results show gains over listed baselines through 16K, mixed ablation effects, and measurable degradation as sequence length grows.

papers.abstract: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. Using an expanded corpus of 722 official UN Security Council (UNSC) records, we measure nation-level bias with five complementary tests, thereby extending prior approaches to cover a broader set of bias expression channels: opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose), and framing (Headliner). To enable grounded bias evaluation, we explicitly define an unbiased status for each test; in particular, for WOW and AK+- where ground truth is difficult to specify, we propose an action-based pseudo unbiased status derived from observable voting behavior to construct a quantifiable baseline. Benchmarking 4 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small, and Qwen3-30B) across the five permanent members of the UNSC, we find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines defined for each test, model outputs lean toward the opposition (red) side for China and Russia and toward the supportive (blue) side for the U.K., the U.S., and France. These results underscore the need to audit IR-facing LLM deployments with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.
authors: Jonghyeon Choi, Yeonjun Choi, Beakcheol Jang
bullets: Evaluates nation-level bias using 722 official UN Security Council records and five complementary tests: opinion ranking, association sorting, vote simulation, opposition attribution, and framing.
Defines test-specific unbiased reference statuses to support quantitative, cross-setting comparisons.
Introduces action-based pseudo-unbiased baselines for opinion ranking and association sorting, derived from observable voting behavior.
Across four evaluated LLMs, outputs lean opposition-oriented for China and Russia, and supportive-oriented for the U.K., U.S., and France.
Highlights the need for grounded, multi-test audits of LLMs used in international-relations applications.

papers.abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.
authors: Jinkyeong Choi, Chaebin Jeong, Junsung Jeon, Donghyeon Park
bullets: Introduces self-consistency bias: the persistence of incorrect claims in incoming memory.
Compares four auxiliary objectives by information content and update sensitivity within a shared recursive interface.
Reward-related prediction achieves the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning among evaluated conditions.
A claim-level analysis shows that errors can persist despite corrective observations.
Motivates tracking error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of auxiliary memory supervision and evaluation. (a) Supervised initialization: the memory generator fθ encodes the update context with the reference memory p∗t under teacher forcing. Reward Preservation (RP), Predictive Preservation (PP), and Semantic Anchoring (SA) supervise the information content of the representation ht or its projection qt (ϕ: fixed text encoder); Update Stability (US) penalizes the sensitivity of qt to a perturbed incoming memory p̃t−1. We compare behavioral cloning (BC) alone, BC with each objective, and BC with all four. (b) Recursive inference, shared across conditions with auxiliary objectives inactive. The generated memory keeps a valid fact but also an incorrect claim inherited from pt−1 (self-consistency bias), which misleads the policy; error persistence is therefore evaluated together with valid-fact retention. papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
authors: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi, Yong Deng, Shuheng Shen, Changhua Meng, Xiaofeng Wu, Jie Yang, Wei Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of static supervised fine-tuning data for evolving MCP agents.
Uses rollout feedback to identify capability gaps and learning targets.
Evolves verified seed tasks while preserving aligned verifiers, then recovers or refines teacher trajectories with reusable skills.
Fine-tunes the student on evolved task–trajectory pairs and repeats the process using new feedback.
Reports absolute gains of 16.5% on Toolathlon, 10.2% on MCPMark, and 12.6% on MCP-Atlas over the initial student.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a co-evolution framework for agents and training data, addressing the static data distribution problem in agent fine-tuning. This is a form of test-time adaptation and continual learning for LLM agents.
papers.title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
papers.tldr: EvoMCP co-evolves MCP-agent tasks and training trajectories in a feedback loop, improving agents by continually targeting newly revealed capability gaps.

papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
authors: Jiedong Zhuang, Peng Zhao, Jialin Tang, Haoji Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate storage in long-context GDN prefill.
Uses a block-adjacent solver for approximate local Delta computation and an input-dependent selector for recurrent-event allocation across head pairs.
Materializes only selected updates and reconstructs token outputs from compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across RULER and 4K–128K contexts, retaining about 29% of recurrent events yields 1.50–1.94× GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including selection overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3 End-to-end SparseGDN execution pipeline. The block-adjacent intra-chunk kernel computes transformed values U, compact update coefficients, and selector scores. The dynamic selector converts these scores into a structured event mask. Only selected events trigger deferred W materialization and recurrent-state updates, producing compact event states. During output reconstruction, the mapped output kernel retrieves the appropriate preceding event state from HBM and applies the accumulated gap decay, while computing group-local interactions and producing outputs for every token.

Figure 1 GDN-core prefill latency across context lengths for Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B. Compared with FLA GDN, SparseGDN additionally includes the online selector overhead. Latency is aggregated over all 24 GDN layers. SparseGDN reduces latency at every context length, reaching 1.93× and 1.94× speedup at 128K for the 9B and 4B models, respectively. Lower is better.

Figure 9 Accuracy--efficiency trade-off across retention budgets. Each panel plots the aggregate RULER score difference ∆, defined in Table 3, against the geometric mean GDN-core speedup over 4K–128K. Point labels show measured recurrent-event keep rates. Solid lines connect nondominated configurations among the evaluated sparse operating points. The cross marks the approximately 49%-keep configuration, which is dominated by the approximately 39%-keep configuration for both models under these aggregate metrics. Speedups include online selection. Higher and farther right is better.

Figure 10 Tail-window ranking quality, scan cost, and illustrative task scores. Left: change in retained nonanchor dense-decode importance mass relative to Tail-16 on 130 stratified 8K requests per model, with task-stratified paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Pair-tier assignments, exact per-pair keep counts, and anchors are fixed to Tail-16. The gray curve reports standalone score-kernel latency per layer at 8K. Right: illustrative 128K score curves. The shaded bands highlight the default Tail-16 window in both panels.

Figure 5 Dynamic event selection and packing. Here, ZBi denotes the i-th 16-token block of the pre-activation output-gate tensor Z within a chunk. Chunk scores determine the retention order within each head pair. Recurrent lifetime and output-visibility proxies weight the estimated gains from larger budgets, which determine the low-, medium-, and high-retention tiers. The example assigns 9, 4, and 3 pairs to these tiers. Selected events are packed in temporal order into CSR chains for recurrent execution.

Figure 11 Complete-model prefill peak allocated memory across context lengths. Measurements use BF16, batch size one, use_cache=True. The shaded region shows the absolute memory saved by SparseGDN wherever both paths complete. The dashed line marks the nominal 80 GB device capacity as a reference. Crosses indicate Native OOM at 256K and are placed on this reference line for display; they do not represent measured allocation peaks. SparseGDN completes at that length for both models. Lower is better.

Figure 7 Per-stage GDN-core prefill latency. The top and bottom rows show Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, respectively. The left column compares native Intra with SparseGDN Intra plus online Selector; the middle and right columns compare H and O. For SparseGDN, H includes deferred W materialization. Each component reports the median of per-iteration CUDA-event times summed over all 24 GDN layers. The stacked Intra-plus-Selector bars sum the two component medians. Boxed values denote the corresponding native-to-sparse latency ratios. Lower latency is better.

Figure 8 GDN-core speedup across batch sizes and context lengths. Speedup is Native/Sparse, includes online selection, and uses batch latencies aggregated over all 24 GDN layers. Crosses mark configurations without a paired speedup because Native runs out of memory. Crosses are placed at a fixed height for display and do not represent measured speedups. The corresponding sparse-only outcomes are detailed in Table 2. Every completed paired configuration favors SparseGDN. Higher is better.

Figure 2 Two empirical structures observed in layer 16 of native-dense Qwen3.5-4B on an 8K RULER input (niah_multikey_3, row 0). (a) Adjacent chunk-boundary states are frequently nearly stationary, while the magnitudes of their changes vary substantially across value heads. (b) The left panel shows |M−1 − I|, averaged over 123 complete 64-token chunks and all 32 value heads. Here M is the native Delta-solve matrix defined in Section 2.3; subtracting I removes the unit diagonal, and absolute values are taken elementwise before averaging. The coefficients concentrate near the causal diagonal and weaken across more distant token blocks. This observed locality motivates the block-adjacent approximation, whose computation support is shown in the right panel.

Figure 6 Tier-aware scheduling of heterogeneous recurrent event chains. High-, medium-, and low-retention head pairs induce event chains with different workloads. Scheduling them in physical-head order can place a long high-tier chain behind shorter tasks, creating an SM straggler and extending kernel completion time (left). SparseGDN orders chains by expected workload and uses event-count-adaptive execution to distribute them across SMs (right), reducing load imbalance and tail latency. The red dashed line denotes kernel completion.

Table 6 Kernel-pipeline ablations at batch size one on a GPU. Speedup is the ratio of reference to optimized median latency over the stages listed in Scope. Each variant uses five warmup forwards and 30 interleaved CUDA-event measurements. Within each measurement, the indicated stage times are summed across all 24 GDN layers before computing the median across measurements. Separately timed Selector work is excluded; statistics fused into Intra remain included. Each row uses its own reference, so the isolated speedups should not be multiplied. Compact+mapped reports the joint effect of compact state storage and mapped output reads.

Table 4 Algorithmic component ablation on all 13 RULER tasks at 4K (1,300 examples per model). Adaptive masks are recomputed for each Intra variant. Bold highlights the proposed method.

Keep is the mean fraction of valid recurrent pair–chunk events retained across evaluation requests; padding chunks are excluded. ∆ = Ssparse−Sbase is the arithmetic difference in aggregate RULER scores, computed from unrounded scores over 7,800 examples per model using the official scoring rules. Scores and their differences are expressed on the percentage scale. Speedup is the geometric mean of the six GDN-core speedups at batch size one under the timing protocol in Section 3.1, including online selection. Higher speedup and ∆ are better.

Table 7 Complete-model prefill peak allocated memory. “Incr.” denotes the peak allocation above memory already live at forward entry. “Incr. reduction” is the relative decrease in this increment, computed from unrounded values. Native OOMs during its first 256K warmup, so no completed-forward peak or increment is available. Lower is better.

papers.selection_reason: Hardware-aware sparse linear attention with recurrent-event selection improves long-context prefill computation and memory traffic.
papers.title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention

papers.abstract: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.
bullets: Evaluates five LLM review paradigms across three input representations and three models using ICLR 2025 submissions.
Direct absolute rating and comparative ranking have similar rank correlation, but direct ratings are heavily compressed above the acceptance threshold.
After base-rate-matched recalibration, Direct Rating agrees more with human scores than Elo while using 24% as many API calls.
Abstract-only input outperforms full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice.
Human scores better predict citations overall; Group Rating uniquely preserves citation correlation after controlling for human scores and ranks within accepted papers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the experimental pipeline. Papers pass through three input representations (top), then through (a) absolute rating methods, which score each paper independently, or (b) comparative rating methods, which infer a latent rating from head-to-head outcomes and rescale it to 1–10. Only the comparative family is rescaled, so inflation and other absolute-error metrics are not comparable across families. Inline metrics give the best configuration in each family on the stratified 232-paper sample at the fixed ≥ 6 threshold.

Figure 7: Score distributions for the five paradigms vs. ground truth (abstract-only, GPT-4o-mini). Absolute methods (Direct, Anchor) compress scores into a narrow 6–8 range, while comparative methods (Elo, Swiss) preserve broader distributions closer to ground truth. Annotated below each: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ (Spearman correlation).

Figure 2: External validity on the 126 test papers carrying a retrievable citation count, a complete set of paradigm scores and a recorded decision. a, Paradigm rank under three evaluation targets; the lines cross, so none is best on all three. The decision target counts the 18 withdrawn submissions as non-accepted, which leaves the ordering unchanged. b, Spearman ρ with citation count, as an open circle (raw) joined to a filled circle (controlling for the mean reviewer score). Only Group Rating retains its correlation after the control (ρ = 0.304, p = 0.0006, surviving Bonferroni correction across the eighteen tests in Table 11). Anchor’s partial value is negative and Swiss’s exceeds its raw value, so the two are given as positions on a common axis rather than as a decomposition.

Figure 3: Population-scale false-positive (strong paper wrongly filtered) and false-negative (low-quality paper wrongly accepted) rates as a function of the accept threshold, swept from 5 to 7. The dashed gray line marks the fixed ≥ 6 threshold used in Table 9; the dotted green line marks the base-rate-matched threshold of Elo and Swiss; Direct Rating’s, at 7.67, lies beyond the plotted range. Direct Rating’s curves are flat across the plotted range because only 1.8% of its predictions fall below 7, which is why a fixed threshold at 6 makes it appear degenerate.

Figure 4: Error localization by ground-truth score bin (population scale, threshold ≥ 6). For each paradigm, blue bars show false-positive counts (strong papers wrongly filtered) and orange bars show false-negative counts (low-quality papers wrongly accepted). Direct’s errors are almost entirely false negatives, since its inflation accepts nearly all low-quality papers, whereas Elo and Swiss distribute the error budget across both classes, with false positives concentrated at borderline ground-truth scores.

Figure 6: Score distributions by input representation (all paradigms pooled, GPT-4o-mini). Violin shapes show density and box plots show quartiles; ground truth (gray) is shown for reference. The three representations differ little in spread (pooled σ 1.56, 1.62 and 1.59 for abstract-only, vanilla and objective), and all are far narrower than ground truth (σ = 2.16). Annotated below each group: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ̄ (mean Spearman correlation with ground truth across paradigms).

Figure 9: Cross-model performance heatmaps. Left: Cohen’s κ (practical decision utility). Center: Spearman ρ (ranking potential). Right: grade inflation (calibration). GPT-4o-mini Elo achieves the highest κ despite slightly lower ρ than Direct.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Based Review Paradigms for Academic Paper Quality Assessment
papers.tldr: LLM review performance depends strongly on calibration, model, input format, and evaluation target, with no paradigm outperforming an always-reject baseline in accuracy.

papers.abstract: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.
authors: Ezza Ali, Sehrish Bibi, Momina Moetesum, Faisal Shafait
bullets: The study isolates replacement operators while keeping the pruning mask fixed across several MoE models and routers.
Survivor gate renormalization can reduce accuracy by 0.8–8.5 points on routers not trained with top-k renormalization and can reverse method rankings.
The proposed tilted novice improves over MoNE’s constant replacement by 3.45 points on OLMoE and 1.37 points on Moonlight at 50% pruning, with small parameter overhead.
Operator performance is model-dependent: trained-scale rerouting leads on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, while partial expert copies match the tilted novice on two models.

Evaluation task and calibration domain matter substantially; multiple-choice retention can overstate performance on math and code tasks, while calibration shifts the pruning mask more than resampling.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free expert pruning for MoE LLMs; directly relevant to efficient inference and large language model architecture.
papers.title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning
papers.tldr: Replacement semantics—especially survivor gate scaling—strongly affect training-free MoE pruning results, and no single replacement operator is best across models or tasks.

papers.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.
bullets: Isolates PRM score aggregation as a separate evaluation target in best-of-N reasoning selection.
Freezes reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and deletion traces so reducers face identical recorded selection problems.
Across seven checkpoints and two benchmarks, product shows higher deletion-induced instability than GM in all 14 stored N=32 cells.
The effect remains under a pre-injection-defined sensitivity analysis, while effects vary across checkpoints and Qwen results are statistically inconclusive by exact paired tests.
Provides versioned outcome records and CPU reanalysis; missing edited-score vectors limit testing new reducers under the same stress.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic evaluation protocol for process-reward-model aggregation in LLM reasoning; directly relevant to language foundation model reasoning and evaluation.
papers.title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation
papers.tldr: StrictPRMBench provides a replayable audit showing that, on its frozen evaluation records, product aggregation is more deletion-sensitive than geometric mean, without claiming universal or deployment-wide harm.

papers.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

A multidimensional framework combines speech-grounding assessment with LLM-based semantic judgment validated by human preference studies.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.
authors: Xuning He, Kai Fan, Runyu Zhang, Binghuan Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong
bullets: Long-horizon agents accumulate costly contexts that can obscure decision-relevant information.

Compact sequences enable reusable KV caches and reduce later-layer computation across the agent trajectory.

papers.abstract: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Huachuan Qiu, Ruocheng Guo, Zijun Shi
bullets: Targets a reliability gap: human-like behavior alone does not ensure clinically grounded interviewees.

Ablations indicate that the two channels support clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

papers.abstract: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
authors: Yunhui Jang, Zach Wang, Jai Doshi, Kangway Chuang, Sidney Lisanza, Taylor Joren
bullets: Targets the limitations of free-form, rewritten language memories for scientific optimization, where experience is measured quantitatively under specific contexts.
Uses domain-grounded identifiers to index insights and accumulates property-oracle measurements through local updates.
Links jointly applied interventions and decomposes evaluated sets to estimate their epistatic interactions.
Improves performance in most tested settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
Scope: results are reported for in silico antibody optimization; the abstract provides no specific datasets or numerical gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMIG. MEMIG constructs an epistasis graph with antibody-grounded identifiers. Directed edges organize property → germline → region → mutation hierarchies, while undirected edges connect co-occurring mutations and store their epistatic effects.

Figure 3: Memory retrieval of MEMIG. Given a starting antibody, MEMIG identifies the matching identifiers, retrieves the corresponding insights with their neighbors, and curates them into natural language. Blue denotes the antibody-grounded identifier and the corresponding node, green its quantitative record, and yellow the epistasis graph neighbors and the curation based on them.

Figure 5: In silico antibody binding optimization. Each numeric label corresponds to an antibodyantigen cluster, clustered by CDR sequence identity. ∗ denotes the structural baselines (dashed), which have access to the complex structure.

Figure 6: Cumulative performance progression. Vertical lines mark memory updates, where the rollouts between two lines are generated concurrently under the same memory. The curves report the centered rolling mean with a half-width of 30 rollouts, computed within each memory step. Notably, the ordering of rollouts within the same memory is random, so a downward slope does not imply performance decrease. Each dot marks the mean over all rollouts of that memory step.
Figure 2: Antibody optimization task.

Figure 7: Cumulative performance progression without a rolling average. Vertical lines mark memory updates, where the rollouts between two lines are generated concurrently under the same memory. Each point is the mean improvement over all rollouts sharing a memory step, and error bars indicate the standard error across those rollouts. The rolling average in Figure 6 smooths the rollouts within each memory step, which can obscure the value of an individual step. To remove this smoothing, we report the mean improvement of every rollout sharing a memory step as a single point in Figure 7, with error bars indicating the standard error across those rollouts. We observe the same trend as in Figure 6, where MEMIG improves over successive memory steps while the vanilla LLM does not, which confirms that the progression is not an artifact of the smoothing.

papers.abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.

On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, both methods perform best on average across general and mathematical reasoning benchmarks at 75% and 50% expert retention.

papers.abstract: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $\alpha_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(\Phi, t_n)$ alone. Here $\alpha_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $\alpha_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.
authors: Jiasong Han, Yunkai Chai, Jintao Wang
bullets: Defines a transfer operator that reevaluates a length-$L_0$ positional kernel on longer grids and computes a pre-training witness $\alpha_L$.
Characterizes relative-head generalization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer and establishes an absolute/relative duality.
Shows that learned-absolute schemes are underdetermined and derives a static expressivity bound.
Experiments on 2,625 controlled trained-model measurements show $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the studied generalizing and non-generalizing positional-encoding/task cells.
The theory does not cover content-dependent tasks such as addition or sorting; the general deterministic case remains an open conjecture.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the method. Select (fit) a single positional head’s kernel at length L0 realizing the task’s target pattern RL0 ; transfer the same kernel to a longer grid via TL (re-evaluate ΦLWΦ⊤ L , no retraining); old rows keep their argmax by the causal-mask identity (Thm 1); score the new rows [L0, L) to read off αL ∈ [0, 1]. The whole pipeline uses only (Φ, tn), with no Transformer training, no data samples, and no learned Transformer parameters (only a deterministic kernel-selection on the PE basis).

Figure 2: The offset taxonomy, derived (Theorem 2, Prop. 4). A relative kernel length-generalizes a fixed relative offset; a clamped learned-absolute encoding does the reverse; and neither handles a growing offset (the shared blind spot, right column). Throughout, the relative statements are for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer, the hypothesis of Theorem 2; the accompanying text explains why it is needed and what the L0-fit contributes. This 2 × 3 verdict is exactly the empirical PE taxonomy, here a consequence of what a single positional head can realize.
Figure 4: Empirical LG (solid) and training-free αL (dashed) vs. test length L (train L0=20), 1L1H. αL tracks both who generalizes and how LG decays with L.

The scale study uses 2 seeds (700 rows), and both columns are computed on the cells the two studies have in common, so the 2L4H entry (0.36) is over 19 cells rather than the 20 of Table 4, where the same quantity over all 20 cells is 0.31.

The bounded-offset cells (prev/skip3) are the only entries whose verdict moves with frequency – they degrade as frequencies are added (num:8→32 drives prev 0.47→0.00); the other cells’ raw αL shifts stay sub-threshold (e.g. first 0.93→1.00) and never flip the verdict. Verdict movement appears precisely at the selection gap and nowhere else.
