papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of length generalization and positional encoding relevant to long-context models.
papers.title: A Positional Realizability Theory of Length Generalization in Single-Head Attention
papers.tldr: A realizability theory explains when positional encodings enable length generalization in a controlled single-head, positional-only attention setting.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.
authors: Shengran Guo, Min Chi, Feifei Qiao, Varad Patwardhan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating symbolic, formula-based answers and distinguishing different skill states behind identical scores.
Uses a shared RoBERTa encoder with regression, ordinal, and classification grading heads, plus Q-matrix-guided prediction of skill mastery and learning gain.
Detects likely Gen-AI assistance and converts assistance probabilities into weights that reduce the influence of potentially unreliable cognitive evidence.
On 49,402 responses across 19 semesters, AICG reduces MAE by 50.3% versus RoBERTa regression and raises QWK from 0.798 to 0.927.
Cognitive supervision drives most of the gains; AI-aware weighting provides additional improvements, especially in recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

papers.selection_reason: Develops AICG, a framework for automated math grading that uses LLMs for cognitive supervision (Q-matrix) and Gen-AI detection to handle complex symbolic reasoning.

papers.tldr: AICG improves mathematical short-answer grading by combining score prediction with skill-level cognitive supervision and Gen-AI-aware reliability weighting.

papers.abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.
authors: Jihao Zhao, Shuaishuai Zu, Pengfei Li, Biao Qin, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Baochuan Yang
bullets: Aggregate acceptance metrics can obscure differences across reasoning, browsing, and tool-use states, especially in later browsing actions.
TraceSpec combines dynamic execution, fixed-prefix replay, and state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps.
TraceSpec-Traj provides 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states from browsing and software-engineering trajectories.
Adaptive intermediate-turn supervision improves replay throughput by 12.5%–22.6% over DSpark across tested target sizes and temperatures.
Scope: results focus on trajectory replay and evaluated agent workloads; findings also indicate workload and phase affect speculative-decoding behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TraceSpec, a framework for improving speculative decoding in LLM agents by connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. This addresses agent execution and LLM architecture.
papers.title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: TraceSpec improves speculative decoding for LLM agents by using trajectory-aware analysis and adaptive draft training, increasing replay throughput over its baseline.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
authors: Zhichang Yu, Baining Cao, Sbaaoui Idriss, Qi Wang, Gangqiang Xu, Ling Qin, Xiaoling Jin, An Liu, Shaohao Cai, Xiaoyang Bao, Shengle Chen, Changchang Ding, Pengfei Zhu, Jingxiang Xu, Yifeng Mao, Lu Liu, Hai Jin, Yingfeng Zhang
bullets: Agentic search harnesses can achieve strong retrieval-augmented answering with simple BM25/grep retrieval, but uncontrolled loops waste queries, reread documents, and fill context windows.
The proposed supply layer compiles documents into structures such as claim-evidence navigation trees, entity graphs, timelines, ontologies, wikis, and memories.
Claim-evidence navigation trees reduced query tokens by 38% on average, with 91% savings when the compiled evidence sufficed and a 1.9% increase otherwise.
A decision gate reduced reported latency from 140 seconds to 30 seconds, while retrieval-round substitution introduces its own latency cost.

Structural artifacts showed no detectable FRAMES accuracy gain under a competent harness, so their value is primarily efficiency, governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, and continuity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Context as infrastructure. Knowledge compilation is the supply side: an ingestion pipeline that enriches raw documents into typed context artifacts. The harness is the control side: it decides which artifact, if any, enters the window and when the loop stops. Tools are the contract between them. Arrows show the flow of context, not control. The navigation tree (highlighted), whose leaves are claim–evidence pairs, is the mechanism measured in this paper; the ontology artifact (highlighted) is the one whose value is primarily commercial rather than benchmark-visible.

Figure 2: Measured token and latency effects. Top: conditional change in total query tokens on FRAMES when projected evidence is sufficient (hit), insufficient (miss), and averaged over the benchmark. Bottom: end-to-end latency with and without the decision gate, with claim-leaf trees present. Negative bars are savings.

Table 2: The deployment ledger. Every row is defined for production collections, not FRAMES; the unit is the collection (or the reviewer team), and the comparison is against the same collection before the artifact or against a shadow control. Targets are pre-registered per deployment; a direction is reported only after the target is met, and audit coverage is an invariant rather than an average. The navigation-tree row refers to the claim-leaf variant; a carrier without claim leaves carries no evidence and is judged only on the organizational terms of Table 1. The mind map is a navigation-tree layout and is judged on the navigation terms of the navigation-tree row, the timeline on the temporal terms of its own row.

The two carrier-only rows remove the claim–evidence leaves, so their deployment value is organizational only—they arrange content, they do not add evidence.

Table 3: Accuracy audit of the structural variants on the full FRAMES benchmark. The two navigation-tree rows share the same carrier; the only change is whether claim–evidence leaves are present. “Neutral” means no improvement large enough to be distinguished from run-to-run variation in a single run, and it does not rule out a small effect below the resolution of this design; “negative” means a loss of that kind. We report the direction and the failure mode the audit supports, not point estimates: each variant was run once. The claim-leaf row is the measured mechanism, not a structural baseline.

Token changes are relative to the uncompiled BM25/grep harness; negative is a saving, and dashes indicate quantities not measured separately. The first three rows are conditional splits of the same benchmark—hit and miss are defined by the gate’s verdict—and the FRAMES average is over all evaluated questions. The last two rows are arm means, not conditional splits: each is the mean change of that arm against the uncompiled baseline over the queries in that arm (evidence present, evidence absent), so −52% is not comparable with the −91% hit figure or with the −38% average. papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'knowledge compilation' as a memory mechanism for LLMs in agentic systems, transforming raw retrieval results into structured, navigable context to reduce token usage and improve efficiency.
papers.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
papers.tldr: Knowledge compilation can make agentic retrieval more efficient by supplying governed, navigable context, even when it does not improve benchmark accuracy.

papers.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
authors: Alexander Detkov, Dashiel Karish, Matthew Oleynikov, Matt Thomson
bullets: Introduces two benchmarks for evaluating deductive reasoning across increasing inference depths.
Uses a controllable formal graph benchmark and a real-world knowledge-composition benchmark.
Compares knowledge supplied in context with knowledge encoded in model weights, without chain-of-thought prompting.
In-context knowledge substantially outperforms deduction over pretrained knowledge, though both degrade with longer compositions.
Findings highlight limitations relevant to prompt-based agent control and continual learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models receive graph adjacency in-context but integrate the information poorly, failing at long-range inferences. DeepSeek, Kimi, Nemotron, and 12 other models answer questions about a random graph of 50–60 nodes given in the prompt as a list of edges, with reasoning off. Each question concerns the nodes exactly k hops from a start node, so k = 1 questions require only direct-neighbor information. a) Verify: is a given node exactly k hops away? Accuracy falls from 93–100% at k = 1 to 49–56% at k = 3, close to chance. b) Count: how many nodes are exactly k hops away? Models count correctly 43–69% of the time at k = 1 and ≤ 16% from k = 2. c) Name one: name a node exactly k hops away. Models name a neighbor at 99–100%, but a node two hops away at only 9–40%. d) Enumerate: list every node exactly k hops away. Models list all neighbors at 71–100%, but no model lists more than 12% of sets correctly from k = 2.

Figure 2: Models compose facts from the prompt far better than from memory. DeepSeek, Kimi, and Nemotron answer k-hop Wikidata questions with reasoning off and information given in context, in memory, or both. a) The chain’s facts are given in the prompt under invented names, among 16 decoy chains with the same relations. All models compose at ≥ 94% up to k = 3, but at k = 6, Kimi composes at 29%, while DeepSeek and Nemotron Ultra fall to chance. b) The facts are recalled from memory without supporting facts in the prompt. Composition reaches only 37–64% at k = 2 and ≤ 12% from k = 4, although every fact is known. c) The facts are given in the prompt under their real names, among 16 real decoy chains, so the model can use both the prompt and memory. Accuracy reaches 36–71% at k = 6.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks LLM knowledge integration across in-context and parametric memory, with direct implications for memory reasoning and continual learning.
papers.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
papers.tldr: ImplicitHop shows that LLMs struggle to integrate multi-step knowledge, with performance declining sharply as inference depth increases, especially for pretrained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.
authors: Huancheng Chen, Xiaodi Sun, Zhaoqiong Huang, Michelle Chang, Jingwen Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of flat SkillBanks, which retrieve skills without modeling the overarching strategy for using them.
Introduces hierarchical routing: coarse-grained talents guide execution and softly prioritize associated fine-grained skills.
Uses matched rollout reward contrasts to train talent selection and group-relative advantages for downstream execution.
Across seven QA benchmarks and two agentic benchmarks, TalentRL consistently improves performance and achieves the best reported results among compared methods.
Reported peaks include 99.3% success on ALFWorld and a 90.7 score on WebShop.

papers.selection_reason: LLM agent skill routing over procedural memory fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: TalentRL: Strategy-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Skill Routing
papers.tldr: TalentRL improves LLM agents’ procedural-memory use by learning high-level strategy selection alongside skill retrieval through contrastive, strategy-guided reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.
bullets: Introduces 400 multiple-choice questions covering answerable inside knowledge and post-cutoff outside knowledge, with abstention available.
Defines NAS and KIS scores to reward searching for outside knowledge and avoiding unnecessary searches for inside knowledge.
Evaluates five commercial LLMs with and without vendor web search, focusing on deployed search behavior rather than verbalized confidence.
GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of outside-knowledge items but only 1% of inside-knowledge items; Mistral Small searches about 20% of outside-knowledge items.
Explicit temporal cues strongly influence search: two selective models’ NAS drops from about 0.72 to 0.57–0.58 without cues.

papers.selection_reason: Studies when LLM agents retrieve external information versus relying on static internal memory, directly informing LLM memory and retrieval decisions.
papers.title: Confident Fools or Careful Searchers? A Behavioural Study of When LLMs Search Beyond Their Static Internal Memory
papers.tldr: A benchmark shows that commercial LLMs vary widely in deciding when to search, with some searching appropriately for recent facts but missing uncued knowledge gaps.

papers.abstract: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
authors: Chenhao Hong, Jiakai Xu, Kaushiki Singh, Yusen Zhang, Eugene Wu
bullets: Targets pre-attempt difficulty estimation for model routing, test-time compute allocation, and tool selection.
Uses a cheap LLM to convert problems into a Constraint Intermediate Representation, which deterministically compiles into a constraint graph.
A graph neural network encodes the constraint structure to predict LLM response correctness.
Evaluated across seven SAT, logic, and math reasoning benchmarks and four LLMs.
Improves prediction over the strongest baselines, lowering NLL from 0.465 to 0.423 and raising AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727.

papers.abstract: There exists little mathematical theory explaining why Transformer architectures are empirically successful even for non-Markovian data. To this end, this paper studies next-token prediction via stochastic optimal control theoretically trained Transformers for such sources, where we consider either stationary and ergodic non-Markovian sources or those which are hidden Markov models of some finite order (possibly non-stationary). In either case, we first obtain error bounds via finite models with finite window approximations. For stationary ergodic sources, the resulting error is bounded by an entropy gap; for $N$th order Markovian sources, it decays at an exponential rate $\alpha^{\lfloor M/N\rfloor}$, where $M$ is the window length and $\alpha$ is determined by filter stability (and the Dobrushin coefficients of the transition and measurement kernels). We then construct a Transformer of depth $M+1$, one head per layer, realizing the truncated filter, and we optimally train it with stochastic control developed in earlier work, which rigorously returns a near optimal Transformer. In particular, we show that for a non-Markovian source, either under stationarity and ergodicity for general models or under filter stability for hidden Markov models, an optimally trained Transformer has arbitrarily small performance error with increasing context length, data, and approximation refinement. Numerical studies accompany the theory.
authors: Ka\u{g}an Akman, Jake Feldman Starosta, Naci Saldi, Serdar Y\"uksel

papers.abstract: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising way to oversee increasingly capable agents. It succeeds in part because current models appear limited in their ability to control what they verbalize in their reasoning traces. We investigate the source of this limitation and link it to an entropy collapse in the first few tokens following the opening thinking tag. We exploit this mechanism to recover CoT controllability through two inference-time interventions on initial tokens: prefilling, where even a single token can substantially increase controllability, and banning frequent opening tokens combined with in-context examples, which improves average compliance by 34-41 percentage points across models. These interventions recover mainly addition and style controllability (adding or transforming information), while suppression controllability (avoiding or removing information) exhibits more varied responses, suggesting distinct underlying mechanisms. Consistent with this, the two groups behave as separate capabilities: across models, performance correlates positively within these groups, while cross-group correlations are mostly negative. Importantly, we find that the relationship with monitorability depends on the evaluation: addition and style controllability more consistently positively correlate with monitorability, while suppression often shows negative associations. Our findings motivate the development of controllability evaluations that distinguish difficulty initiating a specific opening from general limitations of the ability to alter reasoning content, alongside separate reporting of control tasks and categories.

papers.abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

papers.abstract: Training a large language model is compute-bound, and current recipes divide the work between optimizers by hand: orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices, Adam-style updates for the rest. This division rests on human priors about which layer type deserves which geometry, and it fixes a single global update budget that every parameter block shares. We introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer that makes the partition of parameters into blocks the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry by its realized counterfactual return, then freezes the routes and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC), the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, the framework gives two results. First, its FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam (3.2794), the best hand-designed recipe: it recovers the human prior without hand-setting per-layer geometry. Second, FARO-ERC improves on that arm: it lowers the clean-data loss at every one of 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, a modest but robust gain. Its sign test, paired test, and confidence interval all agree, and it exceeds the measured run-to-run noise at no added time or memory. It works by trimming the riskiest blocks rather than expanding the safest, and it holds up under a corrupted stream, still lowering the mean loss and winning the seed majority. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/FARO.
authors: Xiaojun Wu, Cehao Yang, Xuhui Jiang, Chengjin Xu, Jia Li, Jian Guo

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.
authors: Yujian Chen, Hao Jiang, Guang Cheng, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu

Recurrent memory improves DSpark’s metrics, but does not close the longer-sequence gap; teacher probability matching helps Markov GenPPL without improving MAUVE.
More LangFlow denoising steps improve results at lengths 16 and 128, showing that inference refinement affects model comparisons.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45{\deg} Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.

bullets: Addresses the risk that recursive model updates may weaken safeguards or introduce new vulnerabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to solve complex scientific and practical problems via iterative optimization. However, dynamically coordinating diverse search mechanisms as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets evolve remains a critical open challenge. Targeted empirical diagnostics reveal that mechanism effectiveness is highly state-dependent. Motivated by this, we analyze how individual decisions drive final outcomes, decomposing the expected terminal improvement under a shared budget into cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses. Guided by this opportunity-loss theoretical foundation, we propose OptiCom, a unified framework that represents LLM-driven optimizers within a shared configuration space: C=(A,Q,O,E,M,S), corresponding to artifact, query, operator, evaluation, memory, and strategy. Operating within this space, a fast LLM-based Optimization Controller dynamically composes immediate mechanisms through structured Action Packages, while a slower Strategy Adapter refines long-term selection preferences, operator weights, and templates based on accumulated trajectory feedback. Comprehensive evaluations across 32 benchmark groups demonstrate the superiority of framework: OptiCom achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72 among 14 evaluated configurations, securing the top score in 23 groups. Ultimately, these results highlight the broad applicability and high extensibility of OptiCom as a general-purpose paradigm for robust LLM test-time scaling.
bullets: LLM-driven optimization mechanisms vary in effectiveness as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets change.
The framework analyzes terminal improvement as cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses.
OptiCom unifies optimizer components in a shared configuration space covering artifacts, queries, operators, evaluation, memory, and strategy.
A fast controller selects structured Action Packages, while a slower adapter updates preferences, operator weights, and templates from trajectory feedback.
Across 32 benchmark groups and 14 configurations, OptiCom ranked first on average and achieved the top score in 23 groups.

Composing optimization mechanisms. The analysis in Section 4 identifies two factors governing adaptive optimization: the opportunities provided by available actions, ∆t, and the loss incurred when selecting among them, ℓt. Guided by this decomposition, OptiCom dynamically combines complementary mechanisms within the shared configuration space. To maximize opportunities while mitigating selection loss, the framework operates through a continuous, state-conditioned execution loop driven by two core components: an Optimization Controller for immediate mechanism composition, and a slower Strategy Adapter for long-term guidance revision. Both components operate through LLM API calls with fixed model parameters (see Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.1).

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for natural-language logical reasoning, where the final answer is easy to check but the proof behind it is not. In natural-language logical reasoning, an intermediate conclusion should follow from its premises, and the resulting derivation should support the final answer. Existing methods lack machine-checkable verification of intermediate conclusions and answer-supporting proof dependencies, so they may assign credit to invalid or answer-irrelevant steps. We propose Proof-R1, an RL framework from formal verification that trains LLMs to construct verifiable proofs for natural-language logical reasoning. Proof-R1 admits a generated conclusion into the verified proof state only when the corresponding reasoning action satisfies the proof obligations through UNSAT-based machine-checkable formal verification. Proof-R1 also recovers the answer-supporting dependency closure to trace the proof structure of the final answer and align outcome credit with the proof dependencies. Experiments demonstrate that Proof-R1 improves answer accuracy across three logical reasoning benchmarks and four backbone models and outperforms training-free agents and training-based methods in terms of reasoning-process verifiability.
bullets: Existing approaches may reward invalid intermediate steps or reasoning that does not support the final answer.
The framework admits conclusions into the proof only when UNSAT-based verification confirms their proof obligations.
It traces the dependency closure supporting the final answer and aligns training credit with those proof dependencies.
Experiments across three benchmarks and four backbone models improve answer accuracy and reasoning-process verifiability.
The approach targets natural-language logical reasoning and depends on formal verification of generated proof steps.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents require reinforcement learning methods that can assign credit to intermediate decisions under sparse and delayed rewards. Existing group-based methods such as GRPO and GiGPO alleviate this issue by comparing rollout returns or repeated anchor states, but they still fail when the compared returns have no variation. We identify this failure mode as zero-credit failure: during early training, many failed rollouts contain useful prefixes, yet existing methods assign them no task-discriminative advantage. To address this issue, we propose Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization (MVPO), a potential-routed policy optimization algorithm that learns from viable failure prefixes. MVPO estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions, repairs zero-credit groups with potential-difference advantages, and attenuates the potential branch according to relative performance progress. Experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct show that MVPO outperforms eight strong baselines, including GRPO and GiGPO. Under the same training length, MVPO improves over the GiGPO baseline by +4.4 success points on ALFWorld and +5.3 on WebShop, while adding only 0.16%-0.20% advantage-construction overhead.
bullets: Targets sparse, delayed rewards where early decisions are difficult to credit.
Identifies zero-credit failure: failed rollouts with useful prefixes may receive no task-discriminative advantage when returns lack variation.
Uses Union-Find viability regions to estimate prefix potential and construct potential-difference advantages for zero-credit groups.
Attenuates the potential-based learning branch according to relative performance progress.
On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, improves over GiGPO by 4.4 success points on ALFWorld and 5.3 on WebShop, with 0.16%–0.20% advantage-construction overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MVPO. MVPO first estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions using future success, loop statistics, and adaptive milestone progress (§4.1). It then routes step-level credit according to anchor-group availability: informative anchor groups use anchor-based comparative credit, while zero-credit groups are repaired with prefix-potential advantages (§4.2). Finally, the routed step-level credit is combined with the episode-level group advantage for critic-free policy optimization (§4.3).

Figure 1: Motivation and overview of MVPO. Top: an ALFWorld case of zero-credit failure: all rollouts fail, making GRPO/GiGPO assign no task-discriminative advantage, while MVPO identifies viable prefixes using prefix potential. Bottom (a): zero-advantage steps affect over 90% of GRPO steps and about 65% of GiGPO steps in early WebShop training. Bottom (b): higher prefix potential predicts higher future success on ALFWorld. Bottom (c): MVPO reaches 40% success earlier during training. Bottom (d): MVPO improves final success over GiGPO on both benchmarks.

Figure 3: Training dynamics of MVPO. (a) The performance-progress attenuation mechanism works as intended. At the beginning of training, the EMA success rate is low and κt stays close to 1, allowing prefix-potential credit to repair zero-credit groups with full strength. As the policy improves, the EMA success rate increases and κt decreases accordingly, causing the potential branch to fade and leaving more gradient space to anchor-based comparative credit. (b) The learned prefix potential remains directionally meaningful throughout training. Successful trajectories maintain higher mean potential than failed trajectories, while the Union-Find region statistics remain stable. This supports the central assumption of MVPO: potential can distinguish viable failure prefixes from unproductive prefixes before final rewards become frequent.

papers.abstract: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.
bullets: Addresses jailbreaks in non-high-resource languages where models recognize risks in reasoning but still produce unsafe responses.
Introduces Think Gap Score and reasoning-trace substitution to measure cross-lingual gaps in how safety reasoning influences outputs.
Identifies safety-relevant neurons by comparing neuron importance with reasoning enabled versus disabled.
Uses neuron-selective consistency optimization with a frozen judge, without human-annotated responses or preference data.
Across two reasoning models, reduces attack success on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, generalizes to unseen languages, and preserves multilingual task performance while limiting false refusals.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our mechanistic analysis and ACTR framework. Top: TGS measures cross-lingual reasoning-utilization gaps; think-on/off comparisons localize safety think neurons. papers.abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.
bullets: Addresses article-isolated, black-box sentiment prediction in high-stakes financial applications.
Uses SEC 10-K-derived knowledge graphs to provide company profiles or relevance-ranked factual triples as context.
Works with any causal LLM without updating model weights and with nearly no added computational cost.
Attributes sentiment scores to article sentences and retrieved facts for inspectable, human-reviewable evidence.
Simulations show consistent portfolio-performance gains over a state-of-the-art baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of FinLLM-KG. (a) Financial news articles are tagged and preprocessed. In parallel, fixed-relation 10-K triples from FinReflectKG [8] are restricted by a temporal alignment gate to the latest 10-K filed strictly before the article. Eligible facts are supplied either as a company profile or as the top-k retrieved triples and mixed with the article; in the baseline, the context is the article alone. (b) A frozen causal LLM performs sentiment analysis on the resulting context (prompt). The sentiment signal is used in the portfolio construction framework and, for the proposed methods only, can be decomposed into sentence-level and triple-level attributions for explainability.

Fig. 2. Cumulative returns of sentiment-based 35% long–short portfolios under three conditions: Baseline (article text only), Summary (article text with the latest 10-K company profile), and Top-k Triples (article text with the top-k relevance-ranked factual relations), compared against the S&P 500 benchmark.

Fig. 3. Sentence- and triple-level attributions for a top-k triple prediction (s = +0.790). (a) Selected sentence-level Kernel SHAP attributions. (b) Exact Shapley values for the four retrieved 10-K facts relative to the company-anchored prompt. Green and red indicate positive and negative contributions, respectively.

papers.abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.
bullets: Success depends on both sampling correct answers and whether their upper reward tail beats that of incorrect answers.
Extreme value theory identifies correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical regimes.
Finite-sample laws show that under Gaussian rewards, high-variance incorrect responses can win despite lower mean reward.
With incomplete reward models, convergence may be polynomial rather than exponential, unlike oracle selection.
A lightweight tail-tension diagnostic estimates when additional sampling may become harmful; synthetic and real-score experiments support the theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: An illustrative overview of our explanation of BoN for verifiable problems. When n responses are sampled, assuming pass@1 = p, we obtain approximately np correct responses and n(1 − p) incorrect responses, each assigned a reward according to the corresponding reward distribution. Whether BoN selects a correct response is determined by the competition between the maximum reward Mc among the np correct responses and the maximum reward Mw among the n(1− p) incorrect responses. When n is sufficiently large, these maxima are governed by the tails of the respective distributions. Thus, the performance of BoN depends on the competition between the tails of the reward distributions for correct and incorrect responses.

Figure 2: An illustrative explanation of reward hacking in verifiable problems. The blue and orange points represent correct and incorrect sampled responses, respectively, with n points in total. The response outlined in red is the one selected by BoN. Thus, if a blue response is outlined in red, BoN successfully selects a correct response. In the monotonic-improvement case (top row), correct and incorrect responses have reward distributions with the same variance, so their maximum rewards grow at similar rates as n increases. In the reward-hacking case (bottom row), incorrect responses have larger reward variance, causing their maximum reward to grow faster and eventually exceed that of correct responses. Thus, BoN selects a correct response at small n but incorrect one at large n.
Figure 6: Tail-tension early stopping on RAMO-Llama3.1-8B scores. The proposed method mitigates degradation in reward-hacking cases while reducing computational cost.

Figure 5: Experimental validation of the EVT approximated Gaussian scaling law. BoN accuracy follows the predicted finite-n scaling Eq. (12) well. Furthermore, the typicalregion accuracy An(kn;x) closely matches Sn(x) as in Lemma 1.
Figure 7: Full results of the experiment verifying the scaling law using synthetic data.

Figure 3: Overall results for MATH with Pythia-12B, MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and GSM8K with Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The gap between BoN and oracle selection often widens with n, and some settings exhibit non-monotonic BoN accuracy.

Figure 4: Synthetic Gaussian experiments for the four phases. The observed BoN curves match the predicted iA, iiB, iiA, and iB behaviors, and the predicted n⋆ aligns with the empirical optimum in the reward-hacking phase.

Table 3: Properties of the reward distributions for correct and incorrect answers. c, w are subscripts denoting correct and incorrect answers, respectively, and µ, σ2, γ, T denote the mean, variance, skewness, and tail ratio (the ratio of the right tail to the left tail) of the reward distribution, respectively. In all cases, correct answers are assigned higher reward values on average than incorrect answers. On the other hand, except for Sky-Qwen-4B, the reward models have higher variance for the rewards of incorrect answers than for those of correct answers across all three datasets.
Table 2: Limits of An(kn;x) classified by the limiting values of αn and βn as n→∞
Table 5: Experimental comparison of our Tail-Tension Early Stopping with Kalayci et al. [2025].
Table 1: Four phases of BoN n-dependence. The initial trend is determined by Pr(Rc > Rw | x), while the asymptotic behavior is determined by the tail-dominant side in Theorem 1.

Table 4: Goodness of fit of the reward distributions for correct and incorrect answers to representative probability distributions. c, w are subscripts denoting correct and incorrect answers, respectively. papers.title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems

papers.abstract: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.
bullets: Addresses weak explanation-quality evaluation and overly coarse graph-context integration in existing methods.
Introduces a rubric measuring faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, validated against human judgments.
Uses progressive disclosure of neighbor records so the language model can focus on fine-grained relevant context.
Trains the graph agent with rubric-guided trajectory distillation for tool use and structured explanation generation.
Shows consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on three fraud datasets under the human-aligned rubric.

papers.abstract: We study in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained to minimise a logistic loss. Each prompt has a latent logistic teacher, and the learner must infer its direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. We derive an asymptotic prediction for the test logit in a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension, and total training prompts proportional to dimension squared. Our formula cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable effects on in-context performance. Our analysis also identifies the ridgeless separability regime and addresses the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, and sampling temperature on in-context classification performance. The theory's predictions closely agree with finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained linear-attention models, while experiments with standard softmax attention show qualitatively related behaviour beyond the regime assumed by our analysis.
bullets: Models prompts generated by a latent logistic teacher, with the learner inferring the teacher direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples.
Derives an asymptotic test-logit prediction when context length scales with dimension and training prompts scale quadratically with dimension.
Separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable performance factors.
Characterizes effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, sampling temperature, and ridgeless separability.
Predictions closely match finite-dimensional simulations and trained linear-attention models; standard softmax attention shows qualitatively similar behavior outside the theory’s regime.

figures.caption: Figure 7: An analogous comparison to Figure 1, but the logits here are from a trained transformer-style softmax attention block. In particular, we use standard scaled dot-product softmax attention with fully trainable query Q, key K , value V , and output O weights. We initialise these at identity to improve training dynamics. The model is trained for 100 epochs with AdamW with weight decay 0.1 and early stopping. We set d = 32 and β = 4.

Figure 6: Similarly to Figure 1, we compare the theory to full-parameter linear attention, namely, we train the full K,Q, V matrices. Here we plot a quantile-quantile comparison of the model’s output logit on new prompt matrices Z against the theory prediction R and the true latent βGq. In all plots, d = 16, λ = 10−6, β = 1. Regularisation is applied to ∥K∥2F + ∥Q∥2F + ∥V ∥2F .

Figure 4: Effects of data parameters αtrain and τ on anisotropy (a) and calibration (b),(c). We compute a1, a2 (and correspondingly, m, v) using Result 1. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach to training language model agents, but sparse and delayed outcome rewards provide limited guidance for credit assignment across long interaction sequences. Recent work on on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers complementary supervision by evaluating a policy's sampled responses under privileged training-time context. However, our diagnostics show that positive average agreement between outcome and hindsight feedback coexists with substantial local disagreement, raising the question of how to allocate influence between them at each decision. We introduce UniOPSD (Unified On-Policy Self-Distillation), which unifies these feedback sources through adaptive local credit arbitration. UniOPSD constructs comparable credit estimates from environmental returns and successful-peer hindsight at shared interaction anchors. Historical agreement determines the global mixing level, while current signal availability and relative precision adjust each source's influence at individual decisions. The episode-level outcome contribution is retained, and bounded token modulation refines the fused step credit for policy optimization. With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, UniOPSD achieves ALFWorld success rates of $82.8\%$ and $83.6\%$, WebShop success rates of $75.0\%$ and $82.0\%$, and Search-QA aggregate accuracies of $45.3\%$ and $49.8\%$, respectively. On 3B WebShop, UniOPSD improves over SDAR by $7.0$ percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zenghuang-Fu/Uniopsd
bullets: Addresses sparse, delayed outcome rewards and local disagreement between outcome and hindsight signals.
Builds comparable credit estimates at shared interaction anchors from environmental returns and successful-peer hindsight.
Uses historical agreement for global mixing, while signal availability and relative precision adapt influence per decision.
Retains episode-level outcome credit and applies bounded token-level modulation during policy optimization.
Reports success rates of 82.8%–83.6% on ALFWorld, 75.0%–82.0% on WebShop, and 45.3%–49.8% on Search-QA; gains 7.0 percentage points over SDAR on 3B WebShop.

The episode term is retained explicitly; bounded token modulation bk,t = 1− λm + λmwk,t refines the arbitrated step term before PPO. Privileged peer context is restricted to training.

Figure 2: Online validation success rates of GRPO, GiGPO, and UniOPSD with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ALFWorld and WebShop, measured every five training updates. UniOPSD uses successful-peer hindsight with correlation-guided fusion (corr).

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve increasingly diverse reasoning tasks, yet their performance remains highly sensitive to task prompts, intermediate instructions, and the way reusable problem-solving knowledge is incorporated. Existing optimization methods usually focus on only one part of this design space: they either optimize a monolithic prompt, or separately induce and refine skills from model traces. As a result, they lack a principled mechanism for deciding which component should be updated when failures occur, and they rarely optimize prompts, skills, and skill-use policies in a unified framework. We propose SPARO (Skill, Prompt, And Routing Optimization), a framework that jointly optimizes task instructions, reusable skill blocks, and routing rules. It performs controlled counterfactual evaluations, converts examples' effects into a probabilistic responsibility distribution over prompt, skill, and routing components, samples one component from that distribution, and applies the corresponding targeted mutation. This design moves language-program optimization beyond global prompt rewriting toward structured, reusable, and selectively activated task knowledge. Across five benchmarks and five worker models, SPARO consistently outperforms both prompt-centered and skill-centered optimization baselines. These results suggest that effective language-program optimization depends not only on discovering useful task knowledge, but also on deciding where that knowledge should be stored and when it should be activated.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of methods that optimize only prompts or skills independently.
Uses counterfactual evaluations to estimate each component’s probabilistic responsibility for example outcomes.
Samples a prompt, skill, or routing component for targeted mutation based on that attribution.
Evaluated across five benchmarks and five worker models, SPARO consistently outperforms prompt- and skill-centered baselines.
Highlights that optimization requires deciding both where knowledge is stored and when it is activated.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Sparo. Sparo maintains a cross-round evidence pool and optimizes a modular LLM program by performing counterfactual component attribution over the prompt, skill library, and router, then sampling a component from that responsibility distribution and applying the corresponding targeted mutation.

Figure 1: Overview of language-program optimization paradigms. Prompt-only optimization rewrites the global prompt for any failure; skill-only optimization distills reusable procedures but never diagnoses which component is at fault; Sparo treats the program as a modular object P = (p,B, r, t) and edits only the component that its attribution step samples.

Figure 5: Parameter sensitivity of Sparo on CLUTRR. We vary (a) memory capacity relative to the training-set size and (b) router weight allocation: balanced, and positive-, description- and negative-heavy.

Figure 3: Component-selection patterns across tasks for the Qwen3.5-4B (left) and GLM-4.6V-Flash (right) workers. Each column gives the percentage of optimization steps that selected a prompt, skill, or routing mutation, so the three cells of a column sum to 100% up to rounding.
Figure 4: Comparison of component-selection strategies on CLUTRR. Sparo outperforms random selection, roundrobin selection, and prompt-only optimization.

Table 1: Main comparison across five worker models and five benchmarks. The Prompt, Skill, and Route columns indicate which components of the language program each optimizer can edit (✓ supported, ✗ not supported). Within each model block, prompt-centered optimizers are listed first in chronological order (OPRO, TextGrad, GEPA, aPSF), followed by skill-centered optimizers (Trace2Skill, SkillOpt), then Sparo. OPRO is the reference method in each block; subscripts give the absolute difference from it. Best result per model–task setting in bold.

papers.title: Beyond Prompt or Skill? Attribution-Guided Optimization of Modular LLM Programs

papers.abstract: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.
bullets: Enterprise documents can lack current external metadata and reliable organizational context.
The study compares text-to-SQL, HNSW dense-vector RAG, and two-stage GraphRAG using a knowledge graph of changing metadata and identifiers.
GraphRAG answered all three repetitions of 16/20 questions, versus 10/20 for text-to-SQL and 3/20 for vector RAG.
GraphRAG performed especially well on company attribution and single-document questions, and avoided the benchmark’s identity-related falsehoods.
The authors limit their claim to the tested corpus, model, and question set; GraphRAG underperformed on structured aggregation queries.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The three retrieval arms over shared stores. Text-to-SQL and GraphRAG use two LLM calls each; vector RAG uses one and has no query language to repair. In GraphRAG only the first hop is LLM-authored: entity expansion is deterministic and system-authored, which is what prevents one entity’s fan-out from consuming the row budget and the model then reporting that the other entities do not exist.

Figure 6: The economics. (a) Text-to-SQL’s T3 mean is the SQL and not the model: the generated queries join three tables without narrowing first. (b) GraphRAG’s accuracy is bought: it has the highest token cost per passing attempt of the three, the exact figures being in Table 3.

Figure 1: The three facts a multi-hop question needs live in three different containers. Item 1A is narrative prose and is the only section embedded; EX-21 is a structured list attached to the same filing; insider roles are in a separate filing type entirely. Every projected edge carries the accession number of the filing that asserts it.

Figure 2: Corpus shape. (a) EX-21 disclosure is extremely skewed — 275 filers list one subsidiary, 62 list more than 500 — so any generated LIMIT over a join to this table starves whole entities unless rows are balanced per entity first. (b) The small 2025-08 bucket is spillover, since a monthly feed contains filings dated at the end of the preceding month.

Figure 5: Results. The composition in (b) matters as much as the rate in (a): vector RAG’s 45 refusals are a benign failure, text-to-SQL’s 16 uncited answers are right but unverifiable, and GraphRAG was never uncited because the traversal returns accession numbers before any text is read.

Figure 3: Ingestion wall-clock, about 252 minutes total. Document fetch and embedding are roughly 82% of it. The fetch component is bounded externally by EDGAR’s ten-requests-per-second fair-access policy and cannot be parallelized away.
Figure 7: Repair frequency by category. GraphRAG required a repair on all fifteen T4 attempts, which is the entity-resolution category it lost.

Table 7: Cross-model probe on the featured multi-hop question with the GraphRAG pipeline held constant. One question and one attempt per model, so this is a probe rather than a measurement; it supports only the negative conclusion that a single-model benchmark bounds what can be claimed.

Table 3: Aggregate results over 180 scored attempts. Questions solved credits a question only when all three of its attempts passed. Bold marks the best value in a row. The outcome labels partition the attempts, so pass, falsehood, uncited, refused and the residual failures sum to 60 per arm.
Table 9: The twenty benchmark questions. T1 single-document semantic, T2 structured aggregation, T3 multi-hop relational plus text, T4 cross-document entity resolution.

papers.abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.
authors: Steven Yu, Sheng-Yu Wang, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, David Bau
bullets: Introduces CATT, a synthetic fact-tracing benchmark with unambiguous attribution ground truth and independently configurable dataset properties.
Shows that document redundancy and lexical distractors consistently degrade attribution performance.
Finds that causal evidence is localized to a few tokens, but document-wide averaging dilutes it with noise.
Uses negative log-odds gradients and top-token aggregation to recover critical evidence.
Improves ground-truth recall by 35–72 percentage points across baselines and counterfactual retraining performance by up to 4.9× on FTRACE-TREX.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Upweighting more influential tokens with log-odds improves Recall across token budgets. Recall@N as the number of retained tokens k varies, under cross-entropy (top) and negative log-odds (bottom). Columns show the three CATT settings. The yellow regions mark full-document scoring (“all”), with the upper-right endpoint in each column corresponding to the prior-work loss and aggregation choices. Negative log-odds with small token budgets substantially improve several methods, especially with distractors. Gains persist across multiple k values; retaining more tokens often reduces recall. Results are averaged over all dataset configurations and model seeds at |F| = 50 with error bars showing ±2 standard errors.

Figure 2: CATT: fact tracing tasks with controlled datasets. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B models on fictitious knowledge, which ensures our dataset is the sole causal source of its predictions. Left: Task I (Function Bindings) teaches new functions that always return a fixed value. Right: Task II (Routing Rules) teaches rules that sort objects based on their properties. Given a query phrased unlike any training document, we test whether attribution methods can correctly rank ground-truth documents. Unlike static benchmarks (Akyürek et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2026), we diagnose performance by systematically controlling dataset properties: (A) introducing redundancy by teaching the same fact across N varied document styles, and (B) injecting lexical distractors, which are irrelevant documents that perfectly mimic the query format to expose methods that rely on superficial text overlap. Task II omits distractors because each fact uses a disjoint set of attribute words, making it difficult to construct clear lexical overlaps. Browse the datasets on our project page.

Figure 5: The loss determines what type of tokens occupy the top positions. (a) Per-token attributions for one query on one of its ground-truth Rule Routings documents, under cross-entropy (top) and negative log-odds (bottom). Boxes mark the ten highest-scoring positions. Negative logodds moves the document from rank 1499 to rank 12 of 1500. (b) Each token type’s share of the top-10 positions divided by its share of all positions. Cross-entropy favors item names. Explore per-token attributions for other queries and methods in our demo.

This result is from Grad-Dot on a model trained on Function Bindings dataset with distractors (N=50, |F| = 50). View these plots for each dataset, method, and model seed on our project page.
