papers.selection_reason: Introduces SEDATE, a training-free approach to detect and edit aggression neurons in multilingual LLMs to improve safety.
papers.title: SEDATE: Do Large Language Models Share an Aggression Circuit Across Languages?
papers.tldr: SEDATE is a training-free detect–edit–verify method that targets aggression-related neurons to improve multilingual LLM safety while preserving general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Rubric-based rewards enable effective reinforcement learning on non-verifiable tasks. However, because these rewards are typically defined as a weighted measure of rubric coverage, models are trained primarily to maximize a recall objective. As a result, RL-trained models produce responses that are more complete but also more verbose and contain more unnecessary or factually incorrect content, leading them to be less preferred than responses from the base model. To address this issue, we present the FORK reward, which jointly optimizes recall and a novel precision objective, which requires each unit of a model response to be both necessary and factually correct, as measured by rubric-driven necessity credits and a factual-correctness grader, respectively. Our experimental results show that FORK outperforms existing rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality. Compared to the original recall-based reward, FORK substantially improves precision and reduces response length while achieving similar rubric coverage, which leads to significantly higher win rate compared to the base policy (e.g., from 10.6% to 68.0% on RubricHub-Medical and from 22.1% to 74.1% on HealthBench).
bullets: Recall-focused rubric rewards can produce overly verbose responses with unnecessary or incorrect content.
FORK adds a precision objective based on rubric-driven necessity credits and factual-correctness grading.
The method improves precision and shortens responses while maintaining similar rubric coverage.
It achieves Pareto-optimal coverage–quality tradeoffs and higher win rates against the base policy on medical evaluation benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reward hacking in rubric-based RL and our mitigation method. With the standard coverage reward, recall (i.e., weighted coverage of rubrics) quickly saturates, while precision and win rate against a base model continually decreases and responses become more verbose. With a precision objective included in the reward (FORK), the model reaches similar recall while gradually increasing precision and win rate and generating less verbose responses. Here, we train Qwen2.57B-Instruct on RubricHub-Medical and evaluate it on an in-domain test set.

Figure 2: Training with FORK. Given a prompt, a policy model samples a response, which is then divided into units. An LLM grader matches rubrics to units to assign each unit a necessity credit and determines a credit threshold for unit necessity. In parallel, the grader assesses the factual correctness of all units. Precision is defined as the fraction of necessary and factually correct units, and recall follows the standard definition of weighted rubric coverage. We update the policy model using their weighted harmonic mean as a reward.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes FORK, a reward function that balances recall and precision to mitigate reward hacking in rubric-based RL for LLMs.
papers.title: Eat Your Precision: Precision Objective Mitigates Reward Hacking in Rubric-based RL
papers.tldr: FORK reduces reward hacking in rubric-based RL by jointly optimizing response coverage and the necessity and factual correctness of each response unit.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use exhibit inconsistent behavior across independent runs from identical states, calling different tools, producing contradictory outputs, or pursuing divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces the variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox, while improving performance across benchmarks and model scales. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance, without requiring ground-truth labels.
bullets: Addresses the inability of task-completion metrics to capture trajectory-level consistency and inconsistency propagation across future turns.
Defines RSD as expected cumulative semantic disagreement between independent rollouts, using natural language inference and a recursive formulation inspired by bisimulation metrics.
Trains a neural network on independent rollouts to estimate future divergence at each turn without waiting for the full trajectory to finish.
Using RSD as a fine-tuning reward reduces task-progress variation on tau2-bench and toolsandbox while improving benchmark performance across model scales.
Matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance and requires no ground-truth labels.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Diagram illustrating Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD) in LLM agents. The first three panels display trajectory spreads for perfectly consistent, mostly consistent, and highly inconsistent agents over time. The final panel maps an agent’s expanding and converging semantic action space alongside its corresponding RSD score, demonstrating how the metric tracks the variance of semantic divergence at each turn.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a metric for measuring consistency in LLM agent trajectories, applicable to agent memory and behavior analysis.
papers.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
papers.tldr: Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD) measures and reduces how much LLM agent behavior diverges across repeated tool-using runs from the same state.

papers.abstract: Energy-based models have shown promising properties for domain-specific tasks but remain challenging in modeling general-purpose scenarios. To bridge this gap, we design energy-steered models (ESMs) for foundational language modeling. ESMs integrate energy steering and token generation within a single architecture to leverage the energy-guided search to refine token generation. Specifically, ESMs first optimize a latent state over the energy landscape, then leverages the refined latent state for token generation. By performing such energy-guided pre-training on large-scale corpora, ESMs learn generally effective energy landscape where favorable tokens correspond to lower energy values. To explore the scaling behavior of ESMs, we pre-train ESMs on three large-scale corpora, then evaluate across 26 downstream tasks spanning a broad range of domains. Our results demonstrate that ESMs have promising scaling behaviors with increasing model size and training data, and outperform GPTs on most downstream tasks. These findings highlight ESMs as a promising architecture for large-scale pre-training and general purpose problem solving. We fully release the model weights and training infrastructure to enable the community to completely reproduce and extend our results. GitHub: https://github.com/datamllab/openesm HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/collections/guan-wang/openesm
bullets: Targets the challenge of extending energy-based models from domain-specific tasks to general-purpose language modeling.
Combines energy steering and token generation in one architecture by optimizing a latent state over an energy landscape before decoding.
Pre-trains models on three large-scale corpora and evaluates them across 26 diverse downstream tasks.
Reports favorable scaling with model size and training data, outperforming GPTs on most evaluated tasks.
Releases model weights and training infrastructure for reproduction and extension.

papers.abstract: The Muon optimizer applies spectral orthogonalization to matrix-valued updates and has shown strong performance in large-scale neural network training, yet the mechanisms of this transformation in feature learning remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this question through a tractable factual-recall model, where a fact maps each subject-relation pair to an answer, and a linear transformer learns the subject- and relation-dependent information required to recover this mapping. The transformer is optimized with gradient flow (GF), spectral GF, or Sign GF, which are continuous-time limits of gradient descent, Muon, and Adam, respectively. Prior studies (Nichani et al., 2025) have shown that when the number of subjects exceeds the number of relations, GF learns relation-dependent information before subject-dependent information, producing a feature-separation phase during training. We characterize this separation with the learning times when the subject- and relation-dependent components of the prediction reach a target accuracy. With $S$ subjects and $R$ relations, GF has a learning-time ratio of $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{S/R})$, whereas Spectral GF reduces this ratio to $\widetildeΘ(1)$. In addition, for fixed $S$ and $R$, the subject- and relation-dependent errors decay as $1/(T\log T)$ in training time $T$ under GF, but as $\exp(-\mathrm{poly}(T))$ under spectral GF. Finally, we show that GF and spectral GF are equivariant under orthogonal transformations of the token embeddings, whereas Sign GF is not: Different orthonormal embeddings can potentially produce no feature separation, a large feature-separation phase, or even a reversed learning order. These results provide a mechanistic view of how spectral orthogonalization can fundamentally reshape feature-learning dynamics.
bullets: A tractable linear-transformer factual-recall model separates subject-dependent and relation-dependent learning.
Standard gradient flow learns relation information first, with a learning-time ratio of approximately √(S/R) when subjects outnumber relations.
Spectral gradient flow reduces this ratio to approximately constant order and changes error decay from 1/(T log T) to exp(−poly(T)).
Gradient flow and spectral gradient flow are invariant to orthogonal token-embedding transformations, while Sign GF is not.
The analysis offers a mechanistic explanation for how spectral orthogonalization reshapes feature-learning dynamics.

(b, c): Dynamics of subject and relation component accuracies in GF and Spectral GF. papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of spectral orthogonalization in Muon for transformer feature learning; transferable to training large foundation models.
papers.title: Muon Learns Facts Better: Understanding the Role of Spectral Orthogonalization
papers.tldr: Spectral orthogonalization, as used by Muon, can eliminate feature-separation delays and substantially accelerate factual feature learning compared with standard gradient flow.

papers.abstract: Recent Recommendation Agents (RecAgents) offer a promising alternative by shifting recommendation to an active, user-side paradigm, where generative agents autonomously perceive external platforms, reason over user preferences, and execute decisions. However, existing RecAgents still suffer from two critical limitations: brittle item perception based on noisy and heterogeneous item pages, and inefficient long-context reasoning over extended user histories and multi-step interaction traces. To address these challenges, we propose a novel recommendation agent framework, termed as ReMem, that combines OCR-based multimodal perception with time-evolving dynamic memory. Instead of parsing raw HTML, ReMem observes item pages through screenshots and extracts structured multimodal information via an OCR tool, enabling a more humanoid and platform-agnostic perception mechanism. To support long-horizon preference modeling, ReMem further introduces a chunk-wise sequential memory update strategy, where the agent selectively maintains a fixed-size memory of informative historical interactions while processing arbitrarily long contexts with linear inference complexity and bounded context length. This design allows the agent to preserve evolving user preferences without relying on external memory modules or disrupting the standard autoregressive generation process. To enhance the dynamic memory instruction, we further develop a multi-memory GRPO variant, which propagates the final-answer advantage to all intermediate conversations that contribute to the final response. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that ReMem consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 5.16\% across three recommendation agent tasks, namely searching, ranking, and judging.
bullets: Addresses brittle item understanding from noisy, heterogeneous webpages and inefficient reasoning over long interaction histories.
Uses screenshots and OCR to extract structured multimodal item information without relying on raw HTML.
Maintains evolving preferences through chunk-wise sequential updates to a fixed-size memory, enabling arbitrarily long contexts with linear inference complexity.
Introduces multi-memory GRPO to propagate final-answer advantages to intermediate conversations involved in generating the response.
Across three datasets and searching, ranking, and judging tasks, ReMem reports an average 5.16% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the proposed ReMem framework. Inspired by how humans browse item pages while maintaining time-evolving memory, ReMem consists of three key components. a) Instead of relying on raw HTML, ReMem adopts an OCR-based perception module that represents item pages through a unified multimodal view of natural text, images, and interactive elements, better matching users’ browsing behavior. b) User interaction history is processed as a sequential stream of chunks, from which the model maintains a compact, fixed-length memory that is continuously updated to capture evolving user preferences. c) To teach the model what to remember and how to update memory in multi-turn interactions, ReMem employs Multi-Mem GRPO, which propagates the final-answer advantage to all intermediate memories that contribute to the final response.

Figure 1: Motivation of ReMem. (a) Conventional RecAgents read the Web as text: they extract noisy HTML into long contexts and rely on LLMs to recover user intent, which is brittle across modalities and inefficient for long-context reasoning. (b) The proposed ReMem follows a more human-like principle: see item pages through OCR-based multimodal perception and memorize only evolving preference abstractions through dynamic memory, enabling robust modeling of time-evolving user preferences.

papers.abstract: Selection bias in large language models (LLMs) can persist despite instructions to ignore presentation order or prompts that elicit reasoning. Recent efforts to reproduce Jev-style System One behavior have produced a growing family of models that predict probabilities directly over supplied candidates. Yet systematic comparisons of selection bias across Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs remain limited in multi-option tasks. This leaves a central question: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias? We address this question with a simple test that shuffles options while keeping question and candidate content fixed. Across two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs, we trace individual answers through eight presentations and compare them with fixed-order repetition. On our primary collection of 1,700 questions from two benchmarks, Jev's accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27--29\% relative to the original order, with first failures continuing into the final presentation. This loss of initial successes is substantially larger than under fixed-order repetition, even for highly repeatable Jev reproductions. Nor does Jev show a general advantage over the LLM baselines in preserving correct choices. Aggregation offers limited protection: voting yields modest gains for Jev, while even unanimous answers are frequently wrong. These results expose a gap between repeatable decisions and decisions that remain correct across equivalent presentations, showing why stable accuracy alone cannot establish resistance to selection bias.
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
bullets: The study tests selection bias by shuffling options while keeping questions and candidates unchanged.
It compares two Jev versions, 12 Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs across eight presentations and fixed-order repetition.
On 1,700 questions, Jev accuracy changes by under two percentage points, but its cumulative failure set grows 27–29% relative to the original order.
Jev does not generally preserve correct choices better than generative LLM baselines, and first failures continue appearing in later presentations.
Voting provides only modest protection; even unanimous answers are often wrong.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes selection bias in LLMs and Jev-style System One models, demonstrating that stable accuracy does not necessarily imply resistance to selection bias across different presentations.
papers.title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
papers.tldr: Jev-style decision structure does not reliably reduce selection bias: choices may be repeatable yet become wrong when option order changes.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but often require many decoding rounds to complete a response. Efficient generation depends not only on which tokens are easy to predict, but also on how committing to them helps predict the remaining positions. A highly predictable token may provide little useful context, while revealing a less predictable token can help several other positions become predictable sooner. We propose dSpark, a new schedule distillation-based framework for learning when to commit tokens for faster diffusion language generation. To achieve this, we construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal makes other positions easier to predict, reducing uncertainty earlier in decoding. We then distill these schedules into the model to enable faster parallel sampling, with a KL-divergence regularizer to help preserve generation quality. We extensively evaluate our approach across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. On GSM8K, our method achieves remarkable 10.12$\times$ and 5.12$\times$ speedups over the various baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark.
bullets: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel but can still be slow because they require many decoding rounds.
The method prioritizes tokens whose unmasking makes other positions easier to predict, rather than only selecting individually predictable tokens.
These schedules are distilled into the model for faster parallel sampling, with KL-divergence regularization to preserve generation quality.
Evaluated on mathematical reasoning and code generation, dSpark reports up to 10.12× speedup on GSM8K while maintaining superior task performance.
The approach is demonstrated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes dSpark, a schedule distillation framework for diffusion language models (dLLMs) that learns when to commit tokens to achieve significant speedups in parallel sampling while maintaining quality.
papers.title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: dSpark learns which tokens to reveal first so diffusion language models generate responses in fewer decoding rounds without sacrificing task performance.

papers.abstract: Deep research, or any use of large language models (LLMs) to read a large document collection and produce insights, requires synthesizing information from different sources. In this work, we find that LLMs produce long-form research reports that read as confident syntheses but which fail to accurately reflect the underlying documents. We call this failure smoothing. In collapsing diverse and potentially conflicting sources into a single narrative, the model discards the evidential "jaggedness" of its corpus and asserts conclusions more decisive than the citations can support. We introduce a claim level scoring pipeline, SmoothScore, to quantify this effect. Our pipeline extracts key conclusive claims from model generated reports, then finds evidence relevant to each claim and clusters that evidence along high level aspects. Finally, each claim is scored with respect to the evidence to quantify the degree of smoothing done by the agent. Across 7 systems and 4 datasets, we find that agents consistently produce stronger claims than warranted.
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
bullets: The study examines how long-form LLM research reports can misrepresent their source documents.
“Smoothing” occurs when agents discard evidential nuance and make conclusions more decisive than the citations support.
SmoothScore extracts report claims, retrieves relevant evidence, clusters it by aspect, and scores each claim against that evidence.
Evaluated across 7 systems and 4 datasets, agents consistently produced claims stronger than warranted.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SmoothScore, a pipeline to quantify 'claim smoothing' in LLM research reports, identifying that models often assert stronger conclusions than the evidence supports.
papers.title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
papers.tldr: LLM research agents often turn mixed or conflicting evidence into overly confident claims, and SmoothScore quantifies this “claim smoothing.”

papers.abstract: Existing jailbreak attackers fall into two classes: static planners fix their single- or multi-turn adversarial plans in advance, remaining simple but losing sight of the victim's replies, wasting turns and limiting transferability; interactive generators read each victim reply to generate the next-turn attack but require in-loop evaluators for success signals or hints, incurring substantial costs and inflated performance. Bridging this gap, we propose SEMA-Auto, a sighted and efficient multi-turn attacker with autonomy, interacting with the victim model and terminating the session by itself upon success. To stabilize its behaviors and boost its capabilities, SEMA-Auto is trained in two stages. Synthetic bootstrap tuning installs the notion of attack targets and conforming decisions by fine-tuning the base model with bootstrapped trajectories. Decision-supervised reinforcement learning then optimizes two objectives jointly yet separately, reinforcing the attack with higher jailbreak reward while supervising the decision at each turn against an absolute target. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) attack success rates (ASR) across multiple datasets, victims, and judges, outperforming all static and interactive baselines, within almost the fewest turns, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency. For example, SEMA-Auto performs a $76.0\%$ ASR@1 within an average of $3.0$ turns against DeepSeek-V4-Flash on AdvBench, while the best static baseline is $54.8\%$ with fixed $7$ turns and the best interactive baseline is $43.8\%$ in $3.7$ turns. Against safety-hardened frontier models, GPT-oss-120B, GPT-5.4, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and GPT-6-Astra, our counter-trained attacker achieves an average $59.6\%$ ASR@1 on HarmBench, $13.8\%$ over prior SOTA. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/SEMA
authors: Mingqian Feng, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Chenliang Xu, Jialin Song, Qiyao Ma, Chengquan Guo, Carolyn Buractaon, Christopher White, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fixed attack plans that ignore replies and interactive attackers that require costly in-loop evaluators.
Uses two-stage training: synthetic bootstrap tuning, followed by decision-supervised reinforcement learning for attack effectiveness and per-turn stopping decisions.
Autonomously terminates sessions upon success, improving efficiency and reducing unnecessary turns.
Reports state-of-the-art attack success across multiple datasets, victim models, and judges; on AdvBench, it achieves 76.0% ASR@1 in an average of 3.0 turns against DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
On HarmBench against safety-hardened frontier models, a counter-trained attacker reaches 59.6% average ASR@1, exceeding prior SOTA by 13.8 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SEMA-Auto, a reinforcement learning-based jailbreak attacker that achieves state-of-the-art efficiency and success rates by training on decision supervision and bootstrapped trajectories.
papers.title: SEMA-Auto: Sighted and Efficient Multi-Turn Attack with Autonomy
papers.tldr: SEMA-Auto is an autonomous multi-turn jailbreak attacker that adapts to victim replies, decides when to stop, and achieves strong attack success with few turns.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones.These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
bullets: Addresses the interaction between in-distribution generalization and extrapolation to longer sequences.
Derives guarantees based on model parameter sizes, quantization space, and sequence alphabet size.
Characterizes the trade-off between the number of training samples and their lengths.
Shows theoretically that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing sample count.
Experiments support the theory’s predictions.
papers.selection_reason: Joint statistical and length-generalization bounds for transformers inform long-context training and length-scaling tradeoffs.
papers.title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
papers.tldr: The paper develops joint theoretical generalization bounds for fixed-precision, multi-layer transformers across both sample distribution and sequence length, showing that longer training strings can be far more valuable than more samples.

papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), model-reported self-confidence is often miscalibrated, yet it may still be useful for efficient evaluation. At the same time, LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to direct human auditing, but its practical benefit depends on calibration quality and inference cost. This paper develops a unified statistical framework for both evaluation routes under alternative sampling strategies. For direct auditing, confidence-stratified sampling is used to recover population accuracy from partially verified outputs without requiring calibrated confidence. Finite-sample uncertainty is characterized, and the analysis shows how highly uneven confidence strata affect audit efficiency and label allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, the judge is modeled through sensitivity and false-positive rate, yielding an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty. The two routes are then compared through human-label and total-cost efficiency boundaries. Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro show that miscalibrated self-confidence can still support statistically valid stratified auditing. Under highly imbalanced confidence distributions, proportional allocation substantially reduces estimation error relative to equal-per-stratum allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, only a small subset of target--verifier pairs satisfies the idealized human-label efficiency condition, and automated inference costs can further limit potential savings. These findings clarify the statistical and economic conditions under which confidence-guided auditing and automated verification are useful.
authors: Harine Choi (Texas A&M Transportation Institute, Texas A&M University System), Chenchen Kuai (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zihao Li (Department of Civil, Construction and Environmental Engineering, Marquette University), Jiwan Jiang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Yunlong Zhang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zhiwen Fan (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zhengzhong Tu (Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Texas A&M University), Yang Zhou (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University)
bullets: Confidence-stratified sampling estimates population accuracy from partially human-verified outputs without calibrated confidence.
Finite-sample analysis links uneven confidence strata to audit efficiency and label allocation.
Judge-assisted evaluation uses sensitivity and false-positive rates to form an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty.
Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro favor proportional over equal-per-stratum allocation under imbalanced confidence distributions.
Only a small subset of target–verifier pairs meets the idealized human-label efficiency condition; inference costs can erase savings.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified statistical framework for evaluating LLMs using self-confidence stratified sampling and LLM-as-a-judge, characterizing finite-sample uncertainty and cost efficiency.
papers.title: From Self-Confidence to Statistical Accuracy: Scaling Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation with Direct and LLM-Assisted Auditing
papers.tldr: A unified framework shows when miscalibrated model confidence and LLM judges can reduce the cost of statistically valid LLM evaluation.

papers.abstract: Conversational QA systems should fix errors when users push back and signal which answers to trust. We split each follow-up into its speech act (re-ask, agree, or challenge) and its payload (an answer string, correct or not), and measure four confidence signals on the same transcripts: verbalized confidence, length-normalized likelihood, a frozen hidden-state probe, and P(True). Answers change when the user supplies an answer string and almost never under the speech act alone: in every retained full-size cell, the correct answer converts at least four times as many wrong answers as re-asking or agreement. The four signals disagree. On Qwen2.5-7B the frozen probe rises with answer persistence rather than truth; this holds on held-out questions, with Llama-3-8B (cleaned answers) as support, but not on four other models. Among 81 Qwen2.5-7B errors that survive one re-ask, re-asking, a fresh chat, or abstain repair almost none, while a gold answer repairs 75-95%. In two preregistered replications, every repair rate without an answer string stays below 0.15; a larger post-hoc rerun excludes 0.15 except for the empty elicit. With BM25 TriviaQA evidence, sentences that contain the answer repair 67-76% of persistent errors versus at most 12% when they do not. An end-to-end contain-gate cuts harm on TriviaQA, but a deployable gate that does not know the gold answer repairs few errors.
bullets: Separating speech act from payload shows that re-asking or agreeing rarely changes answers; supplied answer strings drive correction.
Four confidence signals disagree, and Qwen2.5-7B’s frozen probe increases with answer persistence rather than correctness; this pattern does not generalize to all tested models.
For persistent errors, re-asking, fresh chats, and abstention repair almost none, whereas providing a gold answer repairs 75–95%.
Evidence containing the answer repairs 67–76% of persistent TriviaQA errors, versus at most 12% for evidence without it.
An answer-containment gate reduces harm, but a deployable gate without gold-answer access repairs few errors.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes confidence signals and answer persistence in conversational LLMs, introducing a 'frozen hidden-state probe' to measure dissociated confidence signals.
papers.title: Not One Belief: Answer Payloads, Persistence, and Dissociated Confidence Signals in Conversational Question Answering
papers.tldr: Conversational QA systems mainly correct persistent errors when follow-ups provide an answer string, while confidence signals often track persistence rather than truth.

papers.abstract: JEV decision models pair a language model backbone with a lightweight scoring head to select among natural-language options. Direct selection compares candidate answers within one request, whereas entailment reranking evaluates each candidate in a separate natural language inference (NLI) request over fixed relation options. We examine whether the readout and adaptation choices used for direct selection remain effective for cross-request reranking. We combine a mean-span readout with selective backbone adaptation. Mean-span pooling replaces the option-ending pointer with an average of the contextualized states inside each NLI option, without adding head parameters. Selective adaptation retains low-rank updates in attention and gated DeltaNet projections while removing feed-forward adapters. On MC11, which averages accuracy over eleven reranking configurations from seven sources, selective adaptation improves NeoHorse-1-4B accuracy over the all-module baseline while cutting trainable parameters by more than half, and mean-span pooling yields further consistent gains at the same parameter count.
authors: Haocheng Mei, Yuchuan Tian, Ye Yuan, Enhua Wu, Chao Xu, Allen Chen, Kai Han, Yunhe Wang
bullets: Studies whether direct-selection design choices transfer to cross-request NLI reranking.
Mean-span pooling averages contextualized states within each NLI option without adding head parameters.
Selective adaptation keeps low-rank updates in attention and gated DeltaNet projections while removing feed-forward adapters.
On MC11, selective adaptation improves NeoHorse-1-4B over the all-module baseline with more than half the trainable parameters removed.
Mean-span pooling provides further consistent gains at the same parameter count.
papers.selection_reason: Improves entailment reranking in language models using selective adaptation and mean-span readouts.
papers.title: Improving JEV Entailment Reranking with Span Readouts and Selective Adaptation
papers.tldr: Mean-span readouts plus selective backbone adaptation improve JEV entailment reranking while substantially reducing trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: An offline language-based support tool is presented to assist pilot training and tactical decision-making in air combat operations. The system, named MATE (Mission Assistant for Training and Evaluation), applies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to answer natural language questions using content extracted from doctrinal and tactical manuals. Built entirely with open-source components, it performs text preprocessing, embedding generation, semantic search, and language generation locally, ensuring full offline functionality. The tool was evaluated by three Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots, who rated the answers produced with three open-weight language models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 14B, and Mistral NeMo 12B) to five tactical questions derived from a publicly available air combat manual. Average ratings ranged from 4.00 to 4.40 on a five-point scale, with Mistral NeMo 12B obtaining the highest score, and the pilots rated the response time of the tool as fully adequate compared to manual search. The relevance of the retrieved content was identified as the main point for improvement. Potential applications are discussed in onboard mission systems, flight simulators, and training environments.
bullets: Uses open-source components for local preprocessing, embeddings, semantic search, and language generation without internet access.
Answers questions from doctrinal and tactical manuals using three open-weight language models.
Three Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots evaluated five tactical questions, giving average answer ratings of 4.00–4.40/5.00.
Mistral NeMo 12B received the highest rating, and response time was considered adequate compared with manual search.
Retrieved-content relevance was the main identified improvement area; proposed uses include mission systems, simulators, and training.
papers.selection_reason: Describes an offline RAG system for tactical decision support in air combat using open-weight LLMs.
papers.title: Offline Language-Based Support System for Tactical Decision-Making in Air Combat Operations
papers.tldr: MATE is an offline RAG-based assistant that helps air-combat pilots retrieve and understand tactical guidance through natural-language questions.

papers.abstract: Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entangled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progressively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. HSE first extracts task-level evidence from individual trajectories, then aggregates recurring evidence within the same repository to form repository-specific skill candidates, and finally consolidates consistent patterns across repositories into transferable skills across repositories. The evolution is driven by an external writer-evaluator loop that generates and assesses skills while keeping the underlying coding model frozen. The loop externally updates the writer and evaluator policies to improve subsequent skill generation and assessment. This hierarchy progressively filters task-specific details while preserving procedures that generalize across diverse coding environments. Successful trajectories yield reusable guidance for future tasks, while failed trajectories reveal recurring failure modes that guide avoidance and recovery. We evaluate HSE on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE, using GLM-5.2 across Pi and Claude Code harnesses and GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with Pi. Across both benchmarks, 10 skills evolved solely from SWE-Gym improve coding performance across all evaluated settings, demonstrating transfer across benchmarks, coding models, and agent harnesses. We further evolve the skill library from target-benchmark trajectories without verifier feedback, relying solely on the learned evaluator for candidate assessment and achieving additional gains through benchmark-tailored skills.
authors: Jun Gao, Yun Peng, Changhai Zhou, Yuhan Zhu, Xiangyu Zeng, Shiyang Zhang Yuhua Zhou, Luozheng Qin, Qian Qiao, Xiaoteng Ma, Baian Chen Weiyi Shang, Zhen Ming Jack Jiang, Lizhi Liao, Xiaoxue Ren
bullets: Addresses the challenge of separating transferable coding skills from task- and repository-specific context.
Aggregates evidence hierarchically: individual tasks → repository-specific candidates → cross-repository skills.
Uses an external writer–evaluator loop to generate, assess, and refine skills, including lessons from both successes and failures.
Skills evolved solely from SWE-Gym improved performance across SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE settings, models, and harnesses.
Benchmark-specific skill evolution produced further gains without verifier feedback, using only the learned evaluator.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE) for coding agents to distill transferable procedural skills from trajectories.
papers.title: Hierarchical Skill Evolution for Coding Agent
papers.tldr: Hierarchical Skill Evolution distills reusable coding procedures from trajectories and progressively generalizes them across tasks, repositories, and benchmarks while keeping the coding model frozen.

papers.abstract: Modeling the latent, multi-step reasoning processes of learners is a core challenge for adaptive tutoring systems, which often rely on simple right/wrong answers rather than understanding how students think. Instantiated here for grammatical reasoning, this study introduces a diagnostic framework that makes students' step-by-step problem-solving visible by analyzing their action sequences in an interactive learning game. The framework computes five interpretable strategy dimensions (e.g., systematic error correction, random guessing), estimates coordination demand from task structure and behavioral patterns, and classifies reasoning into four distinct states. Analyzing 36,234 interactions from 234 students working on 42 morphosyntactic exercises, we found that reasoning strategies vary primarily by context rather than stable traits (intraclass correlation = 0.14), and students show high persistence in unproductive states; specifically, 74.6% of failures driven by high coordination demand (rather than simple knowledge gaps) are followed by another failure without intervention. Our early warning model predicts validation success with strong accuracy (AUC = 0.826 using strategy patterns alone; 0.902 with additional sequential context) while avoiding circular reliance on current error counts. These findings demonstrate that making latent reasoning processes visible enables earlier, more targeted scaffolding that responds to how students are thinking rather than simply whether they succeed. While demonstrated in language learning, the framework provides a generalizable, interpretable architecture for diagnosing complex, structured reasoning in any domain.
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
bullets: Analyzes interactive action sequences through five strategy dimensions, coordination demand, and four reasoning states.
Finds that reasoning strategies depend more on task context than stable student traits.
Students often persist in unproductive states: 74.6% of failures involving high coordination demand were followed by another failure without intervention.
An early-warning model predicts validation success with AUC 0.826 from strategy patterns and 0.902 when sequential context is added.
Demonstrated in grammatical reasoning, with a proposed architecture for interpretable diagnosis in other structured-reasoning domains.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a diagnostic framework for adaptive scaffolding in language learning using LLMs to analyze student reasoning.
papers.title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
papers.tldr: An interpretable framework reveals students’ step-by-step reasoning in structured tasks, enabling earlier and more targeted adaptive scaffolding than right/wrong signals alone.

papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly considered for clinical decision support, where their answers should be grounded in clinical evidence and remain robust to irrelevant information. Prior work shows that a single irrelevant sentence can lower the accuracy of medical models, but not where inside the model its effect can be removed, or how to do so without knowing which sentence it is. We find that blocking attention to a known distractor restores the answer, whereas head masking can suppress correct answers. We also show that the model's hidden states mark the distractor as the sentence that least fits the case even when the model follows it. To remove a distractor's effect without knowing which sentence it is, we propose EXCISE, an inference-time method that blocks the sentence most influencing the answer, but only if the model's hidden states mark it as inconsistent with the case. On MedQA-TD (MedQA with Targeted Distractors), a benchmark we construct in which each distractor targets a specific wrong option, EXCISE gains 16.7-22.8 accuracy points at a 1.5-2.1-point cost on the same questions without distractors, outperforming prompting, rewriting, and steering baselines for all three models. Its gains extend to MedDistractQA and BiasMedQA, as well as chain-of-thought generation.
authors: Yerim Hong, Sohyun Son, Heeseung Chung, Mujeen Sung
bullets: Irrelevant sentences can substantially reduce medical model accuracy, even when the model follows them.
The model’s hidden states often identify the distractor as the sentence least consistent with the case.
EXCISE operates at inference time without requiring the distractor to be known in advance.
On the authors’ MedQA-TD benchmark, it improves accuracy by 16.7–22.8 points, with a 1.5–2.1-point cost on distractor-free questions.
Benefits also transfer to other benchmarks and chain-of-thought generation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes EXCISE, an inference-time method to excise distracting sentences in medical QA to improve robustness.
papers.title: EXCISE: Locating and Excising Distracting Sentences in Medical Question Answering
papers.tldr: EXCISE improves medical question answering by identifying and blocking the influential sentence that appears inconsistent with the clinical case.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase computation per token by repeatedly applying a shared backbone, offering a way to improve language modeling and downstream task performance at a fixed backbone parameter count. However, each loop depends on the preceding loop, so increasing recurrent depth also increases decoding latency. Existing approaches include Parallel Loop Transformers, which reduce latency by overlapping loop computation across token positions, but yield rapidly diminishing marginal accuracy gains at larger depths. To address this challenge, we introduce LoopFold, which folds computation at multiple recurrent depths into parallel batches for the same token prefix. A lightweight predictor estimates inputs to later loops so they can start before earlier loops finish. A corrector then refines the outputs of these later loops using newly available results from earlier loops. All components are trained jointly using only the final next-token prediction loss. In experiments with 1.4B models, deeper LoopFold configurations achieve progressively higher average zero-shot accuracy across eight tasks, rising from 53.41% to 56.38%. Vanilla looped models and PLT show limited gains over the same depth range. Compared with a nine-loop vanilla model, LoopFold uses five sequential stages and additional parallel computation to reduce decoding latency by 46%.
authors: Feichen Song, Boyi Zeng, Yiqin Hao, Shixiang Song, He Li, Yizhou Yang, Zitong Wang, Yifan Liu, Ziwei He, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Looped Transformers improve modeling capacity through repeated use of a shared backbone, but sequential loops increase latency.
LoopFold folds multiple recurrent depths into parallel batches for the same token prefix.
A predictor estimates later-loop inputs early, while a corrector refines them when earlier-loop outputs become available.
Joint training uses only the final next-token prediction loss.
In 1.4B-model experiments, average zero-shot accuracy rose from 53.41% to 56.38%; five sequential stages reduced latency by 46% versus a nine-loop vanilla model.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LoopFold to parallelize recurrent depth in Looped Transformers, reducing latency while maintaining accuracy.
papers.title: LoopFold: Parallelizing Recurrent Depth in Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: LoopFold reduces the decoding-latency cost of deeper Looped Transformers by predicting and correcting later recurrent loops in parallel.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers offer a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling by repeatedly applying a shared backbone. Vanilla looped Transformers use each backbone output directly as the input to the next iteration. These outputs may contain information useful several iterations later, but retaining it across the loop depends entirely on the single hidden state. We introduce StateLoop, which maintains one additional persistent state per token to retain information across iterations. At each iteration, a learned gate controls how much of the previous state is retained and how much information from the backbone output is incorporated. The updated state is projected back and added to the backbone output for subsequent iterations and final prediction. This design reduces Pile perplexity and improves average accuracy across eight zero-shot tasks over Vanilla Looped. Its perplexity advantage over Vanilla Looped grows with trained loop depth, consistent with persistent state becoming increasingly useful as recurrent computation deepens.
authors: Feichen Song, Boyi Zeng, He Li, Shixiang Song, Yiqin Hao, Zitong Wang, Yizhou Yang, Yifan Liu, Ziwei He, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Vanilla looped Transformers rely on a single hidden state, which may lose information needed in later iterations.
StateLoop maintains an additional persistent state for each token across loop iterations.
A learned gate balances retaining prior state with incorporating new backbone output information.
The updated state is projected back into the backbone output for later iterations and final prediction.
It reduces Pile perplexity and improves average accuracy across eight zero-shot tasks; its perplexity benefit grows with loop depth.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces StateLoop, an architectural variant of Looped Transformers that adds persistent state to improve language modeling.
papers.title: StateLoop: Persistent State for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: StateLoop augments looped Transformers with a gated persistent state per token, improving language modeling and zero-shot performance over vanilla looping.

papers.abstract: Both models and minds not only encode features that describe an entity, but can specifically represent which features of that entity are relevant for a given context. This core capability underlies in-context learning in language models and a variety of cognitive phenomena in minds, yet it is unclear how intelligent systems identify and promote relevant features. In this work, we propose Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA), an algorithmic hypothesis that provides an explanation for how relevance is determined in the context of few-shot concept induction --- the ability to infer a latent concept from a small number of positive examples. Under ADA, concept induction proceeds by forming a summary representation of the examples in a feature space that is shaped by amortized knowledge about which features tend to be useful for finding commonalities between items. We investigate and validate ADA in language models using a few-shot concept induction task. This work provides a novel perspective on the mechanisms supporting contextualization in language models and a promising hypothesis for a core aspect of cognition.
authors: Michael A. Lepori, Laila Johnston, Aalok Sathe, Zhuonan Yang, Roman Feiman, Ellie Pavlick
bullets: Addresses how models determine which entity features matter in a given context.
Models concept induction as summarizing positive examples in a feature space shaped by prior knowledge of useful commonalities.
Introduces ADA as an algorithmic hypothesis for relevance determination.
Investigates and validates ADA in language models on a few-shot concept induction task.
Offers a perspective on contextualization in language models and a hypothesis about a related cognitive mechanism.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA) to explain few-shot concept induction and feature relevance in LLMs.
papers.title: An Algorithmic Account of Few-Shot Concept Induction in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper proposes Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA) as an explanation for how language models identify relevant features during few-shot concept induction.

papers.abstract: Mental health research on social media has been dominated by English-language datasets and DSM-5-centered resources, limiting cross-lingual and cross-cultural understanding of online mental health expression. We introduce MATCHA, the first Chinese multi-disorder mental health dataset that links disorder-specific Weibo Super-Topic communities with users' broader public timelines. MATCHA covers seven DSM-5 disorders and a control group, comprising 46,025 cohort-level users and 1.8 million posts. The dataset distinguishes users with explicit self-disclosure evidence from broader disorder-related participants through an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline, and is released in a rigorously de-identified, controlled-access format. Using MATCHA, we analyze behavioral, linguistic, symptom-related, and life-event-related patterns across disorders, and conduct cross-lingual comparisons with Twitter-STMHD. Our analyses show that Weibo Super-Topics function as concentrated spaces for affective and health-related expression, while cross-platform differences between Weibo and Twitter often exceed cross-disorder variation. MATCHA provides a new resource for community-aware and cross-lingual mental health NLP research.
authors: Bingrui Jin, Baihan Li, Zitong Li, Kunyao Lan, Shimeng Li, Kenny Q. Zhu, Mengyue Wu
bullets: Covers seven DSM-5 disorders plus a control group, with 46,025 users and 1.8 million posts.
Links disorder-specific Weibo Super-Topic communities to users’ broader public timelines.
Uses LLM-assisted annotation to distinguish explicit self-disclosure from broader disorder-related participation.
Analyzes behavioral, linguistic, symptom, and life-event patterns and compares Weibo with Twitter-STMHD.
Finds that platform differences often exceed cross-disorder variation, while Super-Topics concentrate affective and health-related expression.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a new Chinese mental health dataset for cross-lingual NLP research.
papers.title: MATCHA: A Chinese Multi-Disorder Mental Health Dataset with Cross-Lingual Analyses on Social Media
papers.tldr: MATCHA is a de-identified Chinese Weibo dataset enabling multi-disorder and cross-lingual mental health research beyond English- and DSM-5-centered resources.

papers.abstract: Automated fake news detection is vital on social media, where fake news is easily rewritten to fool detectors. However, existing approaches typically rely on superficial writing cues or single-style text rewrites, resulting in poor robustness under diverse cosmetic modifications. We construct MANTIS-Bench, a multi-axis presentation-attack benchmark that pairs original news with rewritten views across writing style, emotional expression, and dissemination framing. We further propose MANTIS, an instance-adaptive adversarial framework enabling dynamic worst-case training tailored to each news article with zero inference-time overhead. This reframes fake news defense from heuristic format smoothing into targeted, fact-invariant credibility assessment. Experiments on MANTIS-Bench show that MANTIS reduces the Union Attack Success Rate (UASR) by 3.55 percentage points relative to SheepDog on GossipCop and consistently outperforms prior single-axis defenses on Macro-F1 while maintaining competitive clean accuracy, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-axis and instance-adaptive worst-case training.
authors: Dexin Liu, Fan Yang, Zimu Wang, Xunfei Zhu, Bolin Ren, Bingyan Zhang, Wei Wang, Qi Chen
bullets: MANTIS-Bench tests fact-preserving transformations across writing style, emotional expression, and dissemination framing.
MANTIS performs dynamic worst-case training tailored to each news article.
The approach shifts defense from superficial format smoothing toward fact-invariant credibility assessment.
It reduces Union Attack Success Rate by 3.55 percentage points versus SheepDog on GossipCop.
MANTIS consistently improves Macro-F1 over single-axis defenses while retaining competitive clean accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses adversarial robustness in LLMs for fake news detection using instance-adaptive worst-case training.
papers.title: MANTIS: Multi-Axis News Transformations for Instance-Wise Stress Testing and Worst-Case Training in Fake News Detection
papers.tldr: MANTIS improves fake news detectors’ robustness by training against instance-specific, multi-axis rewrites without adding inference-time cost.

papers.abstract: Constrained decoding guarantees that Large Language Models (LLMs) produce outputs conforming to predefined formats, but is often assumed to inherently degrade reasoning. We examine this assumption through a taxonomy of three constraint types: \emph{format constraints}, which enforce output structure; \emph{validity constraints}, which mask invalid answer; and \emph{reasoning constraints}, which restrict reasoning trajectories. We theoretically show that appropriate constraints can preserve or improve performance by eliminating invalid paths. Across four model families and eleven open-source models, causal ablations on diverse benchmarks using state-of-the-art constrained decoding strategies reveal that apparent performance degradation largely stems from non-equivalent prompting and output formats rather than from decoder-level masking. Meanwhile, validity constraints improve reliability and extractability by eliminating invalid answers, while reasoning constraints can improve reasoning and, consequently, accuracy when they enforce beneficial trajectories. These findings show that the impact of constrained decoding depends on the type of constraint and the output space it removes. Our code is available.
authors: Ngoc Trinh Hung Nguyen, Alonso Silva, Armen Aghasaryan, Mehwish Alam
bullets: The study distinguishes format, validity, and reasoning constraints.
Theoretical analysis shows suitable constraints can preserve or improve performance by eliminating invalid paths.
Across four model families and eleven open-source models, apparent degradation mainly came from mismatched prompting and output formats, not decoder masking.
Validity constraints improve answer reliability and extractability, while reasoning constraints can improve reasoning and accuracy when they enforce beneficial trajectories.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically analyzes how constrained decoding affects LLM reasoning and reliability, fitting the language foundation models topic as a method for LLM reasoning and inference-time behavior.
papers.title: Constrained Decoding: Harmful or Beneficial? Revisiting Its Impact on LLM Performance
papers.tldr: Constrained decoding does not inherently harm LLM performance; its effects depend on the constraint type and the output space it removes.

papers.abstract: Large language models incur substantial training and inference costs in personalized search and recommendation, as growing interaction histories lengthen request inputs and repeatedly expose the same item text to the model. We propose \textbf{C}omposable and \textbf{R}eusable \textbf{I}tem \textbf{M}emory (CRIM), a framework that separates item-level semantic encoding from request-level history modeling. A small set of learnable summary tokens compresses each item into compact continuous memories, while segment-level readout tokens (REC tokens) introduce predictive supervision within the interaction history. These memories are independent of users and queries and can therefore be reused across requests. At inference time, CRIM composes cached memories in interaction order and incorporates an optional query to produce a personalized retrieval representation, reducing repeated item-text encoding while retaining request-dependent contextual modeling. We further introduce a joint training mechanism that combines cached memories with sampled live re-encoding. Re-encoding only a few history items per request allows the retrieval objective to jointly optimize the item and request encoders at limited computational cost, while periodic cache refreshes maintain consistency. Extensive evaluation and cost analysis on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and our new LazSeq dataset show that CRIM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale, while limiting item re-encoding during joint training. We will publicly release our code and dataset.
authors: Haolin Li, Haipeng Zhang, Mang Li, Zhaohui Xia, Xun Zhu, Miao Li, Yu Zhang, Ji Wu
bullets: Addresses rising training and inference costs caused by long interaction histories and repeated item-text encoding.
Separates item semantic encoding from request-level modeling using learnable summary tokens and predictive REC tokens.
Composes cached, user- and query-independent item memories in interaction order, with an optional query for personalization.
Jointly trains cached memories with limited live re-encoding and periodic cache refreshes to maintain consistency.
Evaluations on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and LazSeq report state-of-the-art retrieval with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale.
papers.selection_reason: Cached item memories reduce repeated item-text encoding and inference cost in LLM-based retrieval, matching memory-efficient inference and LLM external-memory interests.
papers.title: CRIM: Composable and Reusable Item Memory for Efficient Personalized Retrieval
papers.tldr: CRIM makes personalized retrieval more efficient by caching compact, reusable item memories while preserving request-specific history modeling.

papers.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly asked to reason over a user's own web traces: group chats, community threads, activity logs and revision histories. On CL-bench Life, a benchmark of such real-life context learning, frontier LLMs solve fewer than one task in five. We find that the request is not the specification: over 80% of the benchmark's rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request, as for a rule set two turns earlier or every record that meets the user's criterion, and LLMs answering directly pass only 67% of these implicit rubrics against 81% of the others. We propose QERA, a Question-driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture that asks before it answers. QERA first turns the request into a requirement checklist and typed information needs, filtered by code for faithfulness to the user's words; it then answers from the whole conversation, asks the same questions again with quotes verified by code, and applies a guarded local repair. It needs no training or rubrics and makes about four LLM calls per task. On all 405 tasks with four frontier LLMs, QERA attains the highest solving rate on every LLM (21.0% on average, against 18.2% for the strongest of three inference-time baselines and 14.6% for direct answering) and leads every baseline significantly when pooled across LLMs, while using fewer tokens than PSCI and 4-5% of the tokens of Ctx2Skill. Ablations on GPT-6-Luna show that the gain is settled before the answer, by a fixed answer protocol (+3.8 rubric points) and the request-specific questions (+1.6), and that it is concentrated on implicit rubrics, with checking afterwards refining mainly numeric requirements.
authors: Jinhu Qi, Minda Hu, Wentao Zhang, Zixing Song, Irwin King
bullets: Implicit requirements are common: over 80% of CL-bench Life rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request.
Direct answering passes 67% of implicit rubrics, compared with 81% of other rubrics.
QERA builds a requirement checklist, asks typed information needs, verifies quoted evidence in code, and performs guarded repair without training or rubrics.
Across 405 tasks and four frontier LLMs, QERA averages a 21.0% solving rate, versus 18.2% for the strongest baseline and 14.6% for direct answering.
Its gains come mainly from the pre-answer protocol and request-specific questions, especially for implicit rubrics; post-answer checking mainly helps numeric requirements.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an inference-time question-driven reasoning architecture for in-context learning.
papers.title: Ask Before You Answer: A Question-Driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture (QERA) for In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: QERA improves LLM reasoning over users’ long-term web traces by asking targeted, evidence-grounded questions before answering.

papers.abstract: Outcome RL raises pass@1 but not pass@k at large k (Yue et al., 2025). But every pass@1 is scored under a token budget. Every recipe also trains under one. On physics and math problems at fixed token budgets, we compare the pass@1 of 20 released RL models (1.5B to 32B) with that of the thinking models they started from. We ask whether each pass@1 gain is changed behaviour or new knowledge. We divide each change in pass@1 into three parts. Finishing measures answering before the budget runs out. Reliability measures being right once finished. Reach measures problems RL solves that its base answered wrongly in all eight tries, minus problems the base solves that RL answered wrongly in all eight. We find four things. (1) Where the base often hits the token budget before answering, most of the change, gain or loss, is finishing (82% at 4k and 8k). Given more tokens, the base closes most of the finishing gap itself. (2) Where the base has enough tokens, the gain is reliability: the RL model is graded right more often, even on problems both finish. (3) By our definition, RL rarely solves what its base cannot. Reach adds at most 2.1 percentage points on any of our four physics and math sets. We checked 144 physics problems that only the RL model solved. Of these, 3.5% hold up when resampled or read. In a random sample, nine of ten new RL steps a human confirmed also appear in the base's samples. (4) In a small-scale RL run on an 8B model, the gain on new problems is finishing, with reliability flat. Supplying each problem's physical setup was not shown to improve on plain RL.
bullets: Compared with 20 released 1.5B–32B RL models and their base thinking models on fixed-budget physics and math tasks, the study decomposes pass@1 changes into finishing, reliability, and reach.
When base models often time out, finishing explains most gains or losses—82% at 4k and 8k tokens—and extra tokens largely close this gap.
When bases finish reliably, RL improves correctness among completed answers rather than discovering substantially new solutions.
Reach contributes at most 2.1 percentage points; only 3.5% of 144 apparent RL-only physics solutions held up under resampling or review.
A small 8B RL run likewise attributed new-problem gains to finishing, with flat reliability; providing physical setups did not improve over plain RL.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes outcome RL effects on LLM reasoning and pass rates under token budgets, relevant to language foundation model reasoning.
papers.title: What Outcome RL Buys: Finishing, Reliability, Rarely Reach
papers.tldr: Outcome RL’s pass@1 gains mainly come from finishing within the token budget and improved reliability, while genuinely reaching new problems is rare.

papers.abstract: Controlling personality in large language models is important for building conversational agents that can be customized to different users and interaction settings. However, existing personality control methods often face a tradeoff between strong trait expression and natural dialogue generation. We introduce FATE-5, Faithful Alignment of Trait Expression for the Big Five, a two-stage framework that separates personality encoding from naturalness alignment. FATE-5 first learns continuous soft prompt representations of Big Five profiles using dialogue supervision and an auxiliary survey objective. It then improves dialogue naturalness through preference alignment based on both dialogue quality and personality agreement. Across three language model backbones, FATE-5 maintains strong trait expression while achieving substantially higher dialogue naturalness than other trait-strong methods. On held-out questionnaires, it achieves monotonicity correlations of 0.97-0.99 and recovery RMSE of 8.9-12.4, substantially improving over the evaluated baselines. These results demonstrate effective continuous personality control while maintaining natural conversational behavior.
authors: Gunhee Cho, Hongyeob Kim, Yun-Gyung Cheong
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between strong personality expression and conversational naturalness.
Uses a two-stage framework: personality encoding followed by naturalness alignment.
Learns continuous soft prompts with dialogue supervision and an auxiliary survey objective.
Aligns responses using preferences that account for both dialogue quality and personality agreement.
Across three backbones, reports monotonicity correlations of 0.97–0.99 and recovery RMSE of 8.9–12.4 on held-out questionnaires.
papers.selection_reason: Fits LLM alignment and controllable generation research under language foundation models.
papers.title: FATE-5: Faithful Alignment of Trait Expression for Continuous Big Five Personality Control
papers.tldr: FATE-5 enables continuous Big Five personality control in language models while preserving natural dialogue.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve factual grounding without guaranteeing that every generated claim is supported. Previous work has studied claim-level conformal factuality in single-stage RAG and, more recently, multi-hop RAG. We examine its behavior in agentic RAG, where a language-model policy adaptively issues follow-up retrieval queries or terminates retrieval before response generation. We retain the retrieval-based relevance-scoring formulation and post-generation conformal filtering and evaluate six model-dataset configurations: GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B on HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA. Each configuration uses 60 fixed questions, 100 seeded 30/30 calibration-test partitions, five conformal target levels, and a no-conformal-prediction baseline. Across the six configurations, higher target levels are accompanied by higher observed full-support rates and reduced answer availability. At the 95% target, non-empty response coverage ranges from 17.23% to 60.17%, claim retention from 10.72% to 43.16%, and full support among non-empty outputs from 89.14% to 95.56%. We formulate the adaptive retrieval trajectory explicitly and characterize the reliability-informativeness trade-off when conformal factuality is applied after agent termination.
bullets: Studies claim-level conformal factuality in agentic RAG, where retrieval adaptively continues or stops before generation.
Evaluates GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B across HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA.
Across six configurations, stricter target levels increase full-support rates while reducing non-empty response coverage and claim retention.
At the 95% target, non-empty response coverage is 17.23%–60.17%, claim retention is 10.72%–43.16%, and full support is 89.14%–95.56%.
The paper characterizes the reliability–informativeness trade-off of applying conformal factuality after adaptive retrieval termination.
papers.selection_reason: Fits retrieval-augmented generation and agentic retrieval memory research.
papers.title: Adaptive Retrieval, Selective Answers: Evaluating Conformal Factuality in Agentic RAG
papers.tldr: Conformal filtering makes agentic RAG answers more reliably supported, but higher factuality targets substantially reduce answer and claim availability.

papers.abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.
authors: Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Moon-Il Joo, Hee-Cheol Kim
bullets: Addresses hallucination and domain-misalignment risks in LLM-based healthcare question answering.
Creates 500 QA pairs from de-identified discharge summaries using sentence decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided formulation, and expert review.
Evaluates six open-source general-purpose and biomedical LLMs before and after parameter-efficient LoRA tuning.
Tuning improved lexical, semantic, and clinical-fidelity metrics; the best model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L 0.40, BERTScore-F1 0.76, and UMLS-F1 0.49.
External PubMedQA evaluation also showed post-tuning accuracy gains for the two tested models; DocTalk was deployed as a secure web platform.
papers.selection_reason: Develops DocTalk, a medical QA system using fine-tuned Llama-3 models with Chain-of-Thought reasoning. This falls under Large Language Models, specifically focusing on instruction tuning and medical domain adaptation.
papers.title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical Decision Support
papers.tldr: DocTalk uses clinically grounded QA generation and LoRA instruction tuning to improve concise, chart-grounded medical answers for clinical decision support.

papers.abstract: Language models now answer questions alongside other claims: a note in the system prompt, a message from another agent, their own earlier answer. We ask what it takes to talk a model out of an answer it gets right on its own, and separate three factors that earlier studies vary together: where the advice sits in the prompt, who is said to have written it, and what the model has already written. On Qwen3.5-27B and four-option MMLU-Pro items, with the rest of the advice held fixed in each comparison, we find three things. First, position matters far more than the API channel, in opposite directions for a bare claim and an argument: a bare "the answer is X" does most harm just before the model answers, while the same claim with a false rationale does most harm before the question, where it raises error on items the model otherwise almost never misses from 1% to 67%; moving the claim between the system message and the user message at the same position changes error by a few points. Second, attributing the note to an authority rather than to another participant, and phrasing it assertively, each raise error by 10-27 points, while the two authorities we tested differ by under two. Third, replaying a correct worked answer before the advice protects it whether the text is shown as the model's own or as someone else's, and the same replay keeps wrong answers from being corrected by a bare correct note. The position result replicates under an independently written prompt. Code, items and all result tables are released at https://github.com/coolkillercat/safety.
bullets: The study separates prompt position, stated authorship, and the model’s prior answer while holding advice fixed.

A bare incorrect claim is most harmful immediately before the answer; an incorrect claim with false reasoning is most harmful before the question, increasing error from 1% to 67% on otherwise easy items.
Moving the same claim between system and user messages at the same position changes error by only a few points.
Authority attribution and assertive wording each increase error by 10–27 points, while the tested authorities differ by under two points.

Replaying a correct worked answer protects it from misleading advice, but also prevents a bare correct note from fixing an existing wrong answer; results replicate with an independently written prompt.
papers.selection_reason: Fits LLM behavior and context-sensitivity research under language foundation models.
papers.title: Position Matters More Than Channel: Talking a Language Model Out of a Correct Answer
papers.tldr: Where advice appears in a prompt can sway a language model’s answer far more than which API channel delivers it, especially when the advice includes a misleading rationale.

papers.abstract: User memory helps personalized systems build on their understanding of users over time.
