Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.
authors: Yufeng Li, Zaijing Li, Fuchen Zhang, Zongzong Wu, Ming Zhao, Fengxiao Tang
bullets: Addresses semantic loss from converting text into discrete graph symbols and modality mismatch between graphs and LLM-pretrained text.
Uses a Semantic Topology Mapper to create context-intact semantic nodes connected by narrative, semantic, and lexical edges.
Applies Energy-Driven Pathfinding to identify query-relevant subgraphs and deterministically linearize them into textual evidence paths.
Outperforms strong baselines across three multi-hop QA benchmarks, including 14.4% EM improvement on HotpotQA and 5.8% on 2WikiMultihop.
Reduces token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline; evaluation focuses on multi-hop QA benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: RAG framework with graph-based external knowledge retrieval and pathfinding, directly relevant to LLM external memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: ThreadRAG preserves contextual coherence in graph-based RAG by organizing documents into semantic topologies and extracting coherent evidence paths for multi-hop question answering.

papers.abstract: Large language models are typically trained with next-token prediction (NTP), which rewards predicting specific tokens rather than explicitly accounting for the semantic similarities between different words or expressions. Prior work has addressed this limitation by augmenting training data with minimally varying sentences that replace a target word with conceptually related alternatives, e.g., "The tired coach ran home" $\rightarrow$ {"The tired trainer ran home", "The tired instructor ran home", ...}. Such concept augmentation improves performance, but it remains unclear whether its effectiveness depends on where in the sentence the concept is expressed. We reproduce and extend prior work $\textit{beyond nouns}$ to verbs and adjectives, asking whether the part of speech (POS) carrying the concept signal affects perplexity and downstream performance. We find different patterns across evaluation settings: concept augmentation improves perplexity most consistently on news, independent of the POS used, whereas verbs provide the most reliable downstream gains. Despite these behavioral differences, representational analyses using CKA and linear probing show that the conditions yielding the largest downstream gains are not necessarily those that most alter the model's internal representations. Together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of concept augmentation depends on where and how conceptual information is introduced during training.
bullets: Extends prior concept-augmentation work beyond nouns to verbs and adjectives to study part-of-speech effects.
Concept augmentation most consistently improves perplexity on news across POS conditions.
Verb-based augmentation provides the most reliable downstream performance gains.
CKA and linear-probing analyses show that representation changes do not necessarily predict downstream improvements.
Results suggest that both the location and form of conceptual information matter during post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Studies part-of-speech effects in LLM post-training concept augmentation, relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: Every Part Has Its Role: Part-of-Speech Effects in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: Concept augmentation helps language models, but its impact depends on whether concepts are expressed through nouns, verbs, or adjectives and on the evaluation setting.

papers.abstract: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. This is a short empirical study, with one conversation and one run per cell. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost-accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.
bullets: Evaluates full context, BM25, Mem0, and Zep across three coding agents and three language models on one 419-turn conversation with 152 questions.
Mem0 improves over full context only for GPT-4o-mini, while constructing its memory costs more than a full-context rollout.
Memory quality is limited by the model that writes it; a stronger reader cannot recover information omitted by a weaker writer.
With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi achieves 99% accuracy for under half the cost of full context.
The study uses one conversation and one run per experimental cell; Pi’s advantage partly comes from reading photo captions unavailable to other methods.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical analysis of agent memory systems and coding-agent memory strategies fits LLM/agent memory.
papers.title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory
papers.tldr: In a small empirical study, strong coding agents that search raw conversation history can outperform designed memory systems at substantially lower cost.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the few practical tools available for overseeing capable AI systems, but it is fragile: a model's reasoning is only useful to a monitor if it remains coupled to what the model actually does. This coupling can be degraded during training through, for example, CoT compression, optimization against a monitor, and out-of-context generalization from synthetic documents. In this work, we propose an unsupervised post-training objective based on maximizing mutual information between CoT and the output for improving CoT monitorability. Across three model organisms with degraded CoT, it recovers most or all of the lost monitorability. Applied to undegraded policies, it further improves judged monitorability, improves prediction of unsafe behavior by CoT monitors and activation probes, and increases the prevalence of consequential reasoning. These results suggest that monitorability should be treated as a trainable attribute of the policy. A dedicated monitorability post-training stage can extend current practices that protect CoT from direct optimization pressure.
authors: Usman Anwar, Tim Bakker, Christos Louizos, David Krueger
bullets: CoT monitoring is fragile when reasoning becomes decoupled from the model’s actual behavior.
The proposed objective maximizes mutual information between CoT and outputs.
Across three degraded model organisms, the method recovers most or all lost monitorability.
For undegraded policies, it improves judged monitorability and prediction of unsafe behavior by monitors and activation probes.
It also increases consequential reasoning, suggesting monitorability is a trainable policy attribute.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Chain-of-Thought monitorability in LLMs through a post-training objective, relevant to large language model safety and architecture.
papers.title: Monitorability Is Trainable: Post-Training for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.tldr: Monitorability of chain-of-thought can be improved through unsupervised post-training that strengthens its connection to model outputs.

papers.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.
authors: Ido Levy, Segev Shlomov, Leshem Choshen
bullets: Introduces LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled, compositional RAG evaluation.
Evaluates 450 pipeline configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora from 5K to 200K documents.
Three individually strong retrieval techniques predicted a 47% combined gain but achieved only 17% together.
Design choices that improve retrieval may reduce answer faithfulness, showing the objectives can diverge.
The best component combination changes with corpus scale, limiting conclusions from small-corpus tests.
papers.selection_reason: RAG pipeline compositionality and retrieval-memory evaluation directly relates to LLM external-memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
papers.tldr: RAG techniques that work well individually may interact poorly, optimize different objectives, and change effectiveness as corpus size grows, so they should be evaluated as complete pipelines.

papers.abstract: Long-term agent memory is shifting from predefined workflows toward learnable policies for memory construction and retrieval. Existing learning-based methods either optimize construction alone or combine retrieval-side online reinforcement learning (RL) with offline construction supervision, limiting co-adaptation between the two stages. In this paper, we explore end-to-end online RL for a unified memory manager (Uni-Mem) that learns both capabilities under a shared policy. However, joint optimization with existing RL algorithms such as GRPO faces confounded group comparisons and sparse feedback over long memory-management trajectories. To this end, we propose Stage-Decoupled GRPO, which alternates construction and retrieval optimization while controlling variation from the other stage within each rollout group, yielding stage-specific learning signals. We further introduce Event-Wise Credit Assignment (ECA), which localizes feedback to responsible events and propagates event-level advantages to their constituent operations. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show that Uni-Mem outperforms the strongest RL-based memory, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly learning memory construction and retrieval via Stage-Decoupled GRPO and ECA.
authors: Zhiqian Xia, Jielong Tang, Ling-An Zeng, Shixiong Kai, Rong Yao, Hao Kong, Xiao Dong, Wei Wang, Mingxuan Yuan, Siyu Xia, Haifeng Xia
bullets: Existing methods typically optimize memory construction or combine offline construction supervision with online retrieval learning, limiting co-adaptation.
Uni-Mem uses a shared policy to learn construction and retrieval end to end with online RL.
Stage-Decoupled GRPO alternates optimization stages while controlling cross-stage variation to produce clearer learning signals.
Event-Wise Credit Assignment assigns feedback to responsible events and their constituent operations.
On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, Uni-Mem outperforms the strongest RL-based memory method reported.
papers.selection_reason: Learns a unified memory manager for long-term agent memory construction and retrieval, directly fitting LLM memory.
papers.title: Uni-Mem: Learning a Long-Horizon Agentic Memory Manager with Unified Online Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: Uni-Mem jointly learns long-term memory construction and retrieval through online RL, using stage-decoupled optimization and event-level credit assignment to address sparse, confounded feedback.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict tabular labels from similar examples, but it remains unclear whether LLM inference improves on direct voting over those same examples. We address this question by comparing four general-purpose LLMs with distance-weighted nearest-neighbor voting (Distance-KNN) using identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular classification datasets. With the number of demonstrations fixed, enlarging the retrieval candidate pool improves accuracy for all predictors, yet Distance-KNN achieves the highest mean accuracy at every pool size. More detailed analyses reveal that LLM gains are concentrated where retrieved neighbors exhibit low label consensus and vary across models. These gains further depend on the average feature-space distance to the test query: under low label consensus, some LLMs outperform Distance-KNN in close and intermediate neighborhoods, but all fall behind on average in the most distant group. Complementary experiments on the number of demonstrations, prompt formulation, retrieval representation, and label-balanced demonstration selection largely preserve the overall findings. These results characterize when LLM inference adds predictive value beyond distance-weighted voting in retrieval-based tabular ICL.
authors: Ziquan Wang, Yuxuan Nie, Jian Ma, Yingjie Li
bullets: Compares four general-purpose LLMs with Distance-KNN using identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular classification datasets.
Expanding the retrieval candidate pool improves all predictors, while Distance-KNN has the highest mean accuracy at every pool size.
LLM benefits are concentrated in low-label-consensus neighborhoods and vary across models.
Some LLMs outperform Distance-KNN for close or intermediate low-consensus neighborhoods, but all lag in the most distant group.
Findings remain broadly consistent across demonstrations, prompts, retrieval representations, and label-balanced selection.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical characterization of when LLM inference adds value over retrieval-based in-context learning; relevant to LLM reasoning and retrieval.
papers.title: Beyond the Vote: When Do LLMs Add Value to Retrieval-Based Tabular Classification?
papers.tldr: LLMs add value beyond distance-weighted neighbor voting mainly when retrieved examples disagree, especially in close or intermediate neighborhoods, but they underperform overall.

papers.abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have shown that final answers do not always depend on the generated rationales. In particular, LLMs may rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than the information provided by their reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate whether context-aware decoding (CAD), an existing contrastive decoding method, can mitigate such shortcut behavior when applied to CoT reasoning. We study this application as Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on the query with and without its rationale, amplifying tokens whose likelihood increases due to the rationale. We provide a theoretical interpretation of this decoding rule via a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments across five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT. Furthermore, intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales reveal that RCD increases the behavioral dependence of final answers on the rationale content. Our findings suggest that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to mitigating query shortcuts.
bullets: Addresses query-specific shortcuts where LLM answers ignore generated reasoning steps.
Contrasts next-token distributions with and without the rationale, amplifying rationale-dependent tokens.
Provides a KL-regularized reward-maximization interpretation of the decoding rule.
Across five reasoning benchmarks, RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT.
Intervention analyses show greater behavioral dependence on both ground-truth and random rationale content.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free contrastive decoding to reduce CoT shortcut reliance; relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding
papers.tldr: Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD) uses context-aware contrastive decoding to make CoT answers depend more on their rationales and improve reasoning accuracy.

papers.abstract: Temporal reasoning is widely assumed to decompose into two modes: temporal arithmetic (date and time calculations), and temporal semantics (understanding temporal and causal relations). This dichotomy shapes how benchmarks are designed, how models are trained, and how progress is measured, yet its empirical validity has never been directly tested. We provide two lines of evidence that challenge it. First, we test whether tasks labelled as arithmetic or semantic by the benchmarks support transferable gains within their purported mode. Finetuning on these subsets yields predominantly dataset-specific gains ($+6.8$ to $+23.1$ percentage points), while transfer to a different dataset in the same mode ranges from $-3.2$ to $+1.1$ percentage points. Across the two benchmark families used in the transfer analysis, this pattern provides little evidence of coherent, transferable temporal abilities. Second, using cognitive-demand-based model evaluation, we examine which capabilities actually drive performance on these benchmarks. We find that quantitative and logical reasoning, the assumed proxies for temporal arithmetic and temporal semantics, are not the primary drivers; knowledge is. Together, these findings show that current temporal reasoning benchmarks do not cleanly realise the arithmetic-semantics distinction and instead largely reward models for remembering how time typically works.
authors: Auss Abbood, Fernando Mart\'inez-Plumed, Jos\'e Hern\'andez-Orallo, Nigel Collier
bullets: Finetuning on arithmetic- or semantic-labelled subsets mostly improves performance only on the same dataset.
Transfer to another dataset within the same purported mode is weak, offering little evidence of shared temporal abilities.
Quantitative and logical reasoning are not the main drivers of benchmark performance; knowledge is.
The findings challenge the common arithmetic-versus-semantics framework for evaluating temporal reasoning in LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of temporal reasoning in LLMs; relevant to language foundation model reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: Keeping Time vs. Understanding Time: Neither Alone Explains Temporal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.tldr: Current temporal reasoning benchmarks do not cleanly separate temporal arithmetic from temporal semantics and largely reward knowledge of typical temporal patterns.

papers.abstract: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.
authors: Jiaru Qian, Yihong Dong, Xue Jiang, Chun-Wah Hsu, Zhi Jin, Ge Li
bullets: Parallel-thinking RL can suffer from mode collapse, with multiple reasoning paths becoming nearly identical.
DPT encourages distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing prefix similarity between parallel paths.
The approach aims to preserve multiple hypotheses and explore the reasoning space more comprehensively.
Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show DPT outperforms prior parallel-thinking methods and achieves state-of-the-art results among the reported baselines.
The work supports path diversity as an important factor in effective parallel thinking.
papers.selection_reason: RL approach to encourage path diversity in LLM parallel thinking; aligns with language foundation model reasoning interests.
papers.title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity
papers.tldr: Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT) uses reinforcement learning to make parallel reasoning paths less similar, improving LLM reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for multi-step reasoning, yet obtaining reliable process labels remains a central bottleneck. Existing approaches typically rely on human annotation, rollout-based estimation, or auxiliary verification. In this work, we explore a different source of process supervision natively exposed by Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: expert routing. We show that simple routing statistics provide an intrinsic process-confidence signal that is competitive with conventional output-logit confidence. Building on this observation, we construct routing confidence by combining overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation, and introduce RoCo-Rethink, which identifies the least confident reasoning step and selectively regenerates the subsequent trajectory. We further introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM. Across multiple MoE architectures and diverse reasoning tasks, both RoCo-Rethink and RoCo-PRM consistently outperform strong baselines, while RoCo-PRM transfers effectively across both model architectures and tasks. Our findings suggest that expert routing is more than a computational dispatch mechanism: it provides an architecture-native source of process supervision for reasoning.
authors: Guanzhi Deng, Zengyan Liu, Haibo Wang, Kuan Wu, Shing Yin Wong, Sichun Luo, Zhuoran Wang, Linqi Song
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of obtaining reliable step-level labels for multi-step reasoning.
Combines routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation into a routing-confidence signal.
RoCo-Rethink regenerates reasoning after the least-confident step.
RoCo-PRM uses a strong MoE to label trajectories and distills routing-derived scores into a standalone PRM.
Across multiple MoE architectures and reasoning tasks, both methods outperform strong baselines; RoCo-PRM transfers across architectures and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Uses MoE expert routing as process-supervision signal for LLM reasoning; directly relevant to MoE-based language foundation models.
papers.title: A Strong MoE Is All You Need for Process Supervision
papers.tldr: MoE expert-routing statistics can provide reliable process supervision for reasoning, enabling targeted trajectory regeneration and automatic training of transferable process reward models.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.
authors: Jian Zhong, Zeyu Liu, Pingchuan Cao, Rongduo Han, Shunye Tang, Guohuan Xie, Mingyuan Qin, Ran Ji, Xiao Liang, Wei Wang, Haining Zhang
bullets: Represents user memory as confidence-weighted beliefs rather than simple append-or-overwrite entries.
Uses Effective Surprisal, combining semantic deviation and contradiction evidence while discounting unreliable retrieval.
Applies a two-threshold gate with three updates: MAINTAIN, PROFILE, and CORRECT.
PROFILE serves as a low-confidence waiting room for ambiguous or potentially noisy evidence.
Reports consistent state-of-the-art accuracy on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2; DiMoBench evaluates adaptation to belief drift.
papers.selection_reason: Predictive memory consolidation framework for long-term dialogue agents; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
papers.tldr: PreCoMem helps long-term dialogue agents preserve stable user memories while adapting cautiously to genuine changes.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.
authors: Fei Bai, Huatong Song, Chuan Hao, Ran Tao, Jian Yang, Bryan Dai, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
bullets: Single fixed-harness training can cause specialization and poor transfer across configurations.
Harness Scaling treats harness diversity as a new scaling dimension for agentic RL.
The approach factorizes the harness space, selects a compact subset with balanced factorial coverage, and coordinates cross-harness training.
Across benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, structured variation improves transfer to unseen white-box configurations.
Training with structured white-box variation also transfers effectively to unseen black-box harnesses, outperforming training on one complex black-box harness.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Harness Scaling' for agentic RL, proposing a new scaling dimension for generalizing agent behavior across diverse tool-use and context-management configurations.
papers.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Training agentic RL across a structured diversity of harness configurations improves generalization to unseen and external harnesses compared with single-harness training.

papers.abstract: Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.
authors: Keith Kwok, Wanting Ning, Tej Deep Pala, Desmond C. Ong, S. Supraja, Renwen Zhang, Soujanya Poria
bullets: Existing evaluations often overlook how disclosure unfolds across conversation history.
TraDE uses predefined disclosure trajectories, grounded in Social Penetration Theory, to isolate history effects under matched current disclosure.
Across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks, accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure influenced whether models accepted or challenged users’ framing.
These effects persisted for several turns after disclosure became shallow again and were not explained by a single vulnerable moment or disclosure order.
Models diverged most from human supporters in ESConv when users reduced disclosure rather than when they first opened up.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces TraDE, an evaluation framework for conversational agents that accounts for disclosure history and trajectory, addressing limitations of state-based evaluation in social AI.
papers.title: Beyond Small Talk: Modeling Disclosure Trajectories in Human-AI Conversation
papers.tldr: TraDE reveals that human-AI responses to equally deep disclosures depend strongly on users’ prior disclosure history, especially as they pull back from deeper sharing.

papers.abstract: Language models relying on verbalized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained to token-by-token generation in the language space, where many tokens serve textual coherence rather than core reasoning. This entangles genuine differences in logical trajectories with superficial variations in verbalization. Moving reasoning into a compact, continuous latent space offers a promising alternative for efficiently representing and exploring diverse reasoning trajectories. However, current latent models remain largely deterministic, capturing only a single reasoning trajectory rather than modeling a distribution over multiple valid alternatives. While stochastic approaches parameterize distributions over latent reasoning steps, they frequently suffer from unstable optimization and limited empirical performance. Furthermore, their reliance on autoregressive latent prediction during training precludes effective parallelization, leading to prohibitively long training times. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning. PLRM adopts a JEPA-style objective in which the posterior infers latent distributions in parallel from observed reasoning trajectories, while the prior learns to predict the subsequent latent distribution via teacher forcing. To model heterogeneous reasoning processes, we introduce a discrete strategy variable together with a mixture-based prior, allowing the model to preserve the Gaussian-mixture structure induced by multiple distinct reasoning trajectories rather than collapsing them into a single Gaussian. Across diverse benchmarks, PLRM achieves performance competitive with deterministic latent reasoning models on single-trajectory datasets while enabling efficient training and consistently outperforming competing stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets.
authors: Seokhyun Lee, Seongjun Lee, Changhee Lee
bullets: Addresses the limitations of token-level CoT and deterministic latent reasoning, which obscure or fail to represent diverse logical trajectories.
Uses a JEPA-style objective with parallel posterior inference and teacher-forced prior prediction to avoid autoregressive latent training.
Introduces a discrete strategy variable and mixture-based prior to preserve heterogeneous reasoning modes instead of collapsing them into one Gaussian.
Matches deterministic latent-reasoning performance on single-trajectory benchmarks and consistently outperforms stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory benchmarks.
The approach is evaluated across diverse benchmarks, with scope focused on latent reasoning and trajectory diversity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for modeling diverse reasoning trajectories in latent space to improve efficiency and diversity.
papers.title: Parallelizable Probabilistic Latent Reasoning for Diverse Reasoning Trajectories
papers.tldr: PLRM is a parallelizable variational latent-reasoning framework that models multiple valid reasoning trajectories more efficiently and effectively than prior stochastic approaches.

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models improve scalability by routing input tokens to only a subset of expert networks, but they often suffer from representation collapse, in which multiple experts converge toward similar functions and lose their intended diversity. Prior work has addressed this limitation either by improving router architectures or by introducing auxiliary loss terms that implicitly penalize similarity among experts. However, router-based approaches remain vulnerable to routing collapses, and loss-based approaches can conflict with the task's original objective during optimization. In this work, we propose GaP-MoE (Gradient Accumulation and Projection in MoE), which induces expert specialization by directly manipulating expert output gradients rather than modifying the loss function. At each training step, GaP-MoE stochastically selects one of the $TopK$ routed experts as a leader based on normalized routing scores, and projects the gradients of the remaining follower experts onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the leader's recent gradients. This removes directional overlap between expert gradients without altering the task loss, allowing specialization to emerge as a direct consequence of the optimization dynamics rather than an externally imposed constraint. We evaluate GaP-MoE in both fine-tuning settings (BERT-based, on GLUE) and from-scratch pretraining settings (GPT-2-based, on WikiText-103, enwik8, and text8), and further confirm its compatibility as a drop-in module for existing SMoE architectures. Experimental results show that GaP-MoE achieves performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.
bullets: Addresses expert representation collapse, where multiple MoE experts learn similar functions.
Selects a routed leader expert using normalized routing scores and accumulates its recent gradients.
Projects follower-expert gradients onto the orthogonal complement of the leader-gradient subspace.
Encourages specialization without changing the task loss or relying on router modifications.
Evaluated in BERT fine-tuning and GPT-2 pretraining settings, achieving performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.
papers.selection_reason: Improves expert specialization in sparse mixture-of-experts LLMs, directly relevant to modern LLM architectures.
papers.title: GaP-MoE : Explicit Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts via Orthogonal Gradient Accumulation and Projection
papers.tldr: GaP-MoE promotes diverse expert behavior in sparse MoE models by orthogonally projecting follower-expert gradients away from a selected leader’s recent gradient directions.

papers.abstract: Mid-training (MT) is a training phase in LLM training pipelines that continues pretraining (PT) on smaller datasets of higher value. Taking the PT and MT phases as a whole, training usually starts with only PT data and then transitions completely to MT data. In this work, we view this complete transition from PT to MT data as a special case of a broader class of data mixing schedules that specify how the proportions of PT and MT tokens in each batch change over training. Under fixed total training compute and MT token budgets, we ask: Is this complete transition to MT data optimal for minimizing final MT loss? We show that the answer depends on the learning rate (LR) schedule: one data schedule may outperform another under one LR schedule, but changing only the LR schedule can reverse the outcome. Specifically, when the LR decays throughout continued training, introducing MT data earlier and mixing it with PT data lowers the final MT loss compared with placing all MT data at the end of training, but this result is reversed if we use constant LR. We therefore study how to jointly choose when to introduce MT data and when to decay the LR through ablation studies, and find that it is better to decay the LR only after MT data enters training. Finally, we develop a theoretical model that explains why the optimal data schedule for a fixed MT token budget depends on the LR schedule.
authors: Haodong Wen, Kairong Luo, Tingkai Yan, Wenguang Chen, Kaifeng Lyu
bullets: The study asks whether switching completely from pretraining (PT) data to mid-training (MT) data is optimal under fixed compute and MT-token budgets.
With a decaying learning rate, introducing and mixing MT data earlier improves final MT loss versus placing all MT data at the end.
With a constant learning rate, this comparison reverses, showing that schedule choices are interdependent.
Ablations suggest delaying learning-rate decay until after MT data enters training is preferable.
A theoretical model explains why the optimal data schedule depends on the learning-rate schedule.
papers.selection_reason: Studies joint data and learning-rate schedules for LLM mid-training, relevant to LLM training and foundation-model development.
papers.title: Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together
papers.tldr: Data-mixing and learning-rate schedules interact strongly in mid-training, so they should be designed jointly rather than independently.

papers.abstract: A transformer MLP gives each hidden channel two roles: a reader that decides when the channel responds, and a writer that decides what it adds back to the residual stream. Read as a key--value memory, the layer can be measured one factor set at a time: the pairing of readers to writers is carried only by their shared index, invisible to any quantity computed from one factor set alone. Yet training couples the two factors through their joint update, so we ask what reading them together shows. The block supplies the joint instrument: the MLP writes back into the very stream it reads, so the exact Jacobian of its update is square, and its agreement with its own transpose resolves into reader--writer terms whose inner products give each channel, read as a couple, a signed pairing coordinate. Ranked by this coordinate, each block we measure has a small core of strongly coupled channels; where initialization gives either sign equally, the core is nearly all opposed: each writer points against the direction its reader responds to. This opposed core recurs from the smallest models trained from scratch to released checkpoints; its sign is in place within a few percent of training and holds while the coupling grows. Read as couples, most channels return their contribution against the reader that fired it, and the readers of later blocks take it up; few show in the logits. Training holds the couples in place: flipping the opposed writers moves the output toward common tokens, and a writer permuted onto another reader regrows to fit that reader while the reader stays.
authors: Giyeong Oh, Sunghee Ahn, Youngjae Yu
bullets: Treating readers and writers jointly reveals coupling that is invisible when either factor set is analyzed alone.
The MLP’s exact square Jacobian is compared with its transpose to derive a signed reader–writer pairing coordinate for each channel.
Across models and checkpoints, strongly coupled cores are usually opposed: writers point against the directions that activate their readers.
Most channels return contributions against the reader that triggered them, while later blocks can take up these contributions; few appear directly in the logits.
Perturbations support functional coupling: flipping opposed writers shifts outputs toward common tokens, and permuting a writer onto another reader causes it to regrow to fit that reader.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes transformer MLP reader-writer coupling, relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Reader--Writer Coupling in Transformer MLPs
papers.tldr: Transformer MLP channels form coupled reader–writer pairs, with a small, rapidly established core whose writers typically oppose the directions their readers detect.

papers.abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.
authors: Feng Liang, Weixin Zeng, Runhao Zhao, Mingjun Zhou, Shaoshi Yang, Xiang Zhao
bullets: Targets temporal semantic drift in KG question generation, where questions may alter the answer field, time condition, reference event, or temporal order.
Builds a Temporal Intent State to explicitly represent the intended question semantics.
Retrieves compatible typed question patterns, adapts them to the graph, and validates the generated question.
Uses validation feedback to revise questions when supported inconsistencies are detected.
Achieves state-of-the-art generation performance on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ; ablations support its component contributions.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented framework for temporal knowledge graph question generation that preserves temporal constraints during generation.
papers.title: ChronoSynth: Constraint-Aware Question Synthesis over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.tldr: ChronoSynth generates fluent questions from temporal knowledge graphs while preserving the constraints that determine their answers.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.
authors: Linus Filbry, Luckeciano C. Melo, Yarin Gal
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs can perform principled Bayesian belief updating in context.
Tests probabilistic coherence, quantitative inference, and effects of non-Bayesian updates on downstream tasks.
Finds that LLMs generally violate Bayes’ rule during belief updates.
Reasoning abilities and code execution markedly improve performance, including on analytically intractable posteriors.
Suggests tool-equipped LLMs may support complex belief updates in scientific discovery.
papers.selection_reason: LLM Bayesian belief updating and posterior recovery evaluation; aligns with language foundation model reasoning interests.
papers.title: From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
papers.tldr: LLM agents often update beliefs non-Bayesianly, but reasoning and code tools can substantially improve their ability to approximate complex posteriors.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly through group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), has emerged as a central paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs). While RLVR is highly effective at enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, it commonly induces \textit{distribution sharpening}, whereby the policy distribution becomes excessively peaked and rare-yet-correct trajectories are progressively suppressed, thus diminishing sample diversity. To this end, we promote flat-reward optima in RLVR to smooth the policy distribution. We theoretically link flat reward RLVR to reduced distribution sharpening, and empirically show improved sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy. Our method, called \texttt{Flat}-RLVR, searches for flat reward regions via sharpness-aware minimization during LLM post-training, combining this with GRPO variants to achieve better trade-offs between sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.
authors: Yeonbum Kim, Hyun Kyu Lee, Sung Whan Yoon
bullets: RLVR can sharpen LLM policy distributions, suppressing rare but correct reasoning trajectories.
Flat-RLVR promotes flatter reward optima to mitigate this distribution sharpening.
The method combines sharpness-aware minimization with GRPO variants during post-training.
Theory connects flatter reward solutions with reduced distribution sharpening.
Experiments report higher sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy, balancing sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.
papers.selection_reason: Sharpness-aware reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for LLM reasoning post-training; relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: Flat-RLVR: Sharpness-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Reasoning Capacity in LLMs
papers.tldr: Flat-RLVR uses sharpness-aware optimization with GRPO-style RLVR to reduce policy over-concentration, improving reasoning sample diversity without sacrificing single-attempt accuracy.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity of up to 4.4 pts on ADLM and up to 7 pts against MDLM. An LLM judge on WikiHow prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline. On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.
authors: Parul Gupta, Satwik, Avni Aggarwal, Bhavesh Gurnani, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Dinesh Khandelwal, Dinesh Garg, Parag Singla
bullets: Addresses the limitation that standard masked diffusion models treat all positions with a shared noise schedule and no explicit generation priority.
Uses two parallel-decoding passes: predict hierarchy distributions for masked positions, then predict tokens conditioned on those hierarchies.
Assigns separate noise schedules to hierarchy levels, creating a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier.
Improves language-modeling perplexity over diffusion baselines on LM1B and WikiHow, with stronger judged generation preference on WikiHow.
Improves Sudoku-solving accuracy by up to 8.6 percentage points over existing diffusion baselines.
papers.selection_reason: New hierarchical masked diffusion language model architecture with hierarchical noise schedules; relevant to language model architectural research.
papers.title: Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: HMDLM improves parallel masked diffusion generation by modeling which token positions should be resolved first through learned hierarchy levels and level-specific noise schedules.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
authors: Hong Ting Tsang, Boyi Zhang, Haoyu Huang, Jiaxin Bai, Yufei Li, Yisen Gao, Zhongwei Xie, Hongyu Luo, Jeff Z. Pan, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Evaluates 923 questions across persona-grounded histories spanning 11–24 sessions and four modalities.
Targets meaningful spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media.
Uses matched controls to isolate failures in representation, retrieval, delivery, and reading.
Finds modality-dependent representation loss, substantial residual reading errors even with gold evidence, and weak abstention.
Moves evaluation beyond a single leaderboard score toward component-level diagnosis.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-term memory and cross-modal reasoning in omni-modal conversational agents; directly relevant to LLM memory and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents
papers.tldr: MOSAIC is an omni-modal benchmark that diagnoses where conversational agents fail when remembering and reasoning over long-term text, image, video, and audio histories.

papers.abstract: Personalized reward models require user-specific preference comparisons, but collecting such feedback is costly and provides only limited supervision for each user. At the same time, large pools of responses can be generated without user identities or preference labels, yet existing personalized reward models leave this data unused. Directly learning from these responses is difficult because pairwise objectives constrain relative scores within a prompt, whereas pseudo-labeling individual responses requires scores that are comparable across prompts for the same user. We propose \textbf{PerSPL} (Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning), a backbone-agnostic framework that uses pair-mean score centering to stabilize this cross-prompt score coordinate and iteratively turns unlabeled responses into user-specific training signals. Against seven representative baselines across four benchmarks---PersonalLLM, HelpSteer2, Reddit TLDR, and Chatbot Arena---PerSPL achieves the highest reported mean accuracy among the evaluated methods for both seen and unseen users. The two latter benchmarks provide real-user preference comparisons in summarization and open-domain chatbot interaction, respectively. These results indicate that unlabeled responses can provide additional supervision for personalized reward modeling when per-user preference labels are scarce.
authors: Xiaoan Xu, Tingzhou Wei, Juncheng Dong, Korel Gundem, Ethan X. Fang, Zhengling Qi
bullets: Addresses the high cost and limited coverage of collecting user-specific preference comparisons.
Uses pair-mean score centering to make scores comparable across prompts for each user.
Iteratively pseudo-labels unlabeled responses to augment personalized preference training.
Is backbone-agnostic and evaluated against seven baselines across four benchmarks.
Reports the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods for both seen and unseen users.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes PerSPL, a framework for personalized reward modeling in LLMs using semi-supervised learning, relevant to LLM alignment and personalization.
papers.title: PerSPL: Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning
papers.tldr: PerSPL improves personalized reward modeling by converting unlabeled responses into user-specific supervision through stabilized cross-prompt score calibration.

papers.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, we establish deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with $(L_0,L_1)$- or $(H_0,H_1)$-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.
bullets: Existing SAM and USAM updates can have unbounded gradient-direction distortion under generalized smoothness, causing cycling or divergence in examples.
The paper derives a necessary condition for uniformly controlling distortion among gradient-aligned perturbations.
CS-SAM scales both perturbations and descent steps using curvature upper bounds.
It proves deterministic convergence rates under $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, including nonconvex, convex, and Polyak–Lojasiewicz settings.
Minibatch computer-vision experiments show competitive performance; the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieves the highest mean best-test accuracy across four reported settings.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization (CS-SAM) to improve convergence guarantees for deep neural networks. This optimization technique is relevant to training large language models.
papers.title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
papers.tldr: CS-SAM adapts SAM’s perturbation and step size to local curvature, enabling convergence guarantees beyond standard smoothness.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive emergent reasoning capabilities, yet they remain constrained by fixed model parameters and finite context windows. Even when augmented with static retrieval, they can produce statements that are unsupported by, or even contradictory to, retrieved evidence. This leads to hallucinations, difficulty incorporating up-to-date information, and failures to correctly interpret or reconcile sources. Recent work addresses these limitations by tightly coupling step-by-step reasoning with interactive search, treating retrieval as an action within an iterative agentic loop rather than a one-shot preprocessing step. This study reviews frameworks that implement such reasoning-search loops by interleaving planning, querying, retrieval, integration, verification, and stopping. We analyze these systems through four architectural axes: retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness. We separately treat the learning signal as a cross-cutting dimension because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can instantiate the same architecture while producing materially different search, stopping, and grounding behavior. We further distinguish benchmark difficulty from RSA-loop demand and synthesize controlled within-study ablations and quality-cost deltas, avoiding invalid pooling across heterogeneous model backbones, retrievers, corpora, and evaluation protocols. Our goal is to clarify the landscape of reasoning-search-augmented LLMs and outline a unified perspective on the design choices shaping future research.
authors: Biswas Poudel, Nilson Chapagain, Amit Kumar, Xianshun Jiang
bullets: Reasoning-search loops address hallucinations, stale knowledge, and failures to reconcile retrieved evidence in static-retrieval systems.
The taxonomy organizes systems by retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness.
Learning signals are treated separately because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can alter search and stopping behavior.
The analysis distinguishes benchmark difficulty from the demands of the reasoning-search loop.
Controlled within-study ablations and quality–cost changes are synthesized without pooling incompatible experimental settings.
papers.selection_reason: Taxonomy and controlled synthesis of reasoning-search-augmented LLMs; directly relevant to LLM reasoning and retrieval methods.
papers.title: Reasoning-Search-Augmented LLMs: An Operational Taxonomy, Benchmark Analysis and Controlled Evidence Synthesis
papers.tldr: This study develops a taxonomy and evidence synthesis for LLMs that interleave reasoning with interactive search to improve grounding and information use.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.
bullets: Continuous diffusion models match human rates for common words but underproduce rare words, with the gap persisting across model sizes.
The issue arises because intermediate denoising averages competing word candidates instead of sampling one discrete candidate.
GRAFT identifies rare words likely to be lost, commits them while the model remains uncertain, and regenerates the sequence with those commitments fixed.
Across three ELF scales and LangFlow, GRAFT raises rare-word frequency from 0.42–0.77× to 0.82–1.10× the human rate.
The method moves word-frequency profiles closer to human text on every tested model, without additional training.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces GRAFT, a training-free method to restore discrete sampling capabilities in continuous diffusion language models to address the long-tail distribution of rare words.
papers.title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: GRAFT restores rare-word diversity in continuous diffusion language models by adding a training-free discrete commitment step during generation.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework's scalability is validated across model sizes (2b-14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.
authors: Ibrahim Khan, Thai Van Nguyen, Yi Xia, Pratch Suntichaikul, Mustafa Can Gursesli, Daniel Fernandez Galeote, Juho Hamari, Ruck Thawonmas
bullets: Evaluates static predefined roles and dynamically model-selected roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading-comprehension tasks.
Tests 20 LLMs on seven benchmarks, with reported gains of up to 44 percentage points over zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines.
Static and dynamic role selection show closely aligned benefits, although static selection achieves the best peak performance.
Ablations indicate that poorly matched or unconventional roles can hurt reasoning, highlighting the importance of task-role alignment.
The approach scales across 2B–14B-parameter models and is presented as a resource-efficient zero-shot prompting framework.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates a prompting framework (RE-ZS-CoT) for large language models, focusing on role-enhanced zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.tldr: RE-ZS-CoT improves zero-shot LLM reasoning by pairing chain-of-thought prompting with task-appropriate expert roles, often outperforming standard baselines.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel. New draft-training objectives are usually credited with the acceptance they add over cross-entropy on externally written responses, yet many pipelines let the target rewrite them. We ask how much of that gain survives. With a vision-language target and a block drafter, we train three objectives on four versions of one corpus: cross-entropy on corpus tokens, token-level distillation from the target, and distillation gated to positions that would survive verification. Distillation and the gate add large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation adds a smaller gain and the gate little or none. The shrinkage persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures and, for distillation, initializations and learning rates. Most of it remains at matched supervised length and at each objective's best measured training length. A second vision corpus shows the shrinkage, as does a text-only replication, for distillation also with an autoregressive drafter. Objective gains should therefore be measured against a target-regenerated baseline and across training lengths. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRegeneration.
authors: Jungseob Lee, Hogun Seong, Euijun Choi, Sugyeong Eo
bullets: The study compares cross-entropy, target distillation, and verification-gated distillation across externally written and target-regenerated corpora.
Distillation and gating provide large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation’s gain shrinks and gating provides little or none.
This shrinkage persists across data ordering, position weighting, verifiers, temperatures, training lengths, and several initialization or learning-rate settings.
The finding replicates on a second vision corpus and in text-only experiments; distillation also shows it with an autoregressive drafter.
The authors recommend evaluating objective gains against target-regenerated baselines and across training lengths.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates target regeneration effects on draft-training objectives in speculative decoding for large language models. Relevant to LLM training efficiency and decoding strategies.
papers.title: Target Regeneration Shrinks the Gains of Draft-Training Objectives in Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Target-regenerated training data substantially reduces the apparent benefits of draft-training objectives for speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $\tau^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.
authors: Tanqiu Jiang, Min Bai, Sadat Shahriar, Wanyu Du, Sandesh Swamy
bullets: Addresses memory injection and poisoning, which hinder safe memory sharing among agents.
Allows agents to retain multi-turn planning and tool choice while mediating environment-derived values.
Proves and machine-checks two Lean 4 integrity theorems under the assumption that only user inputs and gate-confirmed values are trusted.

Reports zero observed attack success on Trojan Hippo with self-verification and lightweight verifiers; up to 90 agents built shared knowledge bases without directly promoting injected memories on τ²-bench.
Community endorsements reduce verification burden and, under stated assumptions, lower both poison promotion and benign-knowledge eviction risks as communities grow.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a persistent memory architecture for LLM agents with machine-checked integrity guarantees, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
papers.tldr: PerMIT secures shared persistent memory for LLM agents by restricting untrusted information through a finite, auditable confirmation interface with machine-checked integrity guarantees.

papers.abstract: Scanning every passage in a long document seems thorough, but does it preserve more useful evidence or produce better answers? We compare 11 retrieval configurations spanning lexical and dense search, hybrid reranking, and full-document scanning with Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Cloudflare Clef. Our evaluation uses 396 QASPER questions and 80 questions from eight complete textbooks, with common passages, a five-passage limit, and a fixed answer generator. On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), compared with 88.7% for Jev full scan and 81.3\% for OpenAI dense retrieval. Full scans examine every passage initially, yet later reduction steps can discard relevant evidence. Higher evidence coverage also does not consistently produce better answers: Hybrid + Decisions achieves the highest observed book Answer Accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence. Full scanning incurs substantially higher latency on books under the tested deployments, while reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as queries accumulate. Most QASPER articles already fit within the hybrid candidate pool, limiting the benefit of scanning. These results highlight evidence retention, answer quality, and reuse cost as complementary criteria for choosing a long-document retrieval strategy.
authors: Juan Terven, Diana-Margarita C\'ordova-Esparza, Julio-Alejandro Romero-Gonz\'alez, Edgar Chavez-Urbiola, Juan Irving Vasquez, Julian Andres Ramirez-Bautista, Silvia L. Chaparro-C\'ardenas, Gendry Alfonso-Francia
bullets: Compares 11 lexical, dense, hybrid, and full-document retrieval configurations across QASPER articles and textbook questions.
On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), exceeding Jev full scanning (88.7%).
Hybrid + Decisions produces the highest observed book answer accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence.
Full scans examine all passages but can lose relevant evidence during later reduction and incur substantially higher book latency.
Reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as query volume grows; most QASPER articles fit the hybrid candidate pool.
papers.selection_reason: Compares retrieval configurations for long-document RAG, directly relevant to external memory and retrieval for LLMs.
papers.title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
papers.tldr: For long-document RAG, hybrid retrieval can retain more useful evidence than full scanning while delivering better latency and reuse economics, though evidence coverage does not guarantee answer quality.

papers.abstract: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule.
