A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.
authors: Mingyu Yang, Sharath Turuvekere Sreenivas, Adithyakrishna Venkatesh Hanasoge, Nima Tajbakhsh, Ashwath Aithal, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Addresses vocabulary and segmentation mismatches that make next-token logits difficult to align across tokenizers.
Uses explicit common-token pairs for one-to-one alignments and autoregressive chain-rule probabilities for other alignments.
Adds a residual event for probability mass outside the explicit support, preserving normalization.
Across evaluated teacher–student settings, CSD achieved the best average performance, with gains of up to 1.8 points and up to 4.2 points for Llama-3.1-8B base students.
The method is evaluated across multiple Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and Phi teacher–student combinations.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation for LLM knowledge transfer; relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: CSD: Common-Support Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Transfer
papers.tldr: CSD enables unified cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation by matching normalized teacher and student distributions over a dynamically constructed common support.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly take part in extended conversations where they can both shape and be shaped by another party's views, yet most persuasion research measures only one side of that exchange. We introduce a controlled LLM-LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position. Across four ordered model combinations involving GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, we track both each role's explicitly reported position and a separate measure of its turn-by-turn behavior inside the conversation. Opinion dynamics differ substantially across model combinations: same-model interactions narrow the opinion gap on average, clearly for only one of the two models, while cross-model interactions widen it. Explicit reports and in-dialogue behavior capture distinct aspects of opinion dynamics, and a blanket instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence. These findings suggest that conversational influence depends not only on assigned roles and initial positions but also on the participating models, with implications for how opinion change is measured in extended LLM interactions.
authors: Mohammad Siahkamari, Phuoc Dat Nguyen, Stephen MacNeil
bullets: Examines repeated debates about climate-change attribution between assigned-stance and unassigned LLM roles.
Tracks both explicitly reported opinions and turn-by-turn conversational behavior.
Same-model interactions generally narrow opinion gaps, while cross-model interactions widen them.
Reported opinions and in-dialogue behavior reflect distinct aspects of opinion dynamics.
Results indicate that assigned roles, initial positions, and model identity jointly shape conversational influence.
papers.selection_reason: Studies opinion dynamics and persuasion in LLM-LLM interactions, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: To Manipulate or Not: Opinion Dynamics in LLM Interactions
papers.tldr: A controlled LLM–LLM debate study finds that opinion change depends on the model pairing and measurement approach, while explicitly instructing a model to persuade does not reliably increase influence.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $\rho^k$, with $\rho$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $\rho$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.
bullets: The study exactly measures gradients omitted when backpropagating through only the last k loops in nine looped language models.

In trained models, the omitted-gradient fraction often stabilizes once total loops greatly exceed k, though behavior varies: on Ouro, retaining two of four loops loses 81% of the final output gradient.
The omitted-gradient fraction decreases by 0.07–0.22 within 300 fine-tuning steps on three of four models, including on held-out problems.
This decrease is not explained solely by the readout layer and also occurs under truncated training.
Gradient-loss measurements did not outperform simple measurement-free rules for predicting truncation cost in a small test on two new models.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes gradient behavior in looped language model architectures; relevant to architectural advances and training of foundation language models.
papers.title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
papers.tldr: Truncated backpropagation can discard a large, loop-count-dependent portion of gradients, but the loss often shrinks during fine-tuning and does not yet reliably predict truncation’s training cost.

papers.abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
authors: Jingzhe Liu, Jiliang Tang, Tong Zhao, Neil Shah, Clark Mingxuan Ju
bullets: Existing harness-evolution methods can degrade when more optimization tasks are added, due to poor evidence selection.
SSR builds diverse evidence combinations using task quality and coverage, then races candidate harnesses under limited compute.
Across three benchmarks and six configurations, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results.
As the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR’s pass rate rises from 64.3% to 68.3%, while baselines decline.
Its racing mechanism reduces validation executions by 60% while identifying near-optimal candidates.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes agent harnesses (instructions, tools) through agentic harness evolution, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing
papers.tldr: Successive Scale Racing improves agentic harness evolution by adaptively selecting and efficiently testing evidence combinations as task pools grow.

papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.
authors: Pedro H. Barcha Correia, Matheus Azevedo de S\'a, Paulo H. Gomes de Senna, Giovanni Mandel Martignago, Victor Takashi Hayashi, Charles Christian Miers, Marcos A. Simplicio Jr
bullets: Introduces a general threat model for memory injection in LLM-as-a-service platforms.
Shows that all evaluated services—ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash—can collectively achieve all NIST attack goals under this model.
Identifies attack vectors spanning personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and MCP-connected resources.
Finds persistent manipulation in fresh sessions, including disinformation, harmful content, and simulated unresponsiveness; Claude also enables organizational spread and prompt exfiltration.
Reports that nearly half of the proposed mitigations are not implemented across the evaluated services.
papers.selection_reason: Studies persistent memory vulnerabilities in LLM services; directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
papers.tldr: Persistent memory turns prompt injection from a session-limited attack into a cross-session compromise that can spread harmful behavior and misinformation across users and connected resources.

papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).
authors: Ming Zhong, Stacy Li, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski
bullets: Evaluates agents on 20 ML-for-science benchmarks spanning 11 domains under in-the-wild, long-horizon conditions.
Frontier agents improved the published best model on every benchmark; Claude Opus achieved a 10.4% mean relative improvement without flagged academic misconduct.
Agents commonly miscalibrate novelty, underuse resources, and quickly narrow into local engineering sweeps.
Lightweight skills for ideation, experiment management, and checklists increased improvements to 20.1% for Claude Opus and 8.1% for Codex.
The testbed tracks progress toward agents capable of domain-level scientific reasoning, beyond routine ML engineering.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Agent4Sci, a testbed for evaluating frontier coding agents on scientific ML tasks, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
papers.tldr: Agent4Sci shows that frontier coding agents can improve scientific ML benchmarks substantially, but mostly through engineering tweaks rather than genuine scientific insight.

papers.abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user. We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that do not require clarification. We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on both classification and quality of clarification generation. Our study shows that hard negatives are an essential ingredient to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context). The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before answer generation. The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.
authors: Lihong He, Lucian Popa, Marina Danilevsky
bullets: Targets ambiguity arising from dialog context or multiple interpretations in retrieved documents.
Introduces ClariEdge, a dataset of approximately 3,900 positive and hard-negative examples.
A fine-tuned LoRA reaches 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted larger-model baselines on classification and clarification quality.
Works in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval stages of a RAG pipeline.
The study emphasizes hard negatives for distinguishing true ambiguity from queries resolvable using context.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses query clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems using LLMs, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: ClariEdge fine-tunes a lightweight LoRA model to detect genuinely ambiguous RAG queries and generate useful clarification questions before answer generation.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.
bullets: Targets LLM agents’ difficulty with continuous reasoning and long contexts in multi-turn, long-horizon tasks.
Uses global-local guidance: task milestones and insights provide global direction, while local hints appear when agents become confused.
Builds short-term memory from guidance and reorganizes relevant task information before storing it in long-term memory.
Evaluated on ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models, where it reportedly improves accuracy and efficiency over multiple baselines.
Its plug-and-play design integrates memory arrangement with task-specific guidance rather than relying on direct retrieval alone.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-agent framework combining long-term and short-term memory for long-horizon tasks; relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
papers.tldr: M-Plan is a closed-loop multi-agent framework that combines organized long- and short-term memory with task-specific guidance to improve LLM agents’ long-horizon task performance.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.
bullets: Addresses the overhead and inaccuracy of loading or retrieving skills from large, flat libraries.
Stores individual skills in Atomic Skill Memory and reusable successful compositions as Skill-DAGs.
Reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates or applies Skill-GNN for structure-aware skill selection.
Learns over time by writing successful executions back into procedural memory.
On ALFWorld and SkillsBench, reports 87.1% success and 38.38% reward while reducing token and runtime costs versus strong baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Structured procedural memory for LLM-agent skill reuse; fits LLM and agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: SPEM improves LLM-agent skill reuse by combining structured procedural memory with state- and dependency-aware skill selection, reducing resource costs while maintaining strong task performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
bullets: Controlled results across 22 benchmarks show that merely increasing inference-time reasoning yields modest gains.
A capability layer standardizes tool access and renders tool outputs as model-readable evidence.
Persistent memory stores images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts across reasoning steps.
A coding interface enables computations that combine outputs from multiple tools.

Across eight open and proprietary backbones, it improves average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, with substantially lower token cost than maximum-effort alternatives in one comparison.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal tool-use harness with persistent agentic memory and evidence composition for MLLMs.
papers.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
papers.tldr: OpenVLHarness improves visual-agent reasoning by combining heterogeneous tool use with persistent multimodal memory for iterative evidence gathering and composition.

papers.abstract: An agentic system issues several structurally different kinds of LLM calls. It routes intent, classifies actions, grounds language in a device registry, plans multi-agent pipelines and writes the Python code those pipelines run. The difficulty of these call sites varies by an order of magnitude, yet in practice a single model, chosen for the hardest site, serves all of them. In this work, we evaluate 9 models from 0.8B to a frontier hosted model across the five call sites of a deployed open-source home-automation framework (Wactorz), using its unmodified production prompts and two real Home Assistant installations (280 cases, 2520 scored calls). We find that capability is not ordered the same way at every site, and that larger models are not uniformly better: one 4B model is worse than its 2B sibling at grounded actuation. Paired testing shows the best local model to be statistically indistinguishable from both hosted models at four of five sites. Only code generation separates them, against a small hosted model (p = 0.039) as well as a frontier one (p = 0.002). Aggregate accuracy also hides a safety failure specific to actuation, where small models resolve the accuracy/refusal trade-off in degenerate ways: one model (Gemma4 E2B) actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site does not own, while another refuses every request it receives. Routing each site to its best local model reaches 91.8% against 95.4% at no per-call cost. In a live deployment judged by a user, hosting only the two generative sites matches hosting everything (39/43 against 39/43) for 28% of the spend, and the actuation gap the benchmark predicted appears as exactly one case in twenty-six. Benchmark, harness and all records are released at https://github.com/waldiez/slm-callsite-eval.
bullets: Nine models (0.8B–frontier) were tested on 2,520 calls from two real Home Assistant installations using production prompts.
Model capability varies by call site; larger models are not consistently better, including a 4B model underperforming its 2B sibling on grounded actuation.
The best local model matched hosted models at four of five sites; only code generation significantly favored hosted models.
Per-call-site routing achieved 91.8% accuracy versus 95.4% without additional per-call costs.
Hosting only the two generative sites matched the full-hosting live-deployment score while using 28% of the spend; actuation safety remains a key limitation.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the efficiency of small language models in a deployed agentic home-automation system, finding that per-call-site optimization is beneficial.
papers.title: Not Every Call Needs a Frontier Model: Per-Call-Site Evaluation of Small Language Models in a Deployed Agentic Home-Automation System
papers.tldr: Evaluating five LLM call sites in a deployed home-automation agent shows that small models can handle most tasks, while code generation is the main site requiring stronger models.

papers.abstract: Enterprise systems increasingly rely on automated workflows, yet many AI-driven solutions remain brittle under non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback. While reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) agents offer partial adaptability, they do not by themselves provide persistent reflection mechanisms or straightforward integration with policy-constrained enterprise operations. This paper introduces Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a cognitive architecture for context-driven enterprise agents organized around a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection (PCAR) loop. AWI treats reflection as a mechanism for continuous policy refinement and combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation to support decision making under environmental drift and operational constraints. We evaluate AWI in a simulated enterprise decision workflow characterized by delayed outcomes and a controlled regime shift. In a drift-and-delay stress test, guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover more rapidly than static automation while maintaining policy compliance. Within this setting, AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, illustrating the stability-agility trade-off introduced by reflective policy adaptation.
bullets: Targets brittleness in automated workflows under changing conditions, evolving policies, and delayed feedback.
Organizes agents in a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection loop.
Combines hybrid reasoning, reflective memory, and feedback-driven policy adaptation.
In a simulated drift-and-delay workflow, adaptive guardrail-constrained approaches recovered faster than static automation while remaining compliant.
Reflective components modestly reduced behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, highlighting a stability–agility trade-off.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a cognitive architecture for enterprise agents using a PCAR loop to handle non-stationary conditions.
papers.title: Adaptive Workflow Intelligence: A Cognitive Architecture for Context-Driven Enterprise Automation
papers.tldr: AWI is a reflection-enabled cognitive architecture for enterprise agents that adapts workflows to environmental drift while preserving policy compliance.

papers.abstract: During post-training of large language models (LLMs) with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), GRPO-style algorithms can exhibit severe late-stage collapse. Prompt-based probing reveals that this is not benign strategic pruning, but a harmful contraction of effective strategy capacity that makes distinct reasoning strategies increasingly inaccessible. To characterize this phenomenon, we define strategies through trajectory-level policy-update interactions and develop a unified theoretical framework combining optimization dynamics and information theory. We prove that major RLVR objectives progressively concentrate probability mass onto a single strategy, while sustaining nontrivial task accuracy requires a minimum strategy capacity. The conflict between these two results provides a mechanistic explanation for catastrophic collapse. We further derive the {Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI)} as a lightweight online warning signal. To prevent collapse, we propose \textbf{Mesh Learning}, which exposes multiple reasoning strategies and prevents any single strategy from dominating optimization. Across AIME26, AIME25, MATH-500, GPQA, and LiveCodeBench, Mesh Learning consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen and Phi model families, with gains of up to 13.4 pp and 11.5 pp, respectively. These results establish strategy preservation as a key principle for stable RLVR. Code is available at https://github.com/Ayanami-0123/Open-Mesh-Learning.
bullets: GRPO-style RLVR can progressively eliminate distinct reasoning strategies, reducing effective strategy capacity rather than merely pruning redundant behavior.
A unified optimization-and-information-theoretic framework shows that RLVR objectives concentrate probability on one strategy, while sustained accuracy requires multiple strategies.
The Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI) provides a lightweight online warning signal for impending collapse.
Mesh Learning preserves diverse reasoning strategies by preventing any single strategy from dominating optimization.
Across several math, science, and coding benchmarks and Qwen/Phi models, Mesh Learning improves performance by up to 13.4 and 11.5 percentage points, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates catastrophic strategy collapse in RLVR post-training and proposes Mesh Learning to preserve diverse reasoning strategies.
papers.title: All Work And No Play Makes Jack a Dull Boy: Understanding and Preventing Catastrophic Strategy Collapse in RLVR
papers.tldr: The paper explains catastrophic strategy collapse in RLVR and introduces MEI and Mesh Learning to detect and prevent it.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents are now playing an increasingly significant role in assisting humans with complex problem-solving. However, it is exactly their extended interaction history that introduces an underexplored execution-safety concern. Under benign interaction conditions, an agent may execute an action that violates a safety constraint specified many turns earlier. We term this failure mode Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns (GHOST), which may cause irreversible damage. Our experiments reveal that GHOST events are not isolated cases: this failure mode, occurring precisely under benign interaction conditions, yields an occurrence rate of 11.5% on GPT-5.5. Furthermore, we theoretically show that if the residual conditional violation hazard along each safe prefix is bounded below by a non-summable sequence, the execution enters the hazard region almost surely. Leveraging this theoretical insight, we further propose STAR-Guard, a two-layer defense coupling historical semantic safety constraint restoration with pre-execution audit. STAR-Guard restores applicable safety constraints to reduce unsafe proposals, while its deterministic audit layer prevents residual violations from reaching the environment. Consistent with this two-layer design, we observe no GHOST events in our experiments under the GPT-5.5 setup.
bullets: Identifies GHOST: violating a safety constraint specified many turns earlier during otherwise benign interactions.
Reports an 11.5% GHOST occurrence rate on GPT-5.5.
Shows theoretically that a non-summable lower bound on residual violation hazard leads to hazard almost surely.
Introduces STAR-Guard, combining historical constraint restoration with deterministic pre-execution auditing.
Observed no GHOST events with STAR-Guard in the GPT-5.5 experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses safety hazards in long-horizon LLM agents, proposing a defense mechanism (STAR-Guard) for overlooked constraints.
papers.title: A GHOST in Long-Horizon Agents: Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns
papers.tldr: Long-horizon agents can forget earlier safety constraints across benign interactions, but STAR-Guard eliminates the observed failures through constraint restoration and pre-execution auditing.

papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.
authors: Yazhuo Liu, Kunqing Ding, Xiaoguo Gong, Zifeng Wang, Yichen Yang, Yifeng Che, Wen Chen, Josh Kacher, Olivier Pierron, Shigenobu Ogata, Ting Zhu
bullets: Targets general asymmetric grain boundaries, which are common in polycrystalline materials but difficult to study because of structural complexity and interfacial mismatch.
Uses an LLM-based modular framework with an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain tools, simulation interfaces, hierarchical memory, and dynamic replanning.
Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt grain boundaries in nickel to characterize interfacial defects and diverse deformation modes.
Shows that secondary grain-boundary misfit dislocations substantially affect sliding resistance, while metastable structures can cause anomalously high shear resistance.
Demonstrates a workflow connecting systematic computational screening with targeted, mechanistic materials analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic framework using LLMs for materials science, relevant to LLM agents and tool use.
papers.title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
papers.tldr: GBClaw combines agentic AI, simulations, and expert-guided analysis to uncover how complex nickel grain-boundary structures control deformation and shear resistance.

papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning remains underexplored for low-resource languages, including Dialectal Arabic. To bridge this gap, we introduce the DAR-MGSM (Dialectal Arabic Multilingual Grade School Math) Benchmark, the first manually curated benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in Dialectal Arabic. DAR-MGSM consists of math word problems (MWPs) requiring multi-step reasoning and covers five major Arabic dialects alongside Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). The benchmark comprises two parallel versions: translated-only and translated & culturally localized. The latter version adapts entities and references to regional varieties. We evaluate eleven Arabic-centric and multilingual large language models on DAR-MGSM. The results show that the performance generally declines on the localized version, highlighting the challenges introduced by culturally grounded adaptations. However, the magnitude of this effect varies across models, with Arabic-centric models exhibiting different levels of sensitivity to localization. A mechanistic interpretability analysis shows that translated and localized variants of the same MWPs often induce distinct internal reasoning trajectories, even when aggregate accuracy remains similar. Overall, our results show that mathematical reasoning performance depends on both linguistic variety and cultural context.
authors: Noor Abo Mokh, Teresa Lynn, Nizar Habash, Ahmed Elshabrawy, Sara Alhajeri, Alaa Elsetohy, Preslav Nakov, Alham Fikri Aji
bullets: Introduces the first manually curated Dialectal Arabic benchmark for mathematical reasoning.
Covers multi-step math word problems in translated-only and translated-and-culturally-localized versions.
Evaluates 11 Arabic-centric and multilingual large language models.
Performance generally declines on localized problems, with sensitivity varying across models.
Interpretability analysis finds distinct internal reasoning trajectories even when accuracy is similar.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for LLMs in a low-resource language, relevant to LLM evaluation and robustness.
papers.title: Benchmarking Arabic Dialects for Math Problems
papers.tldr: DAR-MGSM benchmarks multi-step math reasoning across five Arabic dialects and MSA, showing that cultural localization can reduce and alter model performance.

papers.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.
authors: Arnav Chavan, Chanhyuk Lee, Udbhav Bamba, Jaehoon Yoo, Seunghoon Hong, Aditi Raghunathan, Jinwoo Kim
bullets: Addresses the limited scalability of continuous flow language models compared with established autoregressive approaches.
Uses causal attention over prefixes and bidirectional asynchronous flow within blocks, supporting prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding.
Adapts pretrained autoregressive models and trains models up to 8B parameters using fewer than 30B tokens.
Matches or surpasses autoregressive quality on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, while supporting one- and few-step distilled generation.
A self-speculative decoding scheme verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within the same model, achieving 2.54× AR throughput at comparable quality.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel continuous flow architecture (Lafa) for LLMs, improving parallel generation and throughput via self-speculative decoding.
papers.title: Large Flow Language Models
papers.tldr: Lafa is an 8B-parameter continuous flow language model that enables parallel generation and achieves comparable quality to autoregressive models with up to 2.54× higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models are trained by next-token cross-entropy, yet several recent systems also iterate a hidden state without emitting a token: continuous thoughts, pause steps, and recurrent depth. This note separates three risks on one latent process. The token risk $R_{\mathrm{tok}}$ scores a readout. The teacher-forced latent risk $R_1$ scores a one-step map that sees the true hidden state. The open-loop risk $R_H$ scores the same map after it has been iterated on its own outputs. If the Bayes next-token posterior is a function of a $k$-dimensional statistic with full-rank covariance, a width-$k$ latent, a linear least-squares transition, and a refit unembedding match the Bayes token predictor. The statistic is identified only up to an invertible gauge: whitening the residual stream does not change the token law once the unembedding is refit. The matching obstructions are sharp. A constant latent drives $R_1$ to zero while token cross-entropy falls back to the marginal entropy. A perfect token predictor can still hide a null-space walk whose open-loop error grows linearly in the horizon. A small next-latent loss does not certificate next-token prediction, and a small next-token loss does not certificate free latent rollout, unless a rank or injectivity condition is stated with the number.
bullets: Separates token risk, teacher-forced one-step latent risk, and open-loop rollout risk.
Shows that a full-rank k-dimensional sufficient statistic can support Bayes-optimal token prediction with a width-k latent, linear transition, and refit unembedding.
Establishes gauge freedom: invertible latent transformations, including whitening, preserve token predictions when the unembedding is refit.
Provides obstructions: constant latents can minimize one-step latent risk without predicting tokens, while perfect token prediction can conceal latent drift whose open-loop error grows with horizon.
Concludes that small latent-transition loss or token loss alone does not certify the other objective without stated rank or injectivity conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of predictive latents in autoregressive language models; relevant to LLM latent and continuous-thought mechanisms.
papers.title: Predictive Latents for Autoregressive Language Models: Possibility, Gauge, and Obstruction
papers.tldr: The note shows that accurate next-token prediction and stable autoregressive latent rollouts are distinct goals, linked only under explicit rank or injectivity conditions.

papers.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP
authors: Ning Zhang, Shihao Wang, Jinrui Zhang, Chaodong Xiao, Lei Zhang
bullets: Combines joint autoregressive and block-causal training so one model supports both regular generation and multi-token drafting.
Offers confidence-only, speculative-only, and hybrid decoding without separate draft and verifier models.
Uses accepted-prefix alignment, shared KV storage, and width-specialized CUDA Graph execution to reduce decoding overhead.
Reports 2.1–2.4× speedups on selected Bonsai models and up to 3.3× throughput on Jetson Orin across evaluated tasks and hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Co-design for multi-token prediction on low-bit LLMs, reducing decoding steps and KV/memory overhead in LLM inference.
papers.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
papers.tldr: BitMTP co-designs multi-token prediction with ultra-low-bit LLM execution to accelerate generation while maintaining comparable task quality.

papers.abstract: People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post-training stage, from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model's tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content-matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users' dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one-sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output. Code: https://github.com/kouzhizhuo/cap-accommodation.
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Heming Li, Jian Yang, Junyu Luo, Jingshu Peng, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Post-training stages from SFT through DPO and reinforcement learning tend to standardize responses to informal dialect cues.
Update-level analysis finds DPO favors matching British and Australian spelling more than AAE and Singlish across 10 open model lineages, despite models producing AAE features when prompted.
CAP uses preference pairs that reward dialect matching while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users.
On a fully open model, CAP improves accommodation to unseen dialect features without detectable increases for Standard-English users or reduced instruction following.
One-sided preference pairs achieve similar gains only by overshooting users and imposing dialect.
papers.selection_reason: Studies dialect accommodation across post-training stages and introduces calibrated preference data, directly relevant to LLM post-training behavior.
papers.title: Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training
papers.tldr: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs (CAP) helps chat models match users’ dialect density without imposing dialect on Standard-English users, while revealing selective preferences hidden by uniform outputs.

papers.abstract: We present our solution to the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, where we achieved a score of 0.6836 on the official leaderboard, more than double the baseline of 0.2964. This task requires generating all possible objects for subject-relation pairs using a language model with up to 32 billion parameters, with no retrieval or fine-tuning involved. We show that the prompting methodology is as important as the model architecture: while the instruction-tuned model version achieves 0.5681 with its chat interface, the base model achieves 0.6836 when prompted using text completion. Thus, instruction tuning decreases factual recall; we refer to this effect as the instruction tax, which is caused by the model's weights rather than the prompting method. Our final solution is fairly straightforward: we prompt the base model with some examples from the training data, generate 64--256 outputs, and retain only the repeated ones. Two specialized methods are then applied for each relation: one improves the recall of large answer sets, and the other verifies a person's vitality before predicting their place of death.
bullets: Achieved 0.6836 on the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, over twice the 0.2964 baseline.
The base model scored 0.6836 with text-completion prompting, versus 0.5681 for the instruction-tuned model using chat prompting.
The approach uses training examples in prompts, generates 64–256 candidates, and keeps repeated answers.
Relation-specific methods improve recall for large answer sets and verify a person’s vitality before predicting their place of death.
The findings suggest reduced factual recall is caused by instruction tuning in the model weights, not merely by prompting.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes instruction tuning versus base LLM factual recall; relevant to LLM behavior.
papers.title: The Instruction Tax on Factual Recall: Base Models Can Beat Their Instruction-Tuned Counterparts
papers.tldr: For factual knowledge-base completion, a base model prompted as a text completer outperformed its instruction-tuned counterpart, revealing an “instruction tax” on recall.

papers.abstract: A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts $k$ (i.e., same reduced $k$ across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective $k$ achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective $k$ in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static $k$ reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.
authors: Jakob Steimle, Thomas Elsken, Daniel Ehrhardt, Lukas Rinder, Daniel Cremers, Xi Wang
bullets: Unifies four dynamic expert-skipping methods and compares them with using the same reduced expert count across layers and tokens.
Evaluates methods at matched measured expert-compute budgets across two text MoEs and one vision-language model.
The static baseline is difficult to consistently outperform across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings; observed gains are usually minor.
Calibration can produce an effective expert count that differs from testing, causing inference compute to be over- or underestimated.
Recommends calibration-free, per-modality static expert reduction and validates it on a held-out model and modality.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled comparison of dynamic expert skipping in modern MoE LLMs; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Don't Skip the Baseline: A Controlled Comparison of Dynamic Expert Skipping in MoEs
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that simple static expert reduction is often as effective as dynamic MoE expert-skipping methods and should be the baseline for fair comparisons.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) minimizes empirical risk over observed preference comparisons, implicitly assuming that the training preference distribution matches the deployment preference distribution. In practice, this i.i.d. assumption often fails, as preference distribution shift exhibits a natural hierarchical structure across three levels: group-level shift, prompt-level shift, and preference-level shift. Such multi-level distributional mismatch poses a critical challenge for safe LLM deployment, yet existing robust DPO methods typically either model uncertainty over the joint preference distribution or focus on individual sources of shift, leaving the hierarchical structure of OOD preference shifts underexplored. We propose TPO, a tri-level distributionally robust framework for OOD preference alignment, which jointly models all three levels of distributional uncertainty through a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set. By instantiating it with Wasserstein distance, we derive a tractable and interpretable objective that combines a closed-form preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each governed by an independent radius. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirically validate the effectiveness of TPO over existing robust DPO methods.
bullets: Addresses DPO’s vulnerability to deployment preference shifts beyond the i.i.d. assumption.
Uses a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set to jointly represent three shift levels.
Combines a closed-form preference-margin penalty, adversarial prompt-embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting.
Provides finite-sample convergence guarantees.
Experiments report improved effectiveness over existing robust DPO methods, without details on datasets or numerical gains.
papers.selection_reason: Tri-level distributionally robust DPO framework for OOD preference alignment of LLMs.
papers.title: TPO: Tri-level Distributionally Robust Learning for OOD Direct Preference Optimization
papers.tldr: TPO improves OOD preference alignment by robustly modeling distribution shifts at the group, prompt, and preference levels.

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.
bullets: Local inference can reduce serving costs and rate limits while improving privacy and user control.
The study analyzes multiple models across several GPU generations rather than focusing on one model-device pair.
Self-attention dominates runtime for long-context inference.
Self-attention underutilizes important GPU resources, with newer GPUs often receiving less effective utilization.
Key challenges include KV-cache paging, cache utilization, and GPU synchronization; the paper offers observations and recommendations for future work.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of long-context LLM inference bottlenecks with focus on self-attention and KV-cache data management.
papers.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
papers.tldr: Long-context LLM inference on a single local GPU is constrained not only by memory capacity but also by substantial self-attention and data-management inefficiencies.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises student-generated responses using sampled-token student-teacher log-ratios. A positive log-ratio penalizes a token that the student assigns higher probability to than the teacher, but its current value does not distinguish sustained high penalties from abrupt increases along a response. We examine these local changes by comparing consecutive blocks of tokens within the same response. Our diagnostic identifies penalty jumps, abrupt increases in average penalty that persist on held-out tokens. Across these jumps, penalties rise while teacher confidence decreases. We call this pattern penalty-confidence tension. Boundaries into high-penalty blocks do not exhibit comparable confidence changes, showing that local changes provide information beyond the current penalty value. Motivated by this observation, we propose Adaptive Pullback OPD (AP-OPD). At each detected jump, AP-OPD uses the preceding block as a local reference and uniformly scales all supervision coefficients in the following block so that its weighted average penalty matches the preceding block's original mean. This reference determines the scaling factor without an additional strength constant. AP-OPD improves performance on both mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Guangyu Liu, Siyuan Gan, Shilong Zhou, Linjian Meng, Boyan Wang, Jing Huo
bullets: OPD’s current penalty value does not capture abrupt local increases within a response.
Penalty jumps coincide with rising penalties and decreasing teacher confidence, a pattern termed penalty-confidence tension.
AP-OPD uses the preceding token block as a local reference at each detected jump.
It uniformly rescales supervision coefficients in the following block to match the reference block’s original mean penalty.
The method improves performance on mathematical reasoning and code generation.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive supervision reweighting for on-policy distillation of LLMs on reasoning and code generation.
papers.title: Adaptive Pullback: Reweighting Supervision at Penalty Jumps in On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: AP-OPD detects abrupt, persistent increases in token penalties and rescales subsequent supervision to match the preceding block’s average penalty, improving reasoning and code-generation performance.

papers.abstract: Multilingual evaluations often score a model's opening yes or no, a token that also carries model and language answering conventions. We ask when different ways of eliciting and reading an answer recover the same judgment, and when they measure an answer habit. We collect 1.1 million replies from eight models in six languages on up to 105 moral vignettes, varying the question's form, the answer constraint, and the reading of the reply, token or sentence, in both wordings (the FAR-6 battery). Story-level judgment profiles converge across the tested readouts and question forms, except for the yes/no token after a negative interrogative read under a preset mapping: on the same replies, token and sentence profiles agree at a median r = 0.67 across cells, while sentence profiles agree with free-sentence profiles at 0.94, a known linguistic variability. With each language's story consensus removed, a model's profile is nearest to its own in another language for 39 of 48 model-language cells under proposition labels and 15 under free sentences, against 5 expected by chance. Particle, position, and named-term preferences follow their own patterns. A model can keep its judgment and change its yes: scoring that token requires establishing which proposition it affirms.
authors: Haonan Huang, Yuwei Lu, Chengkun Cai
bullets: The study tests eight models in six languages across up to 105 moral vignettes, varying question form, answer constraints, and whether replies are read as tokens or sentences.
Story-level judgment profiles generally converge across readouts and question forms.

The main exception is a yes/no token following a negative interrogative under a preset label mapping; token and sentence profiles agree less strongly (median r = 0.67), while sentence and free-sentence profiles agree at 0.94.

After removing shared story consensus, models’ profiles are most similar to themselves across languages in 39 of 48 cells using proposition labels, versus 15 with free sentences; particle, position, and named-term preferences show distinct patterns.
Interpreting a yes/no answer requires identifying which proposition the model is affirming, rather than scoring the token alone.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual LLM evaluation of judgment and answer conventions.
papers.title: Same Judgment, Different Yes: Measuring Multilingual Judgment Profiles in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models largely preserve the same moral judgments across languages and elicitation formats, but a standalone yes/no token can reflect answering conventions rather than the affirmed proposition.

papers.abstract: The Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, when applied to long-horizon tasks, it faces severe challenges: i) Due to the high task complexity, the model struggles to sample enough successful trajectories, resulting in slow convergence. ii) Relying solely on sparse final rewards causes all steps to be updated indiscriminately, encouraging redundant step generation. When both the quantity and quality of successful trajectories become difficult to guarantee, the performance is severely constrained. This dilemma stems from the limitations: existing RL paradigms rely entirely on the reasoning capability of base models, lacking the ability to actively optimize trajectories. To address the above issues, we propose a novel trajectory evolution paradigm with hindsight credit assignment, termed TrajEvolve. TrajEvolve not only relies on the trajectory inferred by the model but also generates ``evolutionary trajectories'' by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories, thereby exposing the policy to high-quality compositions that lie within the base model's support but are rarely sampled within practical training budgets. Furthermore, TrajEvolve reformulates step-level continuous credit assignment as a binary classification task, whether each step is necessary for task completion. This simplification not only reduces the learning difficulty but also enables step labels to be obtained through counterfactual verification, achieving precise identification of redundant steps. Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.
authors: Yi Wen, Hao Chen, Wanyu Wang, Maolin Wang, Pengyue Jia, Derong Xu, Huize Tan, Yingyi Zhang, Wenlin Zhang, Weihong Luo, Xiku Du, Xiangyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses sparse-success sampling and indiscriminate updates caused by final-only rewards.
Generates evolutionary trajectories by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories.
Recasts continuous step-level credit assignment as binary necessity classification.
Uses counterfactual verification to label whether each step is required for task completion.
Experiments on two datasets report superior performance, without details in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Trajectory evolution with hindsight credit assignment for RL fine-tuning of LLM reasoning on long-horizon tasks.
papers.title: TrajEvolve: Trajectory Evolution for Reinforcement Learning with Hindsight Credit Assignment
papers.tldr: TrajEvolve improves long-horizon RL for LLMs by evolving low-quality trajectories and assigning hindsight credit to identify necessary reasoning steps.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates expert capabilities into a single student by matching teacher and student final-layer distributions on student-generated rollouts. We investigate whether depthwise prediction transitions, the changes in predictions between layers, can provide additional task-relevant supervision. Our diagnostic study finds that stronger teacher--student agreement in intermediate transitions is associated with higher answer correctness within questions, with correct responses exhibiting lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. These observations motivate On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which augments final-layer distribution matching by aligning teacher and student layer-to-layer log-probability increments on student-generated rollouts. Evaluations across three backbones and eight benchmarks spanning mathematics, coding, and instruction following show that OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation. In the three-domain setting, OPTD recovers $\approx 90\%$ of the overall teacher--student capability gap, compared with $\approx 75\%$ for OPD.
authors: Runyang You, Yongqi Li, Tiezheng Yu, Wenjie Li
bullets: Intermediate teacher–student transition agreement correlates with answer correctness, with correct responses showing lower transition KL.
OPTD augments standard on-policy final-layer distribution matching with layer-to-layer log-probability increment alignment.
Evaluated across three backbones and eight mathematics, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks.
OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation.
In three-domain distillation, OPTD recovers approximately 90% of the teacher–student capability gap versus approximately 75% for OPD.
papers.selection_reason: LLM distillation method aligning layer-wise prediction transitions.
papers.title: On-Policy Transition Distillation
papers.tldr: On-Policy Transition Distillation improves expert-to-student knowledge transfer by matching how predictions change across layers, not just final outputs.

papers.abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.
authors: Anil Srirangapatna Nagesh, Nitin Gupta, Anuj Taneja, Vivek Singh, Shane Eleniak, Theo Zhao, Moulidharan N, Shashank Keshetty
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband, access technologies, and diagnostics in a single practical model.
Builds source-grounded synthetic data from networking taxonomies and expert graphs, yielding 212,559 routed records across 14 networking routes.
Uses Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation: the student generates trajectories, route-specific teachers provide token-level supervision, and only the student LoRA is updated.
Teacher-logit reconstruction achieved 7.26 × 10^-6 mean absolute error and 100% top-1 agreement; the completed run reported zero student-version or token-ID mismatches.
On 2,850 held-out questions, Llama-CalixCLM v1 scored 21.7112/25 micro versus 21.7641/25 for the combined routed teachers and 12.8661/25 for the base model.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end framework for domain-specialist post-training and distillation of deployable telecom LLMs.
papers.title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
papers.tldr: RSOD consolidates six telecom-specialist LoRA teachers into one deployable student while preserving nearly all of the routed system’s evaluated performance.

papers.abstract: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.
authors: Jiahui Ning, Liang Chen, Yuchen Liang, Yi Zhang, Fenglei Fan
bullets: Introduces an ability-centric framework covering procedural reasoning, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition, and persona/style consistency.
Evaluates over 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs using quantization and pruning.
Finds that compression redistributes ability profiles: coarse and surface-level abilities often persist, while long-tail and context-dependent abilities are more fragile.
Quantization generally retains abilities better than pruning, but the practical choice depends on an application’s required capabilities.
Supports capability-aware deployment decisions and provides diagnostics for designing more ability-preserving compression methods.
papers.selection_reason: Ability-centric evaluation of compressed LLMs, directly relevant to LLM efficiency and understanding how compression affects language model capabilities.
papers.title: ACE-Compression: An Ability-Centric Evaluation of Compressed Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ACE-Compression evaluates compressed LLMs by which underlying abilities they preserve—not just by aggregate task accuracy—revealing that compression selectively weakens fine-grained and context-dependent capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise-hypothesis items from $\delta$-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command-line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18-28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at $\leq$5% or $\geq$95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between -3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because $\delta$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies
