It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1
authors: Surya Deep Singh, Ashutosh Tripathi, Gaurav Deep Singh
bullets: Represents legal documents as provision graphs, preserves clause boundaries, and resolves cross-references before embedding.
Combines BM25 and BGE-M3 retrieval using Reciprocal Rank Fusion for precise citation and semantic matching.
Achieves perfect boundary precision, preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references, and uses 40.3% fewer chunks while maintaining section coverage on GDPR.
Improves retrieval substantially across benchmarks, including Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% on LegalBench-RAG and higher Recall@5/HR@5 on Indian, European, and Thai legal queries.
Releases implementation, evaluation queries, annotation methodology, and chunking-quality metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Structure-aware chunking improves retrieval for RAG, directly relevant to LLM external memory and memory retrieval.
papers.title: StrucChunk: Structure-Aware Retrieval for Legal Document RAG
papers.tldr: StrucChunk improves legal RAG retrieval by preserving document structure and combining hybrid search, substantially outperforming conventional chunking across five multilingual legal corpora.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.
authors: Ruiyang Ren, Yuhao Wang, Yinan Zhang, Chunyan Miao
bullets: Controlled replays show that arrival timing changes what agents search for, even with identical initial evidence.
These differences persist after all initial results arrive and through subsequent searches.
The paper introduces CEA, which triggers local reasoning only when each subquestion’s evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order.
CEA reduces acquisition disagreement to near repeat variation, matches complete-input accuracy, and improves accuracy over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points.
Under contention, first-ready allocation reintroduces substantial disagreement, whereas CEA makes decisions earlier and responds faster than waiting for all initial evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Studies evidence acquisition and scheduling in language-model agents, relevant to reasoning in language foundation models.
papers.title: The Scheduler Is a Hidden Retriever: How Asynchrony Shapes Evidence Acquisition in Search Agents
papers.tldr: Asynchronous evidence delivery can permanently steer search-agent behavior, while Confluent Evidence Acquisition largely removes this timing dependence without sacrificing accuracy or speed.

papers.abstract: When a user supplies a document and wants the answer drawn from it, a language model is expected to follow it even when it contradicts its parametric knowledge. Prior work has focused on making the model rely on context by steering activations, contrasting logits during decoding, or instructing it in plain language. We ask whether the document alone, with no instruction written into it and no access to the model at inference time, is enough. We optimize a document suffix by discrete token search, starting from the answer to a single question and extending the objective to a set of passages, to multi-hop questions that follow from the planted fact, and to later turns of a conversation. On counterfactual passages that contradict parametric knowledge of the model, the suffix flips nearly all items the model resists across three instruction-tuned model families, in most settings outperforms the decoding baseline and the strongest instruction we could write, and matches activation steering. Controls show that the suffix largely acts through the passage rather than injecting the answer, and a single suffix per model transfers to unseen passages. Each extended objective carries the effect to its target, so the objective, not only the document, sets how far the effect reaches.
authors: Gia-Bao Dinh Ho, Sekh Mainul Islam, Masahiro Kaneko, Timothy Baldwin, Isabelle Augenstein
bullets: The work studies whether a document alone can override a model’s parametric knowledge.
It uses discrete token search to optimize suffixes for single questions, passage sets, multi-hop reasoning, and later conversation turns.
On counterfactual passages, suffixes flip nearly all resisted items across three instruction-tuned model families.
They usually outperform decoding-based intervention and written instructions, and match activation steering.
Controls suggest the effect mainly operates through the passage; model-specific suffixes also transfer to unseen passages.
papers.selection_reason: Studies optimized suffixes to steer language-model context following, relevant to LLM behavior and instruction-following.
papers.title: Shaping the Document, Not the Model: Optimized Suffixes for Context Following
papers.tldr: Optimized document suffixes can make language models follow contradictory context without modifying the model or adding instructions at inference time.

papers.abstract: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Kewei Fu, Yongqi Tong, Chenzhi Zheng, Wei Wu, Jiang-Ming Yang, Jianshe Li
bullets: Addresses wasted listening time and truncated tool calls in realtime voice agents.
Starts new Thinker invocations on updated partial transcripts while preserving ongoing reasoning and dispatched tools.
Shares completed reasoning and tool results to fill missing arguments and launch dependent calls.
Across three benchmarks, it improves speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse, with benchmark-dependent effects on final quality.
On FDBench v3, tool coverage rises by 16 percentage points and mean final-response latency falls by 36.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Concerns tool-using LLM voice agents with speculative execution and latency reduction, relevant to LLM deployment and reasoning.
papers.title: Heartbeat Thinking: Speculative Reasoning and Tool Execution While Listening in Realtime Voice Agents
papers.tldr: Heartbeat Thinking lets voice agents continue and reuse speculative reasoning and tool calls across speech updates, reducing post-speech response latency.

papers.abstract: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.
bullets: Fixed BPE merge budgets are often chosen heuristically, despite their impact on memory and computation.
The study uses information-theoretic criteria and corpus statistics to compute effective merge sets directly.
Synthetic text augmentation improves unigram and bigram estimates for tokenizer selection in limited-data settings.
Experiments across corpora and downstream tasks find reduced model size with little degradation in performance.
Synthetic data is especially helpful for tokenizer quality in low-resource settings.
papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses the optimization of BPE merge budgets for language models, treating the selection process as a statistical model selection problem to reduce memory and computational cost. This is directly relevant to the architecture and efficiency of Large Language Models.
papers.title: Rethinking BPE: Merge Selection as Model Selection
papers.tldr: BPE merge budgets can be selected as a statistical model-selection problem to build smaller token vocabularies with little performance loss.

papers.abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.
authors: Xiang Wang, Zhaoxiang Liu, Xiang Chen, Liqiang He, Kai Wang, Shiguo Lian
bullets: Targets rigid menu systems, fragmented services, and limited extensibility in public-service voice platforms.
Combines end-to-end speech interaction, two-level hierarchical routing, a voice-agent marketplace, and user memory.
Routes requests to general or specialized agents and uses stored preferences and context for personalized task execution.
Supports dynamic onboarding of task agents as conversational entities, enabling ecosystem-level extensibility.
Validated in China’s 114 hotline, demonstrating low-latency full-duplex interaction, scalable routing, and competitive speech naturalness.
papers.selection_reason: Agent-based voice interaction system with user memory and routing, relevant to agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: VISAGENT: An Agent-Based End-to-End Voice Interaction System
papers.tldr: VISAGENT is an extensible, agent-based voice interaction platform that replaces rigid public-service menus with natural conversation, scalable routing, and personalized agent support.

papers.abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through professional human translation into 12 Southeast Asian languages, spanning both high-resource (e.g., Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese) and low-resource (e.g., Burmese, Khmer, Lao) tiers across five distinct tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation. Extensive evaluation of frontier proprietary and open-weights models reveals that while frontier models like Gemini-3.7-Flash maintain robustness across resource tiers, smaller models face severe performance degradation on low-resource languages. Crucially, models perform better in reasoning and summarization when pivoted through English rather than target languages, exposing a critical dependency on English representations, especially for low-resource languages. Beyond these observations, we provide a cross-lingual error analysis and a cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis. We hope these findings shed light on the development of next-generation inclusive multilingual models.
authors: Jiuzhou Han, Abhishek Bijay Mishra, Trevor Cohn, Shubham Mittal
bullets: Covers five tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation.
Includes professionally translated data across high-resource and low-resource Southeast Asian languages, including Burmese, Khmer, and Lao.
Frontier models are relatively robust across language-resource tiers, while smaller models degrade sharply on low-resource languages.
Reasoning and summarization improve when models pivot through English rather than using target languages directly.
Provides cross-lingual error analysis and cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis to diagnose multilingual limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual evaluation benchmark for Southeast Asian languages, relevant to LLM evaluation and multilingual capabilities.
papers.title: DeepSEA: A Multilingual Evaluation Benchmark for Southeast Asia
papers.tldr: DeepSEA benchmarks multilingual model performance across 12 Southeast Asian languages and shows that low-resource languages remain especially challenging, with models often relying on English for reasoning and summarization.

papers.abstract: External skills provide language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge, yet how models use such knowledge after it is supplied remains poorly understood. We identify Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB), the tendency of language models to increasingly favor an action as its associated procedural pattern is repeatedly exposed in a skill, even when the interaction state and action relevance remain unchanged. We find that PEB strongly depends on how procedural knowledge is represented: presenting the same content visually substantially attenuates exposure-induced shifts in action preference relative to textual presentation. Further analysis shows that this attenuation primarily arises from visual encoding rather than structured layout. Although repeated procedural signals remain recoverable from Visual representations, they exert a weaker influence on downstream action prediction, distinguishing signal accessibility from its use as action evidence. This effect also extends to executable action selection, where increasing exposure more strongly favors the corresponding action under Text than Visual. Layer-wise analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence becomes more pronounced toward the model output, with stronger evidence under Text, while activation interventions reveal architecture-specific roles of internal components in transmitting or counteracting the preference shift. Complete-agent evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop further show that Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all four evaluated models. These findings establish skill representation as an important factor governing how procedural knowledge is translated into agent decisions. All code is available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Vis-Skill.
authors: Qing Yang, Yuqi Xiong, Pengcheng Huang, Zhipeng Xu, Zhenghao Liu, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu
bullets: Identifies Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB): repeated procedural patterns increasingly influence action preferences even when state and relevance are unchanged.
The bias is much stronger with textual than visual skill representations; visual encoding, rather than structured layout alone, drives the attenuation.
Visual representations preserve recoverable procedural signals but reduce their use as evidence for downstream action prediction.
Layer-wise and activation analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence grows toward model output and involves architecture-specific components.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all evaluated models.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates Procedural Exposure Bias in skill-augmented language model agents operating in embodied environments (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld). Relevant to both embodied AI and LLMs.
papers.title: Procedural Exposure Bias in Skill-Augmented Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: Repeated textual exposure to procedural skills can bias language-model agents toward associated actions, while visual representations substantially reduce this effect and improve task success.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/
authors: Yejin Lee, Hyundong Jin, Yo-Sub Han
bullets: Confidence-only decoding overlooks the structure of remaining masked intervals and token dependencies.
BPD selects central pivots within contiguous masked spans, decoding selected positions in parallel.
Balanced pivoting provides logarithmic decoding depth with respect to interval length.
The practical strategy combines confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection.
Evaluated on LLaDA and Dream across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Balance-aware pivot selection for parallel diffusion LLM decoding, improving efficiency via token selection.
papers.title: Balance-Aware Pivot Selection for Parallel Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding accelerates diffusion LLM generation by combining confidence with center-focused parallel token selection to reduce decoding depth.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, although this may weaken the benefit of looping. To study this tradeoff systematically, we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
authors: Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Zihan Shao, Yue Su, Weiyang Jin, Ping Luo, Zhuoran Yang, Xihui Liu
bullets: Looped transformers reuse a shared layer block to add depth without adding trainable parameters.
The study varies model size, training tokens, and forward/backward loop counts across nearly 600 runs.
A unified scaling law models looping and truncation using effective parameters.
When compute is matched, full BPTT with fewer loops consistently beats truncated BPTT.
With model size optimized, two fully trained loops achieve lower loss than a compute-optimal non-looped model using about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and 8% more training compute.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling study of looped transformers with truncated backpropagation; relevant to LLM architecture advances and training-efficiency tradeoffs.
papers.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
papers.tldr: A large scaling study finds that full backpropagation through looped transformers is generally better than truncated training, with two fully trained loops offering an efficient tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.
authors: Abhinav Khattar (NVIDIA), Aishwarya Chhabra (NVIDIA), Ameya Velingker (NVIDIA), Anusha Kamath (NVIDIA), Brandon Norick (NVIDIA), Kanishk Singla (NVIDIA), Kiran Praveen (NVIDIA), Markus Kliegl (NVIDIA), Mohammad Qazim Bhat (NVIDIA), Mostofa Patwary (NVIDIA), Niket Agarwal (NVIDIA), Rajpreet Thethy (NVIDIA), Ramani Akkati (NVIDIA), Raviraj Joshi (NVIDIA), Sai Nishanth Padala (NVIDIA), Shuoyang Ding (NVIDIA), Sriharsha Niverty (NVIDIA), Utkarsh Vaidya (NVIDIA), Vitaly Lavrukhin (NVIDIA), Yev Meyer (NVIDIA), Anoop Kunchukuttan (AI4Bharat), Mitesh Khapra (AI4Bharat), Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan (AI4Bharat), Rudra Murthy (AI4Bharat), Sumanth Doddapaneni (AI4Bharat), Thanmay Jayakumar (AI4Bharat), Ujjwal Sharma (AI4Bharat)
bullets: The corpus contains approximately 2.83 trillion tokens across all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native scripts and 12 in romanized form.
A GPU-accelerated pipeline translates curated English data, evaluates and repairs low-quality outputs, preserves structure and technical content, and maintains source traceability.
Continued-pretraining experiments across 12 languages find that combining synthetic data with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline.
The Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite covers chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation using translated benchmarks plus native-speaker review.
Benchmarking open-weight models reveals substantial variation across tasks and languages; experiments also examine data volume, script coverage, and Indic-data share effects on English performance.
papers.selection_reason: Large-scale synthetic pretraining corpus and evaluation suite for Indic LLMs, relevant to LLM pretraining and evaluation.
papers.title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
papers.tldr: The work releases a large synthetic Indic pretraining corpus and multilingual evaluation suite to support scalable development and assessment of Indic LLMs.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.
bullets: Bridges explicit CoT, which uses generated tokens, and latent thought, which uses recurrence in hidden states.
For loop count L=L(n) and fixed k≥1 with s(n)^(1/k)=Ω(L), the model simulates a time-t(n), space-s(n) Turing machine.
Uses context window O(s(n)/L) and O(t(n)s(n)^(1/k)/L) generated tokens.
These resources are each reduced by a factor of L relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation.
The construction also works with constant-bit-size softmax attention under the paper’s finite-precision kernel.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical construction of looped transformers that internalize chain-of-thought, reducing context and generated tokens; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A constant-bit-size looped transformer can internalize chain-of-thought into recurrent hidden-state computation while reducing context and generated-token requirements by a factor of the loop count.

papers.abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.
authors: Jonathan Leung, Zhiqi Shen, Deheng Ye
bullets: Long-horizon procedural reasoning remains unreliable in large language models.
Procedural memory is proposed as distinct from semantic and episodic memory.
Goal-Oriented Graphs encode goals and prerequisite dependencies in inspectable symbolic structures.
The paper examines graph construction challenges and principles for integrating symbolic structure with neural reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Explicit procedural memory for language agents via goal-oriented graphs; relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
papers.tldr: The paper argues that explicit, modifiable procedural memory represented as Goal-Oriented Graphs could improve language agents’ reliability on long-horizon procedural tasks.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data has two popular paradigms: autoregressive models such as GPT, which factorize a sequence in a left-to-right (L2R) order, and masked diffusion models, which are essentially any-order autoregressive modeling. Rather than competing methods, these are the two extreme points of a single axis -- the generation order. For structured discrete domains without a natural traversal, both extremes may be suboptimal, yet the intermediate choice -- a single well-adapted order -- remains largely unexplored. We introduce OrderGPT, which builds on Any-Order GPT to learn a task-level generation order without canonical-order supervision. Our key observation is that predicting variables from randomly sampled reveal prefixes produces recurring attention patterns in the backbone that provide a model-dependent signal of predictive dependencies. We aggregate this signal into a reciprocal dependency graph and use a spectral teacher to derive continuous generation priorities. A lightweight OrderMLP integrated into the GPT backbone learns to predict these priorities from attention, incorporating order learning into the architecture within a single training run. Training gradually shifts toward the learned order, which is then frozen for subsequent autoregressive training and generation. The same mechanism adapts across modalities: adaptively it recovers near-L2R dependency structure in language, learns anatomically organized factorizations on human pose, and discovers a factorization on tabular data that places statistically and semantically related fields nearby, while improving downstream modeling metrics across all domains. The code is available at https://github.com/Chenhe-yang/OrderGPT/.
authors: Chenhe Yang, Yuhuan Lyu, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Targets structured domains where neither left-to-right nor fully arbitrary generation order is ideal.
Extracts predictive dependencies from attention patterns under randomly sampled reveal prefixes.
Builds a reciprocal dependency graph and uses a spectral teacher to produce continuous generation priorities.
An OrderMLP learns these priorities within the GPT backbone during a single training run, after which the order is frozen.
Adapts across language, human pose, and tabular data, improving downstream modeling metrics across these domains.
papers.selection_reason: Learnable generation order for GPT-style models is a meaningful architectural contribution relevant to LLM foundation models.
papers.title: OrderGPT: Generation Order as a Learnable Modeling Choice
papers.tldr: OrderGPT learns a task-specific generation order for discrete data, bridging fixed-order autoregressive and any-order masked diffusion models.

papers.abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.
authors: Minoo Ahmadi, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: SMC enhances inference-time search by resampling partial generations according to internal confidence or external process rewards.
Multinomial resampling can duplicate high-weight candidates and eliminate alternative lineages, while ESS may miss this diversity loss.
LP-SMC combines Chopthin resampling with a weight floor to preserve unequal weights and give low-scoring lineages opportunities to recover.
Across two base models and multiple reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, LP-SMC improved oracle coverage in every setting and end-to-end accuracy in 11 of 12 settings.
Coverage gains also persisted with an external reward model, indicating separate benefits from diversity preservation and reward guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces diversity-preserving inference-time SMC decoding for diffusion LLMs, directly relevant to LLM decoding and reasoning.
papers.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Lineage-preserving SMC improves diffusion-LLM reasoning and code-generation decoding by maintaining diverse candidate trajectories during reward-guided resampling.

papers.abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly capable of searching the open web and synthesizing evidence, yet they remain poorly suited to controllable report generation in multimodal deep research. This task requires agents to handle interleaved textual and visual inputs, gather multimodal evidence through multi-step web search, and deliver comprehensive illustrated reports under user-specified requirements. Existing systems face two limitations. During reasoning, they often underuse images discovered along the search trajectory; during generation, they tend to produce fixed-form answers with limited control over report granularity, multimodal composition, and evidence grounding. We introduce MIRA, a Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for controllable reports. MIRA integrates textual and visual evidence throughout research and writing. At its core, MIRA-Harness translates user requirements into generation contracts and connects four stages: evidence collection, report submission, feedback-driven revision, and final delivery. Building on this harness, MIRA-Data constructs high-quality multi-hop multimodal research trajectories, and we post-train foundation models to operate within the workflow. Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art performance among open agents on 7 representative, established multimodal-search and deep-research-agent benchmarks, while producing user-aligned illustrated reports with traceable textual and visual evidence.
authors: Hongrui Wu, Kaiwen Tuo, Congcong Wang, Gen Li, Shuai Dong, Xinlei Yu, Yuqi Xu, Haowen Hou, Zelin Peng, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Addresses weak image use during web research and limited control over report structure, granularity, and evidence grounding.
MIRA-Harness converts user requirements into generation contracts across evidence collection, submission, revision, and delivery.
MIRA-Data provides multi-hop multimodal research trajectories for post-training foundation models within this workflow.
Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art results among open agents on seven multimodal-search and deep-research benchmarks.
Produces user-aligned illustrated reports grounded in traceable textual and visual evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces MIRA, a multimodal deep research agent for controllable reports. This involves multimodal reasoning and instruction following, relevant to multimodal and large language foundation models.
papers.title: MIRA: A Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for Controllable Reports
papers.tldr: MIRA is a multimodal deep-research agent that uses textual and visual evidence to generate controllable, illustrated reports with traceable citations.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.
authors: Howard Yen, Nitya Mani, Alex Renda, Christopher S. Hardin
bullets: Introduces 12 datasets covering agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and market/world-event forecasting.
Tests recall, state tracking, and pattern learning across inputs up to millions of tokens.
Evaluates 30 API and open models with context lengths from 8K to 512K tokens.
Finds that models strong at recall can degrade sharply on state tracking and pattern learning with longer contexts.
Reports that thinking models can underperform base models by exhausting generation budgets or oversimplifying tasks.
papers.selection_reason: New benchmark for long-context capabilities (recall, state tracking, pattern learning) in LCLMs, directly relevant to long-context model evaluation.
papers.title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking
papers.tldr: LEAPS evaluates long-context models beyond recall, revealing substantial weaknesses in state tracking and pattern learning as contexts grow.

papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.
authors: Yizhou Yang, Jiahong Fu, Zhiwu Wang, Kailong Fan, Haokun Lin, Yichen Wu, Zhenan Sun, Renzhen Wang, Deyu Meng
bullets: Sequential editing can cause cumulative parameter interference and degrade general abilities.
The paper finds that projection-based methods’ robustness mainly comes from update regularization, not null-space projection.
FisherEdit penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while allowing flexibility for new facts.
Its Fisher-geometry formulation has an efficient row-wise closed-form solution.
Experiments across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 show strong performance and improved preservation of downstream accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Fisher information-guided knowledge editing for LLMs, addressing sequential editing and stability, relevant to model adaptation and memory.
papers.title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FisherEdit uses Fisher-information-guided parameter regularization to add knowledge while better preserving LLM stability and general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.
authors: Shengjing Liu, Feiyang Li, Yuxuan Yang, Yile Wang, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets overthinking caused by lengthy, redundant reasoning in large reasoning models.
Monitors trial-answer consistency at reasoning-step boundaries rather than forcing early termination.
Suppresses action transition point tokens such as “Wait,” “Alternatively,” and “Hmm” during decoding.
Training-free experiments across four models and five benchmarks reduce token use by 18.6%–25.0% while maintaining performance.
Results also report 0.07%–1.48% accuracy improvements and more coherent, concise outputs judged by LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free decoding intervention to reduce overthinking in large reasoning models, relevant to LLM reasoning and efficiency.
papers.title: CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: CALM reduces large reasoning models’ unnecessary chain-of-thought steps by masking redundant transition tokens while preserving—and sometimes improving—accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
authors: Guanda Li, Xuefeng Bai, Yulong Chen, Zhiyong Wang, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang
bullets: Long reasoning traces often mix useful and redundant intermediate steps.
Existing step signals describe model behavior but not each step’s causal contribution to the answer.
Interventional Step Credit (ISC) estimates step importance through targeted parameter-level interventions.
IGPO uses ISC to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages at fine granularity.
Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, IGPO reduces average tokens by up to 62% while improving overall performance versus compared methods.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces redundant chain-of-thought steps in large reasoning models via interventional step credit, directly relevant to efficient LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.tldr: IGPO uses causal, intervention-based step credit to shorten chain-of-thought reasoning while preserving important steps and improving performance.

papers.abstract: An evidence-review system must allocate additional model judgments and control their use. We study these software decisions on 6,164 frozen manufacturing source-task pairs. Benefit-targeted routing learns recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement. On the original 300-case test, 60 consultations yield 202/231 agreements with two human references versus 189/218 for a logistic-risk router. An additional 300 cases were independently annotated twice using equal frozen evidence. Without retraining the historical policies, the corresponding counts are 164/190 versus 163/193; the differences do not resolve an advantage. Strict scalar-Ridge controls share preprocessing, regularization and fitting, and remain inconclusive. Quotation and requested-state replacement gates retain rejected cases and budget costs; their joint gate rejects one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes. Evidence ablations, fusion and bounded updates supply further controls. A completed 200-pair identity audit yields 97.45 percent weighted merge precision after eight author adjudications. This audits a provisional map, while prospective company-disjoint performance remains untested.
authors: Yijiashun Qi, Hanzhe Guo, Yuxuan Li
bullets: Evaluates consultation allocation and revision controls for LLM-based manufacturing supplier evidence screening across 6,164 frozen source-task pairs.
Benefit-targeted routing models recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement when selecting additional model judgments.
On the original test, it achieved 202/231 agreements versus 189/218 for logistic-risk routing; on an independent 300-case set, results were inconclusive (164/190 versus 163/193).
Quotation and requested-state gates preserved rejected cases and budget accounting, rejecting one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes.
An identity audit reached 97.45% weighted merge precision, but this audits a provisional map; company-disjoint prospective performance remains untested.
papers.selection_reason: Applies LLMs to evidence screening in manufacturing. Represents an application of LLMs to a specific domain task, relevant to the general utility of language foundation models.
papers.title: Benefit-Targeted Routing and Bounded Revision for LLM-Based Evidence Screening in Manufacturing Supplier Discovery
papers.tldr: Benefit-targeted routing and bounded revision provide controlled evidence-screening mechanisms, but the routing advantage remains inconclusive and prospective generalization is untested.

papers.abstract: Generator--critic trading systems pair an LLM-based trader that makes trading decisions with a red team agent that evaluates these decisions and provides feedback for revision. However, improving individual trading decisions does not ensure that both agents learn from experience and improve together over time. This raises an important question: how can the trader and red-Team select useful experience and learn from each other's evolving behavior? On one hand, experience that benefits decisions under one market condition may become ineffective or harmful under another. On the other hand, trading outcomes reflect both agents' actions, making it difficult to derive appropriate experience for each role. In this work, we propose ACE-Trader, an adversarial co-evolution trading framework. Specifically, we first develop separate context-dependent memory selectors that learn to identify useful experience for the current trading decision. Both selectors receive shared feedback from net-return differences between complete memory-assisted and memory-free trading pipelines, with online updates emphasizing recent outcomes. We further design a co-evolution mechanism that links role-specific memories through shared trading records. We use these records to evaluate the Red-Team's risk assessments and the effects of the Trader's revisions against realized market outcomes, then derive experience for their respective memories. By linking this experience to the corresponding records, we enable the Trader to improve its proposals based on prior critiques and the Red-Team to adjust its review focus as the Trader's behavior changes. Experiments on U.S. stock trading show that ACE-Trader outperforms all 22 active baselines in cumulative return and achieves the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown across both active methods and passive benchmarks.
authors: Chang Zhou, Jiarun Zhou, Xingtong Yu, Hong Cheng, Hui Zhang, Xinming Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that improving isolated trading decisions does not ensure long-term co-learning between trader and critic.
Uses separate, context-dependent memory selectors for each role, updated from net-return differences between memory-assisted and memory-free trading.
Links role-specific memories through shared trading records to evaluate critiques, revisions, and realized market outcomes.
Experiments on U.S. stock trading report higher cumulative return, the highest Sharpe ratio, and the lowest maximum drawdown among evaluated baselines and passive benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: LLM trading agents with context-dependent memory selectors and co-evolving role-specific memories; fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: ACE-Trader: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Generator-Critic Trading Systems
papers.tldr: ACE-Trader enables an LLM trader and red-team critic to learn jointly by selecting context-relevant experience and co-evolving their memories from trading outcomes.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user's behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent's choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue's price-equivalent: a formally defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits substantially under-resolve seller influence. We run the audit over 113,472 trials, seven models across families, and two product categories. To our knowledge, we also run the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model, Jev, which outputs a choice probability directly instead of generating text; strikingly, its profile is unlike any text model we tested, resisting most cues yet remaining susceptible to the strongest social-proof claims. We release the stimuli, logs, and code as a benchmark that reports each model's cue-price profile rather than a single score, giving developers and auditors a common, reproducible way to measure how content moves AI shopping agents.
authors: Felix Buecheler, Gerardo Berbeglia, Mingyu Guo
bullets: Choice-rate audits saturate when strong cues are selected nearly every time, obscuring differences in influence.
The method raises a cued product’s price until it is chosen half the time, defining the cue’s price-equivalent premium.
Across 113,472 trials, seven models, and two product categories, cues with similar choice rates showed widely different price-equivalent influence.
The decision-native model Jev resisted most cues but remained vulnerable to the strongest social-proof claims, unlike the tested text models.
The released benchmark provides stimuli, logs, code, and per-model cue-price profiles for reproducible auditing.
papers.selection_reason: A benchmark for auditing LLMs acting as shoppers, measuring the influence of seller content. Relevant to LLM behavior and evaluation in specific agent tasks.
papers.title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
papers.tldr: Price-equivalent auditing measures how much seller-controlled cues influence AI shopping choices by converting their effect into an equivalent price premium.

papers.abstract: Autonomous codebase refactoring requires coding agents to restructure working software while strictly preserving externally observable behavior and prioritizing execution performance and compute efficiency over stylistic preference. Existing benchmarks: refactoring benchmarks assess functional correctness while overlooking runtime regressions, whereas code performance benchmarks target isolated micro-kernels that ignore codebase-scale complexity. We observe that refactoring scale is governed by the scope of the observable contract, the caller-visible interface fixing behavioral invariants while freeing private implementations for optimization. Building on this insight, we introduce FrontierRefactor, a benchmark of 60 qualified engineering tasks spanning four scales, from computational kernels to full repositories, across in-place optimization and cross-language rewriting. Evaluating frontier coding agents through a reference-free cascaded protocol across 1,080 execution runs reveals that correctness and speedup are largely decoupled: 41.2% of submissions satisfy functional equivalence yet fail to deliver verified performance improvements, with 19.3% suffering performance regressions and 21.9% trapped in measurement noise. Refactoring paradigms reveal orthogonal engineering bottlenecks: while cross-language rewrites gain speedups from native compilation after passing functional checks, agents struggle with contract fidelity, with pass rates dropping from 65.0% on modules to 32.6% at package scale; conversely, in-place optimization reliably preserves behavioral contracts at 86.5% but rarely achieves acceleration without physical performance profiling. Trajectory analysis shows that agents fall victim to uncalibrated micro-benchmarking illusions, an operational blind spot that multi-turn execution-timing feedback directly resolves, raising strict success from 16.0% to 40.0%.
authors: Shijian Wang, Fanqing Meng, Jiajun Chen, Qiguang Chen, Linxin Song, Runhao Fu, Shuhang Zheng, Shuai Shao, Qizhe Xie, Jieyu Zhao, Mengkang Hu
bullets: Introduces 60 refactoring tasks across four scales, from computational kernels to full repositories, covering in-place optimization and cross-language rewriting.
Uses a reference-free cascaded evaluation protocol over 1,080 execution runs to assess correctness and performance separately.
Correctness and speedup are largely decoupled: 41.2% of submissions preserve functionality but lack verified performance improvements.

Cross-language rewrites can benefit from native compilation but struggle with contract fidelity at package scale; in-place optimization preserves behavior more reliably but seldom accelerates without profiling.
Multi-turn execution-timing feedback improves strict success from 16.0% to 40.0%, addressing misleading micro-benchmark signals.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a benchmark for coding agents performing codebase refactoring. While focused on software, it represents the application of LLM agents to complex tasks, relevant to the general agent capabilities within language foundation models.
papers.title: FrontierRefactor: Benchmarking Multi-Scale Performance-Oriented Codebase Refactoring
papers.tldr: FrontierRefactor shows that autonomous code refactoring must jointly verify behavioral equivalence and real execution gains, which current agents often fail to achieve.

papers.abstract: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.
authors: Guanqun Jiang, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces procedural hallucination: producing retrieval-supported answers that violate a governing skill or procedure.
Presents SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains.
Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% with conflicting retrieval, versus 78.2% and 72.8% with supportive retrieval.
Mechanistic analysis finds the largest answer-preference divergence shortly after generation begins, with repair primarily attributed to value vectors.
Intervening in the identified value pathway improves final answer validity.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates how language models handle conflicts between retrieved context and stored skills, framing skills as a form of memory. Relevant to LLM memory mechanisms and retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models often follow useful but skill-violating retrieval cues, causing procedural hallucinations that can be traced to early value-pathway dynamics.

papers.abstract: Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory internalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Compounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hypotheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt. Varying the retrieved cases gives the memory different perspectives, yielding reflective diversity that is not merely sampled but also grounded in retrieved experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code, and multi-hop QA, CoMem achieves strong overall performance. Additional evaluations show that it generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and enables smaller models to provide effective guidance to stronger solvers.
authors: Yun Shen, Ming Shen, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Addresses repetitive, task-local self-reflection and the grounding–generalization trade-off between retrieved and parametric memory.
Builds a bank of successful and failed reflections, then uses retrieved cases to generate failure hypotheses during training and inference.
Different retrieved cases provide grounded reflective diversity to guide future attempts.
Shows strong overall performance across two backbones and five math, code, and multi-hop QA benchmarks.
Also generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and helps smaller models guide stronger solvers.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces compounding memory for LLM agents, using retrieved experience to anticipate failures, relevant to LLM memory and agent adaptation.
papers.title: CoMem: Learning to Anticipate Failures from Retrieved Experience
papers.tldr: CoMem improves LLM agents’ failure anticipation by conditioning learned reflective memory on retrieved past experiences rather than using retrieval and learning separately.

papers.abstract: Recovering from failures in long-horizon, stateful language agents is challenging because the action introducing a defect, the symptom exposing it, and the persistent state requiring repair frequently diverge. Existing methods largely focus on retrospective failure attribution, leaving sequential diagnosis and state repair poorly integrated under constrained budgets. We introduce TRACE-FIX, a unified recovery framework centered on versioned residual task state. Trace transforms execution logs into a structured dependency-linked ledger, prioritizing unresolved task requirements rather than salient surface errors. Fix formulates recovery as budgeted planning over admissible actions, incorporating outcome forecasting and explicit repair-reserve constraints to prevent premature budget exhaustion. To rigorously decouple localization accuracy from downstream repair capability, we present LongH-Debug, evaluating root-cause attribution, verified-fault recovery, and end-to-end closed-loop execution independently. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that structured residual tracking substantially improves causal localization over raw-trace baselines, while budget-aware sequential planning converts verified fault signals into more reliable task recovery without destructive trial-and-error. Code is available at https://github.com/toffeecat/tracedp.
bullets: Targets failures where the triggering action, observed symptom, and state needing repair occur at different points in execution.
Trace converts execution logs into a dependency-linked ledger focused on unresolved task requirements.
Fix plans admissible recovery actions using outcome forecasts and repair-reserve constraints to avoid exhausting the budget prematurely.
LongH-Debug separately evaluates root-cause attribution, verified-fault recovery, and end-to-end execution.
The framework improves causal localization over raw-trace baselines and enables more reliable recovery without destructive trial-and-error.
papers.selection_reason: Residual task-state ledger for long-horizon agents fits LLM agent memory.
papers.title: From Trace to Fix: Residual Task State in Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: TRACE-FIX helps long-horizon agents diagnose failures and repair persistent task state through structured residual tracking and budget-aware recovery planning.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate more reasoning tokens than needed. Limiting the reasoning budget reduces cost, but forcing an answer from an incomplete trace can hurt accuracy. System-1 decision models select among candidate options without producing a reasoning response. We evaluate Jev as a decision reader of truncated reasoning across seven LLM reasoners and five multiple-choice benchmarks (35 pairs). Jev achieves higher mean accuracy than forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including the estimated costs of reasoning and answering. At a 1,500-token budget, it improves accuracy by 4.1 pp overall and 8.6 pp on truncated questions, with significant gains in 17 pairs under Holm-corrected bootstrap tests. Offline replay estimates 34.5% of the full-run cost, with a 1.13 pp accuracy loss. A policy selected on training folds saves 71.3% of the estimated full-run cost on held-out folds, with a 0.58 pp accuracy loss. We also find that Jev shows strong question-only accuracy, exceeding 500-token forced answering on average (68.0% vs. 65.5%), although this advantage varies by benchmark. These findings suggest that System-1 decision models can complement LLM reasoning and reduce the need for costly reasoning completion.
authors: Zhongyin Wang, Zhaoqian Xue, Junting Mu, Haozheng Liu, Ye Yuan, Haolun Wu, Lingyao Li
bullets: Evaluates Jev across seven reasoning LLMs and five multiple-choice benchmarks, covering 35 model–benchmark pairs.
Jev outperforms forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including reasoning and answer costs.
At 1,500 tokens, it improves accuracy by 4.1 percentage points overall and 8.6 points on truncated questions.
Offline replay estimates 34.5% of full-run cost with a 1.13-point accuracy loss; a learned policy saves 71.3% with a 0.58-point loss on held-out folds.
Jev also performs competitively using only the question, though its advantage varies across benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates system-1 decision models for truncated LLM reasoning under budget, relevant to efficient reasoning and LLM decision-making.
papers.title: Truncated Reasoning Under a Budget: Evaluating System-1 Models as Decision-makers
papers.tldr: Using a System-1 decision model to select answers from truncated LLM reasoning improves cost-adjusted accuracy over forcing incomplete reasoning traces to answer.

papers.abstract: Self-consistency answers a question by generating multiple responses and selecting the most frequent answer. Its evaluation requires both correctness labels and information about which responses agree; correctness labels alone generally determine neither voting accuracy nor the benefit of additional votes. For tasks in which all correct responses map to the same normalized answer, we derive sharp accuracy bounds using classical stochastic majorization, refined by abstention counts and answer-category limits. We also derive sharp bounds on accuracy changes across voting budgets that share a response pool. When answer-category counts are available, we introduce Plurality-U, a count-based dynamic program that exactly averages voting accuracy over all fixed-size subsets, eliminating finite-pool Monte Carlo error. On 1,403,520 stored outputs from recent reasoning models in Scorio Lite and Scorio Trace, recording abstention counts and answer options cuts the width of SuperGPQA accuracy intervals by more than half. For moving from 9 to 17 votes, our bounds reduce interval width by a median of 77.7% on SuperGPQA and 72.3% on 14 GPQA and Adaptive-Consistency pools, compared with a baseline that combines separate accuracy bounds. Exact computation has lower paired median runtime than 2,000-subset Monte Carlo in 14 of 15 tested pool-budget settings. These results clarify what incomplete logs can establish and provide an exact evaluation procedure when answer counts are retained.
authors: Zhengtao Gui, Zexi Chen, Weining Shen
bullets: Correctness labels alone are insufficient to determine voting accuracy or the value of additional votes; agreement information is needed.
For tasks with a shared normalized correct answer, the authors derive sharp bounds using stochastic majorization, abstention counts, and answer-category limits.
They introduce Plurality-U, a dynamic program that exactly averages accuracy over fixed-size response subsets when answer counts are available.
Across stored reasoning-model outputs, adding abstention and answer-option counts substantially narrows accuracy intervals, while exact computation often outperforms 2,000-subset Monte Carlo.
The analysis applies to incomplete logs and clarifies what can—and cannot—be established about self-consistency performance.
papers.selection_reason: Develops exact evaluation methods for self-consistency in LLMs using stochastic majorization and dynamic programming.
papers.title: Which Answers Agree? Evaluating Self-Consistency from Incomplete Logs
papers.tldr: The paper shows how to evaluate self-consistency voting from incomplete logs by deriving tight accuracy bounds and an exact count-based computation method.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility--diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility--diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility--diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.
authors: Jianhao Zhang, Ou Wu, Yi Du
bullets: Targets noisy, redundant synthetic candidate pools and the difficulty of preserving pretrained capabilities during single-stage fine-tuning.
Builds a navigator by applying the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization, revealing recipe-induced capability drift.
Scores candidates by predictive divergence between the navigator and pretrained model to estimate forgetting-aware utility.
Efficiently selects a utility–diversity constraint set, then distills pretrained behavior on it during new-task fine-tuning.
Experiments report a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation with lower selection overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces NADS for mitigating catastrophic forgetting in LLM fine-tuning using a navigator-guided data selection strategy.
papers.title: NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: NADS selects synthetic data using navigator-model drift to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning without access to pretraining data.

papers.abstract: Scientific model discovery requires proposing candidate models of an unknown system and designing experiments that discriminate among them. However, LLM-based approaches typically rely on in-context learning to predict outcomes and select experiments, lacking explicit model evaluation to systematically guide hypothesis search, while Bayesian approaches enable principled model comparison but are confined to a predefined candidate set which results in limited search spaces. To this end, we introduce BMD, which closes the loop between LLM-driven hypothesis generation and Bayesian experimental design. Specifically, an LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits their parameters, weighs them by model evidence, and averages their predictions. Then, BMD chooses the next experimental conditions by maximizing the joint expected information gain over families and their parameters, while feeding the updated beliefs and residual diagnostics back to the LLM to guide its next proposals. Across four scientific discovery benchmarks, BMD achieves lowest final prediction error than in-context learning and LLM-based scientific agents while recovering exact functional forms more often, with ablations supporting numerical feedback and the joint objective.
authors: JooKyung Yuh, Byungmin Park, Eunseo Choi, Jinheon Baek, Junmo Cho, Kyu Hyun Choi, Sung Ju Hwang, Kyong Hwan Jin, Hae Beom Lee
bullets: Targets the limitations of LLM methods lacking explicit model evaluation and Bayesian methods restricted to predefined candidates.
An LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits parameters, computes model evidence, and averages predictions.
Experiments are selected to maximize expected information gain over both model families and parameters.
Updated beliefs and residual diagnostics guide subsequent LLM hypothesis proposals.
Across four benchmarks, BMD achieved the lowest final prediction error and more often recovered exact functional forms; ablations supported its numerical feedback and joint objective.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes BMD, a framework integrating LLMs with Bayesian experimental design for scientific model discovery, advancing LLM agent capabilities.
papers.title: Bayesian Model Discovery with Language Models: Closing the Loop between Hypotheses and Experiments
papers.tldr: BMD combines LLM-generated hypotheses with Bayesian model evaluation and experiment design to iteratively discover scientific models.
