Penalties that do not outgrow the model’s preference for repetition may leave positions permanently locked.
DRY’s breaker-based penalty is capped for short breaker-free runs, so many locked loops remain locked.
Across 11 open models, 66% of locked units with run length g=6 stayed locked under DRY, versus 1% with g=8.
DRY-C adds recurrence-based exponential penalty growth; none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the limit while task completion remained close to DRY’s.
papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis of repetition-loop lock-in and sampler blind spots in LLM decoding, relevant to language model generation.
papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
papers.tldr: Repetition loops can become mathematically unescapable under truncation sampling and bounded penalties, revealing a blind spot in DRY that DRY-C addresses.

papers.abstract: Explicit memory systems transform conversation history into persistent representations intended to improve future access, often at substantial construction cost. Yet it remains unclear whether this added complexity yields better answer accuracy than retrieving directly from raw history. This study compares six state-of-the-art explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled retrieval settings. We find only localized gains for particular question types and tight run-time context budgets, with no consistent advantage over strong raw-history RAG baselines. Oracle retrieval shows that some systems fail to preserve answer-supporting information during explicit memory construction, while others preserve it but fail to retrieve it effectively, despite construction costs reaching hours per conversation. Our findings suggest that while many existing memory systems for AI agents emphasize increasingly elaborate explicit memory construction, they are often evaluated without strong controlled comparisons to raw-history RAG and may underemphasize retrieval. Retrieval remains a major bottleneck when useful information is preserved, suggesting that improving access to existing information may be at least as important as constructing richer explicit memory.
authors: Yongjie Zhou, Shuai Wang, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon
bullets: Compares six explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled settings.
Finds no consistent accuracy advantage for explicit memory, except for some question types and tight context budgets.
Oracle retrieval reveals two failure modes: losing answer-supporting information during construction or failing to retrieve preserved information.
Some systems require hours of construction per conversation, highlighting substantial overhead.
Results suggest improving retrieval may be as important as building richer persistent memories.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a controlled comparison of explicit memory systems against raw-history RAG, finding that retrieval efficiency often outweighs the benefits of complex memory construction.
papers.title: Do Conversational Agents Need Explicit Memory? A Controlled Comparison with Raw-History Retrieval
papers.tldr: Explicit memory systems offer only localized benefits over strong raw-history retrieval, while costly construction and retrieval failures limit their overall advantage.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation-time interventions on Qwen3-4B-Base, measuring how much of its RL-trained counterpart's gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192-token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH-500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with "Alright" recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as "Wait" do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model's diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model's diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/CyrusZhang04/WhatRLBrings.
authors: Siyu Zhang, Yuquan Lu, Yoshua Y. Li, Yifan Ding, Kun Zeng, Yu Huo, Yifu Guo, Rongxiang Weng, Xunliang Cai, Xiaoying Tang
bullets: On 120 AIME problems, power sampling within the same output limit adds no gain over greedy decoding.

Replacing the base model’s tokens only where its greedy choice differs from the RL model—about 4% of positions—recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 improvement; this also holds across three model pairs on MATH-500.

Forcing the opening token to “Alright” recovers 35% of the RL gain, while later replacements add a further 5.2 percentage points; fixed insertion rules for words like “Wait” do not reproduce this benefit.
Sparse replacement preserves much of the base model’s diversity and reaches 67.5% at k=256, versus 61.4% for the RL model and 61.45% for a matched whole-response mixture.
The comparison uses equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, because the replacement method consults both models at every decoding step.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes what RL adds to LLM reasoning through sparse token-level interventions, directly relevant to LLM training and decoding.
papers.title: What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make
papers.tldr: A small number of token-level choices—especially the opening token and later divergent decisions—accounts for much of RL’s reasoning improvement over the base model.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills as a lightweight way to acquire task-specific knowledge. Recent work enables skills to evolve from task trajectories. However, these methods often lack systematic management of evolved skills, making it difficult for agents to reuse and accumulate skills across domains, thus limiting performance on subsequent tasks.To reliably accumulate, reuse, and maintain useful skills across tasks, we present SELM (Self-Evolving Library Management), a framework that formulates skill evolution as library-level management. SELM jointly manages skill retrieval, updating, and lifecycle by maintaining skill confidence and utility signals. It introduces utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills, a Map-Reduce framework to generate targeted updates from task-specific experience, and lifecycle controls to retain or remove skills based on their effectiveness. These mechanisms enable the skill library to continuously accumulate useful experience while preserving and pruning skills across tasks, improving agent performance on complex tasks across diverse domains. We evaluate SELM on four agent benchmarks covering diverse tasks and execution environments, and SELM consistently outperforms in most settings.
authors: Mengxi Hu, Yuxuan Hu, Jinbo Su, Ke Wang, Honghao Shi, Wenli Wu, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of accumulating and reusing evolved skills across domains.
Uses confidence- and utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills.
Applies Map-Reduce updates to incorporate targeted experience from task trajectories.
Manages skill lifecycles by retaining effective skills and removing ineffective ones.
Evaluated on four diverse agent benchmarks, with consistent improvements in most settings.
papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces SELM, a framework for managing a self-evolving library of skills for LLM agents. This directly addresses the need for persistent external memory mechanisms to store and retrieve information (skills) beyond the current context, fitting the 'LLM Memory' subtopic.
papers.title: Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization
papers.tldr: SELM improves multi-skill LLM agents by systematically retrieving, updating, retaining, and pruning skills across tasks.

papers.abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.
authors: Chengyu Xie, Fei Shen, Shuyi Miao, Yue Feng, Jian Yu, Pengyang Shao, Yijun Tian, Xiaoyu Du
bullets: Cross-lingual safety gaps can let attacks bypass LLM guardrails, while existing alignment methods offer limited neuron-level interpretability.
SCAR scores from parallel safe and unsafe prompts identify language-specific safety neurons; their intersection forms the shared Safety Kernel (SK).
Activation suppression and state-transfer interventions validate the SK’s role in cross-lingual safety behavior.
SK-Masked LoRA restricts adaptation to FFN output dimensions associated with the SK.
Experiments report lower attack success across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, with generally limited effects on general capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies a cross-lingual safety kernel of neurons and constrains LoRA adaptation to these shared coordinates to improve defense.
papers.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
papers.tldr: The paper identifies a shared cross-lingual safety neuron subset and uses it to target alignment updates, improving multilingual defense with limited impact on general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs with in-context examples (IC-Train) lets translation models adapt to new parallel data at deployment, but it is unclear whether they actually learn the translations of rare terms from those examples. We formalize this capability as in-context term learning (ICTL). We show that standard IC-Train develops this capability only weakly, and propose RareCipherFT, which strengthens it without any lexical resources. RareCipherFT pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term with it. It then replaces that term with a character-shuffled cipher in both the context and the reference, so the term can only be recovered by copying from context. The ciphered fraction of training data is annealed to preserve translation quality. Across seven translation directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, and four models from 1B to 7B parameters, RareCipherFT raises term recall over standard IC-Train by 5-15 absolute points without lowering COMET. Probes using synonyms, nonce words and controls for shared surface context show that these gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.
authors: Deevyanshu Malu, Deeptanshu Malu, Sunita Sarawagi
bullets: Standard in-context training develops in-context term learning only weakly.
RareCipherFT pairs targets with context examples sharing rare terms, then replaces those terms with matching character-shuffled ciphers.
The cipher forces models to recover translations by copying from context rather than relying on lexical resources or shortcuts.
Across seven English–low-resource language directions and four 1B–7B models, term recall improves by 5–15 points without reducing COMET.
Probes with synonyms, nonce words, and surface-context controls support genuine source-to-translation linking.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies LLM in-context terminology learning and fine-tuning for translation, relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: Training with Ciphers to Enhance In-Context Terminology Learning For Translation from Rare Languages
papers.tldr: RareCipherFT improves rare-term learning from in-context translation examples by training models to copy ciphered term translations from context.

papers.abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.
authors: Junming Zhang, Rubin Wei, Xu Cheng, Hao Sun, Ruoxi Cheng, Xiquan Wang, Peisong Wu, Mingsong Chen, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Targets habit inference across partial evidence, exceptions, habit changes, and unaccepted suggestions.
Builds synthetic histories spanning hundreds of sessions in food, finance, software, and travel.
Uses four-choice tasks with human review to test habit inference and application.
Evaluates eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash.
The best method reaches 33.61% macro accuracy, and performance remains limited even with annotated evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for habit induction in LLM agent memory; relevant to persistent memory evaluation.
papers.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
papers.tldr: HABIT-Bench evaluates whether agent memory systems can infer and appropriately apply user habits from weak, longitudinal evidence, revealing substantial limitations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards assigns one terminal reward to an entire reasoning trajectory, obscuring how individual reasoning steps contributed to the outcome. GRPO broadcasts a group-normalized advantage to every response token, while finer-grained approaches often rely on dense auxiliary rollouts or branching schemes that can also alter the data used for policy updates. We cast the missing middle as budgeted measurement: with a limited rollout budget, which partial solutions should be evaluated, and how should their value estimates refine credit? ProbePO selects partial-solution states with a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their expected verifier rewards under a capped continuation budget. ProbePO redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO's trajectory-level advantage across tokens while preserving each trajectory's mean token-level advantage; probe continuations serve only as measurements. Across three DeepSeekMath and Qwen-family models spanning 1.5B-7B parameters, ProbePO consistently outperforms GRPO and achieves the highest accuracy among the four evaluated methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. Against dense-probing VinePPO on DeepSeekMath-7B, ProbePO achieves higher accuracy on all six benchmarks with 76% less end-to-end training time.
authors: Diyi Hu, Ruizhong Qiu, Lin Qiu, Hanghang Tong, Hanqing Zeng
bullets: Addresses the coarse credit assignment of terminal rewards and GRPO’s uniform token-level advantages.
Selects partial-solution states using a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their verifier rewards with capped continuation probes.
Redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO’s trajectory advantage while preserving each trajectory’s mean token-level advantage.
Outperformed GRPO across evaluated models and achieved the highest accuracy in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons.
Beat dense-probing VinePPO on all six tested benchmarks while using 76% less end-to-end training time.
papers.selection_reason: LLM reinforcement learning with sparse probes and credit redistribution; relevant to language foundation model reasoning methods.
papers.title: ProbePO: Sparse Probes, Redistributed Credit for Critic-Free LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ProbePO improves critic-free LLM reinforcement learning by using a limited budget to probe uncertain partial solutions and redistribute trajectory credit across reasoning tokens.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.
authors: Yu Wang, Zhu Wang, Ning Hu, Yifan Guo, Xiu Ma, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Targets high transient memory from full-prompt KV-cache construction, which limits long-context inference.
Processes prompt chunks layer by layer, retaining full-prompt KV only for the active layer before evicting it.
Preserves full-prompt-aware cache selection while reducing activation and temporary memory.
At 64K context, cuts construction-time transient memory by 83.89% on A100; on RTX 4090, TTFT increases only 1.06%.
Enables 128K prefill on RTX 4090 and Jetson, where matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory.
papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise delayed KV eviction reduces long-context LLM prefill memory; fits KV cache/memory efficiency and long-context inference.
papers.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: TideKV reduces peak memory during long-context LLM prefill by delaying KV-cache eviction until each Transformer layer finishes processing the full prompt.

papers.abstract: While a LLM's chain of thought (CoT) is a promising approach to interpreting model outputs, prior work shows CoT's content does not always accurately reflect the reasoning process. Emmons et al. (2025) finds that models can follow a question hint without revealing so in its chain of thought, but when the hint is sufficiently complex the computation is forced into the CoT. This claim, however, has only been tested on Gemini models, and the datasets and code is closed source. We replicate their proxy task across eleven models from six families and find the necessity effect generalizes. Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models. We also extend the study from Emmons et al. (2025) to measure CoT-necessity and unfaithfulness across five cue families (four of them new) and three difficulty levels. The relationship between when CoT is necessary and unfaithfulness is task-specific and model-specific. For some hint types, models often verbalize their hint-following behavior even when the hint can be decoded in a single forward pass. These results support the case for CoT monitoring when unsafe behavior requires non-trivial computation, and that properties of CoT unfaithfulness are sensitive to model and setting.
authors: Arav Dhoot, Yixiong Hao, Zephaniah Roe
bullets: Replicates the necessity effect across 11 models from six model families, beyond the originally tested Gemini models.
All models follow simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while following concealed complex cues generally returns near baseline.
Extends evaluation to five cue families and three difficulty levels, including four new cue types.
The link between CoT necessity and unfaithfulness varies by cue type and model; some models verbalize hint-following even when it is computationally simple.
Supports CoT monitoring for unsafe behavior requiring non-trivial computation, but cautions that monitoring reliability is context-sensitive.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability across LLMs; relevant to LLM reasoning.
papers.title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models
papers.tldr: Across 11 models, concealed cue-following usually breaks down when it requires complex computation, making chain-of-thought monitoring useful but strongly dependent on the task and model.

papers.abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. Within the same candidate pool, selecting documents with high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains, unlike the evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors. We introduce truncLongPPL to reduce scoring cost by computing key-token density over a truncated prefix. At 128K, scoring the first half of the reference span yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring with a measured $2.28\times$ end-to-end scoring speedup. Across three training seeds, truncLongPPL achieves the highest mean scores among evaluated pipelines, exceeding random-long by 4.54 points on validation HELMET and 3.28 on held-out RULER, with gains most consistent in retrieval. At a 256K target context, it gains 2.82 average RULER points over random-long on Qwen2.5-3B. In short/long mixed training across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo~3-7B, it gains 1.47--7.31 average RULER points over random-long mixing, with seven-task short-context averages within 0.23 points of the corresponding baselines. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Qwen3-8B and OLMo~3-7B models trained with selected long documents outperform their random-long counterparts by 1.13--1.67 points on LongBench v2 and 0.62--1.44 points on MRCR.
authors: Junlong Jia, Jiang Zhou, Xing Wu, Chaochen Gao Tinghao Yu, Feng Zhang, Lilin Wang
bullets: Random sampling of natural long documents outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths under matched training budgets.
Within the same candidate pool, LongPPL key-token-density selection improves downstream performance, while evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors do not.
truncLongPPL scores only a truncated prefix, achieving performance close to full-span scoring with a measured 2.28× end-to-end scoring speedup at 128K.
Across context-extension, mixed-length training, and SFT evaluations, selected documents yield consistent gains, particularly on retrieval-focused tasks.
The study evaluates Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo 3-7B across 128K–256K target contexts, with short-context performance largely preserved.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of long-document selection for context extension; directly relevant to long-context LLM training.
papers.title: Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that selecting natural long documents by LongPPL key-token density—especially with an efficient truncated-prefix scorer—improves context extension more reliably than random or generic-quality selection.

papers.abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. Preserving its value over time is also difficult: our accumulation baseline without consolidation initially improves but eventually performs below a no-memory baseline. Our key idea is to compare attempts at the same task to identify reusable decisions and refine when they apply. We introduce Hippo, a memory framework inspired by selective hippocampal encoding and replay that learns from these comparisons when shortcomings are diagnosed. It compares the resulting experience with existing memory to merge overlaps and resolve conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. This allows prior guidance to be revised without storing every lesson as a separate entry. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web show performance gains in all three settings and substantially fewer retained experiences than the accumulation baseline. The gains extend across the evaluated base models of varying capabilities, indicating that memory-based adaptation remains useful even for highly capable models.
authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren, Tony Qin, Baoyuan Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of extracting reliable lessons from flawed or mixed-quality attempts.
Uses selective hippocampal-style encoding and replay to diagnose shortcomings and compare attempts on the same task.
Merges overlapping memories and resolves conflicts with explicit applicability conditions instead of storing every lesson separately.
Improves performance on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web while retaining substantially fewer experiences than simple accumulation.
Benefits persist across base models with varying capabilities, including highly capable models.
papers.selection_reason: External-memory agent self-improvement via hippocampal replay; relevant to test-time adaptation and LLM memory.
papers.title: Hippo: Training-Free Agent Self-Evolution via Hippocampal Replay
papers.tldr: Hippo enables LLM agents to self-improve without parameter updates by comparing task attempts and consolidating reusable experience in memory.

papers.abstract: Transformers have emerged as a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, with in-context learning (ICL) enabling models to adapt to new tasks by conditioning on prompts, without any parameter updates. To understand the attention mechanism in transformer blocks, a growing line of theoretical work interprets ICL through the lens of classical statistical estimators. Recent works have established a connection between the attention mechanism and kernel methods, while the kernel function is usually assumed to be fixed. In practice, the query and key matrices in the attention mechanism are trained, which allows the attention mechanism to serve as an adaptive kernel method. In this work, we demonstrate that transformers can act as adaptive anisotropic kernel learners. Specifically, we study ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regressions, and conduct numerical simulations to show that the learned attention scores closely resemble the oracle kernels for these function classes. We then develop a general framework to analyze the generalization error of ICL by connecting transformers to the oracle kernel estimator for each function class. Our theory gives an explicit and constructive implementation of the oracle kernel estimators for these function classes using a wide and shallow transformer architecture, illustrating how the prediction is carried out by the interaction between the query token and the context tokens. Our work complements existing studies by providing numerical and theoretical evidence of how the attention mechanism adapts to anisotropic kernels in both linear and nonlinear settings.
authors: Zhaiming Shen, Alexander Cloninger, Rongjie Lai, Wenjing Liao
bullets: Motivated by the gap between fixed-kernel interpretations of attention and the trainable query/key matrices used in practice.
Studies ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regression tasks.
Shows through simulations that learned attention scores closely match oracle kernels for these function classes.
Develops a generalization-error framework linking transformer ICL to oracle kernel estimation.
Provides a constructive implementation using wide, shallow transformers, explaining prediction through query–context interactions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of transformers as adaptive kernel learners for in-context learning; relevant to LLM reasoning and ICL.
papers.title: Transformers as Adaptive Kernel Learners across Tasks for In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: The paper shows that transformers can perform in-context learning by adapting attention into task-specific anisotropic kernel estimators.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate experience, their long-term memories contain many similar observations of recurring scenes, actions, and entities. Answer quality depends on the evidence retrieved from these memories into the model's context. However, query-relevant memories may contain overlapping information, and a fixed retrieval depth may return too little or too much evidence for a given question. To address these challenges, we propose PACE-Mem, Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence, which constructs a complementary evidence sequence and determines its length from the same selection trajectory. For structured memories, query-guided pooling combines records within each clip to obtain relevance scores and representations. Using these relevance scores and representations, maximal marginal relevance (MMR) selection balances query relevance against overlap with previously selected evidence. From the resulting score trajectory, a prefix-length selection algorithm determines retrieval depth by comparing length-normalized adjacent declines, accounting for both score changes and the amount of evidence accumulated. PACE-Mem is a training-free, plug-in retrieval method for clip-based agent memory systems, leaving memory construction and answer generation unchanged. Across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks, PACE-Mem improves question-answering accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k, the strongest baseline at comparable mean retrieval depths. Further analysis reveals that jointly adding and removing evidence is associated with larger net accuracy gains than either change alone.
authors: Shidu Ren, Rong-cheng Tu, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo
bullets: Addresses redundant memories and the mismatch between fixed retrieval depth and question-specific evidence needs.
Uses query-guided pooling and maximal marginal relevance (MMR) to build a complementary evidence sequence.
Selects retrieval depth from the same MMR score trajectory using length-normalized adjacent score declines.
Training-free and plug-in: it leaves memory construction and answer generation unchanged.
Improves QA accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free complementary evidence retrieval for multimodal agent memory; directly fits agent memory and memory retrieval.
papers.title: PACE-Mem: Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence for Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: PACE-Mem improves multimodal-agent memory retrieval by selecting diverse, query-relevant evidence and adaptively determining how much to retrieve.

papers.abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.
authors: Qishun Yang, Shu Yang, Difei Xu, Di Wang, Meng Ding
bullets: Evaluates privacy leakage when complete histories imply a sensitive relation but individual sessions do not.
Introduces 288 synthetic cases with hidden target annotations and compares six memory systems plus full-history and no-history controls.
Separately measures target-attribute visibility in stored/retrieved context and whether the final answer states the complete relation.
A paired test shows that removing shared identifiers or connecting clues can change relation disclosure even when target attributes remain visible.
Scope: synthetic cases focused on cross-session reconstruction during ordinary tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks long-term memory systems for LLM agents across sessions, directly addressing LLM memory and privacy.
papers.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
papers.tldr: MemJoin benchmarks how long-term agent memory can combine harmless-looking cross-session clues to reveal sensitive, person-linked relations that no single session exposes.

papers.abstract: Until April 2026, the National Vulnerability Database labeled nearly every published Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 vector, a severity tier, and a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) weakness type. Now, NIST enriches only the high priority CVEs, leaving many newly published vulnerabilities unlabelled with the classifiers that security teams use for patch triage. In CVE enrichment, we predict the eight base components of CVSS v3.1 vector, base score, severity tier, and CWE from the vulnerability's textual description alone. To prevent leakage between near-duplicate descriptions, all systems are trained only on CVEs published in 2022 and 2023. Results are evaluated on all 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs in the pinned NVD snapshot. All scores are either directly predicted, or calculated from predicted vectors using the CVSS formula. A fine-tuned 3.8B-parameter model Phi-3.5-mini, trained with LoRA in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, achieves 69.9% accuracy on severity and 70.9% on CWE. It matches the official vector exactly for 48.8% of test CVEs, outperforming TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8 to 4.7 points on all accuracy metrics based on zero-exclusion paired bootstrap intervals. When we evaluate the base model with a zero-shot prompt, it achieves 20.8% accuracy on severity in a sample of 2,000 CVEs. In this same sample, its stated scores match its own vector precisely for only 3.4% of CVEs. However, deriving scores from predicted vectors boosts the critical recall of TF-IDF logistic regression from 50.7% to 73.3% with no additional cost. And since the errors of the fine-tuned model and TF-IDF affect different CVEs, at least one system matches the correct severity tier for 75.8% of test CVEs.
authors: Tara Dixit, Jessie Dong, Summer Li
bullets: NIST now labels mainly high-priority CVEs, creating a need to infer missing enrichment from text alone.
The study predicts all eight CVSS v3.1 base components, base score, severity tier, and CWE using CVEs from 2022–2023 and evaluates on 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs.
LoRA-tuned Phi-3.5-mini achieves 69.9% severity accuracy, 70.9% CWE accuracy, and exact vector matches for 48.8% of CVEs.
Deriving scores from predicted vectors improves TF-IDF logistic regression’s critical-severity recall from 50.7% to 73.3%.
The fine-tuned model outperforms TF-IDF by 2.8–4.7 accuracy points, while combining their predictions reaches 75.8% correct severity tiers across CVEs.
papers.selection_reason: Applies fine-tuning techniques (LoRA) to a small language model (Phi-3.5-mini) for a specific NLP task, relevant to LLM efficiency and architecture.
papers.title: Predicting CVSS and CWE from CVE Descriptions with Fine-Tuned Small Language Models
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning a small language model on CVE descriptions enables useful prediction of CVSS severity, vectors, and CWE labels for newly published vulnerabilities.

papers.abstract: Pixel-based language models process rendered text without relying on a fixed subword vocabulary, offering a promising approach to noisy and multilingual inputs. However, their practical value depends on whether they can be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. To this end, we systematically examine this question through fine-tuning behavior, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Under our tested settings, pixel-based models require longer training and broader labelled-data coverage than text-based models, while delayed learning and learning-rate-dependent failures make adaptation less reliable. Our analyses further suggest that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations, placing greater demands on fine-tuning. Once successfully adapted, however, pixel-based models lose substantially less accuracy under typographical noise and achieve higher target-language accuracy than English-pretrained text-based counterparts on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean English performance. Together, these findings reveal a central trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but shifts a central bottleneck to downstream adaptation.
authors: Haowen Tang, Wei Xia, Raoyuan Zhao, Hinrich Sch\"utze, Yihong Liu
bullets: They avoid fixed subword vocabularies by processing rendered text, benefiting typographical and multilingual settings.
Fine-tuning requires longer training and broader labelled-data coverage, with delayed learning and learning-rate-sensitive failures.
Pretrained pixel representations make task-relevant information less accessible during downstream adaptation.

After successful adaptation, they retain substantially more accuracy under typographical noise and outperform English-pretrained text models on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean-English performance.
The central trade-off is reduced input sensitivity at the cost of a more difficult adaptation bottleneck.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes pixel-based language model adaptation, robustness, and crosslingual transfer; relevant to foundation LM architectures.
papers.title: Beyond Clean Accuracy: The Practical Challenges and Benefits of Pixel-Based Language Models
papers.tldr: Pixel-based language models are more robust to noisy and crosslingual inputs, but harder and less reliable to adapt than text-based models.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in annotation tasks with varying success. While several studies have demonstrated the opportunities and shortcomings of LLMs for annotation, a critical question remains unanswered: is it possible to predict how well they will perform on a new dataset? To answer this and related questions, we construct two task families which induce 461 text classification datasets. We find that it is possible to predict LLM performance - to a certain degree - and that contrary to other work which highlights the usefulness of LLM verbalizations of self-confidence, internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal.
authors: Tong Lin, Grant Schoenebeck, Sabina Tomkins
bullets: Addresses whether zero-shot LLM annotation quality can be predicted before labeling a new dataset.
Constructs two task families yielding 461 text-classification datasets.
Finds that LLM performance is predictable, but only to a certain degree.
Internal log-probabilities are more predictive than verbalized self-confidence.
Scope is limited to the constructed text-classification task families and datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts zero-shot LLM annotation performance using internal log-probabilities.
papers.title: Can This LLM Annotate My Data? Estimating Zero-Shot LLM Performance
papers.tldr: LLM annotation performance on new datasets can be estimated to some extent, with internal log-probabilities providing the strongest predictive signal.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/wenzhilics/tar.
authors: Wen-Zhi Li, Sainyam Galhotra, Claire Cardie
bullets: RLVR can reduce reasoning diversity because limited on-policy rollouts under-sample distinct but equally rewarded solution modes.
Under-sampled reasoning behaviors are difficult for standard on-policy RLVR to recover.
TAR stores a compact bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them when suppression is detected.
Across six math benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 scales, TAR improves the balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation while reducing forgetting of correct base-model solutions.
papers.selection_reason: RLVR for LLM reasoning with adaptive replay to preserve reasoning diversity.
papers.title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
papers.tldr: TAR preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors during RLVR by adaptively replaying base-model solutions when they are being suppressed.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models maintain information about the status of their reasoning process through in-context memory. Complex problems require larger context windows and memory requirements. In this scenario, context management without caching risks discarding useful information for reasoning. We propose RCMEM, an approach that extends context management with an external memory to maintain additional information without burdening the reasoning model with additional context. RCMEM significantly reduces computation time on problems that require repeated computation of intermediate steps, while achieving better performance on complex problems. We demonstrate our approach on a few mathematics problems using model sizes ranging from 0.4 to 25 million parameters, and GPT-2.
authors: Man-Ling Sung, William Hartmann, Jiangying Zhou
bullets: Addresses information loss and growing memory requirements in long, complex reasoning tasks.
Uses external memory to retain intermediate information without adding it to the model’s active context.
Reduces computation time for problems requiring repeated intermediate computations.
Improves performance on complex mathematics problems in experiments with small models and GPT-2.
Evaluation is limited to a few mathematics problems and the reported model sizes.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes external memory to extend context management for reasoning models, directly fitting LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Reasoning with Context Management and External Memory
papers.tldr: RCMEM augments context management with external memory to preserve useful reasoning information while reducing context and computation demands.

papers.abstract: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($\alpha\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($\alpha\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
bullets: Prompt-dependent hidden-state differences decay approximately as a power law, t^-α.
Trained models forget faster (α≈0.55–0.7) than untrained models (α≈0.2–0.5).
A finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformer has a prompt-dependent offset bounded by O(P(log t)^{L−1}/t), under bounded logits and nonzero pre-norm activations.
An exactly solvable relay model matches the bound and reproduces the increasing local exponent observed in untrained networks.
Logit-bias experiments indicate that attention dilution is necessary—and, in the studied settings, sufficient—for the observed forgetting.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of prompt retention and forgetting in autoregressive transformers, relevant to LLM architecture and context behavior.
papers.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
papers.tldr: Transformers gradually forget prompt-specific information as generation continues, with direct dilution dominating and relay effects adding only logarithmic corrections.

papers.abstract: Prefix-tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task-specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. In particular, the following question remains open: Given a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, for any input-output sequence pair $(\mathtt{x},\mathtt{y})$, does there always exist a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ such that prepending $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathtt{x}$ induces the model to generate the target output $\mathtt{y}$? In this work, we prove that under the assumption that $\mathtt{y}$ is in the range of the pretrained Transformer, such a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ exists and can be explicitly computed by solving multiple linear systems. We further show that this assumption is necessary, in the sense that such a prefix may not exist when the assumption fails, thereby providing a complete answer to the above question. Our analysis is constructive and the obtained theoretical results hold under fairly general assumptions on model architecture. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B demonstrate that our algorithm produces prefixes with strong control over model outputs.
authors: Peter Cho-Ho Lam, Ziyi Wang, Zirui Zhou
bullets: Establishes existence of a prefix for an input–output pair when the target is in the pretrained Transformer’s output range.
Computes the prefix explicitly by solving multiple linear systems.
Shows the range assumption is necessary: desired outputs may be unreachable otherwise.
Theoretical results apply under fairly general architectural assumptions.
Experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B show strong control over generated outputs.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and constructive analysis of prefix steering for pretrained autoregressive LLMs; directly relevant to LLM control and adaptation methods.
papers.title: Prefix-Tuning for Arbitrary Output Sequences on Pretrained Transformers
papers.tldr: The paper proves when prefix-tuning can force a pretrained autoregressive Transformer to generate any target sequence and gives a constructive way to compute such prefixes.

papers.abstract: Does persistent memory accumulated from previous attempts help an LLM agent solve new problems, and does memory design affect that benefit? We study programmatic Chinese-character drawing across five agent conditions attempting the same 668 items. Accumulated memory produces modest aggregate gains despite substantial growth in the memory stores: free-form notes improve first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points, while a design combining free-form memory with reusable code improves it by 2.8 points. The two designs do not differ significantly overall, but the code bank shows a suggestive advantage on later, harder items. A separate post-hoc comparison finds a much larger improvement when the code-bank agent receives privileged, target-specific structural supervision. The agent can therefore exploit highly informative structural guidance, although the privileged per-item information does not establish what could have been learned from experience alone. These results suggest that memory design may affect where accumulated experience becomes useful, even when its average benefit is modest.
bullets: The study tests five agent conditions on 668 programmatic Chinese-character drawing items.
Free-form notes raise first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points; combining notes with reusable code raises it by 2.8 points.
The two memory designs show no significant overall difference, but the code bank may help more on later, harder items.
Privileged target-specific structural guidance yields a much larger improvement, but does not show what experience alone could teach.
Overall, memory provides modest average gains while influencing where accumulated experience is useful.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the effect of persistent memory design (free-form notes vs. code banks) on an LLM agent's performance in a drawing task.
papers.title: Persistent Memory and Iterative Improvement in an LLM Agent for Chinese-Character Drawing
papers.tldr: Persistent memory modestly improves an LLM agent’s Chinese-character drawing, with memory design affecting which problems benefit most.

papers.abstract: Code generation has become a core capability of large language models (LLMs), and code data is central to the pre-training process that develops it. As obtaining public code of sufficient quality becomes more difficult, further progress cannot rely on corpus expansion alone. Tiered data management instead applies increasingly targeted processing to smaller data pools, producing data states suited to different training objectives. Following this perspective, we present UltraData-Code as four connected data states spanning repository archival at L0, standardized natural code at L1, algorithmic selection at L2, and task-oriented synthesis at L3. L0 preserves repository data and provenance for reprocessing, while L1 applies scalable filtering, normalization, and near-deduplication for broad pre-training. L2 selects high-quality algorithmically relevant files using language-adaptive relevance signals and quality constraints, yielding approximately 400B tokens of UltraData-Code-L2 across 11 programming languages for focused continual pre-training. L3 converts selected implementations into structured programming exercises, yielding approximately 150B tokens of UltraData-Code-L3 across the same 11 languages for task-oriented mid-training or supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Under controlled 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80 percentage points (pp) on EvalPlus and 5.13pp on MultiPL-E. Replacing half of the L2 training tokens with L3 yields a further gain of 8.42pp and 8.07pp on the two benchmarks, respectively. Both gains increase when the training budget scales to 100B tokens. We have released our datasets and classifiers to support further research on LLMs.
authors: Chengying Tu, Hengyu Zhao, Shuaikang Xue, Zhongming Qu, Jihao Zhou, Xinle Lin, Junshao Guo, Zixuan Fu, Qiang Ma, Jie Zhou, Chaojun Xiao, Hongfei Yan, Yudong Wang, Xu Han, Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun
bullets: Organizes code into four data states: archival repositories (L0), standardized code (L1), algorithmically selected code (L2), and synthesized programming exercises (L3).
Uses filtering, normalization, near-deduplication, language-adaptive relevance signals, and quality constraints to tailor data to different training objectives.
Produces approximately 400B tokens of L2 and 150B tokens of L3 across 11 programming languages.
In 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80pp on EvalPlus and 5.13pp on MultiPL-E.
Replacing half of L2 with L3 adds 8.42pp and 8.07pp, with larger gains at a 100B-token training budget.
papers.selection_reason: Tiered code data curation for LLM pretraining; relevant to language foundation model training data and capability development.
papers.title: UltraData-Code: From Raw Repositories to Algorithmically Dense and Task-Oriented Code Data
papers.tldr: UltraData-Code builds a four-level pipeline that transforms raw repositories into filtered, algorithmically focused, and task-oriented code data, substantially improving code-generation performance in controlled training experiments.

papers.abstract: Line-parallel language models advance multiple lines concurrently for substantial speedups. However, frameworks like the Line-Coupled Language Model (LCLM) enforce a fixed commitment schedule across lines. Because dependencies vary within text, a fixed schedule cannot hold back a line whose prerequisites remain uncomputed, forcing premature commitments and cascading reasoning errors. To address this limitation, we introduce the Lattice Language Model (LatLM), making commitment schedules an adaptive decoding-time choice. Text occupies a 2D lattice where eligible frontier tokens are scored each round; a policy commits confident candidates while deferring unready ones for extended context. One forward pass supervises entire sampled trajectories via 2D causal masking, while an append-only cache retains exact states. At 482M parameters, we establish two findings. (1) LatLM matches a data- and capacity-matched autoregressive model on held-out text when decoded sequentially, while its adaptive parallel decoder achieves near-autoregressive accuracy on independent-line tasks using 25--41% as many decoding rounds. (2) When cross-line dependencies cause LCLM's fixed schedule to fail, deferred commitment substantially improves accuracy while retaining parallelism where dependencies permit. On mixed dependency chains, LatLM achieves 96.5% accuracy versus LCLM's 78.5%, using fewer than half the decoding rounds of the autoregressive baseline.
authors: Shaorong Zhang, Shiyuan Li, Longxuan Yu, Greg Ver Steeg
bullets: Addresses fixed line-commitment schedules that can force premature decisions and cascading errors.
Represents text on a 2D lattice and scores eligible frontier tokens at each decoding round.
Uses trajectory-wide supervision with 2D causal masking and an append-only cache for exact states.
Matches a matched autoregressive model under sequential decoding and uses 25–41% as many rounds on independent-line tasks.
On mixed dependency chains, reaches 96.5% accuracy versus LCLM’s 78.5%, with fewer than half as many rounds as the autoregressive baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive parallel decoding for language models with deferred commitment; relevant to LLM architecture and inference efficiency.
papers.title: LatLM: Line-Parallel Language Models with Deferred Commitment
papers.tldr: LatLM adaptively defers uncertain token commitments, preserving accuracy while decoding dependent text in parallel with far fewer rounds.

papers.abstract: LLM agents accumulate valuable task-specific information through their actions, observations, and environmental feedback during multi-turn task execution. When effectively used, this information can help agents refine subsequent decisions and improve task performance. However, the learning value of an interaction depends on its context and subsequent feedback, making it challenging to extract reliable, actionable lessons and revise them as the task unfolds. In this paper, we introduce ReTTT, which enables experience-driven self-adaptation through test-time training on lessons constructed and continually revised within an episode. ReTTT lets the agent reflect on interaction feedback, maintain the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and learn from them by updating an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen. The adapted model then performs both subsequent actions and reflection, coupling policy adaptation with the construction of future learning experience. We evaluate ReTTT on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite using two model families. ReTTT outperforms trajectory-based test-time training across all six model--benchmark settings, improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points. A frozen-reflection comparison further shows a 7.14-point benefit from adapting the reflection policy, while trajectory analysis illustrates how adapted reflection derives more task-specific guidance from failed attempts. These findings suggest that learning to reflect on its own behavior can boost agents' performance on long-horizon tasks.
authors: Kangcong Li, Hangfan Zhang, Shuyue Hu, Shengji Tang, Tao Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of extracting reliable, actionable lessons from context-dependent interaction feedback.
Maintains explicit, revisable experience-based memory and uses it for test-time training within each episode.
Updates an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen; the adapted model performs both actions and reflection.
Evaluated on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite across two model families, outperforming trajectory-based test-time training in all six settings.
Task success improves by up to 12.14 percentage points; adapting the reflection policy contributes an additional 7.14-point benefit versus frozen reflection.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training with experience-based parametric memory for LLM agents; fits test-time learning and agent memory.
papers.title: ReTTT: Reflection-Driven Test-Time Training via Experience-Based Parametric Memory
papers.tldr: ReTTT improves long-horizon LLM-agent performance by continually reflecting on feedback and updating an episode-local LoRA adapter from revised lessons.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to make accurate predictions from demonstrations, but prediction success alone does not reveal the extent to which the underlying concept has been recovered. Existing evaluations typically assess recovery at the level of the whole concept, making it difficult to identify which components are recovered and to separate model limitations from ambiguity in the demonstrations. We introduce a component-level framework for concept recovery that decomposes concepts into their defining components and uses controlled structural interventions to evaluate both component-level and whole-concept recovery under identifiable demonstrations. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and three composition forms, we find that models often achieve high prediction accuracy despite poor whole-concept recovery, with systematic over-specification of relevant attributes and level constraints. Individual structural components are generally insufficient for whole-concept recovery, whereas jointly specifying complementary components, particularly relevant attributes and their level constraints, substantially improves recovery. However, this improvement is fragile: a single plausible but unnecessary level constraint can substantially disrupt recovery. Finally, joint supervision of recovery and implicit prediction substantially improves recovery while preserving prediction performance, with the learned capability transferring across composition forms. Overall, our component-level analysis provides a more diagnostic view of what models recover from demonstrations than the existing holistic view.
authors: Xufeng Liu, Fang Wan, Yi Liu
bullets: Whole-concept prediction accuracy can mask failures in recovering the underlying concept.
Controlled structural interventions separate component-level recovery from ambiguity in demonstrations.
Models tend to over-specify relevant attributes and level constraints.
Complementary components improve recovery, but one plausible unnecessary constraint can disrupt it.
Jointly training recovery with implicit prediction improves recovery without reducing prediction and transfers across composition forms.
papers.selection_reason: Component-level analysis of concept recovery in in-context learning informs understanding of LLM reasoning and context, within language foundation models.
papers.title: Beyond Prediction: A Component-Level Study of Concept Recovery in In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: A component-level framework reveals that LLMs can predict correctly while recovering concepts poorly, and that recovery improves with complementary structural cues but remains fragile to unnecessary constraints.

papers.abstract: Looped language models reuse physical Transformer blocks across logical depth, but established architectures entangle recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent state organization. We isolate these axes in models trained from scratch at matched parameter scale, logical depth, and token budgets, and then test whether the resulting design principles transfer to resident- and active-parameter-matched Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The prelude-recurrent block-coda sandwich architecture consistently improves performance on context extraction and reasoning-intensive tasks. Input injection primarily enhances knowledge retrieval and context utilization, whereas random initialization and separate H/L recurrent states provide mixed or negative returns. Taken together, these results favor the Huginn-style design: at the 730M-parameter and 336B-token scale, the complete Huginn architecture outperforms Ouro across all ten benchmarks. The advantages of Huginn over Ouro transfer to MoE models. At the 8BA0.8B (32BA3B when unrolled) scale trained on 500B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro on nearly all benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, and coding, while also exhibiting more balanced expert routing. Under matched training and inference FLOPs, the Huginn-style model uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE baseline. Despite its smaller physical parameters, it outperforms the feedforward baseline on DROP and GSM8K, matches it on MATH500, and remains competitive on the other benchmarks.
bullets: Separates recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent-state organization under matched training conditions.
A prelude–recurrent block–coda sandwich consistently improves context extraction and reasoning tasks.
Input injection mainly helps knowledge retrieval and context utilization; random initialization and separate H/L states offer mixed or negative benefits.
At 730M parameters and 336B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro across ten benchmarks, with gains transferring to MoE models.
With matched FLOPs, the looped MoE uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE while outperforming it on DROP and GSM8K and matching it on MATH500.
papers.selection_reason: Looped LLM architecture and MoE design study directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design
papers.tldr: The study identifies a Huginn-style looped Transformer design that improves reasoning and context use and transfers effectively to MoE models with fewer resident parameters.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation with privileged context adapts a language model from demonstrations by letting the model, once conditioned on a reference response, teach its context-free copy token by token. Our taxonomy reveals existing methods differ along three entangled axes: (i) the rollout source (student or teacher), (ii) the teacher coupling (frozen, or an exponential moving average of the student at some coupling rate) and (iii) the KL direction (reverse or forward), yet these axes are usually studied in fixed combinations and have led to conflicting conclusions. We formalize a unifying framework to encompass all self-distillation methods vs classic supervised fine-tuning: we train every combination of the three axes, on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs, to systematically investigate the impact of the above axes. We propose a controlled model of the same objective to explain the resulting acquisition-retention trade-offs. We find that (i) the rollout source matters mostly where the task contradicts the pretrained behavior: there teacher rollouts raise acquisition well above what student rollouts achieve, with almost no change in retention; (ii) the teacher coupling changes acquisition most, on every task: acquisition rises with the coupling rate, then falls past a task-specific rate; (iii) switching the KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other so which axis to tune first depends on the model. The controlled model reproduces the three trends.
bullets: Evaluates rollout source, teacher coupling, and KL direction across all combinations, rather than fixed method pairings.
Teacher rollouts improve acquisition especially on tasks contradicting pretrained behavior, with little retention change.
Teacher coupling has the largest acquisition effect: performance rises with coupling rate before declining beyond a task-specific optimum.
Changing KL direction harms retention in one model but not the other, so tuning priorities are model-dependent.
A controlled model reproduces the observed acquisition–retention trends.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies self-distillation and supervised fine-tuning for LLMs using Qwen2.5 and Ministral checkpoints, contributing to understanding and improving modern LLM training.
papers.title: Disentangling Self-Distillation: Measuring and Modeling Acquisition and Retention
papers.tldr: A systematic study disentangles three design choices in self-distillation, showing how rollout source, teacher coupling, and KL direction separately shape task acquisition and retention.

papers.abstract: Current agents remain largely stateless across tasks, limiting their ability to continually improve from prior interactions and making memory essential for long-horizon agentic behavior. Existing memory methods seek to reuse past experience, but most rely on a single memory representation (e.g., trajectories, reflections, skills, structured knowledge) whose effectiveness varies across task distributions. Rethinking this design space, we evaluate 13 memory methods and find that no single method generalizes across benchmarks, revealing the potential of managing heterogeneous memory providers. We formulate agent memory as a routing problem in which a memory agent decides which memory provider to retrieve from, whether to inject short-term memory, and which providers should store the resulting experience. Based on this perspective, we propose MemAgent, featuring a content-aware routing architecture and a training-data synthesis pipeline. The routing architecture combines content-aware probing before retrieval, short-term memory gating during execution, and selective multi-provider storage, while the training pipeline synthesizes phase-specific supervision for routing decisions. Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS, MemAgent improves average accuracy by 10.0% and outperforms every individual memory method across all three benchmarks. These gains come with less than 0.3% routing overhead and a 12% reduction in average task steps.
bullets: Evaluations of 13 memory methods show that no single approach generalizes across benchmarks.
MemAgent frames memory use as routing: selecting providers to retrieve from, gating short-term memory, and choosing where to store experience.
Its content-aware router uses pre-retrieval probing, execution-time gating, and selective multi-provider storage.
A training-data synthesis pipeline provides phase-specific supervision for routing decisions.
Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS, it raises average accuracy by 10.0%, with under 0.3% routing overhead and 12% fewer task steps.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory-routing agent that selects among heterogeneous memory providers for LLM agents, directly matching persistent and external agent-memory mechanisms.
papers.title: MemAgent: Learning to Manage Heterogeneous Memory Providers for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: MemAgent improves LLM-agent memory by learning to route across heterogeneous memory providers instead of relying on a single representation.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.
authors: Jianyuan Zhong, Chenwei Wu, Zhaochen Yu, Xixian Jiang, Xuewei Li, Hao Xiao, Xilin Dai, Junyang Wang, Jiaru Zou, Zhiqing Cui, Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Zhen Zhang, Qiang Gao, Michael Morley, Luis Nakayama, Qiang Xu, Liyue Shen, Tao Gui, Leo Anthony Celi, James Zou, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: Defines valuable, testable hypotheses as evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties paired with feasible investigations, decision criteria, and alternatives.
Uses multi-agent evolutionary search to build hypothesis trees and compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks.
Recursively learns through credit assignment, workflow replay, and rediscovery of improved strategies for new investigations.
Introduces DFM-Bench to evaluate hypothesis quality and cumulative progress across hypotheses, revisions, development paths, and research runs.

Across four life-science domains, hypothesis quality improved from 4.86 to 5.39 after two self-improvement rounds; expert evaluations and post-cutoff correspondence also favored DiscoveryRSI in the reported comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces DiscoveryRSI, a multi-agent framework for scientific hypothesis discovery. It demonstrates recursive learning and self-improvement strategies for LLM-based research agents.
papers.title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
papers.tldr: DiscoveryRSI recursively improves scientific hypothesis generation by evolving evidence-grounded research plans and learning from their outcomes, producing higher-quality hypotheses and stronger alignment with later research.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
authors: Chiatzen Wang, Bill Xu, Haochen Gu, Hongyang Zhang
bullets: Lossless verification preserves output distributions, making accepted tokens per round a useful efficiency proxy; relaxed verification does not.
Across twelve target–drafter pairs, the most relaxed settings accepted 1.34× more tokens per round but produced 1.54× longer completions on average.
Extra accepted tokens often had low target-model probability and contributed to length inflation, especially by extending reasoning traces.
Rules that reduced verifier rounds typically caused substantial accuracy drops, sometimes because continued reasoning exhausted the output budget.
Completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and accuracy should be reported alongside acceptance rates.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the efficiency of speculative decoding, specifically identifying 'length inflation' in lossy verification. This provides important empirical findings regarding LLM decoding speed and verification mechanisms.
