Estimating the covariance between reward and importance-weighted score restores this invariance, matching the standard gradient without ratio regularization.
Group-mean baselines subtract a sample mean, while score centering subtracts a population mean; they produce different unbiased covariance estimators and variances.
For sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit after applying a group-mean baseline.
For token-level importance sampling, omitting score centering while using a group-mean baseline generally causes bias under regularized ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical perspective on policy gradient estimation for LLMs, clarifying the roles of group-mean baselines and score centering in importance sampling.
papers.title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation
papers.tldr: A covariance-based view clarifies when reward baselines and score centering yield unbiased, shift-invariant policy-gradient estimates under regularized importance sampling.

papers.abstract: Verifying the final answer of a long reasoning trace may show that the trace is wrong but it does not distinguish three cases. The problem may lie beyond the model's capability, another attempt would succeed, or one step in an otherwise recoverable trace made the trace fail. Standard hidden-state probes are trained on final-answer correctness, a label that conflates these cases. Monte Carlo rollouts distinguish the cases and locate the failing step at additional inference cost. We test the hidden states of 4B and 8B reasoning models for the failure type and the failing step and compare each probe with the strongest baseline that uses no hidden states. On incorrect 8B traces, the confidence probe, a calibrated correctness probe at a midpoint cutoff, misses 81% of cases in which a single step makes the trace unrecoverable and 47% of cases in which another attempt would succeed. A probe with a different training design over the same states reverses the ordering of these two kinds of failure, so either ordering can be read from those states. At both scales, no single tested probe locates the failing step more accurately than a rule based only on trace length, and at 4B a probe trained to predict that step fails to outperform this rule in any of 10 runs on identical traces. The confidence probe therefore indicates that an answer is wrong, but its failure-type ordering depends on its training design.
bullets: Final-answer correctness labels conflate capability limits, recoverable failed attempts, and single-step failures.
The study evaluates probes on hidden states from 4B and 8B reasoning models, comparing them with non-hidden-state baselines.
Monte Carlo rollouts provide reference labels for failure type and failing step, but require extra inference cost.
A calibrated confidence probe misses many unrecoverable single-step failures and cases where another attempt would succeed; its failure-type ordering changes with training design.
No tested probe locates failing steps more accurately than a trace-length rule, including across 10 runs at 4B.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the effectiveness of hidden-state probes for localizing reasoning failures in LLMs, finding that simple rules often outperform complex probes in this specific diagnostic task.
papers.title: Effectiveness of Hidden-State Probes for Localizing Reasoning Failures
papers.tldr: Hidden-state probes can signal incorrect reasoning traces and distinguish failure types, but tested probes do not reliably localize the specific failing step.

papers.abstract: We study sparse and continual reinforcement learning fine-tuning of language models through attention-head ranking and partitioning. For sparse learning, we rank attention heads by gradient norm to identify a small subset of heads that can be trained effectively. For continual learning, we partition heads across tasks to reduce cross-task interference and preserve previously learned capabilities. Theoretically, we relate gradient norm to training effectiveness, and further characterize why sparse, separated head updates can remain stable. Empirically, across math, instruction-following, and coding tasks, tuning higher-ranked heads consistently outperforms tuning lower-ranked ones while often matching denser baselines, and head partitioning improves retention while preserving adaptation to new tasks.
bullets: Targets efficient sparse and continual reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of language models.
Ranks heads by gradient norm to select a small, effective trainable subset.
Partitions heads across tasks to reduce interference and preserve prior capabilities.
Theory links gradient norm to training effectiveness and explains the stability of separated updates.
Across math, instruction-following, and coding tasks, higher-ranked heads outperform lower-ranked ones; partitioning improves retention while maintaining adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes sparse and continual reinforcement learning fine-tuning strategies for LLMs by ranking and partitioning attention heads to improve training efficiency and task retention.
papers.title: Ranking and Partitioning of Attention Heads for Sparse and Continual Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning
papers.tldr: Ranking attention heads by gradient norm enables effective sparse fine-tuning, while partitioning heads across tasks improves continual-learning retention and adaptation.

papers.abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.
bullets: Existing alignment evaluations often measure compliance but overlook consistency across generator and evaluator roles.
VALCON constructs three benchmark suites—VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, and VAB-Challenge—using dual-role variation.
Experiments across 28 LLMs find widespread cross-role inconsistency, including among models with highly compliant outputs.
Mechanistic probing links this asymmetry to role-dependent representational decoupling.
A representation-directed intervention reduces consistency failures, forming an evaluation–analysis–mitigation pipeline.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VALCON, a benchmark and framework for evaluating value consistency in LLMs when acting as both generators and evaluators, addressing a gap in current alignment evaluations.
papers.title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
papers.tldr: VALCON benchmarks and mitigates whether LLMs maintain consistent values when generating outputs and evaluating them.

papers.abstract: Language models are often asked to make judgments: whether a proposed answer is correct, whether one statement follows logically from another, or whether a response is safe. Yet changing the instructions that specify how the judgment should be expressed can make the final answer less reliable, even for the same input. We ask whether this reflects a change in internal judgment or a failure to express it. Comparing hidden-state vectors for the same input under different instructions, we find that their differences concentrate in a low-dimensional expression subspace. We identify this subspace without benchmark labels and remove its contribution from a linear predictor to obtain an isolated judgment. Across correctness, entailment, and safety, the isolated judgment remains reliable under instructions not used to identify the subspace, even when the model's final answer and the original predictor degrade. When the judgment question is negated, isolation raises the predictor's AUROC from 0.504 to 0.825 for entailment and from 0.480 to 0.891 for safety. We also find that judgment is readable in earlier layers, before the expression subspace begins to disrupt the predictor. Together, these results provide a way to separate judgment from expression and recover internal judgments even when the model's final answers are unreliable.
bullets: Different instructions alter hidden states mainly along a low-dimensional expression subspace, suggesting changes in wording need not reflect changed judgment.
The method identifies this subspace without benchmark labels and removes its effect from a linear predictor.
Across correctness, entailment, and safety, the isolated judgment generalizes to unseen instructions more reliably than the original predictor or final answer.
Under negated judgment questions, AUROC improves from 0.504 to 0.825 for entailment and from 0.480 to 0.891 for safety.
Judgment is readable in earlier layers, before expression-related variation disrupts prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method to isolate a language model's internal judgment from its expression subspace using label-free analysis. This provides a technical insight into LLM reasoning and internal states, fitting 'Large Language Models'.
papers.title: Isolating a Language Model's Judgment with a Label-Free Subspace
papers.tldr: A label-free low-dimensional subspace method separates a language model’s internal judgment from instruction-dependent answer expression, improving judgment reliability when outputs degrade.

papers.abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) relies on the timely identification of emerging threats, enabling organizations and security analysts to support situational awareness and decision-making. Social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter) have become valuable CTI sources because vulnerabilities and attack activities are often discussed there before appearing in formal reports. However, the rapid growth of cybersecurity discussions on social media has created more content than domain experts can realistically review and annotate, making labeled data a major bottleneck for developing supervised learning approaches. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as weak annotators in other domains, their effectiveness for cybersecurity tweet classification and downstream training of domain-specific pre-trained language models (PLMs) remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose a Teacher-Student weak supervision framework in which a selected LLM serves as a Teacher to generate weak labels for unlabeled cybersecurity tweets, enabling the training of cybersecurity-specific PLMs without large-scale manual annotation. Experimental results show that PLMs trained solely on LLM-generated labels consistently achieve F1 scores above 0.92, remaining within 3 percentage points of fully human-supervised models across all evaluated architectures. These findings suggest that LLM-based weak annotation offers a practical alternative for constructing cybersecurity-specific training data when expert annotation resources are limited.
bullets: Addresses the shortage of expert-labeled data for rapidly growing cybersecurity discussions on X.
Uses a Teacher–Student framework: an LLM generates weak labels, which train cybersecurity-specific PLMs.
PLMs trained only on LLM-generated labels achieved F1 scores above 0.92.
Results stayed within 3 percentage points of fully human-supervised models across evaluated architectures.
Supports weak annotation as a practical alternative when expert annotation resources are limited.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLMs as weak annotators to generate labels for cybersecurity tweets, enabling training of domain-specific PLMs. This is a standard application of LLMs in the 'Large Language Models' topic.
papers.title: LLM-Based Weak Annotation for Cybersecurity Tweet Classification: A Teacher-Student Framework
papers.tldr: An LLM teacher can weakly label cybersecurity tweets to train domain-specific language models with performance close to human-supervised training.

papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires an agent to retrieve evidence for a sequence of dependent sub-questions. When a wrong answer lacks a required passage, the passage may be inaccessible to the retriever, or the agent may have failed to issue a query that would retrieve it. Standard retrieval evaluations conflate these two causes. We study how much apparent retrieval failure is instead caused by search drift: the search no longer tracks an unanswered sub-question. Holding the retriever, corpus, and generation model fixed, we introduce ExecutionRAG, a training-free requirement register that records open sub-questions and their supporting evidence. The register changes search guidance but not evidence access, so each gold passage it recovers certifies that the passage was reachable by the original retriever. On 1,000 MuSiQue questions, the number of wrong answers with unretrieved required evidence falls from 382 to 234 with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and from 383 to 274 with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. These counts correspond to 69% to 44% and 66% to 48% of each system's wrong answers, respectively. Crucially, evidence recovery does not produce a proportional reduction in total error: premature resolutions and abstentions increase as missing-evidence failures decrease. The central finding is therefore a shift in the remaining bottleneck, from guiding search toward required evidence to verifying that the retrieved evidence is sufficient.
bullets: Standard retrieval evaluations conflate inaccessible evidence with failures to query for evidence required by an unanswered sub-question.
ExecutionRAG is a training-free requirement register that tracks open sub-questions and supporting evidence while keeping the retriever, corpus, and generator fixed.
On 1,000 MuSiQue questions, missing-evidence wrong answers decrease substantially for both tested retrievers when search is guided by the register.
This recovery does not proportionally reduce total errors because premature resolutions and abstentions increase.
The remaining challenge is verifying evidence sufficiency after improving search guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ExecutionRAG, a training-free method to address retrieval failure in multi-hop RAG by tracking open sub-questions. This addresses retrieval mechanisms and evidence access, fitting 'LLM Memory'.
papers.title: Beyond Retrieval Failure: Understanding Why LLMs Miss Evidence in Multi-Hop RAG
papers.tldr: Many multi-hop RAG failures blamed on retrieval are actually search drift, but recovering missing evidence shifts the main bottleneck to verifying whether the evidence is sufficient.

papers.abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.
bullets: Long-context scaling still faces inference-time compute, storage, and information-selection pressures.
It distinguishes compute-active memory from compute-inactive memory, including offloaded, persistent, and precomputed KV states.
It models writing, offloading, retrieval, injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as information-lifecycle transitions.
A budgeted cost model brings prompt compression, KV-cache management, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory into one framework.
It identifies benchmark gaps and argues for dynamic, governable memory management rather than static, pointwise compression.
papers.selection_reason: A survey reframing long-context compression as memory management for LLMs, introducing a budgeted cost model and state transitions for memory lifecycle management. This is highly relevant to 'LLM Memory' and 'Long-Context Models'.
papers.title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: This survey unifies long-context compression and LLM memory management as lifecycle-aware decisions about what information should enter costly inference, when, and in what form.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.
authors: Bingcong Li, Hao Ma, Michael Muehlebach, Niao He, Yi Ma
bullets: Fine-grained expert segmentation expands routing choices and potential expressiveness.
Shared experts reduce token-representation variability, creating an exploration dilemma.
MirrorMoE uses token-adaptive suppression to shrink the routing space and improve exploration efficiency.
The method consistently improves performance across model scales.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses routing exploration in mixture-of-experts LLM architectures.
papers.title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
papers.tldr: MirrorMoE addresses reduced routing exploration in fine-grained MoE models with shared experts by suppressing unnecessary experts per token.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT), combining feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.
authors: Weijian Luo, Yujian Chen, Hao Jiang, Guang Cheng, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Existing CDLMs typically reuse architectures designed for causal LLMs or image-generation diffusion Transformers rather than language diffusion.
LangDiT combines feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning.
As a plug-in backbone, it achieves leading generation perplexities in LangFlow and Plaid-style CDLMs at both high and low denoising-step budgets.
Improvements are isolated to the Transformer architecture while retaining each model’s representation, training objective, and inference sampler.
The study demonstrates that architectural design is a key source of performance gains in continuous language generation.
papers.selection_reason: Transformer architecture improvements for continuous diffusion language models.
papers.title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: LangDiT systematically redesigns Transformer architectures for continuous diffusion language models, substantially improving generation perplexity across CDLM formulations.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.
authors: Arnav Chavan, Kusha Sareen, Rishabh Tiwari, Abhranil Chandra, Johan Obando-Ceron, Kurt Keutzer, Scott Niekum, Inderjit S Dhillon, Devvrit Khatri
bullets: Addresses capability loss when LLMs are continually fine-tuned, especially with supervised fine-tuning.
Restricts weight updates away from principal singular directions, which are associated with greater forgetting.
Is optimizer-agnostic and compatible with SFT and self-distillation, using dense gradient estimation and subspace refreshing.
Protecting up to 99% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention and can nearly eliminate forgetting for large models.
Produces 2–4× less KL drift than baseline recipes and improves the learning–forgetting tradeoff.
papers.selection_reason: Subspace tuning mitigates catastrophic forgetting in LLM continual learning, directly relevant to continual learning and language foundation models.
papers.title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning
papers.tldr: Subspace Tuning reduces catastrophic forgetting by confining fine-tuning updates to the bottom singular subspace while retaining strong performance on new tasks.

papers.abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.
authors: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee, Roshen Sanjay Nair, Aviral Kumar, Chelsea Finn
bullets: Addresses the limits of reactive retrieval and rigid precomputed structures for cross-document reasoning.
A builder agent converts raw documents into hierarchical synthetic files and reference links.
Workspace construction is modeled as a Markov decision process and optimized for downstream answering accuracy.
The approach improves accuracy by 33 points on BrowseComp-Plus and 31 points on average on BRIGHT, while amortizing construction costs across repeated queries.
Scope: performance depends on upfront workspace construction and is evaluated through downstream answering tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Trains LLM agents to construct reusable long-context workspaces for future queries, directly relevant to LLM memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
papers.tldr: Librarian Agents uses reinforcement learning to proactively organize documents into reusable, query-oriented workspaces that improve long-context question answering.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.
authors: Bangji Yang, Jiajun Fan, Zhaoyu Zhu, Hongbo Ma, Ge Liu
bullets: Eliminates teacher-specific rollouts, gradient steps, and training during specialist consolidation.
For specialists sharing a base model, solves each fused linear layer via least squares using input second moments collected from a few hundred rollouts.
The composition of rollouts is critical: filtering repetition-loop truncations substantially improves mathematical performance.
On Olmo 3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist produce a generalist that preserves most gains across seven math and code benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free on-policy distillation consolidates specialist LLMs with forward passes only, relevant to language foundation model efficiency and merging.
papers.title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: Training-free on-policy distillation fuses specialist models into one generalist using only forward passes and rollout statistics, retaining most specialist gains across math and code tasks.

papers.abstract: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.
authors: Sebastian-Antonio Toma, Jean de Kernier, Mike Ply, Oliviu Matei
bullets: Introduces 30 fact-evolution trajectories across 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels.
Uses paradigm inversion to generate artifacts from known fact trajectories, enabling deterministic ground truth and direct memory inspection.
Finds intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories showing meaningful divergence.
A representative memory system correctly classifies memory operations only 20% of the time, a failure hidden by downstream QA.
Releases the benchmark, document-generation pipeline, and scoring framework for reproducible evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and diagnostic framework for evaluating agent memory, directly relevant to LLM memory assessment.
papers.title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory
papers.tldr: FEB-30 shows that downstream QA alone cannot reliably evaluate agent memory, because it mixes memory correctness with retrieval and generation errors.

papers.abstract: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.
authors: Ian Gemp, Shubhendu Trivedi, Adam Fisch, Fantine Huot, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata, William W. Cohen, Alekh Agarwal, Kate Larson, Jacob Eisenstein
bullets: Addresses market failure at both extremes: perfect clones eliminate profits, while no competition collapses value extraction.
Studies the critical middle ground where heterogeneous agents strategically shade bids to earn positive margins.
Evaluates Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO bidding across three auction protocols.
Finds that imperfect competition preserves agent profitability while maintaining high task success at low cost across diverse domains.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a decentralized market framework for LLM agents to solve multi-step tasks via sequential auctions, relevant to LLM agents and multi-agent systems.
papers.title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
papers.tldr: A decentralized auction market of heterogeneous LLM agents can balance profitable bidding with effective, low-cost completion of multi-step tasks under imperfect competition.

papers.abstract: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.
authors: Tianxiang Fei, Jiazheng Kang, Mao Zheng, Xingyan He, Xiang Yu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited transferability of using general-purpose LLMs as framework-specific memory writers.
Supports Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory through framework-specific write-protocol distillation.
Uses Memory RL with dense chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO.
Carries policy-written memory banks across context windows to better match deployment conditions.
On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, ranked first across four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.
papers.selection_reason: Trains a compact long-term memory writer across multiple memory frameworks using reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing
papers.tldr: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B is a compact, unified memory-writing model trained with distillation and attributed reinforcement learning to improve long-term memory across multiple frameworks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.
authors: Wonjeong Jo, Gyuwan Kim, Ming Shan Hee
bullets: The study defines scale sensitivity as changes in LLM scores caused by rating-scale design, covering both numerical values and score interpretation.
It tests continuous versus ordinal formats, 3–21 point ranges, and signed versus unsigned scales across political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity tasks.
Changing one scale element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts.
Sensitivity is highest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined.
Rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity relative to zero-shot prompting.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the sensitivity of LLM-based text scoring to rating scale design, relevant to LLM evaluation and robustness.
papers.title: Change the Number, Change the Answer: Assessing Rating Scale Sensitivity in LLM-Based Text Scoring
papers.tldr: LLM-generated text scores can change substantially when the rating scale changes, even after normalization, so scale robustness checks are essential.

papers.abstract: The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics: the embedding and the unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods either reuse a fixed lens or treat the states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state the way the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that read it next and adaptive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it by reading a state through the model's own remaining layers with a stated number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, without fitting to the model's output. No lens, with fixed directions per layer, can exceed the square root of the native frame's coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, whereas the first-order frame, LexFrame[1], reaches 0.97 and 0.97 and reads a state within 0.16 nats of the model's output. Its coefficients attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, its lexical basis steers a prediction while sparing other tokens, and its confident readings would let an early exit skip 0.45 and 0.42 of the layers, where lenses skip almost none. In this way, lexical reference frames make every hidden state of the model readable, attributable and steerable.
authors: Jian Gu, Hongyu Zhang, Chunyang Chen, Aldeida Aleti
bullets: Fixed lenses and point-cloud views do not capture the context-dependent semantics of intermediate states.
LexFrame approximates each state’s native reference frame by applying remaining layers, with configurable inter-position attention rounds and typical attention elsewhere.
The first-order LexFrame[1] achieves 0.97 coherence on both SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, reading states within 0.16 nats of the model output.
Its coefficients are more faithful than attribution patching, and its lexical basis can steer selected predictions while preserving others.
Confident readings support skipping 0.45 and 0.42 of layers on the two models, respectively, unlike conventional lenses.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces native lexical reference frames for interpreting and steering LM residual streams, relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics
papers.tldr: Lexical reference frames interpret language-model hidden states using the model’s own remaining computation, yielding highly faithful, attributable, steerable readings and enabling substantial early exits.

papers.abstract: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user-centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neurons, each encoding multiple unrelated concepts, hinder localizing the components behind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personalize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized latents, from which we identify the experts encoding distinct personalization features. The personalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters, exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal interventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model's behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, revealing distinct routing paths for different personalization features.
authors: Sekh Mainul Islam, Pepa Atanasova, Isabelle Augenstein
bullets: Dense LLMs are difficult to interpret for personalization because their neurons are polysemantic.
The authors personalize three open-weight MoE LLMs and train crosscoders on paired personalized and non-personalized activations.
Interpretable personalized latents identify experts associated with distinct personalization features.
Personalized MoEs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters and show lower polysemanticity.
Causal interventions recover personalized behavior and shift non-personalized models toward it by boosting associated experts.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates personalization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs by identifying specific experts responsible for personalization features using crosscoders, relevant to LLM architecture and personalization.
papers.title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
papers.tldr: Personalizing MoE LLMs makes personalization more interpretable by linking distinct user features to specialized experts and causal routing paths.

papers.abstract: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high-surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.
bullets: Entropy-based patching often misses inline computed results because they have ordinary surprisal for the patching model.
Novelty patching starts patches where upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent two-byte context, using a label-free lookup table fitted on raw text.
At 50M parameters, computed-result accuracy rises from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90% at a matched ~11% patch rate.
The benefit is strongest in written math, shrinks on prose, and ties entropy on source code and synthetic execution traces.
Typed uncertainty, post-training rule switching, and a context-aware novelty predictor did not work; learned chunking finds related structure in math and code.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes compute-efficient patch selection for byte-level language models, relevant to token-level efficiency and LM architecture.
papers.title: Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute
papers.tldr: Novelty-based byte patching directs compute toward new content near mathematical computations, substantially improving computed-result and final-answer accuracy under fixed patch budgets.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models expose an inference-time choice: which positions become visible after each denoising pass. Many existing decoding methods use hand-designed rules or require visibility to grow monotonically. We present a $\textbf{T}$iny $\textbf{I}$nference-time $\textbf{P}$olicy for $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{TIPS}$), an approximately $600$K-parameter controller that learns both unmasking and remasking while keeping the underlying language model frozen. TIPS uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select which tokens should be visible, while a fixed schedule controls the expected visible fraction. We train the controller through supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards. On GSM8K and MATH-500 with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the full-canvas and two-block TIPS variants achieve $58.46\%$ and $57.97\%$ micro-averaged accuracy at a budget of $32$ decoder evaluations, exceeding the strongest baseline in our main comparison by $12.1$ and $11.6$ percentage points, respectively. Both variants are trained at a budget of $32$ evaluations and remain competitive at higher budgets without retraining. These results demonstrate that learning when to reveal and reconsider tokens can improve the accuracy-compute trade-off without updating the decoder backbone.
authors: Ya-Shi Zhang, Jian Tang, Pierre-Andr\'e No\"el, Oleksiy Ostapenko
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-designed or monotonically expanding visibility schedules in masked diffusion language models.
Uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select token visibility, with a fixed schedule controlling the expected visible fraction.
Trains a roughly 600K-parameter controller using supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards.

With LLaDA-8B-Instruct at 32 decoder evaluations, TIPS reaches 58.46% and 57.97% micro-averaged accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500, respectively, outperforming the strongest cited baseline by 12.1 and 11.6 percentage points.
The full-canvas and two-block variants remain competitive at higher inference budgets without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a small inference-time controller (TIPS) for diffusion language models to optimize the accuracy-compute trade-off by dynamically managing token visibility, directly relevant to LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: TIPS: A Tiny Inference-time Policy for Scaling in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: TIPS is a small learned inference-time controller that improves diffusion language model decoding by deciding which tokens to reveal or remask while keeping the backbone frozen.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain overwhelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently generated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permissive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evaluation yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine-tuning nine models from three different families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B-32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks.
authors: Daniela Baiamonte, Kamyar Zeinalipour, Elena Fano, Stefano Simonazzi, Andrea Zugarini
bullets: Addresses the lack of open, commercially usable multilingual supervised fine-tuning data.
Contains 502,818 instruction-response pairs in five European languages.
Uses translation and regeneration pipelines, with regeneration for tasks where direct translation is insufficient.
Human evaluations report inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across datasets and languages.
Fine-tuning nine models across three families and evaluation on 13 benchmarks show competitiveness with larger mixtures and official instruction-tuned releases, with clear safety-task advantages.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual permissively-licensed instruction-following dataset for SFT; fits LLM instruction tuning.
papers.title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following
papers.tldr: Multi-SFT is a commercially permissive multilingual instruction-tuning dataset that enables strong performance across five European languages, especially on safety tasks.

papers.abstract: Many hierarchical byte-level language models group bytes into patches using a learned boundary predictor whose view of the next codepoint depends on encoding and lookahead. In UTF-8, codepoints of many scripts take three bytes: 8 of 24 bits mark length and continuation, and the first byte carries only 4 high codepoint bits. After the same left context, a mark extending a grapheme cluster and a letter starting the next can thus share their first byte. Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) keeps one- and two-byte UTF-8 encodings but writes these codepoints as two UTF-16 bytes, low byte first, so its first symbol carries 8 low codepoint bits that can distinguish such continuations. We train small causal predictors on matched FineWeb-2 text and evaluate on FLORES-200 under UTF-8, UBE, and UBE's same-length big-endian variant. At one-symbol lookahead, balanced grapheme-boundary error at codepoint boundaries across 17 languages in 13 Brahmic scripts is 8.76% with UTF-8, 8.62% with the big-endian variant, and 0.06% with UBE. When the target instead retains a parent tokenizer's subword cuts at grapheme boundaries, UBE lowers the mean error relative to UTF-8 at the same lookahead by 72.91% in Korean, 35.29% in Chinese, and 67.32-99.55% in eight more scripts. In the seven of them whose main Unicode block fits on one 256-codepoint page, the big-endian variant stays within 3.0% of UTF-8, so the gain follows byte order, not length. In Korean and Chinese, UBE's mean error falls below UTF-8's final mean error after only 25% and 37.5% of training. Which byte comes first thus affects how much lookahead a byte-level boundary predictor needs.
bullets: UTF-8 can make a grapheme continuation and a following letter indistinguishable from their first byte in many scripts.
Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) retains short UTF-8 encodings but represents longer codepoints as low-byte-first UTF-16.
Across 17 languages and 13 Brahmic scripts, one-symbol balanced boundary error was 0.06% with UBE versus 8.76% with UTF-8.
For parent-tokenizer subword boundaries, UBE reduced mean error by 35.29–99.55% across the reported scripts, including Korean and Chinese.
The comparison with a big-endian variant indicates that byte order—not encoding length—drives the improvement; scope is focused on boundary prediction and the evaluated multilingual text settings.
papers.selection_reason: Studies byte-level tokenization and boundary prediction for hierarchical language models, relevant to LLM architecture and tokenization.
papers.title: The Right Byte First: How UTF-16 Helps Multilingual Boundary Prediction
papers.tldr: Putting the low UTF-16 byte first substantially improves multilingual grapheme-boundary prediction compared with UTF-8 at the same lookahead.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models support ever longer context windows, and evaluations typically treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty. However, context length alone cannot explain why models fail on long-context tasks that require reasoning over complex information. Contexts of equal length can pose very different challenges: a task may be solvable from a single local passage, or it may require integrating evidence distributed across the full context. We quantitatively characterise this difficulty through three properties: evidence scope, how much necessary information must be found; evidence dispersion, how widely that information is scattered within the context; and reasoning depth, how many dependent steps are needed to derive an answer from it. We construct LURCH, a multi-domain question-answering benchmark of 6,550 instances with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs, enabling all three properties to be quantified. Evaluations of proprietary and open-weight models show that: (1) at fixed context length, all our three properties are strongly negatively correlated with model performance; (2) as context length increases, performance degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence, whereas it remains relatively stable on samples with localised evidence; and (3) difficulty compounds across properties, as questions with moderately high values on all three are harder than those with an extreme value on just one. These findings establish evidence scope, dispersion and reasoning depth as measures of long-context reasoning difficulty that complement context length.
authors: Shiwen Qin, Cameron Barker, Henry Gouk, Elliot J. Crowley, Shay B. Cohen, Mirella Lapata, Miao Li
bullets: Introduces three difficulty dimensions: evidence scope, evidence dispersion, and reasoning depth.
Presents LURCH, a 6,550-instance, multi-domain QA benchmark with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs.
Across proprietary and open-weight models, all three dimensions negatively correlate with performance at fixed context length.
Performance degrades more sharply with increasing context length when evidence is dispersed rather than localized.
Difficulty compounds when moderately high scope, dispersion, and reasoning depth occur together.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-context reasoning difficulty with new difficulty measures and a benchmark.
papers.title: Beyond Context Length: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: Long-context reasoning difficulty depends not just on context length, but on how much evidence must be found, how dispersed it is, and how many reasoning steps connect it.

papers.abstract: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. We implement this as Prism-1 (Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models): every option is read in its own block at shared positions, with the model's usual left-to-right attention, in one forward pass. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle, and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions. Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only answers that survive a reordering are counted, while no shuffle changes any of its answers and no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others.
authors: Yao Long Teng, Jianguo Huang, Yanchen Deng, Jiayi Cai, Bo An
bullets: Web System One models should be insensitive to option order and to adding competing options, as required by rational-choice axioms.
Standard SCQ prompting, even with shuffling, sorting, or invariant architectures, violates at least one axiom.
Prism-1 scores each option independently in separate blocks at shared positions, using one forward pass.
Across five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, Prism-1 had no changes under shuffling or irrelevant-option additions.
Its accuracy stayed within one point of the baseline and was 2–4 points higher when counting only reorder-stable answers.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel LLM scoring architecture satisfying rational-choice axioms, relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models
papers.tldr: Prism-1 enforces order- and rival-independent option scoring, eliminating choice changes caused by option reordering or irrelevant additions while preserving baseline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection-to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HeirCommit freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HeirCommit cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68-83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EvoHeir achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited.
authors: Haoyi Yang, Kshitij Mishra, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou
bullets: Self-evolving loops often inherit updates from tasks that appear learnable, even when those updates do not improve correctness.
HeirCommit evaluates frozen candidate models on fresh questions before deciding whether to inherit them.
EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, allowing useful experience to persist despite rejecting its originating model.
The analysis decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors and characterizes selection-induced optimism.
HeirCommit reduces harmful accepted updates by 68–83%; EvoHeir obtains the best reported mathematics and general-reasoning averages across four backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Selection mechanisms for self-evolving LLM training loops; fits LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Selection Is Not Learning: Choosing Model Futures
papers.tldr: HeirCommit and EvoHeir improve self-evolving language-model training by verifying whether updates are useful before inheritance and preserving valuable experience independently of model selection.

papers.abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.
authors: Soumye Singhal, Joseph Jennings, Ka Shun Shum, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary
bullets: Addresses the underexplored midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, where short-context pretraining and synthetic-heavy SFT may limit agentic capabilities.
Trains at 256K context on hundreds of billions of tokens from repositories, pull requests, commit histories, build logs, and a small amount of agent traces.
After identical SFT, gains appear across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-bench Pro, and the long-horizon DeepSWE benchmark on two Nemotron models.
The recipe also improves robustness across agent harnesses.
Proxy metrics from base models were unreliable; the authors instead use short fixed SFT runs and report supporting ablations.
papers.selection_reason: Open midtraining recipe for agentic post-training of LLMs at 256K context; fits LLM training and long-context.
papers.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
papers.tldr: An open midtraining recipe using long-context software-engineering data and limited agent traces improves models’ subsequent agentic post-training performance and robustness.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.
authors: Bruno Arcanjo, Zhaoxing Li, Sebastian Stein
bullets: Addresses preference elicitation when no user choices are yet available.
An LLM describes a new user’s trade-offs, which are mapped to priors over multinomial logit coefficients.
A Bayesian learner updates these priors as user choices accumulate.
Across seven choice datasets, it improves cold-start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5–40 percentage points.
Its benefit is concentrated among early users, with performance comparable to information from roughly 6–40 surveyed users in log-loss terms.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLMs to generate informative priors for test-time preference elicitation, addressing the cold start problem in adaptive systems.
papers.title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
papers.tldr: Agentic-Priors uses LLM-derived, interpretable preference trade-offs to provide informative priors that substantially improve cold-start preference learning.

papers.abstract: Sequence models can generalise in fundamentally distinct ways: extrapolating structures seen in training, or using their prompt to adapt to novel tasks. The prevailing strategy determines how the model behaves beyond its training distribution, controlling potential capabilities and risks. Recent work has characterised many different strategies theoretically, and empirically described the transition between them as the quality and quantity of pretraining data vary. However, there is no learning theory for this competition, hence no fundamental understanding of \textit{why} one solution might be favoured over another. Here we provide such a theory in a solvable topic model---documents drawn from a finite mixture of latent topics, mirroring the heterogeneity of modern pretraining data. The dataset comes with two distinct solutions: a specialised predictor, that stores the finite topic mixture, and an in-context one, optimal for topics never seen during training. Our theory predicts their emergence at distinct sample complexities: the in-context predictor is available early, while the specialised one emerges only after the training tokens outnumber the parameters of the data-generating process. Trained transformers reproduce both scales and the separating crossover in remarkable agreement with the theory, with no fitted parameters.
bullets: Studies the competition between distribution-extrapolating specialized predictors and prompt-adapting in-context predictors.
Uses documents sampled from a finite mixture of latent topics, yielding both solution types.
Predicts distinct sample-complexity thresholds: in-context learning appears early, while specialization requires tokens exceeding the data-generating process’s parameter count.
Transformer experiments reproduce both learning scales and their crossover without fitted parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of in-context learning versus specialization in transformers, relevant to Large Language Model learning dynamics.
papers.title: In-Context Learning Before Specialisation: Theory of Learning in a Solvable Topic Model
papers.tldr: A solvable topic-model theory explains why sequence models first learn in-context adaptation and only later specialize as pretraining data grows.

papers.abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.
authors: Pengfeng Song, Yunkai Zhuang, Liye Shi
bullets: Stores facts as versioned, source-linked records while retaining earlier values for later reference.
Retrieves relevant versions in source order and labels historical records before answer generation.
Combines structured facts with event memory and original dialogue turns to recover missing details.
Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71–97.62% overall and 96.67–100.00% for historical-residence questions.
Used 48.75–56.73% fewer evidence tokens than session-aware RAG; it also outperformed session-aware RAG in a 1,540-question hybrid-memory evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Presents temporal state tracking memory for LLM agents, directly fitting agent memory and persistent external memory research.
papers.title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: TEM is a training-free memory framework that tracks changing facts by preserving version history and temporal labels, improving answers to questions about updated information with compact evidence.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces TagInsert, a Transformer-based model that challenges the common left-to-right (L2R) generation paradigm in Transformers, for sequence labelling tasks where dependencies may not naturally align with a L2R order. TagInsert lifts the L2R constraint by removing the decoder-side attention mask and enabling the model to decide a preferred order of tag generation at inference time. We experiment on the common Part-of-Speech tagging and the more complex Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) supertagging tasks on multiple languages and low-resource data settings. We show that, although encoder-only models like BERT remain strong performers for tagging tasks, TagInsert frequently outperforms a L2R encoder-decoder model, achieves results comparable to encoder-only models under data-scarce conditions, and shows better results on the long-tail of rare categories. Our analyses show that TagInsert alleviates error propagation typical of autoregressive models by learning to defer difficult predictions to later stages in the decoding process.
bullets: Targets POS tagging and CCG supertagging across multiple languages and low-resource settings.
Removes the decoder-side attention mask so the Transformer can choose which tag to generate next.
Frequently outperforms a left-to-right encoder-decoder model and approaches encoder-only performance in data-scarce settings.
Improves predictions for rare categories and reduces autoregressive error propagation by deferring difficult tags.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces dynamic-order sequence generation in Transformers, a technically transferable idea for language model decoding and architecture.
papers.title: Dynamic ordering in sequence generation in Transformers: experiments on low-resource Tagging scenarios
papers.tldr: TagInsert improves low-resource sequence tagging by learning a flexible tag-generation order instead of following a fixed left-to-right sequence.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
authors: Donghoon Han, Minseop Jung, Dong Woo Kwak, SeungJae Lee, Junhoo Lee
bullets: Targets conditional memories whose full embedding table must remain available for lookup.
Encodes each row with a short code and local scale, using a shared Gaussian-trellis reconstruction program.
Adds norm restoration and independently decodable row records for practical access.
Reduces output KL by 41–63% versus 2-bit round-to-nearest quantization.
Cuts DeepSeek table storage from 203GB to 51GB, enabling larger GPU-resident workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Quantizes large LLM n-gram lookup tables with compressed reconstructable codes, drastically reducing model memory footprint while preserving output quality.
papers.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Conditional Program compresses language-model lookup tables to two bits per value while reconstructing requested rows on demand, substantially reducing storage and quantization error.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted information from large language models, but existing evaluations often measure forgetting only on a designated benchmark distribution. We argue that such behavioral forgetting is an insufficient standard for privacy-oriented unlearning, and that evaluation should instead test whether forgetting persists across the access paths through which the same information may be recovered. We demonstrate this with a controlled case study of cross-lingual querying: across multiple multilingual model families, forgetting varies substantially when semantically equivalent information is queried in different languages and scripts. A single access path is therefore enough to expose a real gap between behavioral forgetting and information inaccessibility, motivating broader evaluation of access-path generalization and adversarial recoverability alongside in-distribution forgetting.
bullets: Machine unlearning evaluations often test forgetting only on a designated distribution.
Privacy-oriented evaluation should examine whether forgetting generalizes across ways of accessing the same information.
A controlled cross-lingual case study finds substantial variation across languages and scripts in multilingual model families.
