papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context speculative decoding with position-free far memory; fits KV-cache efficiency and long-context language modeling.
papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: FOLD is a training-free long-context speculative-decoding method that improves drafting by combining exact local positions with sharpened, weight-controlled far-memory attention.

papers.abstract: The success of transformers is attributed to several factors, including their capacity to express formal languages over variable-length inputs, and ability of the attention mechanism to focus on relevant input features. However, there is limited understanding of the training dynamics of shallow transformers, specifically how to decouple the learning of the attention and the output (feedforward) layer. A natural extension of the theory of one-step gradient feature learning in feedforward networks suggests that one could first learn the attention weights with a single gradient step, and then train the output layer. We show that this fails for a shallow transformer trained to recognize a star-free language from unbounded-length input. We prove that the transformer can be trained to recognize the language with a three-phase gradient descent: the output layer is updated first, followed by an attention update, and the output layer is fine-tuned in the third phase. In contrast, the language cannot be learned by training only the attention or output layer, or by a single attention-layer update followed by finetuning the output layer. We empirically show that ``attention learning lagging output layer learning" is beneficial in other language recognition, regression, and in-context learning tasks as well.
bullets: Studies how attention and output-layer learning interact in shallow transformers.
Shows that a one-step attention update followed by output training fails on a star-free language.
Proves a three-phase schedule—output update, attention update, output fine-tuning—can learn the language.
Establishes that training only attention or only the output layer is insufficient for this task.
Empirical results suggest delayed attention learning also helps language recognition, regression, and in-context learning.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of transformer attention and output-layer training dynamics on unbounded inputs is transferable to understanding and improving large language model training.
papers.title: Training Dynamics of Transformers on Unbounded Inputs: Attention Learning Can Lag Output Layer Learning
papers.tldr: For shallow transformers on unbounded inputs, learning the output layer before attention—and then fine-tuning it—can be essential for successful training.

papers.abstract: A ReAct-style agent accumulates observations, intermediate results, and failed attempts in a single context. As this context grows, stale and off-path information consumes its limited capacity and obscures relevant evidence, making focused reasoning increasingly difficult. We introduce TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent's own policy decides where to search. The agent records each intermediate state, with a short summary, as a node in a search tree maintained by the harness. The policy is a single language model that acts in two roles. In the Reflection role, it has a global view of the tree through these summaries and picks a node to resume, together with an instruction. In the Execution role, the harness restores the path that led to that node, and the model carries out the instruction with the usual task tools until it saves a new node or proposes a solution, which Reflection then approves or sends back to another node. Through these choices, the policy decides whether to deepen the current line, branch from or revisit an earlier state, verify a proposal, or stop, without a fixed traversal order or a score for each node. We train navigation, task actions, checkpointing, and proposal review jointly with a tree-aware adaptation of GRPO, using task-level outcome rewards augmented by process rewards. After small-scale RL of a 4B model, with the same active-context limit for all methods, TreeFlex reaches 48.8% accuracy on a challenging deep-research benchmark, versus 41.5% for flat ReAct and 42.8% for FoldAgent, and its Pass@8 is about ten points higher than either. On SWE-bench Verified, with all three systems trained with RL from the same 9B model, TreeFlex resolves 54.9% of tasks, versus 43.3% for FoldAgent and 45.2% for its step-wise variant.
authors: Dongzhuo Li, Fangzhou Cheng, Weiwei Li, Kevin Han, Haixu Ma, Zhongchang Sun, Ruiyi Li, Serena Li, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang, Yuandong Tian
bullets: Addresses stale and off-path information that can overwhelm a ReAct agent’s limited context.
Stores summarized intermediate states as tree nodes and uses the same language model to select nodes, resume paths, execute actions, and review proposals.
Supports deepening, branching, revisiting, verification, and stopping without fixed traversal rules or per-node scores.
Trained with a tree-aware GRPO method combining task-level and process rewards.
With matched active-context limits, achieves 48.8% on a deep-research benchmark and 54.9% on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the compared baselines reported in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: LLM agent framework with external search-tree memory and policy-driven navigation; fits LLM memory and agent memory.
papers.title: TreeFlex: Agents Navigating Their Own Search Trees
papers.tldr: TreeFlex lets an agent navigate a self-built search tree instead of relying on one growing context, improving deep research and software-engineering task performance.

papers.abstract: Multilingual models share capacity across languages, so adding languages can hurt performance on existing ones. Mixture-of-experts models expand this capacity with little additional per-token computation. Given this extra capacity, does adding experts reduce what each additional language costs? To answer this question, we propose a repetition-aware joint scaling law relating number of active parameters, training tokens per language, number of experts, and language coverage. Fitted on 26,300 per-language loss observations from 64 pretrained configurations, our law reduces prediction error on held-out configurations by 28% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. At matched number of active parameters and training tokens per language, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of expanding from 12 to 200 languages by 83% compared with a dense model. Our law further shows that broader language coverage favors more experts across a wider range of compute budgets, guiding capacity allocation as multilingual models scale.
authors: Joel Dag, Nikit Srivastava, Hamada M. Zahera, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo
bullets: Adding languages can degrade existing-language performance because model capacity is shared.
The study proposes a joint scaling law linking active parameters, per-language training tokens, expert count, and language coverage.
The law is fitted to 26,300 per-language loss observations from 64 pretrained configurations.
With matched active parameters and per-language tokens, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of scaling from 12 to 200 languages by 83% versus a dense model.
Broader language coverage favors using more experts across a wider range of compute budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling laws for multilingual Mixture-of-Experts; directly relevant to LLM architecture and scaling.
papers.title: Scaling Multilingual Mixture-of-Experts: How Language Coverage Changes Capacity and Compute Allocation
papers.tldr: A repetition-aware scaling law shows that adding MoE experts substantially reduces the per-language cost of expanding multilingual coverage and helps guide expert allocation.

papers.abstract: We investigate two aspects of multilingual pre-training with limited data, namely how language exposure is distributed across English, Dutch, and Chinese, and how that exposure is ordered during training. In particular, we compare balanced multilingual exposure to language-dominant exposure, where one language is exposed with more training data than the others. We also compare mixed training, where multilingual training data is used throughout training, with curriculum training, where monolingual exposure of the dominant language is followed by balanced multilingual exposure. Our results show that multilingual BabyLM performance varies with both the amount and order of language exposure. Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning across all 15 matched configurations, indicating that simultaneous multilingual exposure is more effective than staged exposure in our setting. Several language-dominant mixed training configurations achieve higher scores than the balanced configuration, suggesting that a balanced distribution is not necessarily the highest-performing configuration in our setting. Interestingly, the Dutch-primary configurations achieve the best overall performance.
authors: JiWoo Hwang, Lukas Edman, Alexander Fraser
bullets: The study examines English, Dutch, and Chinese under balanced versus language-dominant exposure.
It compares mixed multilingual training with a curriculum that starts monolingual and later becomes balanced multilingual.
Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning in all 15 matched configurations.
Some language-dominant mixtures outperform balanced exposure, with Dutch-primary configurations performing best overall.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates language exposure distribution and order in multilingual LLM pretraining; relevant to pretraining strategies.
papers.title: Language Exposure Matters: Distribution and Order in Multilingual BabyLM Pre-training
papers.tldr: Multilingual BabyLM performance depends on both how much exposure each language receives and when that exposure occurs.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used in language-model pretraining. Existing knowledge-corpus synthesis pipelines, including WRAP and Nemotron-CC, usually take a source passage or document segment as input and generate rewritten or QA-style samples from that text. This can improve surface form and prompt diversity, but it does not explicitly require fine-grained source facts -- especially secondary entities, list/table entries, and precise temporal attributes -- to appear in the synthesized corpus. We propose AFCS (Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis), a pipeline that first extracts source-supported atomic facts and then uses each retained fact to drive generation. AFCS uses structure-aware extraction over the document tree, source-grounded verification, local context expansion, and multi-format generation. In continued-pretraining experiments with OLMo-3-7B and a 32B base on the same FineWiki source corpus, AFCS outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA. Granularity ablations show that fact-level synthesis improves over chunk-level, paragraph-level, and entity-level synthesis; and a 100B-token mid-training integration improves factual benchmarks and raises the 12-task general benchmark average by +1.09.
authors: Yunhao Wang, Feng Zhang, Tinghao Yu, Xing Wu, Jiang Zhou
bullets: Targets missing fine-grained facts, including secondary entities, list/table entries, and temporal details.
Extracts source-supported atomic facts with document-structure awareness and verifies them against the source.
Expands local context and generates diverse samples in multiple formats from each retained fact.
Outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA in experiments with 7B and 32B models.
A 100B-token integration improves factual benchmarks and increases the 12-task general benchmark average by 1.09 points.
papers.selection_reason: Atomic-fact-conditioned synthesis improves factual knowledge pretraining; relevant to LLM pretraining methods.
papers.title: AFCS: Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis for Factual Knowledge Pretraining
papers.tldr: AFCS improves factual knowledge pretraining by generating synthetic data directly from verified atomic facts rather than only source passages or document segments.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts.
authors: Yibin Lou, Yi Hu, Jianhui Chen, Chenpeng Wang, Muhan Zhang, Liangming Pan
bullets: Knowledge selection between parametric and contextual information is linearly represented along a single model direction.
The direction generalizes across conflict formats, knowledge categories, and datasets.
A direction learned from simple factual conflicts transfers to RAG, memory, and rule-following tasks.
Steering consistently improves reliance on prompt-provided information across four model families and multiple settings.
The findings indicate a transferable preference for external knowledge, not merely a factual-conflict-specific mechanism.
papers.selection_reason: Shows a single steering direction controls context vs parametric knowledge in LLMs and transfers across tasks; relevant to LLM mechanisms.
papers.title: Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts
papers.tldr: LLMs’ preference between internal and prompt-provided knowledge is encoded in a generalizable residual-stream direction that can be steered to favor external information.

papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine parameter reuse with sparse computation to improve performance under matched budgets. Prior work demonstrates that different loop visits can play different roles even when they share parameters. To probe the contributions of different loop visits, we learn separate residual coefficients in a model that applies a shared block twice, observing a smaller scale in the first visit. Fixed coefficient experiments show that reducing the first visit's scale preserves or improves performance, whereas the same reductions to the second hurt it. This asymmetry motivates us to explore asymmetric compute allocation. We propose \textbf{LatentLoop}, which compresses the first visit's sequence, retains full resolution in the second, and reallocates saved computation to increase the hidden size. We further learn how strongly the first visit updates the full sequence, and share MoE weights across visits while using separate attention parameters to accommodate their different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations spanning 1.3B--7B parameters, with the largest budget exceeding $10^{21}$ FLOPs, LatentLoop consistently lowers validation NLL. At a fitted NLL of 1.988, predicted compute savings are 19.0\% and 7.9\% relative to vanilla MoE and the looped baseline. It also improves average scores on nine benchmarks at all sizes in 0-shot and 5-shot settings. These results suggest asymmetric compute allocation is a promising direction for looped MoE models.
authors: Zefeng He, Yunkai Chai, Xiaoyang Chen, Tong Zhu, Zongliang Wu, Yun Luo, Yafu Li, Yu Cheng
bullets: Different loop visits contribute asymmetrically: reducing computation in the first visit is less harmful than reducing it in the second.
The method compresses the first visit’s sequence, keeps the second at full resolution, and increases hidden size with the saved compute.
It learns the first visit’s update strength, shares MoE weights across visits, and uses separate attention parameters for differing resolutions.
Across 15 configurations from 1.3B to 7B parameters, it consistently lowers validation NLL and improves average scores on nine benchmarks in 0-shot and 5-shot settings.
At fitted NLL 1.988, it predicts 19.0% and 7.9% compute savings versus vanilla MoE and the looped baseline, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Looped MoE language model architecture with asymmetric compute allocation and sequence compression for efficiency.
papers.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
papers.tldr: LatentLoop improves looped MoE efficiency by compressing the first loop visit and reallocating its saved computation to model capacity.

papers.abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.
authors: Minh-Anh Nguyen, Nguyen T. Ha Lan, Xiyan Fu, Dung D. Le, Wei Lu
bullets: Pruned models frequently continue reasoning past a correct answer and exceed the token budget through repetitive loops.
This degradation reflects impaired termination more than impaired reasoning: models often recognize where the dense model would stop.
Terminating and looping continuations show a consistent hidden-state difference across pruned checkpoints.
Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS) adds this shared direction to the residual stream during inference.
Across six models, three pruning pipelines, and math/code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and accuracy while reducing repetition and generation length.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and recovers pruned large reasoning models via termination-guided activation steering.
papers.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: Pruning often makes large reasoning models loop instead of stop, and a training-free activation-steering method can recover termination and accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.
authors: Jiangcheng Song, Haodong Jing, Yulin Mu, Lesong Tao, Jixin Wang, Jin Cui, Tianjing Ren, Runxuan Xie, Yongqiang Ma, Nanning Zheng
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–inference-efficiency trade-off in reasoning over very long documents.
Uses a small language model for parallel evidence selection and a large language model for ordered memory verification and updates.
Trains the two systems through supervised evidence-selection tuning, GRPO-based memory optimization, and joint coordination.
Evaluated on RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, achieving a 9.74× end-to-end speedup and 73.91% fewer output tokens than RL-MemAgent.
The abstract scopes results to the reported long-context benchmarks and evaluation settings.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-process memory framework for long-context reasoning with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
papers.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: MemDuet coordinates fast evidence selection with slower memory verification to improve long-context reasoning efficiency while preserving accuracy as contexts grow.

papers.abstract: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.
authors: Lingxi Cui, Jinhao Ruan, Wenqing Wei, Guo Yi, Li Rao, Ke Chen, Lidan Shou
bullets: Addresses retrieval challenges caused by interleaved threads, channels, time, and speaker-dependent authority.
Builds three complementary forests: Channel for workflows, Actor for speaker context, and Artifact for deliverable lifecycles.
Uses a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges to connect information across views.
Combines message relevance, hierarchical summaries, and cross-view links to assemble evidence.
Outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines on three enterprise-chat benchmarks, with up to 20.85-point accuracy gains over MemOS.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical agent memory for retrieval; fits the LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: EGCForest: Structured Agent Memory Organization for Enterprise Group Chats
papers.tldr: EGCForest organizes enterprise group-chat memory across multiple hierarchical views to retrieve distributed evidence more reliably and efficiently.

papers.abstract: LLMs absorb vast knowledge from training data, yet their inherently probabilistic nature offers no guarantee that this knowledge will surface in their outputs. To bridge this gap, Knowledge Extraction Enhancement (KEE) techniques such as activation steering, decoding adjustments, and prompting modify inference, potentially reinforcing existing predictions or surfacing less accessible answers. Yet their evaluations centered on aggregate accuracy, which obscures diverse effects by collapsing recovered failures and disrupted successes into a single score. We introduce MAPLE, a unified framework for characterizing how KEE techniques affect parametric knowledge extraction. Its diagnostic metrics disentangle these effects at the surface, probability, and beyond-sampling levels by measuring answer recovery and disruption, gold-token rank shifts on unrecovered failures, and recovery of answers missed by fixed-budget sampling. We evaluate six KEE techniques spanning decoding, activation steering, and prompting across three model families: OLMo2, Qwen2.5, and Llama3. Our analysis reveals distinct effects and trade-offs across techniques, highlighting the value of MAPLE for understanding and comparing KEE beyond aggregate accuracy.
authors: Minsuh Joo, Youna Kim, Choonghyun Park, Soo Kyung Kim, Hyunsoo Cho
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can hide whether a technique recovers failures, disrupts successes, or reveals answers missed by sampling.
MAPLE measures effects at surface, probability, and beyond-sampling levels.
Its metrics track answer recovery/disruption, gold-token rank shifts, and recovery beyond fixed-budget sampling.
The study evaluates six decoding, activation-steering, and prompting techniques across OLMo2, Qwen2.5, and Llama3.
Results show distinct trade-offs between techniques, supporting more informative KEE comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic framework for LLM parametric knowledge extraction techniques; fits LLM foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: MAPLE: A Multi-Axis Parametric Knowledge Extraction Lens for LLM Evaluation
papers.tldr: MAPLE provides a multi-axis framework for evaluating how knowledge-extraction enhancements recover, disrupt, or uncover LLM answers beyond aggregate accuracy.

papers.abstract: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW's previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline's final smoothed training loss in 7.2\% fewer steps.
authors: Jiacheng Li, Jianchao Tan, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses SSC’s sensitivity to gradient scale and clipping thresholds.
Uses AdamW’s previous second moment for row/column scaling and an EMA of clipped spectral norms for per-matrix thresholds.
Restores original coordinates before applying the AdamW update.
On a 19.08B-parameter MoE trained for 83.89B tokens, CAST had lower training and mean validation losses than nine baselines.
Produced the fewest relative gradient spikes and matched the best baseline’s final smoothed training loss in 7.2% fewer steps.
papers.selection_reason: History-adaptive spectral clipping for LLM pretraining; directly relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
papers.tldr: CAST adaptively scales and thresholds soft spectral clipping to stabilize LLM pretraining and accelerate optimization.

papers.abstract: Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs.
bullets: Modern vernacular reasoning traces can be verbose, motivating a more compact linguistic register.
The method rewrites only reasoning traces into wenyan while preserving short direct answers, then fine-tunes a Chinese reasoning model.
A compact modern-Chinese control separates register effects from generic compression.
Across three Chinese reasoning benchmarks, wenyan reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding.
Wenyan outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive elsewhere.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates linguistic register for efficient LLM reasoning, relevant to LLM training and efficiency.
papers.title: Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs
papers.tldr: Wenyan Thinking uses Classical Chinese for intermediate reasoning to make Chinese LLM outputs more compact and effective under limited decoding budgets.

papers.abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. These results suggest that effective multi-model orchestration requires considering not only which model to use, but also which behavioral patterns to carry forward.
authors: Youngbin Choi, Sehyun Hwang, Suhyeon Jun, Seoyeon Lee, Sunghyun Choi, MoonJeong Park, Dongwoo Kim
bullets: Model swaps can cause recipient LLMs to adopt the reasoning and action patterns embedded in prior histories.
Behavior transfer is strongest with raw-history sharing and is substantially reduced by summarization.
DASH uses direction- and authorship-aware summarization to preserve desirable behavior and limit weak-to-strong transfer.
Across repeated swaps, DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines.
The findings highlight behavioral history—not just model selection—as a key factor in multi-model orchestration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies history transfer and summarization in multi-session LLM agents, relevant to LLM deployment and agent behavior.
papers.title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Switching LLMs in multi-session agents transfers behavioral patterns through shared histories, and DASH reduces unwanted transfer while preserving stronger-model behavior.

papers.abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.
authors: Nir Yarden, Amit Ben-Artzy, Roy Schwartz
bullets: Query-first retrieval removes state-capacity pressure, yet Mamba still substantially trails Transformers.
Mamba’s selection gates can strongly control outputs, showing that the mechanism is expressive enough for retrieval.
Gate decisions depend on token representations encoding relevance to the query.
Relevance signals emerge gradually across layers, while retrieval-critical gates often act before those signals are available.
The bottleneck is therefore delayed cross-layer relevance alignment, not capacity alone.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes Mamba's retrieval bottleneck and selection gates, relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
papers.tldr: Mamba’s retrieval failures are not just caused by limited state capacity: relevance information often reaches its selection gates too late for effective retrieval.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA.
authors: Fanyao Li, Yuxi Liu, Xiaohao Liu, He Chang, Zhaoxin Wang, Zhulin Tao
bullets: Higher LoRA rank can introduce harmful directions: in a rank-16 diagnostic, keeping only top singular components performed best.
ReGRA uses a two-stage process: it projects calibration-set task gradients away from the first adapter’s induced subspace, then initializes a second adapter from residual directions.
An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to learn complementary information.
Across diverse benchmarks, ReGRA outperforms same-total-rank alternatives and matches LoRA with twice the rank.
The two adapters can be merged into pretrained weights, adding no inference overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank fine-tuning method for pretrained models, transferable to LLM adaptation.
papers.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: ReGRA improves fixed-rank LoRA fine-tuning by adding a gradient-derived, complementary adapter without increasing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
authors: Aryan Das, Arnab Bhattacharya, Vinay Kumar Verma
bullets: Addresses coarse scalar supervision and unstable moving targets in RL with Verifiable Rewards.
Uses a single policy with sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, avoiding a persistent teacher model.
Adds privileged disagreement correction, reliability-adaptive grounding, and quality- and coverage-aware memory.
Reports the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour budget, with roughly 4 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
Reduces peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: RLVR policy optimization for LLM reasoning with temporal self-distillation; relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: FSPO stabilizes self-distillation for reinforcement learning by using sparse historical policy targets and adaptive correction, improving reasoning and tool-use performance with lower memory use.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.
authors: Yuxuan Wang, Guangxiang Zhao, Xinyu Tan, Yahui Han, Xinxiang Yin, Zhonghai Wu, Xiangzheng Zhang, Lin Sun, Tong Yang
bullets: SFT can alter non-target logit margins even when matching a local reference distribution.
SRP-SFT applies a hinge loss to reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs among the reference model’s top-K non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes.
The hinge stops penalizing a pair once its requested margin bound is satisfied, allowing distributional flexibility.
The paper derives the KL cost of margin violations, characterizes feasibility and utility, and provides a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations.
On Qwen3-4B-Base with UltraFeedback, SRP-SFT outperformed CE and LP-SFT across three seeds in the reported MATH-500 and code-generation evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a margin-preserving SFT objective for LLMs, directly relevant to LLM fine-tuning and training.
papers.title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: SRP-SFT preserves selected non-target logit margins without forcing the full reference distribution, improving math and code-generation scores in reported one-epoch experiments.

papers.abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.
bullets: Addresses how typed decision models can invoke additional reasoning without discarding candidate outputs.
Uses a shared candidate-answer reader over a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone, supporting direct decisions and partial reasoning prefixes.
A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests reads, and an entropy rule accepts answers or interrupts generation.
Across 768 ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge questions, accuracy increases from 70.96% to 84.38%.
Compared with 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time drops 46.30% with a 1.17-point accuracy decrease.
papers.selection_reason: Selective reasoning controller for typed decision models; improves reasoning efficiency.
papers.title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
papers.tldr: A selective reading-and-stopping interface improves typed decision accuracy while reducing unnecessary reasoning and pipeline time.

papers.abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Yuren Hao, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Adds direct connections from earlier to later layers beyond standard residual links.
A jointly trained topology predictor plans the full model’s routing at once, rather than layer by layer.
Reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 17–25% over matched vanilla Transformers from 75M to 1B parameters.
Improves mean accuracy on 13 downstream tasks and achieves higher AlpacaEval win rates after instruction finetuning.
Shows greater robustness to structured pruning in five of six tested settings.
papers.selection_reason: Novel Transformer topology predictor for language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
papers.tldr: DAGFormer jointly plans token-dependent cross-layer connections across the entire Transformer, substantially improving language modeling and downstream performance over standard and routed Transformers.

papers.abstract: The lasting gains in AI have come from methods that absorb more computation, and language models already scale computation within a call. Useful work, though, happens across calls: over hours or days, through tools and external systems, among many agents and the humans they work for, and increasingly through code the agents write themselves. Whether that work compounds is enabled by the harness around it, and the harness faces a constraint the model does not: of the three participants in such a computation, the human, the model and code, only the human's attention does not scale, so the computation can grow only if the human is not in every loop. L3M is a runtime built on that premise, written in Lean 4 so that one language implements the harness, states its invariants, and is the language agents extend it in. One computation spans humans, agents, models and code, and all of its state lives in Git: a rich state trajectory -- rather than a chat conversation -- is an object the runtime can resume, rewind, fork, compare and merge. Waiting, communication, delegation and undo are primitives, not patterns the model reasons through each time. When an agent works out a procedure, it can write it once as a sealed Lean program whose type is its permission request, and the harness offers it back as a tool -- machinery for the model to use. To take the human out of the loop, L3M uses reversibility to decide where that is safe: a tool's review tier follows from how far its effects can be undone, so agents act freely where the runtime can recover. Because the machinery can change, the properties that make this safe are stated as kernel-checked theorems about the code that runs. On Terminal-Bench, an untuned L3M reaches about two thirds of its (unsafe) shell-equipped pass rate using only safe (not needing human review) tools.
authors: Carson Eisenach, Robert Joseph George, Vincent Quenneville-Belair, Kate Gwimm, Dean Foster
bullets: Targets multi-call agent work involving tools, external systems, other agents, humans, and self-written code.
Stores the full computation state in Git, enabling resume, rewind, fork, comparison, and merge instead of relying on chat history.
Provides primitives for waiting, communication, delegation, and undo; agents can turn procedures into sealed Lean tools whose types specify permissions.
Uses reversibility to assign tool review tiers, allowing autonomous execution where effects can be safely undone.
An untuned system achieves roughly two-thirds of its unsafe shell-equipped pass rate on Terminal-Bench using only safe tools.
papers.selection_reason: Git-based persistent state/memory runtime for LLM agents; directly relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: L3M: A Verifiable Harness and Runtime for Self-Extending and Self-Improving Agents
papers.tldr: L3M is a Lean 4 runtime that enables agents to carry out long-running, collaborative work with less human oversight by making computation stateful, reversible, and formally verifiable.

papers.abstract: An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310.
authors: Yi Ding, Mengyu Wang, Min Zhou, Menglin Yang
bullets: Early reasoning mistakes can constrain all later generated steps.
Incorrect responses show substantially higher mean token entropy than correct ones, motivating entropy-based error detection.
REWIND is a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to target suffix regeneration instead of choosing regeneration points randomly.
Across three model families and five benchmarks, it outperforms baselines by 0.51–10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
The approach is evaluated for targeted trajectory repair across multiple models and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-guided trajectory repair for test-time reasoning in LLMs.
papers.title: REWIND: Uncertainty-Guided Trajectory Repair for Test-Time Reasoning
papers.tldr: REWIND uses token-entropy signals to detect likely reasoning errors and selectively regenerate affected suffixes at test time, improving performance across models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.
authors: Shijun Li, Yang Liu, Najmeh Sadoughi, Dongmei Wang, Xinjie Li, Zhu Liu, Rohith Mysore Vijaya Kumar, Yuzong Liu
bullets: Existing retrieval-augmented translation retrieves uniformly, despite many inputs being solvable from the LLM’s parametric knowledge.
SRAT uses agentic reinforcement learning to decide whether to retrieve, what evidence to seek, and how to use it.
Joint Plackett–Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training align retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than similarity alone.
Experiments across idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation show consistent gains over never- and always-retrieve baselines.
The approach treats retrieval as a learnable translation action, with benefits shown under both offline and online retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Selective retrieval-augmented MT via RL; relevant to external memory/retrieval.
papers.title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
papers.tldr: SRAT learns to retrieve translation evidence selectively and integrate it when useful, improving translation over fixed never- or always-retrieve strategies.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
authors: Zhaoyan Jia, Chengwei Zhou, Gourav Datta, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Addresses entropy degradation and insufficient exploration in any-order diffusion generation.
Samples continuations from high-entropy intermediate states, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes.
Uses group-relative advantages for continuation selection and Monte Carlo value differences for segment-level credit assignment.
Achieves the best results among evaluated architecture-preserving methods on three of four benchmarks, improving over JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points.
Reduces generated tokens by up to 27.8%; ForkGRPO-Fast provides a 2.49× training speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement learning method for diffusion LLMs, relevant to LLM architecture and training.
papers.title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: ForkGRPO improves reinforcement learning for diffusion language models by exploring alternative continuations efficiently and assigning credit at the reasoning-segment level.

papers.abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.
authors: Minsu Oh, Seunghui Jwa, Chanjun Park, Yeo-Chan Yoon
bullets: Zeroing memory can hurt performance without proving memory improves over a model trained without memory.
Across nine systems, some depend on memory yet perform worse than memory-free trained alternatives.
In story-state prediction, intact memory underperformed a separately trained no-memory model despite zeroing worsening loss.
On TriviaQA, unrelated passage memory increased xRAG F1 from 19.38 to 24.78, while the question’s passage reached 29.88; accepted-answer rates were statistically uncertain.
Evaluations should report comparison models, absolute performance, and generation/scoring conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates compressed memory mechanisms in LLMs, directly relevant to LLM memory research.
papers.title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
papers.tldr: Compressed-memory gains do not necessarily show that models use the correct document information, so evaluations need stronger comparison baselines and metrics.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.
authors: Thomas Zeng, Zelei Cheng, Mingyang Zhou, Sambit Sahu, William Campbell, Genta Indra Winata
bullets: Expert feedback can explain why a student’s actions are incorrect, providing richer supervision than corrected actions alone.
CAFT elicits critiques and corrected actions from an expert on student-generated trajectories, then fine-tunes the agent on both.
Evaluated across four Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 student models in Airline+Retail, WebShop, and related agentic settings.
Adding critiques improved performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation.
CAFT checkpoints also provided a stronger warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT) using textual expert feedback to improve multi-turn LLM agent performance, contributing to agent training methodologies.
papers.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
papers.tldr: Training LLM agents with expert textual critiques alongside corrected actions improves multi-turn agent performance over action-only supervision.

papers.abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.
authors: LLM-jp, :, Chaoran Liu, Daisuke Kawahara, Hideyuki Tachibana, Hirokazu Kiyomaru, Jun Suzuki, Koshi Eguchi, Kouta Nakayama, Qianying Liu, Rio Yokota, Ryo Takahashi, Sadao Kurohashi, Sosuke Hosokawa, Taishi Nakamura, Takashi Kodama, Yun-Ang Wu, Yusuke Miyao, Yusuke Oda
bullets: Introduces 8B dense and 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts models.
Trains both models from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens.
Defines explicit criteria for training data, external models, and software selection.
Publicly documents development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings.
Reports substantial gains over previous LLM-jp models and competitive results against similarly scaled open-weight models.
papers.selection_reason: Technical report on LLM-jp-4, a Japanese sovereign LLM family featuring a dense 8B and MoE 32B model, contributing to LLM training and architecture (Mixture of Experts).
papers.title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
papers.tldr: LLM-jp-4 is a transparent, reproducible family of Japanese sovereign LLMs that achieves improved and competitive performance through large-scale from-scratch training.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.
authors: Liam Davis, Romain Emil-Popescu, Suman Jana
bullets: Existing jailbreak evaluation can misclassify refusals or merely related answers as successful attacks.
Changing only the judging LLM can shift reported attack success rates by up to 82 percentage points.
The method reconstructs the request answered by a response’s substantive content, excluding repeated or refused information.
It compares the reconstruction with the original and decoy requests, while allowing abstention when neither matches.
Across three off-the-shelf judges, it had the lowest mean error against human labels and reduced ASR variation, but may miss some successful jailbreaks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free semantic reconstruction evaluator for LLM jailbreak compliance; relevant to LLM evaluation and safety.
papers.title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
papers.tldr: A training-free semantic reconstruction evaluator makes jailbreak success-rate judgments more reliable by reducing false positives and judge-dependent variation.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.
authors: Qijia He, Zequn Li, Spencer Luo, Tianle Chen, Pradyumna Narayana, Zixian Ma, Ranjay Krishna, Lan Nie, Sugato Basu
bullets: Problem: OPD supervision can become unreliable after large policy gaps or compounding reasoning and tool-use errors.
Method: Segment-level divergence triggers teacher intervention; the student prefix receives OPD supervision, while a teacher-generated recovery suffix is learned via behavior cloning.
Results: DTDD reduced post-warmup peak gradient norm by 8.6× and reached 21.3% held-out math accuracy in 2.6× fewer updates from a base initialization, with similar final accuracy to OPD.
It improved best-observed ALFWorld and agentic-code performance by 4.8 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively.
Scope: Takeover helps when the teacher is substantially better and can recover from student states, while intervention rates must avoid being too high or too low.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive on-policy distillation for LLM reasoning and agentic training; relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.tldr: DTDD stabilizes on-policy distillation by having the teacher take over when student–teacher divergence signals likely rollout failure, improving training speed and best observed performance in several long-horizon and agentic settings.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.
authors: George Ma, Yuhao Zhang, Bing He, Zeren Shui, Ferhat Erata, Murali Krishna Ramanathan, Somayeh Sojoudi, Hao Zhou
bullets: Addresses sparse verifier rewards and policies that exploit or weaken specifications.
Scores partial progress from discharged proof obligations, augmented with hidden reference-proof probes.
Uses an integrity audit to reject specification changes or circular assumptions.
Agents interact with a live verifier over multiple turns alongside a frozen proof specialist.
Verification improves across model sizes and unseen suites, while held-out issue resolution rises from 59.6% to 72.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic RL with verifier-grounded rewards for code generation across Qwen LLMs; directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
papers.tldr: Verifier-grounded agentic RL substantially improves formally verified code generation and held-out software fixes by using diagnostic proof feedback and integrity checks.

papers.abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.
bullets: Uses LLM-generated summaries and translations as higher-quality synthetic training data.
Improves the baseline with a larger model and character-level vocabulary.
Finds that both changes reach their full potential with LoRA-style fine-tuning.
The submitted Qwenfant model ranked first in the 2026 Multilingual track at submission time.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a character-level BabyLM model (Qwenfant) trained on synthetic parallel text, contributing to LLM training methodologies and multilingual language modeling.
papers.title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
papers.tldr: Qwenfant improves Multilingual BabyLM Challenge performance by training a larger, character-level Qwen3 model on concise LLM-summarized and translated text with LoRA-style fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).
authors: Lucas H. McCabe, Sarah Lukens, H. Howie Huang
bullets: Introduces CoffeeBench, a fault-diagnosis benchmark for LLM agents operating on a simulated appliance.
Evaluates diagnostic efficiency, poor-performing models, and heuristics for selectively trusting predictions.
The strongest models can narrow the fault-option space iteratively to eventually reach successful diagnoses.
Initial diagnostic uncertainty and the model’s judged reasoning soundness predict diagnostic success.
Practical improvements include explicitly tracking episode state to reduce timeouts and using deliberation loops to refine hypotheses.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CoffeeBench for diagnosing appliance faults using LLM agents, focusing on agent reasoning and efficiency in a simulated industrial context.
papers.title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
papers.tldr: CoffeeBench shows that LLM agents struggle to reliably diagnose simulated appliance faults from sensor data alone, but iterative hypothesis refinement and uncertainty-based selection can improve practical diagnosis.

papers.abstract: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.
bullets: Studies prediction regret under Zipf-distributed token statistics.
Uses fixed random embeddings to impose an explicit representational bottleneck of variable width.
Derives scaling with model width, vocabulary size, and Zipf exponent.
Recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws in an appropriate regime.
Predicted curves closely match results on WikiText2 and OpenWebText.
papers.selection_reason: Analytical scaling laws for a bottlenecked bigram model as an LLM toy model; relevant to LLM architecture and scaling understanding.
papers.title: Exact Scaling Laws for a Random-Features Bigram Model
papers.tldr: An analytically tractable random-features bigram model derives capacity-driven scaling laws that closely match experiments on natural-language data.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision on the student's own samples, but its targets still come from the teacher. Verifier reinforcement learning (RL) instead uses an outcome signal, but it provides no direct constraint on capabilities outside the verifier. Combining the two is difficult for diffusion language models (dLLMs), because bidirectional denoising makes the policy likelihoods required by ratio-based RL unreliable. We develop a likelihood-free pipeline for a mixture-of-experts dLLM. Each rollout group is routed by verifier outcome. Mixed groups use ratio-free, group-centred REINFORCE. If every student rollout fails but a teacher succeeds, the model receives dense KL supervision on the student's denoising canvases. All other groups are skipped. A KL term anchored to the distilled checkpoint limits changes outside the verifier reward. The tool-calling teacher succeeds on only 18.6% of the training prompts. At 24 denoising steps, distillation exceeds the teacher by 6.77 percentage points, and routing improves the distilled checkpoint by a further 18.31 points. Routing lowers reasoning-trace accuracy by 0.71 points but raises direct-answer accuracy on the same items by 13.21 points. The anchored arm restores trace accuracy. Its tool-calling score differs by -0.16 points, with a confidence interval that includes zero, although this comparison also removes a small fallback distillation route. A domain-conditional recipe retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; a second seed gives 18.23 points and reproduces both preservation results, but the math result is seed-dependent. We pre-registered every arm and evaluated each comparison on paired items in a single sweep on one machine.
authors: Wentao Lu, Tianyu Zhu, Jesse Clark
bullets: Addresses unreliable policy likelihoods in bidirectional denoising, which hinder ratio-based RL for diffusion language models.
