Humans revisited functions and followed local structure, while strong agents broadly fetched information and rarely returned to prior code—a behavior termed “greedy fetching.”
Across 4,000 real-world binaries, context saturation increased with application size and lower-level representations, highlighting the need for selective retrieval and persistent analysis state.
papers.selection_reason: Examines LLM-agent context-window saturation, greedy fetching, and need for persistent analysis state; informative for LLM memory design.
papers.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
papers.tldr: Top AI agents can match skilled humans on compact binary reverse-engineering tasks, but their broad, context-heavy workflows limit scalability to larger programs.

papers.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.
bullets: A frozen LLM stores experience effects as late-layer activation shifts keyed by a whitened conversation gist.
The method assumes stored shifts approximate effects that attention would otherwise recompute for each question.
Memory is selective: about 98% of unrelated replies remain unchanged.
Facts are rarely used correctly—up to 15% clean recall versus 96–98% when provided in context—and preferences transfer only within a narrow strength range.
The subtraction reference determines preference behavior; without subtracting the opposite, dislikes can be recalled as likes.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates activation steering as persistent memory for LLMs; fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
papers.tldr: Training-free activation memories are highly selective but preserve only limited, question-independent information, often distorting facts and reversing preferences.

papers.abstract: Personalized assistants accumulate long conversation histories, and passing the whole history to an LLM with every request is costly. We show that it is also unnecessary. On PersonaMem-v2 (180 questions), with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 as judges, a relevance-filtered context, built by sentence-level retrieval that ranks the history by similarity to the current request and stops at a fixed budget, matches full-history accuracy with only 5% of the text, cutting the judge's input about 20-fold. An LLM summary of the same length performs on par, but it needs an LLM to read the entire history, whereas retrieval needs only a small embedding model. While both sentence-level retrieval and LLM summary perform strongly, retrieval does so while placing the relevant evidence in the context for only 61% of the questions, and an oracle given only that evidence beats the full history by 15.6 points, making better context selection a promising path to surpassing the full history.
bullets: Full conversation histories are costly and often unnecessary for personalized assistants.
Retrieval ranks history sentences by similarity to the current request and selects a fixed-size relevant context.
On PersonaMem-v2, retrieval matched full-history accuracy with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 judges.
Retrieval performed comparably to an equal-length LLM summary without requiring an LLM to process the entire history.
Relevant evidence was included for only 61% of questions; an oracle using that evidence exceeded full history by 15.6 points, highlighting context selection as a key opportunity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a relevance-filtered context method to reduce the memory footprint of personalized LLMs by matching full history with only 5% of text, relevant to LLM memory optimization.
papers.title: Do Personalized LLMs Need the Whole Conversation? Matching the Full History with Only 5% of Its Text via Relevance-Filtered Context
papers.tldr: Sentence-level retrieval can preserve full-history personalization accuracy using just 5% of conversation text, reducing judge input costs about 20-fold.

papers.abstract: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.
bullets: The study compares N-gram memory updates, one continually trained shared LoRA, and per-task LoRAs merged into the backbone under matched conditions.
N-gram updates cause substantially less representation drift on general math and code inputs than either LoRA strategy, with drift plateauing after the first task rather than accumulating.
Generic behavior remains essentially unchanged under memory-only updates, and changes are localized to inspectable, reversible table rows.
Memory-only learning acquires new tasks more weakly and suffers task interference, causing old-task forgetting comparable to shared LoRA.
Forgetting tracks representation drift on learned-task inputs—not generic inputs—and follows an exact frozen-head logit-margin relation.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representation drift in continual LLM updates and compares LoRA with N-gram memory; directly relevant to continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory
papers.tldr: Updating only an LLM’s N-gram memory preserves backbone representations far better than LoRA-based continual learning, but shifts forgetting and interference into the memory itself.

papers.abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.
authors: Bingjie Zhang, Yibo Yang, Qiantong Liu, Benshuo Fu, Yi Chang, Dandan Guo
bullets: Existing experience-based learning often uses only task success, overlooking the quality of the execution process.
Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL) combines task completion with process quality to provide process-aware feedback.
Paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience estimate how much each experience improves trajectory quality.
Experiences are selected by outcome and quality, while learned utility is combined with semantic relevance for retrieval.
Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, TQG-Exp improves Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points with two backbone LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Experience-based learning with trajectory-quality feedback for LLM agents; fits agent memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
papers.tldr: TQG-Exp improves LLM agent experience reuse by evaluating and optimizing execution trajectories, not just final outcomes.

papers.abstract: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) is the task of mapping mentions extracted from biomedical texts to canonical entities or concepts in the standardized knowledge base. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable performance in mapping accuracy, most rely on training with domain-specific datasets, which fundamentally limits their cross-domain adaptability. To address this limitation, we propose BioNEL-RAG, a novel training-free framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs). Within this framework, the RAG module focuses on retrieving candidate entities, while the large language model module plays the role of selecting the most appropriate candidate for entity normalization, which is based on the analysis of the mention's context, with the aid of its remarkable text comprehension capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that BioNEL-RAG achieves performance comparable to existing methods without requiring training on subdomain datasets, whereas these methods necessitate fine-tuning on specific subdomains such as genes, diseases, or chemical compounds.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Hui Liu, Ziyang Ling, Ronald X. Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-domain adaptability of methods trained on subdomain-specific datasets.
Uses RAG to retrieve candidate biomedical entities from a standardized knowledge base.
Uses an LLM to select the best candidate based on the mention’s context.
Achieves performance comparable to existing methods without fine-tuning on gene, disease, or chemical subdomains.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free RAG framework for Bio-NEL, utilizing retrieval to augment LLM context, which is relevant to LLM memory and context management.
papers.title: Training-Free BioNEL-RAG: Advancing Biomedical Entity Linking through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Model
papers.tldr: BioNEL-RAG enables biomedical entity linking without domain-specific training by combining candidate retrieval with LLM-based context-aware selection.

papers.abstract: Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. For the occupation analysis, we compute each occupation's honorific rate across the seven no-pronoun sentence frames. The standard deviation of these 72 occupation-level rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points across models, showing substantial variation in how honorifics are allocated across occupations. Occupation is associated with 3.2\% to 51.5\% of the variance in register choice, compared with at most 1.2\% for gender. Gender effects are much smaller overall: only two of the nine models show significant directional gender gaps, and they favor opposite genders. HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1 across the nine models, showing substantial variation in how evenly the models allocate respect.
authors: Ajwad Abrar, Md Kamrul Hasan, Hasan Mahmud
bullets: Bengali requires choosing ordinary or respectful register, although English source text does not specify deference.
The benchmark contains 2,016 sentences spanning 72 occupations, seven frames, and four pronoun conditions, including one-word-difference gender counterfactuals.
It reports a 0–100 Honorific Bias Score (HBS), where lower scores indicate more even respect allocation.
Across nine models, HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1; occupation explains 3.2%–51.5% of register-choice variance, versus at most 1.2% for gender.
Occupation-level honorific-rate variability is substantial, while only two models show significant directional gender gaps, favoring opposite genders.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a counterfactual benchmark to measure honorific allocation bias in LLMs for Bengali/English translation.
papers.title: Who Receives Respect? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Honorific Allocation Bias in Bengali
papers.tldr: A counterfactual benchmark finds that Bengali honorific choices in English–Bengali translation vary substantially by occupation and model, while gender effects are generally small.

papers.abstract: Nheengatu (yrl), the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral, has 6--10 thousand speakers and is co-official in S\~ao Gabriel da Cachoeira (Brazil), yet remains poorly served by evaluated Portuguese--Nheengatu MT resources. We present the largest parallel corpus assembled for the language (14.5k Portuguese--Nheengatu pairs), anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution; the first MT evaluation set built from transcribed spontaneous speech; and, to our knowledge, the first open-weight MT models dedicated to bidirectional Portuguese--Nheengatu translation. Three findings organize the paper. First, translation into Nheengatu on held-out constitutional articles plateaus on development data regardless of training length or model size, and much of the remaining error sits in conventional legal terms that the written sources do not attest consistently; a terminology success rate over a frozen lexicon shows that glossary mechanisms at training time and lexical constraints at decoding each raise term realization, the latter at a cost in repetitive output that chrF++ barely registers. Second, a corpus expansion that adds transcribed conversation raises speech chrF++ by 24--27 points while leaving written domains unchanged, a register gap that written-only benchmarks cannot see. Third, a larger NLLB model helps translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu on legal or speech text. For Portuguese-to-Nheengatu translation, our final systems reach 31.7--32.8 chrF++ on article-disjoint constitutional text, 64.1--64.5 on the near-domain set (62.1 after removing items with target-side content overlap), and 45.2--47.5 on speech.
authors: Fabr\'icio Carraro, Rodolfo Joel Zevallos, Rodrigo Gon\c{c}alves de Souza, Caio Henrique Faustino da Silva, John E. Ortega
bullets: Assembles a 14.5k-pair parallel corpus centered on the 2023 Portuguese translation of Brazil’s Federal Constitution, plus the first spontaneous-speech MT evaluation set.
Releases the first open-weight bidirectional Portuguese–Nheengatu MT models, with evaluations on constitutional, near-domain, and speech text.
Glossary training and constrained decoding improve realization of legal terminology, though decoding constraints increase repetitive output.
Adding transcribed conversation improves speech chrF++ by 24–27 points without improving written-domain performance, exposing a register gap.
Larger NLLB models help translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu; remaining errors include inconsistently attested legal terms.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an open MT system and corpus pipeline for the low-resource Amazonian language Nheengatu.
papers.title: The Constitution Speaks Nheengatu: An Open MT System and Reproducible Corpus Pipeline for the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral
papers.tldr: The paper introduces an open, reproducible Portuguese–Nheengatu MT resource and shows that conversational data and terminology controls substantially improve coverage of this under-resourced language.

papers.abstract: The predominance of English-language Web content creates an information-access barrier for speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic. This paper presents the design, imple-mentation, and evaluation of a bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system that allows a user to formulate a natural-language question in either Amharic or English and retrieve an answer from documents written in the other language. The system integrates a statistical machine translation (SMT) component for query translation, a maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) component for Amharic text processing, semantic-based indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction. A domain-diverse Amharic-English parallel corpus was used to train the SMT component, while monolingual cor-pora supported language modeling. Documents were normalized, tokenized, stemmed, indexed, and semantically enriched before retrieval. The original evaluation used precision and recall as the principal effectiveness measures. For Amharic-to-English retrieval, the system achieved 72% precision and 79% recall; for English-to-Amharic retrieval, it achieved 65% precision and 70% recall. These findings show that a modular translation-and-retrieval architecture can provide useful cross-language access even under low-resource conditions. This revised article preserves the original experimental claims while situating them in the context of subsequent multilingual transformer and Amharic QA research.
bullets: Addresses the information-access barrier caused by limited Amharic Web content.
Translates user questions with statistical machine translation and processes Amharic text using maximum-entropy NER.
Uses normalization, tokenization, stemming, semantic indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction.
Reports 72% precision and 79% recall for Amharic-to-English retrieval, and 65% precision and 70% recall in the reverse direction.
Demonstrates useful cross-language QA under low-resource conditions; the article also contextualizes the work alongside later multilingual transformer research.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a cross-language QA system for low-resource languages (Amharic/English) using traditional NLP components.
papers.title: Amharic-English Cross-Language Question Answering Using Statistical Machine Translation, Named Entity Recognition, and Semantic Indexing
papers.tldr: A bidirectional Amharic–English question-answering system combines translation, named-entity recognition, semantic indexing, and retrieval to improve access to cross-language information for Amharic speakers.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.
bullets: Introduces memory lifecycle evaluation through repeated reviews and full-horizon counterfactuals.
Includes a controlled Diagnostic tier and a naturalistic customer-service-style interaction tier.
Measures adaptive-choice potential, horizon reversals, and diversity of optimal lifecycle actions.
Finds substantial delayed-decision structure across both tiers, with many states changing preferred actions over longer horizons.
A learned delayed lifecycle policy improves joint utility over the best fixed strategy on the Naturalistic tier.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VitaBench, a benchmark for evaluating memory lifecycle decisions (compression, consolidation, deletion) in language agents, addressing the gap between retrieval and persistence management.
papers.title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
papers.tldr: VitaBench evaluates whether language-agent memories should be preserved, compressed, consolidated, or deleted based on their delayed future value—not just retrieved.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
authors: Yang Xiao, Yusong Sun, Haoyi Wu, Wenyang Hui, Weiqiang Hang, Luqing Wang, Zejian Wang, Zirui Tu, Jingsheng Mao, Shaobo Hu, Yang Luo, Jiale Guo, Jin Zhang, Yudan Liu, Zhaokai Luo, Ren Huan, Yao Hu, Chengyue Jiang, Wenjie Li, Chuan Mu
bullets: Addresses the gap between static or synthetic training data and the evolving behavior needed to infer users’ preferences, intent, and future actions.
Converts anonymized behavior records from 100,000 users into 100,000 tasks across 91 templates, retaining approximately 75,000 tasks with selected trajectories.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on Vela trajectories improves user-related task performance by up to 11.5 points and general benchmark performance by an average of 4 points.
Additional user behavior data provides further gains, while reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points.
papers.selection_reason: Uses user behavior data as supervision to improve LLM intelligence, fitting LLM training.
papers.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
papers.tldr: Vela turns real-world user behavior histories into training tasks and trajectories, improving LLM performance on user-centered and general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.
authors: Rui Hua, Yu Wei, Ziri Jin, Zhuo Sun, Kai Chang, Jianan Xia, Zixin Shu, Xiaodong Li, Dongmei Jia, Fei Dong, Runshun Zhang, Jian Yu, Hao Xu, Haibin Yu, Jiansheng Li, Baoyan Liu, Wenjia Wang, Xuezhong Zhou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating TCM knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, prescription composition, and dosage.
Uses continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, reasoning supervision, and prescription-level reinforcement learning.
Includes 4B, 8B, and 14B-parameter models evaluated on public TCM tasks and a private spleen-and-stomach prescription dataset.
The 14B reinforcement-aligned model achieved 37.0 prescription-generation F1 on the public benchmark and 52.8 herb-level F1 on the clinical dataset, with improved dosage agreement.
Expert heterogeneity affected reward stability, indicating a limitation for prescription-focused reinforcement learning.
papers.selection_reason: Develops TCM-specific LLM family with clinical alignment and reinforcement learning, fitting LLM research.
papers.title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
papers.tldr: Lingdan-V2 is a family of TCM language models trained with staged clinical alignment and prescription-focused reinforcement learning to support herbal prescription recommendation.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.
authors: Yaoxiang Wang, Kai Zhang, Ruobing Xie, Lanrui Wang, Guoliang Zhao, Junhui Li, Jinsong Su
bullets: MoE expert geometry is made explicit by computing expert transformations in a lower-dimensional latent space.
An expert’s local Jacobian rank is bounded by its input dimension and intermediate width; balancing these dimensions maximizes the rank ceiling for a fixed parameter budget.
Controlled experiments across model scales and routing granularities favor near-square expert shapes.

Intrinsic-dimension-guided layerwise allocation, while holding per-layer parameters, activated FLOPs, and communication constant, improves validation loss and downstream performance over homogeneous baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Expert shape and layerwise capacity allocation in MoE LLMs; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
papers.tldr: LatentMoE shows that expert shape and layerwise capacity allocation are key design choices for improving mixture-of-experts models.

papers.abstract: To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. However, human preferences are complex and hard to measure by simplistic criteria, and it is important to incorporate broader and more sophisticated insights about preferred vs. not-preferred language. In this study, we adopt a well-established psycholinguistic theory, Uniform Information Density, to develop a novel preference optimization algorithm, UIDPO. The basic assumption is that humans prefer to produce language in which information is uniformly distributed, because uniformity induces less cognitive processing effort. To implement this idea into the algorithm, we derive a compound metric for information uniformity by combining the global standard deviation and the local second-order difference, and integrate it to the objective of preference optimization. We compare UIDPO with SimPO, a previous state-of-the-art method, obtaining comparable and sometimes better performance on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench. Additional linguistic analysis on complement clauses also shows that UIDPO can better reflect the tendencies of keeping information uniform in natural language than baselines. Our results show that the subtle human preference over the information rate in language is a helpful source for achieving better human alignment for LLMs. The code repository is published here: https://github.com/CLCS-SUSTech/UIDPO.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of simplistic linguistic assumptions in preference optimization, given the complexity of human preferences.
Combines global information-rate variability with local second-order differences into an information-uniformity metric.
Integrates this metric into a preference-optimization objective based on chosen and rejected outputs.
Achieves comparable and sometimes better performance than SimPO on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench.
Linguistic analysis suggests UIDPO better captures human tendencies toward uniform information distribution, though its scope is tied to this psycholinguistic assumption.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a preference optimization algorithm (UIDPO) based on psycholinguistic theory to improve human alignment.
papers.title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
papers.tldr: UIDPO uses Uniform Information Density to improve LLM preference optimization by favoring outputs with more uniformly distributed information.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. To support this approach with comprehensive behavioral traces, we construct a dataset PsyMemBehav-bench from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users (approximately 950 per user) across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Each recorded engagement is modeled as target selection followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation. PsyMemBehav combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO over complete reasoning-action trajectories. Experiments show that PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first in 11 of 12 reported individual-level metrics, improving average response quality over GPT-5.4 from 54.28 to 59.68 (9.95% relative), and obtains the lowest group-level MAE (0.081) and MSE (0.009) among simulated systems. These results support evidence-grounded user modeling for observed-thread continuation; the benchmark remains conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.
authors: Wenji Zhang, Xilong Cheng, Yunxiao Qin, Mai Tu, Tongye Zhu, Yuhao Zhou, JingBo Ji, Yuting Tan, Duoyin Li, Hongjiang Xiao, Yuan Zhang
bullets: Introduces PsyMemBehav-bench with 5.57M behaviors from 5,862 users across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter.
Models engagement in two stages: target selection, followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation.
Combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO.
PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first on 11 of 12 individual-level metrics and reports improved response quality and group-level error metrics.
Scope is limited to observed engagements and does not simulate no-action decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-grounded LLM user simulation with retrieval and DPO; relevant to LLM memory and agent memory.
papers.title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
papers.tldr: PsyMemBehav simulates social-media users by combining psychology-informed profiles, retrieved memories, and two-level reasoning to predict targets, actions, and responses from behavioral traces.

papers.abstract: Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE-Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at https://baidubce.github.io/FM-Agent/FDE-Bench/.
authors: Huaiming Li, Can Huang, Chufan Wu, Danyu Liu, Xiaomin Yuan, Qinze Li, Yui Lo, Wenhui Bai, Qianlong Wang, Zengle Ge, Xiyu Yan, Yuheng Cheng, Jinhui Ren, Guokai Chen, Jiaqun Liu, Haoran Li, Qianhui Liu, Annan Li, Jianmin Wu, Dawei Yin, Dou Shen
bullets: Introduces 49 real-world cases spanning combinatorial optimization and machine learning.
Agents interact with simulated customers to elicit missing requirements, then optimize final artifacts iteratively.
Case-specific evaluators compare outputs with customer-accepted FDE solutions.
Across 18 configurations, the best mean delivery score is 0.5510 versus an FDE reference of 1.0.
The best delivery success rate is 6.12%, indicating that reliable FDE-level delivery remains challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FDE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on end-to-end delivery tasks involving requirement clarification and iterative optimization, relevant to LLM agent capabilities.
papers.title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
papers.tldr: FDE-Bench evaluates whether agents can clarify underspecified business requests and iteratively deliver solutions that meet customer acceptance criteria.

papers.abstract: Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non-specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full-book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce LongHisDoc, the first benchmark tailored for long historical document understanding. LongHisDoc comprises 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs derived from 101 PDF documents, with an average of 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens per document. It spans 10 categories and features four QA types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable. Answering these questions requires integrating multimodal evidence from text, layout, and visual elements. Our evaluation reveals that the top-performing LVLM and LLM achieve only 62.9% and 69.9% accuracy, respectively, highlighting a substantial performance gap. Furthermore, we assess various modal retrievers and the end-to-end RAG performance to provide references for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. We believe that LongHisDoc serves as a comprehensive benchmark to catalyze future research in full-book historical document understanding. The benchmark and evaluation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/qweq12433454/LongHisDoc and https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/LongHisDoc.
authors: Zeyu Shan, Yongxin Shi, Shihang Wu, Peirong Zhang, Yuanyuan Fang, Zhaopeng Wang, Lianwen Jin
bullets: Contains 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs from 101 PDF documents averaging 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens.
Covers 10 categories and four question types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable.
Questions require combining textual, layout, and visual evidence across long documents.
Top reported accuracies are 69.9% for LLMs and 62.9% for LVLMs, indicating substantial challenges.
Also evaluates modal retrievers and end-to-end RAG performance to support future system development.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LongHisDoc, a benchmark for long historical document understanding, challenging long-context capabilities.
papers.title: LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding
papers.tldr: LongHisDoc is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs and LVLMs on multimodal, full-book understanding of long Chinese historical documents.

papers.abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.
bullets: Classification errors increased from 10.9% in formal Chinese to 23.5% in the yinyang (echoic-irony) register, a +12.7-point risk difference.
Lower agreement in the ironic condition indicates some label-uncertainty propagation, but the increase persisted under both reference standards.
Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced intervention-panel errors by 9.6 percentage points.
Across 29 proposition anchors, task forms for consensus estimation, high-stakes decisions, and association ratings produced differing bias readings, especially for irony probes.
The findings support including ironic registers and multiple task forms in Chinese content-governance evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates bias in Chinese LLMs across different registers and task operationalizations, relevant to safety and evaluation.
papers.title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
papers.tldr: A preregistered audit finds that Chinese LLM bias measurements worsen under ironic language and vary substantially with task operationalization.

papers.abstract: Semantic relations organise word senses and are fundamental to lexical semantics. In order to evaluate semantic relation knowledge of large language models (LLMs), we propose a challenging task in which an LLM predicts the relation between two glosses (definitions of senses) presented in two different orders. The predictions for the two orders are evaluated for consistency with the symmetry or asymmetry of semantic relations. Our task is designed for both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, allowing us to examine whether relation knowledge remains accessible when the same senses are verbalised through glosses in different languages. We construct a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs, with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese. Experiments with 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings reveal generally poor performance. In each setting, only eight LLMs achieve a macro-averaged F1 score significantly above a random baseline, and only one (zero-shot) and two (five-shot) significantly outperform a neural baseline. In particular, LLMs often fail to generate bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to make correct predictions for holonymy in either direction. Our results suggest limitations in current LLMs' semantic relation knowledge, both in identifying relations and in respecting asymmetry.
authors: Zhihan Cao, Adam Nohejl, Hitomi Yanaka
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs identify semantic relations consistently when gloss pairs are presented in both orders.
Supports monolingual and cross-lingual testing across English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese.
Uses 3,069 sense pairs to evaluate 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings.
Most models perform poorly; only a minority exceed random or neural baselines significantly.
Models particularly struggle with bidirectional hypernymy consistency and holonymy prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates semantic relation knowledge in LLMs through bidirectional prediction, highlighting limitations in handling asymmetry.
papers.title: Evaluating Semantic Relation Knowledge through Bidirectional Relation Prediction from Gloss Pairs
papers.tldr: A bidirectional gloss-pair task reveals that current LLMs have limited and inconsistent knowledge of semantic relations, especially across relation directions.

papers.abstract: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) genuinely grasp the truth conditions of plural descriptions, or do they force every sentence into true or false? We investigate the Homogeneity Gap, a semantic phenomenon where a plural definite (e.g., the kids laughed) and its negation (the kids didn't laugh) are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, whereas their quantified counterparts (all, not all) remain strictly bivalent. We introduce HomogeneityNLI, a diagnostic dataset of 1,000 minimal-pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions. Evaluating seven open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Bivalence Bias: models assign plural definites their homogeneous truth conditions, reading the kids as all of them and the kids didn't as none of them, yet collapse the truth-value gap into falsity. In the zero-shot setting, no model recognizes the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of scenarios, and negated definites are judged False in 84% of cases. Explicit linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often entrench the bias. Taken together, our findings indicate that current open-weight LLMs have acquired the truth conditions of plural predication but not its trivalent logic.
authors: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Yiping Li, Sachin Giri, Wan Du
bullets: The study tests whether LLMs distinguish plural definites from quantified expressions under partial group membership.
It introduces HomogeneityNLI, a 1,000-item diagnostic dataset spanning determiners, polarity, and ten logical conditions.
Across seven open-weight models, a pervasive Bivalence Bias treats “the kids” as all and “the kids didn’t” as none.
In zero-shot evaluation, no model identifies the gap for both polarities in over 15% of scenarios; negated definites are judged false in 84%.
Rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts have unstable effects and often reinforce the bias.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates logical reasoning capabilities (truth conditions) in LLMs, introducing a diagnostic dataset for trivalent logic.
papers.title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
papers.tldr: Open-weight LLMs largely understand homogeneous plural predication but fail to represent its truth-value gap, forcing mixed cases into false judgments.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.
authors: Haowen Pan, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma, Yanzheng Jin, Naixin Zhai, Xiang Wang, Xun Yang
bullets: Introduces Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of how persistent agent memory is produced and committed.
Benchmarks five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning.
Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats find susceptibility at all five interfaces under the tested protocols.
Shows that successful authentic experiences do not ensure reliable behavior when contextual support, retention, or consolidation order changes.
Finds that vulnerability depends on memory architecture and updater, while evaluated defenses provide incomplete, interface-dependent mitigation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for memory formation poisoning in LLM agents; directly addresses persistent memory formation and interfaces.
papers.title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: MemForm shows that LLM agents can be broadly manipulated through multiple interfaces involved in forming persistent memory, including retention and consolidation order.

papers.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.
authors: Istok Bako, Bonan Min, Tiffany Shao, Claire Cheng, Yashar Mehdad
bullets: Targets accurate, complete retrieval of policy-grounded resolution steps from enterprise support documents.
Uses natural-language instructions, lightweight retrieval and validation tools, and an LLM-generated Wikipedia-style navigation layer.
Implemented in 1–2 engineer days and portable across capable agentic harnesses.
Achieved 99.2% procedural equivalence and 83.3% evidence sufficiency in the reported case study.
Scope is limited to mature corpora, latency-tolerant workflows, and human review; inference took roughly 90 seconds versus 8–9 seconds in production.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a portable skill-based RAG approach for customer support using an LLM-generated navigation layer to structure document retrieval, demonstrating a simple yet effective method for external memory and information retrieval.
papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
papers.tldr: A simple, portable agentic RAG skill with a navigable document index can generate customer-support resolution workflows nearly as well as human-approved procedures, but is much slower than a production assistant.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.
bullets: Targets LLM difficulty with growing constraint interactions and search spaces.
Uses multi-turn tool execution to connect natural-language reasoning with solvers such as Z3.
Combines synthetic verifiable data, supervised warm-up on solver traces, and solver-grounded RL.
Reports substantial gains on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks.
Scope: focuses on symbolic reasoning with external solver tools.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a reinforcement learning framework for LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers (Z3) for logical reasoning, addressing the complexity of LLMs through tool-augmented execution.
papers.title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
papers.tldr: SAT-RL trains language models to solve increasingly complex logic problems by combining reinforcement learning with symbolic solver interaction.

papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.
authors: Minuk Ma, Kaiyun Guo, Jiarui Ding
bullets: Presents 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals for evaluating experimental-data curation.
Targets verification of specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability across long, heterogeneous documents.
Finds that plain LLMs and existing reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents struggle with the task.
LangPoli achieves 83.16% F1 on Paper Classification, compared with 58.22% for its base LLM, and improves performance on LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC re-ranking.
Explores curriculum transfer to reuse strategies from solved tasks for related curation problems.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on LLM agents (LangPoli) for scientific data curation, addressing agent design and test-time learning strategies.
papers.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
papers.tldr: SciCurateBench evaluates whether AI systems can verify detailed, conjunctive experimental criteria in messy scientific literature, and introduces LangPoli, which uses natural-language action policies to improve curation and retrieval.

papers.abstract: Hybrid reasoning models such as the Qwen3 series switch between a THINK mode and a NO-THINK mode through a few chat-template tokens. A popular recipe trains such models with reinforcement learning in NO-THINK mode and reports improved reasoning performance. We provide evidence that much of this gain can be explained by thinking leakage: the gain comes largely from partially reactivating the reasoning abilities of the original model's THINK mode instead of learning enhanced reasoning behavior. We train Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B with GRPO in NO-THINK mode. As accuracy improves, responses become longer and more reflective, are increasingly judged by the original model to resemble its own thinking, and the model's internal activations shift toward its THINK mode. We then investigate at the level of weights, activations, and attention heads: scaling the RL update further elicits THINK-mode behavior and approaches THINK-mode accuracy but does not exceed it; in Qwen3-8B, replacing a low-dimensional THINK-related activation subspace of the RL-trained model with its original-model value removes most of the RL gain, and the reverse exchange transfers a considerable fraction of the gain to the original model; and the RL-induced shift passes through the attention heads that read the empty think block. We further identify a possible mechanism in the GRPO training signal: responses favored by the advantage-weighted update are more THINK-like, and a gradient step computed from this signal moves the model toward its THINK state. Thus, gains in NO-THINK mode can largely reflect reactivation of reasoning abilities already present in the original model.
authors: Wenxuan Zhu, Shuming Liu, Bang An, Aznaur Aliev, Bing Li, Yibo Yang, Bernard Ghanem
bullets: The study examines Qwen3 models trained with GRPO in NO-THINK mode.
Improved accuracy coincides with longer, more reflective, THINK-like responses and activations.
Stronger RL shifts the models toward THINK-mode behavior and accuracy but does not surpass the original THINK mode.
Activation-subspace and attention-head interventions transfer or remove much of the RL gain, linking it to THINK-related components.
The GRPO signal may favor THINK-like responses, causing updates toward the model’s existing THINK state.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes RL-induced thinking leakage in Qwen3 hybrid LLMs via weights, activations, and attention heads; directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: The Thinking Leakage in Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
papers.tldr: Reinforcement learning gains in Qwen3’s NO-THINK mode largely come from reactivating existing THINK-mode reasoning rather than learning substantially stronger reasoning.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse the same layer multiple times, allowing inference compute to be adjusted without changing the model. Recent adaptive-depth methods train the model across multiple loop depths from the beginning of training. We introduce fixed-first training, which varies model depth only during a short final phase of training. At 200M parameters, training a model of fixed-depth 2 for the first 67% of the run reduces modeled training compute by 45% while keeping mean negative log-likelihood (NLL) across inference depths within 0.5% of training across depths throughout. At 1B parameters, training initially at depth 4 reduces modeled compute by 31% to 37% and wall-clock time by 32% to 39%, while keeping final NLL within 0.8% and downstream differences within the observed seed variation. These results show that training over the full range of depths can be reserved for a short finishing phase with only small changes in performance.
authors: Andrei Piterbarg, Sean McLeish, Dhruv Pai, Benjamin Keigwin
bullets: Trains at one fixed loop depth for most of training, then varies depth only near the end.
At 200M parameters, it reduces modeled training compute by 45% while keeping mean NLL within 0.5% of full multi-depth training.
At 1B parameters, it reduces modeled compute by 31–37% and wall-clock time by 32–39%.
Final NLL remains within 0.8%, and downstream differences stay within observed seed variation.
Scope: results concern looped transformers and the tested 200M- and 1B-parameter settings.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive-depth training for looped transformer language models is an architectural and training-efficiency contribution relevant to LLM foundation models.
papers.title: Adaptive-Depth Is a Finishing Stage
papers.tldr: Fixed-first training lets looped transformers defer multi-depth training to a short finishing phase, substantially reducing training cost with little performance loss.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
authors: Hermann Kumbong, Ishan S. Khare, Iddah Mlauzi, Andrew Woen, Charles Ding, E. Kelly Buchanan, Simran Arora, Azalia Mirhoseini, Christopher R\'e
bullets: Addresses diffusion language models’ slow sampling, full-sequence processing, and training inefficiency at few sampling steps.
Uses a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to encode text into hierarchical discrete codes.
A transformer predicts all codes within each hierarchy level in parallel.
Reports faster generation than diffusion baselines across LM1B, OpenWebText, and XSum while maintaining or improving quality.
Outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku reasoning across difficulty levels with fewer function evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a parallel coarse-to-fine text generation architecture, relevant to language model architectural advances.
papers.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
papers.tldr: Next-Concept Modeling enables fast, parallel coarse-to-fine text generation by predicting hierarchical discrete representations level by level.

papers.abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
authors: Yiyang Fu, Zihao Huang, Dongchen Han, Shukai Gong, Zhen Dong, Qiyang Min, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Addresses variable per-turn compute needs without using separate models or rebuilding history states when switching.
Uses lightweight full-token modules, ratio-specific boundary routers, and cross-ratio training in a shared backbone.
Fixed-ratio modes outperform compute-matched MoE baselines in all six reported comparisons and remain competitive with specialists.
Mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy–compute trade-off on CodeChat and CoSQL, with lower FLOPs than the Large MoE.
Under matched turn-wise budgets, it reduces FLOPs versus routing among independent models, demonstrating flexible shared-model inference.
papers.selection_reason: Single shared MoE model supporting multiple compute budgets via token-to-concept compression, fitting efficient AI and LLM architecture topics.
papers.title: One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns
papers.tldr: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE enables one shared model to flexibly use 2×, 4×, or 8× token-to-concept compression across conversation turns, improving accuracy–compute trade-offs while avoiding model-switching overhead.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.
authors: Alexey Zemtsov, Albina Klepach, Vadim Lomshakov, Andrei Polubarov, Nikita Lyubaykin, Alexander Derevyagin, Vladislav Kurenkov, Alexander Nikulin
bullets: Looped transformers reuse one block, making runtime depth dependent on how well state persists between steps.
State tracking depends on the geometry of the residual map used between recurrent iterations.
The proposed blockwise conformal injections split residuals into coordinate-aligned groups and rotate each group independently.
This gives each group a distinct timescale while preserving exact within-group geometry.
Experiments show gains in last-token state-tracking accuracy and language modeling with delayed signal retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Looped transformer architecture for state tracking, relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: Rotate the Loop: Blockwise Conformality for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: Blockwise conformal residual rotations improve state tracking and language modeling in looped transformers by preserving readable information across recurrent steps.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.
authors: Hamed Mahdavi (Pennsylvania State University), Pouria Mahdavinia (Pennsylvania State University), Majid Farhadi (Google), Vasant Honavar (Pennsylvania State University)
bullets: RL with verifiable rewards struggles when correct solutions are too rare or proofs lack checkable final answers.
SPLICE performs verification and repair offline using a reference solution rather than relying on in-loop rewards.
A second model truncates failed traces at the last verified step and inserts increasingly strong hints until progress resumes.
Finetuning on these repaired traces outperforms training on unedited traces on AIME and human-validated olympiad-proof grading.
The resulting model exhibits hint-like branching and increased predictive entropy at difficult reasoning points.
papers.selection_reason: Offline data generation with spliced hints to improve reasoning model training; relevant to LLM post-training.
papers.title: Splicing Hints into Reasoning Traces: Learning from Demonstrator Failures
papers.tldr: SPLICE trains mathematical reasoning models from repaired failure traces, improving performance on answer-checked problems and olympiad proofs.

papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.
authors: Weixian Waylon Li, Jiaxin Zhang, Han Zhou, Chengzu Li, Ke Wang, Fengxiang He, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Addresses the limited supply of hand-written games and game-specific advantage estimators in LLM self-play.
Synthesises games within fixed reward, observation, and hidden-information templates, then verifies and expands them into variants.
Produces 26 new games across 29 families and 336 verified variants from three templates.
Introduces CRAB, which estimates advantages for decisions across all game variants using shrinkage-based position returns.
On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation improves mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, while CRAB self-play reaches 64.9; transfer increases with game-family count.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling LLM post-training via synthesized zero-sum games and self-play; relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
papers.tldr: GameSmith scales zero-sum self-play by automatically generating and verifying diverse games and using a game-agnostic advantage estimator, improving LLM reasoning transfer.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.
authors: Shanfeng Huang, Rongqian Zhang, Zhou Fang, Song Xiao, Hai Du
bullets: Addresses memory challenges from the large parameter footprint of MoE models.
Jointly optimizes prune-and-merge assignments with global Integer Linear Programming rather than separate greedy decisions.
Uses expert-usage frequency in a surrogate objective to favor frequently used experts as merge representatives and improve routing stability.
