Outlines a method for constructing finite sections of the operator.
Uses singular-value spectra to compare tasks and models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a composition-operator/Koopman formalism for analyzing LLM semantic transformations, relevant to language foundation model theory.
papers.title: Using Composition Operators to Linearize LLM Semantic Transformations
papers.tldr: The paper models LLM prompt-to-response transformations as composition operators, enabling finite-dimensional analysis through singular-value spectra.

papers.abstract: Hidden-state hallucination probing - training a linear classifier on an LLM's internal activations to detect whether a generated answer is faithful to the input - is an active area of 2026 research, with recent work reporting 0.90-1.00 AUROC across several benchmarks and languages. However, none of this work has tested probes on code-mixed input, despite the fact that a huge population of chatbot users write in Hindi-English code-mixed text ("Hinglish"). We address this gap directly: does a hallucination probe trained on clean-language hidden states transfer to Hinglish, or does the signal degrade under code-mixing? We construct a 5,674-item Hindi/English/Hinglish QA benchmark, generate and label 17,022 model responses across three open-weight 7-8B LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), extract per-layer hidden states at two token positions, and train linear and MLP probes for in-distribution detection and cross-lingual transfer. We find that the hallucination signal survives code-mixing well: transfer AUROC ranges from 0.88 to 0.99, with gaps of mostly under 0.05 AUROC relative to in-distribution performance, and that Hindi-trained probes transfer to Hinglish more reliably than English-trained probes. As an independent, practically motivated finding, all three models hallucinate substantially more on Hindi and Hinglish than on English for matched facts. We release our code and synthetic Hinglish QA dataset to support further work on code-mixed hallucination detection.
bullets: Addresses whether hallucination signals in LLM hidden states survive Hindi-English code-mixing.
Builds a 5,674-item Hindi/English/Hinglish QA benchmark with 17,022 labeled responses from three open-weight LLMs.
Trains linear and MLP probes on per-layer hidden states for in-distribution detection and cross-lingual transfer.
Transfer AUROC ranges from 0.88–0.99, usually within 0.05 AUROC of in-distribution performance.
Hindi-trained probes transfer to Hinglish more reliably than English-trained probes; models hallucinate more in Hindi and Hinglish than English on matched facts.
papers.selection_reason: Probes LLM hidden states for hallucination detection under code-mixing, contributing to LLM reliability research.
papers.title: Does the Truthfulness Signal Survive Code-Mixing? Probing Hidden States for Hallucination Detection in Hinglish
papers.tldr: Hidden-state probes remain effective for detecting hallucinations in Hinglish, with only small performance drops when transferring from clean-language data.

papers.abstract: Evaluation awareness poses an unprecedented threat to model evaluation, but the mechanisms by which models detect it remain unknown. This study focuses on determining this and identifying contrasting mechanisms between smaller and larger models. While smaller models use the prompt's format sensitivity to detect evaluation, larger models often rely on higher-order reasoning to detect it. We evaluated Gemma 3 (1B, 4B, and 12B), Phi-3 (Mini and Medium), and Llama-3 8B using Chain-of-Thought analysis, representation probing, and Integrated Gradients attribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose a dual-pathway intervention that combines prompt sanitization with activation counter-steering to suppress both external evaluation triggers and their internal representations. Across 200 highly evaluation-aware prompts, our method achieves an average behavioral flip rate of 70.58\%, consistently outperforming either intervention alone. These results provide new insights into how evaluation awareness develops in compact language models and suggest that effective mitigation requires jointly addressing both prompt-level and representation-level signals.Datasets and codebase can be found in this \href{https://github.com/chahal-navi/Evaluation-Awareness-Compact-LLMs/tree/main}{Github Repository.}
bullets: Smaller models detect evaluation mainly through prompt-format sensitivity, while larger models use higher-order reasoning and contextual signals.
The study analyzes Gemma 3, Phi-3, and Llama-3 models using Chain-of-Thought analysis, representation probing, and Integrated Gradients.
The proposed intervention combines prompt sanitization with activation counter-steering to target both external triggers and internal representations.
Across 200 evaluation-aware prompts, the combined method achieved a 70.58% average behavioral flip rate and outperformed either intervention alone.
The findings suggest that mitigating evaluation awareness requires addressing both prompt-level and representation-level signals.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how LLMs detect evaluation and proposes mitigation interventions, contributing to modern LLM behavior research.
papers.title: Evaluation Awareness Shifts from Format to Context with Model Scale
papers.tldr: As compact language models scale, evaluation awareness shifts from prompt-format cues to higher-order contextual reasoning, motivating a dual-pathway mitigation strategy.

papers.abstract: Large language models can process increasingly long prompts, yet their ability to locate and use decisive evidence may degrade as irrelevant or confusable context is added. We formulate this phenomenon, which we call context poisoning, as extreme-value interference in attention: the decisive-evidence score is upper-bounded, while the maximum score among effective distractors grows with their number. Under a softmax retrieval abstraction, we derive a finite-sample upper bound showing that maintaining a fixed accuracy target above base rate requires the evidence margin to scale as $\Omega(\sqrt{\log N})$, where N denotes the effective distractor count rather than necessarily the raw context length. The analysis connects long-context degradation to score aliasing, positional aliasing, and softmax dilution. Controlled experiments show that retrieval accuracy decreases as total context grows in the presence of embedded hard negatives, that the same-format condition produces the largest observed accuracy drop among the tested distractor constructions at fixed context length, and that retrieval gating can improve evidence use while its net benefit depends on preserving evidence recall. These results motivate evidence bottlenecks, alias-resistant representations, retrieve-then-reason architectures, verifier-mediated memory, and contrastive anti-poison training.
authors: Meysam Ghaffari, Nina Fatehi, Bhaskar Sen, Nasim Sabetpour, Carlos Morato
bullets: Formalizes context poisoning using a softmax retrieval model in which the strongest distractor score grows with the number of effective distractors.
Derives a finite-sample bound showing that fixed above-base-rate accuracy requires an evidence margin of Ω(√log N).
Links degradation to score aliasing, positional aliasing, and softmax dilution.
Controlled experiments find lower retrieval accuracy with longer contexts and hard negatives, with same-format distractors causing the largest tested drop.
Retrieval gating can improve evidence use, but its benefit depends on retaining the decisive evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Directly analyzes long-context degradation in LLMs via attention interference and evidence retrieval, fitting the long-context models subtopic.
papers.title: Context Poisoning as Extreme-Value Attention Interference in Long-Context Language Models
papers.tldr: Context poisoning explains long-context failures as extreme-value attention interference, where growing distractor sets overwhelm decisive evidence unless the evidence margin increases with effective distractor count.

papers.abstract: Retrieval over a personal memory store is retrospective: it surfaces what resembles the query, and it is blind to what the user has committed to do. We describe a prospective term for memory retrieval that costs no inference at query time. Commitments are held in an explicit ledger as dated or trigger-conditioned entries; memory items linked to a firing entry receive a salience boost, blended multiplicatively into embedding-based retrieval so that relevance remains sovereign. On a synthetic prospective-memory task set modeled on TriggerBench's published structure (48 blind-authored dialogues, 175 tasks), the term raised recall@5 on the hard stratum from 0.000 to 0.955 at the default blend weight and to 1.000 under a floor variant, with zero false boosts across 53 resolved-commitment tasks. Blind authorship also produced a scope finding: only 17-29% of naturally phrased commitment-trigger pairs defeat embedding similarity, so the term matters on a real minority of cases and must do no harm on the rest, which it does not. We position precomputed commitment linkage as the always-on floor of a layered design whose expansion layer is query-time prospection. Results are preliminary: the evaluation set is author-constructed, and evaluation on TriggerBench proper is committed follow-up work once its data is released.
bullets: Addresses retrospective retrieval’s blindness to users’ future commitments.
Links dated or trigger-conditioned commitments to memory items in an explicit ledger.
Applies a multiplicative salience boost to embedding-based retrieval, keeping relevance primary.
On a synthetic task set, hard-case recall@5 rose from 0.000 to 0.955, or 1.000 with a floor variant, with no false boosts reported.
Only 17–29% of natural commitment-trigger pairs defeated embedding similarity; evaluation is preliminary and author-constructed.
papers.selection_reason: Adds a prospective term to memory retrieval in LLM agents, a direct contribution to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Memory That Looks Forward: A Zero-Inference Prospective Term for Personal Memory Retrieval
papers.tldr: A precomputed commitment ledger substantially improves prospective-memory retrieval without query-time inference while preserving ordinary relevance.

papers.abstract: Large language models can hold knowledge they do not report. A model may sandbag on a capability evaluation, or answer against what it internally knows, and its outputs alone cannot tell whether it is hiding an answer or simply does not have one. We borrow the Concealed Information Test, a forensic method that identifies guilty knowledge by presenting a suspect with the true detail among plausible decoys and measuring a stronger response to the item they recognize. Our method, Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), does the same inside a model. It presents a question with its candidate answers and reads, from the model's internal states, which candidate the model recognizes as correct. PIR is reference-free, needing no honest reference model and no labeled truth corpus. Across eight models from five families (Gemma, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, and Phi), PIR recovers the recognized answer at 0.70 to 0.87 balanced accuracy, well above the 0.28 to 0.40 unknown-item baseline and the 0.25 chance rate. It stays readable across every form of concealment we test, from prompted deception and trained sandbagging to external password-locked and circuit-broken checkpoints, with recognition between 0.85 and 0.93. When the model hides a known answer, recognition stays high. When unlearning removes the knowledge, recognition drops to the level of a question the model never knew. PIR therefore separates a model that will not answer from one that cannot, which supports sandbagging audits and unlearning verification. The signal is causal, adds information beyond black-box behavioral cues, and extends from multiple-choice questions to free-form generation.
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity between deceptive non-answers and genuine lack of knowledge in language models.
Presents candidate answers and identifies which one the model internally recognizes as correct, adapting the forensic Concealed Information Test.
Reference-free: it requires neither an honest reference model nor a labeled truth corpus.
Across eight models from five families, PIR achieves 0.70–0.87 balanced accuracy versus 0.28–0.40 unknown-item baselines and 0.25 chance.
Recognition remains high under multiple concealment methods and drops after unlearning, supporting sandbagging audits and unlearning verification.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PIR, a method to probe internal model states to detect hidden knowledge. This provides a technical approach for auditing LLM capabilities and verifying unlearning, relevant to LLM behavior and test-time learning.
papers.title: A Lie Detector Test for Language Models: Reading Knowledge a Model Won't Reveal
papers.tldr: PIR uses a model’s internal states to distinguish knowledge it is concealing from knowledge it does not possess.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to maintain consistency and personalization over extended interactions. Existing memory systems typically rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, but these designs struggle when heterogeneous information, such as preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates, is embedded in a single mixed representation. The resulting semantic interference makes top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and often leaves relevant evidence poorly ranked. We present AutoViewMem, a data-driven framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views before indexing. AutoViewMem discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary view set, and uses these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design moves semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, allowing standard top-K similarity search to retrieve focused evidence without explicit routing or iterative retrieval. We further apply offline consolidation to improve memory compactness and consistency. Experiments on the LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks, under both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones, show that AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while preserving a simple inference pipeline.
authors: Zijie Cao, Xijun Qu, Zhicheng Gu, Xiaoshu Chen, Duanyang Yuan, Yanning Hou, Sihang Zhou, Jianxing Gong, Jian Huang, Yang Mei
bullets: Addresses semantic interference caused by mixing preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates in fixed memory schemas.
Discovers complementary views from interaction traces and uses them for provenance-grounded structured memory extraction.
Applies offline consolidation to improve memory compactness and consistency.
Evaluated on LoCoMo and PersonaMem with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, improving long-horizon QA and personalization over strong baselines while retaining standard top-K retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes AutoViewMem, a framework for organizing LLM agent memory into self-configuring orthogonal views. This addresses memory interference and retrieval efficiency, contributing to LLM memory and embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory
papers.tldr: AutoViewMem organizes conversational memories into self-configured, low-overlap semantic views at write time, enabling simpler and more focused long-term retrieval.

papers.abstract: Detecting pretraining data in large language models is challenging because high likelihood can reflect either training exposure or strong generalization. In the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, a likelihood-only detector uses a horizontal boundary and can mistake predictable non-members for members. Motivated by this, we introduce an inclined boundary that evaluates prediction loss relative to predictive entropy. Our analysis shows that entropy correction can preserve the expected membership signal while reducing its variance, thereby improving standardized member--non-member separation. We further extend the mean--variance analysis to the more general setting with a nonzero mean entropy gap. Interestingly, this entropy-adjusted score admits a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation, leading to Energy Transfer Detection (ETD), which views pretraining data detection from a macroscopic residual free-energy transfer perspective. Extensive experiments show that ETD achieves the best average detection performance, improving average AUROC by up to 3.5\% and TPR@5\%FPR by up to 5.1\%, while remaining robust across diverse settings.
authors: Chenye Ke, Zirui Liu, Qi Liu, Yan Zhuang, Jintao Zhang, Zhenya Huang, Shijin Wang
bullets: Likelihood alone can mistake predictable non-members for training-data members.
The method uses an inclined decision boundary in prediction-loss–entropy space.
Entropy correction preserves the membership signal while reducing its variance.
The resulting score has a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation, motivating Energy Transfer Detection (ETD).
Experiments report gains of up to 3.5% average AUROC and 5.1% TPR@5% FPR across diverse settings.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an entropy-adjusted free-energy score for detecting pretraining data in LLMs, relevant to LLM analysis.
papers.title: Detecting Pretraining Data in Large Language Models from a Free-Energy Perspective
papers.tldr: ETD detects whether text was in an LLM’s pretraining data by adjusting prediction loss for predictive entropy, improving membership separation over likelihood-only detection.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense, token-level supervision by conditioning a model on privileged information and distilling the resulting teacher distribution back into the model. However, privileged information can change not only what the teacher knows, but also how it behaves, entangling correctness-relevant learning signals with unintended behavioral shifts. We study this effect in reasoning tasks by contrasting attractive self-distillation, which moves the model toward a privileged teacher, with repulsive self-distillation, which moves it away from a privileged teacher. We find that both objectives can induce strong and opposing behavioral shifts: attraction suppresses exploratory reasoning and promotes shorter, more confident responses, whereas repulsion increases response length, can trigger unintended switches into a model's latent thinking mode, and ultimately becomes unstable. Motivated by these observations, we study contrastive self-distillation, which combines attraction toward a correct-solution-conditioned teacher with repulsion from an incorrect-solution-conditioned teacher. In contrast to prior work that combines such distillation signals with a GRPO objective, we isolate the self-distillation objective and study its behavior on its own. We find that the shared behavioral shifts of the two teachers largely cancel, leaving a token-level signal that more directly reflects correctness. Across non-thinking, instruct-only, and already-thinking models, this contrastive objective improves reasoning performance while maintaining stable response lengths.
authors: Anton Baumann, Akmal Ashirmatov, Leo Schmidt-Traub, Frederike L\"ubeck, Jonas H\"ubotter, Thomas Kleine Buening, Andreas Krause
bullets: Privileged information can alter both a teacher’s correctness and its response behavior, entangling the resulting learning signal.

Attractive distillation yields shorter, more confident responses and suppresses exploratory reasoning; repulsive distillation lengthens responses, may trigger latent thinking, and can become unstable.
Contrastive self-distillation combines attraction to correct-solution-conditioned teachers with repulsion from incorrect-solution-conditioned teachers.
The opposing behavioral shifts largely cancel, producing a more correctness-focused token-level signal.
Across non-thinking, instruct-only, and already-thinking models, the objective improves reasoning performance while keeping response lengths stable.
papers.selection_reason: Contrastive self-distillation for reasoning LLMs; relevant to language foundation model training and behavior.
papers.title: On Repulsive and Attractive Teachers: Separating Correctness from Behavior in Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Contrastive self-distillation separates correctness learning from unwanted teacher-induced behavior by combining attraction to correct teachers with repulsion from incorrect ones.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc sparse attention accelerates long-context prefill by routing each query to a small set of token-level interactions. Hard selection, however, assigns zero probability to every omitted chunk: a routing miss cannot be recovered, and a fixed expansion budget spends the same work on easy and ambiguous queries. We introduce Coarse-to-fine Error-aware Dynamic Attention Routing (CEDAR), a coarse-to-fine method that keeps the language model frozen while preserving global coverage. Each semantic chunk contributes a cheap key--value summary to a residual attention path; chunks with high estimated approximation error are then expanded to exact token attention. Exact and summarized contributions are combined in a single softmax normalization, so refinement replaces, rather than duplicates, coarse evidence. We derive an output-error bound governed by within-chunk key/value dispersion and use it to allocate a variable refinement budget. A controlled clustered-attention study shows that residual summaries reduce reconstruction error by more than 98% relative to hard dropping at equal exact-chunk budgets. Experiments on long-context benchmarks demonstrate that CEDAR recovers most of the quality lost by hard sparse routing while maintaining approximately $3\times$ kernel speedup at 128K context.
bullets: Targets routing misses and wasteful fixed budgets in post-hoc sparse attention.
Keeps the language model frozen and summarizes every semantic chunk for global coverage.
Uses an error bound based on within-chunk key/value dispersion to dynamically refine ambiguous chunks.
Combines exact and summarized evidence under one softmax, so refinement replaces rather than duplicates coarse attention.
In controlled and benchmark studies, reduces reconstruction error by over 98% versus hard dropping and recovers most lost quality.
papers.selection_reason: Error-bounded sparse attention routing with residual summaries for efficient long-context prefill; fits efficient attention and long-context methods.
papers.title: CEDAR: Error-Bounded Residual Routing for Efficient Long-Context Attention
papers.tldr: CEDAR improves efficient long-context attention by replacing hard token dropping with error-aware coarse summaries and adaptive exact refinement, recovering most lost quality while retaining about 3× speedup at 128K context.
